name: Daily Montanan
title: A road access dispute saw three men charged with trespassing. They say they’re innocent.
description: Two former Republican legislators charged with criminal trespass in Big Horn County Justice Court said this week Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks relied on inaccurate information when it issued them misdemeanor citations. Last month, former Republican lawmakers Jason Priest and Scott Boulanger, as well as Dustin Temple, a former director of Montana Fish, Wil[...]
text:
Three men were charged this summer with trespass in Big Horn County, but they say the road they were driving on was accessible with permits they possessed. (Image obtained from Big Horn County's Facebook page)Two former Republican legislators charged with criminal trespass in Big Horn County Justice Court said this week Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks relied on inaccurate information when it issued them misdemeanor citations.
Last month, former Republican lawmakers Jason Priest and Scott Boulanger, as well as Dustin Temple, a former director of Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks, pleaded not guilty to criminal trespass and failure to obtain permission from a property owner before attempting to hunt.
The dispute, which included two related incidents, centers on a road on the Crow Indian Reservation and a question about whether it is a tribal or private roadway.
Priest told the Daily Montanan an FWP investigation misidentified the road as private based on incorrect information from Big Horn County. A spokesperson for Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks said the agency doesn’t generally comment on ongoing cases or investigations.
Big Horn County did not respond to questions from the Daily Montanan.
Priest said Bureau of Indian Affairs documents confirm the road is tribally owned, and as such, the charges are invalid. Priest provided BIA documentation that verifies the road is owned by the Crow Tribe and said he had a valid permit to access it, also provided to the Daily Montanan.
“I’m a believer in private property rights and wilderness access,” Priest said in an interview Wednesday. “Those things are not incompatible.” 
Boulanger, in an interview, also said all three men had valid tribal permits the two times they were on the road. They were also using a public lands mapping application, OnX, which showed they were on a valid public road on their cell phones.
Boulanger and Temple initially accessed the road, which has two names — South Hay Coulee Road and BIA Route 750, Campbell Road — on Nov. 11, 2025, according to a criminal complaint. The court record also states Temple had previously been on the road. 
Boulanger and Temple were confronted while driving on the road and told they were on private property and trespassing by an employee of Monette Farms, which owns the land, according to court documents. Boulanger described the incident with the farm employee as “concerning,” saying the man was screaming and yelling at the former legislator while he was in his truck. 
Boulanger also said they were not planning to hunt on Monette Farms property — they were seeking access to tribal land, which they had valid permits to access, only reachable by the disputed road through Monette Farms.
“We play by the rules,” Boulanger said. 
The court record, and comments made by both Boulanger and Priest to the Daily Montanan, indicate the men never exited their truck on Monette Farms property. Boulanger added their sole intention was to find good bird hunting areas on land that they were legally allowed to be on.
Boulanger later accessed the road again, this time with Priest, on Nov. 23, 2025. They had bird dogs with them, but did not leave their truck, and said they thought they were on a tribal road when they were on it, the complaint said. Boulanger is a former member of the state Board of Outfitters and Guides.
“I held a valid trespass license issued by the Crow Tribe,” Priest wrote in an email to the Daily Montanan. “This was totally absent from the affidavit. I was traveling a tribal road to a lawful destination. It was not aimless entry as the complaint alleges, which it must be under Montana law for the complaint to be valid.”
Photographs of their vehicle were taken both times, the complaint said, and they were then charged this summer. On Aug. 31, 2026, the three men entered not-guilty pleas, according to Big Horn County Justice Court.
A Premier Land Company listing for Monette Farms is seen in a screenshot from its website. (Obtained from PLC’s website)
The case is not being prosecuted by Big Horn County Attorney Jeanne Torske, but instead by Michael Gee, with Helena law firm Morrison Sherwood Wilson & Deola, on behalf of the county. Gee said he could not comment on the case to the Daily Montanan, writing in an email “the rules prohibit me from commenting.”
Torske did not respond to questions, including if she recused herself from the case or why Big Horn County was contracting out legal work. The court documents state a game warden reached out to Big Horn County for a determination on the status of the road, and also show that the county responded the road was private.
For a fee, non-tribal members can access tribal lands to hunt or to recreate.
Lincoln Begay, a Transportation Development Specialist with the BIA, wrote in an email to a lawyer representing Priest the road was owned by the Crow Tribe. Federal law dictates roads listed on the National Tribal Transportation Facility Inventory (meaning they are tribally owned) must be “must be open and available for public use.”
Premier Land Company, which manages Monette Farms, the owner of the land in dispute, did not respond to a request for comment. The Monette Farms land is currently for sale by Premier Land Company at a price of $96 million, one of more than 40 Montana properties the company currently has listed.
Priest is charged with criminal trespass and failure to obtain landowner permission. Temple is charged with the same two counts. Boulanger has four counts — two criminal trespass charges and two failures to obtain landowner permission.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson police make first arrest in killing of Tasia Fortune, who was found hanging from a tree
description: A makeshift memorial for Tasia Fortune is seen in the backyard of a vacant home in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. According to authorities, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a vacant home Monday, Aug. 3, 2026.
text:
The Jackson Police Department arrested a 51-year-old man on Friday in the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman who in August was found hanging from a tree next to a vacant home in west Jackson. 
Jarques Ratliff was arrested after the medical examiner’s office classified Fortune’s death as a homicide on Thursday night and police then secured two search warrants, Chief RaShall Brackney said during a news conference Friday.
Fortune’s family was immediately notified of Ratliff’s arrest, Brackney said. She said additional arrests are coming. The case has garnered national attention because the manner in which Fortune was discovered evoked memories of the South’s history of lynching. 
“This is not closure,” Brackney said. “This is just one step as we continue to investigate this case.” 
Brackney said that Fortune knew Ratliff but she would not elaborate on the nature of their relationship. She said officers arrested him on Friday afternoon after they saw him walking along Capitol Street, a road in west Jackson close to the 500 block of Road of Remembrance, where Fortune was found. 
“We understand the questions and desires for answers given Mississippi’s history,” Brackney said. “We understand this case is being viewed through a broader lens, a global lens, and we do not dismiss those concerns. We are taking them seriously. At the same time, we do have a responsibility to make sure that what we say publicly is supported by our evidence and facts.”
Jackson Police Department Chief RaShall Brackney meets with a security technology company in a photo the police department posted to its official Facebook page on Friday, May 29, 2026.  Credit: Jackson Police Department's official Facebook page
The police chief urged people to be patient while the investigation remains active. Brackney touted the department’s work. She said investigators interviewed nearly 15 people but couldn’t execute any warrants until the medical examiner’s office ruled Fortune’s death a homicide. 
As of Friday afternoon, Ratliff’s name did not appear in the Hinds County jail log. JPD Public Information Officer Tommie Brown said Ratliff had a Jackson address. It was not immediately clear whether Ratliff is represented by an attorney.
Earlier this week, Brackney told the Jackson City Council that Fortune’s autopsy was completed four weeks ago but JPD had not received it. Her comments came in response to Ward 3 Councilmember Kenneth Stokes and a letter from Fortune’s mother. 
In August, Hinds County Coroner Jeremiah Howard identified Fortune as the victim. She was a Kentucky native who ran away from home at 16 with someone she had met in foster care, her family told Mississippi Today. 
Fortune’s family said they didn’t know much about her life in Jackson but understood Fortune was struggling with addiction and was often destitute. 
A makeshift memorial has risen at the house where Fortune was found – a small mound of flowers, balloons, teddy bears and pinwheels surrounding a framed picture of her.
Fortune was the mother of four children.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: ‘I didn’t want to compete with myself:’ Critchfield says budget request focuses on 1 priority
description: This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 10, 2026. Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the […]
text:
Idaho State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Sean Dolan/EdNews)This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 10, 2026.
Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students.
Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.”
“I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday.
After budget cuts, Idaho plans to maintain low government spending, state official says

In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget.
All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie.
She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose.
And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.”
However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million.
Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation.
Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly.
Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students.
While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it.
While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment.
This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million.
Becky Sundin Mitchell, Democratic nominee for state superintendent, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Sean Dolan/EdNews)
 Democratic superintendent candidate Becky Sundin Mitchell says special ed needs more funding

Critchfield’s Democratic opponent criticized the budget request last week.
“This shows such a clear lack of understanding,” Becky Sundin Mitchell wrote on her campaign’s Facebook page. “Special education needs more funding, not less.”
Like Critchfield, Sundin Mitchell says she supports a modernized funding formula. Sundin Mitchell says this rewrite must ensure “full and sustainable” special education funding. Idaho schools face an estimated $100 million special education shortfall — the gap between state and federal funding and local needs.
On Wednesday, Critchfield discussed her decision to seek reduced funding for the high-needs program, her top priority from the 2026 session.
Critchfield says she is keeping a promise to legislators — to use cash on hand for her fledgling program, rather than tapping into the state’s general fund budget. But Critchfield says she has less cash on hand. This year’s $5 million comes from interest and carryover from two accounts within the Idaho Department of Education. Next year’s $1.7 million would come from these same depleted sources.
She said she wants to adhere to that plan next year, while trying to focus the Legislature’s attention on a single new budget request: the $20 million line item.
“I didn’t want to compete with myself,” she said.
The state agency requests begin a lengthy budget-writing process — with an election smack dab in the middle.
Critchfield is seeking re-election in November, as is GOP Gov. Brad Little. The winner of the governor’s race will submit budget recommendations to the Legislature on Jan. 11, the first day of the 2027 session. From there, lawmakers will spend three months drawing up and voting on budget bills for all agencies — proposals that will then go to the governor’s desk.
The 2027-28 budget year begins on July 1.

name: Mississippi Today
title: 9/11 overshadows other major events of the past 25 years for many Americans, new poll finds
authors: Linley Sanders and Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press
description: A general view of the New York skyline during an FDNY memorial to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in the Staten Island borough of New York.
text:
WASHINGTON — Twenty-five years later, the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, are still remembered as among the most important historic events in many Americans’ lives, according to a new poll.
A new Ipsos poll finds that about half of U.S. adults name the 9/11 attacks in an open-ended question about the most important historic occurrences in their lifetimes. That’s despite other momentous events that have happened since then, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the elections of Presidents Barack Obama and Donald Trump.
The polling points to the enduring legacy of 9/11, even as many Americans today are too young to have experienced or comprehended the event a quarter century ago. Ipsos found that the vast majority of Americans remember where they were when they heard about the attacks, and about two-thirds of Americans say it impacted the country “a great deal.” Separate polling from Gallup finds about 3 in 10 U.S. adults say they permanently changed the way they live their lives because of the attacks.
Despite the widespread impact, the Ipsos poll finds relatively few Americans will be marking the anniversary in some way. Only about 1 in 10 U.S. adults plans to do something to commemorate Friday’s 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.
Kevin Noel, 51, remembers watching the catastrophe unfold after he got out of a subway station to head to work near the World Trade Center that morning. To this day, the smell of the deadly inferno comes back to him whenever he’s in the area. He views 9/11 as the most historic event he’s lived through and believes “we’re going to be remembering this for the rest of history.” He plans to reflect on it privately on Friday.
“Every Sept. 11, I just — it’s a traumatic day for me where I just go silent,” Noel said.
The 9/11 attacks top the list of historic events in many Americans’ lifetime
For Americans who can remember the Sept. 11 attacks, they were a defining moment.
When U.S. adults were asked to list up to five of the most important historic events in their lifetime in the open-ended question — where respondents answered in their own words — the Sept. 11 attacks overshadowed the much more recent COVID-19 pandemic, which 31% of U.S. adults mentioned.
Other events, including the elections of Trump and Obama, space expeditions and the fall of the Berlin Wall, were cited by many Americans as defining moments. For Americans 65 and older, the most frequently mentioned events were the Sept. 11 attacks, followed by President John F. Kennedy’s assassination, space expeditions and the Vietnam War.
Clara Kiel, 88, says World War II had more impact on her life personally, as it hung over her childhood and she knew people who served. But she recalls the shock of watching 9/11 happen on TV from her living room. She also plans to take a moment to reflect privately on the 25th anniversary.
“It always seems like there’s something in history that changes the way people think,” said Kiel, a retired secretary in Onamia, Minnesota. “9/11 did it for the generation that grew up through that.”
For younger Americans under 35, COVID-19 is more prominent. About half of U.S. adults under 35 say the pandemic was among the most impactful events of their lifetime, while about one-third mention 9/11. A significant share of younger adults were not born when the attacks happened, or were too young to remember where they were at the time.
About 6 in 10 adults who were born after the attacks say they first learned about 9/11 in a class or through schoolwork, according to a Pew Research Center poll conducted in August.
Californian Kainoa Ilac, 18, who’s heading to college in Los Angeles, learned about the attacks from his parents, who are history teachers.
“I think that I and a lot of my peers in my generation still feel the effects of that day,” from airport security to awareness of the government’s ability to monitor communications, he said.
Americans overwhelmingly say the 9/11 attacks impacted the country
About 9 in 10 Americans say the attacks on Sept. 11 impacted the United States “a great deal” or “quite a bit,” according to Ipsos. Roughly 7 in 10 say it had at least “quite a bit” of impact on the world, and about 6 in 10 say it had a significant impact on their generation. Closer to 3 in 10 say it impacted their family or them personally.
Americans ages 50 and older are especially likely to say the attacks affected them personally.
Among the roughly 1 in 10 Americans who plan to mark the day, about 7 in 10 say they will participate in a moment of silence, and most, 56%, will display an American flag.
Lakesha Crowell remembers 9/11 in detail, including where she was sitting in her sophomore world history class in Meridian, Mississippi, when the teacher disclosed that two planes had hit New York’s World Trade Center. She recalls the security changes, the economic fallout, the way some people around her began looking differently upon foreigners, and the sense of vigilance at both individual and national levels.
“It affected us a lot, because it changed our way of living, and it changed our way of thinking,” said Crowell, 40.
Confidence in government’s ability to protect Americans from terrorism is down
Americans are divided on whether the country has become safer from foreign attacks since 9/11.
The Ipsos poll found about one-third of U.S. adults say the country is “more safe,” and a similar share say it is “less safe.” The remaining one-third, roughly, say the U.S. is about as safe as it was before the attacks.
Republicans are more likely than Democrats to say the country has become safer.
Recent Gallup polling found most U.S. adults, 55%, have “a great deal” or “a fair amount” of confidence in the U.S. government to protect its citizens from future acts of terrorism. That faith was at its highest, 88%, in polling conducted in the days after the 9/11 attack. It has ticked down over the 25-year trend, but the most recent measure is among the lowest recorded, similar to a poll conducted just after a deadly 2015 mass shooting in southern California.
Additionally, about one-third say they are “very” or “somewhat” worried that they or someone in their family will become a victim of terrorism. That’s down from about 6 in 10 who said that in the days following Sept. 11, 2001.
David Bronkhurst, a 49-year-old in Bloomingdale, New Jersey, recalls that after the attacks, his then-partner volunteered at the World Trade Center disaster site, handing out supplies to rescue and recovery workers, and some friends changed career paths to join the fire department. Other friends on the city’s police force died from cancers after they were exposed to toxins from the ash and dust at ground zero, he said.
He plans to attend an annual candlelight procession from a neighboring town to his own.
Bronkhurst doesn’t consider the country safer now than it was before the attacks — but he doesn’t worry too much that terrorism might strike him or his family. “You can’t go through life being scared,” he said.
___
Peltz reported from New York.
___
The Ipsos poll of 1,013 adults was conducted Aug. 21-23 using a sample drawn from Ipsos’s probability-based KnowledgePanel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: A crisis of political maturity: How Black leadership in Memphis is mismanaging the moment
description: There are political moments that test our ideology, and there are political moments that test our maturity. Memphis is presently experiencing both. The question before us is no longer simply what Tennessee’s recent congressional redistricting has done to Black political representation in Memphis. That has already shaped the terrain of the November election.[...]
text:
Memphis, picture above, faces a crisis of maturity from Black leaders, writes Rev. Earle Fisher. (Photo: Getty Images)There are political moments that test our ideology, and there are political moments that test our maturity. Memphis is presently experiencing both.
The question before us is no longer simply what Tennessee’s recent congressional redistricting has done to Black political representation in Memphis. That has already shaped the terrain of the November election.
The more urgent question is whether Black political leadership in Memphis possesses the spiritual, emotional and political maturity necessary to respond to this moment with the seriousness it deserves.
So far, I am deeply concerned that too many of us are missing the mark and mismanaging the moment.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
This moment requires the highest levels of maturity. That means personal grudges, bruised egos, intraparty rivalries, institutional territorialism and political pettiness cannot be permitted to become more important than public participation.
And many of Shelby County’s elected officials, including U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen, Memphis Mayor Paul Young, Shelby County Mayor Mickell Lowery, House Democratic Leader Karen Camper, the Shelby County and Tennessee Democratic Party and the Tennessee Black Caucus of State Legislators, must be more assertive as we move toward the November election. 
The most recent example of the leadership vacuum came in Tuesday’s appointment of a Democratic nominee for the state House District 84 seat, which became vacant when longtime Rep. Joe Towns resigned. Towns, who in August was elected Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk, had been running for both his state legislative seat and the clerk seat for months. 
Yet Democratic officials seemed caught flatfooted when he resigned, leaving the district without a nominee. The statutory process for selecting a nominee kicked in but legality is not the only question democratic institutions should ask themselves.  There are also questions of legitimacy, transparency and public trust. 
In the absence of leadership, one Shelby County Democratic Executive Committee member picked the person who will be on the November ballot, unopposed. 



The most recent example of the leadership vacuum came in Tuesday’s appointment of a Democratic nominee for the state House District 84, in which Black Memphis leadership seemed caught flatfooted despite knowing for months there was likely to be a vacancy.  


Why? If personal animus toward another politician, pastor, organizer or advocate determines whether someone will participate in efforts to strengthen democratic participation, that is no longer merely interpersonal conflict. It becomes a leadership problem. A critical election cannot become collateral damage in somebody else’s feud.
If the fragmentation of Black political power in Memphis ultimately accomplishes its intended effect, history should record more than what Republicans in Nashville did through redistricting. It should also record how everybody else responded.
I am marking this moment carefully.
We should remember who was silent, slothful, stingy, stubborn and salacious when this moment demanded that we be sacrificial, smart, savvy and sincere about putting the interests of the people ahead of our individual platforms.
That scrutiny includes our political institutions. After contentious primaries, party organizations face legitimate questions about whether their members publicly support nominees selected by voters and whether their internal procedures strengthen or weaken public confidence. Those questions deserve transparent answers rather than appeals to procedure alone.
The question is whether leaders are using the platforms entrusted to them to encourage broad democratic participation, communicate accurate information, acknowledge and correct misrepresentations and missteps when warranted, and strengthen public confidence in people’s ability to exercise political power.
Too many of them are not. 
And anybody who benefits from democracy should be willing to strengthen democracy.
If you have a constituency, engage it. If you have a congregation, educate it. If you have a platform, use it. If you have an email list, activate it. If you have resources, invest them. If you have volunteers, organize them. If you have influence, leverage it.
When a single member of the Shelby County Democratic Party Executive Committee was responsible for picking the Democratic nominee for House District 94 — in this case, Matthew Szalaj, an aide to Memphis Mayor Paul Young — they did so following a set protocol. But that’s not to say the process was transparent. (Photo: Shelby County Commission)
And if you have a title, earn it.
This is where there can be no excuses.
Leadership in this moment should be measured not merely by titles, press conferences, endorsements, social-media followings or organizational brands, but by whether leaders strengthen people’s capacity to participate in their government. Those who claim to possess influence should be prepared to demonstrate what they are doing with it.
This moment also requires something more difficult: repentance. Political maturity means being willing to acknowledge where governance has failed, where organizing has been insufficient, where rhetoric has been misleading, where relationships have been mishandled and where our own decisions have contributed to public distrust. Nobody gets to demand accountability from everybody else while declaring themselves exempt from it.
None of us should be above scrutiny if our stated objective is communal uplift rather than individual branding.
So between now and November, I am watching. And I know I am not alone.
Show us the voter registration efforts. Show us the voter education forums. Show us the canvasses, phone banks and text banks. Show us the transportation plans. Show us the early-voting strategies. Show us the precinct organizing. Show us the money being invested in civic engagement. Show us how your congregation, organization, office or institution is helping more people exercise political power.
Because if people and institutions with significant platforms remain conspicuously absent from the work of expanding democratic participation during a moment they themselves describe as consequential, the public has every right to ask what their leadership is actually for.
This moment is recording more than election results.
It is recording who put personality above people. Who protected platforms instead of building power. Who remained trapped in yesterday’s grievances while tomorrow’s political landscape was being constructed around us.
And it is recording who understood what time it was.

title: Unvaccinated Valencia County child tests positive for measles, marking 19th New Mexico case in 2026
description: The New Mexico Department of Health on Thursday announced that an unvaccinated child in Valencia County has tested positive for measles, bringing the total number cases in the state to 19 so far this year.
text:
New Mexico Department of Health officials announced Sept. 10, 2026, that a child in Valencia County became the state’s 19th case of measles so far this year. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)The New Mexico Department of Health on Thursday announced that an unvaccinated child in Valencia County has tested positive for measles, bringing the total number cases in the state to 19 so far this year. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state health department’s announcement does not specify the child’s age or gender but says the child is recovering at home. 
Officials listed sites and time periods in Belen in recent days where others may have been exposed to the virus, including: 

The Building Blocks Learning Center at 303 W. Reinken Ave. between 8:30 a.m. and 1:45 p.m. on Sept. 3;
Walmart at the I-25 bypass between 1 p.m. and 3:30 p.m. on Sept. 4; and
Presbyterian Urgent Care at 609 Christopher Road between 8:25 a.m. and 1:45 p.m. on Sept. 8.

State health officials urged members of the public who may have been exposed at those locations to check their vaccination status and monitor for symptoms. 
Symptoms typically appear within one to three weeks of exposure, according to NMDOH, and begin with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. A red, spotted rash often appears on the head or face before spreading down the body. Infected patients are contagious from four days before to four days after the rash appears, NMDOH said.
The most-recent case that state epidemiologists announced involved an unvaccinated adult in southeast New Mexico who tested positive with the disease, likely after contracting it out-of-state, officials said. The majority of the cases this year have been reported in the state’s correctional facilities.
“Every new measles case is a reminder you can protect yourself and your loved ones with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination,” Dr. Chad Smelser, the deputy state epidemiologist at NMDOH, said in a statement Thursday. 
That vaccine is “the best protection against this virus,” he said.
The number of measles cases in New Mexico remains far less than the 100 cases state officials logged between February and September last year. That outbreak marked the first in the state since 1996.

name: VTDigger
title: Somber and hopeful, 47 immigrants become U.S. citizens on 9/11 anniversary
description:
New Americans were sworn in at the Statehouse on the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Somber and hopeful, 47 immigrants become U.S. citizens on 9/11 anniversary.
text:
New Americans take their citizenship oaths during a naturalization ceremony at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Friday, September 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
MONTPELIER — Barbara Colombo became an American on Friday. She registered to vote before she left the building.
Colombo, 52, was one of 47 immigrants sworn in as U.S. citizens Friday at a naturalization ceremony in the Statehouse.
“It was very touching,” said the psychologist and professor, originally from Italy.
Donning a smile and her “I registered to vote today!” sticker, she posed for a photo with her toddler son wearing a full suit.
Immigrants from 21 countries took the oath of citizenship at the Vermont Statehouse on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. Senior U.S. District Judge William K. Sessions III presided and spoke alongside Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., in a ceremony that was at once solemn and hopeful.
Welch said in an interview that the event was “special in its own terms,” but that holding it on the 25th anniversary of 9/11 made it poignant.
For the new citizens, the day carried its own weight. Hussein Amouri, 23, arrived as an asylum seeker from Tanzania. Citizenship, he said, restored something he’d lost.
“Much of my community engagement ended when I couldn’t vote,” he said. “Knowing that now I have the voice … is very, very surreal.”
Amouri went through the process alongside Heritier Mampuya, 23, from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The two met playing soccer at Winooski High School.
Mampuya, an American Airlines supervisor, said that after a last-minute outfit change and a drive from Burlington, he finally felt “at ease.” He was off to apply for a passport ahead of a two-week trip abroad.

New Americans take their citizenship oaths during a naturalization ceremony at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Friday, September 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Sessions has presided over a naturalization ceremony in Montpelier on the 9/11 anniversary every year since 2002, excluding the Covid-19 pandemic. He and then-Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vt., chose the date to honor the victims in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania while celebrating what Sessions called the country’s “heritage of a welcoming country for immigration and new citizens.”
“The United States is a living, breathing experiment in human relations,” Sessions said during the ceremony. “We are made up of many different cultures, of different races, of different religions, from all over the world.”
He recounted a severe brain injury he once faced and how his neurosurgeon, nurse and physical therapist had all been sworn in as citizens by him in years past.
“The people who come to this country as immigrants and as citizens are part of us, and we are part of them,” he said.
The ceremony unfolded against a tense backdrop for immigration in Vermont. Since January, protests at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement digital surveillance office in Williston have led to several arrests. In March, three people were detained in an ICE operation in South Burlington — all later released by federal judges — after agents were met by roughly 150 protesters in a daylong standoff involving state and local police.
Sessions reminded the new citizens of the rights they now hold, as well as the duties that come with them.
“Under our laws, those freedoms are yours as a matter of right, without regard to the persons who may hold any given political office at any time,” he said. “In a free society, every right has a duty, and every freedom has a responsibility.”
While Sessions spoke of weighty obligations, Selle Cisse’s plans were simpler. He came to the U.S. with his family five years ago and said he’ll travel to visit friends. Beyond that, he’s happy staying put in Vermont.
“It’s calming, it’s at peace,” said Cisse, 24. “It’s good people here.”
For Welch, the day was an antidote to a hard season.
“You really have an obligation as a citizen to strengthen the bonds of affection that we need amongst ourselves to be able to get through tough times where we have significant disagreements about the world we live in,” he said during his remarks. “Help is on the way.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis administration misses legislative deadline gets more money for immigration anyway
description: Emergency fund  spending report and legislative budget commission
text:
The Florida Capitol building on March 11, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)As Ron DeSantis’ turn as governor nears its end, a legislative spending committee voted along partisan lines Friday to approve budget amendments allowing the two-term governor to pay for his crackdown on immigration.
The Joint Legislative Budget Commission approved a $240 million general revenue transfer to the Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund and agreed to allow the Division of Emergency Management (DEM), which operates the fund, to spend up to $250 million to pay pending invoices related to immigration enforcement and hurricanes Hurricanes Idalia, Helene, and Milton, and the 2026 wildfires.
The approval came about an hour after the DeSantis administration submitted an overdue report to commission members who were poised to start the meeting. The report, which details in part how money was spent, had been due to the Legislature July 15.
Florida still owes $603 million on immigration enforcement contracts

DEM Director Jared Perdue, who attended the meeting at the Florida Capitol, brushed by reporters refusing to answer any questions. Perdue (the Department of Transportation secretary who DeSantis recently appointed head of the DEM), is a public employee. State records show he earns $298,000 in his capacity as transportation secretary.
The mandatory report was a primary reason the Legislature agreed to sign off on re-establishing the fund, first created in 2002 to give DeSantis flexibility in addressing state disasters. 
In the eyes of DeSantis, Florida has been in a state of emergency due to undocumented immigration for more than three years, extending his initial January 2023 declaration more than 20 times.
The report shows:

As of June, the state owed 592 outstanding invoices related to immigration enforcement, such as the Everglades immigration detention facility dubbed by the DeSantis administration “Alligator Alcatraz.”
Florida has received just $84 million of $608 million in promised federal funds.
The state owes 82 invoices related to Hurricane Milton and 27 related to Hurricane Helene.

The report includes millions of dollars for “logistical services,” “site healthcare management,” and “facility support services.”
The analysis also found that for state fiscal year 2026-27 (which runs from July 1 through June 30, 2027) a deficit of $1.5 billion in the emergency fund would result unless the Legislature agreed to add money.
That finding of the potential $1.5 billion deficit assumes the fund would pay:

 $2 billion to cover the costs of two major hurricanes during the fiscal year, which includes about 80% of the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season (which has been quiet to date) and one month of the 2027 season.
$100 million for severe weather events aside from hurricanes, which the report says is a conservative estimate. 
$500 million for continued immigration enforcement.

Two months late
Outgoing Senate budget Chair Ed Hooper, a Republican from Clearwater, played down the potential bad fiscal news, telling reporters after the meeting that the state has “significant reserves should there be a natural disaster.”
“I don’t know the answer specifically about the dollar amount [in the state trust fund], and I’m not sure Secretary Perdue has been there long enough to actually have looked into that and come up with a finite number. But he’s committed to me that he is going to be transparent as the Legislature requested and I’ll hold him to that, as least for the next 50 days,” said Hooper said, who leaves office soon. 
Democrats questioned the transparency in releasing a report late and approving spending so far after-the-fact.
Senate Democratic Leader Lori Berman suggested the commission lacked time to absorb the report’s findings. She half jokingly suggested that the panel should be as timely in approving the funds as the DeSantis administration had been in submitting the legislatively required report.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There’s just so many different problems with the fact that we’re just getting this report two months late. Should we wait two months to vote on this appropriation? That would not be something that would be feasible, and it’s the same thing with us getting the report two months late,” Berman said. 
Rep. Allison Tant, a Democrat who represents rural counties in North Florida, expressed frustration that her storm-ravaged constituents weren’t being helped when the governor focused his efforts on immigration enforcement.
“In all of these hurricanes and tornadoes, I stood shoulder-to-shoulder with people who were struggling,” Tant said, detailing stories of personally providing aid to constituents in the aftermath of storms. 
The commission also approved a  hird budget amendment that gave the Department of Military Affairs $7.56 million in spending authority to make payroll until the end of the year.
Florida Center for Fiscal and Economic Policy Director Karen Woodall said the push to have the state submit the report was to increase transparency about how DeSantis has spent emergency money. 
“I think it was our hope that by having the Legislative Budget Commission involved, we would have legislative oversight — not of what the expenditures already made are, and signing the check, but of being engaged in discussion about what they were planning to do with money, so that there could be some transparency and some real legislative oversight about the use of tax dollars,” Woodall said.
She added that in the future she wants “actual dialogue and transparency over what these expenditures are going to be.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Electric bills, primary spending, CCSU president complaint: CT politics news
description: Plus: the Blue Ribbon Commission is at work, a foster care prevention grant is awarded, and Lamont announces new Shore Line East trains.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Lamont, Fazio OK millions to lower electric bills
The State Bond Commission — including Gov. Ned Lamont and campaign rival state Sen. Ryan Fazio — voted to approve borrowing up to $145 million on Monday to help lower electric bills.
The bonds will be used to pay down costs from unpaid bills that were allowed to accumulate during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as providing funding for the state’s electric vehicle charging program that had previously been collected through the public benefits charge on customers’ bills.
It was the second time the Bond Commission approved borrowing money to offset those costs. The first time, in August 2025, helped to reduce bills by about $5 to $10 a month. The second round of borrowing was already factored into rate adjustments that took effect Sept. 1.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter  
What Lamont, Elliott spent on primary
Reports filed on Sept. 10 give a final snapshot of spending by Gov. Ned Lamont and his challenger, Josh Elliott, in the Democratic primary won by the governor.
As of Aug. 31, Lamont’s campaign spent just shy of $10.5 million, with the self-funding governor personally donating $10.2 million to the effort.
Elliott, who participated in the voluntary public financing program, spent $4 million. 
— Mark Pazniokas, Capitol Bureau Chief
Complaint filed against CCSU president
Central Connecticut State University President Zulma Toro is under investigation for intimidation and bullying, CT Examiner reported Tuesday.
The complaint stemmed from a specific incident at a staff retreat in August. Toro allegedly screamed at staff members and canceled the retreat after someone called her plans for a newly purchased building unrealistic.
Toro was also the subject of a 2019 complaint that was ultimately dismissed. CT Examiner reports she has previously been criticized for threatening and insulting staff, as well as making them take care of her mother and her dog.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Blue Ribbon Commission crafting problem statements, policy proposals
Subcommittees of the Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability are working on potential changes to special education, school choice, accountability and the Education Cost Sharing, or ECS, formula.
All four subcommittees should be finished with their work by mid-October.
Members of the ECS subcommittee have so far expressed strong interest in tying the state’s main school funding grant to inflation, as legislators tried to do earlier this year. The special education subcommittee has discussed adding a special education weight to ECS and increasing funding for in-district programming.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Foster care prevention grant awarded
Connecticut is among 10 states that will receive federal grant money to reduce the number of children entering foster care.
The grants range from $600,000 to $750,000 for states to create programs that prevent the need for foster care. The total one-time grant funding is $7.3 million spread across states. Connecticut will set up the infrastructure it needs to bill the federal government for more family therapy services, aiming to reduce long wait times.
The announcement comes at a time many states, including Connecticut, are struggling to find placements for children in foster care.
— Ginny Monk, Investigative Reporter
Eversource files lawsuit against Hydro Quebec
Eversource, along with other electric utilities in Massachusetts, filed a lawsuit in federal court on Tuesday accusing Hydro-Quebec of failing to deliver power to the New England electric grid during a severe cold snap this past winter.
The lawsuit is not expected to have an impact on Eversource’s customers in Connecticut, who are not a party to the utilities’ agreements to purchase 9.45 terawatt hours of electricity from the Canadian power company.
Much of that power is fed into New England through a new transmission line that powered on in January, just days before a severe cold snap scrambled the region’s electric grid. Hydro Quebec has argued that the cold snap was a “force majeure” that necessitated cutting off exports of power to the U.S. in order to serve customers in Canada.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter  
New Haven alders signs off on quantum hub development
Supporters of Connecticut’s quantum ambitions got good news this week, as New Haven officials approved a key step in the development of the building that will house much of the effort.
On Tuesday, New Haven’s Board of Alders approved a development agreement between the city and Winstanley Enterprises, the Massachusetts-based developer that will construct a new building to house QuantumCT’s future headquarters. The building will also serve as the home for Unilever’s forthcoming Global Innovation Center.
The deal was approved unanimously, though at least one alder raised a deeper concern about the city’s massive quantum effort, calling for the project to serve all of New Haven. 
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
PURA again dinged over records request
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority was ordered to release hundreds of pages of emails and other communications this week related to the drafting of energy-related bills during the 2025 legislative session.
The order came from the state’s Freedom of Information Commission based on a complaint from Eversource, which had sought access to the records. The FOIC also admonished PURA legal director Scott Muska over his handling of the records request but stopped short of imposing any fines.
The decision marked the latest blemish against PURA’s handling of records requests under the leadership of former Chair Marissa Gillett, who was separately fined $2,500 by the FOIC last December related to another complaint.
Gillett stepped down from PURA last year, and the authority’s board has since been filled with new members appointed by Gov. Ned Lamont.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter  
New consumer survey finds CT households struggling
Connecticut households are facing increased financial strain and feel worse off than a year ago, according to a new report from the CBIA Foundation for Economic Growth and Opportunity and the University of New Hampshire Survey Center’s States of Opinion Project.
In a consumer survey released this week, local residents cited increased household expenses, including housing, groceries and gasoline, as contributing to the worsening issues. A majority of respondents said that the legislature wasn’t doing enough to help, with just 22% approving of lawmakers’ handling of economic and job creation issues.
The survey adds to a growing pile of data pointing to state residents’ mounting economic issues, with recent reports from the United Way of Connecticut and CT Voices for Children adding that low-income households are being hit hardest. 
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Lamont announces new Shore Line East trains
Gov. Ned Lamont announced on Friday that the Department of Transportation will add four new weekday trains to the state’s Shore Line East route between New Haven and New London.
The new trains will begin running on Mon., Oct. 5. The trains will depart New Haven’s Union Station at 2:55 p.m. and 5:55 p.m., before returning from New London at 4:40 p.m. and 7:28 p.m.
The additions to service come as Shore Line East has struggled to attract riders following the COVID-19 pandemic. Lawmakers set aside an additional $3 million to support the route as part of this year’s budget adjustments.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter

name: WyoFile
title: Cam Sholly, ‘once in a generation leader’ of Yellowstone, leaving park service
description:
After 8-year stint leading the nation’s first park through a pandemic, floods and spiking visitation, Sholly exits public service to join the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation.  
The post Cam Sholly, ‘once in a generation leader’ of Yellowstone, leaving park service appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After nearly eight years helming the country’s first national park through a global pandemic, historic floods and spiking visitation, Yellowstone National Park Superintendent Cam Sholly is leaving the federal workforce.
Sholly will join the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the country’s  largest conservation foundation, where he will serve as chief operating officer. 
The move will conclude nearly three decades of federal service for Sholly, who was known for his candid accessibility until 2025, when federal workforce policy implemented by the Trump administration created new communication hurdles at the National Park Service. Those changes also resulted in major staffing cuts and other disruptions within the system. 
Yellowstone National Park Superintendent Cam Sholly. (Yellowstone National Park/Jacob W. Frank)
“Serving as superintendent of Yellowstone has been the greatest professional honor of my life,” Sholly said in a Friday statement from the National Park Service, adding that he looks forward to “continuing important conservation work on a national scale.”
Sholly will be remembered as one of the most impactful leaders in Yellowstone’s history, said Brian Yablonski, CEO of the Property and Environment Research Center. Not only did Sholly accomplish goals he set out to like strengthening infrastructure, addressing worker housing and protecting the park’s wildlife and ecosystems, Yablonski said, Sholly “did it while steering the park through a gauntlet of crises.
“Every so often, a superintendent comes along who doesn’t just run the park well — he redefines what running it well even means,” Yablonski said in a statement. “Cam Sholly has been that ‘once in a generation’ leader.”
Floods and crowds and bears, oh my
Sholly began his National Park Service career in Yellowstone, where he was hired as a seasonal employee in 1990. Working his way up in rank, he served as the agency’s associate director for visitor and resource protection, superintendent of Natchez Trace Parkway, chief of ranger operations at Yosemite National Park and in several National Park Service headquarters leadership positions. He also directed the agency’s Midwest Region, overseeing 61 national parks in 13 states. 
He took the job as Yellowstone’s superintendent in 2018, and oversaw the vast and complex park during an era marked by the global COVID-19 pandemic, record visitation and president Trump’s DOGE disruptions. His tenure at Yellowstone also coincided with historic flooding that devastated sections of the park, a mass shooting attempt by an employee at Canyon Village, a geyser explosion in Biscuit Basin and other emergencies along with more typical mishaps involving bears, bison and tourists.
Yellowstone National Park Superintendent Cam Sholly and Yellowstone Chief of Facility Maintenance Duane Bubac look at damage in the Gardner River Canyon on June 18, 2022. (Jacob Frank/Yellowstone National Park)
Under his leadership, Yellowstone put over $1.5 billion to work in conservation and major infrastructure projects, according to the park service. The park made infrastructure investments; expanded bison transfers to tribal nations; and launched one of the largest public-private employee housing initiatives in National Park Service history. 
“Cam is an exceptional leader who delivered extraordinary results for Yellowstone National Park and the American people,” Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in a press release. “His dedicated leadership leaves Yellowstone stronger, safer and better prepared for the future.”
The National Park Service has begun the process of selecting Yellowstone’s next permanent superintendent.
