name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Gov. Landry’s interest in LSU harkens back to Huey Long. Could it backfire?
description: Huey Long’s involvement at LSU in the 1920s and ‘30s nearly cost the university and its law school their status as reputable institutions with legitimate credentials.  Nearly a century later, Gov. Jeff Landry’s interest in the state’s flagship school has been cited as a reason LSU could be kicked out of the Southeastern Conference.  Almost […]
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry addresses the Louisiana Legislature at the start of a November 2024 special session. (Hilary Scheinuk/The Advocate, Pool)Huey Long’s involvement at LSU in the 1920s and ‘30s nearly cost the university and its law school their status as reputable institutions with legitimate credentials. 
Nearly a century later, Gov. Jeff Landry’s interest in the state’s flagship school has been cited as a reason LSU could be kicked out of the Southeastern Conference. 
Almost from the moment he took office in 2024, Landry has expressed an outsized interest in the affairs of Louisiana’s colleges and universities — especially LSU. And immediately, his interest has drawn comparisons to Long, an extremely powerful, populist and polarizing politician who was at various points an outspoken LSU critic, its de facto president, chair of its governing board, unofficial band director and unwanted football coach. 
Though fans and sports commentators often draw this comparison, they are almost always a glossed-over, glamorized version that romanticizes the long-running politicization of the university and its athletics program.  
In reality, Long’s meddling undermined LSU’s institutional integrity, nearly costing the university its accreditation. His hand-chosen university president, James Monroe Smith, was charged with embezzlement, leading him to flee the state before being sent to federal prison. 
Long, then a U.S. Senator, “exerted undesirable political influence” on LSU’s law school, the Association of American Law Schools wrote in its censure of Long, according to a 1935 Associated Press report. 
This aspect of Long’s legacy was recalled this week when the Southeastern Conference updated its First Amendment lawsuit against LSU, alleging that its current president, Wade Rousse, does not have control over the university, and that state actors, including Landry and Attorney General Liz Murrill, have an outsized impact on the school’s actions. 
“That is completely and totally fictional. Maybe it makes for good drama. But it is false,” Landry spokeswoman Kate Kelly said in a statement. 
Citing the influence of the governor and attorney general, presidents of the SEC’s member schools had planned to vote Thursday on expelling LSU from the league but ultimately postponed the decision. 
Landry did not directly appoint Rousse as LSU president, unlike Long did Smith, but the governor’s support helped Rousse land the job. 
“Governor Landry is an enthusiastic supporter of LSU. However, I have full autonomy to run this institution and expect to be held accountable for the decisions I make,” Rousse said in a statement to the Illuminator. 
Landry and LSU
Landry has been in the spotlight the past two weeks as a legal fight unfolded in Louisiana. It involves former college athletes who had briefly pursued pro careers before an NCAA rule change awarded an extra year of eligibility to the classes that followed theirs. The group of 43 plaintiffs are suing the NCAA to be allowed to compete again at Louisiana colleges, including LSU. 
Landry and Murrill support the athletes and LSU, which is not a party in the lawsuit. Murrill even attended last week’s nine-hour-plus court hearing that ended with a preliminary injunction in favor of the plaintiffs. 
“Don’t hate the player, hate the game,” Landry said in a statement to The Advocate in regards to the conflict. 
Though the conflict seems to have reached a ceasefire, the governor continued to bash the Southeastern Conference and its commissioner this week, saying it’s “extremely dangerous for Greg Sankey” and the league to continue threatening LSU. 
Landry’s interest in LSU athletics — and higher education as a whole — intensified after he became governor in January 2024. He pushed for a slew of bills to increase the governor’s power. One in particular, in its original version, would have given him the power to directly hire university system presidents, as Long could. 
Critics dubbed it the “King Landry bill,” a reference to Long, who was known as The Kingfish. 
The bill was watered down but Landry still gained the power to directly appoint university system board chairs, authority that Long did not possess. 
Landry used that power to appoint mega-donor Lee Mallett chairman of the LSU Board of Supervisors. Mallett, a Lake Charles businessman, was among the most ardent supporters of Rousse’s hiring and also advocated for the return of LSU basketball coach Will Wade, who also had Landry’s support. 
Wade had previously served as LSU’s coach from 2017-22 but was fired for recruiting violations. His return to college basketball was in 2023 at McNeese State, where Rousse became president the next year.  
Landry’s support has also been vital for several other university president hirings, including Ramesh Kolluru at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette and Jimmy Genovese at Northwestern State. 
The Landry president

Landry’s interest in state university affairs has drawn concerns about accreditation. Most university evaluators, including the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges, require the administration of its accredited schools to remain free from undue external influence. 
The accreditor has given notice to several schools where its reviews determined that politics played an outsized role in the university’s operations.
In 2020, the commission determined Gov. Henry McMaster had undue influence on the University of South Carolina’s search for a new president. 
In 2017, the University of Louisville was given two years to address the commission’s concerns after it found Gov. Matt Bevin had exercised undue influence by abolishing the University of Kentucky’s governing board. 
In 2021, the commission opened an inquiry into the University of Florida for denying requests from professors who wanted to serve as expert witnesses in a voting rights case. 
A spokesperson for the accreditor has not responded to questions about whether it has received recent complaints or opened an investigation into LSU. 
And like Long, Landry has taken a strong interest in LSU’s athletics. In 2024, Landry petitioned the university to bring Mike VII, LSU’s live mascot, back to the sidelines of its football games, a practice it ceased in 2015 over animal welfare concerns. 
In 2025, Landry played a role in the firing of football coach Brian Kelly and athletics director Scott Woodward. 
Landry also hosted LSU athletics donors at an event at the Governor’s Mansion in July to discuss the program’s fiscal outlook. 
The Long of it all
Huey Long, a native of Winnfield, started out as a critic of the state’s flagship university. As time went on, he saw what he could do for the university — and what the university could do for him. 
Long’s patronage and interest helped grow LSU in terms of its student body size, acreage and new buildings. Much of it happened during the Great Depression, when Long took advantage of the economic downturn to lure high-profile faculty to Baton Rouge. 
But Long’s involvement with the university was also controversial, such as when he expelled a group of journalism students, now known as the “Reveille Seven,” who wanted to publish a letter to the editor critical of the governor. Or when he attempted to run off a tenured LSU professor who was critical of a Long protegé. 
Landry similarly has called for the dismissal of two LSU professors: Ken Levy, an LSU law professor who criticized the governor and President Donald Trump in profane comments to his class; and Bob Mann, a mass communications faculty member and frequent critic of Louisiana Republicans, publicly called out one of Landry’s deputies when he was attorney general.
Levy was suspended from the law school in January 2025. Mann went on to write “Kingfish U,” a book about Long’s influence at LSU, and resigned from the university shortly after Landry’s election, citing fears for his job. 
The investigations into Long’s influence at LSU stopped only when the senator died from a gunshot wound after an assassin attacked him at the State Capitol. 
According to some accounts, Long’s last words were about LSU: “I wonder what will happen to my poor university boys.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Measles outbreak has sickened 676 in Pa., including four fully vaccinated people
description: State health officials have recorded cases of measles in 37 of the commonwealth’s 67 counties. They included two deaths associated with the virus, announced last month, and four cases among people fully vaccinated for their ages.
text:
State health officials have recorded cases of measles in 37 of the commonwealth’s 67 counties. Photo by Getty Images Plus)The commonwealth’s top doctor stressed the best protection against measles is to get fully vaccinated. During an update on the measles outbreak, Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra L. Bogen said it has now sickened 676 people in the commonwealth.
Additionally, she said state health officials have recorded cases of measles in 37 of the commonwealth’s 67 counties. They included two deaths associated with the virus, announced last month, and four cases among people fully vaccinated for their ages. The Measles, Mumps and Rubella (MMR) vaccine is recommended for children 12 months and older.
“It’s important to know that people who are vaccinated rarely get measles because the two-dose MMR vaccine offers 97% protection against measles. That means for every 100 people who receive both doses, about three individuals may develop a mild case of measles if they’re exposed,” Bogen said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The four infected despite being vaccinated are residents of Center, Jefferson, Lancaster, and Lycoming counties, she said.
Measles is a highly contagious disease that spreads through infected people breathing, coughing or sneezing. Individuals with measles develop high fevers, coughs and red, watery eyes. That’s followed by a characteristic rash starting at the head three to five days after symptoms begin. About 20% of cases require hospitalization.
Among the cases reported in Pennsylvania, 124 patients have been hospitalized, according to health officials.
Pennsylvania has been responding to a measles outbreak centered on Lancaster County since April. Late last month, the Health Department announced it had recorded the first measles-related deaths in the nation this year and the first in decades for Pennsylvania.
The announcement became a flashpoint in the national debate over vaccines. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. questioned the accuracy of the report, delivered by Bogen and Gov. Josh Shapiro. Lancaster County Republican elected officials joined Kennedy, claiming the report was inaccurate.
Photo of a single dose of the MMR vaccine. (Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)
Kennedy has long been a skeptic on vaccine efficacy, linking shots to autism without evidence.
Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni earlier this week released additional information about the deaths. While both infants were infected with measles, one died of a ruptured spleen and the other had a genetic condition that made her highly vulnerable to infection and the measles killed her.
Bogen addressed inquiries about why the Health Department has not released more information about the deaths. She said the department’s work is governed by the state Vital Statistics Law and the Disease Prevention and Control Law, which allow personal information to be released only under narrow conditions that don’t apply in the Lancaster County deaths.
“Unlike the Department of Health, county coroners and healthcare providers have different laws and regulations that govern their work and what they can disclose. So there may be differences in the level of detail made available,” Bogen said.
Bogen said the state Health Department and its partners are responding to the outbreak by deploying resources and personnel and the MMR vaccine. The vaccination rate for Pennsylvania kindergarteners is 93%, she added.
“We are not waiting for Pennsylvanians to come to us. We are making the vaccine accessible to anyone who wants it,” Bogen said, noting state health workers have held more than 120 pop-up MMR vaccination clinics at churches, fire halls, community centers and private homes.
“Dozens of additional pop-up clinics are already scheduled for the upcoming weeks and months, tailored directly to community interest and need,” she said.
Anyone interested in hosting a MMR vaccination event can call the Health Department at 877-724-3258. The MMR vaccine is also available at each of the department’s 59 state health centers, which are listed at health.pa.gov/shc. 
The state provides the latest information about the measles outbreak at pa.gov/measles.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Supreme Court finds deeper meaning in pothole-triggered traffic accident
description: Kansas Supreme Court examines legal claims of negligence by municipal government through the lens of a Topeka traffic accident caused by a street pothole.
text:
Kansas Supreme Court Justice Justice K.J. Wall, center second row, is author of an opinion reversing the Shawnee County District Court and Kansas Court of Appeals to breathe life into a negligence lawsuit filed against the City of Topeka regarding a municipality's duty to maintain streets for benefit of the public. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Supreme Court photo)TOPEKA — Troy Alan Martin was northbound on Topeka Boulevard when his car struck a large pothole, jolting the vehicle with enough force that it slammed into a median, rolled several times and ejected him onto the street.
Martin, who wasn’t wearing a seatbelt, survived the July 2, 2019, encounter with a crater big enough for an adult to place both feet inside. Because of injuries sustained in the crash, Martin filed a negligence lawsuit against the City of Topeka alleging it failed to reasonably maintain the road.
Shawnee County District Judge Jay Befort dismissed the civil case by granting summary judgment in favor of the city. A three-judge panel of the Kansas Court of Appeals agreed with Befort, concluding the state’s public-duty doctrine barred Martin from seeking compensation. While the Court of Appeals declined to embrace Martin’s legal arguments, the judges concluded chuckholes were an “abysmal” plague.
On Friday, the Kansas Supreme Court took a different route and unanimously reversed both lower courts.
Justice K.J. Wall’s written opinion said Kansas recognized since the early years of statehood that a city had a legal duty to keep streets in a reasonably safe condition. Depending on facts in a case, the opinion said, a city could be liable in a lawsuit alleging injuries resulting from disregard of that duty.
“Once a city opens a street and invites public travel, it owes that duty to those who travel the street in response to the invitation. The public-duty doctrine therefore does not bar a claim for breach of that duty,” the opinion reads.
The Supreme Court said questions to be resolved by a Shawnee County jury included conflicting views on whether the City of Topeka knew or should have been aware of the pothole and whether city employees had the opportunity to take reasonable steps to repair the roadway imperfection prior to the accident.
“Whether a street was reasonably safe for public use by travelers exercising ordinary care, whether a defect was discernible enough to call for repair and whether the city had notice of the defect are ordinarily questions for the jury,” the justices said.
The Supreme Court said it was improper for the district court and Court of Appeals to embrace summary judgment on behalf of the City of Topeka and against Martin when material facts of the case remained unaddressed.
During oral argument in May before the Supreme Court, Justice Caleb Stegall said a complexity in the case was that applicable Kansas statute was written in an ambiguous way. He said both sides in the case pointed to the same text while arguing opposite interpretations.
Under Kansas law, the Supreme Court said, “liability is the rule and immunity the exception” and that governmental entities claiming an exception must bear the burden of establishing it. Municipal governments invoke the public-duty doctrine when faced with lawsuits filed in response to actions of law enforcement officers.
Chloe Davis, a Topeka attorney representing Martin, said exclusions for police officers or sheriff’s deputies didn’t cover pothole negligence.
“If a private person would be liable for the underlying fact pattern, then the government should be liable for that same fact pattern unless it is excluded,” she said.
Nicholas Jefferson, an assistant city attorney in Topeka, said the responsibilities of a public entity and private individual were distinct.
“No individuals I’m aware of operate miles and miles of public streets,” Jefferson said. “A city is different from a private person. A city maintains a vast network of roadways. I think if the city does have notice of a specific road defect, I think that changes the argument.”
He said it would be financially difficult for municipal governments to maintain roads at a level that prevented formation of potholes.
Wall, during oral argument four months ago, foreshadowed the opinion released Friday.
“In some of the earlier cases,” the justice said, “they make clear that the city is not obligated to open a street, right? But, once it does, it has the power to assess and maintain those roads and comes with that a duty to keep that road safe for its intended purpose.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa public universities each seek $2M increases in state general education funds
description: Each of Iowa’s public universities are increasing their funding requests to the state for the first time in years as the institutions work to keep rising costs off students’ backs. The University of Iowa, Iowa State University and the University of Northern Iowa have each requested incremental general education funding of $2 million in state […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents will review and potentially approve fiscal year 2028 university funding requests to the state next week. (Photos by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch. Logo via Iowa Board of Regents)Each of Iowa’s public universities are increasing their funding requests to the state for the first time in years as the institutions work to keep rising costs off students’ backs.
The University of Iowa, Iowa State University and the University of Northern Iowa have each requested incremental general education funding of $2 million in state appropriations for fiscal year 2028, according to documents published by the Iowa Board of Regents.
The total general education request from the university comes out to $561.25 million, representing a 1.08% increase from fiscal year 2027. Additional requests from the UI and ISU for specific initiatives bring the funding request’s total increase to $10 million, or a 1.6% increase from last fiscal year. However, the appropriation request for tuition replacement has decreased from $25 million to $21 million, eliminating $4 million from the appropriations ask.
“The University of Iowa, Iowa State University and the University of Northern Iowa are tremendous assets for the State of Iowa,” the board document stated. “The public universities serve the state in a variety of ways, and each one draws on individual strengths for the betterment of Iowans, but they can do more.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Appropriations requests will be discussed and potentially approved by the board of regents at its Sept. 16-17 meeting. The board will also hear updates on its Resource Enhancement and Productivity Study and appropriations requests for university capital projects.
Neither the UI or ISU have requested increases to general education appropriations since 2023, and the last time UNI requested additional money in 2024, lawmakers did not approve it.
“Like every Iowa household and business,” the board document stated, Iowa’s public universities are paying more for utilities, contracts, insurance and other necessities, and increased funding from the state would go directly to offsetting these costs.
The UI’s general education funding request is “intentionally limited in scope” and won’t go toward any new programs or initiatives, with the document stating the university’s fund reallocation and new fund-seeking efforts will handle those areas. State funding will instead go entirely to inflation-risen costs, helping the UI to keep students and families from seeing those increases instead.
One of Iowa’s state universities sees enrollment increase in fall semester

“That affordability protects a workforce Iowa cannot easily replace,” the board document stated.  “Each year the university graduates the nurses, teachers, physicians, pharmacists, engineers and business owners who stay and build careers in Iowa communities. Keeping their education affordable keeps that pipeline open.”
Beyond general education dollars, the UI’s $2 million special purpose unit request from the state is for a “rural physician pipeline” program that would expand partnerships with rural medical providers and grow enrollment of the university’s rural medicine track from 20 to 28 over four years. The university is requesting this be a recurring investment from the state.
UNI stated in the document it is dealing with utilities, health and property insurance and employee wages increasing. While these costs are partially offset by “renewed emphasis on efficiency and internal reprioritizations,” the document stated increased state funding would also help in this endeavor.
ISU has also worked to absorb rising costs of energy, utilities and contracted services through “responsible stewardship,” the release stated, but is requesting the additional $2 million for its general operations to stop the need to place the burden of higher expenses on students.
The Ames university is requesting another $2 million from the state for its AI-Ready Workforce and Innovation Initiative to expand “ethical AI education” across the university’s academic programs. Other priorities for the initiative include integrating artificial intelligence into its areas of advanced manufacturing, agriculture technology and research and biomanufacturing.
According to the request, this initiative and the state funding for it would help create economic strength and opportunities for new products and innovation.
“This investment will also position Iowa State and its partners to compete successfully for major federal investments that drive economic growth across Iowa and the nation,” the document stated.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Almanac, an annual compendium of Vermont life, is shutting down
description:
The founders of the publication say they’re stretched too thin to continue after six years.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Almanac, an annual compendium of Vermont life, is shutting down.
text:
A stack of Volume V of the Vermont Almanac, sitting in Next Chapter Bookstore in Barre in November 2024. Courtesy of Next Chapter Bookstore
For six years, Vermont Almanac has served as a “glorious mix of eclectic content” on Vermont life, from creative essays and how-tos on rural skills to history and nature write-ups. 
“It was like a very cozy, by-the-woodstove book to read,” said longtime reader Naomi Heindel. 
But the almanac said this week that six years would not become seven. Instead of opening up its website for preorders, the publication announced in a newsletter that it was shutting down. 
“I think the original version of Vermont Almanac — the one overseen by me and Patrick and Virginia and Amy — has run its course,” co-founder Dave Mance wrote in the newsletter. 
In an interview, Mance said that “financial realities” were a factor in the decision to close. 
“Lo and behold, it is hard to publish a book in the 21st century,” he said. 
The almanac began with four founding members: Mance, Virginia Barlow, Amy Peberdy and Patrick White, according to its website. The group had previously worked together on Northern Woodlands magazine, but Mance said they were intrigued by the idea of focusing on Vermont, where they all lived. 
“The idea was kind of built around this philosophy that we value Vermont for its rural traditions, its working lands, its nature,” and those things are “almost a given,” he said. But in actuality, “You have to keep declaring your identity.”
When the almanac was conceived, the four received a $15,000 loan from a family member and started reaching out to writers and photographers they knew from their previous work, Mance said. The almanac ultimately worked with hundreds of Vermont contributors. 
Despite its name, the almanac was not a dry compilation of information — weather forecasts, planting calendars and the like — in the vein of the classic Old Farmer’s Almanac. Mance said that caused some confusion at first. 
“We didn’t have the heights of Vermont’s mountains listed, as some of the old encyclopedic almanacs did,” he said. 
Instead, Vermont Almanac was partly inspired by the Foxfire book series, which compiled basic rural knowledge on Appalachia. 
“We did stories on how to make a black ash pack basket, how to identify animal tracks,” Mance said. 
Each edition included essays on Vermont history, from its big names like Calvin Coolidge to lesser-known history like the Barre Fat Man’s Club. And they would feature the natural world, down to the depths of Vermont’s phytoplankton that give lake trout their yellow color. 
A pillar of the almanac was “to really, really illuminate the natural world in a way that you can do as an annual, where you’re thoughtful and selective, in contrast to kind of the social media naturalism that rules the day, which is expansive and can be good, but is just so overwhelming and uncurated that it kind of just melts my mind,” Mance said. 
September’s “Nature Notes” spread from the Vermont Almanac, Volume V. Courtesy of Vermont Almanac
Lisa Cadieux, the designer of Vermont Almanac, said she tried to give it a classic, reflective look and feel like “something that’s intended to last, and be kept and, ideally, treasured.” 
The nonprofit almanac was funded by a combination of sales, sponsors, grants and individual donors, Mance said. Over the course of six years, he said, they sold roughly 30,000 to 40,000 books. 
“People loved what we were doing, and they forked over a little extra because they liked that we existed and were able to document the state like we were,” he said. 
Over the years, Heindel grew from being a reader to supporting the publication by hosting its book launch parties at the North Branch Nature Center in Montpelier, where she serves as executive director. She described a community that has sprung up among the contributors and supporters around the shared values of place-based education, storytelling and stewardship. 
“Much of the work that we do, and much of the work that their stories highlight, is about rural Vermont,” she said. 
But the grassroots nature of the almanac also proved a challenge because it was so heavily dependent on the work of its founders, who have other commitments. Mance is a maple sugarmaker. Co-founder White is a Christmas tree farmer. 
“We did a big sales push of every volume in December, and then in January I was out in the woods, cutting trees off of main lines and getting ready for the sugaring season to come,” Mance said. 
In the newsletter, the almanac put out a call for anyone interested in continuing the publication to reach out. Mance said he was in talks with one interested party, but he couldn’t give specifics. Old editions of the almanac will still be available on the website for the foreseeable future. 
Mance said that even though he’s sad about Vermont Almanac ending, he’s also at peace. 
“(I’m) just feeling really blessed and really grateful to have been able to do this work for six years,” he said. “It was a privilege, and a great joy, and a great adventure.”

title: Trump plan to limit mail voting hinders Democrats more than GOP, analysis finds
text: President Donald Trump has, at times, justified his campaign against mail-in voting in explicitly partisan terms, claiming Republicans’ electoral chances hinge on whether the practice is allowed.A new analysis from a Democratic-aligned voting rights group, shared first with States Newsroom, shows he may be right: Eliminating mail-in voting would be more disruptive to Democratic voters than Republicans.Fair Fight Action, a Georgia-based advocacy group founded by Democratic former state Rep. Stacey Abrams, analyzed vote-by-mail data in seven 2024 swing states and potential battlegrounds for the 2026 midterm elections. Records indicated that Democrats voted by mail more often than Republicans.The partisan differences didn’t swing any battleground states in the 2024 presidential election, all of which Trump won.But if Trump succeeds in restricting mail voting in the 2026 midterms, which he is attempting through a contentious executive order directing the U.S. Postal Service to enforce new requirements, it could help Republicans win key House and Senate seats as each party seeks a narrow path to a majority in either chamber.Dems’ mail voting edgeFor example, in Michigan, one of the toss-up U.S. Senate races that will determine control, more than 2 million voters cast mail ballots in 2024, according to the Fair Fight analysis. Nearly half came from Democrats, while Republicans sent 39%, a difference of about 200,000 votes in Democrats’ favor. That gap represents a smaller number of votes than the margin of victory for the winner of the state in the last three presidential elections.In North Carolina, another state with a close U.S. Senate race in 2026, Democrats voting by mail outnumbered Republicans by about eight percentage points in 2024, though mail ballots accounted for only about 5% of all votes, according to the data.In a Friday statement to States Newsroom, Fair Fight Action CEO Lauren Groh-Wargo blamed Trump for undermining trust in vote-by-mail and encouraged voters to view mail voting as a viable method.“Trump is a desperate loser who has spent years lying to his supporters about mail voting ‘fraud’ – as a result many stopped using a method they once trusted,” she said. “Voting by mail is secure, convenient, and accessible. Whether voting by mail, early, or on Election Day, make your plan to vote now and see it through.”In a statement, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis portrayed the rule on mail ballots as a “commonsense” election security measure.“If securing America’s elections – through commonsense methods like voter ID and proof of citizenship – would make it harder for Democrats to win elections, perhaps they should reconsider the methods they’re using to ‘win,’” Bis wrote.The Fair Fight analysis shows the partisan gap narrows in states with more mail-in voting.In Arizona, where 83% of voters cast mail ballots in 2024, Republicans held a 5-point margin in mail voting, roughly the same as Trump's 5.5-point victory in the state. And in Nevada, where 44% of ballots were cast by mail, the mail-in vote was almost evenly split among Democrat, Republican and “other” voters.Mail voting historyUntil 2020, mail voting enjoyed broad bipartisan support.An April 2020 study published by Stanford University’s Institute for Economic Policy Research found that in the six Western states — Oregon, Washington, Colorado, Hawaii, Utah and California — that had started implementing a system of mailing ballots to every registered voter, the policy did not help either party while modestly boosting turnout.“Vote-by-mail does not have meaningful partisan effects on election outcomes,” the authors wrote.But as states ramped up mail voting in the 2020 election as a response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the issue turned more partisan, with Democrats more likely to stay away from in-person voting. Trump, then running for reelection, cast unfounded doubts on vote-by-mail’s integrity and warned of dire effects for Republicans.“MAIL-IN VOTING WILL LEAD TO MASSIVE FRAUD AND ABUSE,” he tweeted in May 2020. “IT WILL ALSO LEAD TO THE END OF OUR GREAT REPUBLICAN PARTY. WE CAN NEVER LET THIS TRAGEDY BEFALL OUR NATION.”After several cycles of roughly equal rates of mail voting, Democratic mail voters nearly doubled Republicans, 60% to 32%, in 2020. The gap narrowed in 2024, with Democratic voters outpacing Republicans 37% to 24%.Trump’s claimsWhile the Postal Service is now arguing in court its rule based on Trump’s March 31 executive order is not an election regulation but only includes “modest” technical specifications for mail, other statements by Trump show the purpose is directly tied to election administration. Trump’s order justified new regulations on mail ballots to maintain “public confidence in election outcomes” and “enhance election integrity.”He previewed the effort in an August 2025 social media post saying he would “lead a movement to get rid of MAIL-IN BALLOTS” that again made the issue explicitly about partisan advantage.“WE WILL BEGIN THIS EFFORT, WHICH WILL BE STRONGLY OPPOSED BY THE DEMOCRATS BECAUSE THEY CHEAT AT LEVELS NEVER SEEN BEFORE, by signing an EXECUTIVE ORDER to help bring HONESTY to the 2026 Midterm Elections,” he wrote. “Democrats are virtually Unelectable without using this completely disproven Mail-In SCAM. ELECTIONS CAN NEVER BE HONEST WITH MAIL IN BALLOTS/VOTING.”The U.S. Supreme Court is expected to rule soon on whether the rule can be in effect for this year’s midterms.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska teens oppose 20,000 acre industrial park proposal
authors: Grace Yang, Emily Brubaker, Sadie Cooper, Gemma Alderfer, Lupine Reifler
description: The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority’s plans to develop industrial facilities on land that currently belongs to Alaskan citizens has generated extensive criticism for many reasons. As a group of teens working to preserve our environment to the best of our abilities, we feel that it is our responsibility to inform Alaskans about how […]
text:
A screenshot of a map by the Alaska Department of Natural Resources in a proposal for nearly 20,000 acres of land to be transferred to AIDEA near Houston for a proposed multi-use industrial and energy development district that may include a data center. (Alaska Department of Natural Resources)The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority’s plans to develop industrial facilities on land that currently belongs to Alaskan citizens has generated extensive criticism for many reasons. As a group of teens working to preserve our environment to the best of our abilities, we feel that it is our responsibility to inform Alaskans about how our land is at risk. 
The Department of Natural Resources has proposed transferring nearly 20,000 acres of land near Houston, Alaska to AIDEA. That state agency finances and promotes development projects, and the new land transfer could give them control of public lands to be sacrificed for another “industrial park.”
AIDEA is a corporation with a history of bad investments that have resulted in nearly $233.3 million in losses over the last 35 years, according to an analysis by economists Milt Barker and Gregg Erickson in 2022. These investments included an Anchorage fish processing plant (now ChangePoint Church), the proposed Ambler Road and Mustang Oil. These projects, and more, misused Alaskans’ money and received major community backlash or failed on their own.
AIDEA says it plans to build roads, manufacturing pads and a data center on the land. Those plans could affect nearly 41.8 miles of trails used for running, biking and gathering firewood, along with supporting salmon, moose and other wildlife.
Data centers are being built in places all over the country to train and store data for artificial intelligence systems. A single medium-sized data center uses about 300,000 gallons of water a day along with lots of electricity, putting strain on the local communities’ power and water sources. Additionally, researchers have found that data centers harm the environment through carbon emissions and pollution from PFAS, chemicals that don’t break down in the environment over time. 
Alaska Youth for Environmental Action teens from Anchorage are concerned because the proposed industrial park could be vastly harmful. We should not sacrifice our land, water and communities to power an industry serving distant demands. This for-profit development and industrialization can permanently alter the land which is the foundation of our food, culture and livelihoods. Rather, the state of Alaska should prioritize our Alaskan ecosystems and the people that depend on them.
The deadline for public comment is September 14th. It is important to have our voices heard.

text:
Delaware voters still have a few days to cast a ballot ahead of the state’s Sept. 15 primary. Early voting continues through Sunday, Sept. 13, from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., at designated sites that vary by county. Voters can look up their early voting site or Election Day polling place through the state’s Voter Portal at ivote.de.gov.
But there is no in-person voting on Monday, Sept. 14. The primary itself is Tuesday, Sept. 15, when polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
As of Friday afternoon, Delaware voters had cast 30,800 ballots combined through early voting and absentee methods, according to data released by the Delaware Department of Elections (DDOE).

(Pictured: DDOE’s Daily Report through Election Day)
The Department of Elections’ report breaks these totals down by county and voting method, but not by political party, so it does not show how turnout is trending between Democratic and Republican primary voters.
For a full rundown of who’s on the ballot, including contested primaries for U.S. Senate, U.S. House, attorney general and state treasurer, along with New Castle County Council races, see Delaware LIVE’s Sept. 15 Primary Voters’ Guide.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida’s leaders ‘honor and commemorate’ heroes of Sept. 11 attacks
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis led Florida in remembering the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2002, ordering flags lowered throughout the state. “To honor and remember those who were lost on that day, I hereby direct the flags of the United States and the State of Florida to be flown at half-staff at all local and state […]
text:
The aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001 attack on the World Trade Center. U.S. Navy Photo by Chief Photography Mate Eric J. TilfordGov. Ron DeSantis led Florida in remembering the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2002, ordering flags lowered throughout the state.
“To honor and remember those who were lost on that day, I hereby direct the flags of the United States and the State of Florida to be flown at half-staff at all local and state buildings, installations, and grounds throughout the State of Florida from sunrise to sunset on Friday, September 11, 2026,” he wrote in a memorandum
He attended a ceremony in Green Cove Springs.
“At Ground Zero, firefighters, police officers, and EMTs rushed into the smoke clouds and rubble, braving unthinkable danger to rescue as many people as they could. Hundreds of first responders — and passengers on United Flight 93 — made the ultimate sacrifice so that others could live. We will always remember their heroism and owe them a profound debt of gratitude,” he posted on X.
“The 9/11 terror attacks were motivated by a foreign belief system that is still a major aspect of not just the Middle East, but increasingly Europe and even the United States. We should be clear-eyed about the threat posed by Islamic Jihad and do all we can to ensure Never Forget means Never Forget,” the governor continued.
“The monsters who planned this evil attack wanted one thing: to destroy American values, resolve, and unity by terrorizing the American people.” U.S. Sen. Rick Scott posted.
“The terrorists didn’t win in the days after 9/11, and thanks to the incredible resilience of the American people, they will NEVER win in taking us down. Today and every day, may we never forget the great American spirit which guides us through our hardest days, and may we all remember and honor those who lost their lives 25 years ago.”
At a memorial service at U.S. Special Operations Command in Tampa, U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, along with community officials and law enforcement officers, placed a yellow rose in remembrance of those lost and in honor of the police officers, firefighters, and other first responders showed on that day.
“Twenty-five years ago, on September 11, 2001, our nation experienced one of the darkest days in American history. But on that terrible day, we also saw the very best of America. Police officers, firefighters, paramedics, and other first responders ran toward danger to help others. They risked — and in far too many cases, gave — their own lives to save people whom they had never met,” she said.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly attended a ceremony in Naples.
“Twenty-five years later, we remember the lives taken, the families forever changed, and the first responders whose courage revealed the very best of our nation. May we honor them by carrying forward that same spirit of unity, service, and love of country. We will never forget,” he said on X.
GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds proclaimed in a social media post that “we will never forget.”
“We still mourn the 2,977 lives lost on that horrible day — families in New York and across America shattered by an act of cowardly, unthinkable violence. We still remember the heroes — the first responders who ran towards danger, the patriots who rushed the cabin of United Flight 93. We will never forget. @erikadonalds and I are praying for all of the 9/11 families today.”
On her campaign website, Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon recalled the bravery of the first responders that day and the survivors of those killed.
“It is imperative that we continue to fight for them and for those still living with the mental, emotional, and physical toll of that day, advocating for the healthcare they deserve. It is the least we can do to honor their courage and sacrifice.
“‘Never forget’ is not just a phrase but a charge to share these stories with future generations of that day: the bravery shown in moments of sheer terror, and the hope and inspiration born from people coming together,” she wrote.
“That is when we saw humanity at its best, and it’s worth remembering just as much as the devastation we experienced as a nation.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico remembers 9/11
authors: Matthew Mondschein, Danielle Prokop, Leah Romero
description: New Mexico communities marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 anniversary attacks on the U.S. with remembrances.
text:
Harkening to a tradition started  in 2003, Albuquerque firefighters on Sept. 11, 2026, the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, donned full gear and climbed the 22-story Washington Federal Building five times to represent 110 floors — the height of the former World Trade Center’s towers. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)At 8:46 a.m. on the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 terrorism attacks — the time marking the moment when hijackers crashed American Airlines Flight 11 into the World Trade Center’s north tower — dozens of New Mexico firefighters walked between rows of folded uniforms to summit the Washington Federal Building — the taller of the pair that defines Albuquerque’s skyline. 
Harkening to the tradition started by Albuquerque Fire Department Lieutenant Charles Cogburn in 2003, firefighters donned full gear and climbed the 22-story building five times, to represent 110 floors — the height of the former World Trade Center’s towers. The climb honors the 343 firefighters and 78 other first responders that died following the building’s collapse. 
Brannon Porch, a retired firefighter and U.S. Navy Veteran who marched in the honor guard, described the sinking feeling he had sitting in his truck on the westside, grabbing breakfast from the New York Bagels shop and describing rushing to the fire station and watching when the towers fell. 
Firefighters pass out photos of the first responders who died at Ground Zero, pinning them to their jackets or securing them in their helmets. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Workers inside the Washington Federal Building applaud members of New Mexico fire departments before their ascent. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Albuquerque firefighters prepare ahead of the memorial stair climb to honor first responders who died in the wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York City. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Albuquerque Fire Chief Emily Jaramillo greets supporters after the first leg of the stair climb on the 25th Anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
Brannon Porch, a retired firefighter and U.S. Navy Veteran is a pipe major for the New Mexico Fire and Police Pipes and Drums which led the procession from Civic Plaza to the Washington Federal Building. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Firefighters in the Santa Fe Fire Department conduct their stair climb ceremony on Sept. 11, 2026, in remembrance of the 343 firefighters who died during the terrorist attacks on Sep. 11, 2001. (Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)Firefighters in the Santa Fe Fire Department conduct their stair climb ceremony in remembrance of the 343 firefighters that died during the terrorist attacks on Sep. 11, 2001 (Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)Santa Fe fighterfighter pipes and drums march in front of City Hall. for the Sept. 11, 2026, 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. (Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)Santa Fe Mayor Michael Garcia speaks at 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony on Sept. 11, 2026. (Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)Mayfield High School's Air Force Junior ROTC presenting the colors on Sept. 11, 2026, the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. (Leah Romero for Source NM)
“I had two realizations at that moment: all I thought was “Dear God,” and the second, was that we would go to war,” he said. “Twenty-five years later, I still have a lot of emotions about it, so this event pays homage not just to the firefighters but the civilians that lost their lives that day — and paying respect to them is one of the greatest honors of the job.” 
Members of the Santa Fe Fire Department also gathered Friday morning, this time outside City Hall. In two groups, also starting at 8:46 a.m., they took turns climbing five wooden steps while wearing full gear and climbed until they reached a total of 2,200 steps.
“Our nation was forever changed by the acts of imaginable violence that claimed the lives of nearly 3,000 innocent people,” Santa Fe Mayor Michael Garcia said during the remembrance ceremony. “Twenty-five years later, we continue to remember those who were lost, honor the families and survivors whose lives were forever changed and pay tribute to all those who answered the call to serve and protect.” 
In Las Cruces, students at Mayfield High School gathered outside the school Friday morning , where members of the school’s Air Force Junior ROTC led the 25th anniversary remembrance Friday before class with a presentation of the flags. The Las Cruces Police Department joined the ceremony to present the colors to the students who raised the flags to half mast. Las Cruces Public Schools Board of Directors also joined the annual ceremony.
“While many of us here today were not alive to witness the tragedies that took place 25 years ago on Sept. 11, 2001, we take this day every year to honor the 2,996 people who lost their lives that day,” a JROTC cadet said during the ceremony.

title: Iowa State University faculty-student team develops website for AI tools
description: Iowa State University faculty and students who have spent their time diving into the incredibly fast-paced world of artificial intelligence tools turned their efforts to keep up with the latest news into a website they hope helps others do the same. ISU computer science professor Wei Le and a team of graduate students have already […]
text:
Iowa State University students and faculty have created a website hub for the latest AI tools and updates. (Photo via Getty Images)Iowa State University faculty and students who have spent their time diving into the incredibly fast-paced world of artificial intelligence tools turned their efforts to keep up with the latest news into a website they hope helps others do the same.
ISU computer science professor Wei Le and a team of graduate students have already seen more than 150,000 visits to Todaysai.ai, a website the group created and maintains to serve as a hub for news on new AI tools as they launch and receive updates and for educational resources on how to run certain programs.
Le and her students first came up with the idea while trying to keep pace with the day-to-day changes in AI tool development, she said, from new and better programs being released to established resources expanding into new areas. It would also be helpful for other classes touching on AI, they figured, as the technology makes its way further into academic spaces.
Each week in Le’s advanced AI topics course she and students would spend around half an hour discussing the newest tools and their capabilities, which computer science Ph.D. student Anwar Zahid said was his favorite part of the class.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We actually found there’s a need for students to really catch up (on) what’s happening today in AI world, and we also noticed that there are lots of news out there every day,” Le said. “However, we didn’t find a place where we can integrate all the current AI tools and the knowledge in one place, so this is where we think we should build that website.”
Zahid said he was excited to hear the news from Le, and the group put their own personal time — and sometimes their own money — into creating and maintaining the site. Also included on the site is a section housing video demonstrations of how to use certain AI products for different needs, something Le is hoping to expand with additional resources from product developers and user requests.
Since the site launched in May, it states it’s seen more than 151,000 visitors.
Todaysai.ai is a website developed by Iowa State University faculty and students to bring together the latest AI tools and updates. (Screenshot from todaysai.ai)
“The goal here is to put all the most recent AI tools into one place, and we can organize them very well and make it accessible to the general public,” Le said. “We also hope this is a trustable website.”
The group utilizes AI in gathering relevant information and updating the website on a consistent schedule, with students or Le ensuring the accuracy of information before it’s live. They also designed the site so it’s easy for anyone to access and use, with demos, illustrations and descriptions available for different tools whenever possible.
As demand for AI programs increases throughout public spaces, not just academic and technological ones, Le said she wants the website to be a place where people go to learn about the latest innovations in financial software, personal assistance, coding tools and other applications.
The students themselves, as well as their peers and teaching assistants for other courses, are using the site in their own daily lives and work. Md Mahbubur Rahman, another Ph.D. student involved with the site, said he’s used it to check out new tools as they come out and introduce them to his students.
Teaching assistants have been especially thankful for the demos page, as they can show the videos to their students rather than trying to explain how different tools work.
With the site up and running, Le said she’s applying for grants and looking for collaboration opportunities to expand the site more and give the students working with her more support. Le said she hopes the site can help create a learning community around AI, where users and developers can interact and get the newest information as it comes out.
“I hope this is a platform that bridges the builders of AI and also the user of AI,” Le said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump wants Bombardier out of US market. In CT, the company employs hundreds
description: The president wants the Canadian jet maker out of the US market. But in CT, the company has a large operation and skilled training programs.
text:
Ongoing trade tensions between the United States and Canada hit a new level this week, with President Donald Trump calling for a ban on sales by one particular Canadian jet maker with a significant U.S. footprint — especially in Connecticut.
On Labor Day, shortly before new retaliatory tariffs from Canada were set to go into effect, the president threatened to stop sales of jets made by Montreal-based Bombardier, arguing that the company’s U.S. sales should be halted until it moves its manufacturing stateside.
“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank’.”
Bombardier quickly responded with its own statement, pointing out that it’s already active in the U.S. “Bombardier aircraft create tens of thousands of U.S. jobs through the company’s growing American footprint as well as within its supply chain made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states,” the company said.  
That includes Connecticut, a key hub for the company’s maintenance operations and workforce development efforts. 
According to Bombardier, the company supports close to 300 jobs in the state, many through its Bradley International Airport service center, a 140,000 square foot facility that provides aircraft inspections, repairs and other technical support for Bombardier jets flown on the East Coast.
The company has long been involved in the state’s aerospace industry. Local business groups and economic development organizations call Bombardier a key partner. 
“They’re a valued Connecticut company, and we’re glad we have the opportunity to support them,” said Tommy Hyde, the chief of staff for AdvanceCT, which focuses on business recruitment and retention efforts for the state.
As the state faces broader disruptions from the ongoing trade war with its biggest international trading partner, some Connecticut businesses say the president’s criticism adds to already deep concerns.
Dustin Nord, the director of the Connecticut Business and Industry Association’s Foundation for Economic Growth and Opportunity, said even if criticism is leveled at one specific company, it can affect a much broader group.
“That’s the hard part with trade more broadly,” Nord said. “In the instances where you’re impacting a Bombardier, a lot of these subcontractors don’t just work for one company; they’re working across many companies.” 
“It’s very difficult to target these types of tariffs, or, or in this case, a company-specific type restriction, without having a broader impact on unrelated things,” he added. 
Bombardier wants to solve a key workforce issue in CT
Bombardier’s presence in Connecticut dates back years, but it’s taken on a broader role recently — training new members of Connecticut’s advanced manufacturing workforce.
In May, Bombardier announced that it was bringing its FastTrack program, which helps aircraft technicians develop the skills necessary for key industry credentials on an accelerated timeline, to Hartford. The program’s launch was the result of a collaboration between the jet maker,  AdvanceCT and CT Aero Tech, which offers its own program for aircraft mechanics. 
According to AdvanceCT’s Hyde, conversations about launching the program took off in the wake of discussions about Connecticut’s aging aerospace workforce and the need to train a new generation of maintenance workers and technicians. 
The organization has supported the FastTrack program by helping Bombardier make connections in the state. “Bombardier is a very large employer, and it’s a workforce solution that helps them as a company grow and retain their workforce,” Hyde said. “It’s an opportunity for their existing employees to upskill, take on more roles and responsibilities, and get jobs.” 
Bombardier is also working with CT Aero Tech, which is part of the Connecticut Technical Education and Career System, or CTECS. Under the current arrangement, CT Aero Tech provides facility space to the FastTrack project, which is run by Bombardier.
In an emailed statement, CTECS said the company is an important collaborator in the state, adding that the partnership “provides valuable career opportunities and connections for our airframe mechanic and aircraft maintenance students.” 
CT officials have defended Bombardier before
The past week is not the first time Bombardier has found itself facing scrutiny from the federal government. 
During the first Trump administration in 2017, the company faced a complaint from rival Boeing, which alleged the Canadian business was violating trade laws by selling its commercial aircraft at below-market prices. The administration agreed with Boeing, proposing a roughly 300% tariff on Bombardier jets. 
At the time, Connecticut-based Pratt & Whitney was working with Bombardier to build engines for these commercial jets, known as the CSeries, under an agreement that was first announced in 2007.
The administration’s challenge raised concerns among the state’s congressional delegation, with Rep. John Larson, Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Sen. Chris Murphy sending a letter defending Bombardier, arguing the engine deal was “critically important to Connecticut,” and asking the U.S. Commerce Department to “refrain from taking action that will endanger the many jobs in Connecticut that depend upon Bombardier.”
Pratt & Whitney did not respond to a request for comment about the deal, which ended in 2018 when Bombardier finalized the sale of a majority stake in the CSeries project to Airbus. 
In a statement provided to the Connecticut Mirror, Blumenthal said he is once again concerned about the impacts that federal policies, in this case the new tariffs, could have on the state’s aerospace industry.  
“Trump’s threat of a Bombardier ban is just one more example of his self-centered scattershot approach to trade relations with Canada,” the senator said. “Bradley boasts a significant Bombardier workforce and we’re fortunate that the company is an important employer in Connecticut and subcontractor for our aviation and defense industry.”
Aerospace is a key industry in Connecticut. According to AdvanceCT, in recent years the state has ranked first in the nation for its concentration of aerospace and defense manufacturing jobs. Aerospace products and parts accounted for 33% of the state’s exports in the early 2020s.
Because of this, potential disruptions to the industry, like those raised in recent months by the escalating tariffs, are cause for some concern. “We’ve heard from our employers. The majority of employers find that tariffs will negatively impact their business in the year to come,” Nord said. 
Still, the exact impacts of the U.S.-Canada trade war on Connecticut will depend on how long the dispute lasts. While tensions have hit industries like construction, and have raised uncertainty for businesses since last year, some impacts could be longer-term, according to Nord.
Business groups and other organizations say they’re keeping a close eye on things, given how important Connecticut’s trade relationship with Canada is.
“We support a lot of jobs because that trade exists, and while we don’t do all of the elements of the manufacturing process in Connecticut, that doesn’t mean that we don’t have a lot of net jobs in Connecticut,” Nord said. “We gain by having that strong relationship with our trading partners like Canada.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Two Nebraska officials join campaign against online-sports-betting ballot initiative
description: A group announced a campaign to oppose two statewide ballot measures that seek to legalize and regulate online sports betting in Nebraska.
text:
Ron Brown, a former Husker football coach, speaking at the Nebraska capitol on Sept. 10, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN —  A group announced a campaign to oppose two statewide ballot measures that seek to legalize and regulate online sports betting in Nebraska.
Save Nebraska Sports, which includes State Auditor Mike Foley and Treasurer Joey Spellerberg, held a press conference Thursday at the Nebraska Capitol to begin efforts to inform Nebraskans that the group behind it isn’t looking out for their best interests. 
Ron Brown, a former Husker football coach, said gambling and online betting remind him of what “the cat dragged in” when he was younger. 
“It was often a bloody rat. The bloody rats, to me, in this issue, are the consequences of gambling and online sports betting. The sharp claws of these endeavors have sadly dragged in the filth and disease of greed,” Brown said. 
Foley, Spellerberg, Brown and Nebraska Family Alliance Executive Director Nate Grasz argued that the new initiatives would undermine the integrity of college sports in the state. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The group behind the ballot initiatives is called Tax Relief Nebraska. One measure, if approved, would amend the section of the state constitution that voters amended in 2020 to legalize gambling and casinos at licensed racetracks to also allow online sports wagering at those locations. 
The state’s six licensed racetracks, sometimes called racinos, are in Grand Island, Ogallala, Lincoln, Omaha, Columbus and South Sioux City.
Tax Relief Nebraska’s officials have said the initiative would generate “new revenue for local communities and millions of dollars in property tax relief.”
But Foley said Nebraskans will be scammed by a “false promise of property tax relief” because the tax revenue generated in would be “pennies” compared to how much money will be going to FanDuel and DraftKings, which are based out of state. 
The other would amend three existing state laws to define and provide regulation of online sports betting for someone within Nebraska at the time of the wager. Computer servers used to host online sports wagering platforms would need to be located within Nebraska, and gaming operators could conduct wagering through no more than two platforms at one time. The Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission would need to adopt rules and regulations by June 1, 2027, if voters approved the measures. 
Grasz read a statement from former Nebraska football coach Tom Osborne about his opposition to the measure. Osborne wasn’t in attendance. 
This isn’t the first time that Huskers have been involved in political efforts — former Nebraska volleyball middle blocker Rebekah Allick and five Nebraska softball players appeared in a political ad for a successful 2024 ballot initiative that banned abortions after the first trimester in the state constitution, with exceptions for the life of the mother, rape and incest.  
The general election is Nov. 3.
