He was 50.  Vanderhoff joined WLKY, where he was part of the newsroom for about a decade, in 2014. Before that, he worked at numerous outlets, including the Louisville Courier Journal. He had a […]
text:
Louisville journalist Mark Vanderhoff loved spending time outdoors. He died Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo via Everloved.com)Long-time Louisville reporter and anchor Mark Vanderhoff died Friday after a nearly two-year battle against a form of brain cancer, glioblastoma. He was 50. 
Vanderhoff joined WLKY, where he was part of the newsroom for about a decade, in 2014. Before that, he worked at numerous outlets, including the Louisville Courier Journal. He had a reputation as a trusted political journalist in Frankfort and a friendly member of the press corps. 
“Mark Vanderhoff was an exceptional journalist. But his true legacy is found in the qualities no resume can fully capture: his courage, kindness, curiosity, optimism and unwavering willingness to serve others,” a WLKY article said. “Mark was dealt a devastating hand, but he fought brain cancer with positivity and faith. Everyone who had the privilege of knowing him is better because of it.”
Vanderhoff was diagnosed with a brain tumor in late 2024. 
Vanderhoff’s journalism career began at Trinity High School in Louisville, where he was part of the staff for the school newspaper and yearbook. He then attended the University of Kentucky and served as the editor-in-chief of the student newspaper, the Kentucky Kernel. 
According to his obituary, Vanderhoff is survived by several family members including his wife, Sheila and two children, Lucy and Chase. A private funeral service will be held Saturday, followed by a celebration of life at Vanderhoff’s home. 
Vanderhoff was also in the esteem of those he covered. Republican Attorney General Russell Coleman said on X that Vanderhoff “understood journalism was about people and he treated those people with fairness and compassion.” 
“Mark helped bring the work of the Kentucky General Assembly into Kentuckians’ homes, helping people understand the decisions that affect their lives,” the Senate Republicans said on X. “We appreciated the care he brought to that responsibility. Just as much, we appreciated the person we got to work with along the way.” 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, a former state senator, said on X Vanderhoff “cared just as deeply about Kentucky as he did his reporting.”
“He brought compassion, fairness, and dedication to his work, and truly changed our communities for the better,” McGarvey said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas officials speak of importance of passing down 9/11 lessons
description: Standing before members of the military, law enforcement officers and others, Arkansas’ leaders spoke Friday of the importance of educating the next generation about Sept. 11 as they marked the terrorist attack’s 25th anniversary at the Arkansas Capitol. “As the years tick past, there are going to be more and more Americans who have no […]
text:
Attorney General Tim Griffin speaks at a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Standing before members of the military, law enforcement officers and others, Arkansas’ leaders spoke Friday of the importance of educating the next generation about Sept. 11 as they marked the terrorist attack’s 25th anniversary at the Arkansas Capitol.
“As the years tick past, there are going to be more and more Americans who have no memory of 9/11. For them, that day is a blank slate,” said Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. “It’s up to us, the ones who do remember, to remind the next generation why this day is so important in our nation’s history.”
Sanders, 44, was a student at Ouachita Baptist University, and was in a political science class when the attacks began. Her father, Republican Gov. Mike Huckabee, and mother Janet Huckabee were at a conference out of state when the attacks began.
“I’ll never forget trying and failing to call my parents while they were being hustled into the safe room. It was a fear that was felt by millions of Americans all across our country,” Sanders said.
25 years later, Asa Hutchinson reflects on Sept. 11 attacks

Nearly 3,000 people died when hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a rural field in Pennsylvania. The victims included Arkansans such as Sara Low, a flight attendant and Batesville native, and Nehamon Lyons IV, a Pine Bluff native who was killed in the Pentagon attack.
Attorney General Tim Griffin, a Republican who is also a member of the Arkansas National Guard and was in the Army Reserves at the time of the attacks, had moved back to Arkansas from Washington the month before, he said. He heard the news on the Today Show, which was on in the other room.
“I was getting ready for work, and I heard in the background that a plane had hit a building, and they talked about it being an accident,” Griffin said. “And then I heard them describe the second plane, and that’s when I walked from the other room, in front of the television, and it all started unfolding, not as an accident, but as an intentional attack.”
Members of the military present the flags during the playing of the national anthem during a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks in Little Rock. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
Sept. 11 was his generation’s “collective moment,” he said — referring to how many in his parents’ generation could remember exactly where they were when President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in 1963. Griffin said he visits the Pentagon once every month or so, but it’s been so long since the attacks that there are times that he doesn’t think about Sept. 11 when he’s there.
Like Sanders, he said teaching Americans too young to remember what happened on Sept. 11 was imperative.
“We are so much stronger together when we can— We may not agree on everything, but when we can find that common ground,” Griffin said, calling it one of the three great lessons Sept. 11 taught him. “If you want to find common ground with the next generation, you better make sure you’re telling them about 9/11, contextualizing it.” 
America is the only nation with “the capability, the reach, the strength to do what needs to be done around the world,” and if it doesn’t lead, “bad actors” will step up to fill the vacuum, Griffin said.
“The world without an active, strong, leading United States is a more dangerous world,” Griffin said. “When America is engaged overseas — not isolationist, but engaged overseas — we are safer here. I used to say to people, ‘You want to fight in Baghdad or Boston?’”
Both Sanders and Griffin implored listeners to remember the sacrifices of the first responders who lost their lives during and in the aftermath of the attacks, as well as those of the members of the military who joined in America’s military response in the months and years that followed.
North Little Rock’s assistant fire marshal, Capt. Gary Williams, also spoke of survivor’s guilt, and urged people to call their loved ones as much as they could.
Arkansas students learn about 9/11 attacks through oral histories 

“If you, by chance, have those loved ones that you haven’t talked with in a little while, pick up the phone and tell them, “All I wanna do is hear your voice,’” he said.
Before a final prayer, a lone military band bugler stood and played Taps, which is played at the end of the day on military installations and at military funerals, the sound echoing in the Capitol rotunda.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Auburn University faculty protest Board of Trustees’ dissolution of university senate
description: AUBURN — Auburn University’s Board of Trustees dissolved its faculty senate in June with little notice to faculty in order to comply with a state law that does not apply to the flagship university.  On Friday, more than 100 faculty and community members gathered outside the trustees’ meeting to protest the decision and warn that […]
text:
Auburn University associate professor Heidi Hausse, right, speaks with protesters outside the Auburn University Hotel as the university’s Board of Trustees meets on Sept. 11, 2026 in Auburn, Alabama. Faculty, staff and community members protested the abolition of the faculty senate and changes to the curricula. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)AUBURN — Auburn University’s Board of Trustees dissolved its faculty senate in June with little notice to faculty in order to comply with a state law that does not apply to the flagship university. 
On Friday, more than 100 faculty and community members gathered outside the trustees’ meeting to protest the decision and warn that it could have broader consequences. 
“These are the voices for people coming from many parts of the Auburn family. They are current and emeritus faculty. They are students and alumni. They are staff and administrators. They are community supporters,” said Heidi Hausse, a history professor and one of the organizers of the protest.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The two unions on campus – United Campus Workers (UCW) and the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) – asked to read a declaration of concern at the board meeting, but were told that their request was “not supported.”
The declaration had over 600 signatures of support from the broader Auburn community as of Friday morning. 
Auburn’s decision came a few months after the Alabama Legislature passed HB 580, putting limits on the powers of faculty senates. However, that bill specifically exempted Auburn and the University of Alabama, both of which have standing in the state constitution.
Tracy Witte, one of the organizers and a professor of psychology, said the dissolution of the faculty senate – called the university senate at Auburn – felt like a message that faculty was no longer part of the Auburn family. Witte was a university senator from 2015 to 2021. 
“I always thought faculty were part of that family,” she said in an interview Wednesday. “It’s just the faculty that don’t have a representative body anymore. Why is that? Are we not part of the Auburn family?”
Auburn University President Christopher Roberts speaks at the board of trustees meeting on Sept. 11, 2026, at the Auburn University Hotel in Auburn, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Other groups on campus have a representative body – undergraduate and graduate students, and staff. Auburn trustees replaced the faculty senate with the Presidential Academic Advisory Council (PAAC), which will not be independent from the board or university president and will serve a strictly advisory role, according to university policy. 
Auburn’s president will appoint some members of the council, while others will be elected from faculty at each school. The president can appoint faculty or non-faculty members until each college has equal representation. 
Hausse said the advisory council, while advertised as faculty-led, consists mostly of appointed members, and that administrators have emphasized that the council is not a representative body like the university senate. 
“The upper administration has made clear not only are more than half of its members appointed instead of elected, but even its elected members should not be understood as representatives, and we should not use the word representative to refer to those members,” Hausse said.
After recognizing the appointed executive positions of the council at the trustees meeting on Friday, Auburn University President Christopher Roberts said that he is looking “forward to a very constructive and productive partnership with you and the other faculty members that will soon be elected.”
‘Climate of fear’
Auburn resident Jim Newton protests outside the Auburn University Hotel as the university’s Board of Trustees meets on Sept. 11, 2026 in Auburn, Alabama. Faculty, staff and community members protested the abolition of the faculty senate and changes to the curricula. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)
The dissolution of the faculty senate is the most recent action that organizers said have contributed to a “climate of fear” at Auburn over the last year. 
“There’s a lot of fear on campus. People who don’t want to publicly express disapproval of what’s happening,” Witte said. 
Multiple university employees were fired following the death of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk last September for social media posts condemning the commentator’s rhetoric. The firings were celebrated by Alabama Republican politicians like U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who coached football at the university in the early 2000s.
Some of the terminated employees sued the university for violating their First Amendment right to free speech.
Witte said Friday that faculty at the protest are the “front runners in terms of sticking our necks out.”
“This is a peaceful demonstration. Everything that we’re doing is legal. We are safe,” Witte said. “So that the many, many people across campus who right now are like, ‘I think this is terrible, but I’m not going to say anything,’ feel more comfortable for the future.”
New core curriculum
Auburn University professor Konrad Patkowski protests outside the Auburn University Hotel as the university’s Board of Trustees meets on Sept. 11, 2026 in Auburn, Alabama. Faculty, staff and community members protested the abolition of the faculty senate and changes to the curricula. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)
The board also mandated two new classes for all Auburn students at the June meeting, but the curriculum will not be totally created by faculty. The board will have final say on the curriculum. 
Kate Craig, a history professor at Auburn, said in an interview Wednesday that eliminating faculty expertise from curriculum creation harms students.
“It’s not a problem with the idea that U.S. history and civics aren’t valid subjects to teach. Of course they are, but what has fundamentally happened in this policy is that the board has radically restructured the core curriculum at Auburn,” Craig said. 
Vini Nathan, the university’s provost, said at the trustees’ work session Thursday that one of the two new mandated courses – U.S. History and Civic Leadership – will be required for all incoming freshmen in Fall 2027, and both will be required by Fall 2028. 
“We just want to let our faculty lead that, and we want to be able to bring it forward to the board,” Nathan said. “This is in terms of the board directive and in terms of our timeline. This was specific guidance that we got from the board.”
Students will have to take the classes while also meeting all other core curriculum requirements.
“Essentially, they said that we had to do this, and then they told us we had to figure out how to do it,” Craig said.
The board will have final approval for the new courses. 
Hausse said Friday she is worried that the advisory council’s presentation will be focused on board approval instead of maximizing student learning.
“Imagine sitting there thinking instead of, ‘What is the best way that we can teach students about something? What’s the best way that we can broaden their horizons when they come to Auburn?’” Hausse said. “Instead, you’re sitting there thinking, ‘Will the board say yes to this? Is this what the board wants?’”
She said at the protest that political appointees, like the board members, controlling curricula restricts students’ freedom to learn. 
“You have people who are furthest from the classroom curriculum designed in the subject area of a subject saying all students must take this thing,” Hausse said. “How is that good for students? How does that suggest they will get the best education?”
The protest on Friday, Craig said, was not about the faculty losing control or representation. It was always an advisory position, but she said the expertise of Auburn’s faculty has been left out of decisions that will impact every student.
“This is about completely sidelining our expertise and our care and attention to Auburn. I hope that more people recognize, as a result of Friday, that these policies are a bad thing for everyone, that this will have the effect of devaluing students’ degrees,” Craig said. “In the end, thinking about my students. That is really what motivated me because I think that they deserve better.”

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Frustrations, remorse and pain surface on 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 attacks
authors: Ashley Murray, Shalina Chatlani, Shauneen Miranda, Ariana Figueroa
text:
Powerful U.S. officials past and present faced families, survivors and first responders Friday at ceremonies to honor the 25th anniversary of the day 2,977 Americans died in terrorist attacks in Virginia, New York and Pennsylvania.At the Pentagon, Condoleezza Rice, who was serving at the time under President George W. Bush as national security advisor, told the crowd she wanted to share something “deeply personal.”“Those of us in authority on that day did not see the nature of the danger in time to prevent the attack of 9/11. We did what we knew to do, but by definition, it was not enough. … I will always carry deep personal remorse for the pain that you, the families of the fallen, still feel, and for the trauma that our country endured,” she said.Speakers at all three Sept. 11 milestone anniversary events recounted stories of courage and loss as people found themselves in an unimaginable circumstance. Some also flared with frustration at what they say is a lack of justice for those who planned the attacks.

 







An American flag hangs down the side of the Pentagon, Sept. 11, 2026. The flag was unfurled during a sunrise ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. (Photo by Air Force Staff Sgt. Madelyn Keech/Department of Defense)

President Donald Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, speaking at the memorial service for the 184 people who died when the hijacked United Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, highlighted the anniversary as a justification for their stagnant war with Iran. That nearly seven-month-old conflict has killed 18 U.S. service members, injured over 700 more and taken the lives of thousands of civilians across the Middle East.“We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today. We don't have a choice,” Trump said. “There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win. We will always remember the victims and the families of September 11, 2001, very famous date, unfortunately.”Hegseth told the crowd, which was only open to victims’ families, survivors and their families, that Americans were “ignorant of the Islamist threat” 25 years ago.“Every day, enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home, but we are ever vigilant,” he said, adding that the U.S. has killed Iran’s leaders and put their Navy “at the bottom of the sea.”The deeply unpopular war has continued, despite early promises from Hegseth and Trump that it would not morph into the prolonged Middle East conflicts that followed the Sept. 11 attacks.‘No justice’At the site in Lower Manhattan where the World Trade Center’s twin towers once stood, families read names of the 2,753 victims who died inside the towers, on the ground and on the two hijacked airliners, American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175.

 







Two large American flags hang within The Oculus in the World Trade Center in downtown Manhattan on September 11, 2026. (Shalina Chatlani/ Stateline)

Terry Strada, widow of the late Tom Strada, who died in the north tower, slammed recent presidential administrations of both parties for not holding Saudi Arabia accountable for allegations that the kingdom’s officials knew about the attacks.“My husband Tom Strada, you are missed more with each year that passes. But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?” she said to loud cheers from the crowd.“For 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families,” she said.   “President Trump can still change that. Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through. Vice President Vance, thank you for being here today. Please carry that message back,” she said, again receiving loud cheers.Vice President JD Vance sat in a front row at the ceremony alongside former presidents Bush, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton. Former first ladies Michelle Obama and Hillary Clinton, also a former secretary of state, were seated in the row, as was former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.Neither the Embassy of Saudi Arabia nor the White House immediately responded to States Newsroom’s requests for a response.Painful memoriesFamilies at the site in Lower Manhattan shared memories seared in their minds.Bob Lee, 67, was a firefighter in the Bronx that day. He remembers how many first responders had to gather together to clean up the dust and debris that had settled around the city."When you see the people that were down here, everybody's eyes was … full of soot and dust, and their eyes were glowing like bright red because all the stuff that was in their eyes," Lee said. "It was just a crazy scene."

 







Bob Lee, 67, flew in from Kansas City, Missouri to attend the 25th anniversary of 9/11 in New York City. on Sept. 11, 2026. As a firefighter in the Bronx, he was one of the many first responders who helped clean up the debris created in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/ Stateline).

Lee moved to Kansas City, Missouri, shortly after 9/11. He was 42 at the time and realized he had been exposed to a lot of toxic air.“I told them I was retiring," Lee said recalling that he knew a lot of his colleagues would get sick. He was a union representative for his unit in the Bronx. “I lost hundreds of those guys. You know, it's crazy … Quite a few friends have died of cancer.”New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani this week announced that his office had released around 170,000 pages of records that had been closed off over the last 25 years on the level of toxic air pollution people were exposed to in the aftermath of 9/11.The records suggest that New Yorkers were misled about the air quality and that officials downplayed how dangerous it was to breathe the air. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, close to 50,000 people, including first responders and survivors, developed cancer in relation to the event. Christopher Santora, then 23, was a firefighter who responded to the attacks and was enveloped in debris as the towers fell. He lost his life trying to save people that day. His cousin Jason Roettger, 56, was chosen to read the names of people who had died during 9/11 at Friday’s ceremony.

 







Jason Roettger, 56, and his mother, Karen Roettger, 83, attended the 25th anniversary of 9/11 in New York City on Sept. 11, 2026. He lost his cousin in the attacks on the World Trade Center and said he was honored to be chosen to read names of people who had died on that tragic day. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/ Stateline).

Roettger said it was an honor to be a part of the event and to represent his cousin. He said he's glad the air quality records were released.“I think everyone that was here in the city, or even in New Jersey, everyone in this area knew the air wasn't good,” Roettger said. “Even though the government said ‘No, the air is fine.’ I think everyone knew that that was a lie.”Wanda Hernandez, 72, lost her daughter Monique de Jesus, who was 28 at the time. She was working at the World Trade Center. 

 







Wanda Hernandez, 72, lost her daughter Monique de Jesus, who was 28 at the time, on 9/11. Her daughter was working at the World Trade Center. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/ Stateline)

Hernandez said Friday she was focusing on all the beautiful moments she had with her daughter before that day.“We went on vacation for my birthday before it happened, like a month before. Yeah. Yeah, we had a good time, you know, and we went to a wedding like a week before it happened,” Hernandez said. “Two weeks, so that was nice. Had a good time. I was a good mother. She was a good daughter.”‘A vast empty space in the side of the Pentagon’Over a 13-minute speech Friday morning at the Pentagon, Rice, who also served as secretary of state later in the Bush administration, painted a picture of administration officials caught completely off guard by the attacks, orchestrated by the well-known anti-American extremist terror network al-Qaeda.“I was at my desk at the White House that day when my executive assistant, a young Army officer, told me that a plane had hit the World Trade Center. ‘What a strange accident,’ I thought,” Rice said.“I called President Bush, who was reading to children at an education event in Florida. He too thought that it must have just been an accident. But within 17 minutes, a second plane hit the World Trade Center,” she continued.What followed, according to Rice, was a whirlwind as officials rushed to secure locations — Bush to Air Force One, Rice and Vice President Dick Cheney to a White House bunker and CIA Director George Tenet to an undisclosed location. Then-Secretary of State Colin Powell was in Peru “and trying to get home.” Those in the White House “Situation Room,” Rice recalled, just heard the “ringing and ringing and ringing” of Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s phone at the Pentagon, where he had been hosting a congressional breakfast. The late Rumsfeld would end up outside assisting in rescue efforts “as his security detail begged him to flee,” she said.“I remember turning to a television screen, and the horror and the shock that I felt. There was a smoking crater, a vast empty space, in the side of the Pentagon.”Fight with hijackersA morning observance program was also held at the Flight 93 National Memorial near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, to mark 25 years since 40 passengers and crew members died when the hijacked United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in a rural field. Families read aloud the names of the victims during the ceremony.Members of Flight 93 fought with hijackers over Western Pennsylvania and forced the flight to crash, which prevented the hijacked aircraft from hitting the intended destination of the U.S. Capitol.Others expected to speak Friday afternoon included Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.Gordon Felt, brother of Edward Porter Felt, one of the 40 people who died on Flight 93, was set to speak, along with retired United Airlines Capt. Morrie Wiener, who piloted Flight 93 prior to the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service.Mullin ties mass deportation to Sept. 11Outside of the Department of Homeland Security headquarters in Washington, D.C., Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin used the anniversary to promote the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, and said that lack of cooperation from so-called sanctuary cities is what could lead to another 9/11.“It’s a safe haven that incubates terrorist activity and it doesn’t just stay local,” he said.He specifically called out Democratic-led cities of Seattle, Boston and New York City.“It shouldn’t be political,” he said. “When we start looking at the 25th anniversary, if there’s anything we should agree on, it should be that. Why should the Department of Homeland Security be controversial? We’re taking care of your backyard.”Immigration enforcement agencies under the department have been roiled in scandal and carried out alleged illegal orders since Trump’s second term began. The events have included allowing deportation flights to take off against a judge’s order, erroneous deportations of individuals with legal protections, and the killing by immigration agents of two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, of Minneapolis. The latest scrutiny of the department comes after a $20 million no-bid contract was extended in Kentucky to outfit agents with electric shock gloves.Courage and ‘selfless service’Despite the lasting pain, speakers Friday noted that relatives of those killed in the attacks found ways to move forward and persevere.Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine at the Pentagon said the milestone anniversary was not only about remembering those lost, but “it is also a story of great American courage, selfless service, and those who've made the choice to carry those memories forward.” “The courage of those extraordinary Americans in Pennsylvania, in New York, and right here on these hallowed grounds, did not end when the smoke cleared and the fires went out, because survivors and families have carried it forward through service, through sacrifice, and through remembrance,” Caine told the crowd.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Secretary of State Evnen certifies Nebraska’s fall 2026 ballot after lawsuit-heavy summer
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen has officially finalized Nebraska’s fall 2026 ballot, closing a chapter on a lawsuit-heavy, winding path toward certification. At least nine lawsuits were filed to the Nebraska Supreme Court, either directly or on appeal, against candidates, political parties and ballot measures since Nebraska’s May 12 primary.[...]
text:
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen announces the finalization and certification of the candidates and issues that will be advanced to voters at the Nov. 5, 2024, general election. Sept. 13, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen has officially finalized Nebraska’s fall 2026 ballot, closing a chapter on a lawsuit-heavy, winding path toward certification.
At least nine lawsuits were filed to the Nebraska Supreme Court, either directly or on appeal, against candidates, political parties and ballot measures since Nebraska’s May 12 primary. Some were not resolved until Thursday, the day before Evnen needed to certify the ballot, and two remain pending before Nebraska’s highest court. 
Criminal fraud arrests have also clouded multiple petition efforts.
“County election offices and the Elections Division have done an excellent job verifying petitions and ensuring candidates were properly filed so that we could certify the general election ballot on time,” Evnen said in a statement. “We are confident that all the appropriate checks have been completed and confirmed despite the rather unusual number of issues we faced this year.”
Boxes filled with ballots at the Lancaster County Election Commission on April 24, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
With Friday’s certification, the following candidates and issues are set for the ballot:

92 candidates for federal (U.S. Senate and three House seats) and state-level races (governor/lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state, treasurer, auditor, Legislature, State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents).
48 judges who face an up-or-down vote to remain in office for six more years.
Three statewide ballot measures — two related to online sports betting and the other related to sex-based restrictions for K-12 and collegiate sports.
Another constitutional amendment, referred by the Legislature, on whether to expand legislative term limits.

The first finalized ballots must be sent to military and overseas voters by Sept. 18.
Under state law, any candidates wishing to run a write-in campaign must file by Oct. 23 to have votes cast for them counted. If not, votes will not be reported for candidates not on the ballot.
The Nebraska Examiner will launch its 2026 General Election Voter Guide next week, building on the Examiner’s 2026 Primary Election Voter Guide with additional office-specific, policy-heavy answers for candidates and more details on judges and ballot questions.
Lawsuit-heavy election year
Ten candidates joined the ballot after the May 12 primary, all petitioning to do so. They consist of two nonpartisans for federal races and others for new political parties. Leadership of the parties also had to petition to create the new Nebraska Working People Party (three candidates) and America First Party (five candidates). Others petitioned but did not have enough signatures.
The new parties fought to exist before the Nebraska Supreme Court. The chair of the Working People Party, who is running for U.S. Senate, survived a Democratic challenge to her candidacy, too.
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)
One ballot measure from the Respect Nebraska Voters campaign failed to overcome a legal challenge and will not appear on the ballot, the Supreme Court confirmed Thursday.
The measure, if successful, would have raised the threshold for state lawmakers to tweak voter-approved laws from 33 of 49 lawmakers to 40 of 49 lawmakers and implemented that same four-fifths threshold for any laws seeking to change how petitioning operates in the state. 
The ballot measure related to K-12 and collegiate sports, from the Fairness for Girls campaign, will appear on the ballot, but its ultimate validity to appear is still being challenged. The proposal would enshrine in the Nebraska Constitution part of a 2025 law requiring public and certain private schools, colleges and universities to designate sex-separate athletic teams and sports.
The Nebraska Supreme Court will hear the challenge Sept. 30. The justices initially refused to hear the case. The lawsuit was then refiled in Lancaster County District Court. The issue is whether the group’s petition language was legally compliant, which a Lincoln voter disputes. She says the language led her to sign the petition without knowing what the measure would do.
A Lancaster County judge upheld the validity of the Fairness for Girls campaign this week.
In Nebraska’s capital city, voters will also see three proposed amendments to the Lincoln City Charter. The proposals would limit Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms, align odd-year city elections with even-year statewide elections and let certain residents within a 3-mile buffer around Lincoln city limits vote in municipal elections, excluding bond votes.
The Nebraska Supreme Court said Lincoln city officials must place the issues on the Nov. 3 ballot Wednesday. City officials said they will, and they suggested they might still pursue their constitutional authority to also offer “alternatives” for Lincolnites’ consideration.
In other lawsuits this year:

A Nebraska Democratic Party candidate had to sue to appear on the ballot this spring because she had said she would drop out if she won. The Democratic Party then had to sue to defend its decision not to replace her when she upheld her promise.
The Republican National Committee sued to overturn a state law allowing U.S. citizens who have never resided in Nebraska but have a parent registered to vote in one Nebraska county to register in one county. The RNC lost the case but is appealing.

Petition scrutiny
Petitioning this year generally faced heavy scrutiny as significant allegations of fraudulent signatures plagued at least eight different petitions for five different campaigns, including the city charter effort, all four statewide ballot measures and one failed nonpartisan bid for governor.
Six out-of-state circulators have so far been arrested in the ongoing criminal investigation, which is centered in Lancaster County.
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office’s Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, Evnen and county election officials are calling for legislative changes to the petition process. Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers has called the situation a “sad period in Nebraska history.”
This month has marked the end of two lawsuits filed in 2024 against voters’ approval of the legalization and regulation of medical cannabis. The Nebraska Supreme Court last week unanimously upheld the validity of those ballot measures, over objections from longtime marijuana opponent former state Sen. John Kuehn as well as Evnen and Hilgers. 
And this week, the justices unanimously affirmed the dismissal of another Kuehn lawsuit trying to challenge the constitutionality of the same medical cannabis laws.
2026 ballot questions
Evnen certified three ballot measures for the November 2026 general election ballot, which were assigned a measure number between 440 and 442, at random. An additional question, which the Legislature forwarded to voters in May 2025, will also appear on the ballot.


Legalize online sports betting — Legalize online sports betting if conducted through vendors at Nebraska’s six licensed racetracks, in Grand Island, Ogallala, Lincoln, Omaha, Columbus and South Sioux City. (Initiative Measure 440)
Regulate online sports betting — Define online sports betting and require the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission to adopt any needed regulations, no later than June 1, 2027. (Initiative Measure 441)
Sex-separate requirements for K-12, collegiate sports — Make permanent part of a 2025 state law requiring public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state playing against those schools, to designate sports and athletic teams as male, female or coed. The ballot measure itself would not additionally define “sex,” instead relying on the 2025 law. (Initiative Measure 442)
Legislative term limits — Allow state lawmakers to serve up to three consecutive four-year terms, instead of two consecutive terms. (Constitutional Amendment 1)

Evnen’s office will host public hearings on the three statewide, voter-initiated measures in each of Nebraska’s congressional districts in October.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump administration sues Arkansas over in-state tuition for DACA students, other immigrants
description: The Trump administration is suing Arkansas and asking a federal judge to strike down a 2019 law allowing state colleges and universities to charge in-state tuition to students who have legal permission to remain in the U.S. under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, also known as DACA, among others.  The Justice Department on […]
text:
People gather for a rally to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program in Battery Park on June 15, 2022, in New York City. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)The Trump administration is suing Arkansas and asking a federal judge to strike down a 2019 law allowing state colleges and universities to charge in-state tuition to students who have legal permission to remain in the U.S. under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, also known as DACA, among others. 
The Justice Department on Thursday filed lawsuits against Arkansas, Hawaii, the District of Columbia and Utah. The federal government is suing 25 states total over such measures.
The Justice Department lawsuit said the Arkansas law is unconstitutional and called it “blatant unequal treatment.”
The suit challenges a law signed by former Gov. Asa Hutchinson, a Republican, in 2019 that allowed in-state tuition for immigrants who have lived in the state for at least three years and graduated from a public or private high school in the state.
The law applies to DACA students; those who have work permits or whose parents do; and immigrants from the Marshall Islands. 

Act844complaint 
The measure had originally applied to immigrants regardless of legal status but was narrowed to those three categories. It passed with bipartisan support in the majority-Republican Legislature. The lawsuit comes after a federal judge struck down a 2004 law allowing in-state tuition for some immigrants in Kansas on Wednesday. That law had also been challenged by the Trump administration.
Arkansas’ Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin’s office said it was reviewing the complaint to determine next steps but agreed with the Trump administration.
“We agree with the U.S. Department of Justice that federal law preempts state law in this case, and that this state law should not be enforced,” Griffin spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said in a statement.
Supporters of the law said it was a fair move for students who have been living and going to school in the state and would help the state economically by keeping high-skilled students in Arkansas.
Former state Rep. Megan Godfrey, a Democrat who co-sponsored the legislation, said the Trump administration lawsuit was mischaracterizing the law as something that benefitted immigrants who weren’t in the country legally.
“It’s disingenuous to say it’s a law for ‘illegal aliens,’ and it’s a political stunt,” Godfrey said. “It’s an intentional riling up of a base that is so extreme on immigration issues that they are out of step with a Republican supermajority in Arkansas.”
Hutchinson signed the in-state tuition measure along with another bill allowing the state to issue nursing licenses to DACA recipients. It was also the same day he announced his plans to sign a law cutting off funding for “sanctuary cities” that don’t cooperate with federal immigration authorities.
“We’re a welcoming state, and we want to be able to continue that,” Hutchinson said when he signed the tuition measure.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota loses nickel processing to Michigan
description: A Minnesota nickel mining company has chosen a processing site in Michigan over a site in western North Dakota. Talon Metals announced Thursday it will use a processing site in Marquette County, Michigan, and will not use a former coal mine site at Beulah in Mercer County.  State and local officials gathered in Beulah last […]
text:
A Minnesota mining company considered a former coal mine near Beulah, North Dakota, as a processing site for nickel and other critical minerals but chose a processing site in Michigan instead. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)A Minnesota nickel mining company has chosen a processing site in Michigan over a site in western North Dakota.
Talon Metals announced Thursday it will use a processing site in Marquette County, Michigan, and will not use a former coal mine site at Beulah in Mercer County. 
State and local officials gathered in Beulah last year when Talon Metals announced that it would invest $365 million to process nickel and other critical minerals at the former Beulah Mine site.  
Granville “Beaver” Brinkman, the economic development director for Beulah, said Friday he was disappointed in the Talon decision. 
“We would have loved to have Talon here in Mercer County,” Brinkman said. 
He said work continues to find a new use for the former Westmoreland mine, which stopped producing coal in 2022. He said there could be an announcement in the next few months.
Fertilizer from coal a key part of North Dakota critical minerals processing plans

“We have a lot of interest in Mercer County from a lot of different industries, and we’ll keep trying to pursue each and every one of them,” Brinkman said. 
Talon in January acquired the Eagle Mine and Humboldt Mill in Michigan, which gave the company ownership of an operating U.S. nickel-copper processing facility, an experienced workforce, and technical and operating expertise, the company said in a news release. 
Talon said that gave the Michigan site an edge over building a new processing facility in North Dakota. 
The nickel would come from the Tamarack mine in northern Minnesota. 
Talon officials said construction of the mine in Minnesota would begin in late 2028 or early 2029; with processing in 2030.
That timeline largely hinges on the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources environmental impact study, which includes a public comment period that ends this week. Additional permitting will follow depending on the results of the report.
Plans for North Dakota nickel processing unclear as company also evaluates Michigan site

A Talon Metals press release in July referred to both a Beulah and a Michigan processing facility but whether it would operate both was in doubt. 
Talon was awarded nearly $115 million from the U.S. Department of Energy to support the Beulah nickel processing facility. The company said it is working with the agency to determine the future of the funding award with the decision to locate in Michigan.
In Thursday’s announcement, Talon said it appreciated working with officials in North Dakota. 
Talon “is grateful for the relationships built over the past several years and for the time, engagement, and support provided by those who contributed to the project.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas governor and U.S. Senate candidates to clash at state fair debates
description: TOPEKA — The first political debates of the election season come to the Kansas State Fair on Saturday, putting candidates vying for governor and the U.S. Senate on stage along with the normal fair gigs of wood carvers, pig races and cookie demonstrations.  The days leading up to a 10:30 a.m. debate between gubernatorial candidates […]
text:
Political debates have been held for more than 30 years at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson, sponsored by Kansas Radio Networks and 580 WIBW Radio. Shown here are 2022 gubernatorial candidates Gov. Laura Kelly and Attorney General Derek Schmidt. On Sept. 12, 2026, Sens. Cindy Holscher and Ty Masterson will debate as each vies to be the governor. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The first political debates of the election season come to the Kansas State Fair on Saturday, putting candidates vying for governor and the U.S. Senate on stage along with the normal fair gigs of wood carvers, pig races and cookie demonstrations. 
The days leading up to a 10:30 a.m. debate between gubernatorial candidates Sens. Ty Masterson and Cindy Holscher have been rife with social media zingers and denunciations of political strategies and life choices — and arguments about using notes onstage.


Kansas State Fair Gubernatorial Debate
Sen. Cindy Holscher and Sen. Ty Masterson
10:30 a.m. – 2 p.m.
 
Kansas State Fair Senatorial Debate
Adam Hamilton and Sen. Roger Marshall
1:30 p.m. – 2:55 p.m.
Location: Heartland Credit Union Pavilion, Hutchinson, Kansas
Listen: Broadcast live at 580 WIBW
Online: Live-streamed at 580wibw.com or kwch.com or through the 12 News Connected App


Masterson, an Andover Republican, challenged Holscher’s desire to use debate notes, calling them “her emotional support script.” 
In response, Holscher posted a piece of notepaper with her “notes” for the debate, including questions about Masterson’s “million dollar no show job,” “tax cuts for billionaires” and “Brownback 2.0.” 
An email from Masterson asking supporters to cheer him on Saturday tagged his Democratic opponent as “the most radical progressive leftist that has ever run for governor in the state of Kansas.”
In a video, Holscher said she hopes Masterson appears at the debate: “I know showing up for work is pretty hard for him.” She referred to the Kansas City Star report that Masterson received $163,000 a year leading Wichita State University’s Koch-funded makerspace.
 
Senate race
At 1:30 p.m., Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton and Republican candidate Sen. Roger Marshall will take the stage to tout their stances on national issues, agriculture and other topics important to Kansans. 
Marshall approaches the debate stage under fire for where he spends time and whether he’s been available to Kansans at town hall meetings. He also was the subject of a New York Times article about suing his patients over unpaid debts, with 81 being arrested.
In an August Facebook post, Marshall addressed the number of days he’s spent in Kansas, saying “Kansans deserve to know where their Senator spends his time, and there’s been a lot of bologna from big government woke Democrats about this — so I’ll give you the real truth.”
He reported an average over the last six years of 185 days in Washington, D.C., 130 days in Kansas, 35 days of official travel and 20 holiday/personal days. 
Hamilton, an Overland Park pastor, attacked his opponent’s use of the court to enforce medical bills, writing online, “Medical bills should not ruin lives. We must do better than this.” 
Hamilton appeared on the cable channel MS NOW to criticize Marshall’s actions, which he said show something about Marshall personally. 
“This last year, when he could have made sure that people who are vulnerable had health insurance, he voted not to include the subsidies into what they call the One Big Beautiful Bill, and stripped 31,000  to 36,000 Kansans of their health insurance,” he said. 
Marshall, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, has made few comments about the article, but his attorney who litigated the medical debt told the Times that Marshall was not involved in decisions about warrants, arrests or garnishments. 
Marshall had said little about his opponent, but political action committees and national Republican leaders have criticized what they call Hamilton’s liberal stances as a pastor. 
On X, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz linked to a Hamilton sermon, asking: “Why do Democrats keep nominating ‘preachers’ who reject the central tenets of Christianity? This heretical ‘sermon’ directly contradicts the Bible.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Feds propose some Medicare reimbursement cuts. Oklahoma doctors say it will endanger patients.
description: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is proposing a significant rule change that would mean physicians receive half as much in reimbursement from Medicare for services provided on the same day as an office visit. The American Medical Association and more than 150 healthcare organizations, including the Oklahoma State Medical Association, are[...]
text:
A hallway inside the Clinton Regional Hospital, which closed in 2022. The healthcare provider is now receiving federal support to convert to a rural emergency hospital. (Photo by Jillian Taylor/ StateImpact Oklahoma)The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is proposing a significant rule change that would mean physicians receive half as much in reimbursement from Medicare for services provided on the same day as an office visit.
The American Medical Association and more than 150 healthcare organizations, including the Oklahoma State Medical Association, are calling for CMS to withdraw the proposal, arguing it could endanger patient health.
“We are talking about independent practices, rural physicians, who are bringing patients oftentimes with limited transportation and from long distances, to have several medical services performed at the same time,” said Oklahoma State Medical Association President Dr. Julie Strebel. “Under this proposal, we would no longer be able to do that without an up to 50% decrease in our physician fee structure.”
Strebel is a gynecologist and obstetrician with a private practice based in Oklahoma City. On a typical day in September, five of the 25 patients she treated use Medicare. The health insurance program serves people age 65 or older and some younger individuals with disabilities, and depends on federal support.
Strebel said her practice has never turned away patients for not having private insurance. Still, the proposed reimbursement rate reduction could change how she and other physicians treat Medicare patients.
Instead of addressing a patient’s unanticipated health concerns in one appointment, the change incentivizes multiple visits to the doctor’s office, she said.
“For example, in my gynecology practice, a Medicare patient comes in, and she reports that she’s had some bleeding,” she said. “Instead of just being able to take that patient in my office to the ultrasound room and do an ultrasound and do a biopsy, I have to send that patient potentially home, have her come back on a different day … Because if I do it all in one day, I won’t actually get appropriate reimbursement for her visit.”
She said she worries delaying patient care will mean more people go untreated.
“Anytime that a patient walks out of your office, you’re not certain that they’re going to come back,” she said.
The federal government proposed a similar Medicare reimbursement reduction in 2019, but physicians and stakeholders rallied to stop the measure.
CMS said in a press release that the latest proposal will account for “overlap” between duplicative services and reflects “a broader Administration-wide strategy to create a healthcare system that results in better quality, efficiency, empowerment, and innovation for all Medicare beneficiaries.”
Western Oklahoma podiatrist Dr. Brad Nelson said the insinuation that physicians are over-collecting for the healthcare services they provide Medicare patients is “insulting.”
“I’m a Trump administration fan, but I don’t think his administration as a whole has been really great in health care,” he said. “…[Lawmakers] need to just get off their butts, talk across the aisle and fix things, as opposed to just cutting stuff left and right.”
Nelson has been running a private podiatry practice in Oklahoma since 2004, and he said reimbursement rates for Medicare and Medicaid have decreased significantly over the last couple of decades – by at least 33% for his practice, he estimated.
Nelson said about half of his patients rely on Medicare, and many are from rural areas. His office is based in Clinton and has a satellite clinic in Elk City, drawing in patients from Altus, Hollis, Woodward and parts of Texas. The proposed reimbursement cuts would particularly impact rural patients who have to drive long distances to get care, or patients who rely on others to drive them to an appointment, Nelson said.
Nelson and Strebel both said healthcare decisions are often urgent, and shouldn’t be dictated by a fee schedule. During a recent new patient visit, Nelson said he noticed a concerning spot and immediately conducted a biopsy. It came back as a Stage V melanoma.
“Can you imagine him getting delayed treatment because, you know, Medicare wanted to pay us a 50% reduction?” Nelson said.
He said the proposed reimbursement cut could force some physicians to stop serving Medicare clients completely. He said it has forced him to ask difficult questions about his own practice.
“Do I reframe my practice only to private insurance?” he said. “Do I cut employees?”
Strebel said rural hospitals could also be at greater risk of closure if a decreased reimbursement rate for Medicare is stacked on top of other recent cuts to federal healthcare plans.
“It’s been proven, over and over, that when a rural hospital closes, the population that it serves becomes sicker,” she said. “Not only that, we then are losing a vital business in that community … so the domino effect is huge with all of this. It’s not just about cutting payment to a physician.”
The proposed Medicare policy change is open for public comment until September 14. If the change is approved, it will go into effect on or after Jan. 1, 2027.
This article was originally published by KOSU.

name: National
title: Mixed-status immigrant households expected to lose benefits under new public charge rule
description: New rules going into effect next week allow immigrants’ enrollment in safety net resources to be taken into account for lawful immigration status applications, the latest in the Trump administration’s immigration overhaul. The rules will have wide implications for mixed-status households, as people without lawful status may forgo enrollment in public benefit[...]
text:
A 10-year-old Honduran immigrant who came into the United States as an unaccompanied minor carries her baby cousin in 2021 in Indiana. A new federal rule expands public charge considerations in immigrants’ applications for lawful permanent residency, a policy that could contribute to more than a million people disenrolling from public benefits. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)New rules going into effect next week allow immigrants’ enrollment in safety net resources to be taken into account for lawful immigration status applications, the latest in the Trump administration’s immigration overhaul.
The rules will have wide implications for mixed-status households, as people without lawful status may forgo enrollment in public benefits for their U.S. citizen kids and other dependents out of fear. 
The new U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) guidance goes into effect Sept. 18 and affects people applying for a green card, certain visas or admission into the United States. It rescinds the Biden administration’s 2022 public charge regulations, which restricted immigration officers from considering immigrants’ use of non-cash public benefits, including many benefits for low-income families such as Medicaid, housing programs and food stamps.
Trump administration will make green card hopefuls return to home countries before applying

When an immigration officer determines a person could become dependent on government benefits, that “public charge” is a ground for inadmissibility under federal law.
Trump’s new policy broadens immigration officers’ discretion, allowing them to consider enrollment in non-cash public benefits as public charge. That includes Medicaid, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the country’s largest food assistance program.
Those subject to public charge consideration are immigrants seeking adjustment of immigration status to lawful permanent residency, and includes those who are spouses, siblings, parents and children of U.S. citizens; widowers and widows; foreign medical school graduates; U.S. armed forces personnel; certain workers such as those with advanced degrees, and others.
USCIS specifies certain immigrant groups and classifications that are not subject to public charge. Those include asylees, refugees, Afghani and Iraqi interpreters or such nationals who worked for the U.S. government, people seeking temporary protected status, human trafficking victims, self-petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act, Indigenous people born in Canada who aren’t U.S. citizens, among other groups.
Health research group KFF this summer estimated that between 1.4 million and 4.1 million Medicaid and CHIP enrollees living in a household with a noncitizen could disenroll due to the public charge rule or another immigration-related fear.
Last November, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security acknowledged this, saying that the rule would affect U.S. citizens in mixed-status households. The agency said that federal and state spending could be reduced by almost $9 billion annually “due to disenrollment or forgone enrollment in public benefits programs by members of households that include aliens who may be receiving public benefits.”
It also acknowledged “downstream and upstream” effects for states and their economies.
“For example, the rule might result in reduced revenues for healthcare providers, such as hospitals and nonprofits, participating in Medicaid, companies that manufacture medical supplies or pharmaceuticals, grocery retailers participating in SNAP, agricultural producers who grow foods that are eligible for purchase using SNAP benefits, or landlords participating in federally funded housing programs,” the agency wrote in its proposed guidance.
Immigration activity is taking a toll on children’s health, doctors say

Previous studies found that under the first Trump administration’s public charge rules, families were less likely to apply for food assistance or seek healthcare, a point emphasized by the American Academy of Pediatrics this week.
“When a child is hungry, it can affect every aspect of their development and lead to chronic conditions like heart disease and diabetes, even into adulthood,” said Dr. Sural Shah, chair of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Council on Immigrant Child and Family Health, during a news conference Thursday.
“Without accessing WIC, babies and young children will miss out on critical nutrition supports that are important for brain development in the first 1,000 days of life. Medicaid and CHIP are lifeline programs.”
In an executive order he signed a month after his inauguration, President Donald Trump wrote that his administration would “uphold the rule of law, defend against the waste of hard-earned taxpayer resources, and protect benefits for American citizens in need, including individuals with disabilities and veterans.” 
Health clinicians say immigration activity has been leading to fear and isolation among families, causing delayed care and illnesses to advance among children. They also say those with disabilities and complex needs will be among those hit hardest.
The Autism Self Advocacy Network, for example, said immigrants with disabilities will be disproportionately affected, as they tend to use public benefits more than other immigrants. 
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: VTDigger
title: You can’t take this away from me
description:
A yard flag, a broken tradition at Town Meeting, and one Vermonter's stubborn faith that America can still be worth the trouble.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  You can’t take this away from me.
text:
This commentary is by Henriette Mantel, a Vermont-born writer, actress and producer, best known for playing Alice Nelson in the “Brady Bunch” movies and for co-writing and directing the Sundance documentary “An Unreasonable Man.”
I’m sure not many of you remember the chorus of a song the Gershwin brothers wrote in 1937 — “No, they can’t take that away from me” — but lately I’ve been singing it a lot. Not about a love gone wrong but about our American flag, Old Glory. 
Every time I see a truck drive by with the Stars and Stripes on one side and a flag of our current president — I can’t write his name — on the other, all I can do is sing that song. 
Recently, a man walked past our house and asked why we have the American flag in front. My friend rushed to answer before I could get a word out, “Because her father was a WWII hero, is that enough for you?” The tension of that guy thinking maybe I’m not a true open-minded American because I like the flag blew my mind. Hearing my friend, who I pretty much disagree with on all politics, jump on the guy’s question exemplified what’s going on around Old Glory lately.    
Growing up in Vermont, I loved the annual Town Meeting. While so many of my friends took the free ski day at Stratton, I would go watch from the balcony and feel like I had a say in what happened in my town, even though I was too young to vote. It would always start with everyone saying the Pledge of Allegiance. I couldn’t wait to cast my first ballot. My first presidential vote was for George McGovern. 

READ MORE

Last year at Town Meeting, we didn’t say the Pledge of Allegiance. When I asked why, the moderator said we never did. Huh? Was my memory failing me? I asked my Cemetery Committee, of which I am the proud president, and they all said, “Of course we did. It stopped during Covid.” No one knew why.  
I went to the selectboard meeting to find out. The town office is now in the grade school I attended, so I sat in the same spot where I used to sit in sixth grade. I would stare at that same ceiling for hours, studying the tin graphic designs. My teacher used to hand out the Weekly Reader. It was my favorite part of the week. Reading that paper made me feel like it was a huge world out there and I needed to get out in it. I’d personally fix every injustice I read about. 
Most of the selectboard members thought my pitch to say the pledge was a good idea, but there were problems. I told them it would be fine with me if citizens want to get on one knee or tell me to go pound dirt. Either is an OK choice, but come on, I get to say it, don’t I? They promised to call the Vermont League of Cities and Towns and see what the latest protocol is. 
For me, the pledge has always been about possibilities. After I moan and groan about where our country is today, I still believe that America can return to its values of integrity and freedom and justice for all. It might not happen in my lifetime, but there are glimpses of those values everywhere, even if in today’s world you have to look hard. 
Between people getting on my case about my flag in the front yard and then this debate about the pledge at the Town Meeting, I remembered Bruce Springsteen saying, “The America that I love, the America that I’ve written about for 50 years, that’s been a beacon of hope and liberty around the world, is currently in the hands of a corrupt, incompetent, racist, reckless, and treasonous administration.” He’s right. But he always follows up the depressing truth with a call to action challenging us to take “aggressive, peaceful action” in defending American ideals and democratic norms. Let’s not forget the words of the late civil rights leader John Lewis, who said, “Get in good trouble, necessary trouble, and help redeem the soul of America.”
So where is your fight? Where is your hope that we can reclaim this country? Call me Pollyanna, but I find it every time I look at a flag. Of course you don’t have to do a darn thing. You can just sit and complain for all I care. But do me a favor: Next time you hear the Pledge of Allegiance, whether it be at Town Meeting or a basketball game or anywhere the story is told, look at the flag — or your boots — but please don’t give up hope in this country.
And remember when it comes to Old Glory, “No, they can’t take that away from me.”

name: VTDigger
title: Keep calm and carry on: Burlington airport to host emergency response simulation
description:
Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport will test its emergency systems Saturday during regular airport operations.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Keep calm and carry on: Burlington airport to host emergency response simulation.
text:
Passenger jets on the tarmac at the Burlington International Airport in South Burlington in Sept. 2022. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Ambulances, fire trucks and airport personnel will come together Saturday to test the Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport’s emergency response systems.
“Being prepared for an emergency is a responsibility we take very seriously at Leahy BTV,” Director of Aviation Nic Longo said in an airport press release. “While we hope we never have to put these plans into action, this simulation allows us to work side by side with our fantastic emergency response partners, test our readiness, and learn how we can be even better prepared to protect our travelers, employees, and community.” 
The simulation, required every three years by the Federal Aviation Administration, is designed as a drill to test and improve the airport’s procedures for emergency response, communication and coordination with regional agencies. 
The exercise will include 10-15 ambulances, many fire departments, the Airport Fire and Rescue Team and community volunteers who will be acting out an emergency scenario, Jeff Bartley, the airport’s director of innovation and marketing, said in an interview.
The simulation is planned to start at 9 a.m. and finish at noon.
The exercise is designed to be intense, Bartley said, with colored smoke and actors with heavy makeup to simulate injuries. But it’s also designed in a way that will not interfere with regular airport and community procedures.
“You won’t see fire trucks screaming through the communities,” Bartley said. “They’re staged here, and they’re allowed onto the airfield in timed format.”
Bartley noted that ambulances simulating transport to hospitals in the surrounding area for emergency victims will not use sirens or lights during the exercise. 
The simulation will occur on the opposite side of the airfield so as not to affect travelers.
“They might not even see the exercise,” Bartley said.
The simulation also includes a debrief with all involved parties to discuss aspects of the response that worked well and areas that could be improved, Bartley said. 
There will even be a mock press conference with local media.
“We’re stress testing not just the emergency response but our internal emergency communications,” Bartley said. “We’re not posting on social media like we really would, but we’re internally practicing.”
More than 200 community members signed up to volunteer for the event, Bartley said in the airport press release.
“Their support not only allows us to create a realistic exercise, but also enables other organizations, such as our local first responders and hospitals, to test their own systems and readiness,” Bartley said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: The ballot is free. So why does voter suppression still exist in Mississippi, asks JSU student
description: Voters waited for 2 to 3 hours to cast their absentee ballots Saturday at the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson in October 2020.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.

Mississippi knows how to change clothes. We just have a habit of keeping the same problems underneath them. 
Poll taxes and literacy tests are forms of voter suppression we recognize immediately because history has taught us what they look like. They were blatant. But barriers to political power do not always announce themselves so clearly. Policies change. Language changes. Sometimes the struggle underneath them does not. 
But the fight underneath these tools was always bigger than the tools themselves. It was about access. Who gets political power? Who gets to exercise it easily? And who has to work harder just to reach what supposedly belongs to everyone? 
That question followed me recently while trying to navigate Mississippi’s voter-registration system. 
I am 21 years old, study political science and have done civic engagement work. I have reliable internet access and spend more time thinking about elections than the average person. Yet even I found Mississippi’s voter information difficult to navigate. I moved between different state resources looking for answers and eventually called the Mississippi Secretary of State’s hotline.
Jakari Holland  Credit: Courtesy photo
When I asked about transportation assistance, the representative had to search the state’s website while I waited and ultimately told me she would need to call me back with an answer. 
That made me think less about inconvenience and more about equity. If both the person seeking information and the person responsible for providing it have to search for the answer, how accessible is that information in the first place? 
And if exercising a right requires navigating multiple resources, making phone calls, printing and mailing paperwork or finding transportation to complete a process in person, who pays the price for those extra steps? 
What about an older Mississippian unfamiliar with navigating multiple websites, someone in the Delta without reliable transportation, a first-time voter who does not even know the first step to becoming registered, a student away from home, a working parent who cannot easily make it to an office during business hours?
These people may have completely different lives, but an additional step costs each of them something: time, transportation, technology, information or assistance. 
I am a college student with reliable internet access and a laptop, and I still struggled to navigate it. The ballot may be free, but accessing Mississippi’s democracy can be remarkably cumbersome.
Maybe I noticed the difference because I came to Mississippi for college from Georgia, where eligible residents with state-issued identification can register to vote online. Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee also offer online voter-registration options. Crossing one of Mississippi’s borders, and accessing the same fundamental right can suddenly look remarkably different. 
And once I started thinking about the cost of access, it became difficult to look at online voter registration as an isolated issue. 
Mississippi lawmakers already had an opportunity to remove one of those costs. House Bill 593 was introduced during the 2026 legislative session to authorize online registration for eligible first-time voters. It included state-issued identification requirements, identity verification and county registrar review. 
It died in committee. 
Why? 
One bill dying would not tell us much. Mississippi bills die every year. But HB 593 does not exist in a political vacuum. When a proposal designed to remove an administrative barrier dies before reaching the floor, it is worth examining it alongside Mississippi’s other unresolved fights over access to political power. 
Mississippians have been without a functioning statewide ballot-initiative process since 2021. Our state has prohibited ranked-choice voting in state and local elections. And in 2024, a three-judge federal panel found that portions of Mississippi’s legislative maps unlawfully diluted Black voting strength in violation of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, requiring the state to redraw districts. 
Legislation capable of expanding access dies before reaching the floor. A ballot-initiative process that once gave citizens direct political power remains unavailable year after year. Even redistricting intended to remedy the dilution of Black voting strength has become the subject of continued political and legal fights. 
At some point, resistance to change stops being a sufficient explanation. 
When voter access is repeatedly caught in another committee, another lawsuit, another delay, the cumulative effect can stymie political participation itself. 
At some point, we have to stop examining these decisions individually and start examining the pattern. 
Different policies. Different circumstances. But the same underlying question: Who gets access to political power, and how easily do they get to exercise it? 
And I have a hard time accepting that the answer is simply to wait. 
Change in Mississippi did not arrive because institutions suddenly became generous. Black Mississippians, students, churches and communities organized until maintaining the old system became more difficult than changing it.
Maybe we have spent too much time waiting for political power to come down from the Capitol instead of bringing our collective power to its steps. Mississippi’s history has already shown us what happens when ordinary people make their voices impossible to ignore. 
So where do we start? With each other. 
Mississippi already has the infrastructure for collective power within our communities. What if we built a statewide coalition around a simple demand: accessing democracy in Mississippi should not be harder than it has to be? 
The system already knows how to tell us no. 
Maybe it is time we organize enough people that it can no longer afford to.

Jakari Holland is a senior political science student at Jackson State University and a native of Atlanta. He has described his work as centering on political access, economic disinvestment and a simple question: when opportunity is promised, can the people it is meant to serve actually access it? He is particularly drawn to grassroots movements that transform local communities into sources of collective political power and turn that power into tangible change.

The conditional agreement with project[...]
text:
The Record Hill wind farm in Roxbury, Maine. (Photo via U.S. Department of Energy)After a series of failed attempts to add more offshore wind power to Rhode Island’s energy portfolio, the state utility operator has turned landward.
Rhode Island Energy announced Tuesday that it has tentatively agreed to buy 150 megawatts of wind-powered electricity from an onshore wind farm planned for northern Maine. The conditional agreement with project developer Clearway Energy Group remains subject to pricing negotiations — a sticking point for past proposals on offshore wind projects — and also requires approval from the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission.
Onshore wind projects have not been spared from the Trump administration’s attacks on renewable energy projects. Federal regulators paused permits on land wind and solar projects beginning in July 2025, setting off an escalating legal battle as project developers and Democratic attorneys general — including Rhode Island’s Peter Neronha — sought to overturn the federal freeze. A federal judge in Oregon ordered federal regulators to resume previews under a preliminary injunction issued on Aug. 6. 
The 800-megawatt wind farm planned for Maine’s Aroostook County, near the Canadian border, was not listed as one of the 155 projects subject to the federal permit freeze. In August, Maine utility regulators authorized the onshore wind array, along with a high-voltage transmission line to connect the wind turbines to the regional electric grid. Both project developers were chosen from a competitive request for proposals that included input from Rhode Island, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Vermont.
Maine has tentatively agreed to buy 600 megawatts of capacity from the project, leaving the remaining 200 megawatts up for grabs. Rhode Island’s tentative power purchase agreement, if solidified, would generate enough electricity to power 73,000 homes while advancing the decarbonization mandates under the state’s 2021 Act on Climate law.
“We are committed to helping advance a reliable, safe, affordable, and increasingly clean energy future for our customers, while supporting Rhode Island’s 2021 Act on Climate requirements,” Greg Cornett, Rhode Island Energy president, said in a statement. “The proposed project offers the opportunity to secure a significant amount of renewable energy through a competitive regional procurement while supporting broader efforts to strengthen New England’s energy infrastructure and diversify the region’s energy supply.”
The project marks the largest onshore wind farm in New England, expected to create more than 2,500 construction jobs and $2.4 billion in economic output, according to Maine utility regulators. The benefits to Maine ratepayers — roughly $400 million including the transmission line — also offer stability to the regional electric grid that includes the rest of New England.
The timeline for Rhode Island Energy to finalize a contract agreement and submit the pricing proposal to the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission was not immediately available. 
Rhode Island’s first large-scale offshore wind project, Revolution Wind, remains on track for completion by the end of the year. Once operational, the 65-turbine project south of Rhode Island will provide enough electricity to power 350,000 homes across Rhode Island and Connecticut.
