name: New Jersey Monitor
title: ‘You still live in my heart’; families mark 9/11 attacks with stories, calls for justice
description: Federal, state and local officials joined thousands of family members in lower Manhattan Friday to honor the victims of 9/11 and celebrate those who responded, 25 years after the terrorist attack that shocked the world and changed how Americans view the vulnerability of their nation, and even each other.  The event marks the day hijackers […]
text:
People hold up photos of their loved who were victims of the 9/11 attacks during the commemoration ceremony on the 25th anniversary at Memorial Plaza in Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Federal, state and local officials joined thousands of family members in lower Manhattan Friday to honor the victims of 9/11 and celebrate those who responded, 25 years after the terrorist attack that shocked the world and changed how Americans view the vulnerability of their nation, and even each other. 
The event marks the day hijackers commandeered two commercial airlines and flew them into the twin towers on a bright Tuesday morning in 2001. The attack killed nearly 3,000 people from 27 states and more than 90 counties. More than 700 hailed from New Jersey. 
Another 165 people, including several Garden State residents, lost their lives the same day in a similar attack on the Pentagon and when a third hijacked plane crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. 
“We come every year because this is where they are. Their souls are here,” said Freyda Markow, of Brooklyn, who lost her cousin, New York City Firefighter George Cain, on Sept. 11, 2001. 
Markow carried Cain’s picture and wore a sash decorated with at least a dozen mass cards honoring other responders who have died since that day of cancers and other related health issues. “They lost their lives here. Maybe they didn’t die here, but they lost their lives,” she said. 
“Our responders deserve better,” Markow said. “We were promised more.”

(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Former President George W. Bush, Mike Bloomberg and Vice President JD Vance attend the 9/11 commemoration ceremony on the 25th anniversary at Memorial Plaza in Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Micheal Resta of Lakewood, NJ attends the 9/11 commemoration ceremony on the 25th anniversary at the Memorial Plaza in Manhattan, NY on Sept. 11, 2026. Resta lost his brother, John Resta and sister-in-law Sylvia San Pio Resta who was eight-months pregnant. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
 
In addition to the scores of family members, friends and first responders, Friday’s ceremony included Vice President JD Vance, former presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton and their spouses, including former Secretary of State and Senator Hillary Clinton, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, current and former governors of New York and New Jersey, and dozens of local and state officials representing the region. President Donald Trump was set to attend a ceremony at the Pentagon Friday. 
A statement from the White House noted an entire generation has no “living memory” of 9/11. “The passage of time must never dim what will forever burn bright in the conscience of our Nation. Amid the ashes of Ground Zero, we made a solemn vow to Never Forget — a vow that must be renewed in every American heart, taught in every classroom, and honored in every community across our land,” it read. 
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill arrived around 8 a.m. On Thursday, she had issued an executive order calling for U.S. and New Jersey flags to be flown at half-staff today to mark the anniversary. In a statement, she praised those who responded to the attack.
“As a young Naval Officer that day, I witnessed our country confront unimaginable tragedy, but I also saw the extraordinary courage of the first responders and service members who answered the call. We made a promise to never forget those we lost, and New Jersey will always keep that promise,” Sherrill said in the statement. 
The event began under a cloudy sky, with a drum corps and a choral performance of the Star Spangled Banner by the Brooklyn Youth Chorus. Attendees gathered around a podium near the North Tower and strolled throughout the park, many hoisting placards with pictures of their loved ones lost that day. Other families wore matching T-shirts with the names and faces of those who died. 
Germano Riviera, a survivor of the attack, carried an American flag with the names of all the victims. He said he has attended all but two ceremonies at Ground Zero over the past two and a half decades; during the other years, he went to events in Florida, where he now lives. 
“Something I can never forget is the stench,” Riviera said, adding that he spent some seven months volunteering to help recover remains at Ground Zero. The boots he wore during this time are now part of the collection at the memorial museum, he said. 
The crowd grew throughout the morning, as the clouds drew back, revealing sun and a blue sky behind the skyscrapers that have risen since that day. FBI, police and other armed security personnel ringed the site and were stationed throughout the city, at subway stations, bridges and other potential targets, another legacy of the attacks.
The ceremony included what has become an annual tradition of reading the names of those killed in the 9/11 attacks, as well as the victims of the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center, which killed six people and injured more than one thousand. Music by cellist Yo-Yo Ma and others accompanied the reading. 
‘One betrayal after another’
The names are recited by loved ones, with pauses for seven, one-minute silences to mark the time each tower was struck, when each fell, and when the planes crashed in D.C. and then Pennsylvania. The seventh minute of silence honors those who have died in the 25 years since. 
Many of the readers were children and young adults who were not born when 9/11 occurred. “Even though I didn’t know you or Grandma Ruth, you still live in my heart and I love you,” said one of the readers, who honored his grandfather. 
While most people then living in the metropolitan area, and many others around the country, can tell you where they were when the towers were hit, some 100 million Americans have been born since 9/11, according to the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, which was founded to honor those who were killed and hosts the annual ceremony. 
The memorial created a digital toolkit with information about other events and ceremonies dedicated to keeping their memory alive. 
“We never got to meet you, we’ll always remember you,” said another child whose grandfather died in the attacks before he was born. “You blessed us with the Knicks and this year we got our first championship,” the boy said. 
The readings feature snippets of personal memories, prayers, updates on family news, promises to honor their loved one’s legacy and, occasionally, a political message. Terry Sholty Strada, national chair of the 9/11 Families United, drew cheers during her reading when she called for justice, something many family members say has eluded them more than two decades later. 
“It’s been one betrayal after another,” saidStrada, whose husband Thomas, was a partner at financial firm Cantor Fitzgerald and worked on the 104th floor of the North Tower. She decried leaders who “chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with Americans,” and urged the Trump Administration to take action. 
“You can’t protect yourself going forward if you don’t know the real truth,” Strada, a Florida resident who lived in Chatham, New Jersey, at the time of the attack, told reporters later. Stada said readers were told not to share any political messaging from the podium, but she decided to speak up anyway. 
The lack of answers angers Strada, she said, especially as the nation celebrates its 250th anniversary this year. “For a tenth of our country’s existence the victims’ families have been fighting for justice. Think about that,” she said. 
While the FBI has closed its investigation, investigators in the U.S. and abroad say they have amassed evidence that could connect the Saudi Arabian government to the hijacking of the planes that day. The alleged “mastermind” of the attack, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, who was born in Kuwait and has been held in Guantanamo Bay since 2006, and several co-conspirators are set to face trial in June 2028. 
Today the World Trade Center site is a memorial park where white oak trees surround the museum and the two square, black granite-clad pools where the twin towers once stood. 
Names of the victims are etched on the bronze panels at the edge of the pools, where water smoothly cascades into what were once the buildings’ foundations. The letters form mini-vases where visitors leave bright flowers. On Friday, the panels were also bedecked with small American flags. 
The names include dozens of victims from Monmouth, Middlesex and Bergen counties, but also Patricia Cody from Brigantine, in Atlantic County, Deepa Pakkala of Stewartsville, in Warren County, and a handful of residents from Burlington, Gloucester and Sussex counties. New Jerseyans from 17 of 21 counties lost their lives on 9/11. 
A woman places a rose on the 9/11 memorial during commemoration ceremony on the 25th anniversary at the Memorial Plaza in Manhattan, New York, on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Judge clears path for 1-year-old girl to be reunited with mother
description: A judge has cleared the way for a one-year-old girl in foster care to be reunited with her birth mother who is scheduled to be deported to Guatemala and currently is in custody of U.S. Immigration and Enforcement. In an order released Friday, Judge Sara Walter Combs, with the Kentucky Court of Appeals, rejected an […]
text:
A one-year-old child will be reunited with her mother before they are both deported.
(Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)A judge has cleared the way for a one-year-old girl in foster care to be reunited with her birth mother who is scheduled to be deported to Guatemala and currently is in custody of U.S. Immigration and Enforcement.
In an order released Friday, Judge Sara Walter Combs, with the Kentucky Court of Appeals, rejected an emergency appeal by the foster parents who opposed the move and argued they had not had sufficient input into the decision about the child they had cared for since shortly after birth.
In an order that provided more information about the case — which had been confidential, under rules of family court — Combs found details of the case have been “misrepresented and distorted by unwarranted publication in social media or otherwise.”
“Mother has suffered hardship, prosecution, incarceration, and the deprivation of her newborn infant for more than a year,” it said.
Further, it said Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson, who is overseeing the case and had ruled in favor of reunification of the child with the mother, “meticulously sorted out the truth of her trauma” in deciding to return the child to the mother only to have her decision “unjustifiably frustrated and delayed.”
And foster parents, the order said, have never had custody of the girl and state laws “do not give any foster parent a custodial interest in children under their care” nor standing, or legal authority, to pursue the case, it said. 
The child had been scheduled to be returned by the foster parents to the Cabinet for Health and Family Services on Sept. 7, which in turn was to give the child to ICE for reunification with the mother before they both were to travel to Guatemala, according to court records. The transfer was delayed when the foster parents filed an emergency appeal last week with the appeals court seeking to block the move.
Lawyers for the mother and foster parents, who are not identified in Combs’ ruling, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Johnson, the judge in the case, has cautioned parties about public comments on a family court case which by law is confidential.
Combs’ public ruling Friday, based on filings with the appeals court that also were deemed confidential, sheds more light on the mother’s circumstances.
It says that she had a “difficult journey” from Guatemala during which she was sexually assaulted, resulting in a pregnancy, which she carried to term after arriving in the United States.
The mother, 20, speaks no English or Spanish, only a Mayan dialect known as K’iche, which is rare enough that few interpretation services are available, the order said.
The mother did not seek medical help and gave birth to the baby alone at home.
The court does not know whether the mother chose to have the baby because of moral convictions, lack of access to reproductive health care or language barriers that prevented her from seeking help, the order said.
After the birth, she took the child to the hospital seeking help and was charged with abuse after officials suspected mistreatment. Combs’ order said the mother’s inability to communicate was a factor in her prosecution and separation from her child.
 She was jailed and released after pleading guilty in July to wanton endangerment but was then detained by ICE because she is undocumented. She currently is at a detention camp in Louisiana and ICE has delayed deportation to allow the mother to reunite with her child, Combs’ order said.
Combs’s order said the “intolerable reality” is that the family will be unable to reunite if the mother is deported without her child, adding the court “will not allow the foster parents to frustrate the family’s reunification when they lack standing; have never had legal custody of the child; and were given notice and opportunity to be heard before the family court.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Democratic Party files another legal challenge to disqualify House candidate
description: The Alaska Democratic Party filed a petition on Wednesday asking a state Superior Court judge to compel the Alaska Division of Elections to disqualify a candidate for the Alaska State House from the November ballot.  That’s after Republican Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom reversed an Aug. 31 decision not to certify two Republican candidates for the […]
text:
A polling place sign at the State Office Building in Juneau on Aug. 15, 2022. (Photo by Lisa Phu/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Democratic Party filed a petition on Wednesday asking a state Superior Court judge to compel the Alaska Division of Elections to disqualify a candidate for the Alaska State House from the November ballot. 
That’s after Republican Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom reversed an Aug. 31 decision not to certify two Republican candidates for the midterm election. She reinstated Jose Tagle, a candidate for House District 22, on Sep. 4, along with former attorney general, Treg Taylor, who is running for governor.
The petition only challenges Tagle’s reinstatement on the ballot, not Taylor’s.     

Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom speaks after being sworn into office in Dec. 2022. Dahlstrom is a former state lawmaker who served as the Dunleavy administration’s commissioner of corrections before joining the gubernatorial ticket. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

The Alaska Public Offices Commission had officially recommended the division not certify the two candidates after finding that they failed to complete campaign finance disclosure reports within the 30 day period as required by state elections law. 
Dahlstrom had initially followed that recommendation and declined to certify Tagle and Taylor. But she reversed that decision on Sep. 4, and later cited an unusual review by the Alaska Department of Law that found gaps in 91 other candidates’ financial disclosure reports.
“I will not withhold certification from two candidates on recommendations that, in light of this additional information, I cannot apply with confidence across the field of candidates,” Dahlstrom said in a statement announcing her decision. “Certification decisions have to rest on a process that can be defended as to every candidate.”
Officials with the Alaska Democratic Party said in a statement announcing the new legal challenge that she “capitulated after apparently receiving outside pressure.” The statement did not include evidence of outside pressure.
“Dahlstrom’s about-face reflects a broader concern about an election system that has repeatedly required voters, advocacy organizations, and political parties to seek judicial intervention just to get clear answers,” the group wrote. “Alaskans should not have to rely on administrative complaints and litigation to simply understand which rules apply and whether the state intends to stick by its own decisions.” 
Dahlstrom’s office and the Alaska Department of Law did not respond to a list of questions Thursday, including the reason for her decision to reinstate Tagle, whether potential litigation risk was a factor, and if there is a legal basis for reversing her initial decision and rejecting APOC’s recommendation to decline Tagle’s certifcation. 
The new legal challenge stems from a lawsuit filed by the Alaska Democratic Party in June, which argues Tagle was ineligible to run in the primary election after he filed a completely blank financial disclosure report with his application to run for the seat. 
Alaska Democrats sue elections officials after they approved candidate who didn’t disclose finances

In that case, attorneys on behalf of the Division of Elections argued that APOC is the regulatory agency that oversees candidates’ financial disclosures and has authority over candidates’ eligibility and compliance with state disclosure laws —  not the division.  
The judge ruled in favor of the division on Aug. 16, saying APOC has the authority to investigate candidates’ financial reports, while the division and the Lt. Governor’s office has the legal duty to administer elections, including enforcing deadlines for financial disclosures.
The court acknowledged that if the APOC fails to investigate, a candidate cannot advance on the ballot or be elected to office. “The law is clear that a candidate who fails to substantially comply with AS 39.50 within the time limits of AS 39.50.060(b) forfeits nomination and election,” Superior Court Judge Josie Garton wrote. 
In the Alaska Democratic Party’s legal filing on Tuesday, the party argues that is the precise situation of Tagle, given APOC’s official recommendation to the division not to certify him.
“There is no legal basis for the division to reinstate Tagle as a candidate now that APOC has concluded he failed to comply with AS 39.50,” they wrote. “If the statute is to have any effect at all, this court must apply it as written and direct the division to remove Tagle from the general election ballot.”
They argue “at the very least” if Tagle wins the general election the court should prohibit Dahlstrom from allowing Tagle to take office. 
Officials with the Alaska Democratic Party called for consistency from the division in enforcing campaign finance disclosure laws. 
“You cannot tell a court one thing, tell candidates another, and then expect voters to trust whatever answer comes next,” said Jenny Marie Stryker, executive director of the Alaska Democratic Party in a statement Wednesday. 
“This inconsistency is embarrassing and a poor example of public service,” she continued. “Whoever comes into office next will have a lot of work to do, because this DOE seems determined to leave a disastrous mess for others to clean up.”
Tagle did not respond to a text message requesting comment sent to a number listed for him on the division’s website on Wednesday. The voicemail box was full and not accepting new messages.
Following the ruling, on Aug. 16, Tagle updated his financial disclosure report with APOC to include his income and business interests. 
When asked why the Alaska Democratic Party did not also file a legal challenge to the division reinstating gubernatorial candidate Treg Taylor, whose case is similar, a spokesperson said it was because the lawsuit against Tagle’s candidacy was already in play.
“It’s because our previous challenge was only in regard to Tagle. So we’re just finishing what we started,” said Jalen Lee by email on Thursday.
APOC investigated and issued an official recommendation on Aug. 27 that Lt. Gov Dahlstrom and the division not certify Taylor’s nomination for governor after he failed to comply with candidate financial disclosure requirements within the state deadline.
Taylor had failed to disclose the names of his renters at several properties in Anchorage, including a rental and extended stay apartment complex, Inlet View Tower. Taylor applied for a waiver, but was denied. 
Taylor disclosed the first name and last initial of renters in July, but has not updated the report with information as requested by APOC.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Amid uncertainty about mail-in ballots, WA leaders say they’re ready for what comes next.
description: While the state’s lawyers fight in court to repel the Trump administration’s repeated attacks against vote-by-mail, Washington’s election officials are drawing up contingency plans for the November election.  Their main message to Washington’s 5 million registered voters: Don’t worry; we have it handled.  If President Donald Trump succeeds in getting new, re[...]
text:
Washington state election officials encourage voters to return ballots via designated drop boxes to ensure they arrive in time to be counted. In the primary, the state tallied a higher number of ballots with late postmarks than prior years. (Photo by Donna Gordon Blankinship/Washington State Standard)While the state’s lawyers fight in court to repel the Trump administration’s repeated attacks against vote-by-mail, Washington’s election officials are drawing up contingency plans for the November election. 
Their main message to Washington’s 5 million registered voters: Don’t worry; we have it handled. 
If President Donald Trump succeeds in getting new, restrictive postal service regulations approved for the 2026 midterm elections, voters will still be able to print a new ballot and envelope if their regular one gets stuck in the postal bureaucracy. 
Those concerned their ballots won’t get postmarked in time to be counted should use a designated drop box, especially if the election is less than a week away. But if you must use the mail, officials say you should hand-deliver it to a post office and ask the postal clerk to stamp your ballot in front of you. Do not deposit your ballot in an old blue mail box that may or may not be on anyone’s regular pickup route. 
The post office isn’t the only concern.
Election officials, law enforcement, fire officials and government lawyers around the state and the country have been conducting “tabletop exercises” for a variety of other situations, from combating rumors on social media to responding to bomb threats and incendiary devices. 
“We have a lot of contingency plans that are written out and documented,” said King County Elections Director Julie Wise, who has been working in elections for more than 20 years. 
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said last week that more than 20,000 mailed ballots were postmarked too late to count and some didn’t arrive until much later because they were left in damaged mailboxes or boxes for which the post office had lost the key. 
By this fall, King County expects to have 100 drop boxes, with no one in the county living farther than a few miles from one, including people living in rural areas. There are more than 580 drop boxes statewide but they are more spread out in less populous counties. State law requires at least one drop box per 15,000 voters, with at least one in each city, town or census-designated location with a post office. They are also located on tribal reservations if requested by the tribe. 
Hobbs says locating more drop boxes around the state is something his department is working on, in cooperation with local governments and the governor’s office. A new drop box map is scheduled to be published on the Secretary of State’s website on Sept. 18. 
Stuart Holmes, director of elections in the Secretary of State’s Office, emphasized that the state has long had a plan for getting ballots to and from people even if they can’t depend on the post office. 
Not only can you print a replacement ballot on the same website where you can update your voter registration, but you can also print a new ballot envelope and tape or glue it together. People who don’t have a computer attached to a printer at home, may need to print their ballot at a public library or vote in person at a county voting center in the days before Election Day. Your county elections office will post locations closer to the election. 
“We have a very resilient system,” Holmes said, adding that the system continues to get stronger every day. “Election officials: We get it done.”
The legal fight
Washington has filed about 75 lawsuits against the second Trump Administration, including three concerning vote-by-mail that Washington is either leading or co-leading. 
“This is a huge priority in our office. It’s a huge priority personally and professionally for the attorney general,” said First Assistant Attorney General Maureen Johnston.
So far, the Trump administration is mostly losing the vote-by-mail battle in the courts. Johnston said the Department of Justice is 0 for 23, for example, in their quest to get access to private information on state voter lists. That doesn’t mean Washington state officials are allowing themselves to be overconfident that federal government interference will be halted before the November election.
“We’re gaming out what could happen and what are the things we need to do in advance,” Johnston said. “You can’t predict what will happen but you want to have given it some thought.”
On Thursday, a three-judge panel in the U.S. First Circuit Court of Appeals denied the Trump administration’s request to lift a lower court’s order that blocked a USPS rule to implement the president’s vote-by-mail executive order. The case will likely be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
Democrat U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell celebrated the decision in a statement: “That’s right! Harm is being done to voters. Disenfranchisement! Thanks to the Appeals Court decision, the court is saying USPS chaos has got to stop.”
The Washington Attorney General’s Office is also preparing to respond to other potentially disruptive actions of the federal government, such as deploying ICE agents near voting centers or ballot drop boxes. 
The proposed new rules from USPS struck down by the U.S. Appeals Court include changes to ballot envelopes – putting bar codes on outgoing envelopes – that Hobbs says would be impossible to execute in time. For example, ballots to soldiers and other people overseas go out 45 days before the election, which is fewer than two weeks from now.
“The USPS is trying to do everything they can to ruin vote-by-mail,” Hobbs said. “This last rule change is very devastating.”
Earlier this month, the offices of the secretary of state and attorney general jointly released a guide for county election officials that outlines how they should interact with federal officials to make sure the Nov. 3 election will be safe, secure and accurate. The advice ranges from what to do if federal law enforcement officers show up on Election Day to communicating about postal service operations and dealing with people trying to seize voting machines or asking for documents.
‘Everyone cares about elections’
Communication is a big part of the state’s election contingency plan, with a focus on combating misinformation online. 
“Nick always says: Don’t believe everything you read. Be smart about it. Use your head. Demand proof,” Johnston said of her boss, Attorney General Nick Brown, a Democrat. 
The truth she hopes people will hear instead is how voting by mail maximizes participation in our democracy. “Voting is one very concrete way for us to exercise our rights,” she said. 
That is not a partisan opinion, Johnston emphasized. “Everybody should be able to vote for whoever they want,” with an emphasis on everybody having that right. 
Hayward Evans, president of the Seattle King County NAACP, says history teaches that the hard fought right to vote isn’t guaranteed. 
“For Black Americans, the ballot never really came easy,” Evans said. “Progress isn’t permanent unless we protect it.”
Instead of making false statements about vote-by-mail, Wise said the federal government could be doing more to help people vote. “Everyone cares about elections,”  Wise said, adding that both Democrats and Republicans doing her job have voiced concerns about the federal government’s actions. “We are all on the same page of wanting to make sure we have accessibility for our voters.”
Cantwell said she and her Democratic colleagues in the Senate are fighting back, against “people trying to weave a lot of distrust into the system.” She didn’t dismiss concerns about election fraud, however, promising that it would be caught and the penalties would be severe, but Cantwell emphasized that the focus should be on getting out the vote. name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Stein honors North Carolina National Guard on 25th anniversary of 9/11
description: The North Carolina National Guard lost 30 members in direct combat operations over the past 25 years.
text:
Gov. Josh Stein honors the North Carolina National Guard on the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu)North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein joined members of the military and first responders for a memorial ceremony on Friday to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks.
North Carolina National Guard leaders welcomed U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross, several members of the North Carolina General Assembly, the Raleigh Fire Department, and the North Carolina State Highway Patrol to honor the nearly 3,000 people who lost their lives that day.
Military leaders and Gov. Josh Stein laid a memorial wreath to honor members of the North Carolina National Guard lost since 9/11 on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
“We reaffirm our commitment to the values that the armed forces defend: Freedom, justice, security, democracy, and peace,” Stein said, standing in front of a mammoth American flag at the North Carolina National Guard Joint Force Headquarters in Raleigh. 
Despite the horrific events of that day, many heroes emerged, Stein said. 
First responders, firefighters, police officers, and ordinary people rushed into danger to save their neighbors’ lives. In the following days and months, people held vigils around the world to support the country. 
“In one of our nation’s darkest hours, we were not alone,” Stein said.
The governor recognized Greensboro flight attendant Sandy Bradshaw, who was on Flight 93, which crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania after passengers and crew fought back against hijackers who planned to fly it into Washington, DC.  He also recognized John Cerqueira, a then-recent graduate of North Carolina State University who helped carry a woman in a wheelchair down 68 stories of steps in the North Tower of the World Trade Center. 
On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, States Newsroom editor remembers the heroes of Flight 93

In the years following the attacks, citizen-soldiers of the North Carolina National Guard were called upon to serve in wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. 
The North Carolina National Guard lost 30 members in direct combat operations over the past 25 years. Boards at the ceremony displayed their photos and names. 
On Friday, family members of the North Carolina National Guard lost since 9/11 laid flowers at the foot of a battlefield cross in remembrance of their loved ones. Military leaders joined Stein in laying a ceremonial wreath. 
Major General Todd Hunt, Stein’s principal advisor on military affairs, said 9/11 was the day that the National Guard and U.S. Army transformed into a combat-effective organization, with more than 20,000 members of the National Guard deploying to serve the country.
“As we reflect on 9/11 right now today, at this moment, there are many emotions and thoughts going through people’s heads and hearts,” Hunt said. “Let us never forget our country coming together and bonding in anger, sadness, and patriotism.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Sen. Rounds’ senior staffer posts image of obscene gesture after report about ethics concerns
description: After allegations surfaced that his work as a state-level lobbyist is a conflict of interest, a senior staffer for a U.S. senator from South Dakota went to social media and posted an image of an actor with a raised middle finger. The senator’s office has not addressed questions about the post. Rob Skjonsberg, of Fort […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, speaks during a Downtown Sioux Falls Rotary event on Oct. 28, 2024. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)After allegations surfaced that his work as a state-level lobbyist is a conflict of interest, a senior staffer for a U.S. senator from South Dakota went to social media and posted an image of an actor with a raised middle finger.
The senator’s office has not addressed questions about the post.
Rob Skjonsberg, of Fort Pierre, is a senior adviser and former chief of staff for Republican Sen. Mike Rounds and has worked on Rounds’ campaigns. Politico published a news story Sept. 4 about Skjonsberg’s simultaneous work in South Dakota as a lobbyist on behalf of companies including Meta, the parent company of Facebook. Rounds, who serves as co-chair of the Senate Artificial Intelligence Caucus, has been involved in legislation and policy discussions that could affect the company.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Shortly after the Politico story was published, Rounds’ sole opponent in the Nov. 3 election, independent candidate Brian Bengs, called on Rounds to support a ban on government staffers and campaign staffers lobbying for corporations and special interests.
“South Dakotans deserve to know that the people who work for them aren’t using public service as a revolving door to lucrative lobbying jobs,” Bengs said in a news release.
Skjonsberg responded that same evening by posting an image on X (formerly Twitter) of an actor posing with a raised middle finger.
“Like you, the nonsense will be forgotten @BrianBengs,” Skjonsberg wrote in the X post, using Bengs’ X username.
Lobbying and ethics
Records maintained by the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office show Skjonsberg has been lobbying in the state since at least 2023 and is registered on behalf of 14 clients this year, ranging from Meta Platforms to farm groups, equipment manufacturers and mining interests, among others.
Experts from ethics watchdog groups quoted by Politico said it’s inappropriate and a conflict of interest for a U.S. senate staffer to simultaneously work as a lobbyist. Rounds’ Senate spokesperson Dezmond Ward told Politico the senator’s general counsel “consulted with the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics, which provided guidance to make certain there was and is no conflict of interest.” Politico also quoted Ward saying “Senate Ethics guidance continues to be followed today.”
Ward sent similar statements to South Dakota Searchlight, adding that “over four years ago, our general counsel worked with Senate Ethics to establish a structure to avoid any potential conflicts of interest,” and Rounds’ office “also implemented additional safeguards beyond what was recommended by Senate Ethics.” Ward did not respond to follow-up questions from Searchlight seeking further information about the structure and additional safeguards he referenced.
X post questions
Searchlight sent Ward multiple messages including questions about whether Rounds condones Skjonsberg’s X post. Ward’s responses did not address the questions about the post. Instead, Searchlight received a reply from Skjonsberg.
“I did not clear the X with anyone. I can defend myself,” wrote Skjonsberg, who often misspells “Bengs” as “Bangs” in his communications. “Bangs has a habit of bullying people and he picked a fight with the wrong guy.”
Skjonsberg offered no examples to support the bullying allegation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A Democrat, Julian Beaudion, was nominated to run in the Senate race against Rounds and Bengs but withdrew last month while accusing Bengs of being part of a coordinated effort — with a group of Democrats who were pessimistic about Beaudion’s chances of success — to push Beaudion out of the race. Bengs denied that accusation at the time, saying “I entirely reject the notion that there was some behind-the-scenes conspiracy.”
Big tech ties
Bengs issued another news release Monday morning calling further attention to the Politico reporting and also to about $200,000 of campaign contributions — later verified by Searchlight — to the Rounds campaign from people and political action committees with ties to tech companies such as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and Alphabet (owner of Google), and to tech-company investors.
Rounds has been active in legislation affecting the tech industry, including being a sponsor or cosponsor of bills that would promote artificial intelligence innovation in the financial services industry, prevent smuggling of American-made semiconductors into China, and boost American manufacturing of robotics.

Bengs accused Rounds of being too closely affiliated with big tech firms, including companies attempting to build data centers.
“He will claim that he represents us, but the money tells a different story,” Bengs said at a press conference where he released the information.
When Searchlight asked the Rounds campaign for a response to Bengs’ statements about Rounds’ ties to big tech, Skjonsberg replied with a written message saying Bengs’ announcement “stinks of hypocrisy and big government socialism.” Skjonsberg also said, in part, “the governor and the Legislature have already put strict guidelines on data centers in South Dakota, and the top of that list is local control.”
Skjonsberg was referencing a new state law that allows the Public Utilities Commission to assess data center companies the cost of regulatory reviews related to their projects, and another new law that preserves local data center regulations while protecting against excessive water use for data center cooling and data-center-caused rate increases for other electric customers.
Skjonsberg additionally defended Rounds.
“I’ve known Mike for almost half my life,” Skjonsberg said. “He is a man of character and faith.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Federal appeals court vacates Trump order extending operations for a west Michigan coal plant
description: For more than a year, the U.S. Department of Energy has repeatedly extended the lifespan of a coal plant in West Olive, Michigan, arguing the power generated at the facility was needed to help address a national energy emergency. However, a three-judge panel at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, in […]
text:
The J.H. Campbell plant in Port Sheldon Township, operating since 1962, was scheduled to close partially in 2030 and wholly in 2040. Consumers Energy, however, announced in 2021 it was moving the plan up by 15 years for May 31, 2025. [ONN photo/Sarah Leach]For more than a year, the U.S. Department of Energy has repeatedly extended the lifespan of a coal plant in West Olive, Michigan, arguing the power generated at the facility was needed to help address a national energy emergency.
However, a three-judge panel at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, in a ruling issued Friday, said it was unpersuaded by the department’s justifications for keeping the J.H. Campbell Coal Plant online, determining that the department had exceeded the emergency authority granted by the Federal Power Act.
“There is no dispute that for almost a century states have exercised authority, preserved by the Federal Power Act, to regulate in-state power plants for the economic and environmental benefit of their citizens,” Judge Cornelia Pillard wrote for the panel. “It is the states — informed by federal, regional, and load-serving entities’ assessments of available supply and reliability needs — that bear the responsibility to plan for and avert reliability risks on an ongoing basis. To that end, states decide which generation resources must be built, expanded, reduced, or shut down.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The panel ultimately vacated the order.
The Campbell plant’s owner, Consumers Energy, announced a plan to retire the facility in 2021. The Michigan Public Service Commission, which oversees energy companies within the state, and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, the energy grid operator for the central United States, each signed off on the plant’s retirement, with MISO determining the move would not violate its reliability criteria.
“The Department’s position would empower it to pick its preferred power sources in Michigan — or, presumably, any other state — and order them to operate without regard to the multiple procedural and substantive constraints built into state reliability planning processes,” Pillard wrote, determining that the department’s emergency authority “is best read to apply where the Department identifies a risk of substantial harm from inadequate electricity supply that calls for immediate action by DOE in particular.”
This is a developing story and will be updated soon.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Embattled charter school in Canton remains in limbo
description: A sign for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy is shown Thursday, Dec. 19, 2025, in Canton.
text:
SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy seemed poised to close four months ago. At a hearing in May, an attorney for the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board had built a case detailing severe fiscal mismanagement by school executives. 
Discussions at several previous board meetings had also exposed serious problems, such as overprojecting enrollment and other questionable business practices. The issues could cost the school its charter.
But the board couldn’t just act on that information. First, it needs a recommendation from the hearing officer. The officer has not acted, and the school remains open.
Under the leadership of a new provost, SR1 CPSA students attend classes in what was once a daycare facility in Canton. Tamu Green, the school’s founder and chief executive officer, said he plans to enroll 200 students by next school year. He reported 98 students at the end of the last school year.
Hearing officer Kim Turner asks questions during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Lisa Karmacharya, the charter board’s executive director, said Thursday she had anticipated making a decision in time for the current school year if the recommendation was to revoke the school’s charter so parents could find another option that fits their children’s needs.
At the May 14 hearing, hearing officer Kim Turner asked Dillon Pitts, an attorney who represents the charter board, and Jamie Travis, an attorney who represents SR1 CPSA, to submit additional findings of fact and conclusion of law within 30 days of completing the transcript. Then Turner would begin work on her recommendation to the charter board. She said the bulk of the work would be analyzing hundreds of documents submitted by the attorneys.
“I will, within a reasonable time, provide a written report and recommendations to the board,” Turner said at the hearing. She later said the parties “could be several months out” from the board voting on her recommendation.
Turner is also director of the state agencies division at the attorney general’s office. The attorney general’s office did not immediately respond to a request from Mississippi Today for a status update on the transcript or on Turner’s work toward making a recommendation.
At the hearing, Travis suggested he might appeal the recommendation, which could delay the process further. Turner said she would include an appeal deadline within her recommendation.
Mississippi Today asked Karmacharya if the board received evidence of whether the mismanagement that put the school’s charter at risk is still happening. She said she can’t comment because of the charter board’s active investigation into the school. 
Depending on the vote, SR1 CPSA would be the first school in the state to have its charter revoked by the authorizer board. 
Dillon Pitts, attorney for the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, right, questions Letitia Johnson, the board’s finance director, during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Management concerns abounded at the school, Pitts said during the hearing. He described conditions that could affect students’ safety, such as subpar health standards and a lack of documented support for students with disabilities. 
The Canton charter school was out of compliance with federal guidelines that ensure healthy and safe food for students, according to Pitts, who referred to a 2026 inspection of the school cafeteria. Pitts presented evidence that seven out of 11 individualized learning plans, or IEPs, were also missing signatures from parents or guardians. These plans ensure school officials accommodate a student’s disability.
Read more: Mississippi may shut down a Canton charter school for severe fiscal mismanagement
Pitts claimed school officials didn’t disclose the use of credit cards to pay for school supplies they bought from Amazon. Backup documentation such as receipts and invoices were not always provided, he said.
The charter board began the process of revoking the school’s charter in December after determining the school had one day’s cash on hand, or $24,000. The charter board had also discussed revoking its charter in December 2023 because school leaders requested money to serve 150 students but enrolled 12. The school overestimated its enrollment each subsequent year.
Tamu Green, CEO of SR1, confers with Dorlisa Hutton, chief operations officer and vice president for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, during a hearing on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Travis argued the school never missed payments and had a bank account balance that exceeded the required reserve amount mandated by the authorizer board. Green also claimed that charter authorizer board staff offered little technical support to the school business manager.
Green made the same claim in May at a town hall meeting he hosted in Canton for parents, staff and community members. He asked parents to advocate for the school ahead of the critical vote to revoke its charter.
Renee Truss, whose grandson is a first grader at SR1 CPSA, attended the charter board’s June meeting and asked the group to keep the school open. She said it offered her grandson the kind of attention he would not get in nearby public schools.
“Understand that there are students that are affected,” she said. “As a parent, we don’t know about the finances and the monies that the school has. But we’ve been recently made aware of the financial challenges of the school. And being made aware of those challenges, we have rallied behind SR1 in our community because we know the difference that it has made.
“At SR1 it appears that the students’ needs are being met.”
On Thursday, Truss told Mississippi Today she still feels the same way. She said she believes the school can endure with community support.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Senate Democrats propose significant changes to Michigan’s automatic power outage credit
description: After severe weather knocked out power for hundreds of thousands of Michigan residents last week, members of the Democrat-led state Senate are introducing legislation to provide Michiganders facing lengthy outages with hourly payments. Sens. Stephanie Chang (D-Detroit), Erika Geiss (D-Taylor), Mary Cavanagh (D-Redford Township), Sue Shink (D-Northfield Towns[...]
text:
Michigan Capitol building. (Photo by Susan J. DemasAfter severe weather knocked out power for hundreds of thousands of Michigan residents last week, members of the Democrat-led state Senate are introducing legislation to provide Michiganders facing lengthy outages with hourly payments.
Sens. Stephanie Chang (D-Detroit), Erika Geiss (D-Taylor), Mary Cavanagh (D-Redford Township), Sue Shink (D-Northfield Township.) and Jeff Irwin (D-Ann Arbor) introduced six bills earlier this week to provide energy customers with credits on their bill based on the amount of time they are without power. 
The proposed change to the state’s outage credit would start at $5 for customers without power for an hour, increasing to $25 an hour for those whose power is out for 72 hours or longer. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The package also proposes credits for individuals who face four or more outages a year, and reimbursements to local governments and to renters whose utilities are covered by their landlord to help recoup the cost of lost food.
“Power outages continue to disrupt daily life for Michiganders across the state, and our communities should not be forced to pay the price,” Geiss said in a statement. “These blackouts disproportionately impact low-income and Black and Brown communities. This injustice is unacceptable, and utility companies must be held accountable to reimburse ratepayers and local governments bearing the brunt of their failures.”
On Thursday, members of the Michigan Public Service commission increased the current outage credit to $44 per day for those who face more than six outages a year. Customers facing outages for more than 16 hours under normal weather conditions, 48 hours under gray skies and 96 hours under catastrophic conditions are also eligible for the daily credit.
The package, which includes Senate Bills 1170–1175, was referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Environment for further consideration. An identical package of bills was introduced by lawmakers in the Republican-led Michigan House in 2025 and remains sitting in the House Energy Committee.
Michigan’s major utilities have been the subject of criticism as customers complain of high energy bills and poor reliability.
“These increased outage credits are vital to properly compensating people for their spoiled food and medicines, hotel rentals, gas generators and all the other costs they suffer every time our monopoly utility companies fail,” said Alex Kellogg,  the energy accountability manager for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, in a statement. “Our bills are too damn high already with the constant rate hikes DTE and Consumers demand, so Michiganders deserve a Ratepayer Bill of Rights and they should remember in November who is standing up for them and who is not.”
Katie Carey, the director of media relations for Consumers Energy, one of the state’s largest energy companies, said the company is reviewing the bills.
“Michigan and New York are currently the only states that require electric utilities to issue automatic bill credits or compensation to customers, and Consumers Energy complies with the outage credit requirements established by the Michigan Public Service Commission,” Carey said in a statement via email. “On the topic of outages, investing in reliability improvements and restoring power safely and quickly will remain our top priorities.”
Connecticut Law also requires energy companies to provide customers with a credit for outages longer than 96 hours after an emergency. In other states, customers must file a claim in order to receive compensation for lost power, spoiled food and medication and damaged appliances.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Line 5 opponents challenge state environmental department permits, calling them ‘legally deficient’
description: As state officials scrutinize permits that would allow a Canadian energy company to build a tunnel beneath the Straits of Mackinac, four Tribal Nations and a host of environmental groups have filed a challenge in hopes of overturning the state’s decision. On Thursday, The Bay Mills Indian Community, Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, […]
text:
Anti-Line 5 sign at a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Detroit District public scoping meeting regarding the Line 5 tunnel project, Saint Ignace, Sept. 8, 2022 | Sharon FighterAs state officials scrutinize permits that would allow a Canadian energy company to build a tunnel beneath the Straits of Mackinac, four Tribal Nations and a host of environmental groups have filed a challenge in hopes of overturning the state’s decision.
On Thursday, The Bay Mills Indian Community, Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians and Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians submitted a request for a contested case on a set of permits the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy issued in July.
The Environmental Law and Policy Center, Flow Water Advocates, the Michigan Climate Action Network and the National Wildlife Federation also requested a contested case in a separate petition. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both challenges come on the heels of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s announcement that the state was taking another look at the permits following a Michigan Supreme Court decision, which determined state energy regulators had failed to consider the environmental impacts that could come from extending the lifespan of Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline when they approved another permit for the project.
Enbridge Energy’s Line 5 pipeline stretches 645 miles from northwestern Wisconsin, through Michigan, into Sarnia, Ontario. The pipeline diverges into two segments within the Great Lakes, with the dual pipelines resting on the lakebed.
Tribal nations, environmental activists and state officials have pushed to have the pipeline shut down for years amid concerns that the pipeline could rupture, spilling crude oil into the ecologically sensitive Straits of Mackinac.
Following a 2018 anchor strike which dented the pipeline in three places, Enbridge and the state agreed to build a utility tunnel below the lakebed to house a replacement segment for the pipeline.
While the company has championed the tunnel as a solution to the threat of future anchor strikes, and as a means of containing any potential oil spills, pipeline opponents argued the tunneling process poses a significant threat to the environment, as well as to Indigenous cultural resources.
“The Line 5 tunnel project, if allowed to proceed, will irreversibly destroy tribal cultural resources including burials, tribal lifeways, and the Straits of Mackinac, a sacred space for the Anishinaabe,” said David Gover, a managing attorney for the Native American Rights Fund.
The fund is representing the Bay Mills Indian Community, Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians and Earthjustice.
There is no way to mitigate the impact to these resources, Gover said in a statement, stressing that they would be permanently destroyed.
In a statement, Dave Scott, a senior attorney at the Environmental Law and Policy Center, argued the water resource permit EGLE approved is “deficient under Michigan environmental laws.”

“That’s even clearer after the Michigan Supreme Court’s recent opinion,” Scott said. “Michigan law requires a robust environmental review and analysis of alternatives to the tunnel. We look forward to presenting our arguments and we hope that EGLE will do the right thing and ultimately deny this legally deficient permit.”
Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy directed the Michigan Advance to a statement it issued in response to Whitmer’s request to reexamine the EGLE permits.
“Let’s be clear — we already have an agreement with the State of Michigan to advance the Great Lakes Tunnel Project,” Duffy said. “Without years of litigation and political intervention, this project would be moving toward completion.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Energy company eyes adding data center west of Fargo
description: A company building a solar farm west of Fargo has plans to add a battery storage facility and potentially a data center in the area.  Minnesota-based Geronimo Power says it has been working with stakeholders in Harmony Township to explore the potential development of a data center. The company said the data center is expected […]
text:
Workers prepare the ground for what will become a solar farm north of Mapleton, North Dakota, on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)A company building a solar farm west of Fargo has plans to add a battery storage facility and potentially a data center in the area. 
Minnesota-based Geronimo Power says it has been working with stakeholders in Harmony Township to explore the potential development of a data center.
The company said the data center is expected to be powered by new power generation, which may include renewable energy, battery storage and natural gas. 
Geronimo Power started construction on its Harmony Solar project north of Mapleton this summer. 
Harmony Solar will supply about 200 megawatts of power. The company also is developing Harmony Storage, a battery site capable of storing 200 megawatts of power produced by the solar farm for up to four hours. 
Geronimo Power did not provide an exact location for a data center, but the company’s website said it seeks to locate new data centers near its power projects. 
Data center nondisclosure bill dies in North Dakota Senate vote

Cass County Administrator Robert Wilson said he met with officials from Minnesota-based Geronimo Power on Wednesday, though specifics such as size and exact location were not discussed. 
Geronimo did not provide details of the size or energy needs of a potential data center. 
Data centers need large amounts of energy to keep banks of computers cool. A data center under construction at Harwood north of Fargo is expected to use as much as 280 megawatts of power at peak demand times. 
Wilson said there will likely be further talks with Geronimo officials, but nothing was planned at this time. He said much of the discussion focused on road access.
“That’s really our role,” Wilson said. 
He said the situation could be similar to the Applied Digital site near Harwood, where the company paid to add a turn lane to a county road and make improvements to ease traffic congestion during construction. 
Wilson said zoning and permitting decisions would fall to Harmony Township officials. 
An electrical substation is adjacent to a solar farm north of Mapleton, North Dakota. The area could also become home to a battery storage site and a data center. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Mike Blevins, zoning administrator with Harmony Township, said Thursday there are no applications submitted for a data center. 
According to documents filed with the North Dakota Public Service Commission, the Harmony Township Board of Supervisors approved an amendment to its zoning ordinance on July 21, allowing for a battery energy storage system at the solar farm site. 
The Public Service Commission on Wednesday set a public hearing for the battery project for 10 a.m. Oct. 23 at the Days Inn in Casselton. 
Geronimo’s Harmony Storage anticipates starting construction in 2027 and being in operation by 2028. The 12-acre project about 3 miles north of Mapleton has a cost estimate of $249 million with an estimated lifespan of 30 years.
A noise assessment it filed says there are no noise standards in Cass County or with the state for battery storage projects, but the project would comply with the noise standards the state has set for wind farms. 
This is the third battery storage project the commission has considered this year. 
The Public Service Commission has siting authority over energy facilities such as solar farms, wind farms and battery storage sites, but not large power users such as data centers. 
Data center development has become a top issue in North Dakota. A proposal for a statewide moratorium was rejected for consideration in the recent special legislative session. 
Legislators debated a bill to ban nondisclosure agreements between data center developers and public officials and agencies. Lawmakers rejected the proposal, though the issue could reemerge in the 2027 legislative session that begins in January. 
Opponents of data centers cite the potential for higher utility bills, water demand, noise, effects on health and loss of farmland. 
Supporters say data centers provide jobs, property tax revenue and help meet growing demand for artificial intelligence.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Will Kosta Diamantis get jail time? Judge gets wildly different asks
description: A judge was presented with two wildly different proposals for how to sentence the former public official convicted of bribery and extortion.
text:
What type of punishment should a high-ranking public official receive for soliciting bribes from construction companies, fixing government contracts for those businesses and repeatedly lying in order to cover up those crimes? 
That’s what a federal judge in Bridgeport will need to decide next week during the sentencing hearing for Konstantinos Diamantis, Connecticut’s former deputy budget director and the one-time leader of the state’s school construction office. 
U.S. District Court Judge Stefan Underhill has been presented with two wildly different proposals for how to resolve the federal corruption case, which resulted in a jury convicting Diamantis on 21 charges of bribery, extortion, conspiracy and lying to federal investigators.
Diamantis’ defense attorney, Norm Pattis, asked the judge last week to sentence his client to home confinement and community service, as well as prohibiting him from holding public office or working in any government setting again. 
Meanwhile, federal prosecutors are requesting that Diamantis, who is also facing another corruption trial in December, be sentenced to 10 to 12 years in federal prison to pay for his crimes and to send a message to other government officials who might consider profiting off their public office. And they pointed out that length of prison sentence is what the federal sentencing guidelines call for. 
The sentencing memorandums filed by Pattis and the U.S. Attorney’s Office present two starkly different descriptions of Diamantis, who served for 12 years a Democratic lawmaker before being appointed by Gov. Ned Lamont to run the state’s school construction program.
To bolster the case for home confinement, Pattis portrayed Diamantis as an aging family man who has already been severely punished for his role in the multi-year bribery scheme. 
“The public consequences here are unmistakable. A former legislator, attorney, military veteran, and senior state official has been prosecuted, tried, convicted, publicly disgraced, financially ruined, stripped of his profession, and permanently excluded from positions of public trust. Those consequences convey a powerful warning: abuse of governmental authority can destroy a lifetime of professional accomplishment and financial security,” Pattis wrote.
Pattis also noted that Diamantis, who is 70 years old, could have his state pension revoked or reduced as a result of his conviction, and if he is sentenced to prison, he won’t be able to collect on Social Security.
“A lengthy sentence would likely return Mr. Diamantis to the community at a greatly advanced age, without assets, a profession, stable income, or a dependable supportstructure,” Pattis wrote. 
David Novick, one of the U.S. Attorneys who led the prosecution, cast Diamantis in a completely different light.
Novick described Diamantis as a brash, money-hungry state official, who used his “nearly unfettered control” over Connecticut’s school building program to bully and intimidate construction contractors and local officials alike. 
The federal prosecutor also reminded the judge of the mountain of evidence that was presented at trial, including text messages and voicemails in which Diamantis demanded bribes from two of the school construction contractors he oversaw: Acranom Masonry and Construction Advocacy Professionals. 
Novick recounted how those contractors delivered cash bribes to Diamantis at coffee shops, a Hartford restaurant and at his home in Farmington, and how one of them hired his daughter. 
“Diamantis’s principal crime was a years-long, brazen breach of public trust by a senior state official who used his government office to line his own pockets by extorting businesspeople bidding to provide valuable services to state taxpayers on multimillion dollar school construction contracts,” the prosecutors wrote. 
“Diamantis solicited, cajoled, intimidated, and outright threatened two contractors,” he added.
Novick told the judge that the seriousness of Diamantis’ crimes could not be overlooked, and he took issue with Pattis’ argument that Diamantis should be credited for the decades he spent as a public official, which ended as a result of the federal criminal investigation. 
He also called out Diamantis for claiming to be a military veteran. 
“While he refers to himself as a ‘military veteran,’ the (presentence investigation report) clarifies that Diamantis served less than a month in Officer Candidate School before being honorably discharged due to a knee injury.”
Diamantis’ request to avoid a federal prison sentence is even more noteworthy, Novick argued, given that he has yet to show any level of remorse for his crimes. 
The federal prosecutor pointed to Diamantis’ conviction on several charges related to lying to federal agents and Diamantis’ testimony during the trial in which he denied participating in any bribery or extortion scheme. 
“Diamantis’s continued insistence, in the face of overwhelming documentary evidence to the contrary, that he has done nothing wrong points to a serious flaw in his own moral and ethical calculus, which merits significant consideration by the court,” Novick wrote.
“Even now, in anticipation of sentencing, Diamantis has offered no acknowledgment of responsibility for his crimes,” he added. 
More recently, Diamantis has sought a federal pardon from President Donald Trump.
Despite that request, Pattis told the judge that Diamantis recognizes the severity of his crimes and the damage he has caused. 
“Mr. Diamantis does not minimize the seriousness of the jury’s verdict or his breach of the public trust. He asks the Court, however, to impose an individualized sentence based on all the circumstances rather than treating the advisory range as presumptively appropriate,” Pattis wrote.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office disagreed, and argued that the judge needs to sentence Diamantis to prison in order to send a message to other public officials who might exploit their positions of power. 
“Crimes by public officials are particularly susceptible to general deterrence because bribery is a premeditated crime — those tempted to sell out the public have plenty of time to weigh the risks and rewards before doing so,” Novick wrote.
“A guidelines sentence sends an important message to another public official tempted to use their office for personal gain, namely, that the consequences will not just be the loss of office and reputation, but substantial loss of liberty as well,” he added.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Sen. Moreno drafting Trump bill to give adults $5,000 if Republicans wins midterms
description: U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno is drafting legislation to fund President Donald Trump’s new promise: $5,000 to every adult citizen if the Republicans maintain their majority in the midterms. Trump acknowledged in his speech at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday that this year’s elections are competitive. He offered an unprecedented incentive to vot[...]
text:
Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno speaks with reporters in the Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno is drafting legislation to fund President Donald Trump’s new promise: $5,000 to every adult citizen if the Republicans maintain their majority in the midterms.
Trump acknowledged in his speech at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday that this year’s elections are competitive. He offered an unprecedented incentive to vote.
“If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them, because of our economic, tremendous economic success… I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said.
This money would have stipulations, the president added, saying it could only be spent in the United States.
Michael McGovern, president of progressive organization Innovation Ohio, said it’s another empty promise.


“This is the same party that has cracked down on people’s ability to give out water or pizza to people waiting in line to vote, now is throwing around $5000 but ‘only if you vote for us?'” McGovern said. “I don’t know if that passes the smell test, and really reeks of desperation.”
Legality
The president did not give details on how he would provide $5,000 to all 270 million adults, costing more than a trillion dollars.
“Is it possible? The short answer is no, unless Congress were to appropriate the money,” retired Case Western Reserve University law professor Jonathan Entin said.
Moreno, Ohio’s senior senator who attended the speech on Wednesday, was the first to offer help.
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election … because Republicans (and America) will win!” Moreno said in a post on X.
It’s illegal to buy votes, but the payouts wouldn’t just go to Republicans, Entin said.
“It says, ‘I will pay every American however they voted,'” he explained.
And even if it feels like a bribe?
“Who is going to prosecute him?” Entin asked. “Even former presidents have very broad immunity from criminal prosecution in connection with their official actions.”
In an interview Thursday, U.S. Senator Jon Husted said he wanted to learn more.
“I’ll get some more details about exactly how that would work, but the principle is right in line with what the working family tax cut plan is about — giving people more of what they earn to spend on their priorities rather than sending it to Washington,” Husted said.
The national debt is around $40 trillion, and the senator added that he does care about how much Congress is spending.
Senate race
Husted also spoke at the convention, amid a U.S. Senate race that is considered one of the most competitive in the country. In his Wednesday speech, he mainly attacked opponent Sherrod Brown, but also talked about benefits of the GOP.
“Prevented a huge tax increase, cut taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and gave working families expanded child care credits,” he said in his speech.
Brown’s team took shots at Husted for being in Dallas instead of Ohio with only about 50 days until the election. In a previous interview, Brown said he didn’t think Husted cared about everyday concerns.
“Jon Husted, who keeps giving more tax cuts to rich people and doesn’t look out for the cost of groceries and the cost of gas,” Brown said in an August interview.
Brown has also criticized Husted for voting in favor of keeping the Iran war going. Trump said that conflict will end following the midterms.
“They can’t hold out any longer,” Trump said in comments to reporters prior to attending the convention. “They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there.”
McGovern said this is another policy proposal he doubts will happen.
“I don’t believe a word that comes out of Donald Trump’s mouth when it comes to the war in the Middle East,” he said. “We’ve seen these promises again and again that the war will be over soon.”


Follow WEWS Statehouse reporter Morgan Trau on X and Facebook.
This article was originally published on News5Cleveland.com and is published in the Ohio Capital Journal under a content-sharing agreement. Unlike other OCJ articles, it is not available for free republication by other news outlets as it is owned by WEWS in Cleveland.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: 25 years later, coming together on 9/11
description: David Lawrence Angell. Carol Marie Bouchard. Mark Lawrence Charette. James Edward Hayden. Amy Nicole Jarret. Kathryn L. Laborie. Shawn M. Nassaney. Renee Tetreault Newell. Jessica Leigh Sachs. Their names were read aloud by Col. Darnell Weaver, superintendent of the Rhode Island State Police, on Friday morning at the Rhode Island Veterans Memorial Cemetery i[...]
text:
Sharon Serio-Valente, left, mother of 21-year-old fallen Marine Lance Cpl. Matthew Serio, and Margaret Nassaney, right, mother of Shawn Nassaney who lost his life on United Flight 175 on 9/11, carry a wreath at the Rhode Island Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Exeter on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)David Lawrence Angell. Carol Marie Bouchard. Mark Lawrence Charette. James Edward Hayden. Amy Nicole Jarret. Kathryn L. Laborie. Shawn M. Nassaney. Renee Tetreault Newell. Jessica Leigh Sachs.
Their names were read aloud by Col. Darnell Weaver, superintendent of the Rhode Island State Police, on Friday morning at the Rhode Island Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Exeter on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All nine Rhode Islanders died in the terrorist attacks against the United States on Sept. 11, 2001.
Over 100 people attended the solemn 45-minute ceremony with state leaders, first responders, and Gold Star families.
The names of over 20 military service members from Rhode Island who died in the global war on terror in the years after 9/11 were read aloud by Maj. Gen. Andrew J. Chevalier, the adjutant general of the Rhode Island National Guard.
Gov. Dan McKee, who spoke at the ceremony, directed U.S. and Rhode Island flags to remain at half-staff at all state facilities and buildings on Friday. McKee also urged Rhode Islanders to lower their flags as a sign of respect.
“Twenty-five years later and the pain of September 11th still feels fresh for so many,” McKee said in prepared remarks. “Nearly 3,000 Americans lost their lives in the tragic attacks in New York City. Among them, nine Rhode Islanders were taken from us too soon. We may never fully know the pain their families and friends feel. But today and every day, Rhode Island stands with them and their loved ones.”
McKee noted that the uncertainty, fear, and grief that swept across the country immediately after the attacks.
“It’s a feeling and a moment we must never forget,” he added. “But we also remember the inspiring bravery and heroism. Firefighters, police officers and first responders running into the towers to help strangers, not knowing if they’d ever make it out. And after the smoke cleared and the dust settled, everyday citizens united hand in hand, lifting each other up to help in any way they could. That unity is what defines our nation. It echoes the principles of liberty: freedom, independence and perseverance on which this nation was built upon.”
McKee paid tribute to military members, Gold Star families, and all who served in the aftermath of 9/11.
“And we pay tribute to those who gave the ultimate sacrifice,” the governor said. “We will always remember their valor, and we are stronger for it. Today, we remember the lives lost and thank those who have sacrificed so much to preserve our freedom. Twenty-five years later, we have not forgotten and we will never forget. Thank you all for being here.”
George Chasse, a firefighter with the Exeter Fire Department performs the ‘Striking of the Four Fives,’ a custom dating back to 1860 in the New York City Fire Department. A solemn service tradition in which a four series of five strikes on a bell honor a firefighter who has died in the line of duty. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
