name: Kentucky Lantern
title: EPA seeks more public comment on rule that affects Kentucky water protections
description: The U.S Environmental Protection Agency is again seeking public comments on a proposal to redefine what waters receive federal environmental protections, a move that could also have a broad impact on state water protections in Kentucky.  The Trump administration is allowing public comments until Oct. 9 on a “supplemental” rule to redefine federally protected[...]
text:
A section of Three Mile Creek. Photo by Richard Durtsche in Land, Air & Water via Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet)

The U.S Environmental Protection Agency is again seeking public comments on a proposal to redefine what waters receive federal environmental protections, a move that could also have a broad impact on state water protections in Kentucky. 
The Trump administration is allowing public comments until Oct. 9 on a “supplemental” rule to redefine federally protected Waters of the United States under the Clean Water Act. It’s an action the EPA said would allow it to “evaluate a wider range of options” following a 2023 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that severely curtailed the federal government’s ability to regulate water pollution over certain types of wetlands. 
It’s the second time the EPA is collecting public comments on the proposal. In January, Republican Kentucky Attorney General Russel Coleman and other Republican attorneys general wrote in a public comment that the federal government has long tried to overreach in their authority to regulate water pollution, arguing state governments are better suited to do so. 
“For too long, the agencies have over-expanded the definition — far exceeding lawful congressional authorization. The fallout from that overreach has been severe,” the attorneys general wrote. “Expansive definitions stripped states of their ability to regulate their own waters. Congress never intended that affront to traditional state authority.”
But environmental advocacy groups including and Kentucky’s own water pollution regulators have warned the redefinition could also mean a drastic rollback of state regulatory power over water pollution. 
The GOP-controlled state legislature passed a law in 2025 — arguing the need for industry regulatory relief — that largely ties the definition of protected state waters to the federal definition of navigable waters. At the time, environmental advocacy groups warned that ceding water protection limits to the federal government could threaten the groundwater of hundreds of thousands of Kentuckians.
In January, the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet published online infographics that warn at least 74% of stream miles, or an estimated more than 80,000 miles of streams, could lose environmental protections under the federal redefinition. The cabinet also wrote only 14% of Kentucky wetlands would be protected under a proposed federal redefinition. 
In an infographic, the cabinet wrote the state is in a “uniquely vulnerable position” because state water protections are tied to the federal definition of Waters of the United States. 
“This means that questions about what waters the state protects will depend on
which political party is in power rather than a true scientific or geological standard,” the cabinet wrote.
The cabinet warned of the potential for more water pollution, less protection against flooding and impacts of waterfowl habitat.
Those interested in submitting a public comment on the federal proposal can do so online or by other means including mail.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Republicans attack ex-GOP Mayor Ballard in party’s opening secretary of state ad
description: The first television ad from Republicans in this year’s Indiana secretary of state race is an all-out attack on Greg Ballard’s time as the Republican mayor of Indianapolis.
text:
An image from an Indiana Republican Party campaign ad attacking Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard. (Screenshot)The first television ad from Republicans in this year’s Indiana secretary of state race is an all-out attack on Greg Ballard’s time as the Republican mayor of Indianapolis.
The 30-second commercial that started airing Friday doesn’t mention Republican candidate Max Engling a single time. But the narrator and on-screen text repeatedly denounces “liberal Greg Ballard” and says he failed as the city’s mayor.
Ballard, who is running under the Lincoln Party banner, responded that he is proud of his record in office from 2008 through 2015 and described the ad as “built on fiction.”
Indiana secretary of state hopefuls clash over voting rules, office audit

“This is a panic move from the Indiana Republican Party,” Ballard said in a statement. “You don’t attack candidates you’re not afraid of. Part of the reason I’m running for this office is to reduce the toxicity and negativity of political campaigns.”
The Ballard campaign also quoted a 2014 statement from then-Indiana Republican Party Chairman Tim Berry on Indianapolis Ballard’s decision not to seek re-election as mayor.
“I would like to thank Mayor Greg Ballard for his tireless work and dedication to public service. He has made Indianapolis financially stronger and more vibrant than when he took over eight years ago,” Berry said. “Ballard fought to protect taxpayers, bolster businesses, expand education opportunities and make Indiana’s largest city, a destination city. His focus was always making Indianapolis a better place and that’s certainly a part of the legacy he will leave behind.”
The ad paid for by the state Republican Party picks up on attack lines used by the Engling campaign about local tax increases and crime rates in Indianapolis under Ballard.
Republicans started broadcast ads a month after Democratic nominee Beau Bayh’s commercials first hit the airwaves. 
Bayh also isn’t mentioned in the new Republican ad, which is part of $1 million in media spending announced Thursday by the state GOP and Gov. Mike Braun’s campaign to support Engling’s campaign.
That announcement described the push as “part of a statewide effort to make clear the choice facing Hoosier voters in the secretary of state race and highlight what’s at stake this November.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT enjoys robust pension investment returns
description: CT’s 15.1% return ranked in the top 23% of returns achieved by major public pension funds over the past fiscal year.
text:
State Treasurer Erick Russell reported a 15.1% increase last fiscal year investing Connecticut’s pension assets, a gain of roughly $11 billion for retirement programs for state employees, teachers and other municipal workers.
The returns, presented this week to the Investment Advisory Council, mark the fourth consecutive year pension investments have eclipsed the 6.9% target the state hopes to average over the long term. More importantly, Connecticut’s results ranked in the top quarter of all major public pension funds nationally.
“These results strengthen the retirement security of Connecticut’s teachers and state employees, while reducing pressure on future state budgets and helping us continue the progress we have made in strengthening the financial foundation of our state,” Russell said.
The treasurer, a New Haven Democrat who oversees $76 billion in pension assets, won his first term in November 2022 and began reforming a system which had lagged other states’ investment results for more than a decade.
Russell has reduced investments in emerging ventures, put more funds into private and domestic markets, and curbed reliance on investment managers who receive fees for their work. His reforms mirror many suggestions Yale researchers made in 2023.
Connecticut’s 15.1% return ranked in the top 23% of returns achieved by major public pension funds over the past fiscal year, and in the top 25% achieved over the past three, Russell said. The treasurer reported a 10.1% return last fiscal year and 11.5% two years ago.
But not that long ago, Connecticut’s pensions were in far worse shape.
A severe recession first focused officials on the problem in the late 2000s, when mandatory pension contributions skyrocketed due to a lack of overall funding. Those increases, coupled with declining revenues, helped trigger three big state tax hikes between 2009 and 2015.
According to the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, Connecticut governors and legislatures failed to save adequately for pension benefits for more than seven decades prior to 2011. This deprived the state treasurer of huge assets that otherwise could have been invested to generate billions of dollars in revenue over those seven decades.
Connecticut legislators enacted aggressive budget caps in 2017 that forced unprecedented surpluses. Those dollars were used largely to build reserves for the first two years. But since 2020 Connecticut has poured $11 billion in surplus into its pension funds, including $1.3 billion Russell deposited earlier this month from the fiscal year that ended June 30.
That’s in addition to the roughly $3 billion in regular contributions built annually into the state budget, which still consume a hefty 12% of the General Fund.
But Gov. Ned Lamont’s fiscal analysts project the required annual payments would be nearly $1 billion greater, were it not for all the surplus dollars redirected to wipe out pension debt.
Connecticut still carries more than $30 billion in unfunded pension obligations, a burden it’s not projected to pay off entirely until well into the 2040s, according to the Office of Policy and Management.
“Connecticut has made tremendous progress in strengthening our pension system and putting the state on a more sustainable financial path,” Lamont said. “Strong investment performance, combined with the additional contributions we have made in recent years, is helping us reduce pension debt and lower costs for taxpayers over the long term. This progress is the result of disciplined fiscal management, and it gives us greater flexibility to make investments in education, housing, and other priorities that strengthen our economy and improve quality of life for people across our state.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Cabinet approves process to designate CAIR and others as domestic terrorist groups
description: In a procedure that took less than two minutes, Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet voted Friday to approve a rule governing the Florida Department of Law Enforcement’s designation of Florida groups as domestic or foreign terrorist organizations. The approval paves the way for the state to thus designate the Council on American Islamic […]
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaking in Tampa on July 1, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)In a procedure that took less than two minutes, Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet voted Friday to approve a rule governing the Florida Department of Law Enforcement’s designation of Florida groups as domestic or foreign terrorist organizations.
The approval paves the way for the state to thus designate the Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR), the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa more than two months after DeSantis announced he had received the recommendations from FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass.
The rule establishes that the state’s Chief of Domestic Security, at the moment Glass, will notify the governor and Cabinet of plans to designate an organization as a domestic or foreign terrorist organization.
The Florida Legislature passed a bill (HB 1471) earlier this year empowering the FDLE chief to label organizations domestic or foreign terrorist groups on evidence of specific criteria, including engagement in terrorist activity as defined by Florida law, subject to ratification by the governor and Cabinet.
The legislation prohibits any state agency, political subdivision, or public school district from expending or accepting state funds to support groups thus designated. It bans public schools or school districts from spending state or federal funds or maintaining programs on campus that “promote” a designated group.
The law also says any college or university must report information relating to the status of a student who is attending that school on a student visa if the student “promotes” an terrorist-designated organization. Students found to have promoted the group can be expelled.
The ACLU, the ACLU of Florida, and two other legal groups representing CAIR and CAIR Florida filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the legislation in July in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida.
“As Florida chief of domestic security, I know there are imminent dangers to public health, safety, and welfare due to increasing risks from foreign and domestic terrorist groups,” Glass said Friday.
“This provides an appropriate framework where that they can take action appropriately so that they can defend the people of Florida against possible actors and terrorist groups. So, I move to approve the item as presented,” DeSantis said.
‘Dangerous new designation regime’
The governor attempted to designate CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood as domestic terrorist organizations through an executive order in December. CAIR Florida filed a legal challenge in March, and a federal judge shortly thereafter issued a temporary injunction blocking that designation. The DeSantis administration has appealed the ruling.
“From Day One, Florida officials’ use of this dangerous new designation regime has violated the Constitution,” Hina Shamsi, director of the ACLU’s National Security Project, said in July.
“Gov. DeSantis has simply no legitimate basis to brand our clients with one of society’s most reviled labels, let alone to force them to shut their doors under threat of crippling criminal penalties, and leave the Floridians they serve without a crucial civil rights voice. In the United States, CAIR and all nonprofits have the right to criticize the government, protect religious freedom, and advocate for the causes they believe in.”
In addition to CAIR, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa, DeSantis said in July that the state had received recommendations to designate more than 90 groups as foreign terrorist organizations, including but not limited to Cartel de Sinaloa; Tren de Aragua; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran (IRGC); Cartel del Noreste; and Cartel del Golfo.
Under the rule change approved Friday, any designation would become effective 30 days after publication in the Florida Administrative Register. Organizations placed on the list would have seven days after being noticed to object in writing and provide documentation the organization believes would counsel against the designation.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: US Senator
description: Roswell Republican Larry Marker challenges U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján, a longtime elected official, for one of New Mexico's U.S. Senate seats. Source NM spoke with both about their race.
text:
Roswell Republican Larry Marker is challenging U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján, a longtime elected official, for one of New Mexico's U.S. Senate seats in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. Above: The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)(Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)The race to represent New Mexico in the U.S. Senate took an unconventional route last spring.
Incumbent U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) soundly defeated his opponent in the June 2 primary election with an 84%-16% victory. The Republican race, however, appeared blank on the ballot.
While the Republican Party of New Mexico failed to officially field a candidate for the race, Republican Larry Marker of Roswell decided to run as a write-in candidate, meaning his name didn’t appear on the ballot. He still managed to garner nearly as many votes — through voters writing his name in — as Luján’s Democratic primary opponent, Democrat socialist Matt Dodson.
Luján and Marker will face each other on the Nov. 3 general election ballot.
Whoever wins will hold a six-year term with an annual salary of $174,000. Source NM spoke with both candidates about the race, their vision for the state and how they’d navigate the remainder of President Donald Trump’s second term. Their answers have been edited for clarity and concision.
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján
(Courtesy of Ben Ray Luján)
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján, one of five Democrats who make up the state’s congressional delegation, first won this seat in 2020, but has worked in public service in New Mexico for more than 20 years.
He first won election to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission, which oversees the state’s utilities, in 2004 and later won a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 2008. He served as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2018 as Democrats sought to regain a House majority during Trump’s first term.
Luján sits on U.S. Senate committees for Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry; Budget; Commerce, Science and Transportation; Finance; and Indian Affairs. His late father Ben Ray Luján Sr., served in the state Legislature for nearly 40 years, including more than a decade as House speaker.
He survived a stroke in 2022 and, citing that experience, helped secure $3 million for a new MRI scanner at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center, which will enable researchers to more closely study brain chemistry.
Luján told Source NM he’s running for reelection because he believes the office lets him practice the “golden rule” he learned about as a churchgoing child — “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you” — on a statewide scale.
“I grew up on a small farm in northern New Mexico. I still live on that farm today,” he said of his Nambé roots. “I’m very proud of my work ethic and what I learned on that farm — lifting up and helping neighbors and raising food and helping to share that everywhere that we can.”
What is the most important issue currently facing New Mexico?
Right now, I don’t know that there’s just one issue. The two issues at the top of my list after talking to people around New Mexico is the cost of everything and water.
Both of these issues matter so very much, whether I’m down in the southern part of the state, in the Middle Rio Grande Valley or up north.
All of the tariffs and the policies coming out of this administration now are just arbitrarily hurting folks. 
If reelected, what piece of legislation would you prioritize sponsoring in the next term?
One of the pieces of legislation that I’ve been working on now with colleagues throughout the country that will make a big difference in a positive way for families back in New Mexico is to provide more support to middle-class families for home healthcare; for caring for a parent, grandparent, a sibling, a child, a grandchild.
Right now, there are so little, if any, programs that provide that kind of support.
This is something that I learned about with a diagnosis with my mom. Myself and my three siblings now stay with mom every night to make sure that she has care and people around her.
How would you describe the impact of the Trump administration on New Mexico and what would your approach be to working with the Trump administration if re-elected?
With the passage of the ‘Big, Beautiful Bill’ and many of the aspects in there, what President Trump’s policies have done…is make families in New Mexico sicker and make families in New Mexico poorer.
When I was serving in the U.S. House under President Trump’s first term, after we were able to win back a majority, there’s still room to work with him. I’m proudly working with Democrats and Republicans on a farm bill. I believe that we could actually get a farm bill across the finish line that will provide more support for food programs, help families in New Mexico and support families and ranchers, especially in western states.
What policies would you support as it relates to border security?
We need to have smart immigration policy and strong border security in America. I’ve advocated for 100% screening — inbound and outbound — of our southern border for some time.
The U.S. Senate has several proposals pending related to data centers, ranging from a moratorium to requiring data centers to foot the bill for their energy use. Where do you stand on these measures?
Whether it’s AI data centers or any other industry, in New Mexico, drinking water needs to be for drinking and agriculture needs to be for agriculture. Plain and simple.
Do you believe the U.S. voting system is secure?
The voting system in the U.S. is a secure voting system. When President Trump and my Republican colleagues in the U.S. Senate say that they’re moving legislation that is simply about voter ID, they are misleading and arguably lying to the American people. What Republicans and President Trump are trying to do right now is end vote by mail for every American across the country, and they’re trying to scare people all across the U.S.
What do you see as the most meaningful accomplishments of your current term?
I’ve been honored to work with my Democratic and Republican colleagues to pass significant pieces of legislation that are making a positive difference for families in New Mexico. The Radiation Exposure Compensation Act was a piece of legislation that most observers suggested would never be done.
I was very proud that I led an initiative to create a fund specific for the victims of the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire that was very similar to something (former U.S. Sen.) Pete Domenici created after the fire that started in and around Los Alamos National Laboratory in Cerro Grande.
You’ve consistently opposed the current administration’s actions when it comes to policies that acutely affect New Mexico, particularly ICE operations and Medicaid cuts. How would you approach these issues in a second term?
My approach always has been that I’m willing to work with anyone when it comes to helping people in New Mexico. But if you’re going to bully New Mexico, we’re not going to get along.
Your opponent has criticized you for prioritizing what he describes as ‘hand-out’ social programs. How do you respond to that?
I was proud to lead an initiative, working with my Republican colleagues, that required the plugging of all the orphaned and abandoned oil wells in New Mexico and on federal land across America. That was a job creator and that was one that put a lot of people to work and invested millions of dollars in job creation and opportunity throughout New Mexico. If my opponent wants to call that a hand-out, then he’s clearly out of step with people back in New Mexico, especially in one of the fields that he purports to know the best.
Larry Marker
(Photo courtesy of Larry Marker)
Larry Marker, a self-employed oil and gas businessperson, previously ran unsuccessfully for state land commissioner and the state senate.
Born in Hobbs and raised in Roswell, Marker told Source NM that rural New Mexico needs a senator who will fight for economic development opportunities. He’s vowed to work toward a secure border, support the oil and gas industry and boost New Mexico’s farmers and ranchers.
Marker acknowledges, though, the difficulties of his campaign. 
Republicans have not won a statewide race in New Mexico for a decade and he won his party’s nomination with no competition. Now, he faces an incumbent with strong name recognition largely because his party failed to field candidates in the June primary election.
“I definitely can beat Ben Ray Luján,” Marker told Source NM by phone while waiting to board a plane to Dallas, where he planned to seek national funding at the national Republican midterm convention. “I’m just going to have to outwork him.”
What is the most important issue facing New Mexico?
New Mexico has a lot of excess income, you know, they’re just basically drowning in money right now while the federal government isn’t. Where I’m going to be working in Washington, D.C., I believe the biggest issue — and it does affect New Mexico — is the $40 trillion in debt, and then we need to figure out a way to stabilize Social Security.
If elected, what piece of legislation would you prioritize sponsoring in the next term?
The first thing I want to look at when I get there — and I’ve got a pretty solid plan — is how we can stabilize Social Security. 
People are concerned about Social Security. They’re worried about the economy, and the economy’s tied directly to the deficit and the debt of the federal government and, of course, taxes. Affordability is a big issue. We could solve a lot of those problems if we solved the debt and the deficit.
How would you describe the impact of the Trump administration on New Mexico and what would your approach be to working with the Trump administration if elected?
His policies have affected New Mexico. Of course in the oil and gas industry, those guys are excited about the price of crude (oil) being up, but they realize that that’s not really good for the economy.
My position on Donald Trump is that I do support most of Trump’s policies. He doesn’t have the constitutional authority to levy tariffs — that’s an issue that I struggle with. And as far as waging war in Iran, I believe the Constitution intended to limit the president’s ability to wage war, but we haven’t done anything about that since 1953…Until Congress and the Senate decide to step in and actually do something and do their job, it’s going to be a mess.
What policies would you support, if elected, as it relates to border security?
We need a very, very strong, secure border, but we do need a way for people to migrate into the U.S. — a legal method that is not real cumbersome and especially not real expensive.
There are several proposals in the U.S. Senate related to data centers, ranging from a moratorium to requiring data centers to foot the bill for their energy use. What is your position on these measures?
We need to treat data centers like you would treat a feedlot. They don’t need to be close to town. They don’t need to be anywhere where they can destroy the resources of the area they’re in. And they need to be someplace where they’re not over a shallow water table or a water table that they can contaminate.
Do you believe the U.S. voting system is secure?
Do I believe that it’s secure and completely hack-proof? No, no.
Do I believe that people need to get out and vote and that they need to quit worrying that their vote won’t count because somebody’s going to steal it or do whatever? We need to get out and vote and say that our county clerks are doing the best they can to provide us a good, stable voting process in New Mexico.
I don’t believe the federal government should be able to control the elections, but what I do believe is people have got to have confidence in our voting system.
What would you do differently than your opponent?
Small-town New Mexico is in serious trouble. What I’m going to be doing differently is my time is going to be focused on providing people opportunities to make a living, to make a good life, to go out there and get something accomplished.
We need to rebuild our mining industry. We need to get a handle on the government putting the independent oil and gas producers out of business. We need to provide opportunities right here in New Mexico.
I believe in helping people by giving them a hand up, but don’t give them a handout. 
Republicans have not won a statewide race in New Mexico in a decade. How do you plan to compete with an incumbent who has name recognition?
I would not have done this if I didn’t think that I could win this race.
If you look at the voter registration numbers for the state Republican Party, we’ve got about 55,000 more registered Republicans now than we had in 2020, which is the last time this office was up for election.
For the first time in the history of New Mexico, less than 40% of the registered voters are Democrats. So, that tells you things are swinging.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC approves state funding for Flock cameras despite growing privacy concerns
description: Some SC law enforcement are doubling down on the use of Flock cameras, even as scrutiny of the surveillance devices has mounted nationwide.
text:
A Flock Safety license plate reader camera near Casa Grande, Arizona, in October 2025. (Photo by Jerod MacDonald-Evoy/Arizona Mirror)COLUMBIA — Some South Carolina law enforcement are doubling down on the use of Flock cameras, even as scrutiny over the AI-powered surveillance devices has mounted nationwide.
State legislators approved $365,000 in the state budget for four police and sheriff’s departments seeking to add automated license plate readers to their crime fighting arsenals or expand their existing fleet of Flock cameras.
The funds will go to law enforcement in Cameron and Florence, as well as McCormick and Marlboro counties.
The money is part of a larger $350 million list of legislator-sponsored spending that includes parks, building renovations, water and sewer upgrades, and equipment for first responders. Earmarks, or what legislators call community investments, designate state taxpayers’ money to local projects at legislators’ request.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In addition to the funding for local law enforcement, the state public safety agency, which includes the state Highway Patrol and Statehouse security officers, is in the process of renewing an existing contract for readers near two of the agency’s buildings.
Controversy surrounding Flock
Flock cameras are a brand of license plate readers that utilizes artificial intelligence to track and store detailed data on vehicles. The cameras photograph passing vehicles and record information, including the make, model and color as well as details like bumper stickers and dents.
Departments that use Flock cameras also can allow other agencies to access their devices, creating a massive nationwide network of more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states and thousands of law enforcement agencies.
There are some 1,650 Flock cameras across the Palmetto State, according to DeFlock, a grassroots group that tracks license plate reader deployments.
“We should not deprive law enforcement of tools that have the potential to prevent and solve crimes,” Gov. Henry McMaster said in a statement. “If and when those tools are misused, those responsible must be held accountable.”
Flock came under fire following reports of police officers accused of using the camera network to track friends, relatives and romantic partners, adding to concerns about how the data can be accessed and shared.
Opponents also criticized the technology after inaccurate license plate information contributed to wrongful police stops and arrests.
In response, more than 100 communities have canceled, suspended or rejected a Flock contract or deactivated their cameras since the beginning of 2026, according to DeFlock.
And Texas’ Republican Gov. Greg Abbott last month ordered all state agencies to pause funding for Flock cameras.
People have also vandalized cameras around the country. In South Carolina, police reported vandalism to the devices in Irmo, Bluffton, Traveler’s Rest and Ridge Spring, as well as Chesterfield, Union, Chester and York counties.
In Oconee County, elected officials are considering an ordinance barring the use of county funds to pay for Flock cameras and other mass surveillance systems.
What legislators are saying
One state House member pulled his support for a $375,000 request from Irmo police for a “Flock Drone Responder.”
“I was able to help the Town of Irmo with its fire department, but I had some additional questions about the drone request and Flock camera, particularly about how the data they collect will ultimately be used and protected,” Rep. Nathan Ballentine told the SC Daily Gazette.
“I’m fully supportive of law enforcement and public safety, but we also have to protect people’s privacy,” the Irmo Republican added. “I have some legitimate concerns that need to be addressed before I can support another request like that one.”
In the Pee Dee, Rep. Jason Luck said he was surprised that a request from the Marlboro County Sheriff’s Department for various equipment included more than $300,000 for 30 Flock cameras.
The Bennettsville Democrat said the technology is impressive but he has yet to see it used in a way that “complies with the U.S. Constitution.”
The cameras were part of a larger $1.2 million request, which in addition to the cameras included money for radios, TASERs, body armor, a training facility and software for officers to write up their reports while in the field. The Legislature ultimately agreed to send the department $500,000 for its needs.
“We are currently experiencing a staffing shortage, which includes investigators,” Sheriff Larry McNeil wrote in his request. “(License plate reader) technology is a tool that allows for real-time use by supervisors to obtain crucial information to bring dangerous incidents to a safe resolution.”
McNeil also said the technology has helped police in surrounding jurisdictions make “critical” arrests but did not go into further detail.
The sheriff did not respond to messages left by the Daily Gazette.
Luck said while he supported the larger request, he hopes the sheriff will reconsider the license plate readers.
As ‘smart cities’ tools grow nationwide, so do privacy and ethical concerns

Behind Marlboro County, the second largest request for the cameras came from Clarendon County, but at the request of the state legislator sponsoring it, the sheriff promised to divert the funding to pay for dash cameras instead.
“I think a lot of of people want to live their lives without the encroachment of the government,” said Rep. Fawn Pedalino, the Turbeville Republican who sponsored the request. “People feel like, if they’re not doing anything wrong, why should they be watched.”
Sheriff Tim Baxley, in his request, said his office already has 15 Flock cameras and would like $160,000 to add more “to aid in many of our problem areas where drive-by shootings, robberies and property thefts occur.”
He said the existing cameras were “instrumental” in solving past cases, as well as locating missing people.
The cameras were part of a larger, $1 million request approved by the legislature, which also included renovations to the sheriff’s department and new reporting software.
Rep. Jerry Govan, who sponsored the $35,000 request from the rural town of Cameron, said that application came before the national debate around the technology heated up. But it was what the town’s leaders said they needed.
The Orangeburg Democrat acknowledged users can abuse the technology, as well as cameras in general, particularly as artificial intelligence advances.
“This technology is moving so rapidly it’s mind boggling,” he said, and legislation governing it is not keeping pace.
“We certainly have a lot of catching up to do,” Govan added, in terms of safeguards.
A state contract
Outside of local law enforcement, the state Department of Public Safety has had Flock cameras near its main headquarters building and near its support services building for several years and is in the process of potentially renewing its contract, according to spokesman Kyle McGahee.
McGahee said the readers only photograph the plates of cars entering and exiting the headquarters campus. They’re not aimed at traffic on nearby roads. At the support building, cameras might pick up some non-law enforcement vehicles traveling on the access road, but coverage doesn’t reach the much busier street of Shop Road.
Authorized staff has access to the Flock network for investigative purposes, but the agency “takes extensive measures to maintain accountability on how the information is accessed and used,” McGahee added.
Despite widespread interest, only 3 states passed license plate reader laws this year

Changes announced
Flock recently announced changes amid the blowback against its technology.
The company said it’s recommending police agencies only retain license plate reader data for seven days, down from 30, while adding tools to restrict data sharing between agencies and detect potentially abusive searches. Flock also plans to require law enforcement attach case codes to searches and will automatically suspend users whose activity is flagged as abnormal.
“These changes, like I said, are the next chapter of a long book I hope to write on how we build a better version of America that’s both safer, protects our privacy and holds those who have power accountable,” Flock Safety co-founder and CEO Garrett Langley said in a video statement.
Still, advocates from the American Civil Liberties Union say some of the safeguards have been tried before and question whether the company’s changes address broader concerns about a system that can create a record of people’s movements, even when they are not suspected of a crime.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How many people ride CT’s historic river ferries?
description: Rides on the Chester-Hadlyme Ferry and the Rocky Hill Ferry last only a few minutes, but they're popular with commuters and sightseers alike.
text:
Two historic river ferries operate in Connecticut — the Chester-Hadlyme Ferry and the Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry. Both carry thousands of passengers, cars and some bicycles across the Connecticut River each season.
The Chester-Hadlyme Ferry was established in 1769 as Warner’s Ferry and is one of the nation’s oldest continuously operating ferries. It sails back and forth between Chester and Lyme. The Rocky Hill Ferry is the nation’s oldest, and it runs between Rocky Hill and Glastonbury.
And even though neither of the ferry rides last more than a few minutes, they remain popular for commuters and sightseers alike. Both operate seasonally from April to the end of November, but the Chester-Hadlyme is currently closed for repairs.
Across the two boats, tens of thousands of Connecticut residents travel each month during ferry season. July is the most popular, with nearly 20,000 passengers riding the ferries during that month in 2024 and 2025.
In the summer months, one Connecticut’s ferry might cross the river more than 2,500 times.
The Chester-Hadlyme Ferry made 2,527 river crossings in July 2025. That’s an average of more than 81 crossings per day.
The two ferries run seven days a week, but some times are busier than others. The majority of crossings are made on weekday afternoons and evenings. Weekday mornings and weekends see fewer crossings.
The vessels collect modest fares from each passenger. Walk-on riders are charged $2 a trip and vehicles cost $5 per vehicle on weekdays, $6 on the weekends.
There are also commuter packages for those who take the ferry regularly, priced at $60 for 20 rides.
Last year, there were more than 91,000 ferry rides taken between the two boats. But the inexpensive fares mean the revenue the ferries generate is limited.
In 2024, they brought in $227,995 in rider fees for the season, excluding rides purchased through Token Transit, an app that launched for the two boats in 2024. Last year, ferry fare revenue dropped to $193,427, but nearly 1,000 more tickets were sold through Token Transit.
The vessels played an important part in Connecticut history.
The Chester-Hadlyme route, which many take today to get to Gillette Castle State Park, was used during the Revolutionary War to transfer supplies across the Connecticut River. 
The current ferry traversing the route has been in operation for more than 75 years. Earlier this summer, state officials announced $8 million in state and federal grants will be used to replace the vessel, known as Selden III.
The Rocky Hill Ferry is older than the Chester-Hadlyme route, dating back to 1655. In fact, it’s the oldest continuously operational ferry in the nation. The setup for the Rocky Hill-Glastonbury crossing, known as “towing on the hip,” consists of a tugboat that is secured to the side of a barge — the “Hollister III” — that carries cars, bicycles and passengers on foot.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: 11 Indiana counties can apply for state debris removal reimbursement
description: Eleven Indiana counties hit by severe storms in August are eligible for state and federal assistance to reimburse a majority of debris removal costs as part of the federal major disaster declaration. The Federal Emergency Management Agency will reimburse 75% of eligible debris removal costs in Delaware, Fayette, Franklin, Hamilton, Henry, LaPorte, Lake, Madi[...]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun joins a debris assessment in Connersville on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Gov. Mike Braun's office) Eleven Indiana counties hit by severe storms in August are eligible for state and federal assistance to reimburse a majority of debris removal costs as part of the federal major disaster declaration.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency will reimburse 75% of eligible debris removal costs in Delaware, Fayette, Franklin, Hamilton, Henry, LaPorte, Lake, Madison, Porter, Tipton and Wayne counties.
And Gov. Mike Braun’s office committed Thursday that the state would cover 75% of the remaining share — or 18.75% of the total eligible cost — so local governments will only need to pay 6.25% of costs for eligible projects known as FEMA Category A.
“I want to make it clear that Hoosier communities, from our rural towns to the suburbs of our capital city, will not shoulder the recovery effort alone,” Braun said in a news release Thursday. “Debris removal is the next phase of this marathon, and we are with Hoosiers every step of the way.”
State treasurer to provide upfront cash for storm-hit communities

The money will come from an Indiana Department of Homeland Security contingency fund. There is no estimate for how much will be spent.
The announcement coincided with state Treasurer Daniel Elliott’s pledge Thursday to make $50 million available to local governments, schools, libraries and municipal utilities for public infrastructure repair, with or without a disaster declaration.
The rules for FEMA reimbursement are more strict: Eligible projects must be in the public interest, eliminate immediate threat to life, public health and safety and be the result of a declared disaster to qualify for reimbursement under FEMA Category A.
The Braun administration has also secured contractors to assist with debris removal and management, with the first state-led debris removal operations starting in Fayette County.
The Braun administration is urging local governments to work with county emergency managers to report waterways, rights-of-way and private property for debris removal.
Property owners should contact Indiana 211 for assistance, while local governments interested in reimbursement should email debris@erassist.com.

title: ROOTS Plants Seeds for a Different Kind of Delaware Education
description: ROOTS offers four-day school programs as an alternative to traditional education, along with one-day and two-day enrichment options for homeschooling families. By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE At ROOTS Farm & Forest School, a garden can become a science lab, caring for an animal can teach responsibility, and a walk through the forest ca[...]
text:
ROOTS also emphasizes individualized instruction. With a student-to-teacher ratio of 6-to-1, educators can recognize different learning styles and give children room to progress at their own pace while continuing to challenge and support them.
ROOTS offers four-day school programs as an alternative to traditional education, along with one-day and two-day enrichment options for homeschooling families.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
At ROOTS Farm & Forest School, a garden can become a science lab, caring for an animal can teach responsibility, and a walk through the forest can inspire questions that lead to a day of discovery.
The Delaware nature-based learning community serves children ages 2 to 14 at campuses in Georgetown, Milton, Clayton and Townsend. Its preschool, elementary and middle school programs combine traditional academics with outdoor exploration, project-based learning and practical experiences. A high school program is also planned.
ROOTS offers four-day school programs as an alternative to traditional education, along with one-day and two-day enrichment options for homeschooling families. Students learn math, reading, writing and science, but lessons are often connected to real situations rather than limited to textbooks, worksheets or memorization.
The school’s outdoor classrooms include gardens, food forests, natural play areas and spaces where children help care for animals. Students may also build with natural materials, participate in community service, complete STEAM activities, create art and stories, and work with others to solve problems.
“We learn by doing,” the organization states on its website, identifying one of the four beliefs at the heart of its educational philosophy.
The other three are taking responsibility, staying curious and solving real problems. Together, those principles are intended to help students understand not only what they are learning, but also why it matters and how it can be used outside the classroom.
Five foundational pillars guide the ROOTS curriculum: community, environmental stewardship, homesteading, nature studies and animal husbandry. Rather than treating those areas as isolated subjects, teachers weave them into students’ daily experiences.
A gardening project, for example, can introduce children to plant biology, weather, food systems, mathematics and environmental responsibility. Caring for animals can help students develop patience, empathy and dependability. Collaborative projects can strengthen communication, leadership and problem-solving skills.
ROOTS also emphasizes individualized instruction. With a student-to-teacher ratio of 6-to-1, educators can recognize different learning styles and give children room to progress at their own pace while continuing to challenge and support them.
Programs are designed for neurotypical and neurodivergent students, with teachers working to create an inclusive setting where children feel valued and capable. Auditory, visual, tactile and kinesthetic learning styles are incorporated into the school’s approach.
The school’s leadership has pursued specialized training in nature-based education and outdoor inclusion. Founder and director Talon Holleman has completed the Level 1 Nature-Based Teacher Certification Course through the Association of Nature-Based Education. Holleman and co-founder Travis Holleman are also certified as Forest School Teachers and Directors through the Forest School Teacher Institute.
That training complements the school’s focus on educating the whole child. Along with academic development, ROOTS seeks to nurture resilience, creativity, independence, social and emotional growth, and a lasting connection to the environment. “Our goal isn’t simply to help children succeed in school,” the ROOTS website states. “It’s to help them become capable, compassionate people.”
Families who select ROOTS are also invited into a broader learning community. The organization works with schools, libraries, youth groups, small businesses and other community partners to provide workshops, field trips and hands-on programs. Adults can become involved through volunteer opportunities, gaining the chance to learn alongside the children while supporting the school’s programs.
At a time when many parents are considering alternatives to conventional classrooms, ROOTS offers an educational model grounded in experience, curiosity and connection.
Its mission is straightforward: empower children to care for themselves, their community and their environment. At ROOTS, those lessons begin with children rolling up their sleeves, stepping outside and discovering what they are capable of doing.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A pilot program in Plymouth hopes to crack the code on insurance in coastal communities
description: The insurance challenge for coastal states like Massachusetts has been a vexing one. Inflation and tariffs are scrambling rebuilding costs, and the rise in climate-driven natural disasters has contributed to a recent increase in private insurers not renewing policies and the state’s insurer-of-last-resort seeing a growth in the number of enrollees.
text:
ONE COASTAL COMMUNITY in Massachusetts is preparing to spend the next nine months diving into the wonky insurance issues plaguing a critical 500-property zone that’s vulnerable to sea level rise. 
The rest of the state might want to pay attention. 
In Plymouth, a seaside town known for the arrival of the Pilgrims to its shores, is now confronting a volatile future as encroaching waters threaten its people, economy, and tax base. 
So, the town of 68,000 has launched an effort, backed with nearly $300,000 in state money, to figure out what to do about the potential higher insurance costs and lost tax revenue preparing to wreak havoc on communities like Plymouth as the impacts of climate change intensify. 
InnSure, a Cambridge-based nonprofit that helps communities navigate insurance markets through local planning, is building a digital platform that models how different building improvements and climate resiliency projects within the specific zone in Plymouth would affect insurance costs and reduce risk to extreme weather events. 
The new system, which builds on a pilot project launched in Salem last year, will be able to break down benefits as granular as, say, what happens if 300 of the 500 identified properties are raised by three feet, or if 200 properties install upgraded fortified roofs to protect against wind damage, or if the town installs a new marsh at the shoreline. 
The idea is that both town leaders and individual property owners will be able to determine what investments they should make in order to minimize risk — and therefore lower their insurance premiums.  
To Steve Brandt, chief development officer at InnSure, that means that town climate, energy, and planning officials are “firing up” the desktop application “every day to help inform decisions around the community.” 
“There are so many incredible resilience efforts happening here in Plymouth, but where the disappointment comes is, ‘Hey, we did all this great work, we spent all this money. Why doesn’t the insurance industry now recognize that with value in their pricing?’” Brandt said. “The whole purpose of this program is to turn the process on its head, where the community with this new data is in control of their insurability as opposed to hoping the industry responds to what they’re doing.” 
The insurance challenge for coastal states like Massachusetts has been a vexing one. Inflation and tariffs are scrambling rebuilding costs, and the rise in climate-driven natural disasters has contributed to a recent increase in private insurers not renewing policies and the state’s insurer-of-last-resort seeing a growth in the number of enrollees. 
The home insurance market in the Bay State is in far better shape than in hard-hit California or Florida, but the catastrophic losses there driven by wildfires and hurricanes create a sense of urgency here.  
Chunks of shoreline lost to rising seas and more frequent floods not only reduces the town’s property tax base, but it also threatens the livelihoods of people who depend on the town’s maritime economy, said Michael Cahill, climate resiliency and sustainability planner for Plymouth. 
The issue isn’t theoretical for Plymouth, either, which found itself in the bullseye of a record-breaking winter storm earlier this year that pummeled it with 25 inches of snow and took out power for 80 percent of the town. 
Unlike parts of the Massachusetts coast dotted with mansions and second homes, the immediate waterfront neighborhood in Plymouth is lower income, with three different Census tracts totaling around 2,000 households on or near the water earning 65 percent or less of the statewide median income.  
Those neighborhoods are the backbone of a bustling harbor key to the town’s economy, including a robust fishing and aquaculture industry and various cruises and boat tours coming through Plymouth.  
A lobster boat pulls up to a dock on a sunny September day in Plymouth to unload its catch. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
In total, 85 percent of the town’s revenue is generated by property taxes, said Derek Brindisi, Plymouth’s town manager. 
“An important part of this is what are the consequences if we don’t do this work?” he said. “Because of sea level rise, we’ll lose a portion of our coast, which means we’ll lose a portion of our economy and a portion of our revenue. That has a consequence on the services that we can provide — public education, public safety. So this work that we’re doing today has a trickle-down effect in so many other different areas.” 
Massachusetts could experience over $1 billion in coastal property damage each year by the 2070s, according to a state report released last year. 
That’s led the state to consider whether and how communities should retreat from the coast altogether, something under active consideration through a potential voluntary buyout program. And Massachusetts lawmakers are weighing a new requirement for property sellers to disclose its flood risk to new potential buyers. 
It’s against this backdrop that Plymouth is looking for solutions.  
Even as it pursues this effort with InnSure, the town has already embarked on a project to raise a frequently-flooded boat ramp by three feet and is studying how best to rebuild a sea wall separating the harbor from its downtown. And it’s one of about 20 communities in Massachusetts that offers residents discounts on flood insurance premiums through a federal program.  
A sea wall separates Plymouth’s downtown from the harbor. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
Plymouth is planning to raise a boat ramp that is frequently flooded. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
The scope of the problem of sea level rise — and the limited ability of one town alone to do much of anything about it — means partnerships like the one Plymouth has with InnSure are all the more powerful in arming residents with actionable information, Brandt said. 
“Climate change can be a highly charged conversation,” he said. “Data and personal experience with disaster or insurance negates some of that and can take a lot of that noise away. It becomes really practical because you boil it down to, ‘Here’s what could happen. Here’s what you could do to mitigate that risk. And here’s the implications if that’s not done.’” 
While InnSure’s project, which is set to be completed by the end of the fiscal year, promises to provide direction for how Plymouth and other coastal communities can grapple with rising seas, it also exposes two uncomfortable realities. 
Even if various resilience improvements lead to avoided damages and savings on insurance costs down the line, the up-front investments required can be prohibitive.  
There’s hope that the new data can help the town and local property owners win more grants to help fund the improvements, especially as the state readies an infusion of money through an environmental bond bill that the Legislature will likely send to Gov. Maura Healey’s desk this fall.  
But the initial cost of these projects risks slowing progress as communities up and down the coast — and increasingly inland ones, too — bear the constant drain of their budgets to beef up shoreline protection and refix roads, docks, and properties that have suffered repetitive losses.  
Then there’s the prospect that InnSure’s work will reveal large insurance gaps — and that it could take people paying more, not less, in insurance costs to close them. 
Just 4 percent of US homes have flood insurance, since only homeowners in the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s flood zones are required to purchase it. That leaves many properties that are at risk without coverage should disaster strike. Many general home insurance policies don’t cover damage due to flooding. 
“There are massive gaps out there in terms of what is insured,” said Chris Stark, executive director of the Massachusetts Insurance Federation. “I don’t envy the leaders that are going to have to get the buy-in from everybody to tackle this problem.”  
Plymouth officials know the tradeoff in embarking on such a localized deep dive into the insurance needs and opportunities of one part of town could uncover some unsettling realities and trigger a backlash.  
But they argue it’s better to understand where the vulnerabilities are and work to rectify them than not know at all. 
“If we get data that’s not favorable, it’s our role as the municipality to provide people with the most accurate information available to help them make sure that they’re making informed decisions,” Cahill said. “That will give us information on where, as a municipality, we should be focusing our efforts.” 
Plymouth Beach is a popular destination in town, but rising seas threaten the town’s economy. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
InnSure chose Plymouth in the first place as the site of this project because the town has been forward-thinking both in its approach to climate issues and its entrepreneurial spirit, Brandt said: The town declared a climate emergency in 2022 and is supporting the growth of several startup companies to grow its blue economy.  
Now, the hope is that the model works as a key part in the toolkit used by municipalities and residents to plan for the future and fend off the climate-driven insurance collapse that has taken hold in other parts of the country. 
“The goal for what we’re trying to build is to prove that this model works, take it to the rest of the town, and then work with the state to expand this,” Cahill said. “If we can really internalize and identify risk properly, we’ll be much more prepared to make actual changes that impact people’s lives.”

title: Wartime oil prices continue to benefit Alaska’s state treasury, new figures show
description: The price of North Slope crude oil topped $100 per barrel on Wednesday, crossing that mark for the first time since June, according to figures published by the Alaska Department of Revenue. Though the rising cost of diesel, heating oil and gasoline is hitting individual Alaskans hard — nationally, the price of diesel topped $6 […]
text:
U.S. Marines from the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit board M/T Celestial Sea, an Iranian-flagged commercial oil tanker suspected of attempting to violate the U.S. blockade by transiting toward an Iranian port, May 20, 2026. American forces released the vessel after searching and directing the ship’s crew to alter course. (U.S. Marine Corps Photo)The price of North Slope crude oil topped $100 per barrel on Wednesday, crossing that mark for the first time since June, according to figures published by the Alaska Department of Revenue.
Though the rising cost of diesel, heating oil and gasoline is hitting individual Alaskans hard — nationally, the price of diesel topped $6 per gallon on Thursday — the high cost of crude oil caused by the Iran war continues to increase the amount of money available for services and Permanent Fund dividends in Alaska.
Preliminary figures published Aug. 31 show the state earned just under $7 billion in general-purpose revenue during Fiscal Year 2026, which ended June 30. 
That estimate will be revised and updated later this fall, acting Revenue Commissioner Janelle Earls said in a memo containing the estimate. 
The new figure is more than $500 million above a prediction from March, which itself was another $500 million higher than a prediction from last fall. 
This spring, legislators and Gov. Mike Dunleavy approved $6.4 billion in general-purpose spending on services and this year’s Permanent Fund dividend. 
They also made plans for what would happen if more money was available, and those plans are now being executed, Earls said.
The wartime windfall means another $128 million for Permanent Fund dividends, enough to raise this year’s payment to $1,200 per recipient. Those payments will start Oct. 1. 
It also means an extra $115 million for local school districts and $15 million more for the state’s bulk fuel loan program, which fronts local governments the money needed to buy fuel for the winter.
After that spending, more than $341 million was left over for a deposit into the state’s Statutory Budget Reserve, a savings account that can be accessed with a majority vote of the state House and Senate and the assent of the governor.
Since July 1 and the start of Fiscal Year 2027, oil prices — and thus state revenue — have continued to run ahead of the March forecast.
In March, the Department of Revenue forecast that North Slope oil prices would average $75 per barrel for FY27. Through the first two months of the fiscal year, prices have instead averaged $84 per barrel. 
On Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he does not expect oil prices to decline until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
If that holds true, the result would be tens — if not hundreds — of millions of dollars extra for state lawmakers and Alaska’s new governor to budget when the 35th Alaska State Legislature convenes in January.  
Already, the Legislative Finance Division is projecting a $106 million surplus in FY27, according to a newsletter published Sept. 4.

title: Nebraska Supreme Court tosses medical cannabis federal preemption case, for now
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court on Friday decided a longtime medical cannabis opponent will not have another day in court to try to overturn the state’s voter-approved medical cannabis laws, at least for now. Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke, in a unanimous 29-page ruling, agreed with a lower court judge’s decision that former state Sen. John […]
text:
Attorney Eddie Greim of Kansas City speaks in Lancaster County District Court during a hearing on a lawsuit arguing Nebraska's medical cannabis laws are preempted by federal law. He represents the plaintiff, former state Sen. John Kuehn, at right. May 20, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court on Friday decided a longtime medical cannabis opponent will not have another day in court to try to overturn the state’s voter-approved medical cannabis laws, at least for now.
Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke, in a unanimous 29-page ruling, agreed with a lower court judge’s decision that former state Sen. John Kuehn of Heartwell did not have standing to challenge Nebraska’s medical cannabis laws.
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)
Kuehn argues that such state laws, including Nebraska’s voter-enacted legalization of medical cannabis, are “preempted” by federal law under the U.S. Constitution’s supremacy clause defining marijuana as a more dangerous drug that states are precluded from regulating.
“We conclude that Kuehn did not have either taxpayer standing or standing for a matter of great public concern to challenge the constitutionality of the acts,” Funke wrote. “We therefore affirm the district court’s order dismissing Kuehn’s operative complaint without prejudice.”
“Without prejudice” means Kuehn could bring a similar case in the future if circumstances change. For instance, since June 2025, the Nebraska Legislature has appropriated more funds to the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission and passed new legislation around cannabis.
What is ‘standing’?
For a case to proceed, a litigant must prove they’ve suffered an “injury in fact” by the time a case is filed or later amended. Kuehn filed his case in December 2024 and last amended it June 2025. Kuehn conceded he had not yet suffered the direct injury but sought to use exceptions.
Lancaster County District Judge Susan Strong listens to opening statements from attorneys on the first day of the civil trial to determine the validity of the medical marijuana ballot measures at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Tuesday, Oct. 29, 2024, in Lincoln. (Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)
“Standing refers to whether a party had, at the commencement of the litigation, a personal stake in the outcome of the litigation that would warrant a court’s exercise of its subject matter jurisdiction and remedial powers on that party’s behalf,” Funke explained in the opinion.
Lancaster County District Judge Susan Strong dismissed Kuehn’s case on June 26, 2025. She also presided over and ruled against a preelection challenge from Kuehn, filed in September 2024. 
The Supreme Court last week affirmed Strong’s ruling on the validity of Nebraska’s medical cannabis laws, also in a unanimous ruling from Funke.
Shifting federal guidance
During oral arguments in April in Kuehn’s preemption appeal, no attorneys or justices asked about shifting federal guidelines on marijuana. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche federally downgraded state-licensed medical cannabis to a Schedule III drug in April, down from a Schedule I drug. 
Schedule I drugs, such as heroin, LSD, ecstasy and peyote, are drugs the federal government has classified as having a high likelihood of abuse and no currently accepted medical value. Schedule III drugs are defined as those with moderate to low potential for physical and psychological dependence, such as Tylenol with codeine, ketamine and testosterone.
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska’s Medical Cannabis Commission is working toward implementing a state-licensed program and has licensed four cultivators. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and Attorney General Mike Hilgers signed off on a first set of regulations for the commission this summer.
The commission is rewriting its regulations to add fees before moving to license product manufacturers or dispensaries. The Legislature authorized the commission to do so this year.
Access to legally purchase medicine in Nebraska is still months, if not at least a year, away.
Standing exceptions
Kuehn tried to use two “narrow” exceptions to the standing rule: that he should be able to sue to try to prevent an “illegal expenditure” of public funds (taxpayer standing) or because the laws constitute a “matter of great public concern” (“great public concern standing”).
“It is not enough to wait for the United States government to one day come to Nebraska and challenge these acts,” Kuehn’s attorney Eddie Greim of Missouri had told the justices. “Instead, Nebraska’s courts should be open to Nebraskans who want to hold their Nebraska state government to its constitutional limitations.”
Nebraska Supreme Court Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke. May 4, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Funke wrote that other jurisdictions might find Kuehn had taxpayer standing, such as in other states, but Funke said doing so for Nebraska would be “inconsistent with our jurisprudence.” Funke also wrote that Kuehn’s claims did not present the “rare” circumstances to justify an exception for great public concern.
Unlike in other taxpayer standing cases that try to block public spending alone, Kuehn sought to go further and declare the Nebraska medical cannabis laws unconstitutional. 
Had the case proceeded and later returned to the Supreme Court, it would take five justices to declare the laws unconstitutional. For standing, Kuehn needed a simple majority, or four judges.
AG’s Office: Others could sue
Zachary Pohlman, the state deputy solicitor general defending five state officials from Kuehn’s lawsuit, had argued that at least five parties would be better suited to sue than Kuehn, such as the federal government, Hilgers, a property owner, a prospective medical cannabis user or a criminal defendant charged with illegally possessing cannabis asserting the laws as a defense.
Nebraska Deputy Solicitor General Zach Pohlman, representing Nebraska Secretary of State of Bob Evnen, presents his case during a hearing at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)
The Supreme Court ruled that its finding whether Kuehn lacked standing was not related to whether others could sue in Kuehn’s place.
Pillen was named in the suit, as were Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Department of Health and Human Services CEO Steve Corsi, former State Treasurer Tom Briese and Tax Commissioner Jim Kamm. 
Kuehn had also sued the 2024 ballot sponsors behind the voter-approved laws and current and former members of the Medical Cannabis Commission.
The Nebraska Attorney General’s Office had threatened to sue the state Medical Cannabis Commission if it issued licenses. But no such challenge materialized when the commission licensed the first cultivators in October 2025. No other state lawsuits have been filed at this time.
Nebraska Supreme Court upholds validity of state medical cannabis laws

Hilgers’ office has joined a federal lawsuit seeking to challenge the DOJ’s rescheduling of marijuana, which President Donald Trump is calling for.
In an unsigned statement Friday, Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana said another “desperate lawsuit, designed to erase the will of Nebraska voters and destroy medical cannabis, has failed.”
“For nearly two years, people with powerful political connections and deep pockets have thrown everything they can at us,” the statement said. “Lawsuits, accusations, obstruction and delay, because they refuse to accept what 71% of Nebraskans overwhelmingly decided.”
The group, which led the 2024 effort to legalize and regulate medical cannabis, said no matter the money, influence or political power behind the “next attack,” it won’t erase that vote.
The next Medical Cannabis Commission meeting is Monday.
