title: No way: Wisdom and, or, but, politics
description:
The wisdom of ancients offers guidance for our modern, confusing times, writes columnist David Romtvedt.
The post No way: Wisdom and, or, but, politics appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

It was in high school when I first read the “Tao Te Ching” (The Book of the Way), the sixth or seventh century B.C.E. text by Lao-tzu that translator Stephen Mitchell has called, “the classic manual on the art of living.”  Others say it’s a book about good government, both of the self and the state. 
The opening words are:

The way that can be spokenis not the constant way.  The name that can be namedis not the constant name. The unnamable is the eternally real.

Maybe that means the only people who should run for office are those who don’t belong to a political party.
I’m old enough to have been thought of as a sage in ancient China. That is, if I were in ancient China and also wise.  For better or worse, I’m a 21st century American and, in this country and time, a person of my age is simply old, notwithstanding the honorific title “senior citizen.”
Alaska writer John Haines wrote about the God whose name we cannot say, what he called the owl in the mask of the dreamer, the reality behind reality, the words on the tip of the tongue. That one might mean “don’t vote for those who are glib.”
I imagine myself at the edge of the continent looking out to sea. I can’t see the other shore. I jump in and the waves roll over me, the undertow drags me along the bottom and spits me up once again into the air. I shake the sand from my hair and look back to see the next wave on its way. “Oh, Lord,” I say. “No way.” Really, I’m eager to be dragged under again.
Or consider this: I ride a bicycle. In winter, I float down a snowy hill, drifting as if I were sailing on a great white sea. In summer, I haul my daughter behind the bike in a lightweight nylon and aluminum trailer. But now my daughter is grown. I feel bereft, riding toward my dissolution. It’s my attachment to my daughter, to the past, to the bicycle, and to my own legs churning that hurts. Still, it’s not so bad to feel these attachments — I’m happy because of them.
The English poet John Keats said that truth is beauty, and I thought he was wrong. I agreed with the Jamaican-born American poet Louis Simpson who, commenting on the Holocaust, wrote, “There is the truth, you show me the beauty.” Now I think both were right. My father would beat me then go outside to tend his iris beds.
I’m aware that this is a risky stance to take, especially in politics. I must embrace some ways of living and repudiate others. Will I follow the path of truth or beauty? Are truth and beauty linked? Can there be beauty in the ugly truth? At some point in life, each of us is asked to stand for what we believe. What if we’re not sure?
In “The Gift,” author Lewis Hyde reminds us that in some cultures a person of substance is recognized for what is given, for being a vehicle through which gifts flow. In our culture, the big person is measured by getting rather than giving. If you start a dot-com company with $4,000 borrowed from your in-laws and sell the company three years later for a billion dollars, you are a success. 
Ours is an age of exaggeration. Everything must be bigger, bolder, louder, longer, more nerve jangling and upsetting. Even the movies must be drenched in blood as the world itself, a thing as real as we are likely to know, is drenched in blood.
Twenty-five hundred years after Lao-tzu wrote the “Tao Te Ching,” that miracle of gemlike lucidity and deep wisdom offering guidance in the conduct of life. Donald Trump now leads the free world. The book lies open with its warning — abandon the way and great beings fall while the mediocre rise to prominence. How prescient they were, those ancients.
But it’s not helpful to dwell too long on what can go wrong in society. Even as the Tao offers a warning, it also reminds us that there is beauty everywhere and there are people worthy of our admiration and respect. That’s a good place to begin.
The post No way: Wisdom and, or, but, politics appeared first on WyoFile .

title: Contempt hearing over gender-affirming care at Children’s Hospital Colorado begins
description: On the first day of a contempt of court hearing, attorneys for Children’s Hospital Colorado and families of transgender kids outlined their conflicting opinions of what compliance looks like with a court order that directed the hospital to resume gender-affirming care for patients under 18.  Children’s Hospital Colorado stopped offering gender-affirming care[...]
text:
Children's Hospital Colorado is pictured on June 23, 2026, at the Anschutz Medical Campus in Aurora, Colorado. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)On the first day of a contempt of court hearing, attorneys for Children’s Hospital Colorado and families of transgender kids outlined their conflicting opinions of what compliance looks like with a court order that directed the hospital to resume gender-affirming care for patients under 18. 
Children’s Hospital Colorado stopped offering gender-affirming care to minors in January due to threats from the Trump administration. Four families sued Children’s Hospital after it initially stopped offering care to their children. The families are referred to by pseudonyms in the lawsuit due to safety concerns.
Attorneys for the hospital say it is in compliance with the order since it added gender-affirming care for minors back into its scope of services, despite medical providers’ refusal to prescribe such medications and patients’ inability to access them. The plaintiffs argue that’s not enough, and the hospital cannot blame providers who independently decided not to prescribe or renew gender-affirming medications. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Colorado Supreme Court ruled in May that the hospital violated the state’s anti-discrimination law when it stopped offering care like puberty blockers and hormone therapy to transgender patients under 18 but continued offering it to cisgender children for some hormonal conditions. The hospital has never provided gender-affirming surgeries for minors.
The state’s highest court directed a lower court to issue a preliminary injunction against the hospital. The lower court in June issued the injunction, which required Children’s Hospital to resume gender-affirming care for patients under 18.
Suspended gender-affirming care brings on dire mental health concerns for trans kids in Colorado

Despite the court order, providers who offer gender-affirming care through Children’s Hospital’s TRUE Center for Gender Diversity “each independently decided not to prescribe or renew gender-affirming medications for minors,” according to a statement from the hospital. 
A letter the providers wrote to patients says they each made the decision due to “the serious risk of federal action that could result in the inability to continue serving and caring for any patients for years into the future.” Providers said they intend to continue offering appointments to patients for education, counseling and other resources as they have since January. 
Plaintiffs filed a motion in June asking the court to hold the hospital in contempt, and a scheduled three-day hearing on the motion for contempt began Thursday. After opening statements from attorneys on both sides, Denver District Court Judge Ericka Englert closed the courtroom to the public while providers testified. She issued a court order that granted anonymity to the providers to protect their identities.  
Two plaintiff parents, referred to in the lawsuit under pseudonyms Denisha Doe and Grace Goe, testified about their daughters’ experiences receiving gender-affirming care from the TRUE Center and working with their providers. Both mothers said they sought care for their daughters from the TRUE Center because they wanted what was best for their children, and they understood the TRUE Center was the best place to receive gender-affirming care. 
Doe and Goe said they both contacted the TRUE Center through Children’s Hospital Colorado to initiate gender-affirming care for their daughters, not any providers directly. Both mothers said they did not choose who their provider would be — the TRUE Center assigned them a provider — and all communications, billing and scheduling went through the hospital, not the providers. 
In August, Englert granted the plaintiffs’ request to make the lawsuit a class action, meaning it applies to “All transgender adolescents ages 18 and younger who were receiving or will seek to receive gender affirming medical care from Children’s Hospital Colorado and were then denied or will be denied gender affirming medical care after January 2, 2026.”
Opening arguments
Elliot Peters, one of the attorneys who represents Children’s Hospital, said the preliminary injunction does not require the hospital to guarantee that providers will prescribe gender-affirming medications. He referenced language in the Supreme Court’s opinion, which says that the hospital “can’t force providers to prescribe gender-affirming care to individual patients, but it can define the scope of services it offers.”



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Plaintiffs asked the hospital to allow providers to offer the care to youth if deemed necessary, not to force doctors to provide the care, the Supreme Court opinion says. 
Providers had “ample reason” to fear threats from the federal government, and declining to offer gender-affirming care is not a decision doctors who have dedicated their lives to caring for transgender and gender diverse patients made lightly, Peters said. 
A brief plaintiffs filed ahead of the contempt hearing says the Supreme Court opinion focuses on whether care is provided to patients, which, given the providers’ refusal to prescribe medications, it is not. It says the hospital needs to make more of an effort to direct the decisions and actions of providers, since it is not a “powerless bystander,” the brief says.
“CHC has already shown the ability to forbid the Providers from providing medical gender-affirming care and has, for years, imposed a code of conduct on the Providers,” the brief says. 
John McHugh, an attorney representing the plaintiffs, said the duty to comply with the court order rests with the hospital, not the providers. 
Plaintiffs asked the judge to fine the hospital $50,000 for each day it is not in compliance and to direct the hospital to comply with the June order. 
Mothers testify
Doe’s 15-year-old daughter, called Danielle in court papers, had an appointment already scheduled after the announcement that the hospital would not provide medical gender-affirming care to transgender youth. She said she was surprised the hospital didn’t cancel the appointment, but she went anyway. 
At the appointment, their provider told Doe that they could only offer prescriptions to young adults age 18 or older, but added they can still order blood work and have conversations with younger patients like Danielle. She did not get any prescription refills at that appointment. 
After providers announced their decision not to offer prescriptions to transgender minors, Doe talked to her daughter’s provider on the phone. Doe said during testimony the doctor cried on the phone, after Stan Garnett, an attorney for the hospital, asked her if the provider was disappointed to make the decision. 
Doe confirmed after a question from Garnett that she heard providers during their Thursday testimony say they made the decision not to continue medical care independently and not with the hospital. Goe also confirmed she heard providers testify about how they came to their decisions to stop offering medical care. 
Goe’s daughter, called Gabriella in court papers, is 10, so she has not yet received gender-affirming medical care. Goe said they have not returned to the TRUE Center for counseling or monitoring for signs of puberty since it stopped offering medical care, because the reason she brought her daughter there was to establish a relationship with a provider who would eventually be able to prescribe the necessary medications when her daughter reached puberty. 
McHugh asked Goe if it is likely that her daughter will start puberty while the Trump administration is still in office, and she said yes, since she estimated it can start as early as age 11 or 12. 
Goe has not spoken with her daughter’s individual provider, and she confirmed that it was her decision not to bring her daughter back to the TRUE Center. She received an automated communication from the hospital about scheduling an appointment. After she asked for clarification on whether that meant it resumed medical care, the hospital responded that it is not providing medical gender-affirming care.
Federal threats
A December declaration from U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy threatened to pull Medicaid and other federal funding from any facility that provided gender-affirming care to minors. Colorado joined several other Democratic-led states in suing over that policy, and an Oregon judge ruled the declaration was unlawful in March. 
In July, the Department of Justice subpoenaed Children’s Hospital for patient data as part of an investigation into off-label use of prescriptions for gender-affirming care. The hospital is fighting that subpoena.
Denver Health also stopped offering gender-affirming care to youth in January and has yet to resume that care. Some primary care offices offer gender-affirming care to transgender minors, but Children’s Hospital and Denver Health were the largest providers. Cessation of care at Children’s Hospital is estimated to have affected about 800 patients. Many offices that specialize in gender-affirming care have long waitlists for patients. 
While Colorado has shield laws that protect gender-affirming care providers and patients from criminal prosecution and subpoenas by other states, those protections don’t extend to the federal government. Colorado also passed a law that prohibits insurance plans from limiting or denying gender-affirming care that a doctor identifies as medically necessary.
Hospitals in Texas and Ohio have stopped offering gender-affirming care as a result of settlements with the U.S. Department of Justice. A grand jury in Texas is pursuing criminal charges against gender-affirming care providers.
A jury trial for the families’ lawsuit against Children’s Hospital is scheduled for early January 2027.

title: How the US House could overturn the midterm election results
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump tried to maintain power following his loss in the 2020 election by exerting pressure on state election officials to, in some cases, “find” the votes.Loyalist Republicans in Congress then attempted to deny Joe Biden the Oval Office when lawmakers gathered to certify the Electoral College, bringing to light loopholes and deficiencies in the law that could have denied voters their choice. Similar flaws exist for U.S. House elections. With concern mounting among GOP lawmakers they may lose control of that chamber following November’s midterm elections, it is not a stretch to imagine state officials could, once again, receive calls from the White House or powerful Republicans in Congress.What’s less understood is that the House itself has the ability to investigate and potentially overturn the results of any of its 435 races. In a House narrowly controlled by one party or the other, disputes over a handful of seats could become significant. “The House and the Senate, they are the final judge of their own elections,” explained John C. Fortier, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank.“So, in theory, if a state went through a process and counted all the votes and certified the votes and sent in the results, it still could be questioned by Congress,” he added. “The House has done this in the past. It is much less common today. There was a time in the 19th century where it became extremely common.”Experts and officials interviewed by States Newsroom pointed to several circumstances that could occur.State officials could hold back an election certificate, a member-elect could seek to block another member-elect from taking the oath, or legitimate challenges could occur under a federal law dealing with contested elections.States act firstThe first step after votes are counted, or in some cases recounted, is for a state’s top election official, typically a secretary of state, to certify the results and send the certificates of election to the U.S. House clerk. But that doesn’t always happen.New York state election officials held back Republican Rep. Claudia Tenney’s ability to join the House following the 2020 elections amid a legal battle in an extremely close race.It wasn't until a state Supreme Court justice ruled in Tenney’s favor that she took her oath of office in February 2021, more than three months after the election.Fortier detailed another particularly messy example of a disputed House race in North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District following the 2018 election.The state board of elections opted not to quickly certify either Democrat Dan McCready or Republican Mark Harris as the winner given concerns about mail-in ballots. It took until late February, nearly four months after Election Day, for the board to call for a new election after Harris testified during a hearing that “his political operative orchestrated a fraudulent absentee ballot scheme,” according to an article from NC Newsline. That September, Republican Rep. Dan Bishop won a special election over McCready.And while the House didn’t step in at the time, it could have. “They essentially deferred and kind of waited it out,” Fortier said. Neither of those holdups determined control of the House, but a few state officials deciding not to send certificates to the clerk later this year could have an impact come January.State officials are not exempt from political influence from Washington, something that was on full display beginning in 2025 when Trump and Republicans in Congress called on state legislatures to redistrict to give them an advantage in this fall's elections. The results have rolled out even through September.House members can try blocking members-electAnother potential roadblock emerges on the first day of a new Congress when any member-elect can try to block another member-elect from being sworn in. That happened in 2021 when Texas Republican Rep. Chip Roy objected to lawmakers from Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin taking their oaths. The Democratic-controlled House voted 371-2 to approve a resolution directing the speaker to swear in everyone. The House has two additional options should a member-elect challenge another member-elect taking the oath. The first is to “provisionally or conditionally” seat that person and refer the case to the House Administration Committee for investigation. The second is to vote to not seat anyone and refer the dispute to the panel to determine who is entitled to it, according to a report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.The report notes that “it would be under only the most exceptional circumstances for the House to refuse to seat, even provisionally, a Member holding valid election credentials from the state, and it appears that this third option has happened since 1933 only two times on the first day of the new Congress, and once during the Congress concerning a special election.”The House voting not to seat anyone “would effectively nullify a certificate of election that was previously issued by the executive authority of the state,” according to CRS. How the House can probe election resultsThe Federal Contested Elections Act of 1969 provides another avenue for lawmakers on the House Administration Committee to investigate any election once a complaint is filed, typically by the losing party. This has happened dozens of times throughout the decades, including in December 2020, when Iowa Democratic candidate Rita Hart asked the House to decide whether Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks actually won the race, triggering a months-long investigation. The FCEA allows the committee to “impound records, ballots, tally sheets, ballot stubs, poll books, ballot boxes, voting machines or other electronic voting systems, and irregular or defective paper and absentee ballots,” according to CRS. The committee has the option to use the vote count sent by the state or “conduct its own recount and make its own determinations and findings,” the CRS report states.House members conducting a probe can even instruct states how to handle ballots.“Where state law requires destruction of ballots after an election, the committee may notify the state election officials to preserve the ballots despite the state law,” the report says. The panel would eventually make a recommendation and the House would decide by a simple majority vote which candidate to seat or whether to declare the seat vacant. That vote is the final decision “regardless of whether or not the Member-elect had been sworn in on the first day of the new Congress,” says the report.Decisions about how to decide any contested elections would be made by the new House that will convene in early January, not the one that will return to Capitol Hill during the lame-duck session that’s set to last several weeks in November and December. “It's not as if the outgoing Congress could just make a decision as to who's contested and who won the election,” Fortier said. “It's the new Congress that would do that.”But not just anyone can file a contest with the House. The person who challenges the results “must show that but for the voting irregularities or acts of fraud, the results of the election would have been different and the contestant would have prevailed,” according to CRS. Those investigations typically take months. The Iowa case of Hart v. Miller-Meeks began in December 2020 when Hart, the Democrat, filed her contest. The Administration Committee held a hearing in March 2021 after Miller-Meeks tried to dismiss the case. Then-Chairwoman Zoe Lofgren, D-Calif., argued against those efforts, saying “the American people deserve to know who actually won this election. And the people of Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District deserve to be represented by that person.”The case ended several weeks later after Hart withdrew her challenge. ‘As far as someone's willing to burn it’ Casey Burgat, legislative affairs program director and associate professor at George Washington University, said while any member-elect can challenge another member-elect’s ability to take the oath on the first day of the new Congress, it is somewhat unlikely a genuine attempt is made to do that next year.But that comes with a caveat.“I think the prospect for the tit-for-tat or the brinkmanship goes up exponentially if it is a close majority,” he said. “That just creates an opportunity for parties to see majority status and find reasons to not seat the other side.”Whether any potential challenge is taken seriously would likely be determined by who makes it. “If it's just a flamethrower, a Chip Roy-type person, I think that'll be discounted more than if it's led by someone like a Mike Johnson or someone in leadership or Steve Scalise,” Burgat said. “I've had conversations with a lot of these members and staff of like, how far can this go. And my response to them is often, as far as someone's willing to burn it.” Sarah A. Binder, senior fellow in governance studies at Brookings, said it’s unlikely that any Republican could successfully challenge a Democratic member-elect taking the oath if Democrats have a true majority and have elected their speaker.“There have been some years where the member-elect whose seat is being challenged is prior to that told to sit down, not to stand when the rest are to be sworn in,” she said. “But other times they actually swear in everybody because your winning seat could still be contested after the swearing in.”Then there’s the rogue clerk theoryIn addition to the possibility a state official holds back an election certificate, a member-elect seeks to block another member-elect from taking the oath and legitimate challenges occur under the Federal Contested Elections Act, some Democrats have raised concerns about the clerk of the House.The nonpartisan official’s office assembles the list of members-elect once they receive a certificate of election from a state official. And that list determines who votes for speaker, which takes place on the first day of the new Congress before any of the 435 members are actually sworn in. The House cannot move on to any other business until a speaker is elected. AEI’s Fortier said the clerk’s authority is ministerial and that whoever holds that office doesn't really have discretion over who to add to the member-elect list once the state sends in the certificate of election. The clerk going rogue during the vote for speaker also is highly improbable, he said. “I think it is not a very likely scenario, even though I think people are thinking about it. I am not even sure it's realistic,” Fortier said. “I think this is very difficult to imagine.”Burgat from GWU had a similar assessment that the House clerk doesn’t hold the authority to disregard election certificates once they arrive or to try to meddle in who can vote for speaker. “The minute that the secretary of state or its equivalent certifies the election and transmits to the clerk, a nonpartisan position, it goes on the roll,” he said. “The politics comes in after that fact.”The clerk’s office wrote in a statement that it “receives and verifies Certificates of Election from every state, placing on the Roll of Representatives‑elect only those individuals whose credentials show they were regularly elected.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: TN officials want waiver to speed up process to choose developer of Nashville parking lots
description: The Department of General Services has requested a waiver to speed up the process of choosing a master developer for state-owned land near the Tennessee Capitol. The department wants to put out a request for qualifications to find a master developer for 10 acres of parking lots surrounding the State Capitol. The goal is to […]
text:
The Tennessee Department of General Services received a waiver to keep the bidder for redeveloping 10 acres of state parking lots confidential. The bidder will also receive an option to renovate the James K. Polk Building, pictured above. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Department of General Services has requested a waiver to speed up the process of choosing a master developer for state-owned land near the Tennessee Capitol.
The department wants to put out a request for qualifications to find a master developer for 10 acres of parking lots surrounding the State Capitol.
The goal is to turn the lots into a mixed-use development with housing, hotel, retail and parking for state employees. The lots up for redevelopment include the one on which Elon Musk’s Boring Company is building the first phase of its underground tunnel for Tesla vehicles.
The parking lots that could be redeveloped are 16, 26 (Gold lot), 27 (Blue Lot), 28, and 29. (Photo: Tennessee Department of General Services)
Michelle Parks, a spokesperson for the Department of General Services, said the waiver does not make any part of the bid process private.
For public-private partnerships, the department must submit plans during the budget cycle, which the state legislature typically approves in April each year.
“The Department of General Services did not anticipate pursuing this procurement during the last budget cycle, so it was not included,” Parks said. “ The State Building Commission has the authority to waive that disclosure requirement, which allows us to move forward with the Request for Qualifications rather than waiting until the next budget cycle. The procurement will be openly advertised and competitive.”
The department’s request came before the Tennessee State Building Commission Thursday, where the board deadlocked 3-3 on a vote to approve the request-for-qualification and the disclosure waiver. Instead, the commissioners agreed to meet in two weeks to vote on General Services’ proposal, after concerns expressed by State Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, during public comment on the project.
Campbell, who is not on the building commission, said she favored the state redeveloping the parking lots into a mixed-use project, but was concerned the Department of General Services was trying to steer the project to a single bidder without a competitive process.
“The department certainly sounds like they already have someone they want to pick,” Campbell said. “It seems like they’re trying to rush this before the end of Gov. Bill Lee’s term.”
Lee is term-limited, with his final day in office coming in January 2027.
The redevelopment of the state lots is part of a broader plan by state officials started in 2022 to offload or redevelop some of the state’s downtown Nashville real estate holdings.
The Department of General Services submitted a request for information in September 2025 on the “feasibility of a private developer” building on those state parking lots.
As part of its request for qualifications process, whoever builds on the state lots will also receive an option to expand its development to the James K. Polk Building, which currently is home to the Tennessee Performing Arts Center, TPAC.
TPAC has already announced a plan to move to Nashville’s East Bank, near the new NFL stadium currently under construction.
Adam Kleinheider, the spokesperson for Republican Lt. Gov. Randy McNally, said McNally voted against approving the request for qualifications Thursday because he had additional questions and concerns.
“The request for qualifications was not in its final form until the morning of the meeting,” Kleinheider said.
Deborah Fisher, executive director of the Tennessee Coalition for Open Government, said she still didn’t understand why approving the project couldn’t go through its normal disclosure process.
“The legislative session starts in four months,” Fisher said. “That review step by lawmakers during the budget process is a healthy step. Less scrutiny from lawmakers means less scrutiny from the public.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: One man picks state rep in Memphis
description: The term “one man, one vote” is taking on new meaning in Memphis where, in the haste to fill a vacant seat, a lone member of the Shelby County Democratic Party selected the next state representative for House District 84. You could call it the perfect storm, or you could call it a cluster.  Either […]
text:
Matthew Szalaj, right, an aide to Memphis Mayor Paul Young, was selected over Kyler Gilkey to replace retiring Rep. Joe Towns of Memphis on the November ballot for House District 84. Gilkey came in second to Towns in the August primary. (Gilkey photo: submitted; Sjalaj: Shelby County Commission)The term “one man, one vote” is taking on new meaning in Memphis where, in the haste to fill a vacant seat, a lone member of the Shelby County Democratic Party selected the next state representative for House District 84.
You could call it the perfect storm, or you could call it a cluster. 
Either way, to replace retired Rep. Joe Towns on the November general election ballot, the party had just one person on its executive committee choose between two candidates: Kyler Gilkey and Shelby County Commissioner Matthew Szalaj. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Szalaj, a special assistant to Memphis Mayor Paul Young, received the appointment this week from Coleman Thompson, officials told the Lookout. Thompson was the only person remaining on the committee from District 84 after party leaders recently discovered two others had moved out of the district.
The appointment, rather than a special election, makes Szalaj the new state rep for two years. After receiving an appointment to the commission in March, he faces no opposition in the November general.
Shelby County Democratic Party Chairman Willie Simon and state Rep. Torrey Harris, who chairs the Shelby County Democratic Delegation, weren’t exactly enthused with the process, but both said this week they followed the rules.



Quotation







I have really studied this process, and we have to make some changes. I will be very blunt about that, because one individual cannot make a decision, or should not make the decision, for 72,000 individuals in a district.


– Rep. Torrey Harris, chair, Shelby County Democratic Delegation


Secretary of State Tre Hargett and Tennessee Elections Administrator Mark Goins also gave guidance on the process, along with the Tennessee Democratic Party, according to Harris.
Secretary of State’s Office spokesman Ben Hill confirmed that Goins provided a governing statute, which lists who participates in the selection depending on how executive committee members are picked.
Harris acknowledged that vacancies previously were filled through the same process but that changes were made in the last decade or so in how party executive committee members are chosen. That might have led to the small number of decision-makers, creating a bit of outcry among Memphians who follow politics.
Stockard on the Stump: Towns’ departure opens seat for Shelby Dems appointment

“I have really studied this process, and we have to make some changes,” Harris said Thursday. “I will be very blunt about that, because one individual cannot make a decision, or should not make the decision, for 72,000 individuals in a district.”
Gilkey and Szalaj made their case in an executive committee meeting before a group of residents who asked questions, according to Simon. But Thompson, who could not be reached for comment, had the lone vote and went with Szalaj.
But Simon and Harris both said he explained his vote by saying Szalaj called him first and that he promised his support, refusing to renege. 
Apparently, cell phone agility is critical.
To say Gilkey was disappointed in the process would be an understatement. He knocked on doors and campaigned all year, only to lose to Towns, who then resigned in late August after capturing the Criminal Court Clerk’s post.
“Ultimately, I think the process has some flaws in it,” Gilkey. “I don’t feel as though one person should be able to decide the representation for 70,000 people in a district.”
Even if three people on the party’s executive committee had voted, it wouldn’t be “indicative of how a democratic process should play out,” he said. Gilkey added that the voices of 1,500 voters who cast ballots for him in the primary “were essentially null and void.”
Gilkey said Thompson didn’t give him a chance to sway him or look at his qualifications “because of basically a pinky promise that he made to his lodge mate and frat brother.” 
Szalaj did not return a call seeking comment. 
Regardless, the concept of each person’s vote carrying equal weight appears to be slipping in a city that once depended on “one man, one vote” to gain a seat at the table. On the other hand, some people are more equal than others.
We’ll think about it
Tennessee Comptroller Jason Mumpower notified House Democratic Caucus Chairman John Ray Clemmons this week that he would consider taking a close look at the Department of Transportation’s process for selecting a contractor team for the I-24 southeast Nashville toll lane project.
Mumpower said in a letter that his office, including the Division of Investigation and Division of State Audit, “will review and assess the information (Clemmons) provided to determine what action, if any, is warranted, including whether to examine this process as part of our next audit of the Tennessee Department of Transportation, which is scheduled to be released in 2027.”
Clemmons went to the comptroller for help after Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti rebuffed him, saying his office doesn’t have “general investigative authority” to probe the toll lane contractor selection. 
Tennessee Comptroller Jason Mumpower is weighing a request from Rep. John Ray Clemmons of Nashville to examine the process by which the Tennessee Department of Transportation selected a contractor for the state’s toll road process. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Skrmetti narrowed it down, saying “Instead, it only has authority to conduct investigations into certain matters.” He cited an AG’s opinion from 2005 and claimed it doesn’t allow the type of investigation Clemmons requested.
The state’s Transportation Modernization Board and Gov. Bill Lee caught some folks’ attention when they chose a consortium of companies led by Spain-based Ferrovial to design, build and operate Tennessee’s first venture into toll lanes. The group of six mostly foreign companies called DriveTN offered to build the lanes to Murfreesboro and along I-40 East and I-440 in southeast Nashville for $9.2 billion while promising to pay the state nearly $25 billion in concessions, a tad bit higher than the two next closest bidders who guaranteed payouts of $7 billion-plus.
DriveTN’s upfront costs are expected to be paid during the eight-year construction phase. Eventually, motorists are to be able to jump on these express lanes for a fee based on traffic load.
The bid jumped out at some analysts.
Bank downgrades Ferrovial stock over I-24 toll lane bid

One international bank, UBS, lowered Ferrovial’s stock rating to “neutral” because of uncertainty about the deal, including questions about upfront spending, capital expenditures, the rate of return and the possibility that motorists will be charged high rates to pay the debt.
In a letter to Mumpower, Clemmons said recent news reports “give the impression” the 50-year lease was awarded because of “alleged financial relationships with former Lee Administration officials.” He added that people deserve to know whether the process was handled according to the law.
Transportation officials said last week that former TDOT chief of staff Steve Townsend, who took a job with Ferrovial, was not allowed to participate in its bid after leaving state employment. No doubt, we can all take comfort in that.
Transportation Commissioner Will Reid also said that the fees motorists ultimately pay will be determined by demand and have no connection to DriveTN’s massive payment to the state. 
But consider this: Taking an ultra-conservative outlook, if it costs $10 a trip to use an express lane one way each day, that equates to $100 a week, $400 a month, and about $4,000 a year. $20 a trip comes to roughly $8,000.
Only folks with some disposable income will be able to use them, leaving the rest of the unwashed masses to go without meat and curse the bread. (Apologies to Edward Arlington Robinson and “Richard Cory.”)
Wait a minute, man
Democratic Sen. Heidi Campbell of Nashville says she’ll be pushing legislation in 2027 to give local legislative bodies a vote over data centers as public opposition to the facilities grows statewide.
In addition to Metro Nashville, the Don’t Tread on Tennessee Taxpayer site created by Campbell shows multiple counties have paused data centers, including McMinnville, Coffee County, Knox County, Washington County, Johnson City, Jonesborough, Bristol, Grundy County, Cedar Hill, Anderson County and Hawkins County. Most of those send Republican lawmakers to the State Capitol.
Republicans and Democrats sponsored multiple bills this year to put more controls on data centers, which require large amounts of power and depend on gas-powered turbines to function, creating pollution. Only one GOP-sponsored bill passed, even though the others were legitimate efforts.
“If someone wants to build a facility the size of a small city next to your kid’s school and plug it into your power supply, the people who live there ought to get a vote,” said Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, over her proposal to let local communities have a say in approving data centers. (Photo: Nick Fantasia for Tennessee Lookout)
Campbell’s measure would be similar to the Jackson Law that gives locals a vote on landfills, she said, although some groups would like to see that buried under a pile of trash.
“If a company wants to build a facility the size of a small city next to your kid’s school and plug it into your power supply, the people who live there ought to get a vote,” Campbell said in a statement to the Lookout.
With Republicans starting to catch heat over data centers, expect more focus on them when lawmakers return to Nashville in January (Gee, we can hardly wait.) It will take a herculean effort, though, by Campbell to move her bill out of the first committee. Such is life in the superminority.
The same with Democratic Rep. Aftyn Behn who wants to shine more light on the tax exemptions Tennessee gives data centers. 
A break here, a break there, and pretty soon you’re break dancing. Well, maybe in 1984.
“Get, get, get, get, get on the dance floor, baby”*
* “More Bounce to the Ounce” — Zapp

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Department of Education seeks dedicated program funding in budget request
description: The Alabama State Department of Education (ALSDE) plans to request a $5.9 billion budget for fiscal year 2028 and establish line items for education programs that have previously been funded with supplemental funds.  The request is $77.8 million more than the department’s FY27 appropriation, or a 1.3% increase, and provides funding to the state’s classrooms.[...]
text:
Alabama State Schools Superintendent Eric Mackey talks to Alabama State Board of Education members during a meeting on Feb. 12, 2026. The board discussed likely the final version of the Alabama State Department of Education's fiscal year 2028 budget request on Thursday, which includes "memorializing" programs into the budget rather than using supplemental funding. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama State Department of Education (ALSDE) plans to request a $5.9 billion budget for fiscal year 2028 and establish line items for education programs that have previously been funded with supplemental funds. 
The request is $77.8 million more than the department’s FY27 appropriation, or a 1.3% increase, and provides funding to the state’s classrooms. State Superintendent Eric Mackey said in an interview after the board’s meeting Thursday that he hopes to establish funding for programs like school safety, security and climate in the annual budget. 
“That would be a big win to me because we want to establish that line item in the direct budget,” Mackey said. “The problem with the supplemental budget is because it’s supplemental, it’s not memorialized. When you pull the budget from year to year, the supplemental funds don’t appear anywhere, and we need them.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The program was mainly funded through the Education Trust Fund (ETF) supplemental appropriations for FY26 with $25 million and $2.5 million from the ETF for FY27. The board plans to request $27.5 million from the ETF for FY28. 
The ETF, which is funded mostly through state income tax, currently holds about $9.8 billion, according to the Legislative Services Agency’s fiscal dashboard. Lawmakers and agencies have been warned that the ETF is “tightening” and FY28 will be a “very, very challenging budget” year for the General Fund. 
The board will also request $14 million for school breakfasts, which was funded entirely in the supplemental budget for FY27 at $7.3 million. 
“That would cover the gap for all schools to be able to offer breakfast,” Mackey told the board.
The price of diesel fuel has impacted school buses. According to AAA, the price of diesel reached $5.71 a gallon on Thursday, the highest ever recorded average in Alabama. The national average is $5.98 per gallon. One year ago, a gallon of diesel in Alabama was $3.46 on average and $3.71 nationally.
The department will request $56.1 million more for its transportation program, a 9.6% increase from its FY27 appropriation.
“I don’t even have any idea how we’ll get ahead of that if the price of diesel doesn’t stabilize between now and next year, but hopefully it will,” Mackey said.
For about half of Alabama students, the bus is the only option and routes can take over an hour in rural parts of the state, Mackey said.
“When kids are six years old, they think it’ll be exciting to ride the school bus. The truth is, there are very few kids riding the school bus because they want to,” he said. “It’s a basic service. It’s got to be there for the kids to learn. They’ve got to get to school.”
The board will approve its final budget request in October, but can continue to make adjustments as finalized school data is released this fall and a new administration takes office.  The Legislature will have the final word on the budget.

text:
The flyer for Lefty’s Alley and Eats NFL Launch Kickoff Party on Sunday, September 13. Photo Credit: Lefty’s Alley and Eats.
Lefty’s Alley and Eats is welcoming in the new NFL season with NFL Kickoff Launch Parties at its Lewes and Newark locations with raffles to support local nonprofit organizations.
 
Lefty’s Alley and Eats will celebrate the start of a new NFL season with NFL Kickoff Launch Parties at its Lewes and Newark locations on Sunday, September 13, according to a company press release sent on September 9. The launch parties will feature food and drink specials throughout the day, raffles and giveaways in addition to the football action.
Raffle tickets will cost $5 and the winners will be announced at halftime of the 1:00 p.m. slate of games. All raffle proceeds will be donated to two local nonprofits. Each Lefty’s location will match the total amount raised on site and make additional donations to each locations respective organization. 
The Lewes location will be donating to Home of the Brave which is an organization based in Milford, Delaware, trying to reduce homelessness for Military Veterans, according to the organization’s website. The Newark location — the company’s newest location — will support Special Olympics Delaware which provides sporting opportunities for children and adults with intellectual disabilities. 
(To learn more about Lefty’s Newark location click here.)
“Football season is always a big part of the experience at Lefty’s, but we wanted this year’s kickoff to be about more than just watching the games,” Lefty’s Alley and Eats founder and owner, DJ Hill, said via the press release. “It’s an opportunity for our guests, our team and Lefty’s to come together, have some fun and make a meaningful contribution to organizations doing incredible work right here in our communities.”
Representatives from each nonprofit organization are expected to be in attendance at the respective locations to share more about their organization and the work being done in the community. 
Lefty’s launch parties are the start of its gameday schedule for the 2026-2027 NFL season. 
Starting on September 20, Lefty’s will follow a “Sunday Game Day routine” that features a raffle with one free entry, a jersey giveaway at halftime of the 1:00 p.m. slate of games and food and drink specials throughout the day. The routine is scheduled to take place across all 18 NFL regular season Sundays.

title: Federal judge dismisses claims ICE detained Nashville journalist in retaliation for her reporting
description: A federal judge has dismissed a petition by a Nashville Spanish-language news reporter that alleged her detention by federal immigration agents this year was an unconstitutional retaliation for her critical reporting on immigration raids. Estefany Rodriguez, a reporter for Nashville Noticias, was the subject of a targeted arrest on March 4 by Immigration and[...]
text:
Estefany Maria Rodríguez Florez, a reporter for the Spanish-language news outlet Nashville Noticias, was arrested by ICE March 4 south Nashville. (Photo: Courtesy of Nashville Noticias)A federal judge has dismissed a petition by a Nashville Spanish-language news reporter that alleged her detention by federal immigration agents this year was an unconstitutional retaliation for her critical reporting on immigration raids.
Estefany Rodriguez, a reporter for Nashville Noticias, was the subject of a targeted arrest on March 4 by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who surveilled her leaving her home with her husband and 7-year-old daughter in a car displaying the news outlet’s logo before pulling the couple over to make the arrest after the child had been dropped off at school.
Rodriguez was held for two weeks in federal facilities in Alabama and Louisiana before her release was secured by attorneys.  She has alleged mistreatment during her detention.
In court filings, Rodriguez’ attorneys alleged her arrest, initial denial of bond and swift transfer to out-of-state facilities “indicated retaliation against Rodríguez in violation of the First Amendment due to her work as a journalist, including reporting on ICE.” They also alleged other constitutional violations in her apprehension and detention and sought an injunction preventing “any enforcement action against (Rodriguez) to retaliate against her for past speech or to chill future speech.”
Nashville journalist released from ICE detention details retaliation claims 

U.S. District Judge Eli Richardson dismissed those claims largely on procedural grounds Wednesday, ruling it was improper to include them as part of a so-called habeas corpus petition. Habeas corpus petitions challenge the lawfulness of an individual’s detention.  
“What [Rodriguez] seeks here is a wide-ranging injunction against all sorts of potential unlawful behavior in the future that is separate and apart from any specific challenge made (in her habeas corpus petition) to her March 4, 2026 arrest and subsequent detention.”
Richardson also ruled the petition, originally filed before Rodriguez was released from physical custody, is now moot. Rodriguez was released from a detention center on March 19, 15 days after she was initially detained. She remains free on a $10,000 bond.
Federal prosecutors alleged Rodríguez is illegally residing in the country after overstaying a tourist visa. Rodriguez subsequently filed for asylum based on threats she received reporting on government corruption in Colombia. She is now married to a U.S. citizen and is seeking permanent status through her husband, according to court filings.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: 25 years later, Asa Hutchinson reflects on Sept. 11 attacks
description: Asa Hutchinson had been leading the Drug Enforcement Administration for a month when he was in New Mexico on Sept. 10, 2001 for a 90-minute debate about marijuana legalization with that state’s governor.  The world changed the next day, and eventually so did Hutchinson’s mission. Hutchinson, a former two-term Republican governor, had a front-row seat […]
text:
Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson, accompanied by his wife Susan, speaks to reporters and friends and supporters at the state Capitol on Nov. 10, 2023, after filing papers with the Secretary of State to run for president in Arkansas.(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate) Asa Hutchinson had been leading the Drug Enforcement Administration for a month when he was in New Mexico on Sept. 10, 2001 for a 90-minute debate about marijuana legalization with that state’s governor. 
The world changed the next day, and eventually so did Hutchinson’s mission.
Hutchinson, a former two-term Republican governor, had a front-row seat to the changes the U.S. went through in the months following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people. He went from leading the country’s drug enforcement efforts to becoming one of the first top officials at the Department of Homeland Security that was formed in response to the attacks, which occurred 25 years ago.
That morning, Hutchinson and his staff expected to fly back to Washington. But when they woke up, it was to the news that a plane had rammed into the World Trade Center in New York. It was one of four hijacked planes that crashed into the Trade Center, the Pentagon and a rural field in Pennsylvania. 
“We went ahead to the airport, knowing I needed to get back to Washington, and the second plane goes in,” Hutchinson told the Arkansas Advocate in an interview this week. “And of course, at that time all of the commercial aircrafts are grounded, and so we had no means immediately of getting back. President Bush wanted me back, and so sent a military aircraft for me.”
Arkansas students learn about 9/11 attacks through oral histories 

That was how Hutchinson ended up in his home state of Arkansas that day. As the military plane refueled at Little Rock Air Force Base, Hutchinson said he checked in with his children in Washington, his wife in Arkansas and with the Department of Justice. He learned the Barbara Olsen, wife of then-Solicitor General Ted Olsen, died on the flight that crashed into the Pentagon, calling that the moment “when it got really personal.” 
It didn’t get easier. The DEA’s headquarters overlooked the Pentagon. Some of his staff witnessed the plane’s crash. The explosion that followed the crash shook the building’s foundations.
“The emotions were raw,” Hutchinson said. “It was a difficult day for everyone.”
Hutchinson, a former federal prosecutor who had served as a congressman in northwest Arkansas’ 3rd Congressional District, had been sworn in as DEA’s top official in August 2001. Changes began to happen at the DEA following Sept. 11, as agents began asking their informants about possible terrorist threats instead of about drugs. 
“All of a sudden, security at every level of American life has become a priority,” Hutchinson said. “On 9/11, the shift happened quickly, and with increasing intensity over the last 25 years.”
Sept. 11 unleashed a national reckoning about security and how to protect the country, and saw the passage of controversial surveillance powers via the PATRIOT Act. Months after the attacks, Congress approved legislation creating the Department of Homeland Security and the Transportation Security Agency. 
Hutchinson was nominated and confirmed as the department’s first undersecretary for border and transportation security, overseeing TSA and other agencies in 2003. He remained with the department until 2005, returning to Arkansas for an unsuccessful run for governor. Hutchinson went on to win the 2014 governor’s race..
But Hutchinson said the most important thing for people to understand about those days was how America and the world responded. The nation’s allies in Europe “came to our defense,” while Americans united in a way that hadn’t been seen since the attack on Pearl Harbor, he said. 
“We are divided today, and while it takes an emergency sometimes to unite us all, there are ways that we can reflect on the spirit of 9/11, our response at that time, and say, as a nation, we can do better,” Hutchinson said. “It didn’t matter whether you’re Democrat or Republican or independent. After 9/11, we were together, united, seeing what needed to be done to make sure that our freedoms were strong and our country was protected.”

title: Over 500 people completed Colorado’s new safety course for semiautomatic guns in August
description: Around 500 people in Colorado have completed a firearm safety course and exam required by a new state law to buy certain popular guns during the first month of the law’s implementation. That’s according to a legal filing in a lawsuit against the new law, created by Senate Bill 25-3. The law established a process […]
text:
Demonstrators hold signs during a Here4TheKids gun violence prevention sit-in at the Colorado Capitol on June 5, 2023. (Chloe Anderson for Colorado Newsline)Around 500 people in Colorado have completed a firearm safety course and exam required by a new state law to buy certain popular guns during the first month of the law’s implementation.
That’s according to a legal filing in a lawsuit against the new law, created by Senate Bill 25-3. The law established a process for people to purchase semiautomatic firearms with detachable magazines in the state. Opponents say it is an onerous hoop to jump through to practice a right guaranteed by the Second Amendment.
But “a person with a genuine intent to comply with (the law’s) requirements for obtaining a specified semiautomatic firearm (‘SSF’) can do so within a matter of days,” says a Sept. 1 filing from state lawyers, headed by Attorney General Phil Weiser, representing defendants Gov. Jared Polis, Colorado Parks and Wildlife head Laura Clellan and Weiser.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Over 3,500 people submitted applications for an eligibility card in August. Then, 1,125 of those cards were issued at 39 sheriff’s offices and 502 people went to complete a safety course and pass the exam, according to the filing. The number of people who completed the basic four-hour course available for people with hunter education was 409, and 93 people went through the 12-hour extended course.
It’s unclear how many people submitted an application but failed to follow up with a sheriff to get an eligibility card. Eligibility cards are valid for five years, so the 623 people who didn’t take a course still have plenty of time.
The data came from a declaration from Kirk Teklits, the manager of business operations for CPW. The declaration was part of a response to a request for a preliminary injunction against Colorado’s permit-to-purchase scheme.
“That’s a 14% completion rate. That does not show that this is a system that’s functioning well,” Daniel Fenlason, the Colorado State Shooting Association director of operations, said in a video posted to the organization’s YouTube account.
Anecdotal evidence
The new law went into effect Aug. 1. It requires prospective buyers to pass a background check, obtain an eligibility card from a county sheriff and complete a safety course to buy semiautomatic rifles and handguns with detachable magazines on a list developed by the state’s Department of Revenue. The process makes someone eligible to buy those guns for five years. CPW operates a database so industry professionals can keep track of who has an eligibility card and who has completed a safety course. Teklits wrote that 330 firearm instructors have created accounts with that database system.
Colorado prepares overhaul of semiautomatic gun sales

CSSA sued Weiser, Polis, Clellan and El Paso County District Attorney Michael Allen over the law last September, but then asked the judge to issue a preliminary injunction after the main components of the law began in August. In that newer request, the plaintiffs argue that it is too burdensome to buy the type of gun considered under the new regulations.
Lawyers for the state, however, contended in their response that the number of people who have successfully undergone the new process undermines CSSA’s argument, which was mostly supported by anecdotal evidence and speculation over wait times and costs.
“The four intended-purchaser declarants who have attempted to satisfy SB25-03 offer no factual support for Plaintiffs’ speculative concerns about ‘lengthy waits’ or ‘exorbitant’ costs, and in many instances undercut them,” the response says.
Declarants in that CSSA motion for a preliminary injunction said they experienced an application timeline of less than two weeks and application costs of $82.



Quotation







Coloradoans interested in going through the (firearm) purchase eligibility process have been able to do so reasonably quickly and in large numbers, particularly given how new this process is.


– Dan Coil, CPW’s firearm safety program manager


Teklits wrote in his declaration that the average time in September between a person’s completed application and when they got an eligibility card from a sheriff was 10.9 days. The average time between the card issuance and course completion was 11 days.
“The number of individuals who have already successfully completed the course is a testament to the fact that the courses are widely available and that the materials are understandable and accessible to participants,” wrote Dan Coil, CPW’s firearm safety program manager, in his own declaration for the filing. He wrote that he has received “unsolicited positive feedback” from people who have undergone the process, which he helped design.
“While the Motion for Preliminary Injunction relies on anecdotal accounts to characterize
the Firearm Safety System as dysfunctional, the statistics tell a different story,” he wrote. “Coloradoans interested in going through the SSF purchase eligibility process have been able to do so reasonably quickly and in large numbers, particularly given how new this process is.”
Lawyers also contended that costs and wait times are attributable to third parties, such as firearm instructors and sheriffs who refuse to process applications for eligibility cards. CSSA filed a declaration from Teller County Sheriff Jason Mikesell, who said his office is not participating in the program due to financial and constitutional concerns.
“The refusal of a particular sheriff to meet SB25-03’s requirements may subject them to injunctive relief by affected persons in a different lawsuit; it does nothing to demonstrate the law’s unconstitutionality in this case,” state lawyers wrote.
Lawyers also contend that the “shall-issue” licensing plan the law creates is constitutional under New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen, the landmark U.S. Supreme Court case that requires a historical analogue for firearm regulations. The law creates a narrow and specific standard and is analogous to licensing requirements throughout the country’s history.
Additionally, they wrote, historical tradition doesn’t include the widespread civilian use of guns like AR-15s, a model that began with military use in the Vietnam War.
“Colorado’s licensing regulation for SSFs is lawful for another reason: the state could, like ten other states have, prohibit possession of SSFs outright. All but one circuit to consider assault weapons bans since Bruen have upheld those laws’ constitutionality,” the filing says. “This Court can and should reach the same conclusion. The SSFs subject to SB25-03 are not arms protected by the Second Amendment.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: As Election Day 1876 neared, politicians hit the stump in Colorado’s mining boomtowns
description: With Republicans in control in Denver and southern Colorado considered solidly Democratic, the swing counties in Colorado’s 1876 election lay in its mountain mining districts. Voters in these diverse, rough-and-ready boomtowns had been an important constituency since the early days of the Colorado Territory. They were pivotal in defeating an 1864 attempt at[...]
text:
The town of Lake City, Colorado, is pictured in this photograph dated between 1880 and 1883. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-64)With Republicans in control in Denver and southern Colorado considered solidly Democratic, the swing counties in Colorado’s 1876 election lay in its mountain mining districts.



Sept. 3–9
Sept. 10–16 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

Voters in these diverse, rough-and-ready boomtowns had been an important constituency since the early days of the Colorado Territory. They were pivotal in defeating an 1864 attempt at statehood out of concern about taxes and other government intrusions, and in 1874 they were instrumental in electing Democrat Thomas Patterson, an Irish-American Denver lawyer, as the territory’s non-voting delegate to Congress.
Patterson’s 1874 election sent shockwaves through a Republican establishment that had long dominated territorial politics, and now the “Little Tiger,” as the newspapers called him, hoped to return to Washington as the Centennial State’s first full-fledged congressional representative. He faced Republican nominee James Belford in what was shaping up to be the marquee race in Colorado’s inaugural state elections, set for the first Tuesday in October.
Colorado’s predominantly GOP-leaning press was forced to admit that Patterson was an energetic campaigner and gifted public speaker, even as they urged readers to remain loyal to the Republicans.
“Mr. Patterson as an orator has few equals,” said the San Juan Prospector of a Patterson speech in Del Norte on Sept. 11, 1876. “But while Mr. Patterson, by the suavity of his manner has taken a fast hold on the people of this country … many do not coincide with him in his views in regard to National questions.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 1876, Colorado railroads extended only as far west as Floyd Hill in the present-day Interstate 70 corridor, and Cañon City in the south. For statewide candidates like Patterson and Belford, campaign stops in frontier mining camps entailed long stagecoach trips over rugged mountain wagon roads. Despite “not feeling very well owing to his long ride,” the Prospector noted, Patterson addressed citizens in Del Norte for an hour and a half.
Dueling Democratic and Republican meetings in Georgetown on Sept. 9 “had the effect of bringing the miners to town by the hundreds, and persuading nearly all the residents to come out,” reported the Colorado Miner.
“We could note but little difference in the size of the audience in the two halls,” the paper added. “Both parties certainly manifested enthusiasm in giving their respective speakers good houses, and applauding them at every opportunity.”
In Lake City, more than 1,200 people turned out for a Sept. 14 event featuring both Patterson and Belford, one of the campaign season’s few face-to-face debates between two candidates for the same office.
“There being no hall in the town of sufficient seating capacity to contain the audience, the meeting was held in open air,” reported the Silver World newspaper.
Corruption scandals, silver coins and grasshoppers were the hot topics in Colorado’s 1876 election

Belford took to a stand erected in front of the town drugstore and spoke for an hour and 15 minutes, followed by a 90-minute speech by Patterson, after which Belford was given a 15-minute reply.
“Despite the lateness of the hour and the growing chilliness, (Belford) held the audience till the close, and when his time was up was greeted with cries of ‘go on,’ but the terms of the agreement were adhered to and at half-past ten o’clock closed the largest and most enthusiastic political meeting ever held in San Juan,” concluded the Silver World.
As statewide candidates hit the stump across Colorado, county-level party conventions met to fill out their slates with nominees for the state Legislature and local offices, adding to the month-long political frenzy. Some newspapers, like William Byers’ Rocky Mountain News in Denver, were rabidly partisan and churned out a flood of commentary as Election Day neared.
“A big crowd … came out at Granite last night composed mostly of miners. Belford’s position on the silver question suits the people exactly,” reported a front-page item in the News on Sept. 12. “The Republicans are wide-awake and will elect the whole ticket.”
“The prospect south is very encouraging,” it added the following day. “The people are wide awake to the important issues of the day and alive to the danger of placing the government of the nation in the hands of the (Democrats).”
Other publications spilled far less ink on the day-to-day campaign drama. Especially in small-town papers, the printed material gathered to fill column inches could vary widely from week to week. On Sept. 16, the front page of the Colorado Springs Gazette featured poetry, an excerpt from a Rutherford B. Hayes campaign biography, and a short article on the latest fashion in fall bonnets, republished from Harper’s Bazaar.
And in Georgetown, the Miner’s Sept. 16 issue featured a short story about a boy who, upon being punished by his aunt with the chore of painting a fence, had “a great inspiration burst in upon him,” and contrived to trick his friends into doing the work for him.
“WHITEWASH — Tom Sawyer’s Discovery in Human Nature,” read the headline. “From Mark Twain’s New Book.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Senate Health chair wants WV to reinstate death penalty for egregious sexual crimes against children
description: Sen. Brian Helton, a member of Senate leadership, says he’ll push legislation to reinstate the death penalty in West Virginia. Under his plan, capital punishment would be an option in cases where a person was found guilty of felony sexual battery against a child less than 12 years old.
text:
Sen. Brian Health, R-Fayette, plans to reintroduce legislation that would reinstate the death penalty in cases where a person was found guilty of felony sexual battery against a child less than 12 years old. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Sen. Brian Helton, a member of Senate leadership, says he’ll push legislation to reinstate the death penalty in West Virginia. Under his plan, capital punishment would be an option in cases where a person was found guilty of felony sexual battery against a child less than 12 years old.
It would also apply to individuals who, in an attempt to commit sexual battery on a child, injures the sexual organs of the minor. 
“I want to use every tool in our arsenal from a justice standpoint to protect babies and protect innocent children from this atrocity,” Helton, R-Fayette, said in an interview Thursday. 
West Virginia’s death penalty was eliminated in 1965.
Helton introduced a bill reinstating the death penalty for egregious sexual crimes against young children earlier this year, but it didn’t get any traction during the legislative session. He plans to prioritize the legislation in the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January.
“I think we’ll have tremendous support,” Helton said. “Regardless of your party affiliation or your political views, if you cannot get behind standing up for our most precious young, innocent children who are absolutely devastated by this, then you really need to answer to your voters.” 
Helton disagrees with a 2008 ruling by the U.S. Supreme Court in the case of Kennedy v. Louisiana, where justices ruled 5-4 that the Eighth Amendment prohibits the death penalty for the rape of a child when the child did not die or the crime was not intended to result in death of the child. 
His legislation from earlier this year said the Supreme Court ruling “was wrongly decided and an egregious infringement on the states’ power to punish the most heinous of crimes.”
According to Helton’s legislation, jurors would have the ability to recommend the sentence of death or life imprisonment without the possibility of parole to the judge. The judgment of conviction and sentence of death would be automatically reviewed by the West Virginia Supreme Court. 
Helton is a close ally of Gov. Patrick Morrisey and serves as chair of the Senate Health Committee, where he is tasked with oversight of the state’s child welfare system. 
The Senate is overwhelmingly Republican, he believes that his bill on capital punishment will have bipartisan support. 
When asked about the possibility of faulty DNA evidence which would be used in prosecuting the sexual crime, Helton said an appeals process is available to defendants as a secondary safeguard.
“I don’t think we can just throw our hands up in the air and say well you know, someone may be wrongfully convicted, so we can’t have harsh penalties for people for these sort of crimes,” Helton said.
Senators considered a bill earlier this year to reinstate the death penalty for people convicted of first-degree murder and first-degree sexual abuse of children in the same proceeding. The bill didn’t make it out of the Senate Finance Committee by deadline.
A cost estimate prepared by the West Virginia Division of Corrections and Rehabilitation estimated that each execution would cost the state $91,000. The division said construction of an area to hold death row inmates along with a building to carry out the executions would cost $20.4 million. 
In 2025, the Senate also considered a bill to reinstate the death penalty for individuals who are sentenced for intentionally killing a law-enforcement officer or first responder in the line of duty.
