name: Alabama Reflector
title: Rhett Marques pledges business support in AL-02 race
description: The Republican nominee for Alabama’s 2nd  Congressional District pledged Thursday to reduce taxes and regulations for businesses shortly after he secured the endorsement of a business group. Speaking at an Enterprise tire store he once owned, Republican Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, cited his support for eliminating taxes on overtime pay and said he woul[...]
text:
State Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the Republican nominee for Alabama's 2nd Congressional District, speaks at a news conference Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, alongside Rosemary Elebach, Alabama state director for the National Federation of Independent Businesses (NFIB). Marques said he would reduce the regulations and taxes on small businesses if elected to Congress in the fall. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector).The Republican nominee for Alabama’s 2nd  Congressional District pledged Thursday to reduce taxes and regulations for businesses shortly after he secured the endorsement of a business group.
Speaking at an Enterprise tire store he once owned, Republican Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, cited his support for eliminating taxes on overtime pay and said he would pursue similar measures in Congress.
“As a state representative over the last eight years, I have worked hard to make sure that we have put more money into the hardworking people of this state,” he said at the news conference.
The campaign for U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, the incumbent and Marques’ opponent in the race, said in a statement Thursday that Marques is lying about the congressman to distract voters away from his own voting record.
“Instead of spinning up foolishness, Rhett should quit dodging debates and explain to voters why he’s voted to raise taxes more than 20 times,” the statement said. “I look forward to voting for myself in November and defeating Rhett’s unaffordable agenda.”
Marques received the endorsement from the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) just as The Center for Politics from the University of Virginia shifted the rating for the election toward Figures, from likely Republican to leans Republican.
Rosemary Elebach, the Alabama state director of the organization, said Marques “was a voice for small business owners” in the Legislature.
The Alabama Legislature redrew the map last May by putting in a map the Legislature approved in 2023 that federal courts later deemed racially discriminatory against Black voters.
The U.S. Supreme Court in Louisiana v. Callais, a decision handed down in April, weakened a section of the Voting Rights Act that led to that decision, which the court formally overturned a few weeks later.
Marques won the Republican primary for the seat in August after a campaign in which he emphasized his endorsement by President Donald Trump.
The Alabama Legislature in 2023 approved  HB 217, sponsored by House Minority Leader Anthony Daniels, D-Huntsville, which exempted hourly employees from state income taxes on overtime. The tax exemption expired in 2025 and was not renewed.
Marques said he would try to implement other Alabama business laws in Congress. One bill Marques and Elebash cited was SB 221, sponsored by Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, that excluded credit card transaction fees from sales and use taxes. According to the fiscal note, the bill decreased the sales and use tax receipts to the Educational Trust Fund budget as well as county and municipal funds.
Marques also echoed Republican concerns about turnout in the fall. GOP turnout in the May 19th primary fell over 2022, and just 5% of eligible voters cast ballots in the Aug. 11 special congressional primaries, which mainly featured Republican races.
“That is disappointing for a state that is heavily veteran, who have put their lives on the line for our right to come and vote,” Marques said. “It is very important for every member of this state to go vote and give their opinion because it is going to matter, not only for this state but for the direction of our country.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia has tightened online safety rules. Now comes the hard part.
description: West Virginia has already taken action to protect minors online. The harder question is whether the protections now on the books match the problems families are actually trying to solve.
text:
Facebook owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)West Virginia has already taken action to protect minors online. The harder question is whether the protections now on the books match the problems families are actually trying to solve.
For parents, online safety is not only about what children can access. It is also about what happens after they open an app: the notifications that pull them back, recommendation systems that determine what they see next, and endless feeds designed to keep them engaged.
That distinction matters because West Virginia’s newest online-safety law addresses a specific problem, not the entire digital environment.
What West Virginia’s new law actually does
House Bill 4412, which took effect June 12, requires certain websites and applications to verify that users are at least 18 before providing access to material harmful to minors when it makes up more than one-third of the site’s content. It also limits how verification information can be retained.
That is an important protection, but HB 4412 is not a general social media law. It does not regulate infinite scrolling, personalized recommendations, notifications or other engagement features. Its focus is narrower: restricting minors’ access to websites and applications dominated by sexually explicit material.
The law is also the latest in a series of West Virginia efforts to address online safety. Lawmakers previously considered bills focused on children’s online privacy, broader social media restrictions and parental controls over app access. None became law.
That history shows West Virginia has been testing different approaches. HB 4412 is a narrower step. The question now is whether it addresses the risks West Virginia families actually face online — and whether additional protections are needed.
The problem is bigger than access
The scale of young people’s digital lives helps explain why this distinction matters.
According to Pew Research Center, 97% of U.S. teens use the internet daily, and 40% say they are online almost constantly. Nearly half, 48%, say social media has a mostly negative effect on people their age.
Those numbers do not prove that social media causes mental health problems, and frequent use should not automatically be labeled addiction. But they do show why questions about how digital platforms operate deserve serious attention.
Research into problematic social media use is also developing. A review of 32 studies examining social media and anxiety found positive associations in more than half of the studies, with stronger associations in studies measuring problematic use and screen time. Association, however, is not proof of causation.
Good policy has to hold both ideas at once: children deserve protection, and policymakers should be careful about claiming more than the evidence establishes.
A law is only as strong as its effect
West Virginia is not alone in confronting these questions. States across the country are experimenting with different approaches to children’s online safety, creating a patchwork of rules covering age verification, parental involvement, privacy and platform design.
That makes implementation just as important as legislation.
Are families aware of the protections? Are covered websites complying? Are enforcement mechanisms being used? And are the rules actually reducing the risks they were designed to address?
Those questions should not be treated as criticism of HB 4412. They are the questions any state should ask after passing a law.
West Virginia also has a reason to pay attention to what happens beyond its borders. State Attorney General JB McCuskey recently joined other state attorneys general in a multistate settlement with Meta that requires additional child safety measures on Facebook and Instagram. The agreement followed allegations that Meta’s platforms harmed young users and encouraged problematic use — allegations Meta disputed.
The settlement does not answer every question about youth online safety. But it reinforces an important point: protecting children cannot be reduced to a single statute or a single type of online content.
West Virginia has taken a step. Now it should measure what that step accomplishes.
The goal should not be to regulate technology simply because it is new, nor to assume that every problem involving a teenager and a phone is the platform’s fault. Parents have responsibilities. Young people have responsibilities. Platforms have responsibilities, too.
The real test is whether West Virginia’s rules recognize all three — and whether, when a child goes online, those rules provide meaningful protection rather than simply another law on the books.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Black and minority business owners press NC leaders for new state contracting goals
description: GREENSBORO — For years, Gerald Carr knew where to turn when his Charlotte construction company needed help navigating North Carolina’s state contracting system.  Now, Carr said, the rules have changed and businesses like his are scrambling to figure out what comes next.  Carr, CEO of All-Pro Builders and Restorations, was among the dozens of Black […]
text:
Business leaders and advocates trickle into the town hall meeting at the International Civil Rights Center and Museum in Greensboro on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)GREENSBORO — For years, Gerald Carr knew where to turn when his Charlotte construction company needed help navigating North Carolina’s state contracting system. 
Now, Carr said, the rules have changed and businesses like his are scrambling to figure out what comes next. 
Carr, CEO of All-Pro Builders and Restorations, was among the dozens of Black and minority business owners and advocates who gathered in Greensboro Thursday to press state leaders for new contracting opportunities. The move follows the dismantling of the state’s Office for Historically Underutilized Businesses.
The town hall, held at the International Civil Rights Center and Museum, was organized by The Collective, a coalition of minority business organizations including the Greensboro Business League, the Greater Durham Black Chamber of Commerce and the NC Black Alliance. 
The message from the business owners and advocates in the room was straightforward: The state needs to make sure minority-owned and other small businesses don’t lose access to state contracts. 
The group is calling for all businesses previously certified through the HUB program to be transferred into the state’s Small Business Enterprise program, which is intended to provide contracting opportunities to small businesses across North Carolina. The group also called on Gov. Josh Stein’s administration to create a new Advisory Council on Black Affairs.
The asks come less than two months after lawmakers eliminated the HUB office as part of the state’s 2026 budget. As part of a greater state effort, House Republicans also overrode multiple vetoes from Stein, passing bills to cut government spending on diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
The fine print: NC’s $34B budget includes DEI cuts, ferry tolls, AI, prison funds and more

The office was created in 1999 following an executive order from then-Gov. Jim Hunt. The HUB office helped minority small businesses compete for state and local government contracts. 
Businesses certified through the HUB received dedicated training, were directly notified of new bidding opportunities and were part of a public searchable database. 
The budget change ended the state’s recognition of HUB certifications for state government contracts. The state Department of Administration said businesses can continue pursuing state contracts, but HUB certifications won’t be renewed. 
The distinction offers little comfort to some business owners who say the certification was an important part of how they found work and built relationships with larger contractors. Carr said he worked closely with the HUB office when he needed support competing for contracts and connecting with other construction companies. 
He said his company lost a contract worth more than $400,000, just three days after the HUB office was shut down. 
Left to right: N.C. Rep. Amos Quick III, D-Guilford, N.C. Sen. Gladys Robinson, D-Guilford, business owner Gerald Carr and Michelle Clark Jenkins speak on a panel in front of business leaders and advocates in Greensboro on Sep. 10, 2026. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline).
“This whole thing is a game. If you don’t understand the rules of the game, you can’t play,” he said. “Not only is it happening, but it’s also happening at full speed.” 
Carr’s experience was part of a larger discussion at Thursday’s gathering about how the loss of the HUB office could affect more than just individual businesses. Other speakers described the closure as a disruption to businesses that had spent years building relationships and pursuing contracts through the state system. 
Rep. Amos Quick III, D-Guilford, said the state needs to do more to communicate the economic effects of programs designed to support minority-owned businesses. 
“We must begin to amplify the impact and the positive impact that these types of initiatives and policies have,” he said. 
The criticism comes as the state tries to build a replacement system. 
At the event, state officials announced a new accelerator program scheduled to open Oct. 15. The program is expected to help businesses affected by the HUB office’s closure navigate the transition and fast-track small-business certifications. The state Department of Administration will oversee the program. 
Gabriel Esparza, the department’s secretary, said more than 6,000 businesses were enrolled in the HUB program when it closed. That left many business owners trying to understand what the changes meant for their existing certifications and future contracts. 
“We want to make this the best thing it can be, not only for small businesses but also to honor the spirit and legacy of all of the work that so many of you did and continue to do to lift Black businesses, minority businesses, and women-owned businesses across the state,” he said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Students no longer remember 9/11. SC teachers aim to make sure they never forget.
description: Teaching about the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, remains vital in understanding what happened after, educators said.
text:
Teachers for younger students are instructed focus on the "helpers," such as first responders, when talking about the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, as depicted on the Memorial Wall dedicated to the 343 New York firefighters who died that day. (Photo by Seanna Adcox/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — At 8:46 a.m. Friday, K-12 schools across South Carolina will go silent.
Although most students know why they’re observing a moment of silence, none were alive the moment American Airlines Flight 11 struck the north tower of the World Trade Center.
Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, that killed 3,000 people, teachers are tasked with explaining to students the significance of what happened that day. Roughly one-third of the country wasn’t alive when the attacks took place, which means it’s even more important to make sure students understand the significance of the attacks and their consequences worldwide, educators said.
“It is increasingly moving out of (students’) lived experiences, into their historical memory,” said advanced government teacher Patrick Kelly. “It is incumbent on schools to make sure that memory is vivid and alive.”
Patriot Day
Under state law, every Sept. 11 is designated Patriot Day in schools.
On Patriot Day, representatives of certain organizations, such as Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts, Big Brothers, Big Sisters, Boys and Girls Clubs, and Future Farmers of America, can request to speak to students about patriotism and civic involvement. As long as approved representatives give principals enough of a heads up, state law gives them the right to talk to students for up to half an hour.
Many schools also hold ceremonies to remember the attacks and the people killed, said Department of Education spokeswoman Christy Cox. Those might include history lessons, school choir performances and Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps presentations.
Those assemblies give “students across grade levels opportunities to remember the lives lost, honor the courage and sacrifice of first responders and service members, and reflect on the unity and resilience demonstrated by the American people,” Cox said in an email.
In the classroom
Although no state law requires certain discussion around the Sept. 11 attacks, teachers are expected to include them in lessons on major events in American history, Cox said.
“As we approach the 25th anniversary of 9/11, we recognize that an entire generation of students has grown up without firsthand memory of these events,” she said. “That reality makes our responsibility even greater — to ensure they will truly never forget.”
The state standards require one lesson focused on the Sept. 11 attacks. When students are in 5th grade, they are expected to learn about what happened and how the country responded through foreign policy, according to the state’s academic standards.
Teachers might weave the attacks into other classes about American history. For instance, during a unit in 8th grade on how world events affected the country or a 6th grade unit on global interdependence, teachers might use 9/11 as a way of exploring conflict, change and global connections, according to the education department.
High schoolers might learn about the attacks during their modern world history class, where students look at how the connections between the U.S. and the rest of the world changed because of major cultural, economic or political shifts. Or, the topic may become part of U.S. government classes, in which teachers could talk about the policy and national security shifts the attacks caused.
For the most part, specifics on how to address the attacks are up to school districts and teachers, Cox said.
Kelly, who teaches at Blythewood High School, considers the attacks an essential part of talking about modern government. Discussing the way government works in any great depth is impossible without at least mentioning Sept. 11, 2001, he said.
“That’s still shaping the way our government operates,” Kelly said.
On Sept. 11 each year, Kelly makes sure to mention the attacks and have a moment of remembrance. He lines up the anniversary with the start of discussions about federalism, using 9/11 and the government’s response as one of several case studies on how the U.S. government’s structure differs from that of other countries, he said.
The topic comes up again throughout his course, including during units on the country’s war powers and civic engagement, he said.
“It’s a constant source of discussion, because modern government was completely reshaped by Sept. 11 and its aftermath,” Kelly said.
Teachers can decide to talk about the attacks at any grade level. As part of the Palmetto Civics Project, which provides teaching resources on major historical events, the state provides teachers age-appropriate topics and activities to broach the subject.
For instance, elementary school classes might focus on the first responders who helped get people out of the wreckage, while middle school students might learn more about what people saw from the ground and how the country responded.
In all grade levels, teachers should make sure to branch out from talking just about the World Trade Center strikes, the handout suggests.
“Many students are familiar with the Twin Towers but may not realize that Americans were also attacked at the Pentagon and that the passengers of Flight 93 demonstrated remarkable courage in resisting the terrorists,” the pamphlet reads.
Changing memories
Although the events feel far removed for many students, some might still have personal connections through parents or other relatives, Kelly said. Especially in a city like Columbia, which has an active military population, students may know someone who fought overseas in the Afghanistan or Iraq wars.
Even for those without a personal connection, the Sept. 11 attacks feel closer to them than other major historical events, such as the attack on Pearl Harbor, Kelly said.
That’s at least partially because of their recency and partially because of how many photos and videos still circulate regularly. Unlike the attack on Pearl Harbor, which is preserved only through black-and-white photographs and a few grainy audio clips, 9/11 is remembered through a huge archive of photos and video, he said.
“Our students are part of that media ecosystem,” Kelly said. “They are exposed to that.”
Jonathan Hepworth, a history professor at Clemson University who does research on how people remember historical events, asks his students each semester which historical event most interests them. A growing number each semester has said 9/11, including this most recent semester, he said.
The reasons varied, he said. Some had a personal connection to the incident. Others got intrigued after watching a documentary, either about the attacks themselves or the conspiracy theories that sprang up in the aftermath.
That suggests the attacks are still significant to students, though the ways they understand what happened is different from how people understood it 24 years ago, or 15 years ago, or even five years ago, Hepworth said.
“It’s always secondhand to them,” Hepworth said of his students. “There’s always a certain amount of distance.”
Over time, collective memory of historical events shifts because of what happens afterward, he said. What felt like a dividing line in history for those experiencing it, even from afar, might feel like more of a curiosity to younger generations, he said.
Making sure young people know what happened, though, is essential, Hepworth said. When people stop talking about major historical events, they disappear from the public consciousness.
Hepworth pointed to the 1918 influenza pandemic as an example. Although the flu infected about a third of the world’s population and is estimated to have killed at least 50 million, the pandemic fell out of popular memory within decades, he said.
People considered the mass tragedy too painful to talk about, Hepworth said. But that led many to forget it happened.
That’s not the case with 9/11. Even though students are more removed from the event a quarter-century later, they are still talking about what happened, which means the difficult work of talking about a massive tragedy is successful, he said.
Losing that collective memory would mean losing vital context about why the world is the way it is, Hepworth said.
“The fact is that everything that we have and decide at any given point is the sum of all the decisions made before us,” Hepworth said. “If we can’t understand what decisions were made and why and people making the decisions they did, we are not going to have a very good understanding of why we are where we’re at.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Rutgers still focusing on care for 9/11 responders, survivors 25 years later
description: At least 6,900 New Jerseyans who survived the 9/11 terrorist attack on New York City have received free treatments for cancers, lung diseases, mental health issues, and other health conditions linked to the terrifying and toxic soup at Ground Zero.  Their care is coordinated through the World Trade Center Health Program at Rutgers University, part […]
text:
Vicente Benavidez has blood drawn for testing at the World Trade Center Worker and Volunteer Medical Screening Program Oct. 1, 2003, in New York City. Benavidez worked for four months removing asbestos from Ground Zero following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. The World Trade Center health program continues to treat first responders, survivors, volunteers and others suffering from the toxins in the air and the trauma surrounding the attacks. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)At least 6,900 New Jerseyans who survived the 9/11 terrorist attack on New York City have received free treatments for cancers, lung diseases, mental health issues, and other health conditions linked to the terrifying and toxic soup at Ground Zero. 
Their care is coordinated through the World Trade Center Health Program at Rutgers University, part of a nationwide program that has benefitted more than 144,000 Americans since two commercial airliners struck the Twin Towers 25 years ago. The attack killed nearly 3,000 people, including close to 700 from New Jersey. 
Decades later, patients — a mix of first responders and people who lived, worked or attended school near Ground Zero — continue to enroll in the federal program, which is part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That includes some 3,500 Americans who signed up in 2025, according to program data. 
“We are still here and would love the privilege of taking care of you,” said Dr. Iris Udasin, a Rutgers professor of environmental and occupational medicine who is medical director of New Jersey’s World Trade Center program, one of six centers of excellence providing this care. 


Need medical care?
For program information, eligibility details and applications, visit the World Trade Center Health Program website.


The federal program also serves people who experienced the attack on the Pentagon as well as responders to the airline crash in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Care is provided by a handful of New York clinics, the centers of excellence, and a national network of clinicians who diagnose, treat, and monitor patients for 9/11-related issues, with zero out-of-pocket costs. 
Udasin said some cancers and chronic illnesses can take decades to emerge. Nationwide, some 40% of participants have been treated for cancers, 30% for chronic lung issues, 25% for gastrointestinal concerns, 16% for asthma and 13% for PTSD, program data shows. 
Capt. Kristi Anderson, a physician who is the federal program’s chief medical officer, said the diagnoses make sense, given what patients experienced at Ground Zero. Like certain cancers, she said mental health issues can take years to surface. 
“People have coping mechanisms, they’re just busy, they don’t think about their mental health. Then sometimes later in their life, when they can sit down and have a chance to breathe, they realize they have symptoms,” said Anderson, an officer in the United States Public Health Service. 
The federal program often sees an uptick in interest following the anniversary of the attack, Anderson said, something she and others welcome. “It seems to happen every year, but this one will be pretty impactful,” she said. 
New research shows the World Trade Center health program — which spent $355 million on medical claims for 61,000 people nationwide in 2025 alone — is helping participants lead healthier, longer lives. Enrollees lived 35% longer than lower Manhattan residents of the same age, Anderson said, results she said likely reflect access to regular disease screenings, free care, and the sense of community the program offers. 
The nationwide program grew out of New York City-based efforts to provide free care for firefighters and other first responders who were at Ground Zero and soon experienced symptoms, including breathing issues and PTSD, according to its website. 
U.S. Rep. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-NY, is shown in 2015, with others supporting the permanent reauthorization of the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Reauthorization Act, which provides money for healthcare for first responders and others suffering from diseases from the 9/11 attacks and for the families of those who have died. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
After years of first responders and their advocates fighting for federal funding for health care, Congress, in late 2010, finally passed the James Zadroga Act, named for a New York Police Department detective who died from his exposure at Ground Zero. In early 2011, President Barack Obama signed the bill which set aside $1.6 billion over five years for what had become a nationwide program. In 2015, Obama extended the program through 2090 and it received supplementary funding several times before President Donald Trump approved the current federal spending plan, which includes nearly $1 billion for the World Trade Center initiative. 
Since its start, New Jersey — where nearly 17,000 people have received free cancer screenings, or other diagnostic work — has been home to the second-highest number of participants, after New York. Florida is third and Pennsylvania is fourth. Thousands of patients also live in Texas and Arizona, while more than 10,000 are Californians, according to program data. 
“That highlights the importance of having that nationwide provider network, so patients don’t have to come back to the New York metropolitan area to get care. They can just get it where they live,” Anderson said. 
As time passes, Congress has expanded the effort to include more diagnoses, like uterine cancer, which was added to the covered conditions list in 2023. The program has also provided nearly $200 million in research to support more than 150 studies related to environmental health concerns. 
Program eligibility is limited to people who lived, worked or were in school within a specific zone near Ground Zero, or those who responded to the attacks. It covers diagnosis, treatment and monitoring only for certain conditions that have been linked to that experience. Participants must have some form of insurance, Anderson said. 
While the program continues to grow over time, Anderson said estimates suggest there were some 400,000 people who lived, worked, or attended school in the Ground Zero area when the towers were struck and crumbled. That means more than 250,000 who remain eligible for care. 
“It’s a lot of people that could potentially receive benefits,” Anderson said.

title: Virginia rolls out more secure EBT cards to curb SNAP benefit theft
description: Virginia is replacing traditional food-assistance benefit cards with chip-enabled versions designed to make it harder for thieves to steal SNAP benefits from families. About 749,000 state residents receive assistance through the program.  Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced Thursday that the state has begun mailing new Electronic Benefits Transfer cards equipp[...]
text:
A SNAP welcome sign is displayed in a storefront. Virginia is rolling out new chip-enabled EBT cards designed to better protect food assistance benefits from theft and fraud. (Photo by Getty Images)Virginia is replacing traditional food-assistance benefit cards with chip-enabled versions designed to make it harder for thieves to steal SNAP benefits from families. About 749,000 state residents receive assistance through the program. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced Thursday that the state has begun mailing new Electronic Benefits Transfer cards equipped with chip-and-tap technology to households enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
The change is aimed at combating “skimming,” in which criminals capture card information at the point of sale and drain benefits before recipients can use them. Unlike magnetic stripes, chips generate a unique, encrypted code for each transaction, making the cards more difficult to skim or duplicate.
Households do not need to request a replacement, and benefits will continue without interruption during the transition, according to the administration.
The SNAP program is essential for Virginia families, Spanberger said, even as forthcoming changes from the federal spending bill H.R. 1 will reduce the program’s funding by up to $187 billion over the next 10 years, levy more of the cost onto states and change eligibility requirements for recipients. 
“At a time when many families are struggling to keep up with the rising price of groceries and Republicans in Washington are making the deepest cuts to SNAP in the program’s history, we are taking this step to make sure families have secure, accessible support — and are protected from bad actors,” Spanberger said in a statement. 
The first cards are going to areas that have experienced high levels of benefit theft, including Chesterfield, Colonial Heights, Clarke, Fairfax City and County, Giles, Lynchburg, Madison, Manassas Park, New Kent, Norfolk, Northampton, Orange, Patrick, Portsmouth, Radford, Richmond, Roanoke, Smyth, Surry, Washington and Wythe.
A second round will begin at the end of October, with all Virginia EBT cardholders expected to receive replacements by the end of the year. 
“If a family qualifies for food assistance to help them buy groceries, they should not have to worry about someone stealing them,” Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa said. “These new cards are a practical step to protect families and make it harder for criminals to take advantage of the system.”
Recipients will be able to insert the chip or tap the card at checkout through a dual-interface system. The state recommends tapping when possible because it provides the strongest protection. 
Virginia is the eighth state to adopt chip-enabled EBT cards and the fifth to use technology supporting both tap and insert transactions, the administration said. 
Other states have seen theft reports fall after introducing chip cards. California reported an 83% decline after making the switch in January 2024, and the administration said Alabama has reported similar results. 
“SNAP benefits are often what stands between the families we serve and an empty table, and no one should have to worry about going hungry because a criminal targeted the help they depend on,” Virginia Department of Social Services Commissioner Duke Storen said. 
“The threat of benefit theft is real, and this modernization strengthens the security of the benefits Virginians count on.”
Before the rollout, testers visited retailers across Virginia to make sure point-of-scale systems properly handled both successful and declined transactions. The Department of Social Services also tracked mailing times, card activations and transaction problems during testing. 
“Throughout the testing and rollout process, this has been a true collaboration, and the result is a stronger, more secure system,” said Travis Smiley, executive director of the Virginia Food Industry Association. “When families’ benefits are better protected, those dollars stay in our communities and support local grocers and businesses across the commonwealth.”
Because replacement cards will be mailed directly to recipients, households should make sure their local services department has their current address. After receiving a card, recipients will need to verify their information, activate it and select a personal identification number using the enclosed instructions. 
The Department of Social Services recommends locking cards through the ConnectEBT app when they are not being used and changing PINs regularly. Recipients should also never provide their card number or PIN in response to an unsolicited phone call, text message or email. 
More information is available through Virginia’s EBT chip card website. Cardholders can also reach the EBT Call Center around the clock at 866-281-2448.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: The day terror changed us and a Virginia governor stepped up to lead and restore confidence
description: There are times when I sit alone and think back — trying to unearth details best left buried — and it all still feels like a nightmare, one that hasn’t softened even through the gauzy filter of 25 years gone by. It’s not just in the reliving of the undiluted horror from that cool, clear […]
text:
In this handout provided by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, first responders pour water on the fire on scene following an attack at the Pentagon on September 11, 2001 in Arlington, Virginia in this undated image. American Airlines Flight 77 was hijacked by al Qaeda terrorists who flew it in to the building killing 184 people. (Photo by Federal Bureau of Investigation via Getty Images)There are times when I sit alone and think back — trying to unearth details best left buried — and it all still feels like a nightmare, one that hasn’t softened even through the gauzy filter of 25 years gone by.
It’s not just in the reliving of the undiluted horror from that cool, clear second Tuesday morning of September in 2001. Not since Pearl Harbor had murder at such mass scale touched our shores, and we didn’t know how to handle that.
It’s not just the lives that vanished from our midst in a twinkling, leaving an unfillable void where love and warmth and laughter and family once was. Two thousand, nine-hundred and seventy-seven innocent people perished that day in fire and torn, twisted steel. More have died since from its injuries and effects.
It’s not just the freedoms that we as a society willingly forfeited in the name of security after 9/11 — everyday liberties we treated as a birthright then but are hard to fathom in today’s paranoid surveillance state.
It’s all of it. Combined and compounded over time. On its silver anniversary, it washes over us, stirring old memories and fresh fears; reopening wounds still unhealed.
Each person of sufficient age and awareness on that day has those memories, unique to individual perceptions, locations and feelings. Those close enough to witness those strikes — who felt impact concussions and the searing heat of the flames, who heard the screams, who smelled death up close — are haunted by an experience they will take to their graves.
We have no words or comforts to assuage the still-raw grief of those who lost loved ones to those unholy attacks. The pain the rest of us feel is puny in comparison.
The 9/11 Memorial Plaza in New York City. (Photo by Jake Hirsch/NJ Governor’s Office)
To those of us in Virginia’s Capitol that morning, it began as a routine day with an odd twist. 
We had heard fragmentary reports of a small plane that may have flown into one of the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York. It occurred to me that a terrorist bomb in the underground parking deck of that complex in 1993 had killed six people and injured more than 1,000, but I dismissed the thought.
We were in the Capitol to cover a news conference that could roil that year’s statewide Democratic Party ticket in a gubernatorial election year. To the Democrats’ advantage, the news conference disintegrated halfway through when a Capitol correspondent at the event learned from her editors that a passenger jetliner had slammed into the Pentagon.
Whatever was happening, it was just a two-hour drive north of us on Interstate 95 in Virginia. On a television in the press office of Gov. Jim Gilmore on the third floor of the Capitol, I watched as the first of the twin towers collapsed in Lower Manhattan. On the same screen, I could see orange balls of burning jet fuel leaping from the destroyed western facet of the Pentagon, staining the deep blue sky of a perfect autumn day.
We were a nation instantly at war and gripped by terror. And in that terror, there was word that another hijacked jetliner was bound for Richmond with either our state Capitol or the Federal Reserve Bank as its target.
People of differing stations and functions — janitors, office workers, a legislator and the press corps among them — left the Capitol and gathered outside as word spread. I was among them, wondering if we were far enough from the Capitol should a plane strike it.
It was a false alarm. It evidently arose from the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 over the Midwest that was turned around and aimed at the U.S. Capitol. Flight 93 crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing all on board, after passengers, selfless and patriotic beyond comprehension, overpowered Al Qaeda terrorists who had taken control.
In those few dreadful hours as the unthinkable became lived experience, I was keenly aware as a journalist that rumors were not immediately distinguishable from facts, and each briefly had the same currency. The scared and uninformed were leading the scared and uninformed.
That’s when Gilmore stepped into the moment he was made for and calmly, confidently led Virginia. Our darkest day was his finest.
“I wasn’t really afraid. I was aware that maybe there would be some further attacks that we didn’t know about. There was some uncertainty,” Gilmore told me last week.
“We didn’t know the parameters of the plot. We knew there had been a strike at the World Trade Center, that there had been a strike in Virginia at the Pentagon, but we didn’t know what else was going on. The goal was to take charge of the situation and do the best we could,” he said.
He activated the state Emergency Operations Center in Richmond and instructed police statewide to directly report episodes of gunfire to officials there during the crisis.
The key was sound information communicated promptly. To that end, our 68th governor updated the media from his office conference room almost hourly through the day, and then addressed the commonwealth on live television that night.
“There is a public role to an officeholder, and it’s an opportunity — a duty — to communicate,” Gilmore said. “People sometimes think that talk is nothing, but actually talk — communicating to the citizens of Virginia — is everything, and that’s calming.”
Plus, he knew what he was talking about.
Gilmore served in U.S. Army intelligence, posted in Germany during the Cold War. He had been commonwealth’s attorney for Henrico County and state attorney general before becoming governor, so he was hardwired into statewide conduits of official information.
Most importantly, however, for three years before 9/11, he had headed the Gilmore Commission, a federally chartered panel that examined the nation’s exposure to terrorism and recommended ways to deal with it. His deputy on the commission was James Clapper, who served as the Director of National Intelligence.
Virginia Governor Jim Gilmore applauds for U.S. President George W. Bush as he announces the reopening of Reagan National Airport October 2, 2001 in Arlington, VA. (Photo by Mark Wilson/Getty Images)
That day changed us. Until 9/11, it was common to prop open the ground floor east and west doors to the state Capitol on beautiful spring and fall days, and anyone could amble inside without being stopped or questioned. That ended forever on Sept. 12.
Gilmore detests the Orwellian legacy of 9/11 and the toll it still takes on our freedoms and privacy.
“The lesson of ‘1984’ was that you never knew whether you were being watched by the authorities or not,” he said.
“The 9/11 attacks were a watershed. I’m not sure whether the public demanded it, whether the insurance industry demanded it, or whether the police demanded it, … but it’s transformed us into a security society, a society that is now being watched. I absolutely deplore this,” he said.
But hope abides, he said, noting public outrage that has forced numerous jurisdictions and agencies to suspend or cancel their use of automated license plate reading technology by Flock and other providers.
“I am frankly surprised and pleased that the Flock camera thing is being pushed back on by individual citizens,” Gilmore said. “People are saying, ‘Wait a minute, we don’t want to be watched all the time.’ And artificial intelligence, as it develops, will supercharge this problem.”
And when it comes to security, the man knows what he’s talking about.

name: National
title: Divorce becomes next battleground as states debate family values
description: Cerina Fairfax, a Virginia dentist and mother of two, spent nearly two years living in the same house as her husband while she was trying to divorce him. Virginia state law required couples with children, like the Fairfaxes, to wait a year before being allowed to file for divorce. Cerina’s husband, former Virginia Lt. Gov […]
text:
Missouri Republican state Rep. Cecelie Williams, flanked by Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe and Democratic state Rep. Raychel Proudie, speaks in April about legislation that clarifies the right to divorce while pregnant. In recent decades, most of the states that have tweaked their divorce laws have made it easier, not harder, to get one. But that may be changing. (Photo by Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent)Cerina Fairfax, a Virginia dentist and mother of two, spent nearly two years living in the same house as her husband while she was trying to divorce him.
Virginia state law required couples with children, like the Fairfaxes, to wait a year before being allowed to file for divorce. Cerina’s husband, former Virginia Lt. Gov Justin Fairfax, had also tried different legal tactics to prolong the process.
In March of this year, a judge granted Cerina sole custody of their children and ordered Justin to move out.
A few weeks later, with just days left before his move-out deadline, Justin fatally shot Cerina and then himself, police say, while their two teens were also in the house.
The tragedy focused national attention on state divorce laws, which have remained mostly static since 2010, when New York became the last state to allow no-fault divorce. In the years since, most of the states that have tweaked their divorce laws have made it easier, not harder, to get one. Virginia, for example, relaxed some of its requirements just days before Cerina Fairfax’s death.
Now that could be changing.
In recent years, more conservatives have turned to divorce as a “family values” talking point, with some pushing to make it harder for couples to divorce. By doing so, they’ve relaunched a national conversation that would have been nearly unthinkable just a few years ago.
In 1969, California became the first state to allow no-fault divorce, which allows one member of a couple to file for divorce without proving that the other person engaged in wrongdoing such as adultery, abuse or abandonment. No-fault divorce emerged from the women’s rights movement of that era, promising women greater freedom to escape from unhappy or abusive marriages.
But the loss of that freedom suddenly seems more plausible, particularly for those whose confidence in federal protections for women’s rights was shattered after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the constitutional right to abortion in 2022. And as state lawmakers ramp up restrictions around birth control, fertility treatments and pregnancy loss, new limits on divorce seem less far-fetched.
“What’s different now is that it’s actually gaining some traction,” said Marcia Zug, a family law professor at the University of South Carolina School of Law whose work focuses on the legal history of marriage. “Simply the idea that we’re talking about it seriously, that it’s part of some Republican party platforms, that it’s not just laughed out of the room.
“Even if we’re not anywhere near eliminating it, that is the major change.”
Earlier this year, for example, an Iowa Senate subcommittee approved a bill that would allow couples to opt out of no-fault divorce when they’re registering for marriage licenses.
“In the last generation, we have seen the chaos of — the circus of — pure no-fault divorce, (and) the ugliness of divorce and the breakdown of marriage,” Iowa state Sen. Jesse Green, a Republican, told his colleagues during a February hearing on his bill, which later died in committee.
“A lot of people are not getting married anymore because maybe, in some cases, they feel the lack of support and accountability with our law,” he said.
Oklahoma bill would end incompatibility as grounds for divorce

In Texas and Nebraska, the official state GOP platforms call for ending or limiting no-fault divorce. Other state Republican parties, such as in Louisiana, have considered similar party planks.
Republican lawmakers in states including South Carolina and South Dakota have filed bills to limit no-fault divorce or make the process harder.
Oklahoma state Sen. Dusty Deevers, a Republican and pastor, filed a bill in 2024 to abolish no-fault divorce, after saying he wanted to see public shaming for those who cause divorce.
At the same time, some prominent social media influencers have been using their platforms to call for streamlining divorce laws.
Hadley Vlahos, a Mississippi registered nurse with 2.2 million followers on TikTok, used her platform this summer to talk about her three-year-long divorce, which included an 11-day trial and hundreds of court filings. She has called for changes to Mississippi’s divorce law, one of only two in the country that doesn’t allow a no-fault divorce if one spouse objects. Her petition to change state law has more than 30,000 signatures.
Jen Hamilton, a nurse and content creator North Carolina who has 7.2 million followers across TikTok and Instagram as well as a bestselling book, called for changes to the divorce laws in her state after separating from her husband.
She recently appeared at a fundraiser with North Carolina state Sen. Woodson Bradley, a Democrat who co-sponsored a bill that would shorten the required separation period before divorce in certain circumstances. That bill remains in committee.
Hamilton’s goal, she told her followers, “is to do everything that I can to get North Carolina law changed to protect women — and some men — from these archaic, paternalistic laws that keep people trapped in marriages that are either unhealthy or dangerous.”
A paradox
Divorce has been declining in the U.S. for more than 40 years.
Four of the five states with the highest divorce rates — Oklahoma, Nevada, Mississippi, Wyoming and Alabama, as of the most recently available data — are Republican led; Nevada has a Republican governor but a Democratic-controlled state legislature.
But state laws aren’t an effective way to raise or lower the number of divorces, said Krista Westrick-Payne, a marriage and divorce researcher and assistant director at the National Center for Family & Marriage Research at Bowling Green State University.
“The more significant things that affect whether or not a couple decides to divorce has much more to do with their relationship and their personal situation,” Westrick-Payne said.


Religious areas tend to see higher divorce rates, according to her research. So do areas that are more politically conservative.
“That feels like a paradox,” she said. But those areas generally see more people marrying at younger ages — one of the biggest predictors of divorce.
“So it’s not to say religious people are divorce prone; it’s just they have all these other risk factors, and underlying population dynamics that affect this.
“People like to get on social media and make these overarching statements, flattening a very complex issue,” she said. “And I don’t think that serves anyone very well.”
The most dangerous time
The Iowa proposal to allow couples to opt out of no-fault divorce faced strong opposition from domestic violence advocates, who said such laws especially burden people fleeing domestic violence — who are overwhelmingly women — and can leave them stuck in a dangerous marriage while they try to prove to a court that they’re being abused.
“For someone experiencing domestic violence, leaving is already incredibly complicated, and for a lot of survivors, it is the most dangerous time,” said Lindsay Pingel, director of community engagement at the Iowa Coalition Against Domestic Violence, which represents 25 victim service provider organizations across the state.
Then-California Gov. Ronald Reagan, himself divorced, signed the law that made his state the first to allow no-fault divorce. Prior to that, a person trying to divorce had to prove in court that his or her spouse did something wrong. But such things are difficult to prove in court, and subject to a judge’s interpretation.
“We know that domestic violence doesn’t always come with the kind of documentation that someone who’s never experienced an unhealthy relationship might expect,” Pingel said. “There might not be a police report, or medical records, photographs or witnesses.”
Most survivors of domestic violence don’t talk about it with others until they’ve decided to leave, she said. And many don’t feel safe involving authorities in a situation that could make it more dangerous.
“We have to stop asking why survivors continue to stay in unhealthy relationships when we continue to put barriers in place that prohibit them from leaving.”
Cerina and Justin Fairfax tragedy underscores new Va. laws that could help prevent similar violence

Women who talked to Stateline about their divorces described years-long court battles with convoluted rules, fraught custody arrangements and uneven protections in cases of abuse.
Some states require months- or years-long waiting periods where a couple must be separated before they can file for divorce. At least three states — Arkansas, Arizona and Louisiana — allow so-called “covenant marriage,” a legally binding agreement that comes with additional requirements and is harder to end through divorce. Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is from Louisiana, is in a covenant marriage with wife Kelly.
Recently, some states have made it easier for couples to divorce. Maryland, for example, moved to a purely no-fault divorce process in 2023.
Virginia’s new divorce law includes some narrow changes, including an option for speeding up the divorce process. It also created a legislative work group to study whether the state should eliminate fault-based divorce entirely.
And in Missouri, Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe in April signed a new law clarifying that pregnancy can’t prevent a divorce from being finalized.
Pingel, of the Iowa domestic violence coalition, said supporting healthy marriages and protecting vulnerable people from dangerous marriages aren’t competing goals.
“Children benefit from safety and stability,” she said. “and keeping someone legally tied to a person who is causing harm doesn’t necessarily create a healthier family.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland 9/11 victims’ families fear others no longer remember the day they can’t forget
description: In the 25 years since the 9/11 attacks, family members of the 69 Marylanders who were killed that day said they're coping but the pain is still with them, but they worry that others are beginning to forget.
text:
Part of the memorial to the five residents of University Park who died in the 9/11 attacks. Besides a marker, the memorial includes a reflection garden with five prominent stones. (Photo by Steve Crane/Maryland Matters)Devora Kirschner had only been married to Lt. Darin Pontell for six months when he was killed in the Sept. 11 attack on the Pentagon 25 years ago.
Pontell, 26 at the time, had been working as an intelligence officer in the Navy when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon. A Columbia native, Pontell was one of 69 Maryland residents killed in the attacks.
“It seems like forever, but then I can quickly bring myself back to that time and have it feel like just yesterday,” Kirschner said this week.
Lt. Darin Pontell was working in the Pentagon when it was hit by American Airlines Flight 77 on Sept. 11, 2001. (Photo courtesy of Devora Kirschner)
It’s been 25 years since the terror attacks that flew two passengers jets into the World Trade Center and one into the Pentagon, and crashed a fourth into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, when the passengers tried to wrest control back from the hijackers. In that time, Kirschner worries that the unified support that existed between people at the time has dissipated.
She finds it disrespectful that people, specifically on social media, continue to fuel conspiracy theories about the attacks, when family members and friends of victims are still grieving their loved ones.
Combating these notions is what pushes her to continue talking about Pontell, supporting the Naval Academy and creating awards in his name. Kirschner had known Pontell since they were both in the sixth grade, and she continues to see his family regularly today.
“The further away you are, it doesn’t resonate as much,” Kirschner said. “I want people to have that understanding and have a connection … we all suffered because so many good people were lost that day.”
Basmattie Bishundat said she kept the faith when she heard of the attack on the Pentagon, where her son, Romeo Bishundat, was working as an information technician officer in the Navy. She had been on the phone with him earlier that morning and despite being unable to reach him by phone afterward, she said she was still hopeful he would come home.
Romeo, who grew up in Waldorf, had been working in the Pentagon’s Naval Operations Telecommunications Center since April 2001. He would have turned 24 just a few days later, on Sept. 14.
Naval information technician officer Romeo Bishundat would have turned 24 just days after the Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the Pentagon. (Photo courtesy of Devita Bishundat)
“I don’t even know how I’ve survived 25 years without my child,” Bishundat said. “The pain I’ve been through … I don’t know how much more a heart could take.”
As Bishundat looks back on the last 25 years, she said she feels there’s outdated information and not enough educational resources circulating about the attacks anymore. The new generations of kids who weren’t alive and don’t understand the implications of the attack deserve to learn from those who were there, she said.
Sharon and Alan Linton Sr. of Frederick echoed that sentiment. Their son, Alan Linton Jr., was working as an income analyst on floor 102 of the World Trade Center’s South Tower that day. They wish there was the same level of awareness and unification now as there was in the immediate years after, especially for younger generations.
“Fifteen years ago, I think everybody knew about it,” Sharon said. “Somewhere along the line, the school system decided it wasn’t necessary to recognize that day.”
Alan had called his parents minutes after American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower to let them know he was safe. As United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South tower he was in, his parents continued to call, but heard no word back from him. Sharon, Alan Sr. and several of their family members drove to the city to search for him the morning after, in hopes that he was alive and in a hospital somewhere.
Frederick native Alan Linton Jr. was on floor 102 of the World Trade Center’s South Tower when it was struck by United Airlines Flight 175 on Sept. 11, 2001. (Photo courtesy of Sharon Linton)
They held a “celebration of life” about a month after the attack, though officials hadn’t identified more than a few of his remains and didn’t confirm his death until nine months after. Sharon and Alan Sr. organized a funeral about five years later, when officials said they wouldn’t be able to identify any other body parts.
They later helped to partially fund the creation of an emergency center named after their son at Beyond Shelter, a homeless shelter in Frederick, as a way of supporting a cause Alan Jr. felt passionate about.
The pair doesn’t always do something special for Sept. 11 but said their family typically gets together for a meal at Outback Steakhouse – Alan’s favorite restaurant in Frederick at the time – on his birthday.
“There are very, very few days that we don’t discuss him in some ways,” Sharon said. “Alan loved food, and when we eat his favorites, we think about him, talk about him.”
Bishundat said she’s changed since Romeo’s death and strives to take after his outgoing, “playful” personality. She has grown to accept the situation and release her grief, though there have been days in the past 25 years where it’s been difficult to do so.
No matter the amount of time that has passed, families will always be emotionally affected by their losses, Bishundat added.
“If it’s a mother, if it’s a sibling, everybody is living a nightmare, a roller coaster, a tsunami,” Bishundat said. “It’s just different stages, different days.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Secretary of state race is setting the bar for a quality contest
description: What a delight the current secretary of state race is. It has everything that a quality election contest should have — most importantly, open and accessible candidates. No one is hiding from constituents or ducking media interviews. And Hoosiers have four genuinely good choices. In reverse alphabetical order, to mix things up, they are Libertarian […]
text:
The four secretary of state candidates gather before OneZone’s Voices of Leadership Luncheon Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Greg Ballard campaign)What a delight the current secretary of state race is.
It has everything that a quality election contest should have — most importantly, open and accessible candidates. No one is hiding from constituents or ducking media interviews.
And Hoosiers have four genuinely good choices.
In reverse alphabetical order, to mix things up, they are Libertarian Lauri Shillings, Republican Max Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh and Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard. They all have varying levels of public and private sector experience to bring to the table.
And they are busy. They are actively knocking on doors, running ads, attending community events.
The quartet already had one formal debate, and another by the Indiana Debate Commission is coming up Oct. 7. There are numerous other forums and events happening around the state involving the race, which tops the Indiana ballot this year.
And they have ideas! You heard me. It’s my favorite part about a campaign: the proposals.
Two Indiana secretary of state debates planned

Mitch Daniels’ 2004 run for governor was the first major race I covered. He had a new proposal every week, whether it be using Indiana contractors more, changes to the state’s economic development structure or stronger ethics rules. He had a literal foldout roadmap that had dozens of plans, and you could mark them off as he accomplished (most of) them.
It was a true campaign platform. He created buzz and conversations among voters and other candidates in the race.
That was a high-water mark, though. Over the years, candidates have backed away from detailed policy proposals. Instead, they trot out national talking points on issues that the office doesn’t even involve. There’s been some of that in this race but at least it’s not predominant.
Ballard is leading the way. He first suggested a state-crafted and -distributed voter guide and then followed that up by pushing a nonpartisan recount commission makeup involving former judges. And this week he proposed clerk and poll worker training.
Shillings believes an overhaul of the agency’s website is needed and supports more voter education resources.
Engling wants to use the office to identify — and eliminate — so-called chameleon trucking carriers that shut down after safety violations only to reopen under a different name. He also supports closing Indiana’s primary voting system. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Bayh is pushing a comprehensive audit of the office. He supports eliminating straight-ticket voting and allowing voters to put measures on the ballot.
Many of these items would need legislative buy-in, but smaller things can be accomplished administratively.
Debate the ideas all you want. Are they too expensive? Is that an important topic? That means people are thinking.
The race is worth uplifting, as many candidates in other races around the state have no interest in doing some of this kind of work.
During the primary, we sent out more than 100 surveys to candidates for our voter guide. We are a small staff and simply can’t do that many one-on-one interviews. We got a 40% return rate.
Another round went out for our general election voter guide, and it is looking even worse. Many incumbents – but not all – refuse to fill it out. Some don’t have emails where you can reach them and don’t answer calls or direct messages.
That’s not good for anyone in our political system. And that’s why I’m so excited by the secretary of state race.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia governor candidates target cost of living, but details remain murky
description: The two competing candidates for Georgia governor are both focusing on affordability but putting forward starkly different proposals aimed at easing household expenses. At a time when voters are anxious about the rising cost of living, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, is pitching a plan to allow local governments to exempt […]
text:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at a campaign event on on Aug. 27, 2026, and Republican Rick Jackson speaks at a press conference on Sept. 2, 2026, both in Atlanta. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder The two competing candidates for Georgia governor are both focusing on affordability but putting forward starkly different proposals aimed at easing household expenses.
At a time when voters are anxious about the rising cost of living, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, is pitching a plan to allow local governments to exempt sales taxes on groceries, qualifying take-home family meals, baby formula, diapers and feminine hygiene products. Cities and counties would have to opt in, either permanently or temporarily when grocery prices surge. To help with the transition, she proposed a one-year $250 million “Local Tax Relief Stabilization Fund” that local governments can tap into.
“What we are proposing is very simple. It makes common sense,” Bottoms said at a recent event. “It allows local governments the opportunity to suspend or even eliminate their grocery sales tax. Very simple. There are some states that don’t tax groceries. The state of Georgia doesn’t tax groceries, but local municipalities do. We want to be responsible and thoughtful about how these local municipalities balance their budgets and the relief that they may want to offer to people in their counties and their cities.”
Bottoms’ platform also includes eliminating the income tax for teachers.
Rick Jackson pledges ‘intelligent’ Medicaid expansion, but offers few specifics

Republican Rick Jackson, a wealthy businessman in the healthcare industry, wants to address affordability concerns with a 50% cut in the state income tax for all taxpayers, a sales tax exemption on some household utilities and an automatic gas tax suspension when those prices surge. He is also proposing a property tax freeze to allow officials time to reconsider how local governments assess property values while creating transparency for residents as well as eliminating taxes on tips.
“I want to start where most Georgians actually feel the affordability crisis: at the gas pump, the power bill, and then the paycheck, especially after taxes come out of the tip … The heart of this plan is immediate relief at the pump, on the monthly utility bill and in the paychecks of working Georgians. I’m not going to pretend that one governor can control every price, but when government can act to lower a bill, it should. And when an outside crisis hits, relief should move as fast as the crisis,” Jackson said at a recent press conference.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But both candidates’ proposals face financial and operational questions.
Bottoms’ grocery plan relies on local governments choosing to opt in. Clint Mueller, deputy director at the state association that represents counties at the state Capitol, said that sales tax makes up a significant share of local governments’ revenue, especially in rural communities with limited commercial activities, and that it’s also unclear whether exemptions would be voted on by local governments or if voters would approve them in a referendum.
Bottoms ups the ante in feud over debates in race for Georgia governor 

“And if so, who makes that decision to put it out to the local voters?” Mueller asked. “Think Gwinnett County,the county that has 17 municipalities, and they all negotiated agreements on these sales taxes. Well, if somebody’s got to make a decision on exempting groceries, who does that? Does the county have to get all the cities to agree, or do they have to get an agreement and then put it before the voters?”
Danny Kanso, the vice president of public policy at the nonprofit Georgia Budget and Policy Institute, said that while it remains to be seen how local governments could make up the revenue gap, eliminating those taxes would help lower-income families more than an income tax cut, which he said disproportionately benefits higher earners.
“There are revenue substitutes that could be found that might make this a little bit more palatable for localities where they wouldn’t necessarily have to choose between cutting spending or exempting groceries from taxation, but that would require broadening the proposal out a little bit to look for some of these revenues,” Kanso said.
Jackson’s plan to address affordability also offers few specifics about how he might achieve his proposals. Kanso estimated that cutting the income tax in half would cost the state budget more than $8 billion, and it wasn’t clear how the state would replace that revenue.
“[It’s] a hugely expensive proposal and not a lot of indication of how that would be paid for, or where the tax burden would be redistributed to, or what spending cuts would be made to achieve that,” Kanso said.
And like Bottoms’ grocery tax cut, Jackson’s tax cuts on household utilities and fuel would help lower cost for lower-income families, Kanso said, but that it remains to be seen how the state would pay for those proposals without cutting services or raising taxes elsewhere.
“It seems a lot of folks don’t want to talk about the how versus the what, and those are the details that are kind of necessary to determine if this is something that on the net would be positive or negative,” he said.
