name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Faith-based programs help fill the state’s childcare access void. They have their own challenges.
description: For 37 years, Emmanuel Child Care Center operated out of Emmanuel Church in Rochester, providing infant, toddler, and preschool care to families on the Seacoast. On Aug. 28, the center closed its doors.  According to Pastor John Tate, the childcare program was no longer the best use of the space to meet the community’s needs. […]
text:
Londonderry Presbyterian Church is home to Kids by the Common Early Learning Center. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)For 37 years, Emmanuel Child Care Center operated out of Emmanuel Church in Rochester, providing infant, toddler, and preschool care to families on the Seacoast. On Aug. 28, the center closed its doors. 
According to Pastor John Tate, the childcare program was no longer the best use of the space to meet the community’s needs. Instead, it is going to be home to a growing community food pantry. 
“We had a wonderful center that operated excellently for a very long time, and we made the difficult but lighthearted decision to move on to a different use of the space,” Tate said. 
For years, buildings of worship have been reliable places for families to find childcare. By providing faith-based teachings, access, or community, these programs with a limited presence in New Hampshire are giving families options for a different kind of care. 
Kids by the Common, located in the Londonderry Presbyterian Church, was a “mission of the church” created to help bring more families to the church and serve the community. For more than 50 years, Kids by the Common has offered full-day kindergarten, something public schools in Londonderry did not offer until this year, as well as preschool and infant and toddler care.
“We’re hoping to be able to help grow the church as well, get families involved and hope that they want to set roots in the Presbyterian Church,” said center director Beth Connolly. “It’s very welcoming to all family makeups, all family structures. So we have to make it a welcoming environment and have everyone feel like they can be who they are when they’re here” 
Connolly said that while the program is connected to the church and does offer care guided by religion, their goal is to teach children “to be kind.” 
“Our philosophy is based on teaching children to be good humans, to be kind to our earth, be kind to our property, and be kind to each other,” Connolly said. “So we kind of incorporate the church’s belief through that. It’s not necessarily through daily prayers or anything like that. During Christmas time, we talk about the birth of Jesus and take kind of an overview of it and put it at a children’s level, something that they can understand. … That’s kind of the gist of our religious teachings.” 
Gina Walsh, who operates Little Blessings in Northwood, rents space from St. Joseph’s Catholic Church. Her program is not directly connected to St. Joseph’s or Catholicism. Walsh said she teaches nondenominational Christianity through her infant, toddler, and preschool out-of-school-time programming, and homeschool enrichment. 
“We include a religious piece to our curriculum,” Walsh said. “We have themes every month, and part of our themes has a faith-based piece. … We also say a prayer before we eat. We usually do Bible verses.” 
Both programs are state licensed, receive state childcare assistance funds, and adhere to state early-learning standards. Walsh believes she has a quality program, but enrollment growth has been slow, she said, because of the religious aspect of it. 
“I’ve heard people calling us a Catholic program, and they don’t know if because we’re in a Catholic building, people perceive us that way and don’t understand that we’re open to all faiths or no faiths,” she said. “It’s not a requirement to be Catholic to come here, or to be a practicing Christian. I think there might be some misconceptions about families that are welcome here, or other faith-based programs for that matter.” 
A classroom at Kids by the Common in Londonderry. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Kids by the Common, however, has grown exponentially recently. In 2024, it expanded the program from two classrooms to six to care for more kids and offer more full-day programming with help from the Presbyterian Church. Enrollment expanded from 27 to 62 children in a year and a half. 
Connolly said her program’s increasing enrollment is due to several factors. She said she’s noticed a lot more families moving to Londonderry over the past few years because of its booming housing market, good public schools, and location near the employment hubs of Manchester, Concord, and Boston. She said the church’s and program’s inclusivity, small size, and family-oriented community are driving factors.
“There’s lots of families who are moving into town. So they’re looking at, ‘If I can’t purchase a house, can we rent a townhouse? Get into town and the school system?’” Connolly said. “The young kids start here with us.” 
Depending on a program’s relationship with the church, it can be subject to the church’s issues. Childcare programs are interconnected with what happens there, making things potentially unpredictable. 
Emmanuel Child Care closed because the church decided to repurpose the space. With five months’ notice and help from the state’s resource and referral agency, Child Care Aware of N.H., families and staff were given new placements and jobs. 
Tate said the program had been a blessing to the church, and he is happy to have it end on decent terms. He also said that while the decision was not financial, the program was a challenging endeavor for the church. 
“We didn’t operate it as a business, so it wasn’t really profitable,” Tate said. “But it wasn’t something that the church always had to subsidize either. There were years the church would subsidize the center, and there were years the center was in the black.” 
This year, St. Joseph’s decided to open a pre-kindergarten through eighth grade school in the same building as Little Blessings. Enrollment for Walsh has gone down this year due to the overlap, although she said she hopes to figure it out with the school and the parish. 
“That was a pretty hard hit for us that we weren’t really expecting,” she said. 
At the moment, Kids by the Common is the primary user of Londonderry Presbyterian. The church does not currently have a pastor, and the congregation’s numbers are low. As a nonprofit, the childcare program makes a weekly donation to the church to help cover utility bills and other expenses. 
Childcare programs, regardless of whether they are nonprofit or church-affiliated, operate on thin financial margins due to high operating costs. Connolly contributes financially to the church while also trying to maintain affordability for families. 
“We do some fundraisers throughout the year to kind of help balance out the budget,” she said.  “We’re very careful with what we purchase. We do a lot of Facebook Marketplaces, but we try to be mindful and you know just try to keep things as low cost as we can while still enhancing the program.” 
The closing of Emmanuel Child Care Center was emotional, Tate said. But he has hope for the future. In the final weeks of operation, leaders met with someone who is looking to start a childcare program in their church. 
“We know it leaves a hole,” Tate said. “But we are praying that God will raise up another center that will carry that on and pass the baton to somebody else.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT needs job coaches for people with disabilities. A new state pilot could help.
description: The SPARK-CT pilot will offer 10 months of paid training for specialists in job coaching — a workforce that was hollowed out during COVID.
text:
Thousands of workers with disabilities in Connecticut face barriers to employment, from lower wages to segregated work opportunities. Addressing those issues has only become more pressing as the state pushes towards “competitive integrated employment,” encouraging workers with disabilities to be hired alongside workers without disabilities, with equal chances for improved wages, benefits and promotions. 
But to make that transition, the state needs to overcome a related challenge: a shortage of the counselors, coaches and support staff who help workers with disabilities succeed in the workplace. 
As efforts to address broader caregiving, special education and other support-oriented workforce shortages continue across the state, the Bureau of Rehabilitation Services is stepping in with a program targeted at creating a pipeline for these workers, part of a larger group known as direct support professionals or DSPs, in Connecticut. 
“We’re building to ensure that we have the right supports accessible to all corners of the state,” said David Doukas, the director of the BRS. “We believe that we can train people entering the workforce in this and that they’re going to provide the best support possible.”
Earlier in the summer, the agency announced it was launching a pilot for a 10-month paid training program called SPARK-CT, also known as Strengthening Professional Advancement in Rehabilitation Knowledge via Certified Training. The planning and development of the pilot was funded through federal grants, and the pilot is expected to cost around $3.7 million from the initial planning phase through completion and project closeout, according to program information shared with The Connecticut Mirror. 
The money will be used to help develop a new cohort of Direct Employment Support Professionals, a uniquely trained subset of DSPs who specialize in job coaching and providing a wide range of employment services.
Over the course of the program, selected trainees will complete experiential and field work with community-facing rehabilitation organizations, while also receiving direct training from BRS on how to provide job coaching, handle administrative tasks and support workers with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
 By the end of the program, successful participants will have the knowledge necessary to take the National APSE Certified Employment Support Professional (CESP) Examination, a credential that trainees can point to as proof of their skills. 
The SPARK-CT pilot gives the state a chance to test how it can help to develop a key workforce, while also producing a cohort that can immediately fill vacant roles in a range of local organizations. 
“We’re all fishing in the same ponds for the same workforce,” Doukas said. “So the more that we can build, it is really going to benefit the entire system and the populations that we jointly serve.” 
The front door to employment
The Bureau of Rehabilitation Services, which falls under the Department of Aging and Disability Services, focuses on what is known as vocational rehabilitation, helping people with disabilities prepare for, find and keep employment. The agency also contracts with nonprofit and community-based organizations, known as community rehabilitation providers or CRPs, that help provide services directly to those in need. 
These CRPs are often the front door to employment services and other vital resources in communities, with people working with CRP staff and counselors to receive support.
But the state has faced a shortage of support staff at these community organizations for years, a trend that accelerated as DSPs left the workforce during the COVID pandemic. Reports suggest that the vacancy rate for DSP workers in Connecticut falls somewhere between 18% and 23%.
Connecticut is far from the only state dealing with this issue. “What’s happening in Connecticut is exactly what’s happening across the country,” said Chaz Compton, the project director for the Interwork Institute, an education and research center at San Diego State University that supports accessibility and inclusion efforts for people with disabilities.  
“During the pandemic the numbers of rehabilitation clients dropped because people were not coming out of their homes,” he said. “That lack of referrals impacted the ability of those community rehab programs to even stay open. Many of them closed completely.”
Years removed from the pandemic’s disruptions, the demand for services has returned, but the workforce challenges remain.
In recent years, salaries in the industry have been a concern, with workers often making at or close to minimum wage. In 2025, local DSPs, a workforce that is largely made up of women of color and other workers from marginalized backgrounds, earned roughly $19.65 per hour, or close to $41,000 a year working full time before taxes.
The pay for an entry-level DSP, meanwhile, starts at around $18.00 an hour.
Local advocates argue that increasing pay is key to improving DSP retention. “A for-profit can offer $25 an hour, but at a caregiver or caregiver agency, the starting wage is $17.25 or $18. You see that gap,” said Pamela Fields, the CEO of MidState Arc Inc. a local nonprofit that supports people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. “They’re going to go where the money is.”
The current DSP shortage is affecting people seeking services, contributing to longer placement times for people with disabilities. A national survey of community providers found that in 2025, 52% of community-based providers considered additional program cuts due to ongoing staff recruitment and retention challenges. Nearly two out of three providers said they turned new clients away because of staffing issues.
While the state does not have an exact figure showing the need for DSPs, more than a hundred roles are currently posted on the Department of Developmental Services’ online DSP job board.
In 2023, Connecticut’s Bureau of Rehabilitation Services hosted a daylong conference for employers, vocational services agencies and state agencies to learn about job programs for individuals with disabilities. Credit: Courtesy of CT Bureau of Rehabilitation Services
By providing a full-time financially-supported training that combines classroom, online and experiential instruction, the BRS hopes that it can help close this gap, particularly focusing on DSPs that can provide employment services.
The Bureau of Rehabilitation Services held information sessions about the SPARK-CT program earlier in the summer, and selected trainees began onboarding at the participating CRPs in August. Doukas said around 30 participants will be involved in the cohort, which will run until next summer.
Successful participants will be eligible for a number of financial incentives, ranging from $1,300 in completion bonuses over the course of the program to an additional $1,000 for obtaining the CESP credential. Participants will also receive roughly $32,000 in pay for their work over the course of the program. 
Meeting an urgent need
At Marrakech, Inc., a 55-year-old organization that supports people with disabilities and other vulnerable groups, hiring more DSPs has become an urgent need.
“It’s a big job that has not been recognized traditionally,” said Heather LaTorra, the president and CEO of the organization, which assists more than 1,000 people a year. 
Marrakech, Inc. is one of four CRPs partnering with the Bureau of Rehabilitation Services on the SPARK-CT program.
Even before joining the state, the organization had launched various programs to build up its staff, including a four-week “Earn & Learn” program that provides paid classroom instruction to prepare entry-level DSPs.
The organization also operates its longstanding Academy for Human Service Training, an 8-week program that blends classroom instruction and experiential work, with participants learning topics mandated by the Department of Developmental Services in addition to gaining certifications in CPR, first aid and other areas. 
LaTorra has worked at the CRP for four decades, moving her way up from a volunteer and intern to leading the organization. When it comes to training a prospective DSP, she says that Marrakech, Inc. focuses on potential more so than specific qualifications. Trainees are asked to have a drivers’ license, GED or high school diploma and clear a background check. 
Almost everything else can be taught, so long as a trainee is open-minded and ready to serve. 
The state’s new SPARK-CT training pilot, LaTorra hopes, can help this work progress even further. 
“This is going to help so many people,” she said. “It’s going to help get people off waiting lists. It’s going to help the organizations hire qualified people that are well trained. And the people going through it are getting paid from day one, have a full-time job and will have many options in this field going forward.” 
The SPARK-CT program arrives as the state works to support people with disabilities, particularly when it comes to employment and workforce development. 
According to data from the Center for Research on Disability, the national unemployment rate for workers with disabilities was 9.3% in 2023, compared to 3.9% for workers without disabilities.
In Connecticut, the disparity was roughly the same over the same period, with workers with disabilities facing a 9.7% unemployment rate while unemployment for workers without disabilities stood at 4.1%.
In 2023, the median annual earnings for workers with disabilities in the state was $31,660 compared to $52,990 for workers without disabilities. In other words, a worker with a disability made roughly 60% of what a worker without a disability made.
A survey published earlier this year by DataHaven found that while 1 in 4 adults in the state live with disabilities, there continues to be significant unmet need in Connecticut. Looking specifically at economic well-being, the report authors found “ a particularly large difference in overall self-rated financial well-being,”  between people with disabilities and those without.
A different approach to career pathways
“What we have seen, particularly since COVID, are two pressures on the workforce,” said Rep. Lucy Dathan, D-New Canaan, a co-chair of the legislature’s bipartisan IDD Caucus, which focuses on promoting laws and state initiatives that support people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. “There is pressure for the people that are providing the services: the nursing assistants, the paraeducators, the folks who are providing day programming. But then there’s also the ability for people with IDD to get meaningful jobs for themselves.”
The issue has spurred legislation in recent years. In 2023, lawmakers passed House Bill 5001, a multifaceted measure that expanded disability support in the state, including in employment and housing, with the larger goal of reducing lengthy waitlists for services. The bill came with a sizable fiscal note, including more than $30 million from the General Fund over two years. 
In an interview, Dathan acknowledged that the legislation was a significant step, but one that requires additional follow-up work. In the future, she’s particularly interested in advancing legislation around “supported decision-making”, an alternative to conservatorship and more strict guardianship arrangements.
On the workforce side, she said that finding ways to support direct support professionals could also be worth looking into, adding that the SPARK-CT pilot seems like a helpful step forward. 
“I’m really hopeful that this program is something that’s going to be meaningful for our state,” she said. 
Still, even with its potential, the SPARK-CT program faces some challenges. For one, while the training program offers pay and incentives, it still pays less than competitive full-time salaries in the area. The program also offers a pathway into the field that could help with entry-level staffing shortages, but it does not address the longstanding issue of low wages and the need for additional support for more experienced workers already employed as DSPs in the state.
Members of the SPARK-CT training pilot, joined by BRS and local CRP staffers, pose for a photo during a kickoff event in Meriden on August 26, 2026.  Credit: Photo courtesy of Bureau of Rehabilitation Services
Advocates say that even with these caveats, the pilot could be deeply valuable, training more people who can work as DSPs providing employment services.
“Being able to have programs that focus on those things and develop those things are hugely helpful to the sector as a whole,” said Danielle Middlebrooks, the advocacy director for the Arc of Connecticut.
The SPARK-CT pilot will end in mid-2027, and the current funding will only support one round of the programming. BRS is looking for ways to incorporate the lessons of the pilot into its work moving forward.
The ultimate goal, Doukas says, is to create a long-term pathway into DSP jobs for people in the state. But even more than that, he believes that programs like SPARK-CT, if given more permanent support, can usher in a larger shift, boosting Connecticut’s declining workforce more broadly by providing a foundation that can help people with disabilities as they take on new jobs.
“We aren’t doing this because it’s just a good thing to do. Our agency doesn’t exist because it’s philanthropic,” he said.  “Individuals with disabilities can bring meaningful contributions to the state’s economy, they represent part of the workforce solution in general.” 
“If given an opportunity by employers,” he added, “they’re going to be able to fill roles.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas must be ruthless in spending its millions from social media settlements
description: When Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, settled a lawsuit a few weeks ago, the tech giant agreed to pay more that $17 billion to a collection of 47 states, including Kansas. Over the next 10 years, Kansas will receive an estimated $134 million to address the damages of social media among teens. […]
text:
Kansas will soon have to figure out how to spend a multimillion dollar settlement from Meta over social media use among young people. (Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)When Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, settled a lawsuit a few weeks ago, the tech giant agreed to pay more that $17 billion to a collection of 47 states, including Kansas. Over the next 10 years, Kansas will receive an estimated $134 million to address the damages of social media among teens.
The sensible goal for that money is clear: Prevent the next generation of Kansans from joining social media at all. 
The middle schoolers on Instagram. The tweens on Snapchat. The teens on TikTok. The kids on YouTube.
Prevention is an ambitious goal that won’t happen by accident. It will demand ruthless coordination and execution.
Like an orchestrated military attack or political campaign, a 10-year barrage should swamp Kansans in messages about social media, ensuring that teens don’t have their first two decades defined by heart-shaped likes and the endless scroll, by extreme makeover filters and social media addiction.
Using the most ruthlessly effective practices from advertising, public relations and psychology, we can shift thinking among the youngest Kansans and their parents. Imagine today’s 4-year-olds growing up to understand social media in a different way: with realism.
It’s tempting to compare this first social media settlement to the landmark payoff from tobacco companies to states. In 1998, cigarette manufacturers began direct payments to states. The so-called Master Settlement Agreement has provided about $50 million per year to Kansas over the last 25 years, according to the Kansas Children’s Cabinet and Trust Fund.
Since the settlement, overall smoking rates and teen smoking rates have plummeted in Kansas and across the country. 
That, however, doesn’t mean that Kansas has used the settlement money in a targeted way. Reports from the Campaign for Tobacco Free Kids show that Kansas spends a small fraction from the tobacco settlement on smoking cessation programs.
During last fiscal year, the nonprofit reported that Kansas spent only 1.6% of the year’s settlement money on tobacco prevention ($2.3 million of $140.9 million). That amount lags far behind the percentage that the Centers for Disease Control recommends.
If we hope to make improvements with young people and social media, Kansas must be far more aggressive with settlement funds from Meta and any other tech companies that eventually settle (all eyes on you, TikTok, Snapchat and Google). 
Smoking rates didn’t just fall because of anti-cigarette commercials and public pressure campaigns on teens. Many factors changed our collective attitudes about tobacco: health warnings on cigarette packs, bans on smoking in public, higher costs for cigarettes, raising the minimum age for tobacco sales, restricting tobacco advertising and more. Being ushered out of your favorite restaurant for smoking will change your tobacco use pretty quickly.
Efforts to shift social media use likely won’t have the same significant parallel reforms. Meta agreed to some changes to its apps, including limiting teens’ browsing time and eliminating certain features, such as the “like” button. These reforms are at once commendable and minuscule. Changing how young people use technology will not be accomplished by changes that technology companies implement voluntarily, even to settle a lawsuit. 
To change how young Kansans interact with social media means changing parents’ minds and behavior. We parents (yes, me included) hand our kids smartphones largely unlocked to social media. In many Kansas homes with kids younger than 16, an iPhone gift at Christmas or the iPad birthday present both come with unlimited data plans.
To return to the comparison with tobacco, we parents might as well be buying cartons of cigarettes from the convenience store and standing at the front door with a lighter as our kids slouch out the door for the middle school dance, casually taking a drag and stuffing the rest of the pack into their pockets. We are their supply.
At the time of the tobacco settlement in the late 1990s, American parents weren’t reckless enough to hand packs of Marlboro Reds to their 10-year-old. They understood and acted on the dangers, even the parents who smoked themselves. 
We are doing the equivalent now with cellphones. 
Parents must be convinced that social media is fundamentally dangerous. After all, 12-year-old Sydney cannot buy her own cellphone and cellphone plan. Parents control access.
Ideally, state legislators would have long ago spent public money on campaigns to redefine social media in the minds of both parents and teens. States such as Kansas could have passed more regulations than simply banning cell phones in K-12 schools. It would have also helped for those laws to be more meaningful and exist before 2026.
Although this isn’t going to happen, the most useful way to spend millions of dollars in Kansas might be informing state legislators about the pitfalls of social media. Imagine robust state laws that penalize social media companies from doing anything that they know will create addictive behavior in any user, from children up to adults. 
Or, perhaps an embargo on the state’s universities partnering with any social media company that doesn’t comply with a list of wellness standards. If we can learn anything from reforming tobacco use in America, it’s the power of government restrictions to create norms. 
Another option would be to treat social media addiction as such: an addiction that demands treatment for each individual. Academic studies reveal effective interventions for compulsive use of social media. These range from mindfulness techniques to hypnosis to residential treatment programs. 
Even $10 million or $20 million each year could never provide such services to every Kansan who likely needs them. It’s an indication of how paltry the Meta settlement is in context — plus how widespread and problematic social media use is.  
What option remains? A focused campaign to reframe social media as poisonous and invasive — especially to the lives of young people. Describing apps this way might strike you as an overreaction, but half-measures won’t produce results. 
Parents need to see apps as harmful. Children need to see them as a long-term health risk. When I attended high school and college, this was precisely what anti-tobacco messaging told my parents and me. Along with many others from my generation, we believed it and reacted — because we saw the product as deadly and its marketing as deceptive. 
Producing such a change in public sentiment demands every dollar from the Meta settlement and any others that follow. The settlement should not fund any other program or create political pet projects. Every dollar should be aimed at reducing the use of social media among young Kansans. 
Some politicians will likely argue that the money could be spread among many initiatives — not just combatting social media. This is naive. Remember that social media companies run their own advertising campaigns to encourage us to use them over competitors. 
Meta, for instance, spends about $2 billion each year on advertising its products, according to its SEC filings. That is more per year — yes, more! — than what it will pay out to states over the next 10 years as part of the settlement. There’s no guarantee that the company won’t ramp up spending to promote itself in the future. 
Even funded by 100% of the settlement dollars, our social media problem might hold steady at best, given Meta’s own campaigns.
Two paths present themselves to us as Kansans. Down one road, we fritter away the Meta settlement over the next 10 years on a buffet of programs that are feckless and disparate, creating little to no influence on social media use among young people. 
The other road defines our state as a bold leader, truth-teller and ardent reformer of social media. Our next generation of Kansans, when they travel to neighboring states, appreciates that they understand the risks of social media better than young people from other states, such as their roommates at college roommates or their friends at work. 
Our reality will hinge, at least in part, on how ruthlessly and strategically we spend Meta’s money. 
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana higher ed commission to review dual-college credit accessibility
description: State officials want to see more Hoosier students earn college credits or career certifications before they graduate high school. Indiana leads the nation for students finishing at least one college class in high school, but many students are just one or two classes shy of earning a credential upon graduation. Others earn high school credit […]
text:
Indiana Education Secretary Katie Jenner speaks to the Indiana Commission for Higher Education Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of Indiana Higher Education Commission livestream)State officials want to see more Hoosier students earn college credits or career certifications before they graduate high school.
Indiana leads the nation for students finishing at least one college class in high school, but many students are just one or two classes shy of earning a credential upon graduation.
Others earn high school credit for career technical classes when dual-college credits are available for the same course.
The Indiana Commission for Higher Education shared those statistics when it issued a Request for Information Thursday to improve access to career technical classes and the Indiana College Core, a block of dual-credit classes designed to easily transfer toward a college diploma.
Students who finish the entire 30-credit block earn the equivalent of a full year of college credits for minimal cost.
They also satisfy the credential requirement for Indiana’s new Enrollment Honors Plus diploma seal, which grants them acceptance to any of Indiana’s public universities and a host of private universities.
Lawmakers directed Education Secretary Katie Jenner to assess dual-credit, career technical and advanced placement offerings before the next legislative session, with the goal of better aligning the state’s $30 million early college investment with its new high school diploma seals.
“When we consider how we can make higher education more affordable and increase educational attainment, we have an incredible opportunity to expand access to high-quality early college credit for every high school student,” Jenner said in a statement Thursday.
“Providing no-cost early college credit is an essential step in helping more students find the path that’s right for them and improving their long-term outcomes,” she said.
Indiana College Core is available at 328 Indiana high schools, which partner with colleges and universities to offer dual-credit, dual enrollment and online classes at little to no cost to students.
But the commission found 22% of Hoosier students attend a high school where the Indiana College Core is not offered.
That disparity is primarily due to insufficient enrollment or limited availability of teachers certified to teach dual-credit courses, said Sam Rourke, assistant commissioner for career and technical education.
The commission will review proposals in the coming months to alleviate barriers to early college access, with a report from Jenner due later this year.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin files constitutional challenge to state abortion restrictions
description: Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin is challenging state laws that restrict abortion access, arguing they unconstitutionally infringe on Wisconsinites right to “liberty and bodily autonomy.”  Tanya Atkinson, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Wisconsin, said during a virtual press conference Thursday that the case seeks to address a “powerful promise” in th[...]
text:
Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin's Water Street Health Center in Milwaukee. (Photo courtesy of Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin)Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin is challenging state laws that restrict abortion access, arguing they unconstitutionally infringe on Wisconsinites right to “liberty and bodily autonomy.” 
Tanya Atkinson, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Wisconsin, said during a virtual press conference Thursday that the case seeks to address a “powerful promise” in the state Constitution. The Wisconsin Constitution states that “all people are born equally free and independent and possess inherent rights, including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” The organization is seeking to establish a constitutional right to abortion with the suit. 
The lawsuit was filed Thursday by Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin in Dane County Circuit Court on behalf of its staff and patients against Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne, the state Medical Examining Board and the Board of Nursing. 
It challenges two restrictions in Wisconsin law: one that requires that only physicians provide abortion care and one that requires patients to wait 24 hours between a consultation appointment with a physician and an abortion appointment with the same physician. 
“In this case, we ask our Court to recognize what we believe that promise means — that our constitutional freedom includes the ability to make deeply personal decisions about our reproductive healthcare without unnecessary government interference,” Atkinson said. 
Since Roe v. Wade was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, access to abortion has been in flux in Wisconsin. Planned Parenthood first ceased providing abortion services due to an 1849 law interpreted as a near-total abortion ban that was later declared invalid by the state Supreme Court. It again paused abortion services in Wisconsin due to federal changes included in President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” law, though it has since resumed those services. 
“Whether you can receive healthcare shouldn’t depend on what happened in court that morning. It shouldn’t depend on whether your appointment happens to fall before or after the latest political fight,” Atkinson said. “We cannot continue allowing access to essential healthcare to be this fragile, and that’s why today isn’t simply about defending what we have, but about moving forward… There’s an entire generation of young people growing up who have never experienced reproductive freedom that many of us once took for granted. We have an opportunity to change that trajectory.” 
This is not the first time Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin has sued to establish a constitutional right to abortion. 
It previously sued to establish a constitutional right to abortion in a challenge to the 1849 law.  The case was dismissed by the state Supreme Court after it overturned the 1849 law in a different lawsuit on the basis that the law was invalid due to subsequent laws that had been passed to regulate abortion, including the ones now being challenged.
“None of our courts have decided whether or not the Wisconsin Constitution, in fact, protects this fundamental freedom,” Atkinson said. “We believe it does.”
The new lawsuit argues the restrictions unconstitutionally limit access to healthcare. 
“Through this case, we are asking Wisconsin courts to recognize that these restrictions conflict with the freedoms and protections guaranteed to each of us under our state’s Constitution, and if we are successful, this will be a generational step forward for reproductive freedom in Wisconsin,” Atkinson said. 
There are a handful of state laws that require a physician to provide abortion care including one that says it is a Class I felony for anyone who is not a physician to perform an abortion. Atkinson said there are other healthcare providers who could safely provide abortions including advanced practice nurse practitioners, physician assistants and certified nurse midwives. 
The 24-hour waiting period, which requires a delay between a face-to-face consultation with a physician and the induction of an abortion, was implemented in 1996 under a law signed by Gov. Tommy Thompson.
Allison Linton, a board-certified OB-GYN, the Chief Medical Officer of Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin and plaintiff in the lawsuit, said during the press conference that the restrictions may be presented as medically necessary, but they are not and can be a hindrance to patients accessing care. She said she sees patients every week who struggle to make time for two separate trips to the office for care. 
“They tell us, ‘I don’t have another sick day. I just started this job. I’m afraid I could lose my job if I ask for more time off. I don’t have someone who can watch my children again. I have to get home,’” Linton said, adding that she has cared this week for patients who traveled from Texas and Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. “These burdens fall especially hard on people who already face barriers to healthcare — people who work hourly jobs, people with limited financial resources, parents who need childcare and patients who have to travel long distances to reach us.” 
Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin has three clinics in the state that provide abortion services — in Milwaukee, Madison and Sheboygan. According to the complaint, Planned Parenthood sees patients five days a week at its Madison and Milwaukee centers. However, due to restrictions that require patients to undergo a physical exam and ultrasound, receive information and provide consent, the facilities only offer medication and procedural abortions two to three days per week on average. The Sheboygan location provides a limited number of medication abortion appointments about one day a week.
Michelle Velasquez, the chief strategy officer for Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin, said a successful lawsuit would not necessarily mean there would be no limits on abortion access in the state. 
“Many other states have state-recognized constitutional rights,” Velasquez said. “We see those states still involved in litigation as their state legislatures pass different laws related to abortion, and so the limits of that constitutional right would very much still be in play and dependent on the type of review that would be applied to this right, and then, of course, testing various laws that may be passed in the future up against that state constitutional right. I would anticipate that if the state courts in Wisconsin do in fact affirm that there is this fundamental right to bodily autonomy that an entire sort of new body of law will develop over time.”
The lawsuit comes as control of Wisconsin’s governor’s office and the Legislature is up for grabs, though Atkinson said the fact that it’s an election year did not play a role in the suit. 
“To have the elections be a calculus in when we file a lawsuit, just underscores how normalized it is to have abortion and politics mixed together. The reality is abortion is healthcare. People need access across the state, and for too long, women have had incredible barriers in the state of Wisconsin because of politics,” Atkinson said.
Wisconsin’s abortion laws could change depending on how the elections go. Democrats, if they gain control of both houses of the Legislature and the governor’s office, hope to advance legislation that would roll back restrictions. 
One proposed bill from Democrats, which Assembly Minority Leader Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) recently promoted on X, would roll back a number of restrictions including the provider ban, the 24-hour waiting period, an ultrasound requirement for women seeking an abortion and healthcare coverage restrictions.
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor, celebrated the lawsuit in a statement, saying it is “a reminder that Wisconsin must elect a governor who will protect reproductive rights and keep politicians out of private medical decisions.”
A group of about 11 Republican lawmakers, including Rep. Lindee Brill (R-Sheboygan Falls), Sen. Romaine Quinn (R-Birchwood) and Sen. Cory Tomczyk (R-Mosinee), condemned the lawsuit in a statement, saying that it is an attempt to “usurp the duty” of the state Legislature. 
“If pro-abortion radicals want to change the law in Wisconsin, they should go through the legislative process,” the lawmakers said. “However, Planned Parenthood has not deigned to proceed that way due to their impatience and desperate urge to encourage a culture of death.” 
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor, said in a statement that he would “uphold Wisconsin’s current laws” if elected. Tiffany previously supported legislation to restrict abortion access during his time in the state Legislature and in Congress. He voted in 2015 while in the state Senate for the state’s ban on abortion after 20 weeks. In Congress, Tiffany cosponsored a bill in 2023 that would have made it a crime for doctors to perform abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Unique stretch of New England forest under threat after proposed rollback of roadless rule
description: At first look, the trailhead for Wheeler Brook trail is unassuming. Sitting just off of Route 2 in Gilead, north of Caribou Mountain, the passing traffic of cars and logging trucks is no different from other roadsides across the state. But just a short hike into the woods and the noise of civilization quickly fades […]
text:
Frances Killea with the Natural Resources Council of Maine (left) and Sally Stockwell with Maine Audubon, hiking Wheeler Brook trail in September. The area is part of an unbroken stretch of land across the New Hampshire and Maine border, and would be affected by the Trump Administration's proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule protections. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)At first look, the trailhead for Wheeler Brook trail is unassuming. Sitting just off of Route 2 in Gilead, north of Caribou Mountain, the passing traffic of cars and logging trucks is no different from other roadsides across the state.
But just a short hike into the woods and the noise of civilization quickly fades away, as the trail follows Wheeler Brook, crossing over the (currently dry) streambed and offering a serene forest for visiting hikers, as well as varied, valuable habitat for wildlife. 
It’s one of the few unbroken stretches of land in New England, reaching across the White Mountains that straddle the border of Maine and New Hampshire. And the unique ecosystem is under threat.
Last month, the U.S. Department of Agriculture filed to rescind “in its entirety” the national 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which prohibits road construction, logging and mining on about 30% of lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service.
“The attempt to rescind this is not just an attempt to remove robust protections for healthy habitat, animal migration, healthy soil — it’s really an attempt to try to steal a public health resource,” said Jeff Swayze, a registered New Hampshire guide and mental health counselor. “It’s a way to try to steal agency from the American citizens who own these lands.” 
Swayze joined other conservationists Wednesday at the trail to emphasize the importance of the area for local plants, animals and surrounding human infrastructure. 
Although most roadless areas are in the western U.S., there are still areas in the Northeast that are protected under the rule, and would be affected by the proposed change. 
(Image via Natural Resources Council of Maine)
“There’s obviously a much lower proportion of roadless areas in the East, but it doesn’t mean that they’re any less meaningful to us as humans, and certainly from a habitat perspective as well,” said ​​Frances Killea, with the Natural Resources Council of Maine.
Namely, 235,000 acres in New Hampshire that are part of the White Mountains National Forest, and an additional 6,000 acres that stretch across the border into Maine: the Caribou and Speckled Mountain extension. 
Killea said that even Maine’s north woods are often broken up by logging roads, making the roadless area in Western Maine and New Hampshire all the more important. 
“To have a parcel that is mostly undivided, mostly unfragmented by roads is really special, especially in the East, a much more developed area in the U.S. than places out West,” Killea said. 
An ecosystem under threat
The area is home to several bodies of water, and the forested ecosystem stretches through a variety of elevations — all of which provides valuable habitat for a range of plants and animals. 
“There are very few places left in Maine where we really have older forests that are structurally complex — that have at least three layers of vegetation, that have trees that are of different species, different sizes, different ages,” said Sally Stockwell with Maine Audubon. 
Much of the wooded area is still not considered true, old growth forest, Stockwell said. But it’s well on its way after the end of industrial logging in the region, which in the early 1900s stripped most of the lumber. 
“This forest has some time yet to grow into that truly old, older forest stand, but it’s on its way, and that’s what we need,” Stockwell said. “We need these places where it can continue to grow into these older forests. And when they’re much more structurally complex, we have many more wildlife species.”
The area is an important habitat for a wide variety of wildlife, including several rare, threatened or endangered species. That includes golden eagles and peregrine falcons, both of which are considered endangered species in Maine. 
The habitat for birds is particularly important, Stockwell said, as many species have seen steep declines across North America in the last 50 years.
Jeff Swayze, a mental health counselor and registered New Hampshire guide, stands in a stream bed along the Wheeler Brook trail in Maine. The area is currently protected from development by the federal roadless rule. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)
“There just aren’t as many birds when we go out into the woods anymore,” Stockwell said. “And so anything we can do to create good nesting habitat for those birds gives them a fighting chance because they got all kinds of other threats that are bringing them down too.”
And any loss of habitat is in this protected area is likely to have a direct impact on vulnerable species, she said.
“If we lose these places, we’re likely to lose a lot of those creatures as well,” Stockwell said.
Swayze, the mental health counselor and registered guide, said that these protected areas also have benefits for people. 
“These are intact, rich ecosystems,” Swayze said. “But as human beings, we’re also ecosystems too, and so connecting these places is a part of having well-regulated, emotionally healthy American citizens. And you really cannot put a price tag on that.”
Protecting these woods also protects people who live downstream of the watershed, said Adam Nordell with Environment Maine. 
“We’re also protecting drinking water supplies for the greater Portland area, and all of the towns in Maine that are served by the Saco River,” Nordell said. 
Roadless lands and wildfires
Brooke Rollins, head of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, first proposed rolling back the rule in August 2025, and said at the time that the move would support President Donald Trump’s executive orders meant to increase logging and energy development on federal lands.
That notice of intent set off a 21-day public comment period that brought in more than 600,000 comments, most of which expressed opposition to any changes that would erode the Roadless Rule’s prohibitions on development. Federal officials have not held a single public meeting since then.
In her August announcement, Rollins said the rollback of the rule was driven by wildfire prevention, and that the roadless protections have led to “overgrown stands, insect outbreaks and disease” turning “healthy landscapes into tinderboxes.”
“For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities,” she said.
But research into wildfires contradicts Rollins’ claim that roads will reduce fires. 
Oregon State University Professor Chris Dunn and his colleagues found that most wildfires in Western national forests between 1984 and 2018 started near roads. And the U.S. Forest Service’s own research also shows the majority of human-caused ignitions occur on roadsides, and 20 years of monitoring data does not support assertions that repealing road prohibitions will improve forest health. 
“So constructing more roads and having more public or private access can only serve to cause more wildfires,” Killea said.
Swayze said that just because an area doesn’t have roads, that doesn’t mean that the area is untouched or unmanaged. 
“There’s already provisions for fire mitigation and treatment in roadless areas,” Swayze said. “You just can’t punch a road in to do that.” 
Conservationists will hold two more events next week to share information with the public, on Wednesday in Freeport and Thursday online.
The USDA has extended the public comment period to Tuesday, Oct. 6.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio governor’s race: Where the candidates stand on education issues
description: Ohio’s candidates for governor have differing ideas when it comes to the future of education — from funding public schools to school vouchers and teacher pay.  Ohio Democratic candidate Amy Acton, Ohio Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, and Ohio Libertarian candidate Don Kissick are running for governor in the November election. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine is [[...]
text:
Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton. (Photo by WEWS.)Ohio’s candidates for governor have differing ideas when it comes to the future of education — from funding public schools to school vouchers and teacher pay. 
Ohio Democratic candidate Amy Acton, Ohio Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, and Ohio Libertarian candidate Don Kissick are running for governor in the November election. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine is term-limited. 
Acton’s campaign did not respond to specific questions sent by the Ohio Capital Journal, but instead sent a statement. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Growing up in Youngstown, public schools and libraries saved Dr. Acton’s life,” said Addie Bullock, spokesperson for the Acton campaign. 
“Dr. Acton knows firsthand how important it is to invest in Ohio’s public education system to ensure that all of our kids get a great education. … Fully funding and protecting Ohio’s public schools benefits all of us.” 
Acton has been endorsed by both state teachers unions — the Ohio Federation of Teachers and the Ohio Education Association.
Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to questions sent by the Ohio Capital Journal. 
As the campaign season has gone along, the gap between the candidates when it comes to various education issues has become clear.
Private school vouchers 
Acton’s campaign website states she will “bring reform to our corrupt school voucher system,” and that “public money should be for public schools.”
Ramaswamy has spoken in favor of school vouchers, even saying Ohio should “go further in the direction of school choice,” during an interview last year with Columbus television station WCMH. 
“I think it’s the civil rights issue of our time,” he said. “I think kids in our inner cities or in rural parts of Ohio deserve to go to the best possible schools they can.”
Ohio lawmakers increased the EdChoice private school expansion eligibility to 450% of the poverty line in 2023 through the state budget — creating near-universal school vouchers.
This means K-8 students can receive a $6,166 scholarship and high schoolers can receive a $8,408 scholarship funded by the state.
Ohio spent more than a billion dollars on private school vouchers in the 2025 fiscal year, the second full year with near-universal eligibility, according to data from the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce. Nearly half of the money — $492.8 million — went toward the EdChoice expansion. 
“Acton calls out the voucher program as unaccountable, and on the other hand, Ramaswamy seems to want to give even more funding to vouchers,” said Piet van Lier, deputy director of the advocacy group Honesty for Ohio Education. 
Kissick supports EdChoice, but would examine “whether assistance can be better targeted toward families facing the greatest barriers to educational choice,” according to an email sent by Kissick’s running mate, James Mills.
“School choice should create genuine educational mobility and encourage schools to compete on quality, rather than simply becoming another subsidy for families who already have access to alternatives,” Mills said. 
Fair School Funding 
Acton has said she will continue to implement Ohio’s Fair School Funding Plan. The funding model was initially passed in 2022 with bipartisan support, and was designed to fund schools based on actual need for each school district. 
The Fair School Funding Plan almost made it through its six-year phase-in, but Ohio Republican lawmakers decided to abandon the plan during last year’s budgeting process. 
The most recent state operating budget included a $226 million increase in school funding, but the Fair School Funding Plan model needed at least triple that amount to maintain its initial projections and keep up with inflation.
Kissick’s campaign said he supports “the goals of making school funding more equitable and predictable.”
“As we work to reduce and ultimately eliminate reliance on property taxes, we would protect school funding while first examining what schools actually need, what Ohio already collects, where it is being spent, and what can be redirected before simply replacing one tax with another,” Mills said.  
Math and literacy 
Acton’s campaign said she will “invest in new, 21st century approaches to math and literacy and create workforce training programs.” 
Ramaswamy’s campaign said he will “raise academic standards with a focus on 3rd-grade literacy, 8th-grade numeracy, and 12th-grade civics.”
He has said would bring back the recently ended policy that required the state to hold back students if they struggle to read. 
Kissick’s campaign said he supports continuing funding the Science of Reading model for Ohio schools, which is based on decades of research that shows how the human brain learns to read and incorporates phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension.
“The state should provide good evidence and resources, measure outcomes transparently, and give qualified educators the freedom to apply those tools to the students in their classrooms,” Mills said. 
DeWine wants his successor to continue the literacy work he started, including the Science of Reading. 
School meals 
Acton supports free school breakfasts and lunches. 
“No child in Ohio should go hungry,” her campaign website reads. “Providing this support ensures that all of Ohio’s kids have the fuel they need to learn and thrive.” 
Ramaswamy’s campaign website said he promotes “healthy meals and daily physical education.”
Teacher pay 
Ramaswamy has said he wants to “pay our best teachers more by rewarding excellence and attracting top talent into the profession.” 
Acton is advocating for raising teacher pay across the board, according to van Lier. 
Higher education 
The next governor will appoint trustees for Ohio’s colleges and universities. 
Ramaswamy previously said he wants to consolidate Ohio colleges and universities. After receiving much push back, Ramaswamy clarified and said he never wanted to close the colleges, but rather close programs within the colleges.
Just this week, incumbent Gov. Mike DeWine told a crowd of community college leaders that a plan like the one Ramaswamy proposed wouldn’t happen in Ohio.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: The Trump administration’s culture war on childcare is hurting Wisconsin families
description: Vice President JD Vance is promoting a Trump administration plan to siphon off federal money that helps working parents afford childcare and use it to subsidize parents who stay at home. The man who ran for office mocking “childless cat ladies” is now trying to stir up a cat fight between working and stay-at-home moms. […]
text:
One in four Wisconsin childcare providers said they will likely close their doors after the loss of federal subsidies. The Trump administration to direct remaining childcare funds to stay-at-home parents will exacerbate the crisis.  (Photo by Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent.)Vice President JD Vance is promoting a Trump administration plan to siphon off federal money that helps working parents afford childcare and use it to subsidize parents who stay at home. The man who ran for office mocking “childless cat ladies” is now trying to stir up a cat fight between working and stay-at-home moms. That’s not remarkable coming from a federal government run by social media trolls. But the main effect of the actual policy Vance is promoting will be to make the lives of already stressed working class families, especially in Wisconsin, even harder, more expensive and noticeably worse than before.
Childcare funding has been in crisis in Wisconsin ever since the pandemic relief money that briefly stabilized providers ran out. Without that money, which “prevented system collapse” according to the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association, supporting more than 430,000 children in nearly 6,000 programs, parents are priced out of care and one in four providers say they will likely have to close their doors. 
Unlike Massachusetts and Vermont, Wisconsin does not treat childcare as a state budget priority. Ours is one of only a handful of states including Idaho, Indiana, Nevada and Ohio that failed to spend any money on childcare beyond what was required to draw down federal dollars, according to a 2025 report by the advocacy group ChildCare Aware. In 2026, the state created a new school readiness program for 4-year-olds. It was a first step toward acknowledging the needs of preschoolers and their parents. But it did nothing to address the massive shortage in care for infants and toddlers.
That’s all fine with JD Vance, who wrote on X that “normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force.”
But Vance is not offering to do anything about the fact that the U.S. is the only wealthy nation on Earth that doesn’t offer paid maternity leave, even though 68% of mothers with children under 6 are employed. Nor is he promoting the kind of high-quality early childhood education system that allows parents in Denmark, after their six months of paid parental leave, to enroll their preschoolers in beautiful, enriching childcare programs they don’t have to feel guilty about.
Instead, what Vance is proposing is to take an already paltry federal childcare subsidy and make working parents fight over crumbs with nonworking parents. Mainly, his aim seems to be to punish single parents. That’s not going to leave anyone in good shape — least of all children. 
One of the saddest aspects of the attack on childcare is that very recently parents, educators, business leaders and politicians of both political parties were finally coming together around the idea that childcare is an essential public good that requires public support.
The “mommy wars” attack Vance wants to revive is long out of date. It has been decades since most American families had the luxury of subsisting on a single wage-earner’s income, trad wife fantasies notwithstanding. 
Another major recent breakthrough is policymakers’ realization that the magic of the free market is not going to provide childcare parents can afford. 
“It was the Biden administration that put a ton of money into childcare during COVID, and we learned from that,” says Ruth Schmidt, executive director of the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association. “The lesson was not just the importance of keeping childcare open so that essential workers could work, but the other piece that’s really interesting is that it demonstrated what can positively happen in childcare when you put a little more money into it.”
Thanks to direct payments to providers during the pandemic, center closures dropped off, the number of teachers leaving the workforce slowed down, tuition stopped climbing and, Schmidt says, “this industry for the first time was finally able to say, ‘Our work is important. It is essential to the functioning of our country. It’s worth investing in, because if you invest in it, these positive things can happen.”
Then came Trump. 
Schmidt calls the rollout of Trump policies that slashed supports for families “death by 1,000 cuts.” During the second Trump administration, cuts to food assistance, Medicaid and Head Start, along with the federal government’s move to loosen safety standards and increase staff ratios in childcare centers have taken a huge combined toll on Wisconsin families.
If it were just ideological — if the Trump administration were actually pursuing the kinds of pronatalist policies that make getting married and having children more attractive, as Vance likes to claim, it wouldn’t be as bad. But instead, while spouting rhetoric about valuing families, this administration is subjecting little kids and their parents to more and more misery.
Wisconsin could do more to protect vulnerable kids. Before leaving the Capitol to hit the campaign trail, state legislators failed to pass a bill that would have used state money to fill the gap after federal childcare stabilization funds lapsed. That set off a vicious cycle, says Paula Drew of the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association. Subsidies for families were cut and their out-of-pocket payments skyrocketed, so cash-strapped parents withdrew their kids from care. Under-enrollment meant less revenue for childcare centers, so they raised their rates. “It just sort of snowballed,” Drew says. “Programs said things like, ‘We’re gonna have to lower salaries for staff.’ … so I think we’re going to lose our educators, and in fact I think we’ve already lost a big percentage of our skilled, seasoned educators.”
An unintended consequence of the state’s investment in 4-year-old pre-K is that it creates a disincentive to provide care for infants and toddlers, which is already more expensive, Drew says. “Wisconsin serves very few infants and toddlers in regulated care,” she says. “And now, with additional funding going into the Get Kids Ready pre-K program, we expect that to be even lower a year from now.”
To make matters worse, the state no longer has a surplus of federal Temporary Assistance to Needy Families funds, which it has used to cover some childcare costs for low-income families. 
Sooner or later, Wisconsin is going to have to start dedicating state revenue to childcare. Schmidt and Drew hope that, with a new governor and a new Legislature, Wisconsin will use the state surplus, payroll taxes or a tax on hemp products and gambling, as Louisiana has done, to subsidize childcare. Only then can Wisconsin reduce the astronomical tuition rates that parents pay ($13,000 for home care and $17,400 for center-based care, according to state data), give providers a better wage (currently $13.55 per hour), and stop the wave of childcare closures. 
They especially want the state to shore up disappearing infant and toddler care and retain experienced teachers — not just by giving them a raise but also by allowing them to continue to get higher education “and make this a profession, not just a fleeting step to something else,” says Drew. 
“We need supply of care; supply means educators that can work in programs. And then we want to help parents pay for care on the demand side. … You can’t do one and not the other, because it simply won’t work,” says Drew. “You can’t just help parents pay for care, but not tend to the supply of care available. And you can’t just tend to the supply of care available, but pretend you don’t see that parents are literally going into poverty to try to pay for childcare.”
“Childcare is infrastructure,” says Schmidt. “If we turned around and said to parents with 5-year-olds, you’ve got to start paying $17,000 a year for your child to be in school, we would see empty classrooms, right? We treat these as two very dramatically different concerns. But all of it is about families’ ability to work outside the home, impact the economy, all those kinds of things. “ 
It’s also about having a decent society that values families and takes good care of children. That’s the kind of society we need to come together and focus on, instead of being distracted by the rage-baiting bluster of internet trolls.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Issue 3 campaign employs used car salesman tactics to duplicate rules already in Ohio law
description: It is almost a cliché. The sleazy used car salesman. The high-pressure sales tactic to buy extra stuff you don’t need. Worn-down car buyers give in and pay more for junk add-ons like fabric protection, rustproofing, overpriced gap insurance, extended warranties, etc. It is a game of manipulation done to jack up dealership profits. Unnecessary […]
text:
(Photo by Pat Sutphin/Idaho Capital Sun)It is almost a cliché. The sleazy used car salesman. The high-pressure sales tactic to buy extra stuff you don’t need. Worn-down car buyers give in and pay more for junk add-ons like fabric protection, rustproofing, overpriced gap insurance, extended warranties, etc. It is a game of manipulation done to jack up dealership profits. Unnecessary extras mean higher out-the door costs. The ruse fools gullible customers for company gain.
The same kind of ploy can be pulled on the public for political gain. Take Ohio Issue 3, a proposed constitutional amendment to give Ohio voters extra insurance for election security — on top of the extensive, systemic security coverage that has kept Ohio elections safe, secure, and highly accurate for decades without incident.
The GOP legislative initiative would put a state photo ID law — that Republican legislators also insisted voters needed in 2022 — in the state constitution as a partisan add-on. The law, rammed through the gerrymandered Republican super-majority in the Statehouse required a photo ID before in-person voting. It was considered one of the most restrictive photo identification laws in the country. Ohioans adapted to the gratuitous GOP hurdle to voting and waited for the next one. Many will be puzzled to see a statewide amendment on the November ballot requiring the same photo ID restrictions on voting that were implemented three years ago.
The same party that sold that extreme measure, for no evidence-based, rampant voting fraud reason, now wants gullible voters to buy duplicate insurance on established state law via the constitution. But the sales pitch from Republicans about why a redundant constitutional amendment is a must-have for voters was suspect from the start.
First, the the Republican nominee for governor, tech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, dropped an op-ed calling on the state legislature to fast track Ohio’s photo ID law into the constitution as a midterm election referendum. Not coincidentally, the issue polls well with voters and might boost turnout in the fall election, a possible gain for the Ramaswamy campaign. The day after the op-ed ran, Republicans rushed identical resolutions in the Ohio Senate (presided over by Ramaswamy’s running mate and Senate President Rob McColley) and the Ohio House to enshrine photo ID for voting in the constitution with statewide ballot Issue 3. Republican lawmakers said amending the constitution with voting restrictions was necessary to ensure election integrity — a favorite “Chicken Little,” sky-is-falling refrain Republicans repeat when they’re not boasting about Ohio’s failsafe, gold standard elections.
Issue 3 is also intended to block any future tinkering with the GOP measure if hell freezes over and controlling Democrats move to expand, not restrict, voting rights. Changing a constitutional amendment on photo ID would be much harder than revising a statute on the books.
Ohio Treasurer Robert Sprague, who is running for Ohio Secretary of State, parroted the party spiel about a locked-in photo ID amendment being fundamental to secure elections in a recent speech.
“We have to have photo ID in the state of Ohio,” he said. (Again, we do)
“We have to have it for in-person voting. (Check)
We need to add that to the Ohio Constitution.” (Because we’re doing Ramaswamy a solid?) 
Not exactly a dealmaker. Unexplained is why the hurry to cement voting restrictions instead of, say, voting access in the Ohio Constitution? The “default premise of a constitution is to protect rights and Ohio Issue 3 is a constitutional amendment to enshrine a limitation of rights,” said University of Cincinnati political scientist David Niven.
“It is enshrining into binding permanence a limitation on voting, one that is already law and for which adding this to the constitution does nothing in practical terms,” Niven said.
But Sprague suggested the binding permanence of the Republican photo ID law was chiefly about “making sure that the other party or other people that want to deconstruct these institutions, like our election system, aren’t able to take that (photo ID law) away from the people of the state of Ohio.”
I suspect weaving wild conspiracy theories into a redundancy argument for amending the Ohio Constitution won’t clinch the deal, either.
But manipulating voters with a popular ballot issue to impact election outcomes certainly has precedence in the state. The closest parallel to Ohio Issue 3, said Niven, was the 2004 constitutional amendment that banned same-sex marriage (currently unenforceable). Ohio Republicans had also passed a statutory ban earlier that did the same thing as the anti-gay amendment. The Republican nominee for president campaigned hard on the issue, overwhelmingly supported by voters, which ultimately allowed former President George W. Bush to eke out a win in Ohio by roughly 2 percentage points.
“I think that very much like their work on marriage in 2004, Issue 3 is like steroids for turnout,” Niven concluded. “Republicans aren’t sure they can excite people on the strength of their candidates and campaigns so let’s try to stimulate things with a valid question.”
But the political scientist doesn’t believe the tactic will work in 2026.
“It just doesn’t have the excitement, you know, especially when it doesn’t do anything. I think you need to offer folks something a little bit more exciting if they’re going to drag themselves to the polls when they don’t really like the candidates,” the UC professor said.
Still, Niven predicts the ballot issue will pass.
“From the average voter’s perspective, I think they’ll scratch their heads, say ‘don’t we already have this?’ and then assume we’re doing some kind of voting do-over.”
Pols pushing binding constitutional permanency to voters, who broadly back photo IDs, aim to juice turnout for partisan advantage. The political game, agreed Niven, “has a sleaze to it that would make a used car salesman blush.”
