title: Statewide officials, candidates respond to Haitian student’s death
description: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. Ohio officials and candidates alike have reacted to the death of a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant who died by apparent suicide after being bullied because of his immigration status and the […]
text:
State Rep. Munira Abdullahi, D-Columbus, speaks at a vigil honoring Haitian immigrant Pierre Damas Bel on the grounds of Columbus City Hall on Sept. 3. Abdullahi called for changes to the immigration system in the U.S. 
(Photo by Megan Henry / Ohio Capital Journal)This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.
Ohio officials and candidates alike have reacted to the death of a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant who died by apparent suicide after being bullied because of his immigration status and the ankle monitor he was required to have.
Pierre Damas Bel was a Springfield High School graduate and Wright State University student at the time of his death, when he walked into Interstate 70 traffic on Aug. 31. Social media posts from Damas Bel’s account talked about his desire to pursue his education in the U.S., to build a future and play college-level soccer while working toward medical school.
“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” Damas Bel wrote.
His father said Damas Bel had told him earlier in the day on Aug. 31 that he hadn’t been “feeling okay mentally because of the bullying” he was receiving due to the ankle monitor.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement required the tracking anklet after the Trump administration eliminated Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants living in Springfield and across the country.
At a vigil for Damas Bel on Sept. 2 at Columbus City Hall, state Rep. Munira Abdullahi, D-Columbus, related to Damas Bel’s story of hoping to better the country with his presence. She decried the process that brought with it an ankle monitor and discouragement for the young student.
“We can not accept an immigration system that loses sight of people over paperwork and political dogma,” Abdullahi said. “Pierre deserved better. His family deserves better.”
A sign is shown on the ground at a vigil in Columbus for Haitian immigrant Pierre Damas Bel, who died after walking into traffic on Aug. 31.(Photo by Megan Henry / Ohio Capital Journal)
She demanded the end of “cruelties,” the release of those in ICE detention, and “for my colleagues across the aisle and our Congress members to stand up and do something about this and end it.”
More than 40 Haitians living in Springfield had already been detained by ICE at the time of Damas Bel’s death.
Abdullahi’s fellow state Rep. Latyna Humphrey, also a Democrat representing Columbus, released a statement honoring Damas Bel and talking about the “devastating toll” the immigration process had had on him.
“There are real human beings behind every immigration policy and every government action,” Humphrey said. “…Whatever our political disagreements about immigration may be, our government should never lose sight of the dignity and humanity of the people affected by its decisions.”
The Ohio Senate Democratic Caucus released a joint statement calling Damas Bel’s death “a direct result of this administration’s inhumane and racist immigration policies.”
Democratic Ohio U.S. Rep. Greg Landsman said his office has “reached out directly to the Department of Homeland Security to end the use of ankle monitors on our Haitian neighbors who have done nothing wrong.”
According to the letter dated Sept. 3, Landsman mentioned Damas Bel by name in pushing for the Department of Homeland Security to “reconsider the policy of requiring former TPS holders with no criminal history to wear ankle monitors while going through the legal immigration process.”
“Our country needs border security and immigration enforcement, but the manner in which we prioritize deportations and allocate resources is skewed,” the letter read. “We are wasting time, money, and lives targeting good, law-abiding people rather than clearly prioritizing threats to public safety.”
In a separate statement, Landsman said the U.S. House has passed legislation to extend temporary protections for Haitians for three years, but the U.S. Senate has not taken up the measure.
Federal immigration officials have encouraged Haitians to “self-deport,” despite the fact that the U.S. Department of State still lists Haiti at a Level Four “Do Not Travel” advisory because of the risk of “crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare.”
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has made previous comments disagreeing with the decision to end the Temporary Protected Status for Haitians in Springfield, believing that “it will hurt us in the long run.”
“You’ve heard me talk a lot about what I consider to be a very misguided and wrong policy in regard to mass deporting people from this country,” DeWine said in comments on Sept. 1.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.He said there are consequences to mass deportation, just as there are for other things done by the government. In defending the work of immigrant populations, he said one-third of caregivers in nursing homes and home healthcare workers are immigrants.
“I think we have to ask ourselves: Is it really good, is it what we want done, to see people like this being picked up and facing deportation,” DeWine said. “Do we want that done in our name? And my position has been that it’s a mistake.”
DeWine also said, however, that he felt the Trump administration “has done a very good job with regard to the Southern border, and I think that’s what people wanted.”
Former congressman and Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Sherrod Brown said in a Substack post about Damas Bel that he agreed with DeWine on the issue of immigrants in Springfield, adding that the decision to suspend TPS for the Haitian community “was wrong and has done nothing to make our communities safer.”
The incumbent in the Senate seat for which Brown is campaigning, Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, did not release a statement about Damas Bel. In a Sept. 3 press conference, he said his office plans to help those who have had their Temporary Protected Status taken away “to find out if there are any other methods for them to stay here legally,” but his office plans to maintain “the rule of law,” according to the Springfield News-Sun.
The Democratic candidate for governor, Dr. Amy Acton, released a statement saying she was “devastated by the tragic passing” of Damas Bel.
“Everyone in Ohio deserves to feel safe and to be treated with dignity, and we can uphold the rule of law without creating chaos and fear in our communities,” Acton said in a statement. “Ohio, this is a moment where we are all being asked to stand up for our common humanity. We must build a better way forward.”
In terms of immigration enforcement, Acton has made comments that conflict with Ohio Democratic Party stances, saying she wouldn’t prevent local law enforcement from working with federal law enforcement. 
Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy didn’t release comments on Damas Bel, but has previously made comments that the Trump administration’s general mass deportation policy was “pragmatic.”
Back in 2024, Ramaswamy attended a town hall in Springfield, in which residents expressed concerns about the number of Haitians in the community. Ramaswamy said he didn’t blame the Haitian migrants who were brought here “by unconscionable means,” instead blaming “federal policies,” according to coverage of the meeting by WSYX.
At the time, Ramaswamy also said he supported mass deportation, but “if you’re going to pick a limited number, you may as well pick the ones who are most likely able to assimilate, most likely to participate in economic action, and those who are able to actually integrate their kids into the schools.”
Megan Henry contributed to this article.

title: Gov. DeWine assures universities that Ramaswamy’s consolidation proposal won’t happen — for now
description: Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine is assuring public universities that a proposal to shut down “subpar” institutions, as suggested by candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, will not happen. In a crowded auditorium at The Ohio State University, DeWine gave a speech to community college leaders as well as four-year program presidents and trustees. Kent State University Pre[...]
text:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine delivers the final State of the State address of his second term at the Ohio Statehouse in Columbus on March 10, 2026. (Pool photo by Adam Cairns, Columbus Dispatch.)Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine is assuring public universities that a proposal to shut down “subpar” institutions, as suggested by candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, will not happen.
In a crowded auditorium at The Ohio State University, DeWine gave a speech to community college leaders as well as four-year program presidents and trustees. Kent State University President Todd Diacon listened near the back of the theatre.
“We’re an access institution that takes people that don’t always come from wealthy families, and we prepare them to succeed after they graduate,” Diacon said in an interview following the event.
Kent State’s fall semester is in full swing. Although college enrollment has declined, Diacon said he’s proud to see an upturn when it comes to their priority programs.
“We just enrolled our largest freshman class of nursing students at Kent in 10 years,” he said.
But Diacon raised concerns about a proposal made by Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy.
“We have too many of them,” Ramaswamy said in a video posted to his Threads account in March. “They need to be consolidated.”
In an opinion article he wrote for The Columbus Dispatch, Ramaswamy encouraged shutting down what he called struggling universities. He referred to Kent, Cleveland State, the University of Akron, and Central State University as having previous challenges.
He tripled down on that idea in April.
“I don’t think you should be funding subpar universities,” Ramaswamy said to a student asking a question at a Turning Point USA event.
Colleges shouldn’t replicate each other, he said, and the strongest programs should be the ones to survive.


DeWine is now trying to assuage universities’ fears. In his speech, he sent a message to Ramaswamy.
“The idea that we would get rid of any of our state universities, I think, would infringe upon our efforts to continue to broaden our access,” he said.
It is “not a good idea,” the governor continued, to applause.
College consolidation “can’t and won’t happen,” he added. But DeWine only runs the state for a few more months.
Asked what will happen to students if the legislature approves of Ramaswamy’s idea to consolidate colleges, DeWine called it “speculation,” something that’s happening before anyone knows who’s going to be elected governor.
“Second, we don’t know if they will embrace that at all,” DeWine said. “I think that it’s unlikely that anyone would really make that proposal.”
Although DeWine endorsed Ramaswamy after taking time to consider his options, he has shown disapproval of some of his policies on education and taxes.
Since the summer, Ramaswamy has tried to backtrack on his earlier statements. He is now saying that he never wanted to shut down the colleges, but rather shut down programs within the colleges.
“I think that we have too many duplicative programs in our universities,” Ramaswamy said in July. “When I look at a region, I want to look at Ohio in terms of regions like regional governance; I want every region to have the best higher education institutions available for people in that region. But not every university needs to offer every program.”
The candidate has previously noted that university leaders probably don’t like his idea.
Diacon noted that Kent’s eight separate campuses serve vastly different populations — from up in Ashtabula to two hours south in Tuscarawas County.
“They are important members of their communities, and it’s not just in terms of ‘we employ people in those communities,’ but the tax bases of those communities,” the university president said.
After having his university called out by Ramaswamy, Diacon said it made him feel as if the candidate just doesn’t know much about Kent.
“We don’t spend a lot of time calling attention to ourselves. We just go about doing our work. We tend not to brag about our strengths and successes. We just go about doing our work,” he responded.
“I think the downside of that approach is that people in the general public and in other areas may not appreciate the impact that our university has on the region and on the nation.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: 25 years later, a news man remembers 9/11
description: The days following September 11 remain the saddest I’ve experienced in a nearly 50- year career reporting news on television.
text:
It was 8:30 on a warm, sunny morning in Philadelphia 25 years ago when I walked off the train from my commute to work and ducked into the coffee shop in historic Old City for a cup of hazelnut with a touch of half and half before heading to work in a TV newsroom a block away.

Jeffrey Cole

 Waiting for my cup, I glanced at the row of televisions hanging above the counter to watch American Airlines Flight 11 strike the North Tower of the World Trade Center at 8:46 a.m. I can’t recall if I got my coffee, but I vividly remember sprinting to the station, taking the elevator to the third floor and bursting into the newsroom to find my colleagues staring at the TVs, what are called monitors in broadcast newsrooms, in stunned disbelief.
Quickly, along with my photographer, a veteran of the business with a sharp eye and quick, cutting sense of humor, we were racing to New York in the station’s SUV with WCBS Newsradio 88 blaring the nearly unimaginable details of the second strike on the South Tower at 9:03.
As we hurtled north the traffic seemed to fall away as news of the suspected terrorist strikes quickly spread. We both called our wives to share our sorrow and to let them know we were driving to Manhattan to try to get to what would later be known as ground zero. My wife calmly reassured me she would pick up our son from his first day of kindergarten and our younger boy from childcare.
On we drove, pulling off to take a quick spin around an eerily deserted Trenton-Mercer Airport before jumping back onto 95 and arriving along the Hudson River in Hoboken, New Jersey directly across from the smoking remains of the twin towers. The billowing plumes rising from lower Manhattan stopped us where we stood. Quickly joined by another crew from our Philadelphia station, we spoke to each other of the abject horror at what we were witnessing. 
I’m certain more than a few expletives were said before we set up our equipment and interviewed survivors as they were taken across the river by New York Ferries and even private boats. Some were still covered in ash from the collapse while others had survived in nearby buildings. Almost everyone wanted to talk about what they’d seen; how they’d survived; how fortunate they felt to be alive.
As night fell, the PATH trains linking northeastern New Jersey and New York City halted after the attacks, reopened and we climbed on board from Hoboken with a plan to go as far as the train would take us and walk the rest of the way to ground zero. Our ride was short. The trains were going nowhere near the disaster site. So, we trudged, tv gear in our arms, to the lower Manhattan campus of Pace University arriving after 10 p.m. It was there police at a check point told us we would go no further. It was then we noticed a volunteer group preparing to haul supplies to rescue crews at the scene and there were far more supplies than people to carry them. We offered to help by carrying the materials the four blocks to the scene to get them where they were needed while allowing us to report. The police didn’t object.
Sometime around 10:30 on the evening of September 11, we laid eyes on the hellscape that was the twin towers. Standing in front of a battered men’s clothing store, we shot video of a massive pile of smoldering debris with hard-hatted rescue workers pawing at the twisted metal in a desperate search for survivors. An officer on the scene, directing us to stay out of the way, said there was a makeshift emergency room on one side of us and a temporary morgue on the other. We never saw anyone taken to the ER while the morgue was active. Directly in front of us we saw a leaning section of one of the towers with what looked to be the bent, scorched, twisted steel frame of the other a few yards away. The exact same image later emerged as an iconic photo of the early hours after the attack.

Firefighters make their way through the destruction at  New York’s World Trade Center after the terrorist attack on the twin towers of lower Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001. AP photo by Alex Fuchs.

The streets were piled high with ash. It was as if it had snowed but there was no white, only gray and black soot, reeking of smoke and swirling in the air, filling your nose and mouth. Spotlights sent streaks of light angling across the pile of smoldering debris at ground zero while the surrounding buildings were dark, vacant with blown out window and a layer ash.
We left and hustled to the Fox network newsroom where we cut our video for multiple reports during the morning news in Philadelphia and other stations across the country. Eventually, we finished our reporting and crossed the Hudson for a few hours of sleep in a New Jersey hotel before returning to lower Manhattan.
The days following September 11 remain the saddest I’ve experienced in a nearly 50- year career reporting news on television.
In the hours after the jets struck the towers, loved ones of missing family members rushed to New York City in a desperate search to find them. Mothers and fathers would approach holding pictures of a daughter or son and ask, often through tears, if we’d seen them. If we knew where they were and could we direct them. They would plead; often beg for any information we had. We had none. And if they told me their sons and daughters, their brothers and sisters had been in the towners at that time of the strike, having stood at the smoldering pile of debris just a few hours earlier, I would not try to tell them what I’d seen. Through their grief, I was convinced they knew the news was dire.
It seems impossible 25 years have passed. I’m retired and we’ve left Philadelphia. My sons, little boys back then, are men living on their own with careers, friends and reckoning with parents asking when they’ll visit. The memory of September 11 remains ever constant: The nighttime scene of abject devastation. The searing agony etched on the faces of loved ones. The firefighters, police and rescue workers atop the pile searching for survivors and finding only death. The nagging sense that the America of September 10, 2001 was gone.
Jeffrey Cole of Madison is a former news anchor for WFSB in Hartford and more recently retired as an investigative reporter at Fox 29 in Philadelphia.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: 9/11: We remember. We honor. We stand together
description: We must never allow Sept. 11 to become merely a chapter in a history book or an image on a screen.
text:
Twenty-five years have passed since Sept. 11, 2001 – a day that forever changed America and shattered our sense of safety and peace.
Today, we remember the innocent lives taken in an act of unimaginable evil. But the loss did not end that day. For families who lost parents, spouses, children, siblings, friends, and loved ones, every anniversary renews the pain of lives and futures stolen too soon.

Tony Hwang

We honor the extraordinary courage of the first responders who ran toward danger as others fled. We remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice that day, as well as those who later died from illnesses linked to their service.
We also honor the generations of American servicemen and women who answered the call to defend our nation, our freedom, and the democratic principles we hold dear. Their courage and sacrifice must never be taken for granted.
With time, the rawness of grief may fade. Memories of fear, uncertainty, and disbelief may grow less vivid. But we must never allow Sept. 11 to become merely a chapter in a history book or an image on a screen.
From unimaginable tragedy emerged courage, resilience, determination, and unity. In our darkest hour, Americans stood together, helped one another, and demonstrated the enduring strength of our nation.
Twenty-five years later, remembrance is more than looking back. It is a responsibility we carry forward: to tell their stories, honor their sacrifice, support the families who still bear the loss, and teach future generations what happened and why it matters; and how it can never happen again.
We remember. We honor. We stand together. And we must never forget.
State Sen. Tony Hwang  represents the 28th District of Bethel, Easton, Fairfield and Newtown.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Immigrant rights, advocacy groups sue Trump administration for ‘warrantless arrest’
description: Immigrant and legal advocacy groups sued the Trump administration Thursday for violating the Fourth Amendment and other laws with the they called the government's "arrest first, ask questions later" policy of immigrant arrests.
text:
Austin Rose, at lectern, a managing attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, spoke Thursday as advocates announced a lawsuit against the Trump administration for "warrantless arrests" of residents in immigration stops. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Immigrant and legal advocacy groups sued the Trump administration Thursday for violating the Fourth Amendment and other laws with the they called the government’s “arrest first, ask questions later” policy of immigrant arrests.
The 56-page lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Baltimore, accuses Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents of engaging in “warrantless arrest” that sweeps up people without cause beyond the fact that they appear to be immigrants.
It said 80% of those arrested by ICE in Maryland since 2025 had no criminal convictions and that of 1,300 arrests made in Operation Safe Community, a two-week ICE enforcement surge in Maryland and Virginia last month, less than a third had criminal convictions.
The lawsuit also said that of the more than 7,ooo street arrests in Maryland since Jan. 20, 2025, the day President Donald Trump (R) was sworn in to his second term, 93% of those arrested have been citizens of Latin American or Caribbean countries, in what one attorney called racial profiling.
“Over the past 21 months, plainclothes, masked, armed, unidentified and untrained federal agents have terrorized Maryland communities,” said Shana Kader, legal director for We Are CASA, during a news conference at the group’s multicultural center in Langley Park. “From the Eastern Shore to Park Heights to the mountains of Washington County, these agents have stalked primarily brown and Black neighborhoods, arresting those they perceive to be brown or Black immigrants without warrants and without probable cause.”
“Shame!” some people yelled after Kader spoke.
Sonia Kumar, senior staff attorney with ACLU of Maryland, talks about a lawsuit over the Trump administration’s immigration arrests. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Besides We Are CASA, other groups involved in the suit are the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, the ACLU of Maryland and the National Immigration Project.
Plaintiffs include three men and one woman from Maryland, three identified only by their initials. Defendants are the Homeland Security Department and its secretary, Markwayne Mullin; ICE and its acting director, David Venturella; the Justice Department and Attorney General Todd Blanche.
Representatives from ICE and Homeland Security did not respond to requests for comment on the suit Thursday.
The lawsuit was filed on the same day We Are CASA announced Tiago Alexandre Sousa Martin was released from ICE custody and returned home after being shot by ICE agents in an Anne Arundel County neighborhood on Dec. 24.
And it comes less than a week after ICE agents who converged on a Frederick neighborhood were seen on video grabbing and pushing protestors in front of a house. At least one agent can be seen hitting a person on the ground with a baton, according to video provided by Hagerstown Rapid Response.
Austin Rose, managing attorney with the Amica Center based in Washington, D.C., said the lawsuit isn’t directly connected to the incident in Frederick.
“They [ICE agents] staked out a neighborhood for 40 hours, apparently looking for someone, and then some brave neighbors came and intervened,” said Rose, who was born and raised in Frederick. “It just shows what ICE is doing, which is they’re creating problems for themselves by just randomly showing up in neighborhoods.”
‘We are Maryland’
The named plaintiff, Samuel Guzmán, 24, is a Maryland native. He is also a member of We Are CASA and a resident of Anne Arundel County.
Several people held signs and posters Thursday at We Are CASA’s multicultural center in Langley Park. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
On June 7, Guzmán was detained by ICE agents after coming out of a 7-Eleven. Even though agents saw his identification and Guzmán pleaded that he’s a U.S. citizen, “the agents immediately handcuffed” him, put him in a truck and drove to a nearby parking lot along with other recently arrested “Latine” individuals.
“After finally reviewing Mr. Guzmán’s identity documents a second time, the agents returned him to the 7-Eleven parking lot and released him with no explanation,” the suit says. “Mr. Guzmán continues to take the same route to work on which he was arrested in June, and he faces substantial risk of re-arrest. He fears he or his Latine family members in the Annapolis area will be arrested in the future.”
A 38-year-old woman, identified in the suit as “K.M.,” was approached by ICE agents Jan. 12 while she parked her car near a friend’s house in Salisbury. Agents in six unmarked vehicles ordered her out of the car, “threatened to shoot her” and then handcuffed her. They detained K.M. for several hours at the Salisbury ICE office, interrogating her about her children and husband, who is deceased.
She was eventually released with an ankle monitor, “which causes her significant discomfort and shame at work and in public, and she must attend monthly ICE appointments.”
Similar incidents and fears were expressed by two other We Are CASA members Thursday, who went by their initials.
State Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s) was on hand for Thursday’s announcement to at the multicultural center to express his support for the suit.
“As much as the Trump administration wants to terrorize us, as much as the Trump administration wants to hate us, we are Casa. We are Maryland, and we are America,” Augustine said. “We stand with We are Casa and all who are part of this suit for constitutional due process. We will fight together, and we will win because when we fight … ”
“We win,” chanted those in attendance.

title: Vance blasts Dem ‘crazies’ in convention speech seen as possible 2028 audition
text: Vice President JD Vance took to the GOP convention stage in Dallas on Thursday in what served as a re-introduction ahead of a widely anticipated run for the party’s presidential nomination in 2028. The former U.S. senator from Ohio sought to rally the GOP base on the second and final day of the unusual gathering, as Republicans vie to retain control of the U.S. House and Senate in the midterms less than two months away, even as President Donald Trump faces anemic approval ratings amid the war in Iran and concerns surrounding the economy. Vance repeatedly maligned Democrats as “crazies,” referencing some of the more controversial statements recent primary winners have made. And he urged the enthusiastic crowd to put aside policy differences with GOP candidates to keep “the party of common sense” in power.“It’s so much more than having good politicians in Washington,” he said. “It’s about sending a message to the Democratic Party that if you send your crazies, we’re going to send you packing.” At one point during his speech, members of the crowd chanted “48” — an apparent signal of support for Vance to become the 48th president. Vance responded: “We got to take care of business this November — then we’ll worry about what comes next.” ‘Birthright’Vance infused the recent birth of his fourth child into his speech. He and his wife, second lady Usha Vance, welcomed son Alec Neel Vance in July.  And he portrayed what he called Republicans’ support for Americans’ “birthright” as a major theme heading into November. “I believe that our founders built this nation on a promise that echoes our creator: That every American child is born an heir — is born with a birthright,” Vance said, adding that “that birthright, ladies and gentlemen, is what this November is all about.” Several times, Vance accused immigrants living in the country illegally of stealing what should belong to U.S. citizens. He said that Democrats, particularly former President Joe Biden, encouraged that theft.“My little boy, he is now our fellow citizen, though he doesn’t know it,” he said. “And I think about what the Democrats have said about our shared birthright as Americans, or frankly, the lack thereof.” Vance said the birth of his youngest son shifted his focus to the future.“Now, because we got a new kid around, I can’t help but look at the future of this country through the eyes of the future of my son,” he said. “And I can’t help but think about what it is that we’re fighting for and what it is that we want for all of our children.” Vance honors Charlie KirkThe vice president also paid tribute to his late friend and conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot while speaking on a Utah college campus one year ago Thursday. Vance praised Kirk as a devoted husband and father, addressing Kirk’s two young children, saying: “For those of us who loved your dad, we knew him as something even better than a great man. He was a good man.” Later in his speech, Vance urged voters to “do what Charlie did: Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater — don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.” ‘Trump’s most loyal puppet’Kendall Witmer, rapid response director for the Democratic National Committee, blasted Vance as “Donald Trump’s most loyal puppet,” noting that the vice president is “working in lockstep to enact an agenda that has hiked prices and made life unaffordable for working families,” in a statement Thursday night.  “Vance has defended even their most disastrous policies, proving his loyalty to Trump over the American people,” Witmer said. “Vance will continue to gaslight Americans, but voters know the truth: Trump and Vance have tanked the economy, plunged the country into more endless wars, and failed to make life more affordable for everyday Americans.”Vance is slated to deliver remarks Monday at an industrial manufacturing facility in Olathe, Kansas, during an event hosted by Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc. On Monday, he will also visit a federal law enforcement facility in Kansas City, Missouri, where he is set to speak on the Trump administration’s sweeping anti-fraud effort, which he has helmed.

title: Republicans close out GOP midterm convention vowing to keep control of Congress
text: President Donald Trump and Republicans wrapped up their two-day midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday night, urging voters to ensure the party has another two years with unified control of government. Speakers, many vying for seats in Congress, insisted Democrats regaining power would be disastrous for the country, some going as far as implying they’d lead to the nation’s downfall. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said the results of the elections “will determine the fate of our Republic and the future for our children and our grandchildren.”He argued that the GOP maintaining control of both chambers represents the best way to address border security, crime, defense and economic concerns, though he didn’t detail any specific bills he’d try to enact during the next two years. Johnson didn’t bring up the war in Iran or rising gas prices during his speech, but did say he doesn’t intend to let Democrats flip the House from red to blue next year. “We cannot and will not allow them to take the majority of the Congress,” he said. “We're not going to do it.”RFK Jr.Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke at length about his family’s history as Democratic leaders and how the party has evolved since the 1960s. Standing in front of an electronic backdrop displaying a farm field and the “Make America Healthy Again” slogan, Kennedy’s speech focused predominantly on his experiences and Trump. The vast majority of his 25-minute speech didn’t address the campaigns for Congress, with Kennedy only mentioning the fight for control of the House and Senate in two sentences at the end. “We need to elect a Republican Congress to keep this momentum going,” he said. “Let's go out and do that.”Vice President JD Vance spoke just before Trump arrived on stage.‘I am on the ballot’Trump closed out the convention with his second speech in two days, urging Republicans to vote in the midterm elections so the party could make additional changes to immigration and implement nationwide changes to voter identification requirements. “On Election Day, Nov. 3, you got to do me a favor, you got to get out and vote,” he said. “And you're going to pretend I'm on the ballot because, in a way, I am on the ballot.”He then had everyone in the stadium raise their right hand to recite a pledge to vote that included comments about cheating. He then said anyone who didn’t vote would go to hell. Trump didn’t mention specific candidates much during his speech but did recognize Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is seeking the state’s U.S. Senate seat. Trump said he didn’t like the way Paxton dresses, talks, or looks, but urged Republicans in the state to vote for him during the general election. “I don't know if he's going to ever speak to me again, but you know I don't care as long as he wins,” he said. “I really don't. I don't know. I don't have to speak to him. He's going to vote the way we would vote, so I don't have to speak to him. I don't care. You got to vote for him.” After speaking for about 25 minutes, Trump introduced opera singer Christopher Macchio to perform “America the Beautiful” and “All I Ask of You” from “Phantom of the Opera” as balloons fell from the ceiling.

title: Demuth proposes teacher performance pay, wants changes to free school meals
description: House Speaker Lisa Demuth on Thursday said as governor she would bolster school safety, implement a teacher “pay for performance” model and allow districts to opt out of mandates, like paid family leave. Academic outcomes for Minnesota students have stagnated since the pandemic, with fewer than half of Minnesota public school students meeting grade-level rea[...]
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth and running mate Ryan Wilson present their education plan during a press conference at the Minnesota Capitol on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)House Speaker Lisa Demuth on Thursday said as governor she would bolster school safety, implement a teacher “pay for performance” model and allow districts to opt out of mandates, like paid family leave.
Academic outcomes for Minnesota students have stagnated since the pandemic, with fewer than half of Minnesota public school students meeting grade-level reading and math expectations last year. Many school districts have yet to return to pre-pandemic test scores.
Demuth, the GOP nominee for governor, cited her decade of experience on her local school board — prior to serving in the Legislature — as a needed qualification for getting student achievement back on track.
“We’ll be focusing on the fundamentals of reading, math and science. We want to make sure that we are spending wisely with fewer mandates. We’ll provide safety for all students in all schools,” Demuth said at a Capitol press conference Thursday.
Demuth is facing Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar in November. Klobuchar has pledged to raise student achievement, ban cell phones in classrooms and work with school districts to limit screen-time. Demuth said she would encourage school districts to limit screen-time, rather than a blanket ban.
Demuth said the state will also implement teacher performance pay, because “better teachers deserve better pay.” She was unable to say what metric would be used for teachers to receive additional pay. Some states and districts use student academic performance or classroom observations to determine a teacher’s pay, in part.
Education Minnesota, the state’s teachers union, has endorsed Klobuchar for governor.
Asked whether she would continue Minnesota’s free school meals program passed during the Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta in 2023, Demuth said children from wealthy families shouldn’t be eligible.
“When a family is making six- and sometimes seven-figure incomes, their kids do not need free meals,” Demuth said.
Demuth said as governor she would opt into more federal education funding, like the new $1,700 tax credit for taxpayers who donate to scholarship-granting organizations. The tax credit was passed last year in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and it allows nonprofits to use the money donated to offer scholarships for public or private school programs.
The Minnesota Department of Education has said the tax credit, which is a circuitous form of a private school voucher program long championed by conservative activists, would disproportionately help wealthier Minnesotans.
Demuth’s education plan also says she will remove “‘woke’ standards adopted by the Walz status quo.” Asked what standards the plan refers to, Demuth said her administration will do an evaluation of the state’s education mandates and remove standards that “are pushing our kids away from the basics of reading, math and science.”
Demuth’s plan also includes changes to the state’s teacher licensing board to ensure the board is working to “prepare the next generation of workers and not the next generation of activists,” referring to conservative assertions that the schools are being used to indoctrinate Minnesota students in progressive politics.
The House speaker highlighted that her plan focuses on school safety and said public, private and charter schools would be eligible for state school safety aid. In recent years to help address budget shortfalls, DFL Gov. Tim Walz has proposed cutting state aid to private schools, but those cuts didn’t pass the Legislature.

text:
Five Republican precinct caucuses were held at Franklin Jr High in Des Moines Jan. 15, 2024. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa’s Republican caucuses will again kick off the national presidential nominating calendar in 2028, the Republican National Committee decided Thursday during its midterm convention in Dallas.
The RNC left in place the lineup of previous presidential cycles, with the Iowa caucuses followed by the New Hampshire primary and then contests in Nevada and South Carolina.
 “Today’s vote preserves the path to the Republican presidential nomination and gives our voters a strong voice in the process,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said in a news release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Republican Party of Iowa Chairman Jeff Kaufmann chaired the RNC’s Presidential Nominating Process Committee, which recommended preserving the traditional carve-out system for 2028. According to the RNC’s release, “the only substantive change provides additional flexibility for states holding later contests regarding delegate allocation.”
“I’m pleased to announce that Iowa’s First in the Nation status is officially preserved through 2028,” Kaufmann said in a news release. “… Democrats may have abandoned Iowa, but Republicans under President Trump and RNC Chairman Gruters are committed to ensuring the Iowa Caucuses remain a defining part of the presidential nominating process.”
The Democratic National Committee in July denied Iowa Democrats a waiver to hold their presidential caucuses in the early window before Super Tuesday.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Rogers uses RNC midterm platform to attack El-Sayed as Dems push back against Islamophobic rhetoric
description: The campaign of Michigan Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers had a national audience on Thursday night as he spoke at the party’s midterm convention — a platform he used to level attacks against his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. Much of Rogers’ speech, however, focused on the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade […]
text:
Michigan Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers, of White Lake, Mich., speaks at the second day of the Republican National Convention held on Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. (Screenshot courtesy of C-SPAN)The campaign of Michigan Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers had a national audience on Thursday night as he spoke at the party’s midterm convention — a platform he used to level attacks against his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed.
Much of Rogers’ speech, however, focused on the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center and at the Pentagon, relating the threat of Islamic terrorism to the campaign of El-Sayed, which Democrats on Thursday said was just another example of Rogers using Islamophobia to negatively portray his opponent.
Although Rogers has pounced on El-Sayed’s progressive platform since the latter became the Democratic nominee, highlighting his stances on Medicare for All and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a large part of Rogers’ campaign has centered on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, his Egyptian heritage and his support for the people of Palestine in the ongoing war between Israel and Hamas, the radical political group that has governed the Gaza strip for many years now.
That continued to be a cornerstone of the Rogers campaign, but at scale, on Thursday as millions of Republicans tuned into coverage of the Republican National Committee’s midterm confab. Rogers invoked El-Sayed’s connection with leftist influencer Hasan Piker, and the streamer’s belief that America deserved the Sept. 11, 2001 tragedy. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’ve spent much of my life confronting this enemy head-on. I know what they’re capable of, and I know what happens when America becomes afraid to call evil by its name,” Rogers said from the stage. “That’s why I never imagined that 25 years after 9/11, I would be running against somebody that campaigns with Hasan Piker, who thinks America deserved it. Yeah, but here we are.”
A common attack against El-Sayed has focused on the Piker connection, and Rogers has said — hyperbolically — that Piker was El-Sayed’s running mate. Of note, candidates for the U.S. Senate are solitary nominees, and do not run for office in teams with deputies much like a president or a governor.
El-Sayed has been adamant since becoming the Democratic nominee that Piker does not speak for his campaign, but El-Sayed has yet to denounce the influencer or distance himself from Piker in a profound way. 
El-Sayed’s choice to not do so has only led to more personal attacks from the GOP, alluding to Piker and El-Sayed holding the same political ideologies. El-Sayed has said that wasn’t true and one of the biggest distinctions between them is that El-Sayed does not view himself as a Democratic Socialist, but rather a capitalist concerned with the current state of capitalism.
Rogers was undeterred in evaporating that distinction.
“Together, they attack America. They excuse extremism. They treat our country like it’s the villain,” Rogers said, just before pivoting to a GOP talking point that El-Sayed has accepted campaign cash from terrorist organizations, like the Muslim Brotherhood.
There is no evidence that El-Sayed has ever pledged his support to the organization or accepted money from them, let alone ever having explicit ties to the group.
That said, the National Republican Senatorial Committee has in recent days fixated on a story from conservative Michigan news outlet The Midwestern, which sought to tie El-Sayed with the dealings of his biological mother, Fatten Fathy Elkomy.
The Midwesterner noted that in 2004, the U.S. Department of Treasury designated the Islamic African Relief Agency, which was focused on worldwide healthcare for disadvantaged people in war or conflict zones, as an organization supporting terrorism. 
In its examination of that connection, The Midwesterner also noted that Elkomy worked with the Islamic African Relief Agency between 1999 and at least 2004.
Rogers did not explicitly mention El-Sayed’s birth mother in his remarks, but it was a piece of the overall campaign rhetoric used by the NRSC to advertise Rogers’ address.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, and political influencer Hasan Piker, right, take questions from the media before an event on the campus of Michigan State University in East Lansing, Mich on April 7, 2026 (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Fact checkers, however, have found that the claims about El-Sayed’s biological mother and her work with the IARA were either false or missing key context. The same goes with Rogers’ assertion on the Muslim Brotherhood.
Snopes, in an attempt to debunk the claim, reported that it was not possible to find any evidence that the humanitarian aid group knowingly financially supported terrorist groups or Islamic militants.
The Midwesterner had referred to charging documents filed by the U.S. Department of Justice in 2007 the Islamic American Relief Agency. Elkomy worked for the African branch. Snopes noted that although the DOJ convicted several of the group’s former officers of unlawful financial transactions with Iraq during the 2000s-era war, there were no charges filed related to knowingly supporting terrorism.
El-Sayed’s campaign also said that Elkomy, a nurse practitioner in Missouri, had never been accused of wrongdoing and was neither charged or named as a defendant in the Department of Justice’s case.
That said, Snopes reported that it could not definitively label the claim as a lie or patently true — only that it was misleading.
The Muslim Brotherhood line has long been debunked as a conspiracy perpetuated by conservative firebrand and former state Sen. Patrick Colbeck. The former Republican senator made the claim during his campaign for governor in 2018, when El-Sayed was also seeking the office on the Democratic side of the aisle.
Considering those facts, the Advance asked the NRSC if it was fair to use his birth mother’s ties to the organization in a direct attack against him.
Samantha Cantrell, the NRSC’s regional press secretary, said it was fair game.
“Abdul El-Sayed’s true views on 9/11 should concern every Michigander given he still refuses to condemn Hasan Piker, told Americans to ‘center’ our reaction to 9/11, and has refused to condemn his mother’s work funneling money to terrorist organizations assisting Osama Bin Laden,” Cantrell said in a statement to the Advance.
Rogers also asserted that El-Sayed sympathized with the man who perpetrated the attack on Temple Israel, a Jewish temple in West Bloomfield. The attacker’s brother was later identified by the Israeli government as a Hezbollah leader killed in an Israeli airstrike.
El-Sayed at the time called the situation a tragedy but also said, “hurt people hurt people,” in reference to the attacker.
The Democratic nominee recently apologized for that statement during an annual, pre-Michigan Democratic Convention meeting of the Michigan Jewish Democratic Caucus, known as their Summer Simcha and held in the weeks following the August primary
Rogers did not acknowledge that El-Sayed had apologized or reexamined his past remarks.
Democrats label Rogers’ remarks as pure Islamophobia
In response to Rogers’ address, El-Sayed spokesperson Roxie Richner said Rogers and his allies were “resorting to shameful lies” about the Democratic nominee “to try and distract from Rogers’ deep record as a corrupt career politician who has taken millions from Big Pharma.”
“But Michiganders see right through it,” Richner said. “And they’ll send Mike Rogers packing in November, once again, so he doesn’t get another opportunity to make himself and his billionaire donors richer while selling out working families.”
Christyna Thompson, press secretary for the Democratic-led Senate Majority PAC, said that “this is what Republicans do when they can’t outrun their own record.”
“They rewrite history. They point fingers. They’ll do whatever they can to make people forget how they voted,” Thompson said in a statement. “You don’t get to wrap yourself in 9/11 after turning your back on the people who answered the call. It’s spineless behavior and it turns voters off. “
Thompson said that Rogers voted against the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act when he was in Congress. The act created the federal health program that treats 9/11 responders and survivors from Ground Zero, the Pentagon, and Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
In direct response to Rogers’ focus on El-Sayed’s religious and cultural background, Thompson told the Advance that voters should “take it as a sign of where the GOP playbook stands 50 days out.”
“They’ve got nothing better beyond casual Islamophobia and fake promises of free money they pray would win voters over,” she said. “Pretty stupid strategy altogether.”
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel, in a statement issued following Rogers’ speech, addressed that fact that throughout his speech, Rogers didn’t address skyrocketing prices on goods and services, the new trade war President Donald Trump has opened with Canada, or the new hot war he’s engaging in with Iran.
On Rogers’ rhetoric on El-Sayed’s heritage, Hertel said Rogers was “trafficking in dishonest, Islamophobic attacks because he wants to distract from how his and Trump’s agenda is spiking costs and hurting Michiganders.”
“Rogers’ remarks were dangerous and desperate, and they were beneath the office he seeks,” Hertel added.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska gubernatorial candidates vow support for the seafood industry while revealing some splits
description: At a fisheries forum held Wednesday night in Kodiak, all four candidates remaining in Alaska’s gubernatorial race found plenty of common ground. Former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, and the three Republicans, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, former state Attorney General Treg Taylor and business owner and talk-show host Bernadette Wilso[...]
text:
udience members are packed into the Gerald C. WIlson Auditorium at Kodiak High School on the evening of Sept. 9, 2026, to listen to the four remaining gubernatorial candidates discuss seafood-related issues. Every election year, the Kodiak Chamber of Commerce holds debates that are focused solely on fisheries. Kodiak is one of the nation's main seafood portss, and fishing is a mainstay of its economy. (Photo by Brian Venua)At a fisheries forum held Wednesday night in Kodiak, all four candidates remaining in Alaska’s gubernatorial race found plenty of common ground.
Former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, and the three Republicans, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, former state Attorney General Treg Taylor and business owner and talk-show host Bernadette Wilson, described the seafood industry as a pillar of the state’s economy and fish as part of the state’s identity.
All four gubernatorial candidates, who are set to face off in the general election in Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, said they consider bycatch — the accidental interception of nontargeted species — to be an urgent problem for salmon runs. 
All said they want to appoint a special adviser on fisheries, something that past governors have done but that current Gov. Mike Dunleavy has not.
All said they wanted to appoint members of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, the panel that oversees practices in federal waters, and the Alaska Board of Fisheries, which has jurisdiction over state waters, who would represent state interests broadly, including non-commercial interests.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

All vowed a commitment to science, support for the state agency that markets Alaska’s seafood and investment in the infrastructure in coastal communities.
But there were differences that emerged at the event, sponsored by the Kodiak Chamber of Commerce. Those started with the candidates’ personal connections to and knowledge of seafood issues.
Kreiss-Tomkins, who is from the coastal town of Sitka in Southeast Alaska, which he called “a community that was built by fisheries,” provided evidence of the closest connection to fishing and the seafood industry. He spent summers during his college years working as a fishing crew member, and he is the only one of the four candidates who has personal experience fishing commercially and participating in the seafood industry, the Kodiak event revealed.
Wilson said she was connected to the fishing industry through her family. Her grandmother was born in the Bristol Bay community of Naknek, and her father operates a business “that is responsible for hauling all of the fish out of Valdez.”
Republicans Treg Taylor and Dave Bronson, who live in Alaska’s largest city, indicated in a lightning round held near the start of the forum that they had personally engaged in both sport and subsistence fishing; Wilson indicated sport fishing experience but not subsistence experience.
Taylor, who spent part of the debate talking about non-fishery issues like crime, confessed to a certain lack of knowledge about the subject. “This is admittedly an area that I’m not an expert in,” he said. He learned a lot preparing for the Kodiak forum and even “learned a ton during this debate listening to the responses from the other candidates up here,” he said.
Much of the event focused on trawling, the practice of using large nets in the midwater zones or bottom-water zones to scoop up large amounts of pollock and other groundfish. The pollock harvesters in particular have been accused of damaging the state’s salmon runs through bycatch, the accidental harvesting at sea of fish that would be otherwise returning to in-state spawning areas.
Pollock, which is caught mostly in federal waters, is the top-volume seafood harvest in the nation and accounted in 2023 and 2024 for 60% of the Alaska commercial seafood harvest volume, according to the most recent industry report by the McKinley Research Group, a consulting company. But pollock is a low-priced fish species, and the state’s pollock harvest accounted for only 29% of the value of the state’s total commercial seafood harvest, according to the McKinley Research Group. In contrast, salmon, caught mostly in state waters, accounted for only 13% of the volume but 31% of the total value of Alaska’s commercial seafood harvest in those years, according to the McKinley Research Group.
Bycatch a hot campaign topic
In different ways, candidates at the Kodiak event discussed what they consider to be the threats to salmon from bycatch in the trawl fisheries that target pollock and other groundfish species.
It is a hotly debated issue because it pits different sectors of the fishing industry against each other, including in Kodiak, a community dependent on both trawl harvests and salmon harvests.
Bronson defended his broad anti-trawling stance, which he admitted might not be popular among some people in Kodiak, including some audience members at the forum, which was held in the Kodiak High School’s auditorium.
Drastic reductions in trawling are needed to protect faltering runs of salmon, such as Interior Alaska river king salmon runs that have collapsed, he said.
“We’ve been trying to fix this by pushing all these little buttons. We reduce limits on sport, on subsistence, and we’re doing all this, and it’s not working,” he said. “Where are the kings? Where are the king crab? They’re gone. It’s time to start pulling the big levers, the big ones, and it’s going to devastate some people.”
There are already established areas of federal waters where trawling is banned. None of the candidates named any specific federal areas where they believe new bans should be established.  
 

Fishing boats line the docks at Kodiak’s St. Paul Harbor on Oct. 3, 2022. Kodiak is a major U.S. seafood port, and the Kodiak Chamber of Commerce holds candidate debates every election year that focus solely on fishery issues. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	There have been efforts to ban trawling in state waters, which are within three nautical miles of shore, including bills considered by the Legislature. Trawling is not a widely used harvest practice in state waters, though it occurs in some areas.
Wilson also criticized the trawling practice, but she said there has to be a distinction between the large-scale industrial operators and the “mom and pop” small-scale operators.
To address bycatch, she called for some new efforts to bring together different parties. She called for the establishment of a task force and a symposium to “get everybody to the table, all the different user groups, all in one spot.”
She also called for incentives to spur industry’s use of better technology and practices to mitigate bycatch. “We need to talk about the gear that’s being used. We need to talk about observers that are on boats. We need to talk about how we can bring AI into that conversation,” she said.
NOAA already has a program that funds the development of bycatch reduction technology, and it was not clear if Wilson was referencing that.
NOAA’s national Bycatch Reduction Engineering Program, which distributes grants annually to companies and agencies working on innovative technology, has been in existence for two decades. Technology developed includes trawl nets with features that allow accidentally caught salmon to escape; a 2024 scientific study identified ways to improve the design to protect more salmon.
Taylor used some strong language to describe bycatch, though he did not offer specific suggestions for action.
“We have to end practices that destroy our habitat, and we’ve got to get a handle on bycatch issues throughout the state,” he said.
Kreiss-Tomkins expressed skepticism about Wilson’s symposium and task-force suggestions.
“I’m not so bullish on task forces. I’m more bullish on action,” he said. He pointed to improvements that have already started to ease the bycatch problem. He cited, as an example, his advocacy more than a decade ago of stricter numerical limits for Chinook salmon bycatch in the Gulf of Alaska fisheries, which were approved by the North Pacific FIshery Management Council. He also cited his advocacy for stricter limits on halibut bycatch, which the council approved through an “abundance-based management” system that went into effect at the start of 2024.
Among the responses to a question about the state ferry system and investments in coastal infrastructure, Kreiss-Tomkins provided the most specifics.
Along with bolstering the troubled ferry system and using the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities’ Municipal Harbor Grants Program to support communities, he had other suggestions. The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority should prioritize investment in coastal communities and the seafood industry, something it is not currently doing, he said. Additionally, “general obligation bonds can help build out the waterfronts and harbor infrastructure in Alaska,” he said.
On environmental science, some differences emerged.
Kreiss-Tomkins said the state can respond to the challenge of climate change by investing in research, particularly at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. UAF’s College of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences “has incredible capacity and worldwide renown,” he said.
The Republican candidates demurred on the question of climate change.
Wilson and Bronson said changing conditions in the ocean are nothing new and that there is nothing the state can do about them.
Wilson referred to her Naknek-born grandmother, who advised that “the waters were constantly warming and cooling,” affecting fish runs that would change in size year to year. “It is an ongoing issue that we’ve been well aware of for decades,” she said.
Bronson made a similar comment. “Whether it’s North Pacific or North Atlantic or any other body, oceanic body of water. The temperature is always on cycles, and it’s always changing,” he said.
Taylor said it is important for the state to invest in scientific research to counter federal efforts to impose burdensome environmental regulation. He referenced his own legal fights as attorney general against the Biden administration, particularly concerning NOAA’s 2022 designation of nearly 160 million acres of marine territory as critical habitat for bearded and ringed seals. Both populations are protected with threatened listings under the Endangered Species Act.
Taylor claimed success in the fight. Those critical habitat designations “would have shut down mass portions of Northern and Western Alaska. We beat that with good sound data,” he said.
Taylor’s seal information is outdated. While U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason ruled in 2024 in the state’s favor, finding that the designation was overly broad, the state ultimately lost in the case. The 9th circuit court of appeals in March ordered the reinstatement of the seal species’ designated critical habitats. The day before the Kodiak forum, the appeals court rejected a state petition to revisit the decision.
Outside of the judicial system, the Trump administration has been pushing to reduce the scope of Endangered Species Act protections in general. In July, the administration issued a rule limiting future critical habitat designations.
The Kodiak Chamber of Commerce is set to hold two more fisheries-focused candidate forums on Saturday, one for contenders in the U.S. Senate race and the other for the U.S. House contenders.
Gubernatorial candidcates at the Sept. 9, 2026, fisheries debate in Kodiak hold up signs indicating whether they have participated in subsistence fish harvests. From left are former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, former Attorney General Treg Taylor, business owner and radio talk-show host Bernadette Wilson and former state Rep. Konathan Kreiss-Tomkins. Bronson, Taylor and Wilson are Republicans; Kreiss-Tomkins is a Democrat. Wilson indicated that she has participated in sport fishing but not subsistence harvsting. The four have advanced to the general election, in which Alaska will used ranked-choice voting to select their next governor. (Photo by Brian Venua)

title: Alaska Legislature will support state’s bootlegging penalties in front of U.S. Supreme Court
description: The Alaska Legislature will join Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s administration in seeking to defend the state’s anti-bootlegging punishments in front of the U.S. Supreme Court. On Thursday, the joint House-Senate Legislative Council voted to hire an outside attorney to draft a friend-of-the-court letter — formally known as an amicus brief — in support of the state […]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States NewsroomThe Alaska Legislature will join Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s administration in seeking to defend the state’s anti-bootlegging punishments in front of the U.S. Supreme Court.
On Thursday, the joint House-Senate Legislative Council voted to hire an outside attorney to draft a friend-of-the-court letter — formally known as an amicus brief — in support of the state and against Ken Jouppi, a former Bush pilot whose plane was seized after a bootlegging conviction.
Jouppi has repeatedly challenged that seizure, saying it represents an illegal punishment because it is out of proportion to the crime he committed. 
The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the seizure in 2025, but Jouppi appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, which agreed earlier this year to hear the case. Oral arguments are expected in December.
The Legislative Council has frequently clashed with Dunleavy over the governor’s interpretations of state law and the Alaska Constitution and has funded multiple lawsuits against the governor, but on this case, the state’s executive and Legislature are aligned.
The state Department of Law, which is defending the state’s anti-bootlegging laws, requested in late August that legislators get involved with the issue.
“At its core,” wrote Senior Assistant Attorney General Kaci Schroeder in a memo to the Legislative Council, “the case implicates an important legislative judgment: how seriously Alaska may treat the illegal importation of alcohol into communities that have affirmatively chosen to prohibit it, and what sanctions the Legislature may impose to deter individuals from using aircraft to circumvent those local decisions.”
Schroeder wrote that Alaska’s penalties for bootlegging were the result of the Legislature “responding to the real-world consequences of local alcohol abuse.”
Having the Legislature provide its input could help the Supreme Court understand Alaska’s historic concerns over alcohol and the role that Bush planes have in serving rural Alaska.
The Legislature’s hired attorney is expected to send its letter to the Supreme Court by mid-October, said Rep. Sara Hannan, D-Juneau and chair of the Legislative Council.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Amid PFAS pollution lawsuits, Perdue wants to increase its discharges. Residents are skeptical.
description: For years, Perdue Agribusiness has been embroiled lawsuits over claims it polluted local groundwater with PFAS, the cancer-causing "forever chemical." So neighbors were skeptical when Perdue asked to increase the treated wastewater it pours in a local stream.
text:
A Maryland Department of the Environment emergency response vehicle is on display at a 2025 press conference in Essex. (Photo by Christine Condon /Maryland Matters)When Perdue Agribusiness sought state permission to increase the amount of treated wastewater it pours into a local stream, some Salisbury-area residents were skeptical.
For the past several years, Perdue has been embroiled in a pollution scandal over allegations that it polluted local groundwater with PFAS, the cancer-causing substances known as “forever chemicals” because they do not readily break down in the environment.
The company, which runs a 294-acre campus near Salisbury with soybean processing facilities, hatcheries, grain storage areas and a truck garage, faces twin lawsuits from more than 550 area residents who rely on well water.
But it initiated legal action of its own in May, suing 3M, which produced firefighting foam containing PFAS, and Johnson Controls, which maintained a firefighting system that used the foam at Perdue’s soybean processing plant. Perdue believes the firefighting foam is the sole source of the PFAS contamination.
Now, the company is asking Maryland Department of the Environment regulators to approve its request to discharge an average of up to 1 million gallons per day into the Peggy Branch, compared to its current average flow of about 205,000 gallons per day.
“If the Perdue facility can’t discharge clean water at the levels it’s discharging now, I don’t see how MDE is going to enforce clean drinking water at a level five times what it is now,” Matt Godbey said during a Wednesday night hearing on the request at Wor-Wic Community College.
He was one of a handful of residents who took the microphone to express concerns about the new permit. A public comment period for the permit remains open until 5 p.m. on Sept. 14.
Four years after ban, fire departments stuck with hazardous PFAS foam

Perdue says it needs to increase its discharges into the stream precisely because it’s upgrading its wastewater treatment system. Perdue is planning to do away with a series of lagoons that previously stored wastewater, which have attracted concerns about the potential for pollutants to leech into groundwater.
“The project is tied to long-planned upgrades to the facility’s wastewater treatment system,” wrote a spokesperson for Perdue in a statement, “including replacing existing lagoon infrastructure with modern treatment tanks and providing capacity to support future operational needs.”
Under the proposed new five-year discharge permit under the Clean Water Act, Perdue would face new limits on PFAS discharges into the creek.
For the first two years, Perdue would simply have to notify regulators and take corrective actions if it detects two of the most common PFAS compounds during monthly testing. After that, detectable levels of the two PFAS chemicals — anything over 4 nanograms per liter — would be considered a permit violation and could bring fines or other penalties from MDE.
In 2025, Perdue voluntarily installed a PFAS treatment system at its wastewater facility, which has reduced PFAS concentrations to “trace” amounts, according to the company’s website. The company noted that it believes the last known discharge of PFAS-containing foam on its campus was in 2019.
In many other categories, Perdue’s pollutant limits are staying roughly the same — even though the permit would allow Perdue to increase the amount of water it sends into the environment, said MDE’s Jonathan Rice, chief of the Industrial and General Permits Division for the Wastewater Pollution Prevention and Reclamation Program.
“Despite the fact that the facility has asked us to increase their flow by up to five times, we are not increasing the loading limits,” Rice said during Wednesday’s meeting, “If they increase their flow, they have to offset that by decreasing the concentration of the pollutants.”
James Parrigin, who has lived with his wife and children close to Perdue’s Salisbury campus since 2014, said he chose to purchase a home water treatment system after learning about the PFAS contamination, and pays for a costly new filter each year. Parrigin said Perdue’s request makes him worry that won’t be enough.
“It will make me wonder if the filtration system I’ve installed — that is, the one I could afford — will be robust enough to continue to protect us,” Parrigin said during Wednesday’s meeting. “Will I need to change my expensive filter every six months? Will I need to purchase these expensive water tests several times a year? I’m worried to see elevated PFAS levels in my kids’ blood tests that we get. I’m worried that folks will turn a blind eye to this in the interest of profit and expansion.”
Maryland, South Carolina lose bid to try PFAS contamination cases in state courts

During his remarks, Parrigin suggested that Perdue should be required to show that its PFAS readings are “nondetect,” or not high enough to be measured by lab tests, before it can increase its discharge into Peggy Branch, which empties into Johnson Pond, a Salisbury fishing pond that later flows into the Wicomico River.
Margarita Rosado, who has lived near the Salisbury facility since 1991, said Perdue’s request has alarmed her, adding to fears for her safety that began in earnest in 2024, when testing on her well revealed levels of certain PFAS far exceeding federal drinking water guidelines.
“I had planned to live in my home until my dying days,” Rosado said. “Now, for the first time, I don’t think I want to stay, and that’s something I never thought I would ever say about my home.”
For its part, Perdue argues that it has taken a variety of steps in response to the groundwater contamination, which MDE testing first revealed in 2023. The state identified the company as a “responsible person” for the pollution, and Perdue paid to investigate it, testing 679 wells throughout the community.
The company’s website states that it has performed well testing on all the homes where it was requested, and it has installed free point-of-entry water treatment systems, or POETs, for every homeowner who has asked, covering 91% of the impacted properties.
“Perdue will continue to perform substantial additional monitoring and testing for the surrounding properties, as well as installing and maintaining additional POET systems,” read a Perdue legal filing from May.
But Perdue denies liability for the pollution, arguing that 3M and Johnson Controls should be held liable if the court deems the residents’ claims actionable.
Perdue’s recent legal filings say the Salisbury campus processes soybeans into oil using a highly flammable solvent called hexane. As a result, the plant’s fire suppression system included not just water, but Aqueous Film-Forming Foam, or AFFF, which for decades included PFAS chemicals now known as health hazards.
Perdue wrote that its fire suppression system used the firefighting foam manufactured by 3M starting in 1986. Beginning as early as 2012, Johnson Controls was maintaining Perdue’s system.
“On several occasions,” Perdue’s filing said, workers from Johnson Controls “released large volumes” of the firefighting foam into the environment, without the knowledge or consent of Perdue.
Neither 3M nor Johnson Controls responded to requests for comment.
In legal filings, Perdue has argued that it has since installed a new fire suppression system using fluorine-free foam.
