title: Reykdal seeks $2B infusion for WA public schools in next budget
description: The leader of Washington’s public school system on Thursday outlined his multibillion-dollar budget request he says is needed to ensure the state meets its legal obligations to fund basic education for more than 1 million students. Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal wants Gov. Bob Ferguson and state lawmakers to provide nearly $2 billion more[...]
text:
Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal on Thursday discussed his request for nearly $2 billion in the next state budget. He is seen here testifying to a House committee in January. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)The leader of Washington’s public school system on Thursday outlined his multibillion-dollar budget request he says is needed to ensure the state meets its legal obligations to fund basic education for more than 1 million students.
Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal wants Gov. Bob Ferguson and state lawmakers to provide nearly $2 billion more for public schools in the 2027-2029 budget that they will write in the coming legislative session.
Of the total, $1.2 billion is needed to amply fund education as set out in the state constitution and upheld by the state’s highest court in the landmark case known as McCleary. In 2012, the court ruled the state was underfunding schools. It took until 2018 before justices found the state had met its obligations.
The remainder of the budget request is to expand learning assistance for students from low-income families and restore funding to the popular Transition to Kindergarten program.
Reykdal knows it is a big ask with lawmakers and the governor staring down another budget shortfall. 
“We understand it’s going to be a heck of a battle up there,” he said in a news conference. “We fundamentally believe that we are no longer being amply funded, that the constitution is not being met and the Supreme Court order in McCleary is not being met. We’re urging lawmakers to get to their constitutional duty before everything else.”
Reykdal, who will formally submit his request to Ferguson on Monday, said schools across the state are struggling to cover the ever-rising cost of ongoing operations. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US




A record number of schools, 11, are now on binding conditions with the state, an arrangement that requires state oversight of day-to-day financial operations, according to the superintendent’s office.
“With our state’s affluent economy, it is inexcusable that schools are being forced to choose between paying their insurance bills or laying off the teachers and paraeducators that support the student learning and progress we expect,” Reykdal said in a statement.
Reykdal wants to boost funding for materials, supplies and operations by $408.6 million next fiscal year and another $463.4 million in the following year.
A good chunk of those dollars are to pay for insurance and utilities. In May, roughly 130 school districts participating in a risk management program were notified that their electricity rates will increase by an average of 45% in this school year, according to the superintendent’s office. 
The proposal also calls for providing $100 million more in the next budget to pick up costs of substitute teachers now borne by school districts.  And he’s asking for nearly $225 million more for improving salaries of classified state and paraeducators.
Additionally, Reykdal wants to restore funding for Transition to Kindergarten. Earlier this year, superintendents began preparing to cut teachers and seats for students after the governor signed into law a budget that cut the early learning program by $27 million.
One item not in his request: funding for free school lunches. This puts Reykdal at odds with Ferguson, who has vowed to use money from the state’s new income tax on high earners to cover the estimated $140 million cost in the 2029-31 budget.
Washington now covers meals for roughly 70% of its public school students. Though Reykdal has long supported covering 100%, this isn’t the right time to try to do it, he said.
“That’s the goal. Is it the short-term goal for my agency? No. When school districts are shutting down programs because they can’t hardly afford their insurance bill or their utility bill, that’s a bigger priority because that’s causing school districts to cut direct service and direct programs to students and families,” he said. “It’s kind of a bummer, but meals is not constitutionally protected basic ed.”
Ferguson is drafting his first two-year budget proposal. It will be released in mid-December for the Legislature to consider early next year.  
Monday is the deadline for budget requests to be submitted by state agencies as well as departments run by other statewide elected officials. The Office of Financial Management posts the requests online.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Clean Energy group calls for more public scrutiny of data center energy costs
description: A clean energy group is calling on the Iowa Utilities Commission and policymakers to ensure utility companies don’t use data center energy demands to build new facilities and pass the costs on to ratepayers.  Iowa Business for Clean Energy, in a news release Thursday, said Alliant Energy Corporation is using “loopholes” and “secret” rate agreements […]
text:
A clean energy group is calling for greater scrutiny of a utility company's plans surrounding data centers. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)A clean energy group is calling on the Iowa Utilities Commission and policymakers to ensure utility companies don’t use data center energy demands to build new facilities and pass the costs on to ratepayers. 
Iowa Business for Clean Energy, in a news release Thursday, said Alliant Energy Corporation is using “loopholes” and “secret” rate agreements with data centers to build natural gas “peaker” plants without proving they are in the best interest of ratepayers. 
“Iowa law does not require Alliant to prove this is the best option for ratepayers, nor do they need to prove the data center rates will cover the cost before these plants are built,” Bob Rafferty, executive director of Iowa Business for Clean Energy, said. “That’s backwards, it’s unfair and it’s wrong.”
Alliant Energy said in a statement that “existing customers will not pay for new large-energy-user growth.”
“As energy demand grows across the communities we serve, we are obligated to serve all customers,” a spokesperson for Alliant wrote. “We are also required to plan for and ensure that all customers receive reliable, cost-effective energy service, both now and into the future. Growth from new large energy users also helps spread costs across a larger customer base and supports long-term rate stability for customers.” 
Rafferty flagged the planned construction of several natural gas plants, combined with confidential rate agreements between Alliant and data center projects, as reasons for concern that ratepayers, rather than data centers, could be “stuck” paying for plants. 
Further, Rafferty argues that Iowa’s “utility friendly laws” mean that the Iowa Utilities Commission will not have to determine the “appropriateness” of the decision to build the peaker plants until the utility’s next rate case, at which point the plants will already be built.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Peaker plant ‘loophole’ 
Alliant Energy is planning three natural gas plants that would serve as “flexible” energy sources, able to quickly turn on and off during times of peak electricity demand. The proposed plants, often called “peaker plants” include the Morgan Valley Energy Center in Cedar Rapids, Bobcat Energy Center in Marshalltown and Riverhawk Energy Center in Cerro Gordo County. 
Per the project websites, Alliant says these projects are necessary to “meet growing demand and load obligations” and specifies that the plants are not because of data centers. 
Recent earnings reports from the company, which serves customers in Wisconsin and Iowa, show 3.4 gigawatts of contracted demand from data centers, and that the company anticipates 60% load growth by 2031. 
Iowa Business for Clean Energy argued, in its news release, that Alliant is using data centers “as an excuse” to build the plants. Rafferty said the plants would increase profits for Alliant. 
Iowa groups ramp up campaigns for and against data centers

According to the most recent levelized cost of energy analysis from the industry group Lazard, gas peaker plants are the most expensive form of new energy generation.  
Growing Iowa’s Economy, a group dedicated to promoting “responsible” data center development in Iowa, put out a news release Thursday afternoon arguing against the Iowa Business for Clean Energy claims. 
On this point, the group said the generation methods compared in the Lazard study are “not necessarily interchangeable on a one-for-one basis” and that a resource designed to provide flexibility should not be evaluated “as though it were intended to operate continuously.”
According to Alliant’s application for a certificate of public convenience filed with the IUC for its Morgan Valley Energy Center, daily operations at the plant are dependent on “system loads and market conditions” which it says is largely dictated by the time of year. The document also states that operation at the plant could vary based on “anticipated increased customer and system loads” and other factors like diminished solar and battery capacities.
Rafferty argued that utilities don’t have to show that the capital expense of building a peaker plant is in the ratepayers’ best interest, prior to its construction.
“Alliant doesn’t even need to show the gas plants are needed, that the plants are the best option or that the data centers will pay their fair share to receive Iowa Utility Commission approval to build that massive amount of added capacity,” Rafferty said. 
Growing Iowa’s Economy argued that because the investments will be evaluated at a future rate case, it is not accurate to “imply that billions of dollars can simply be added to customer rates without Commission scrutiny.” 
The Iowa Utilities Commission did not respond to a request for comment Thursday. 
Alliant’s spokesperson said customers have “stability” through the end of the decade due to the utility’s five-year base rate freeze. 
“In addition, the costs of new generation facilities are not included in customer rates unless and until they are reviewed in a future rate proceeding before the IUC,” the spokesperson said. “Rates for large energy users are designed to ensure those customers bear the costs associated with serving their growth.”
‘Secret’ rates for data centers 
Alliant has filings with IUC for individual customer rates with QTS for its Cedar Rapids data center. These rates, which are confidential to the public, exist to “spur economic development through attraction of incremental large loads,” according to Alliant’s request for review of individual customer rate service agreements with QTS filed with the IUC. 
The filing says the individual customer rate is “designed to recover no less than the marginal costs to serve a customer over the term of the service agreement.”
Iowa Business for Clean Energy, citing the levelized cost of energy comparison, said the marginal costs – the cost of producing additional electricity – are “approximately half of the full costs” of peaker plant developments. 
US Department of Energy awards up to $1.9B loan for nuclear plant restart

Rafferty said if data center usage “does not materialize” then “expenses would show up in public rates paid by Iowa households, small businesses, manufacturers, farms, schools, and local governments.” 
Alliant said the individual customer rate agreements “protect existing customers while supporting economic growth.” The tariff rates, the spokesperson said, are “reviewed and approved” by the IUC and include “protections not available under standard customer tariffs.” 
“The agreements are structured to ensure large energy users pay the full cost of serving their load, including costs associated with new infrastructure, rather than shifting those costs to existing customers,” the spokesperson said. 
The review filed with IUC also states that the contract terms ensure the company will “recover its costs to serve the customer while protecting all other customers from bearing costs to serve the new load.” 
Jesse Harris, a spokesperson for Growing Iowa’s Economy, said “it is fair” to question major energy investments.  
“It is not fair to tell Iowa families they are being handed a multibillion-dollar energy bill while ignoring the agreements, regulatory oversight and customer protections specifically designed to prevent that from happening.”
Rafferty said if the projects are “good for Iowa,” then the “numbers should be able to withstand public scrutiny.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Former US House candidate sends $200,000 to local Democratic causes in Alaska
description: Matt Schultz, the former Democratic candidate for Alaska’s lone U.S. House seat, is sending $200,000 in leftover campaign funds to the Alaska Democratic Party, the organization said Sept. 4.  About half of that figure will be distributed to state House and Senate candidates, and the other half will be kept for long-term projects, said party […]
text:
Democratic U.S. House candidate Matt Schultz is seen in an undated photo published on his campaign website. (Screenshot)Matt Schultz, the former Democratic candidate for Alaska’s lone U.S. House seat, is sending $200,000 in leftover campaign funds to the Alaska Democratic Party, the organization said Sept. 4. 
About half of that figure will be distributed to state House and Senate candidates, and the other half will be kept for long-term projects, said party chair Eric Croft.
“This money was never meant to be the entire campaign for any legislative race, but rather as a powerful supplement to what the campaigns are already doing,” he said.  
One hundred thousand dollars is a notable contribution to the normally quiet races for state Legislature.
While outside groups spend tens of millions of dollars on Alaska’s U.S. House and Senate races, Alaska Public Offices Commission records from the 2024 election show that competitive legislative races typically involve less than $200,000 per candidate. 
Federal candidates typically distribute leftover campaign funds to charity or supporters after the general election; Schultz suspended his campaign ahead of the August primary in order to support independent candidate Bill Hill. 
Despite the suspension, Schultz still finished third in the primary, behind Hill and the front-runner and incumbent, Republican Rep. Nick Begich III. 
Schultz, a pastor, formally withdrew from the race on Aug. 31 and announced the redistribution of funds later in the week.
“I ran for office because of a moral calling to care for our neighbors, fight for working people, and build a future where every Alaskan has the opportunity to thrive,” he said in a prepared statement on Sept. 4. “I’m proud that investments in my campaign will continue advancing those values by helping elect leaders across Alaska ready to serve with integrity, compassion, and courage. Although my campaign may have ended, the work we started together carries on.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Cyberattack disrupts Mississippi student financial aid application processing
description: Jackson State University's School of Lifelong Learning where the Institutions of Higher Learning Board of Trustees hold its monthly meeting.
text:
The Mississippi Office of Student Financial Aid is temporarily unable to process student applications and payments after a cyberattack on Monday. It’s unclear when that issue will be resolved. 
The cyberattack struck the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning offices, which include the student financial aid office. The attack affected the student financial office the most, agency spokesman John Sewell confirmed Thursday, but he did not provide details about the broader impact. 
It is still possible to apply for aid online through the Mississippi Aid Application dashboard, or MAAPP,  because that operates separately from IHL’s affected system, Sewell said. There have been no reports of the cyberattack affecting individual colleges or universities.
IHL officials are working with federal law enforcement and cybersecurity professionals to determine what happened and whether confidential or sensitive data were accessed or compromised, according to Sewell and a news release from IHL.
Sewell also declined to provide additional details about what happened, what type of cyberattack occurred and why the agency announced the incident days later on Thursday.
The attack against IHL is the latest example of cybersecurity disruptions at state institutions so far this year. 
In May, the criminal extortion group ShinyHunters attacked Canvas, a learning management system used by Mississippi State University and thousands of other educational institutions globally. The incident disrupted finals week at MSU, blocking access to coursework, classes and grades — and leaving students scrambling. 
A Feb.19 cyberattack forced the University of Mississippi Medical Center to cancel appointments and elective surgeries for nine days. Medical staff had to care for patients without access to Wi-Fi or phone lines. Roughly 650 surgeries were delayed. A month later, the ransomware group Medusa claimed credit for the cyberattack and demanded payment to prevent the publication of stolen data.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: 1 year after Charlie Kirk shooting, campus safety reviews are still in the works
description: One safety analysis is scrutinizing Utah Valley University, while another focuses more broadly on Utah's higher education system.
text:
People visit the courtyard where Charlie Kirk was hosting an event when he was killed at Utah Valley University in Orem on Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)After conservative political activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed at Utah Valley University in Orem, the college commissioned a security review, a new task force started scrutinizing campus safety and Utah lawmakers looked into changes they could mandate to prevent similar tragedies in the future.
A year after Kirk’s death, none of that work is done, though some of it is nearing completion. 
Utah Valley University expects to release findings of an independent review in about a month, a spokesperson said Thursday, adding a date has not yet been set. The school had originally planned to make the report public in late spring, but that timeline was tentative, said Sharon Turner, senior director of communications for the university.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’re just hoping for a way forward that improves on methods we’ve already put in place,” Turner told Utah News Dispatch. “There’s always room for improvement, and I think being aware of that is beneficial to our students, who are the most important part of our jobs.”
At an outdoor speaking event attended by some 3,000 people last year, Kirk was shot while answering a question. The sound of the gunshot sent his audience running for cover and triggered a manhunt for the suspected shooter that lasted almost a day and a half. 
A judge last week ordered 23-year-old Tyler Robinson to stand trial for aggravated murder in Kirk’s death. Robinson, accused of using his grandfather’s hunting rifle to fatally shoot Kirk from a rooftop on the campus, has pleaded not guilty. If he’s convicted, prosecutors said they’ll seek the death penalty. 
The university did not hold classes Thursday, the one-year anniversary of the shooting, and Gov. Spencer Cox declared it Charlie Kirk Day in the state. Turning Point USA, the group Kirk co-founded, was scheduled to hold a memorial Thursday evening at an arena on the UVU campus it rented for the occasion.
Before last year, much of the discussion surrounding campus safety in Utah revolved around sexual assault involving students. The killing of University of Utah student Lauren McCluskey in 2018 then drew the focus to intimate partner violence and stalking.  
Kirk’s death seven years later shined a spotlight on safety planning for events. Experts criticized the light security for Kirk’s appearance last year, staffed by six UVU officers and without assistance from deputies from the Utah County Sheriff’s Office. 
Backpacks and other items are strewn around the courtyard area where conservative political commentator Charlie Kirk was shot and killed during an event at Utah Valley University in Orem on Wednesday, Sept. 10, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Separate from the review commissioned by the university, the Utah System of Higher Education launched a task force last year to study campus safety. The group is evaluating safety across Utah’s eight public colleges and universities and plans to recommend a set of standards for those institutions, though a spokesperson said there’s no timeline yet for when its findings will be made public.
Those recommendations will inform parts of a broad school safety proposal that Rep. Ryan Wilcox said he’s planning to sponsor in next year’s legislative session, which convenes in January. But he said he won’t give details on his bill until the task force releases its report, which he expects to happen by the end of this year. 
K-12 schools in Utah must conduct safety assessments every three years under a 2024 state law. Wilcox proposed a similar requirement for colleges the following year, but the state Senate rejected that component early in 2025, before Kirk was killed. 
Wilcox had considered bringing back his push for school safety assessments this year, but opted to coordinate with the Utah System of Higher Education on improving the colleges’ security measures and planning ahead of campus events.
“If there’s anything comforting that we could communicate, it would be that by no means is USHE — or us — sleeping on the issue,” said Wilcox, a Republican from Ogden and chair of the House Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice Committee. “We’re still wide awake and watching, and involved in those conversations.”

title: Brattleboro Memorial Hospital commits to keeping birthing services
description:
The Brattleboro Memorial Hospital Board of Directors affirmed its commitment on Thursday to continuing obstetric and birthing services, including the BMH Birthing Center.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Brattleboro Memorial Hospital commits to keeping birthing services.
text:
Supporters of Brattleboro Memorial Hospital’s birthing center march in the town’s recent Fourth of July parade. File photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Sept. 10, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — Birthing services are no longer on the chopping block at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital, where financial challenges have prompted the consideration. 
In an announcement on Thursday, the Brattleboro Memorial Hospital Board of Directors affirmed its commitment to continuing obstetric and birthing services, including the BMH Birthing Center, thanks in part to funding through Vermont’s Rural Health Transformation Program. Previously, the board had plans to do away with the services. 
“The board’s decision recognizes both the importance of the service and the financial challenges facing BMH,” the announcement states. “The hospital has sustained significant losses, including from obstetric and birthing services, and continues to focus on stabilizing its overall financial position.”
BMH reported an actual operating loss of $16 million in FY2025. As a result of operational improvements implemented during FY2026, the hospital said it now projects an operating loss of about $9.5 million for the current fiscal year. The FY2027 budget reflects an operating loss of $7.1 million, the announcement states, “indicating continued progress as the hospital executes its multi-year turnaround plan.”
Hospital leadership developed an improvement plan that includes operational efficiencies, staffing changes, increased appointment availability, improved coding and charge capture, and efforts to increase the number of births delivered at BMH, according to the announcement. The hospital also anticipates an increase in expected births in updated FY2026 projects. 
“The board believes strongly that access to local maternity care is essential to the health and well-being of our community,” Chloe Learey, chairwoman of the BMH Board of Directors, said in the announcement. “We are encouraged by the progress that has been made and by the opportunity to continue improving how we deliver care.”
Learey acknowledged the need to “grow and endure through innovation, transformation, and financial and budgetary discipline.”
On Tuesday, the hospital learned it will receive funding through Vermont’s Rural Health Transformation Program. The grant will support exploration and development of new models for delivering obstetric and birthing services, and is seen as an opportunity to evaluate innovative approaches to the future delivery of maternity and related services in southern Vermont.
The hospital also plans to continue working with state and federal legislators on payment reform and potential models to strengthen the hospital’s financial stability, including exploration of Critical Access Hospital and Federally Qualified Health Center models.
The board noted that maintaining local maternity care will require continued collaboration among BMH leadership, employees, unions, community members and government officials. Community philanthropy, grants and other financial support also will be needed, according to the announcement. 
“We are deeply grateful for the outpouring of support from our employees, community members and state and local officials,” Learey said. “The strong commitment to preserving these critical services reflects how important local maternity care is to our region.”
Learey called for turning “that commitment into action.”
“The board is focused on advancing both near-term and long-term solutions that will secure the financial sustainability and stability of these services,” she said. “Families in our region deserve the opportunity to receive maternity care close to home.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont awards first batch of $195 million in federal rural health funds
description:
Rural workforce development and nursing homes receive the first round of $11.7 million in funds.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont awards first batch of $195 million in federal rural health funds.
text:
Hand of an elderly woman with her caregiver. Adobe stock photo

The first $11.7 million of $195 million in federal rural health funds earmarked for Vermont have been awarded, with the lion’s share going to tuition for students in healthcare fields.
Today’s announcement directs $9 million to the Vermont Student Assistance Corporation toward tuition benefits for students in nursing, dentistry and other healthcare fields who commit to working in the state for at least five years. 
The remaining $2.7 million is directed to three nursing homes in Vermont and to four teaching institutions for the training of licensed nursing assistants working in long-term care. 
“As a small state, our workforce shortage makes it difficult to expand healthcare services in rural communities,” Governor Phil Scott said in a press release issued by the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The funding will help Vermont secure well-paying, healthcare-related jobs and expand nursing home resources, he added. 
The money comes as part of a much larger sum of rural health transformation funds designated for Vermont at the end of 2025, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and Vermont’s Agency of Human Services. 
“We must do all we can to ensure our systems of care are prepared to meet growing demand as well as the changing and complex needs of Vermonters as we age,” said Dr. Jill Bowen, the agency’s Department of Aging, Disability and Independent Living’s commissioner, in a press release. 
The Agency did not provide a response to VTDigger’s questions by publication. 
The state has until the end of the year to allocate the $195 million to subgrantees and has been racing to award all of it across different healthcare needs.
The federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025, set aside $50 billion to be allocated in $10 billion allotments over the next five years. Every state is guaranteed $100 million, while the remaining half of the annual fund is awarded on a state-by-state basis each year. The fund has been seen as an attempt to absorb the financial blow that Medicaid cuts and the loss of a provider tax, which helps states fund their Medicaid programs, are expected to have on rural hospitals. 
Rep. Alyssa Black, D-Essex Town, who chairs the house health committee, pointed out that the legislature and healthcare advocates have been asking the Agency of Human Services to make a plan for broad hospital and healthcare transformation work for years. She’s concerned that the roll-out of the federal health dollars is rushed and near-sighted.
“It’s a shiny object meant to distract us from the impending cuts coming. That’s what we should be paying attention to,” she said, referencing the Medicaid cuts and loss of the provider tax.
The Vermont Student Assistance Corporation loan benefits have been part of the state’s budget in years past, but the governor and legislature struck it from this year’s approved budget. 
“And then what?” Black asked. “We cannot build a work force in 5 years.” 
Around 600 students are receiving tuition benefits this academic year in exchange for working in rural communities in Vermont for five years after the degree completion, said Patrick Leduc, Vice President and Chief Operating Officer at Vermont Student Assistance Corporation. 
The state previously allocated funding for tuition benefits for nursing and dental hygienist workforce programs, but did not set aside funding this year in anticipation of the $9 million in rural healthcare funds, Leduc said. The federal funds for the programs this year apply to a wider range of health care workforce development programs, such as mental health related fields and emergency medical services, he added.
Additionally, a separate pot of the awarded funds will go towards training licensed nurse assistants for long-term care. Northeastern Vermont Regional Hospital, Hartford Town School District and Brattleboro Development Credit Corporation all have been awarded part of the $2.7 million in funds to become “regional LNA (licensed nursing assistants) Training Hubs.” 
The Community Colleges of Vermont has been awarded additional funding to develop a state-wide licensed nursing assistants training hub program. 
Helen Labun, executive director of the Vermont Health Care Association, said the COVID-19 pandemic caused a shortage in health care workers nationally, and Vermont has faced a crisis in long-term care workers as a result. 
The state identified the workforce shortage and high use of traveling staff as a driver for nursing home financial troubles, prompting it to award nursing homes around $40 million in bailouts since 2020. 
Two of the selected nursing homes will use the federal award to build out their ventilator units. The Pines at Rutland Center for Nursing and Rehabilitation has been selected to buy new ventilators, while the St. Johnsbury Center for Living and Rehabilitation has been selected to use the funds to build out a new ventilator unit in its facility. 
In Springfield, the funds will go towards the creation of a “dialysis den” at Springfield Center for Living and Rehabilitation, allowing patients to receive local dialysis rather than traveling for the service as they currently do. 
The St. Johnsbury Center for Living and Rehabilitation and Springfield Center for Living and Rehabilitation were cited by the state for systemic care problems last year after the two nursing homes were purchased by Allaire Health Services, VTDigger reporting revealed. The St. Johnsbury and Springfield facilities are currently in compliance, according to the state survey database.
Suzanne Anair, spokesperson for Allaire Health Services, wrote in an emailed statement that this federal funding for the dialysis den and ventilator units creates an opportunity to expand specialized health care access for patients closer to their homes. 
Black said she is frustrated by how much time and attention the state has poured into rapidly drawing down these federal dollars, rather than bolstering the healthcare system for the long term. After five years, the state can no longer rely on these federal dollars.
“I wish that the state could give back every dollar of the rural health transformation money,” she said in an interview.  “We are flitting away one-time money on things that are not sustainable.”

name: VTDigger
title: Jury selected for Jason Eaton trial, with opening arguments due Monday
description:
Many of the questions to potential jurors focused on whether they could return a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity and not criminally responsible, if the defense had proven that during the trial.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Jury selected for Jason Eaton trial, with opening arguments due Monday.
text:
Jason Eaton listens as Chttenden State’s Attorney Sara George, right, speaks during a hearing in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Friday, August 28, 2026. Eaton is charged with shooting three Palestinian students in 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON — Lawyers quizzed potential jurors for nearly a full day before selecting the panel that will weigh the case of the Burlington man charged with shooting and wounding three Palestinian students nearly three years ago. 
The process of seating 12 jurors and four alternates in the case against Jason Eaton began Thursday morning in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington. By late Thursday afternoon, all 16 members had been selected. 
However, it didn’t happen without a loud hitch.
Just as the attorneys and Judge John Pacht had whittled down the jury pool, a fire alarm in the building sounded.
“We do have a jury,” Pacht shouted to the room packed with potential jurors, attorneys, media members and other onlookers. 
Pacht then told everyone to evacuate the building, saying he would provide more information when they were able to safely return.
Burlington Fire Capt. Nathan Perkins said the alarm was set off by a broken sprinkler head in a parking garage that is part of the courthouse building. 
About 45 minutes later, with the alarm no longer sounding, everyone returned to the courtroom and the selected jurors were told to return Monday for the start of the trial with opening statements. The trial is expected to run a week.

Firefighters respond to an alarm activation at the Chittenden Superior criminal court Thursday afternoon, prompting a large crowd of lawyers and a large pool of jurors to evacuate the building during jury selection of the high-profile case against Jason Eaton. Photo by Alan J. Keays/VTDigger

The case centers on Eaton’s mental condition at the time of the shootings, with his attorneys expected to raise an insanity defense. Experts for the defense and prosecution are expected to offer differing views on whether Eaton meets the legal standard for insanity.
Eaton’s mental health has been a central component of the case leading up to the trial, with the judge repeatedly ruling that Eaton is competent to stand trial.
Eaton has pleaded not guilty to three counts of attempted second-degree murder in the shootings of Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad in Burlington on the same evening in November 2023. Awartani remains paralyzed.
The three out-of-state university students were in Burlington visiting friends and family over Thanksgiving that year. At the time of the shooting, according to court documents, the three men were wearing keffiyehs, a traditional scarf that is a symbol of Palestinian identity.
If convicted of even one of the charges, Eaton, 51, faces up to life in prison without parole. 
The judge said about 100 potential jurors had been called to court Thursday for the jury draw in the high-profile case. As part of the process, some of the jurors were called into the courtroom one at a time to explain answers they gave in a questionnaire that was used to help screen the pool. 
Eaton, who for previous court hearings had appeared in green prison attire, wore a gray sportcoat, dark pants, white shirt and blue tie Thursday as he sat at the defense table between his attorneys.  
Many of the questions from the attorneys focused on whether potential jurors could return a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity and not criminally responsible, if the defense had proven that during the trial.
“I think I can,” replied one man.
“If evidence for that was evident,” a woman told the attorneys. 
“I could follow the law,” another man added.
Not every one of the potential jurors said they could. Those people were struck from the pool.
One man said he saw the insanity defense as something some people use to escape accountability for their actions. Another person said their values kept them from returning a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity. 
Several potential jurors were also asked whether they learned anything about the case from social media or the news. Some said they had heard about it but hadn’t formed strong opinions on what happened and believed they could still be fair and impartial as a juror.
One woman said that based on reports she had seen, it appeared the shootings were racially motivated. She added that she could keep an open mind if she ended up on the jury.
No clear motive for the shootings has been revealed, and the prosecutors have not charged Eaton with a hate crime in connection with the shootings. 
Eaton had contended at an earlier hearing that he was acting on behalf of a federal government agency, but no evidence has been presented supporting that assertion.
Later Thursday afternoon, a group of potential jurors was brought into the courtroom and questioned together by Margaret Jansch, one of Eaton’s attorneys, and Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, the prosecutor.
Then the attorneys gathered with the judge at the bench, holding papers with grids on them as they worked to pick the final jury members and alternates.
Eaton has been held without bail since his November 2023 arrest.

“Twenty-five years after 9/11, we honor the heroes who ran toward danger, remember the innocent lives taken and recognize the extraordinary unity and patriotism that emerged from that terrible day,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a statement Thursday. “Nearly a quarter of Americans alive today were born after 9/11 and never experienced it firsthand. That makes it even more important that we pass its lessons to the next generation. We must keep alive the legacy of those we lost and those who served by teaching our children to remember, to honor, and to love our country. God bless America.”
In a column written in 2024, Little said he remembers exactly where he was when heard about the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks – driving back from his ranch to Emmett.

“We will never forget 9/11, and we must never relent in helping future generations understand the lesson of patriotism that grew out of 9/11 – that all of us, despite our individual and varied political opinions – can live out a love for our country during a tragedy, and every day,” Little added.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Department of Justice presents Mark Zuckerberg deposition in state’s Facebook case
description: New Mexico Department of Justice attorneys led the second day of the state’s trial against Facebook by showing the jury a video deposition of founder Mark Zuckerberg regarding allegations that his company’s leaders publicly misrepresented how they stored and shared users’ data.
text:
Randi McGinn, an attorney representing the New Mexico Department of Justice in its latest trial against Facebook, showed jurors a video of Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Sept. 9, 2026, in Santa Fe’s First Judicial District Court. (Photo by Nathan Burton/The New Mexican)New Mexico Department of Justice attorneys led the second day of the state’s trial against Facebook by showing the jury a video deposition of founder Mark Zuckerberg regarding allegations that his company’s leaders publicly misrepresented how they stored and shared users’ data.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the video deposition, attorney Randi McGinn, who’s representing the NMDOJ in the case, asked Zuckerberg a series of questions about the company’s data privacy policies. Although the case is largely focused on allegations that Facebook — now known as Meta Platforms — exposed personal information in data breaches such as the Cambridge Analytica scandal, McGinn spent much of the deposition questioning Zuckerberg about the company’s practices regarding content moderation and combatting misinformation.
“Despite your promise to treat politicians the same as ordinary users, Facebook created something known as a ‘whitelist,’ which shielded politicians from being fact-checked, didn’t it?” she asked Zuckerberg, who answered that he wasn’t familiar with such a list.
After nearly an hour, their conversation turned to the case’s central themes: whether, and how, third-party apps on the website improperly obtained millions of users’ personal data.
In the Cambridge Analytica data breach, an academic posted a personality quiz on the website. When people clicked on it, they surrendered their data, as well as their Facebook friends’ data, which the creator then sold to a consulting firm that aided President Donald Trump and Ted Cruz’s political campaigns.
Attorneys for the state have alleged that the pattern of exposing the data of everyone on a Facebook user’s friends list was common for years.
Zuckerberg disputed that characterization in his deposition.
“You’re missing the most important part, which is that the person had to grant the app developer permission” to access their data, he told McGinn.
His statements echoed an argument Facebook’s attorneys made in their opening arguments in Santa Fe Wednesday — that many of the case’s relevant details are outdated.
For example, Zuckerberg pointed to the data vulnerabilities associated with using third-party apps. It was popular in the social network’s early days to play games like FarmVille or Words with Friends on a computer while logged into Facebook, but that changed once social media use increasingly migrated to smartphones.
“Before maybe 2012, most of the use of Facebook was on our website. Now it’s in mobile apps,” he said. “We had a developer platform that allowed developers to build things that would go inside the website. On mobile apps, that’s not how it works, because of the rules around Apple and app stores and things like that. So, it’s evolved quite a bit over time.”
The trial, which stems from a lawsuit former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas filed in 2021, is expected to run through early October. NMDOJ attorneys on Thursday also began questioning witness Samuel Woolley, a University of Pittsburgh professor and expert on computational propaganda, after finishing the recording of Zuckerberg’s deposition. Witness questioning is expected to continue Friday.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: University faculty in the South report culture of fear, doxxing and threats
description: A survey of higher education faculty in the South found professors are concerned about the political environment around higher education, with some fearing for their physical safety. The annual survey from the American Association of University Professors included an open-ended question that allowed faculty to detail the problems they’re facing. Compared wit[...]
text:
A fleur de lis sculpture is the centerpiece of the quadrangle fountain at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)A survey of higher education faculty in the South found professors are concerned about the political environment around higher education, with some fearing for their physical safety.
The annual survey from the American Association of University Professors included an open-ended question that allowed faculty to detail the problems they’re facing. Compared with previous years, there was a significant spike in faculty scared not only for their careers but also for their physical safety. 
“I teach a subject that is now considered ‘controversial,’” a professor in North Carolina wrote. “As a result, I have had a non-student with a gun enter my classroom to intimidate me. I have received an email death threat from a student.” 
The AAUP survey polls faculty at schools in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia. The association received about 2,700 responses, with 41 coming from Louisiana universities. 
Across the nation, state leaders have put higher education under a microscope. The scrutiny has been particularly acute in conservative Southern states, where changes to education laws have been extensive. 
In Alabama, lawmakers eliminated faculty governance at its public institutions, where professors and instructors previously had a say in campus policy decisions. 
In North Carolina, faculty are now required to post their course outlines publicly, which survey respondents said has led to them receiving threats. 
In multiple states, legislators have passed laws banning the teaching of divisive topics and prohibiting diversity, equity and inclusion programs. 
Dozens of faculty members said they had to fight back against angry alumni, political officials and student activists who attempted to get them fired or doxxed them. Doxxing is the act of publishing someone’s private information without their consent in an attempt to bring harm to them. 
“I was targeted for harassment and experienced death threats,” a full professor in Virginia wrote. ”I feel less safe doing my job than in the past. I have to think through the consequences of words I write in manuscripts.” 
Numerous faculty said they either self-censored or were told not to use certain “off-limits” words such as gender, racism and even transportation because it includes the word “trans.” Some faculty said administrators used AI-screening tools to review their syllabi for certain words.
Some survey respondents reported that the anti-faculty fervor has also spilled off-campus. 
“I had to leave my church because the youth pastor expressed from the pulpit that academics were enemies of the faith. This impacts my work as a faculty member as an important aspect of my personal life has become inaccessible,” an assistant professor in Florida wrote. 
Faculty also described fears that their students might record them and use their lectures or course materials out of context. The responses mention several incidents in which students publicized faculty comments, assignments or curricula to highlight areas of conflict with their personal beliefs. 
At LSU, law professor Ken Levy was suspended in early 2025 after mentioning Gov. Jeff Landry and President Donald Trump in profane comments to his class. Levy fought that suspension in court and lost. His comments came to light when someone shared a video of his lecture with Landry, who posted it online. 
The survey also found that 29% of faculty have applied to jobs in other states since 2024 and the same share are considering applying. 
The top reason faculty gave for wanting to leave the South was its political climate. Other leading answers included diminished academic freedom, changes to diversity, equity and inclusion policy, low pay, limited LGBTQ+ rights and limits to reproductive healthcare. 
Additional findings included 14% of faculty saying they view artificial intelligence as a threat to their academic discipline, and 13% reporting they have lost federal grants since Trump returned to office. 
The Trump administration has revamped the government’s approach to academic research funding, which has included cancelling millions in grants and slashing resources for administrative costs related to research.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State health officials issue vaccine schedule amid ongoing shifts in federal vaccine guidance
description: Maryland health officials issued a first-ever state vaccine schedule Thursday ahead of the annual flu and respiratory illness season, under a new policy created to buck anti-vaccine messaging from the Trump administration in recent years.
text:
From left, Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller, Health Secretary Meena Seshamani and Public Health Deputy Secretary Meg Sullivan testify in February on Moore administration priority legislation known as the Vax Act. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Maryland health officials issued a first-ever state vaccine schedule Thursday ahead of the annual flu and respiratory illness season, under a new policy created to buck anti-vaccine messaging from the Trump administration in recent years.
The guidelines were issued by Health Secretary Meena Seshamani using her new authority under the Vax Act, which authorizes the state to set vaccine recommendations based on guidelines from established health groups, independent of federal guidelines from of agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The law also ensures that those treatments are covered by insurance companies in Maryland and allows pharmacists to administer vaccinations to anyone age 3 or older without a prescription from a doctor.
“Vaccines remain one of the most effective public health tools we have to protect our families and keep our communities safe from a preventable disease,” Seshamani said in a call with reporters Thursday. “As a parent navigating back-to-school germs and the upcoming respiratory virus season, I know how overwhelming it can be to filter through the shifting federal news.”
Vaccination protections ‘teetering’ as state declares measles outbreaks in 3 counties

There aren’t many surprises in the state vaccine schedule, which aligns with recommendations issued by medical societies such as American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
It recommends a familiar list of about a dozen vaccinations for children, including polio, measles chicken pox and more, before they enter school. Annual flu and COVID-19 shots are rec0mmended for adults, and additional vaccinations may be recommended for those who are immunocompromised.
The state vaccine schedule is part of a larger effort by the Moore administration to push back against anti-vaccine messaging from the Trump administration.
Since Trump began his second term in office, various agencies in his administration have bucked decades of vaccination recommendations supported by scientific research and top medical organizations. That has led to public confusion over vaccine safety and best practices, say Maryland health officials.
Earlier this year, the CDC reduced the number of vaccinations recommended for all children. Vaccinations protecting children against rotavirus, influenza, COVID-19 and hepatitis A and B are now recommended only for those with severe health complications, or after consultation with a health care provider, rather than being broadly recommended for all children, as they had been.
The Vax Act, passed this year, allows the health secretary to reference federal guidance from the CDC or the federal Food and Drug Administration, but neither agency was explicitly credited as guideposts for the Maryland vaccine schedule unveiled Thursday.
Instead, Maryland’s Deputy Director of Public Health Services Meg Sullivan said the state recommendations emphasize the importance of certain vaccines where messaging from the Trump administration has created more “confusion” over vaccine safety and effectiveness.
“First and foremost, our goal with these recommendations is try to create one place where there is clear recommendations to try to eliminate the confusion,” Sullivan said. “This includes continuing to recommend the hepatitis B completed series, beginning with the birth dose. Continuing the importance of the MMR [measles, mumps and rubella]  vaccine given as a single vaccine … meaning giving all three components together. Continuing to stress the importance of respiratory virus vaccines.”
Sullivan said the recommendations do not create any vaccine mandates, and the vaccines needed to enter school are unchanged.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The new recommendation also comes on the heels of recent measles outbreaks declared a few weeks ago in St. Mary’s, Cecil and Carroll counties. Sullivan said that the number of confirmed measles cases in the state has risen to 40 this year, compared to a handful in a typical year, but she hopes the new recommendations can help encourage vaccination uptake in areas where vaccine coverage is lower.
“Measles in the state are very top of mind and something we are watching very closely,” she said. “We’re hoping this schedule is part of a broader effort to continue to maintain our high MMR vaccine rates across the state and hopefully prevent future cases of measles.”
With the upcoming respiratory illness season coming up, Sullivan urges families to plan to get their annual vaccines soon so they are protected. She suggested that the end of October is a “good target date” to get those vaccinations done.
“This is a good time to be thinking about your annual flu shot and reviewing the recommendations for the updated annual COVID vaccine and the RSV [respiratory syncytial virus] vaccine,” she said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Eric Pratt’s congressional campaign staffer resigns over white nationalist social media posts
description: In March, from a now-deleted account, Austin Brown posted on an X thread: “You hate Trump because you think he’s Hitler I hate Trump because he’s not Hitler. We are not the same.” Just two months later, Brown was on the payroll for Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt’s campaign for the 2nd Congressional District, according […]
text:
Sen. Eric Pratt, R-Prior Lake, deliberates during a floor session Tuesday, April 9, 2024. Pratt announced the resignation of his campaign staffer Thursday over the staffers' social media posts. (Photo by A.J. Olmscheid/Senate Media Services)In March, from a now-deleted account, Austin Brown posted on an X thread:
“You hate Trump because you think he’s Hitler
I hate Trump because he’s not Hitler.
We are not the same.”
Just two months later, Brown was on the payroll for Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt’s campaign for the 2nd Congressional District, according to public campaign spending filings. Brown said he was Pratt’s field director, according to a now-deleted post, which was released by the campaign of Matt Little, Pratt’s Democratic-Farmer-Labor opponent.
Little’s campaign released screenshots of several other of Brown’s antisemitic, anti-Muslim, racist and homophobic social media posts. In other posts, Brown describes himself as a white nationalist and a “groyper,” a term referring to far-right supporters of the far-right, antisemitic commentator Nick Fuentes.
Little’s campaign held a press conference on Brown on Thursday and within hours Pratt announced Brown’s resignation.
“The central theme of my campaign has been stability over chaos,” Pratt said in a statement. “Throughout my career, I have prided myself on the ability to lead with compassion, accountability and focus. I have always been clear that antisemitism, racism, and discrimination of any kind have no place in our politics or our communities.”
Brown did not respond to an Instagram message for comment. His other social media accounts appear deleted or were otherwise inaccessible. Pratt’s campaign also did not respond to emailed questions.
Republican politics have been roiled in recent years by the injection of far-right extremism into its professional political class. Politico reported last year, for instance, on Telegram chats among Young Republican leaders in New York, Kansas, Arizona and Vermont that were openly racist and antisemitic. The conservative writer Ron Dreher said he’s been told that as many as 30 or 40% of Gen Z congressional and administration staffers are so-called groypers.
The south metro 2nd Congressional District, currently held by U.S. Rep. Angie Craig, is Minnesota’s most competitive. In 2024, over $13.3 million was spent on the race, most of which supported Craig’s campaign, down from over $31 million in 2022, according to campaign spending tracker OpenSecrets. Craig turned the district blue in 2018 and has won close races ever since, widening her victory in 2024 despite the Republicans’ victory nationwide.
Craig announced last year she was not running for reelection. She lost a Democratic primary for U.S. Senate last month to Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.
According to campaign spending filings, Pratt’s campaign paid $10,500 to Austin Brown from May to July.
Little is the former two-term mayor of Lakeville who represented the area in the state Senate from 2016 to 2020, when he lost to a Republican. Little positioned himself as the progressive candidate in his party’s three-way primary election.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah’s status quo problem: Why we resist change even when it hurts us
description: Every time new data emerges about women’s equality, gender gaps, or violence against women and children in Utah, I watch a familiar pattern unfold: instead of asking what the numbers might be telling us, many rush to defend the state’s reputation. I’ve seen scholars publish counter analyses, commentators insist the rankings are flawed, and community […]
text:
People take in the sunset outside of the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Every time new data emerges about women’s equality, gender gaps, or violence against women and children in Utah, I watch a familiar pattern unfold: instead of asking what the numbers might be telling us, many rush to defend the state’s reputation. I’ve seen scholars publish counter analyses, commentators insist the rankings are flawed, and community voices explain away the concerns as misunderstandings or exaggerations. Even in my own personal relationships, I hear the instinctive refrain that “Utah is doing just fine.” But decades of research show that this reflex is not unique to us; it’s human. When people feel deeply connected to a system — whether a state, a culture, or a church — acknowledging its flaws can feel threatening. So, we rationalize, reinterpret, and reassure ourselves that everything is as it should be.
Yet this instinct to protect what we love has a cost. When we rush to defend Utah’s image, we unintentionally silence the very data that could help us make the state safer, stronger, and more equitable. A well‑established body of research explains that people often “rationalize away … defects” in the systems they depend on, not because the systems are flawless, but because admitting otherwise feels destabilizing. In Utah, where identity, faith, and community are deeply intertwined, this reflex is especially powerful. It’s easier to believe that violence is rare, that gender gaps are exaggerated, or that national rankings simply misunderstand us. It’s harder to sit with the possibility that our systems, like all human systems, have weaknesses that deserve honest attention.
This tendency is reinforced by another well‑documented pattern: people cling to familiar systems even when those systems are underperforming. Research on status‑quo bias shows that individuals often prefer “the way things are” not because the current approach is effective, but because change feels risky, uncertain, and socially disruptive. Studies on organizational change reveal that when people perceive a shift as threatening, they double down on defending existing structures, even if those structures are contributing to harm. In Utah, where cultural continuity is often equated with moral strength, this bias can make it difficult to acknowledge that our approaches to gender equality, sexual violence, or family well-being may need updating. The familiar feels safe, even when the familiar is failing too many women and children.
These dynamics are amplified by another cultural pattern we rarely name out loud: Utah’s passive‑aggressive communication style. As I’ve written elsewhere, we often avoid direct conflict, soften hard truths, and express frustration sideways rather than openly. That tendency may feel polite, but it also makes it harder to confront systemic problems head‑on. When you combine a strong system‑justification reflex with a cultural norm of indirectness, the result is predictable: instead of addressing concerns about gender inequality or violence directly, we deflect, minimize, or quietly hope the issue will resolve itself. Passive‑aggression becomes a social strategy for maintaining the status quo — protecting harmony on the surface while preventing the deeper conversations that real change requires.
The danger of these patterns is not abstract. Research from the Utah Women & Leadership Project shows that when communities minimize or reinterpret evidence of harm, violence becomes easier to ignore and harder to prevent. In our recent report on the roots of sexual violence in Utah, I found that cultural silence, institutional defensiveness, and a reluctance to confront uncomfortable truths all contribute to conditions where abuse can persist. When people insist that “things aren’t that bad,” or that national data simply do not apply here, they unintentionally create an environment where victims feel less safe coming forward and leaders feel less urgency to act. Defending the status quo may feel loyal, but it can also leave the most vulnerable among us unprotected.
At some point, though, loyalty to our systems must include the willingness to improve them. Humility is not an admission of failure; it is an act of stewardship. Courage is not criticism; it is care. Utah has never been strengthened by pretending its challenges don’t exist. We are strengthened when we face them directly, when we listen to data even when it unsettles us, and when we allow evidence — not defensiveness — to guide our decisions. The systems we value can evolve, and the communities we cherish can grow safer and more equitable, but only if we choose honesty over comfort and curiosity over fear.
If we want Utah to be the place we believe it can be, we must replace defensiveness with determination. Our rankings, our data, and our lived experiences are not attacks on Utah’s character; they are invitations to strengthen it. We can choose to listen more carefully to victims, to examine our policies with honesty, and to confront cultural patterns that keep us from seeing the full picture. We can build systems that protect women and children (and men) not just in theory, but in practice. And we can do all of this while still loving our state, our communities, and our faith traditions. Progress has never required perfection. But it does require the willingness to see clearly and act boldly. Utah is capable of that kind of courage. The question now is whether we will choose it.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Magaziner calls a press conference to vilify his ‘J6er’ opponent. His opponent showed up.
description: That didn’t take long. The morning after Rhode Island’s Republican voters chose their nominee to take on Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner in the November general election, Magaziner launched the opening salvo against his 2nd Congressional District opponent, Vic Mellor. Joining Magaziner at a podium on the marble plaza outside the State House for a […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner speaks outside the Rhode Island State House in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, alongside law enforcement officers who defended the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)That didn’t take long. 
The morning after Rhode Island’s Republican voters chose their nominee to take on Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner in the November general election, Magaziner launched the opening salvo against his 2nd Congressional District opponent, Vic Mellor.
Joining Magaziner at a podium on the marble plaza outside the State House for a news conference were two officers who had been on duty at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, the same day Mellor participated in a march on the U.S. Capitol. A mob of President Donald Trump’s supporters attacked U.S. Capitol Police officers and pushed through barricades that day, sending lawmakers fleeing from a joint session of Congress where the results of the 2020 presidential election were being certified. 
“The officers who defended the Capitol that day are heroes, and the rioters who attacked police and attacked our democracy are villains,” Magaziner, who is seeking a third term, said. “Vic Mellor is one of those villains.”
Less than 30 feet away stood that “villain” himself with a handful of his own confidants in tow watching Magaziner’s press conference, or Mellor’s assessment, “political hackness.”
But for Harry Dunn, who served 15 years with the U.S. Capitol Police, standing alongside Magaziner Thursday was part of his personal mission to vanquish narratives which “downplay” or “whitewash” Jan. 6.
“January 6 was every single police officer at the Capitol that day — I can guarantee you — it was the worst day of their life,” said Dunn, who has unsuccessfully run twice for congressional seats in Maryland. “So imagine law enforcement experiencing the worst day of their lives, and somebody who’s running to serve the people of Rhode Island calling that one of the best days of his life.” 
Magaziner’s event was over in 15 minutes, and a press gaggle quickly formed around Mellor after Magaziner’s press conference ended. Did he regret his outing to the Capitol five years ago?
“Absolutely not,” Mellor said, and offered a similar reply when asked if he had anything to apologize for.
“I didn’t do anything wrong, so no, I don’t apologize for anything either,” Mellor said.
Mellor, who defeated his state GOP-endorsed opponent Dr. Stephen Skoly in Wednesday’s primary, has previously described himself as a “J6er” with no interest in repentance for his participation that day. On Thursday, he continued to describe the now-infamous day as one in which he did not personally witness excessive violence but instead ecstatic freedom.
“I wasn’t around the violence,” Mellor said. “Again, to me, it was an amazing day. It’s a big building. There was a lot going on in that building.” 
It was also a father-son excursion for Mellor, one he dubbed a “euphoric” experience that he shared with his son, then 18.
“We were in D.C. We’re just part of this huge movement,” Mellor said. “I was just around tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of patriots celebrating their First Amendment rights.” 
Mellor suggested that the entirety of security footage from that day needs to be released — although more than 44,000 hours of U.S. Capitol Police security footage from Jan. 5 and 6 have already been made publicly available online by the House Administration Committee.
Mellor suggested that “undercover FBI,” “Antifa” and “BLM” were involved in the events of Jan. 6 and that “The violence should be looked into, and we should know who did that violence.” 
“Release the video,” he added. “You’ll know exactly what I did.”
Harry Dunn, a former U.S. Capitol Police officer who defended the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, speaks outside the Rhode Island State House in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. At left is D.C. Metropolitan Police Officer Daniel Hodges, who was injured at the Capitol that day while in the line of duty. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Worst day ever. Best day ever.
Dunn and D.C. Metropolitan Police Officer Daniel Hodges had a different side of the story to tell.
“Mellor was part of the crowd that punched me, kicked me, tried to gouge out my eye, crushed me against a doorframe, ripped off my gas mask and beat me in the head with a riot baton,” Hodges said. “Mellor is proud of his association with the mob who viciously attacked my colleagues.”
Jan. 6 was Hodges’ first time in the building, and he was defending a tunnel at the Capitol’s Lower West Terrace when he was assaulted by members of the mob. Federal prosecutors later accused one rioter of taking Hodges’ gas mask as well as his baton, which one rioter used to beat him. Hodges was later pushed against and crushed between doors and bled from his mouth.
Hodges later told media outlets in January 2021 that “it was absolutely my pleasure to crush a white nationalist insurrection.”
“While I was defending the Capitol, Congress, the vice president, congressional staff, the lawful transfer of power of the presidency, Victor Mellor was at best supporting the terrorists that wanted to install an unelected dictator against the will of the people of the United States,” Hodges said.
Not only was he not part of the violence, Mellor emphasized to reporters that he’s never been charged for any crimes relating to Jan. 6.
“Obviously, I condemn any kind of violence,” Mellor said. “I wasn’t part of any kind of violence at the Capitol, and if I was, the FBI would have at least knocked on my door.”
Mellor’s campaign issued a statement after Magaziner’s event in which he added, “Anyone who laid hands on a cop was wrong. I condemn it.” 
When asked about the personal accounts he heard from Dunn and Hodges Thursday, Mellor offered only a few words.
“Those are their stories,” Mellor said. “I’m just going to say I thank them for their service.”
He did not speak with Magaziner Thursday, he said, and had shown up to the event “to represent myself and to stand up for myself.”
But, Mellor added, “I have no problem speaking to him. I’m sure at some point him and I will have face-to-face conversations.”
Republican congressional candidate Vic Mellor, second from right, listens to U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner’s press conference outside the Rhode Island State House in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. Mellor attended the event a day after winning the Republican primary for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Socialism or MAGAism?
The State House sits in Rhode Island’s 1st Congressional District, but the city’s downtown and West End — where the majority of voters supported Rep. David Morales, the democratic socialist winner of the Democratic primary for mayor on Wednesday — are in the 2nd.
The 2nd Congressional District’s large share of unaffiliated voters, 54%, plus its Democrats’ range of beliefs and priorities became a talking point in the one and only debate between Skoly and Mellor, broadcast over Labor Day weekend.
The Sept. 4 WJAR NBC10 debate showcased the two Republicans’ shared rancor for socialism. Skoly specifically referenced the Democratic primary for Providence mayor as an example of what more moderate Democrats fear about their party’s direction. Morales, now the Democratic nominee, defeated Providence Mayor Brett Smiley by 5 percentage points in still unofficial results.
A decisive victory and a potential new chapter for Rhode Island’s capital city

“They don’t like what they see happening in Providence,” Skoly said during the debate recorded at WJAR NBC 10 on Sept. 4. “How Providence runs is how our state runs.” 
Skoly predicted Mellor’s zealotry would ultimately lead to Magaziner’s victory in November. Mellor, meanwhile, argued that his job is to represent Republicans, not Democrats. 
Skoly’s first public statement following his defeat came Thursday morning. 
“I leave this race with my head held high, my principles intact and my gratitude for Rhode Island deeper than ever,” Skoly stated.
Mellor acknowledged that to defeat Magaziner in the general election, he would need more votes than he got Wednesday night.
“Of course,” he said, “but CD2 is really close…My message is to all those conservatives that have kind of dropped out of the system. I’m appealing to the Democrats also because they don’t want socialism.”
Did Mellor see the Providence mayoral race connected to his efforts in CD2?
Yes, the candidate replied, and in “a totally direct way.” 
“What happened here in the mayoral race is a travesty,” Mellor said. “But it’s a byproduct of a broken state for decades. Our youth have no opportunity here in Rhode Island. So they’re looking for socialism as an answer…That’s because the state is broken. There’s no future for them here.”
Skoly made no endorsement of Mellor in his statement. Mellor said Thursday that he had not received a concession call from his primary opponent.
Mellor called his 58% of the vote — a victory of 16 percentage points over Skoly — a “mandate.” He said the state’s Republicans would now unite behind him.
“They’re going to have to reevaluate everything they do,” Mellor said of the state GOP, which endorsed Skoly in the primary. “I’m not stopping. I’m not asking their permission for anything…I absolutely will talk to them. We need to come together to do this.”
