name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Keeping the story of Flight 93 alive, as living memories become fewer
description: For around 100 million Americans born after 9/11, and millions more born in the years shortly before, that day that shifted the nation’s course is an abstract day in history.
text:
The American flag flies at the entry to the pathway that leads to the Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Pennsylvania. The visitor center is in the background. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert)A pair of blue baseball-patterned boxer shorts takes the center of a display case at the Flight 93 National Memorial museum.
If the underwear seems out of place, not far from where the airliner came to earth Sept. 11, 2001, near Shanksville, Somerset County, that’s part of the point. 
It tells a story from the life of passenger Lauren Catuzzi Grandcolas, who persuaded her colleagues at PricewaterhouseCoopers to wear brightly colored shorts over their business suits to a boardroom meeting with execs from whimsical underwear maker Joe Boxer.
Her move convinced the company’s CEO that Grandcolas’ team understood their products and won them the job.
“I can’t think of anything that you could put in there that would make her more proud,” her husband Jack Grandcolas later told National Park Service staff.
Betsy Keene, curator at the memorial and three other NPS sites in western Pennsylvania, said that made Grandcolas’ shorts a clear choice to include in one of several new displays at the memorial.
Betsy Keene, curator at the Flight 93 National Memorial and three other NPS sites in western Pennsylvania, has overseen the new displays of personal effects belonging to the passengers and crew of the hijacked plane that crashed near Shanksville, Pa., on Sept. 11, 2001. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
They feature personal effects of the 40 passengers and crew who fought to keep the hijacked Boeing 757 — which investigators believe the four attackers aboard planned to crash into the U.S. Capitol — from becoming another weapon against the United States on 9/11.
”I just want people to see something that will help them relate to the story, that will tie them in,” Keene said of the selections in the cases, which are the first official expansions of the museum’s exhibits since it opened in 2015. 
Twenty-five years after the attack on the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the crash of United Airlines Flight 93 into a reclaimed coal mine in Stonycreek Township, the memory of the day is still strong with those who lived through it. 
But for around 100 million Americans born after 9/11, and millions more born in the years shortly before, that day that shifted the nation’s course is an abstract day in history. 
Stephen Clark, superintendent of the Flight 93 memorial, said that aspect sets it apart from other memorials in the national park system.
“I like to use the word raw,” he said. “It’s as if it just happened yesterday.”
A visitor pays her respects at the Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Somerset County, during the 2010 remembrance event. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert)
And despite that, it tends to be the 9/11 site that’s overlooked amid replays of the abject horror of the twin towers – beacons of the nation’s financial might – and the headquarters of its military afire and collapsing, Clark said.
“This is real, and our rangers, and our staff, and our ambassadors come in contact on a daily basis with people who are part of this story of 9/11,” he added.
Increasingly, the memorial’s role is to teach, in addition to commemorating, how the passengers and flight crew made a desperate decision to fight for their lives and succeeded in preventing an attack on American democracy itself. 
Even newer members of the federal law enforcement and intelligence communities, with whom the park staff work regularly, sometimes don’t have vivid memories of 9/11, Clark said.
“I want them to come here and feel this place, and understand what happened here and the bravery aboard that airplane, to motivate them for their entire career to ensure that they do everything they can to never have another 9/11,” he said. “It’s a daunting task.”
The mission to educate visitors happens every day, Clark said, but on Friday the Flight 93 memorial will host its observance of the 25th anniversary of the attacks. Each year it begins at the Wall of Names with a reading of the 40 names timed to coincide with the moment the plane crashed at 9:03 a.m. 
At 1 p.m. a public ceremony will begin featuring music by the Somerset County Youth Chorus and remarks by retired United Airlines Capt. Morrie Weiner, who flew Flight 93’s Newark to San Francisco run for a decade before retiring 10 days before the attacks; Gordon Felt, whose brother Edward Felt was a passenger; Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.
Keeping Flight 93 stories alive
Every year since 2003, Scott Marsh has led a trip for eighth grade students at Mechanicsburg Middle School in western Ohio, where he teaches social studies, to the Flight 93 memorial and then on to Washington, D.C.
“Those kids had that memory,” Marsh said of the first students he took on the trip more than two decades ago. “And as every year went by, [his students] remembered less because we were moving away from that time.”
Now, when Marsh brings his classes to the memorial, concepts like love and sacrifice and courage are what bind them to the story of Flight 93. Marsh said he can see when the story’s significance clicks into place.
“They get really quiet and then they look at you. I mean, they stare right at you as you’re telling the story, or you’re telling them what I want from them and why it’s important,” he said. “And you know, usually eighth grade kids are kind of all over the place. But they are totally locked in.”
Marsh said his students find it particularly impactful to learn Grandcolas was pregnant and to find the almost ghostly inscription “and unborn child” carved in the wall of names beside hers. 
The name of Lauren Catuzzi Grandcolas also bears the inscription “and unborn child” on the Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
At least 40 states have either required or suggest that public schools teach students about 9/11, according to the Associated Press. Pennsylvania passed a law in 2024 that requires schools to hold a moment of silence each anniversary and requiring the state Department of Education to provide a model curriculum on 9/11
On an August morning, Diana Bigwood of Greencastle, Franklin County, strolled the memorial plaza overlooking the wildflower-filled field where the impact of Flight 93 is marked with a red-hued boulder. She spoke softly to her great-grandson Ryker as they walked.
“There’s too many of his little friends that when we say we’re going to the Flight 93 memorial,  they don’t even know what you’re talking about,” she said.
Bigwood said the memorial is an emotional place. She said she cries every time she visits and can no longer stand to listen to recordings of the passengers’ last messages left via the plane’s on-board AirFones.
If youngsters like Ryker don’t learn the stories of 9/11, the nation risks losing pride in its first responders and the vigilance to stop another attack, she said. 
“I’m so proud of the people that yes, they lost their lives, but look how many more people, had they went to their destination in D.C., … could have died that day,” she said.
A grasshopper sits on a wall at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, where the hijacked airliner crashed after passengers and crew attempted to regain control on Sept. 11, 2001. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
David Beamer, father of Flight 93 passenger Todd Beamer, said he shares concerns that young people aren’t learning about the actions of his son and fellow passengers. Todd Beamer was one of a handful of passengers able to make a phone call after the plane was hijacked. 
He relayed information about the hijacking and the passengers’ and flight attendants’ plan to fight back to a telephone operator, who he also asked to pray with him. She later relayed his final words, “Are you guys ready? Okay. Let’s roll,” as they advanced toward the cockpit. His words became a slogan of national resolve in the days and weeks that followed.
“I believe that plane was headed to the nation’s capital, and the damage and the loss of life would have been another big big win for our enemies,” David Beamer said. “It didn’t happen because regular people became soldiers that day … The blessing is they had the opportunity to fight back, and they did.”
Beamer said he used to fly around the country speaking to school groups. At 84, he’s cut back on travel but still speaks at church events. He noted there are a number of groups including the 9:57 Project, founded by veterans and educators to connect with young people and carry on the legacy of Flight 93. 
This Sept. 11, Beamer said he will attend the ceremony at the memorial for the first time and read his son’s name.
“We’ve been to the memorial many times, but we choose to go on quieter days,” he said.  “I determined this time I’m going to read. I’m gonna say Todd Beamer, and it’s the time in the program that we’re remembering each individual, so I felt like I wanted to do it this year.”
Teaching 9/11
Friends of Flight 93 National Memorial was founded in 2009 to keep the story and the memorial meaningful and relevant for generations to come, Executive Director Donna Gibson said. It works hand-in-hand with the National Park Service to provide programming and volunteers.
For several years the organization has held the National Day of Learning to Teach to Remember 9/11, which has now evolved into two weeks of programs, curriculum and lessons for teachers. 
In June, Gibson said, it held a symposium for educators from around Pennsylvania where teachers were placed in groups and asked to create lesson plans. 
“We found that we were coming to this point where you had people who had the lived experience that really didn’t know how to manage their emotions in the classroom because it was such a horrific day for them, and they didn’t want to scare their students by being upset,” she said.
The Ceremonial Gate — made of wood from hemlock trees — at the Flight 93 National Memorial separates the Wall of Names from area where United 93 crashed on September 11, 2001. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
From that event, two lesson plans were selected to be made available to educators across the country. One has students design a military-style challenge coin depicting on one side what defines them as a person — community, environment and education, for example — and then research a passenger or crew member and do the same for them on the other side.
A second lesson has students create a passport for people enmeshed in the Flight 93 story by researching their lives and finding connections to other passengers, crew or family members. The feedback from teachers has been positive, she said.
“They were surprised, one, their students never heard of Flight 93,” Gibson said. “And two, how engaged they were with the whole project, learning about the passenger, learning about the person that was in their passport.”
Beyond the challenges of time, distance and teachers’ comfort levels with the subject matter, impressing the significance of 9/11 as a world-changing event presents a challenge of making it immediately relevant to students’ lives, said Adam Shaffer, a Shanksville native and chief of interpretation and education at the memorial. 
“First is connecting with other relevant, significant world and national events that have directly impacted them, because that’s something that they all have at least some level of exposure to,” Shaffer said, noting that many have family members who served in Iraq or Afghanistan during the Global War on Terror.
Another touchstone he said is relatable for some students is the COVID-19 pandemic.
“It’s just a ‘you know where you were at whenever it happened,’ kind of a moment,” Shaffer said.
Park rangers also use current events to show the effects of 9/11 are still echoing through society, Shaffer said, noting that a victim of the World Trade Center attack was identified last month.
He added that some of those responsible for the attacks are still facing trials. A trial for one of the men who plotted the attacks was, last month, scheduled to begin in June 2028
“There are still pieces of the 9/11 story 25 years ago that are still here and tangible and very real in the world that they’re growing up with, and I think it’s those connecting points that draw them into wanting to understand more than about that day,” he said. 
Today’s students, who don’t know a world without smartphones, also engage with the communications aspects of the Flight 93 story and how different it was in 2001.
Because Flight 93 took off from the Newark, New Jersey, airport late, the passengers learned about the planes that had struck the World Trade Center and realized the hijackers aboard their plane didn’t intend to land safely. They did so using credit card-activated seatback AirFones that many airliners had before cellphones were ubiquitous.
“While they didn’t have the supercomputer that we have in our hands right now … the passengers and crew were just also able to do that using the technology of that time,” Shaffer said.
The crash of United Flight 93 is marked by a boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County on August 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
New connections to the passengers and crew
Among the exhibits in the visitor center museum is a simple white cordless phone with an answering machine, doubtless similar to those where some of the passengers left their final words to loved ones. 
That’s one of tens of thousands of items in the park’s collection, most of which have never been displayed. 
Through a $2.3 million donation to the National Park Foundation specifically for enhancing visitors’ experiences at the memorial before the anniversary, the park service was able to purchase several new display cases to allow some of those artifacts to be shown for the first time.
They include paper, textile and leather objects recovered from the crash site that are too fragile to be exposed to the light of day that will be housed in cabinets with special electronic light-blocking glass. One item is passenger Nicole Miller’s driver’s license that became fused with a piece of the fuselage in the heat and violence of the crash. 
“It’s a very, very personal object because it’s a driver’s license, but also it reflects that violence, and so it’s a remarkable sort of thing that does both parts of that story at once,” Keene said.
Others include clothing and personal effects from the lives the passengers and crew had hoped to return to on their flight. In one case, the freshly dry cleaned uniform of flight attendant Lorraine G. Bay stands next to the wrinkled field jacket of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologist Richard J. Guadagno, who was returning from a trip to visit family in New Jersey.
Beneath it, Guadagno’s day planner, yellowed with age, is open to Sept. 11, 2001, with the annual leave he used for the trip penciled in.
“It’s actually a ‘Far Side’ calendar, which always makes me chuckle,” she said, referring to the absurd science and animal themed comic strip popular in the 1990s. “Again it’s one of those little details that sort of twinkle at you that help you get drawn in.”

name: VTDigger
title: The one story from 9/11 that I can’t forget. And I don’t want to.
description:
Bob Dow lost the love of his life in the south tower. Nearing the 25th anniversary of the attack, he taught me why we still need stories like his — and journalists to tell them.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The one story from 9/11 that I can’t forget. And I don’t want to..
text:
A Port Authority police officer lays a flower at the Sept. 11 Memorial in New York, Thursday, Feb. 26, 2015. Photo by Seth Wenig/AP Photo
When Bob Dow reached out by email asking me if I wanted to write again about his loss on Sept. 11, I said yes. 
I said yes because Bob’s loss of the love of his life, Ruth Ketler, is resonant even today. I said yes because learning how he had continued in the world over the past 25 years since I wrote a story about his search for Ruth, would also help me — and others — to heal.
I have spent my life as a journalist. I most recently served as editor-in-chief of VTDigger. I now teach journalism at the UC Berkeley School of Journalism, where I tell my students that they are doing a service when they interview people and listen — listen deeply. The gift of your attention, of your presence, is never to be underestimated, I say.
Listening to people’s stories transforms you. Journalism is, in many ways, the discipline of moving toward other people’s pain and listening deeply enough that their stories can be known, shared and borne by the larger world. In this way, it heals.
Bob met Ruth in the mid-1980s, when he was tending bar. They became friendly, but he thought they were too different to be a couple. He was politically liberal; she was a Republican. He was a poet and a writer; she had spent her career in banking. But in 1993, after a dinner together, a romantic relationship began.
On Sept. 11, Bob was 50 years old and living in Manhattan with Ruth. He spent most of the week in the city but commuted to western Massachusetts a few days each week to teach at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Ruth, who was 42, worked as director of research at Fiduciary Trust Co., on the 94th floor of the World Trade Center.
That morning, a friend called to tell him a plane had crashed into one of the towers at the World Trade Center. Then Ruth was on the phone from her office in the south tower. 
“Leave the building,” he told her. She’d been told to stay, she said: “I love you. I got to go.” 
Minutes later, the second plane hit her building. The attacks that day killed nearly 3,000 people when hijackers flew commercial planes into the twin towers, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania, the deadliest terrorist attack on American soil.
I was at home in Manhattan when the first plane crashed into the World Trade Center. It was a little before 9 a.m., and I was getting ready to leave my children with our babysitter and take the subway to work as a reporter at the Wall Street Journal. I would spend the next month interviewing Bob and others whose loved ones had been killed. Even as the Journal staff fled our offices next door to the World Trade Center, we covered the aftermath from our homes and a back office in New Jersey.
But at home, I turned off the TV and refused to speak about the falling towers. I believed my kids, age 1 and 3, would never sleep peacefully again if they watched on television the buildings falling and overheard grown-ups describing people plunging to their deaths a few blocks away.
I am, by nature, fearful. I do not crane my neck to see what has happened when I pass an accident scene on a highway. Once a doctor sewed a gash on my daughter’s shin, and my sister had to hold her hand because the sight of the needle and the sound of her cries almost made me pass out. “Delicate,” is how my mother kindly referred to my temperament.
But for the three decades that I worked as a newspaper reporter, journalism propelled me toward the pain and loss that I would have otherwise tried to escape. 
The grief, the struggle and the courage of Bob and the other people I have interviewed have changed me in ways that I am only now beginning to appreciate. They have turned me into a braver human being, more fully alive for the whole of life, not hunched over in a crash position trying to avoid the pain.
‘A willingness to see and feel’
I entered the field of journalism in 1989, first at a weekly newspaper on Cape Cod, then at the Rutland Herald.
While there, I wrote about a woman who escaped domestic violence and a nurse who became addicted to her child’s Ritalin. I probed how a father came to be wrongly accused of molesting his child. Through the interviews, I learned what it is like to survive the fear of being killed by your partner, sliding into drug addiction and being falsely accused of a crime against your child. And through my stories, the readers of the Herald did, too. 
In the years since, I have worked as a foreign correspondent for the Journal and later The New York Times. In 2008, assailants from Pakistan held two of Mumbai’s fanciest hotels hostage for two days. I stood outside the Trident Hotel most of that time with the wife and daughter of a banker who hadn’t emerged since going to dinner inside. When the hotel was finally freed by government forces, the banker’s family learned he had been killed in the early hours of the siege.
I’ve gone on to teach journalism and serve as dean of the UC Berkeley School of Journalism. And last year, I led the newsroom at VTDigger, this pioneering news publication that is part of a movement to reinvent the business model of journalism as a nonprofit, akin to public radio.
At VTDigger, reporter Auditi Guha spent hours interviewing Wilmer Chavarria, a school superintendent in Winooski who was interrogated at George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston as he returned from vacation in Nicaragua last year. Chavarria, a U.S. citizen, described being separated from his spouse and questioned in a windowless room without clocks, at times with four officers towering above him as he sat in a metal chair. They mocked his 15-year marriage and his insistence he was employed as a school superintendent. 
Through Auditi’s story, Chavarria’s humiliation was known and borne by the larger world.
In my conversation with Bob this past August, I asked him how he has managed to go on after losing Ruth. I told him about my dad, who became an alcoholic after losing his business. How he never recovered from that loss.
In Bob’s case, he said it helped that he continued to teach. Two weeks after Ruth died, he drove up to Amherst to engage his students in his class, “America at War.” He continues to teach, making the same commute between Manhattan and Amherst.
Teaching, as Bob sees it, is “a tool to unlock the heart and soul and mind of others.”
Bob aims to teach his students “a willingness to see and feel — best we can — the suffering of others and empathize and understand that which may be beyond our immediate reach and understanding.” 
In many ways, that’s what journalism does, too.
I have a daughter who is a recovering addict, and I attend parents’ meetings every week to hear that same love of life and desire for survival that Bob seeks out in others’ stories. My daughter has been sober for the past 14 months, a testament to her courage and strength. But if left to my own fears, I find myself hunkering down, afraid that she could relapse and die.
At Al Anon Family Group meetings, parents speak openly about how their children are living on the streets or have died of overdoses. I listen, weeping. But knowing these parents have endured such loss and can still laugh on their grandchildren’s birthdays, vacation with friends and support other parents so lovingly, enables me to unfurl from the crash position. It lets me know that if the worst were ever to happen, I just might be able to survive.
As the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 approached, Bob watched documentaries about the attacks and the survivors. I ask why he moves toward those stories rather than away, as I imagine I might have done.
At first he says he doesn’t know. Then it comes to him. 
“I see, I feel, I hear the stories of others,” he says. “It is healing to see the love of life and the desire for survival in others.”
Indeed, Bob tells me, “The reason I listen is the reason I reached out to you.”
Geeta Anand, the former editor-in-chief of VTDigger, lives in Plainfield.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas public television hopes to regain donors lost after attempt to cut PBS ties
description: Arkansas’ public television station hopes to regain lost donors and shore up new sources of financial support following the backlash over an attempt to cut ties with PBS, the interim CEO of the Arkansas TV Foundation said Thursday. More than 3,700 donors withdrew their support last winter after the Arkansas TV Commission began taking steps […]
text:
From left: Arkansas TV Commission Chairman Gary Newton, Commissioner Cynthia Nance, and Arkansas TV Education Director Sajni Kumpuris listen as Arkansas TV Foundation interim CEO Pamela Owen updates the commission on the public television station's donor base at its Conway headquarters on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas’ public television station hopes to regain lost donors and shore up new sources of financial support following the backlash over an attempt to cut ties with PBS, the interim CEO of the Arkansas TV Foundation said Thursday.
More than 3,700 donors withdrew their support last winter after the Arkansas TV Commission began taking steps to disaffiliate from PBS. The commission reversed course in June after donors rallied to raise more than $2 million to cover PBS dues for the fiscal year that started July 1.  
CEO Carlton Wing and chief financial officer James Downs told the station’s governing board that they expect to be able to fully afford PBS dues for the next two fiscal years.
Wing, a former Republican lawmaker, said Arkansas TV has become “one of the great stories in public media across the country” after having “a very, very uncertain future” less than a year ago.

UPDATED: PBS programs will remain in Arkansas after commission accepts funds raised for dues

 

Arkansas was the first state to attempt dropping PBS after federal funding cuts led the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to close, forcing public television networks nationwide to find new ways to pay for PBS shows.
Arkansas TV gained half as many new donors between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026 compared to the previous year, said the foundation’s interim head, Pamela Owen, who succeeded retiring CEO Marge Betley in August.
The percentage of repeat donors from the 2025 to 2026 fiscal years dropped from 87% to 78%, Owen said.
In addition to the $2.1 million covering PBS programs through June 30, 2027, the foundation secured commitments of more than $1.5 million each toward the cost of PBS dues in fiscal years 2028 and 2029. Owen reminded Wing, Downs and the commission that these pledges won’t cover the full price of dues for both years.
The foundation also expects to have to keep up with “significant increases” to Arkansas TV’s operating expenses, Owen said.
“This will likely significantly draw down our buffer that we’ve built over the years in the foundation,” she said.
Commissioners and network leaders said they appreciated the $500,000 in state funds that the Legislature and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders directed to Arkansas TV in June to help with operating expenses. The funds specifically helped the network maintain its emergency alert broadcast towers, commission chair Gary Newton said.
Emails show viewer backlash over PBS program’s removal from Arkansas TV

Commissioner Cynthia Nance presented a resolution expressing gratitude to former Arkansas first ladies Barbara Pryor and Gay White for leading the effort to crowdfund PBS dues. Nance is the only current commissioner who opposed last year’s move to leave PBS. The commission approved the resolution with no dissent.
White and Pryor said in June that they were frustrated with Arkansas TV’s decision to remove “Washington Week with The Atlantic” from its schedule and move “PBS NewsHour” from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. on weeknights as of July 1.
Viewers told the network they believed the move was ideologically driven, echoing complaints heard earlier this year when Arkansas TV was poised to drop PBS entirely.
In a July email to Newton, the former first ladies asked for the programming changes to be reversed and said the move undermined the public trust that fueled the successful crowdfunding campaign. Newton said the programming changes were unrelated to the network’s aborted effort to leave PBS.
The privately-raised funds for PBS shows should have “freed more than $1 million annually within Arkansas TV’s budget to strengthen local programming and future initiatives,” White and Pryor said in the email provided to the Advocate by their fundraising effort, Friends of Arkansas PBS.

Comms emails July Aug to Sept 13 2026 Redacted 
Wing has said since taking the reins of Arkansas TV a year ago that the network should prioritize Arkansas-focused programming. New, locally-made shows that have premiered this year focus on topics ranging from Arkansas history and politics to health and nature. The public affairs show “Arkansas Week” has also expanded from 30 minutes to one hour.
The programming changes went into effect July 1, and since then dozens of Arkansans have continued to express their displeasure and cancel their donations to the network, according to emails the Advocate obtained via a public records request.
Some viewers, including those who still donate, said they have no interest in the shows airing in place of “Washington Week” and “PBS NewsHour.”
“The current 6:00 [p.m.] lineup is tediously unimpressive, much of which is not locally produced at all,” one viewer wrote to the network Wednesday. “It smacks of censorship. It IS censorship.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: FBI director Kash Patel attends Gov. Landry’s alligator hunt fundraiser
description: President Donald Trump’s controversial FBI director, Kash Patel, was a guest this week at Gov. Jeff Landry’s annual alligator hunt in the Atchafalaya Basin.
text:
FBI Director Kash Patel, center, speaks at a gathering of law enforcement officials Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2025, in Lafayette, accompanied by Gov. Jeff Landry, right and U.S. Rep. Clay Higgins. (Photo courtesy Congressman Clay Higgins' Facebook page)President Donald Trump’s controversial FBI director, Kash Patel, was a guest this week at Gov. Jeff Landry’s annual alligator hunt in the Atchafalaya Basin. 

The annual event, now in its 16th year, is Landry’s signature campaign fundraiser and often draws high-profile conservative figures. Donald Trump Jr. and his son have attended in previous years, as has Kristi Noem, Trump’s former Homeland Security director, according to social media posts. 

Patel appears to have attended the fundraiser’s law enforcement night Wednesday based on a photo Attorney General Liz Murrill shared online the next day. It shows her, Landry and Patel together, with Patel wearing a “57 Landry” shirt and a LSU-themed hat with the alligator hunt logo. Landry is the state’s 57th governor.

Great to have @FBIDirectorKash join us this year at Gov. @JeffLandry gator hunt on the Atchafalaya Basin. Showed him how we get things done down here in South Louisiana!  pic.twitter.com/RjhV3WkTNP
— Liz Murrill (@LizMurrillforLA) September 10, 2026

Patel also posted photos Wednesday of a meeting he held in Lafayette with Landry, Congressman Clay Higgins, U.S. Attorney Zach Keller of Louisiana’s Western District and dozens of law enforcement officers. 

“In the field with some of our great Louisiana law enforcement partners — talking about some of the huge strides we’ve made together these last 18 months,” Patel said in his post.

In the field with some of our great Louisiana law enforcement partners – talking some of the huge strides we’ve made together these last 18 months making America safe again, covering issues like fraud takedowns, crushing violent crime, improved technology through use of AI,… pic.twitter.com/4SFdXXqEOv
— FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) September 9, 2026

Patel’s travel has been under a significant amount of scrutiny. FBI directors are required to use government planes, even for personal travel because it allows them to maintain secure communications wherever they go, according to several news reports. 

FBI directors are expected to reimburse the government for themselves and family members who use government planes for personal travel. Patel often blends official travel with leisure activities, which has led congressional Democrats to question whether he is properly accounting for his personal use of government resources, according to the Associated Press. 

For example, the AP reported that Patel went snorkeling around the submerged USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, which is very rarely allowed, a few days after visiting the FBI field office in Honolulu.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin DNR tells Enbridge to stop work on pipeline after natural gas leak
description: The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources has told the oil and gas company Enbridge to halt construction on the Line 5 pipeline across northern Wisconsin after a massive spill of natural gas liquids in Iron County late last month.  The spill, which occurred near the town of Saxon and at 1.3 million gallons of natural […]
text:
Laina G. StebbinsThe Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources has told the oil and gas company Enbridge to halt construction on the Line 5 pipeline across northern Wisconsin after a massive spill of natural gas liquids in Iron County late last month. 
The spill, which occurred near the town of Saxon and at 1.3 million gallons of natural gas liquids was the largest in the company’s history, was caused when an unoccupied truck rolled over a valve while crews were doing construction work. The company is in the process of rerouting Line 5 off the Bad River tribe’s reservation — a controversial project which has triggered numerous challenges to the DNR and federal permits. 
Since the spill, environmental activists, tribal members, candidates for office and elected officials in both Wisconsin and Michigan have renewed their calls for the pipeline to be shut down. 
After the spill, Enbridge began working to bypass the damaged valve so the pipeline could again be used to transport Canadian oil and gas. On Wednesday, the DNR issued a notice of noncompliance to the company, noting that Enbridge was constructing the bypass without the proper permits from the DNR. 
In the notice, and in an accompanying letter from DNR Secretary Karen Hyun, the agency said that it had told the company on three separate occasions it could not conduct the bypass work without approval from the state, and possibly from both the county and federal governments. 
The notice states that the bypass construction involves matting placed in nearby wetlands and close to Spoon Creek, which is considered a navigable waterway regulated by state law. 
In her letter, Hyun said she was “deeply concerned and incredibly frustrated” by Enbridge’s actions, especially the potentially harmful effects caused by the “significant discharge” of pollutants known as volatile organic compounds — which can be harmful to people’s health and the local environment. 
“Enbridge has continued to add to the growing list of environmental concerns and violations, demonstrating disregard for the environment, human health, and the statutory authority of the department,” she wrote. “Regarding the Line 5 reroute construction, Enbridge has caused additional discharges to the environment since my earlier letter, which have caused continued frustration and profound unease for the department and the people of Wisconsin. Additionally, at the location of the Line 5 Natural Gas Liquids (NGL) spill on August 25, Enbridge has made the decision to start unpermitted construction of a bypass, despite the extensive efforts of the DNR to educate Enbridge on the necessary permits and approvals for this bypass construction and a commitment to review submitted materials in a timely matter. Based on this pattern of noncompliance demonstrated by Enbridge, my concern over the environmental impacts of Enbridge’s activities over the past weeks has only heightened.”
In a statement, Enbridge spokesperson Juli Kellner said the company is working “around the clock” to clean up the spill site and return the pipeline to service. 
“Enbridge continues working towards both priorities related to the third-party line strike near Saxon, Wis. — the safe control and remediation of the incident site and completing a temporary bypass to allow the pipeline to return to service, which will help resolve energy supply disruptions,” she said. “Around the clock work on both priorities is being done in parallel. Line 5 is critical infrastructure delivering energy to millions of people in the Midwest and Great Lakes regions. We continue to work with the Wisconsin DNR on relevant permitting and separately on environmental conditions at the incident site.”
Rob Lee, an attorney for Midwest Environmental Advocates who has worked on the challenges to Enbridge’s Line 5 permits, said that the company doesn’t get to decide that restoring the pipeline is more important than following state law. 
“Enbridge knew it needed authorization before it started this work. The DNR told the company that repeatedly. Enbridge went ahead anyway. That shows extraordinary disregard for Wisconsin’s environmental laws and for the state agency charged with enforcing them,” Lee said. ““Enbridge cannot simply decide that getting Line 5 back in service is more important than following Wisconsin law. They’ve been out there moving earth, crossing waterways and disturbing wetlands without permits. They need to stop treating environmental requirements as obstacles to work around and start following the law. If they don’t, DNR should revoke the permits for the reroute.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Supreme Court justice recused from 2 cases challenging constitutionality of new 3-judge panel
description: A Utah Supreme Court justice now won’t participate in two cases — the first dealing with gerrymandering and another on abortion — that are each challenging the constitutionality of the Utah Legislature’s newly created rotating three-judge “constitutional court” specifically meant to hear challenges to state laws.  Utah Supreme Court Justice John Nielsen, who[...]
text:
Third District Judge John Nielsen speaks during the announcement of his appointment to the Utah Supreme Court. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)A Utah Supreme Court justice now won’t participate in two cases — the first dealing with gerrymandering and another on abortion — that are each challenging the constitutionality of the Utah Legislature’s newly created rotating three-judge “constitutional court” specifically meant to hear challenges to state laws. 
Utah Supreme Court Justice John Nielsen, who was first appointed to the state’s highest court last fall, has recused himself from both cases. 
His most recent recusal came last week after Planned Parenthood Association of Utah sought to disqualify him from the case stemming from an ongoing challenge to the state’s near-total abortion ban that has been blocked from going into effect since 2022. 
In 2024, the Utah Supreme Court opted against lifting the injunction blocking the law — which infuriated the Republican supermajority of the Utah Legislature. Today, abortion remains legal in Utah up to 18 weeks gestation. 
Utah governor swiftly signs bill to create 3-judge ‘constitutional court’ to hear challenges to laws

In a motion filed in July, Planned Parenthood’s attorneys argued that Nielsen should be disqualified from the case because his “impartiality might reasonably be questioned” because Nielsen, during his time as a private attorney, helped file an amicus brief on behalf of Pro-Life Utah in 2022, during the ongoing legal fight over Utah’s abortion ban. 
The Utah Attorney General’s office, in an Aug. 5 filing, argued Nielsen shouldn’t be disqualified, saying the state has “no concerns” about Nielsen hearing the appeal to the three-judge panel. 
“The mere fact that two different appellate court proceedings separated by several years and involving entirely different issues sprang from the same underlying case should not necessarily mean they involve the same ‘matter in controversy’ or raise an objectively reasonable concern about impartiality,” the Utah Attorney General’s Office wrote. 
In July, a clerk for the Utah Supreme Court wrote that Nielsen “does not believe that amicus representation is a basis for disqualification,” but he disclosed his previous involvement in the case “as information that the parties or their lawyers might reasonably consider relevant to a possible motion for disqualification.”
However, on Sept. 3, Nielsen reversed course and decided to recuse himself from Planned Parenthood’s challenge to the three-judge panel. 
In Utah redistricting fight, plaintiffs ask judge to block Legislature’s new ‘constitutional court’

“Though Justice Nielsen still believes that there are strong reasons supporting the duty to sit here, he concludes on further reflection that the duty to recuse is stronger,” a clerk wrote in the recusal notice. 
“The duty to sit and render judgment on a case and the duty to recuse from a case both reflect
important values, including judicial independence and public confidence in the judiciary,” the clerk wrote. “Sometimes those duties come into tension and create difficult questions. This is one of those cases.”
Now a judge from another court will be invited to take Nielsen’s place. The Utah Supreme Court is scheduled to hear oral arguments in the case on Oct. 5. 
Shireen Ghorbani, President & CEO of Planned Parenthood Association of Utah, issued a statement expressing appreciation for Nielsen’s recusal. 
“The rules about recusals are objective and clear — a judge should recuse when their impartiality might be reasonably questioned,” Ghorbani said. “We appreciate Judge Nielsen for recusing in our case.” 
Previously, in April, Nielsen “voluntarily disqualified” himself from hearing the challenge to the three-judge panel stemming from an anti-gerrymandering case. 
At the time of his recusal, he cited work he did as a private attorney representing the Utah Republican Party in a prior appeal in the underlying anti-gerrymandering case brought by the League of Women Voters of Utah, Mormon Women for Ethical Government and other plaintiffs. 
“Though amicus representation is not in itself disqualifying, then-counsel Nielsen worked very closely with the Legislature’s counsel and offered advice on the broader litigation to the point that he felt for purposes of recusal that he had acted as counsel for the Legislature rather than just for amici,” a Utah Supreme Court clerk wrote in Nielsen’s recusal notice. 
Soon after the Utah Legislature created the three-judge panel to hear constitutional challenges to state laws, Utah’s attorney general and the Legislature moved to transfer several cases — including the anti-gerrymandering case and the abortion case — to the new “constitutional court.” The plaintiffs in those cases also reacted swiftly, asking the courts to block the legislation that created the three-judge panel as itself unconstitutional. 
Opponents of the new three-judge panel argued it enables state leaders to “forum shop” court cases away from judges who haven’t given them favorable rulings, while proponents including Senate President Stuart Adams, R-Layton, argued it was structured to avoid any concerns of “forum shopping” because judges that would serve on the panel would be randomly selected. 
The creation of the new three-judge panel has led arguments in the underlying court cases to be put on pause while the courts hash out whether the new court is constitutional or not.  
Challenges to the new “constitutional court” have since gone to the Utah Supreme Court to decide — at a time when the state’s highest court is undergoing major changes. 
The Utah Legislature earlier this year expanded the court from five to seven justices, prompting two openings on the bench that Gov. Spencer Cox recently filled with the appointments of Stephen Dent and Jay Jorgensen, both of whom the Utah Senate confirmed in June. 
Then, two more openings came after the resignation of former Justice Diana Hagen amid controversy and the retirement of longtime Chief Justice Matthew Durrant. Late last month, Cox nominated attorney Michael Manssen and 5th District Judge Matthew Bell to fill those seats. Their appointments are pending confirmation from the Utah Senate, with confirmation hearings scheduled for Friday and Monday. 
Nielsen took his place on the bench last year after he was appointed to fill a vacancy left by former Associate Chief Justice John Pearce.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota public university enrollment drop includes fewer undergrad and international students
description: South Dakota public university enrollment decreased by 294 students this year, according to numbers released Thursday by the state Board of Regents. Overall enrollment, which includes graduate and undergraduate students, is 35,797. Enrollment dropped at three universities and increased at the three others: Black Hills State University in Spearfish increased[...]
text:
The Coughlin Campanile at South Dakota State University in Brookings. (Courtesy of SDSU)South Dakota public university enrollment decreased by 294 students this year, according to numbers released Thursday by the state Board of Regents.
Overall enrollment, which includes graduate and undergraduate students, is 35,797. Enrollment dropped at three universities and increased at the three others:

Black Hills State University in Spearfish increased by about 2% to 3,502 students.
Dakota State University in Madison grew by about 3.5% to 3,975 students.
Northern State University in Aberdeen grew by 4% to 3,890 students.
South Dakota Mines in Rapid City decreased by 2% to 2,489 students.
South Dakota State University in Brookings decreased by about 2% to 11,901 students.
University of South Dakota in Vermillion decreased by 3.5% to 10,040 students.



System-wide enrollment peaked at 36,662 in 2017, and no year since then has equaled that mark.
“Enrollment is one measure of the health of our universities, but the larger story is what those students are preparing to do,” which is to build the state’s workforce and contribute to its communities, South Dakota Board of Regents Executive Director Nathan Lukkes said in a news release.
International student numbers decline in South Dakota amid immigration crackdown

The numbers could be a sign of the “2025 cliff” feared by higher education officials, attributed to a lower birth rate during the Great Recession of 2007-2009. A 10% decline in high school graduates was expected nationally from 2025 to 2037, Lukkes told lawmakers in 2024.
Undergraduate enrollment systemwide decreased by 401 students this year, to 29,738, including decreases of 377 at South Dakota State University and 175 at the University of South Dakota.
Systemwide international student enrollment decreased by 237. International enrollment also dropped by 76 students last year. The decreases come amid federal immigration policy changes during the Trump administration that have made it more difficult for some foreign students to enter and stay in the country.
Graduate student enrollment systemwide increased by 107 students, and 56 more South Dakota high school graduates are pursuing higher education in the state than last year, according to system data.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana FWP analyzing nonresident hunting impacts, seeks hunter input
description: Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks is collecting data on the impacts of nonresident hunters on deer, elk, upland game birds, and water fowl hunting in the state, and is asking hunters to provide feedback about how nonresident hunting impacts how licenses are allocated. The survey is part of a study bill — House Bill 568 […]
text:
Silhouette of a hunter aiming his shotgun. Photo illustration by Getty Images.Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks is collecting data on the impacts of nonresident hunters on deer, elk, upland game birds, and water fowl hunting in the state, and is asking hunters to provide feedback about how nonresident hunting impacts how licenses are allocated.
The survey is part of a study bill — House Bill 568 — passed by the 2025 Legislature. The Montana Hunters First Act, sponsored by Republican Rep. Courtenay Sprunger, directed FWP to conduct an impact study on nonresident hunting.
The bill requires the department to look at how nonresident hunting impacts deer, elk and bird hunting in each of the seven regions across the state, as well how lands enrolled in hunter access program are utilized and game population trends.
During the 2025 session, lawmakers also passed a bill increasing the base cost of a nonresident hunting fee by more than 500%, which is expected to raise nearly $7 million annually.
While the final results of the study will be released in December, the department released some preliminary data this week showing that nonresident license sales have grown during the previous decade, “though some of that has tapered a bit in recent years,” according to FWP, while remaining higher than 2016 numbers.
Nonresident total elk license purchases, which includes deer-elk combo and elk only licenses, grew from 19,914 in 2016 to 22,092 in 2025, while deer licenses peaked in 2021 at 42,557 and dropped to 40,614 in 2025.
The share of nonresident deer and elk hunters climbed from around 17% in 2016 to a peak of more than 20% in 2021 before dropping off a percentage point in recent years.
Since 2016, the largest uptick in hunting license sales has been in migratory bird licenses, which rose from 3,490 in 2016 to 5,539 in 2025 — a 58% increase.
Nonresident upland game bird license sales increased 15% from 3,490 in 2016 to 5,539 in 2025.
In general, license sales are sold according to state law, which can change with every legislative session. The Fish and Wildlife Commission can also dictate how licenses are distributed and has cut back on some licenses for nonresident in recent years.

House Bill 568 requires FWP to identify “specific issues for consideration” for the legislature, the department and the Fish and Wildlife Commission about nonresident hunter impacts. However, the bill does not make any immediate changes to hunting seasons, license quotas, or resident/nonresident allocations.

Hunters can participate in the survey through FWP’s website.
The department will publish a publicly accessible report by Dec. 1.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Bill would make NJ lawmakers ‘practice what they preach’ on cell phone use
description: Cell phones are so distracting during legislative sessions they should be banned, just as they were in schools, a GOP lawmaker said.
text:
Rep. Brian Bergen (R-Morris) says so many legislators scroll their cell phones during voting sessions that he has introduced a bill to ban their use. (Photo by Hal Brown for New Jersey Monitor)With New Jersey students now banned from using their cell phones during the school day, one state lawmaker wants his fellow legislators to follow in their footsteps and stop scrolling during legislative sessions.
Assemblyman Brian Bergen (R-Morris) introduced a bill Thursday he cheekily dubbed the “Practice What We Preach Act” to bar legislators from using or even possessing their phones or other digital devices during voting sessions and committee meetings.
Lawmakers would have to leave their devices in lockers that would be installed outside every chamber entrance and committee room and not pick them up until proceedings adjourn, “the same way a sophomore gets her phone back at 2:45 p.m.,” Bergen said.
“The argument for banning phones in schools was that these devices are distracting, corrosive to attention spans and harmful to engaging with the people in the room,” Bergen said. “I sit in that room. I have watched members shop, scroll, post and play games while we spend billions of dollars of other people’s money. A kid on a phone in algebra misses a formula. A legislator on a phone during a vote misses a budget.”
Bergen was one of just three legislators — all Republican — who voted against the bell-to-bell phone ban for students, which took effect in K-12 public schools at the start of this current academic year. He has complained that New Jersey’s 1989 law banning beepers on school property remains on the books.
The bill he introduced Thursday would make it a disorderly persons offense for legislators to use phones during voting sessions and committee meetings — the same penalty beeper ban violators face.
As a Republican in a legislature long controlled by Democrats, Bergen knows his bill is unlikely to advance.
But he hopes the proposal will at least shame some of his Statehouse colleagues from reaching for their phones the next time legislative leaders gavel in a new session.
“They all know it’s true. It’s an issue. Like people playing Candy Crush while I’m giving a speech. Like come on! It’s crazy,” Bergen told the New Jersey Monitor. “They can rest assured that I’m going to call them out on the floor if they’re not paying attention, 100%.”

title: Hatcher says he’s amenable to Molder’s challenge to debate before 5th District election
description: A debate — or a series of debates — may be on the horizon in Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District race.  Columbia Mayor and Democratic candidate Chaz Molder on Thursday morning formally challenged Republican competitor Charlie Hatcher, a farmer and former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, to a series of three debates across the district. Molder suggested[...]
text:
Charlie Hatcher, left, said he is open to a debate with fellow 5th Congressional District candidate Chaz Molder, right. (Photos: John Partipilo, left, and Brad Vest, right, for Tennessee Lookout)A debate — or a series of debates — may be on the horizon in Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District race. 
Columbia Mayor and Democratic candidate Chaz Molder on Thursday morning formally challenged Republican competitor Charlie Hatcher, a farmer and former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, to a series of three debates across the district.
Molder suggested holding debates at Columbia State Community College, Rhodes College in Memphis, and the University of Tennessee at Martin. 
The challenge came after Hatcher told The Daily Memphian that “voters deserve to hear from the two nominees in this important race.”
“As a mayor, I don’t wait for an invitation to show up. I listen to folks at church on Sunday morning, around kitchen tables, at the ball field, and in my office at city hall, whether they voted for me or not,” Molder said in a Thursday news release. “The politicians who gerrymandered this district gave us a lot of ground to cover.”
“We are the ones asking for the job, so we ought to be the ones doing the traveling. No voter should have to drive three hours to hear their congressional candidates debate,” he said in the release. “Three debates will give people across this district a chance to hear from both of us in person, close to home.”
Hatcher told the Lookout Thursday that he’s open to the idea if both campaigns can agree on scheduling.
“I want a well-structured forum,” perhaps organized by an association, he said in a telephone interview from Dallas, where he is attending the Republican Midterm Convention hosted by President Donald Trump.
“I’ve been meeting folks where they are in every nook and cranny of this district for months,” Hatcher added in a written statement. “I look forward to a discussion on the issues at a time and place that works for both candidates throughout the district.”

name: WyoFile
title: What would it take for a third-party candidate to win Wyoming’s race for governor?
description:
The Constitution Party is betting on former Republican Rebecca Bextel and five other candidates this year in push to gain major party status. 
The post What would it take for a third-party candidate to win Wyoming’s race for governor? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
No minor party candidate has ever won a statewide elected office in Wyoming. 
Voters have exclusively elected Republicans and Democrats to the state’s top positions for the last 136 years. Though third-party candidates have frequently qualified for the general election in recent decades, one has yet to either capture a statewide race, or garner the requisite support to upgrade to major-party status. 
Constitution Party Chairman Joshua Shimkus says this year is different. 
“We’ve gone from relative obscurity to entering a political dialogue realistically,” Shimkus told WyoFile. “Our goal is to become a legitimate party. The first big step of that is becoming a major party.” 
There are six Constitution Party candidates on Wyoming’s general election ballot this year — the most high-profile being gubernatorial candidate Rebecca Bextel, the Teton County conservative activist at the center of the Checkgate controversy that dominated the 2026 legislative session. 
When Bextel announced her run in May, she said she would only stay in the race if Republican voters nominated Gillette Sen. Eric Barlow in the primary election. Hard-right Republicans saw Barlow as too moderate to represent Wyoming’s conservative movement. Barlow nevertheless triumphed, beating out GOP candidates backed by President Donald Trump and the Wyoming Republican Party. Bextel will now challenge Barlow in the general election alongside Democratic candidate Kenneth Casner. 
Republican gubernatorial candidates Eric Barlow and Megan Degenfelder participate in a primary election candidate forum organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming at Casper College on WJuly 22, 2026. Barlow won the primary election and will face Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel and Democratic Party candidate Kenneth Casner in November. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Meanwhile, Tamara Trujillo, a former Republican lawmaker in Cheyenne, is running for secretary of state, while Jeffrey Haggit, of Mountain View, is running for Congress for the third time. The three other Constitution Party candidates are seeking seats in the Legislature. 
Shimkus said he didn’t know Bextel before the Checkgate controversy — she was perhaps best known until then for her opposition to affordable housing measures in Teton County — but recruited her in the months afterwards when he saw a potential ally in his vision for his party, as WyoFile previously reported. 
“We discussed strategy, and how this might be a vehicle for all conservatives in the state of Wyoming,” Shimkus said in May.
In Wyoming, a minor party can elevate to major-party status if one of its candidates for governor, secretary of state or U.S. House collects at least 10% of the total vote for that office in the general election. 
Shimkus said he’s confident that will happen this year. 
“We’ve been able to position the party in a way that we can have meaningful political conversation,” he said. “Part of that is recruiting Rebecca Bextel and Tammy Trujillo for office.”
“We’re going out to win,” Shimkus said. 
Third-party obstacles
Others say several obstacles remain in the way of a third-party candidate’s prospects this cycle. 
“All you have to do is look back. No third party or independent candidate has won a statewide office,” Jim King, a retired University of Wyoming professor, told WyoFile. 
The most successful third-party gubernatorial candidate in Wyoming history was the Populist Party’s Lewis C. Tidwell, who won 11.28% of the vote in 1894 — only four years after statehood. Tidwell’s success effectively spoiled the Democratic Party’s candidate’s shot for governor and helped the Republican Party win back the office. 

Sources: Wyoming State Archives and Wyoming Secretary of State’s Office. Timeline by Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile
Wyoming’s political landscape, however, is now a much deeper shade of red. 
“If the Republicans and Democrats were more evenly matched, then a third-party candidacy may matter more,” said Ryan Williamson, an associate political science professor at UW. “But seeing how lopsided it is, it would be more difficult for a Constitutional candidate to be a spoiler and change the outcome.” 
King also pointed to Wyoming’s Republican supermajority and said in other states where independent or third-party candidates have won, it’s often “a situation where the two parties are at such war with each other,” a third type of candidate appeals to voters. 
Or, King said, it’s “usually someone who has already been successful politically.” 
A question of time
Timing is another huge obstacle, he said. 
While Bextel announced her tentative plans in May, she didn’t start campaigning in earnest until earlier this month — two months shy of the general election. Barlow, meanwhile, announced his run in August 2025 and has since set new fundraising records and carried out an extensive on-the-ground campaign across the state. 
Plus, running as a third-party candidate “immediately robs you of a lot of the tangible and intangible resources that are available to major party candidates,” Williamson said. 
One, he said, is “an existing political infrastructure,” such as political action committees related to a party, or association with other members of a party. Another is brand recognition, Williamson said. 
Running as a minor-party candidate, “people don’t really know what that brand represents as much,” he said. “People may not know as much about Eric Barlow, but they do know they’re a Republican and they’re going to show up and vote for the Republican. And that’s just kind of uniformly true throughout the United States, across different levels of government and points in time.” 
The pool of voters is another challenge, King said. 
Third-party candidates often have a more “narrow view of what government responsibilities should be, and most people do not subscribe to those positions,” he said. 
“Yes, people want smaller government, but they still want all the services they’re getting from government,” King said. “So a third-party candidate who typically is pushing the idea that they’re going to reduce government’s role is fighting an uphill battle. There just isn’t the size of a constituency out there for candidates like that.” 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting for most residents starts Oct. 6.

text:
The Kansas Statehouse dome and a U.S. flag stand out against a blue sky on May 1, 2025. (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Gov. Laura Kelly ordered flags to be flown at half-staff Friday in recognition of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
The lowering of flags from sunup to sundown will honor those who lost their lives in the attacks, Kelly said Thursday.
“Twenty-five years after the unthinkable tragedy that claimed the lives of nearly 3,000 Americans and injured thousands more, we uphold our commitment to remembering those whose lives were permanently altered by a horrific terrorist attack,” Kelly said. “We will never forget the bravery demonstrated that day by so many, including our nation’s first responders, who saved countless lives despite losing more than 400 of their own. Their sacrifice and service will never be forgotten.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Senate race mud-throwing will continue to the bitter end, but do voters care?
description: Watchers of the Nebraska Senate debate at the state fair saw a microcosm of the yearlong campaign between Sen. Pete Ricketts and Dan Osborn.
text:
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn are in a heated Senate race. 

(Photos by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND — It only took about a minute into the Nebraska State Fair Senate debate for the name-calling to start.
Incumbent Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts called nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn “Democrat Dan” 40 times throughout the hourlong event, leading Osborn to joke that there should be a “third podium” for him as he tried to pitch himself as being a working-class populist above party lines.
Osborn didn’t attack Ricketts as much, but he accused Ricketts of being part of the “rigged game” in Washington, D.C., and assisting the “biggest transition of wealth in human history,” referring to Trump’s tax and spending bill. After the debate, Osborn’s campaign made fun of how many times Ricketts said “Democrat Dan” with a drinking game. 
News coverage of the debate noted how fiery it was. Debate watchers saw a microcosm of the yearlong campaign.
Ricketts’ strategy has been maintaining a consistent drumbeat painting Osborn as a “secret” Democrat, vowing not to make the “same mistake” as U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 by ignoring him. 
Ricketts touted Congress’ passing President Trump’s tax and spending bill, securing the southern border, and investing in defense against foreign adversaries as examples of him fighting for Nebraska. He also repeatedly pointed to his accomplishments as governor. 
Ricketts is seeking his first full six-year term in the Senate. The former two-time governor easily beat Omaha Democrat Preston Love Jr. in a 2024 special election to finish the final two years of former U.S. Sen. Ben Sasse, R-Neb., who resigned to lead the University of Florida.
He has Nebraska’s dominant political operation behind him, known for its no-holds-barred approach to campaigning. 
Meanwhile, Osborn — whom some national media outlets describe as the independent candidate who refused to go away — has tried to win over enough voters statewide without alienating Democrats or Republicans, seeking a better finish than his 2024 7-percentage-point loss to Fischer. 
Osborn’s strategy has come with its own problems. 
University of Nebraska-Lincoln political science professor Kevin Smith said Osborn’s biggest challenge was always going to be getting enough Republicans to vote for him in a ruby-red state where Republicans outnumber Democrats 2-to-1, with a growing number of nonpartisans.
“Based on his race against Fischer, he did persuade some Republicans. I don’t see how he got as close as he did without some Republicans crossing over,” Smith said. “That’s just the way the math works out in the race.” 
The Senate race has drawn national attention for its nontraditional political dynamics, serving as a trendsetter as other red states, like South Dakota and Idaho, saw Democrats step aside for independent candidates. In Nebraska, former Democratic Senate nominee Cindy Burbank dropped out to clear the field for Osborn. Ricketts and national Republicans have tried to use the Democratic strategy as proof that Osborn will side with Democrats in Congress and said he is being dishonest with voters. 
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’s podium sign at Lincoln’s Country Club in Lincoln on June 12, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
This election season has also seen twists and turns in lawsuits related to the Democratic primary, new political parties that have faced allegations of being spoilers in the race, and candidates suspending their campaigns to support Osborn. 
With November approaching, the national political environment has continued to trend more favorably for the party out of the White House. The Senate, once a pipe dream for Democrats, appears within reach, with races in Iowa and Texas seen as toss-ups by election analysts. 
The Nebraska Senate race is still viewed as favorable to Ricketts. There has been a noticeable public shift in how Ricketts has talked about the race compared with earlier in the cycle, when he said Nebraska could determine which party controls the Senate. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz told a crowd of Republicans in Lincoln earlier this year that this race is a “real” one. 
There have been no polls other than internal polling from the Osborn campaign showing a close race. Smith said it’s hard to tell how the race is going without any high-quality polling. 
At a Lincoln campaign event last month at the Rosie’s South Harvester Room, Ricketts told supporters that the election is a contrast between “a man who wants to complain about everything but offers no solutions” and himself as someone who has “been delivering for Nebraskans for over a dozen years.” 
Ricketts told the Examiner after the event that he doesn’t view his campaign as negative, saying that “pointing out the contrast with (Osborn) is not being negative.”
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts waiting to speak at his event on Aug. 17, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
“We’re just pointing out that he says one thing and does another,” Ricketts said. 
Throughout the campaign, Osborn has had to play defense against controversies amplified by Ricketts and Republicans, such as explaining why he paid himself and his extended family for campaign work — which is legal but often comes at a political price. Osborn called a Federal Election Commission complaint from a conservative watchdog group “baseless.”
The group alleged that payments from Osborn’s campaign committees to his immediate and extended family members and their businesses far exceeded fair market value. The FEC currently doesn’t have enough members for a quorum, so it can’t look into complaints or do much beyond publishing candidates’ financial disclosure reports and other basic tasks.  
In the debate, Osborn acknowledged that some political advertisements funded by dark money support his campaign, but said he doesn’t stand by ads that don’t include his approval of the message. In the debate, each candidate accused the other of benefiting from “dark money,” referring to large political donations made by anonymous contributors.

Osborn’s campaign is no stranger to trying to create social media moments; It has produced skits and videos attacking Ricketts for accepting corporate donations and for his stance on marijuana. Osborn’s campaign even has music videos — and the Ricketts campaign has its own song about Osborn. 
Osborn held an impromptu press conference to showcase a large fake bank check made out to “My sweet baby boy Pete Ricketts” from Ricketts’ father to “buy a Senate seat,” after fundraising reports showed the senator had donated $5.2 million to his own campaign.
Ricketts said he has contributed to his own campaign because he believes in Nebraska and that is where his roots are. 
Republicans attacked Osborn because the largest share of contributions in his latest fundraising report came from donors in California and most of his money came from Democrats.
Osborn separated himself from former Maine Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Graham Platner, accused of sexual assault by a former girlfriend, after Republicans pointed out that the two had shared consultants at one point. 
Reporting from the Flatwater Free Press showed that Osborn staffers from his 2024 campaign infiltrated the Legal Marijuana NOW Party and tried to dissolve it. 
Leak, leak and even more leaks
The former labor union leader also had to endure, or push back against, multiple leaks of audio recordings of his campaign events and town halls by conservative and national outlets. The audio leaks were brought up during the debate. In one recording,  Osborn said that he would be “f—ed” as a candidate if he said that he wanted to “abolish ICE,” and that he couldn’t win in Nebraska if he said, “Oh, I love trans people, and they should be able to play in sports.” 
In another audio leak after the debate, he told Latino and Black Democrats that President Doanlnd Trump’s border wall is “a symbol of racism” that “does nothing” in a private meeting in July, according to Politico. 
Osborn addressed some of the leaks during the debate, saying that Ricketts’ campaign ads using the recordings are a “joke” because they take snippets of what he says out of context. At one moment in the debate, Osborn said he didn’t know what Ricketts was referring to when he said Osborn had compared U.S. law enforcement to Nazi Germany and called officers “chicken sh–.”
Independent U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn speaking during his rally in La Vista on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Ricketts was referring to an article in the online outlet Plains Sentinel quoting Osborn criticizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents for wearing masks. At a town hall, he said, “Take your masks off, chicken sh— … If you have to wear a mask to do your job, you’re probably doing something wrong,” according to the Plains Sentinel. 
On the debate stage at the State Fair, Osborn said he tried to calm the “temperature down” with some people at his events because they were very passionate. 
Smith, the UNL professor, said he was unsure how effective Ricketts’ attacks would be in the grand scheme of things, but pointed out that it might be meaningful for the outcome if it can “persuade just a small portion of wavering Republicans,” if the race is as tight as Osborn’s internal polling claims. 
Osborn is currently on a statewide tour that includes rallies and town halls. 
He told the Examiner last month after a campaign event at Bourbon Theatre in Lincoln that one of the reasons for his tour is to set the “record straight” with voters, as those “controversies” have often been brought up at his events. 
Osborn said he wants to be asked those questions, as he can answer voters face-to-face rather than through a TV or radio ad. 
“Ricketts … he wrote himself a check for five and a quarter million dollars, and now he’s up on TV, and he’s lying about me … I am not enriching myself or my family,” Osborn said. 
The campaign has been marked by endless attacks from both candidates. It wasn’t used during the debate, but Osborn has called Ricketts “Pocket Pete” on social media and at rallies. He has told voters that Nebraskans have been “abandoned” by their elected officials for “corporations and special interests funding their campaigns.” 
Ricketts and Osborn have attacked each other about the late Florida sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Osborn attacked Ricketts about “voting against” the release of the Epstein files — Ricketts did vote with the rest of the state’s federal delegation for the U.S. House’s Epstein Files Transparency Act. 
Ricketts attacked Osborn for a canceled fundraiser with a long-time Democratic donor who was mentioned in the Jeffrey Epstein files — the donor said “nothing pertaining to me in the March 2024 email” was true.
On the trail, Osborn has lumped in the Ricketts family with Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel and Mark Zuckerberg, calling them “modern-day robber barons stripping” the country bare.
“This ain’t a damn football game”
Nebraska Democrats’ support of Osborn has been a focus of multiple news cycles in the race. 
Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb said during a late July press conference that having Democrats’ support doesn’t  hurt his chances because some Republicans are “frustrated with Ricketts.” 
A Dan Osborn shirt at an Omaha office of the Nebraska Democratic Party on April 3, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/ Nebraska Examiner)
“I think a lot of folks are putting their kind of partisan ideology aside this election cycle and looking to see who can deliver better on promises,” Kleeb said.
Osborn said after a campaign event last month that he wasn’t aware that state Democrats had endorsed him, adding that he wants to be endorsed by everybody. 
Kleeb endorsed Osborn last year, and it was widely reported. 
Osborn, in the same private meeting in July, told the group of minority Democrats there are “two separate pots in politics. Campaigning is not being a U.S. senator, so it is about trying to win votes in a Republican state.”
“This isn’t about [partisanship] anymore. …This isn’t Team Red versus Team Blue. This ain’t a damn football game,” Osborn told the Examiner in August. “This is up versus down.” 
Smith, the UNL professor, said he expects the race to be competitive, but whether Osborn is in “striking distance” is a different question. He added the “wild card” in the race is that November is likely to be tough for Republicans nationwide. 
“Your crystal ball is as good as mine,” Smith said. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Supreme Court rejects primary loser’s appeal to force Democratic Party to replace candidate
description: The Nebraska Supreme Court unanimously ruled that the loser of the Democratic Senate primary election incorrectly interpreted state law.
text:
The Nebraska Supreme Court is housed at the Nebraska State Capitol Building in Lincoln. (Rebecca S. Gratz for the Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court unanimously ruled that the loser of the Democratic Senate primary election incorrectly interpreted state law. 
William Forbes had sought to force the Nebraska Democratic Party to replace its Senate nominee, who dropped out. He appealed to the high court after a Lancaster County district judge dismissed his case.
Forbes and his lawyers argued that the law’s language requires a replacement, saying the law is meant to prohibit what they described as a “scheme” by the Democratic Party to clear the field for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn. 
Lawyers for the Nebraska Democrats said the statute Forbes cited addresses the process a party must follow if it chooses to replace a nominee, whereas the law about a candidate declining the nomination says a party “may” replace the person. The high court said the party’s reading of the law was correct. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“After Burbank’s withdrawal, Nebraska statutes did not obligate the Democratic Party to nominate a replacement candidate. Forbes’ lawsuit contending otherwise lacked merit, and the district court was correct to dismiss it. Accordingly, we affirm,” part of the Supreme Court order reads. 
Cindy Burbank won her May primary against Forbes comfortably. She then dropped out of the race one day after the secretary of state verified Osborn’s signatures to be on the fall ballot. 
This ends the drawn-out drama in the Democratic Senate primary, which saw allegations that both Forbes and Burbank were “plants” to help either incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts or Osborn. Both Ricketts and Osborn have denied any involvement with the other two candidates.
The deadline to certify the ballot is Friday; the Senate field has five candidates. 
In addition to Osborn and Ricketts, the others are Legal Marijuana NOW’s Mike Marvin, who suspended his campaign but will still appear on the ballot; Nebraska Working People Party’s Robin Richards; and America First Party candidate Chuck Conboy. 
The general election is Nov 3.
