name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana lawmakers will consider closing domestic violence firearm loophole in 2027
description: In the 2027 legislative session, Montana lawmakers will consider a bill aimed at closing a loophole in state law that permits individuals convicted of domestic assault to purchase or possess firearms.  The Criminal Justice Oversight Council at its meeting last week voted 9-to-7 to advance draft legislation strengthening Montana’s partner and family member as[...]
text:
The dome of the Montana State Capitol pictured on March 28, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)In the 2027 legislative session, Montana lawmakers will consider a bill aimed at closing a loophole in state law that permits individuals convicted of domestic assault to purchase or possess firearms. 
The Criminal Justice Oversight Council at its meeting last week voted 9-to-7 to advance draft legislation strengthening Montana’s partner and family member assault law and clearly state that misdemeanor convictions can result in revocation of firearms possession. 
“I generally don’t support legislation that increases penalties, but I think that this is a real public safety issue,” said Rep. SJ Howell, a Democrat. “We hear about it every session. We hear about it every interim. We have Montanans who come in and tell really heartbreaking stories of their loved ones who’ve been murdered in situations like this, and I think this is an opportunity for us to really dig in and say, ‘Is there something we can do to actually prevent some of these violent crimes?’”
More than half of female homicide victims are killed by current or former male intimate partners, according to the National Institute of Health. Firearms are used in more than 50% of those homicides.
A federal law passed in 1994 prohibits individuals convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence from having firearms, but a loophole exists in Montana statute due to the difference in how state and federal statutes define domestic violence. 
Montana has more comprehensive laws protecting victims of domestic violence by allowing threats of violence or emotional injury to be enough for a conviction, a more stringent standard than federal law. 
In January 2025, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals held that the mismatch in definitions means that the federal law prohibiting possession of a firearm didn’t apply to a conviction under Montana’s law. 
That opinion came from a federal district court case that convicted Michael B. DeFrance of possessing three guns after having been convicted of a misdemeanor for assaulting his ex-girlfriend, Jermain Charlo. 
Charlo, a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai tribes, has been missing since she was last seen in Missoula on June 16, 2018. DeFrance is not named as a suspect in her case. 
His charges were overturned in a ruling the three-judge panel called “absurd,” for having a weaker consequence stemming from a stronger state misdemeanor law. 
Last fall, the Criminal Justice Oversight Council drafted a letter to Montana’s federal delegation asking them to consider a congressional workaround to better align federal and state statutes, before forging ahead with drafting legislation for state lawmakers. 
Under the draft bill, which is likely to be carried by Democratic Sen. Laura Smith, a judge would have broader discretion to prohibit a convicted offender from possessing or purchasing a firearm, regardless of whether a gun was used in the assault. 
The bill would also change the state’s laws around unlawful possession of a firearm by adding the partner and family member assault misdemeanors to the list of convictions that prohibit owning a gun. 
Both sections would give the state broader ability to keep firearms away from individuals with domestic violence convictions without relying on the federal statute.  
Shantelle Gaynor, who works in the Missoula County Community Justice Department and serves as the council’s crime victims representative, voted to advance the draft legislation, saying it would help not only victims, but law enforcement. 
“Just as a reminder, it’s also quite important to law enforcement safety,” Gaynor said. “These are the kinds of calls that law enforcement are harmed by, especially when there are guns and a fact pattern that is showing escalating violence and disregard for law enforcement.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Republicans starting ads for Engling a month after Democrat Bayh hit the airwaves
description: Indiana Republicans say they’re starting a statewide advertising campaign to boost secretary of state candidate Max Engling — a month after Democratic nominee Beau Bayh’s ads first hit the airwaves.
text:
Republican Max Engling speaks to reporters after a debate on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Republicans say they’re starting a statewide advertising campaign to boost secretary of state candidate Max Engling — a month after Democratic nominee Beau Bayh’s ads first hit the airwaves.
The state Republican Party announced Thursday plans for the $1 million effort in support of Engling, with the cost split between the state party and Gov. Mike Braun’s campaign.
The Engling ads were set to begin airing this week, state GOP spokeswoman Kylie Glatfelter said, but video of the initial commercial wasn’t immediately released.
The Republican Party’s announcement said the ad spending “reflects Braun’s strong support for Engling,” a staffer to U.S. Sen. Jim Banks who defeated current Secretary of State Diego Morales during June’s state GOP convention. 
“I’m proud to put my full support behind him, and this campaign is about making sure voters across our state know what’s at stake in this race,” Braun said in the Republican Party’s statement. 
Beau Bayh ad kicks off potentially expensive Indiana secretary of state campaign

The spending by Braun and state Republicans helps Engling close the fundraising gap between him and Bayh in what is poised to be an expensive campaign that includes former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard running under the Lincoln Party banner. Libertarian Lauri Shillings is also on the ballot.
The Bayh campaign launched its broadcast advertising about four weeks ago and has had the political airwaves to itself since then.
Bayh, the son of former Gov. Evan Bayh, ended June with about $2.3 million in his campaign fund, making him the best-financed Democratic candidate in years as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a statewide office since 2012.
Engling had a late start in fundraising as he launched his successful GOP nomination challenge in May. Engling’s campaign had about $150,000 as of June 30, according to Election Division reports.
Since July 1, Bayh’s campaign has reported nearly $450,000 in large contributions. Engling’s campaign has received about $200,000 in large contributions during that time.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Federal judge dismisses complaint against Indiana citizenship verification voting law
description: Voting rights groups challenging Indiana’s citizenship verification statutes as discriminatory have less than a month to refile their complaint after a federal judge on Thursday dismissed it. The plaintiffs — League of Women Voters of Indiana, Common Cause Indiana, Hoosier Asian American Power and Exodus Refugee Immigration — filed suit last October in the U[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballots for the May 19, 2026, primary election at Fox Hollow Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Voting rights groups challenging Indiana’s citizenship verification statutes as discriminatory have less than a month to refile their complaint after a federal judge on Thursday dismissed it.
The plaintiffs — League of Women Voters of Indiana, Common Cause Indiana, Hoosier Asian American Power and Exodus Refugee Immigration — filed suit last October in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana.
They allege a pair of recently approved state laws discriminate against voters who have become U.S. citizens by subjecting them to citizenship verification that natural-born citizens will never face.
The state of Indiana has rejected or canceled the voter registrations of more than 60% of immigrant Hoosiers challenged under a recent proof of citizenship law — not including several hundred with pending cases.
Indiana voting rights advocates sue over ‘unnecessary’ proof of citizenship laws, cite ‘stale’ data

The four groups have argued the laws have forced them to spend significant money and other resources to counteract the laws’ impacts on the people they serve, distracting from their missions.
But their alleged injuries, according to federal Judge Matthew P. Brookman, don’t hold up to recent precedent established in a 2024 U.S. Supreme Court decision.
“The Court confirmed that an organization cannot ‘manufacture’ its own standing by ‘divert(ing) its resources in response to a defendant’s actions,'” he wrote in a Thursday order.
“These allegations no longer suffice to establish organizational standing because they do not pass muster” under the new test established by FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, he added.
Now, plaintiffs must show the challenged statutes affect or interfere with their core business activities, not just their organizational missions, to illustrate their injuries.
“Here, Plaintiffs do not say what their ‘core business activities’ are, so they have failed to allege facts as to this prong of the AHM organizational-standing test,” the judge opined.
He dismissed the complaint without prejudice and offered the plaintiffs 28 days to file an amended version.
Brookman also denied a motion for a preliminary injunction — which would temporarily pause enforcement of the laws — noting that his dismissal of the complaint leaves no claims pending on which to grant injunctive relief.
Secretary of State Diego Morales has said the statutes boost election security.
Neither he nor lawyers for the plaintiffs immediately responded to requests for comment on the judge’s decision Thursday afternoon.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Turtle Mountain chairman encourages civic, youth engagement
description: Tribal leaders should support their community’s youth to spur growth and break away from old politics that hinder opportunities, the leader of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians told college students, instructors and other tribal officials Thursday.  Tribal Chairman Jamie Azure said he wanted to break away from that “standard approach” soon after h[...]
text:
Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians Chairman Jamie Azure speaks at the Tribal Leaders Summit in Bismarck, N.D., on Sept. 10, 2026.
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Tribal leaders should support their community’s youth to spur growth and break away from old politics that hinder opportunities, the leader of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians told college students, instructors and other tribal officials Thursday. 
Tribal Chairman Jamie Azure said he wanted to break away from that “standard approach” soon after his entry into tribal government as a council member in 2016. He outlined how his tribe worked to engage youth and drive toward goals for the Turtle Mountain community after trainings on strategic planning for Native nations showed why opportunities were lacking.
“We learned that if we are going to move forward as a nation, we needed to start planning on moving forward by using correct data, by using higher education, by showing people that our sovereign nations weren’t just little specks on a map,” Azure told an audience at the 29th Tribal Leaders Summit in Bismarck. 
Tribal leaders call for sovereignty as federal support wavers

In 2018, Turtle Mountain leaders and the Native Governance Center organized a youth summit with roundtables to ask young people what challenges, opportunities or lack thereof they saw in the community, Azure said.
The tribe began a 10-year strategic plan based on that feedback, “and that’s still going through to today,” the chairman said. 
The tribe built a water park for a safe, fun place for families and job opportunities for young people, and a recovery center to help people move forward from addiction, Azure said. 
The tribe raised its minimum wage to $15 an hour and made youth employees eligible for a 401(k) retirement account and insurance after six months, he said. 
“That to me is sustainable security for our people for the next 40, 50 years,” the chairman said.
Additionally, the tribe’s natural resources group and 25 to 50 youth workers cleaned up and transformed the beaches of Gordon Lake into Sky Chief Park. The youth asked the tribal council to prohibit alcohol at the lake, which passed, Azure said. And those teenagers began to enforce the rules, he said. Parking and camping areas got cleaner, he said. 
US Supreme Court sends North Dakota tribal redistricting case back for review

“You can sit back and you can watch our young ones really just take a grasp and say, ‘This is who we are.’ That’s true sovereignty. That’s people coming together and saying, ‘We have the power,’” Azure said.
Tribes can take the example of the youth at Turtle Mountain and other tribes and “say we need to come together unitedly” and move forward on issues together, he said. He noted Turtle Mountain and Spirit Lake brought a voting rights lawsuit regarding North Dakota’s legislative redistricting that is ongoing.
“We continue to fight and we continue to move forward,” Azure said.
He said he’s become more connected with other tribal leaders across North Dakota the last two years, especially over developments at the federal level, such as tribal college funding cuts. 
“Sovereignty does not mean that we work alone,” the chairman said. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico environmentalists host ‘people’s public hearing’ to decry Roadless protection removal
description: The United States Agriculture Department’s move to repeal protections for roughly 45 million acres of federal forestland nationally without a public hearing prompted New Mexico environmentalist groups to host their own forums across the state this week, including one Wednesday evening at a basketball gymnasium in Albuquerque’s Barelas neighborhood.
text:
Emmet Yepa, a Jemez Pueblo member and government affairs director of the Semilla Project, leads a prayer Sept. 9, 2026, to kick off a “people’s public hearing” in Albuquerque regarding the federal repeal of the Roadless Rule. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)The United States Agriculture Department’s move to repeal protections for roughly 45 million acres of federal forestland nationally without a public hearing prompted New Mexico environmentalist groups to host their own forums across the state this week, including one Wednesday evening at a basketball gymnasium in Albuquerque’s Barelas neighborhood.
USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins on Aug. 18 announced that the department had formally proposed repealing the 2001 Roadless Rule, which currently protects federal forestland, including roughly 1.6 million acres in New Mexico, from road construction and timber harvesting. She unveiled the proposal last year in Santa Fe during the Western Governors’ Association annual convention.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rollins said the roadless rule has “frustrated” local forest managers and impeded wildfire suppression and prevention, though studies show that wildfires, most of which are human-caused, occur less frequently in protected “roadless” areas than in unprotected forestland.
The USDA’s announcement made no mention of public forums to host public feedback on the proposal. Instead, the department is accepting online comments on the repeal through Sept. 21. 
A USDA spokesperson did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Thursday about why the department is not holding public forums.
Such public forums are typical for USDA rule changes, according to leaders of environmentalist group New Mexico Wild.The proposed enactment of the Roadless Rule 25 years ago featured hundreds of such public forums across the country, according to the Federal Register.
The USDA has also opted to hold public hearings for other recent proposed rule changes, including those about reducing salmonella in poultry products and regulations for South Texas onion growers.
Approximately 80 people, including U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) attended the “people’s public hearing” on Wednesday in Albuquerque, hosted by New Mexico Wild and other local environmentalist groups. Organizers said they would submit testimony from speakers at the hearing to the USDA. Other forums will be held in Pecos, Las Cruces and Silver City in the coming days. 
By the #s: Nearly a quarter of the Gila is protected as ‘roadless.’ Those protections could be nixed

Heinrich told those gathered Wednesday that he attended the public forums in the late 1990s regarding implementing the Roadless Rule. Those forums improved the eventual policy that has remained widely popular for the last 25 years, he said. 
“Let this administration know that it’s not okay not to have a public forum,” Heinrich told attendees. “That public process is at the heart of good democracy, good governance, and we won’t accept anything less than that.”
Other speakers said they were concerned that repealing the rule will increase light pollution, harm wildlife, damage watersheds, impede Indigenous cultural practices and remove the experience of solitude from the outdoors, all in service of profit for timber companies. 
Emmet Yepa is a Jemez Pueblo member and government affairs director at Semilla Project, a youth environmental justice group. He said the Roadless Rule has protected lands sacred to his people in the Santa Fe National Forest.  
“As public lands, these areas should remain protected for the public good rather than open for development,” Yepa said. “We have a crucial opportunity to preserve these ecosystems while they are still healthy. Once lost, they cannot easily be restored.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fazio, Lamont trade blame for tolerating corruption in Hartford, D.C.
description: Democrats embraced Trump's call for GOP candidates to serve as his stand-ins, while Republicans argued Dems tolerate corruption in Hartford.
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Ryan Fazio tried Thursday to refocus Connecticut voters on the ethics and performance of Gov. Ned Lamont and away from President Donald J. Trump’s promise to pay every adult American a $5,000 bonus if Republicans retain control of Congress.
On the morning after Trump urged voters to pretend he is on the ballot in November, Lamont and other Democrats were happy to take his advice, while Fazio did his best to ignore a president hard to ignore and make the case that Lamont is a “laissez-faire” governor tolerant of corruption and malfeasance in Hartford.
“When you are in office, you should take responsibility for what occurs on your watch,” Fazio said at a press conference with Republican legislative leaders and other candidates outside the state Capitol.
He ticked off items he deems disqualifying to Lamont earning a third term: A $250,000 no-bid contract to a former education commissioner; a credit card scandal that toppled a university chancellor; a former administration official convicted of soliciting bribes from school construction contractors and accused of conspiring to cancel an audit into Medicaid fraud; and a federal investigation into legislative earmarks.
“After eight years in office, the governor has had enough time to clean up Connecticut state government, but instead the scandals and corruption has only metastasized,” Fazio said. Recycling a line used by GOP nominee Bob Stefanowski four years ago, Fazio said taxpayers are paying a “corruption tax.”
Less than a mile away on Pratt Street, a brick-lined pedestrian way in downtown Hartford, Democrats reveled at their good fortune in the insistence of an unpopular Republican president staging an unusual midterm convention that abets the Democrats’ goal of defining the midterms as a referendum on Trump.
Luke Bronin, the former Hartford mayor and winner of a Democratic congressional primary that all but assures his election to Congress, set the tone at the Democratic event, embracing Trump’s call from a stage in Dallas to treat Republicans on the ballot this year as stand-ins for him.
“We don’t have to pretend he’s on the ballot,” Bronin said. “He is on the ballot because the truth is that there is not a single Republican who is willing to stand up to Donald Trump, even as Trump’s reckless war drives up costs, as his crazy tariffs drive up costs, as he tries to interfere in our elections through the postal service and in every other way he can, as he takes corruption to levels we have never seen in this country before.”
House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, who has reason to expect that his 102-49 Democratic majority is safe or even likely to grow, was next.
“If you don’t like what you see in Washington, if you don’t like the corruption, if you don’t like the blind loyalty to one person, the team behind me is your team,” Ritter said, standing with Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, Comptroller Sean Scanlon, Treasurer Erick Russell and Attorney General William Tong.
Lamont challenged the credibility of Fazio or any other Republican to question his ethics, given their tolerance of a president whose net worth has grown by more than $2 billion since returning to the White House, while his attorney general signed off on a deal ending the IRS examination of his taxes.
“You’ve got a president who’s added well over a billion dollars to his income on gross malfeasance and corruption. I didn’t hear a word from any of the Republicans, I didn’t hear one word from Ryan Fazio,” Lamont said. “You know what I heard was crickets.”
Gov. Ned Lamont greets House Speaker Matt Ritter, right, and Treasurer Erick Russell at Democratic rally on Pratt Street in Hartford. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org
Fazio, a state senator from Greenwich who had refused to identify his choice for  president in 2016, 2020 and 2024 as he ran for reelection to the Senate in a district where Trump was unpopular, initially declined to comment on the president’s offer of a $5,000 payout to adults if the GOP wins this year.
“I’m not going to comment on every single federal issue that comes about,” he said.
Fazio, who disclosed his votes for Trump once he announced his candidacy for governor, relented when pressed to express an opinion on the promised bonus.
“I think it is a very bad idea,” Fazio said. “I support broad-based middle-class tax relief. I always have. I think that is the path to prosperity, straightforward equality under law, pro-growth, pro-opportunity, pro-affordability. I think what was talked about last night — I only read a short account of it, so I don’t know exactly what it is or any context — it sounds like a very bad idea.”
The confluence of Trump’s speech, Fazio’s press conference and a Democratic rally in which the governor and his ticket hewed to a message of Connecticut’s fiscal stability under Lamont and U.S. economic instability on the president’s watch illustrated the challenge to Republicans in blue states.
Fazio, who is 36 and the youngest gubernatorial nominee in Connecticut since 1990, has significant resources after qualifying for $18 million in public campaign financing, but he is competing for voters’ attention in a time of national and international volatility in a blue state where an incumbent governor has not been defeated at the polls in 72 years.
He suggested he would amplify his message about Lamont as a less-than-engaged governor in advertising, without saying to what degree.
“We’re going to primarily run this campaign to present a vision to the public of change in Connecticut, and that’s not just one talking point, one 30-second ad. It’s about the full body of what’s being proposed,” Fazio said. “Yes, many people are busy in their daily lives. They’re not going to see every little thing we put out. But we want to give the public as much as we can give in order to paint a picture of what new leadership can look like, and transparency and accountability and affordability in the state can look like.”
Fazio is trying to draw voters’ attention to back the inappropriate p-card spending by the former chancellor of Connecticut State Colleges and Universities, who was removed but retained a well-paying faculty job. And the ongoing FBI examination of how Sen. Doug McCrory, D-Hartford, funneled legislative earmarks to Hartford nonprofits. McCrory lost a primary last month.
They also called out Lamont for awarding a $250,000 no-bid contract to Miguel Cardona, Connecticut’s former education commissioner who also served as President Joe Biden’s education secretary. Cardona’s firm was hired by the state to do research and make recommendations for an education workforce commission he also leads as chair.
Lamont expressed no regret for hiring Cardona.
“You say, ‘Oh my gosh, you’ve got a guy who used to be secretary of education leading our [Career] Pathways Commission.’ You’re damn right, because he knows what he’s doing,” Lamont said. “He was commissioner of education for us. He was secretary of education for the president. He knows best practices going on around the country. If you want to give every kid the very best opportunity and pathways, make sure they know what they can do educationally and know what they can do work-wise, he’s the best person for the job.”
Fazio, who has served in the state Senate since 2021, unveiled a plan at the press conference to “crack down” on alleged corruption and misspending in the state government if he is elected in November.
Fazio’s plan includes proposals that would add additional transparency to the legislative earmark process that was utilized by McCrory to direct money to organizations in his district. It also called for strengthening the state’s Freedom of Information Act and implementing new rules policing no-bid contracts, like the one that was awarded to Cardona in July. 
Bob Stefanowski, the Republican who competed with Lamont in 2018 and 2022, failed to make the issue resonate when he, too,  called on Lamont to end the “corruption tax” on Connecticut taxpayers. A difference this cycle is that at least one of the federal corruption cases that Republicans have cited in recent years has now resulted in criminal convictions.
Lamont’s former deputy budget director Konstantinos Diamantis was found guilty last year of soliciting bribes from a pair of construction contractors that he oversaw as the head of Connecticut’s school construction office. Diamantis is set to be sentenced for those crimes next week. 
Fazio and the other Republican leaders at the press conference said that policing and preventing such corruption needs to be a top priority in the next administration. 
“Time and again, we are seeing these scandals popping up in the state of Connecticut,” House Minority Leader Vincent Candelora, R-North Branford, said. “We are on a merry-go-round cycle of corruption.”
Lamont proposed and helped to pass several reforms to the state budgeting process to increase reporting and oversight around legislative earmarks. The governor also fired Diamantis in 2021, prior to his arrest.
Matt Corey, the Republican running for lieutenant governor with Fazio, said Lamont is “reactive” to corruption in the state instead of being “proactive.” And in the case of Cardona’s consulting contract, they noted that the governor personally approved the contract that will provide $250,000 to the former U.S. Education Secretary.
On Pratt Street, the Democrats indicated a willingness to compare their record and stewardship of government with the Republican brand established by Trump. Tong, the Democratic attorney general, said Trump is more than a convenient talking point for Democrats: He is a source of material harm in Connecticut that Fazio ignores.
“He has a tolerance for the harms, the dangers that this president visits upon Connecticut,” Tong said. “This discussion about Trump is not about Washington. It’s about Connecticut. It’s about the damage he’s doing in Connecticut.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Respect Nebraska Voters measure will not appear on Nov. 3 ballot, Nebraska Supreme Court affirms
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed Thursday that a ballot measure seeking to constitutionally make it harder for lawmakers to amend voter-approved laws or add more hurdles to petitioning is too broad and won’t appear on the November ballot. In a 6-1, unsigned 18-page decision, the high court said it agreed with Nebraska Secretary of […]
text:
Advocates for a proposed amendment to the Nebraska Constitution hoped to make it harder for legislators to tweak ballot measures approved by voters. Advocates, including ballot co-sponsor Jo Giles at podium, host a launch event in Omaha. Jan. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed Thursday that a ballot measure seeking to constitutionally make it harder for lawmakers to amend voter-approved laws or add more hurdles to petitioning is too broad and won’t appear on the November ballot.
In a 6-1, unsigned 18-page decision, the high court said it agreed with Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s determination that the Respect Nebraska Voters measure had too many subjects. State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh, a Democrat from Omaha, and former state Sen. Curt Friesen, a Republican from Henderson, had filed the initial objection.
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Photo courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)
Under the Nebraska Constitution, voter-proposed ballot measures can contain only a “single subject,” a standard the Supreme Court has wrestled with in consecutive election cycles.
“We conclude that the initiative violates the single subject rule,” the court wrote. “Accordingly, the secretary does not have a duty to place it on the general election ballot.”
‘Deeply disappointed’
The Respect Nebraska Voters campaign said it was “deeply disappointed” with Thursday’s ruling and noted it had started due to “statewide frustration” over legislative action, particularly around minimum wage increases and promised paid sick leave.
“In the face of increased and sustained attacks on the initiative process and the undermining of both voter-passed legislation and the process itself, this issue is more critical than ever,” campaign leaders said in an unsigned statement.
The statement added that the campaign would continue to engage with Nebraskans to ensure community voices are heard and respected by lawmakers.
Evnen had determined the campaign had at least two different subjects: one, to raise the threshold to amend voter-approved laws from 33 of 49 lawmakers (66%) to 40 of 49 (80%), and the other to add new restrictions on or outright prohibit the Legislature from regulating the petition process in certain cases, also at a new four-fifths threshold.
“These two subjects are not naturally and necessarily connected,” the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office, representing Evnen, wrote in a brief to the court. “The people could protect the initiative process without regulating its results, or vice versa. Neither subject requires the other.”
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The AG’s Office said the “bundling” was meant to improve the electability of the measure and violated the “fundamental limitation” of the single-subject requirement.
Former state Sens. Andrew La Grone and Julie Slama, Dunbar attorneys who submitted the objection to Evnen on behalf of Cavanaugh and Friesen, made similar arguments.
What is a single subject?
Attorneys for the campaign had told the justices that Evnen had a “ministerial duty” to place qualifying measures on the ballot and no discretion to invalidate it on single-subject grounds.
The campaign had also broadly asked the justices to reconsider past reasoning in single-subject cases and apply the same standard to legislative bills and voter-proposed ballot measures. The court refused.
In any case, the campaign attorneys argued, the measure clearly involved a single subject.
“The general subject of the Initiative is limiting the Legislature’s ability to interfere with the people’s reserved power to make laws,” the attorneys wrote in a brief. “And the initiative’s components are naturally and necessarily connected to this subject.”
The attorneys added: “Secretary Evnen’s hair-splitting review of the Respect Nebraska Voters initiative cannot be squared with the text, purpose or application of the single-subject requirement.”
Nebraska Supreme Court Justice Jonathan Papik listens to arguments from attorney Richard Griffin on behalf of the Nebraska Association of Public Employees. Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Justice Jonathan Papik of Omaha, writing in dissent, agreed with the campaign and said he found the measure had one subject. He did not dispute that it would have amended the constitution in more than one way. However, “at a more fundamental level,” he questioned whether the court should continue using its “natural and necessary connection test” to confirm whether an issue constitutes one or more subjects, or consider another standard.
Papik said the Supreme Court has defined a “general subject” with “considerable breadth,” particularly between the legislative context and voter-led ballot measure context.
“In my view, a general subject of the Legislature’s authority over the people’s reserved power to make laws is not any broader than the general subjects of which we have already approved,” Papik wrote in his eight-page dissent.
Papik also dissented in 2020 when the Supreme Court invalidated a proposed constitutional amendment to legalize medical cannabis, finding that version was too broad.
Similar Missouri ballot measure
As part of its arguments, the Respect Nebraska Voters campaign had also asked the Nebraska Supreme Court to take notice of a “remarkably similar lawsuit” from Missouri, dealing with the “Respect MO Voters” campaign.
In that proposal, the Missouri Constitution would be amended to make the initiative and referendum process a “fundamental right,” prohibit the Legislature from weakening those powers and prohibit the Missouri Legislature from changing voter-approved laws or reimplementing voter-rejected laws without approval of at least 80% of lawmakers in the two houses.
In Nebraska’s one-house Legislature, the 80% requirement would not apply to recent voter-repealed laws. There have been two recent cases: outlawing the death penalty, which was reversed in 2016, and funding a state program to cover some private school attendance costs, which was reversed in 2024.
On Sept. 3, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the Missouri issue was a single subject and that all provisions “relate to the single overarching subject of ‘protecting Missouri citizens’ constitutionally reserved lawmaking power.’”
Evnen’s deadline to certify the fall ballot is Friday. The general election is Nov. 3.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Brownsberger edges Lander by 35 votes after Senate race recount
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service and Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: The results conclude a nail-biting primary race for the Suffolk and Middlesex District, which became a proxy war over voter dissatisfaction with the Beacon Hill status quo and a test of Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's political prowess.
text:
SENATE PRESIDENT PRO TEMPORE William Brownsberger of Belmont has narrowly won his reelection bid following tense recounts that saw him capture a 35-vote lead over challenger Daniel Lander of Boston.
The results conclude a nail-biting primary race for the Suffolk and Middlesex District, which became a proxy war over voter dissatisfaction with the Beacon Hill status quo and a test of Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s political prowess after Brownsberger helped quash her tax reclassification push in 2024. Brownsberger was the highest-ranking lawmaker facing a primary challenge this cycle, and there is no Republican candidate on November’s general election ballot.
Last Thursday, Wu-backed Lander was leading by three votes — 12,132 to Brownsberger’s 12,129, according to unofficial tallies from the Tuesday primary. By Friday afternoon, Brownsberger was up by 34 votes. Both candidates filed petitions for district-wide recounts, which are permitted in races with a margin of victory of less than 0.5 percent of total votes cast.
Brownsberger, joined by a large crew of senators, closely monitored the recount underway at Boston City Hall on Wednesday. The Suffolk and Middlesex Senate district includes western neighborhoods of Boston, parts of Cambridge, and surrounding communities of Belmont and Watertown.
Unofficial Boston counts had shown Lander with 5,135 votes to Brownsberger’s 3,373. After the recount, Lander had 5,131 votes to Brownsberger’s 3,369, according to the Boston Election Department. City election officials did more work Thursday, after the Lander campaign requested an additional review of absentee and vote-by-mail ballot materials.
In Belmont, Brownsberger’s hometown, certified counts initially showed the incumbent senator at 4,010 votes compared to Lander’s 1,809.
Altogether, Brownsberger picked up one vote in the recount from the most recent unofficial tally, ending with 35 votes more than his challenger.
Brownsberger’s election night watch party at Donohue’s Bar and Grill in Watertown captured the drama of the race. He told supporters at one point, “Not looking too good tonight,” according to the Harvard Crimson. About an hour later as the results turned in his favor, Brownsberger declared, “We’re actually up by a [expletive] thousand right now.”
In a statement about the recount results, Lander congratulated Brownsberger and said his own campaign showed “this district is hungry for change.”
“While this race did not end as we’d hoped, I am so deeply proud of the campaign we built. I know we have woken up the State Senate and sent a message loud and clear that the days of delay and inaction must end now,” Lander said. 
He promised to continue to be “shoulder to shoulder” with those fighting the Beacon Hill establishment “every single day over the next two years.” 
“To hold our State Senate accountable, and to fight to build a more just Massachusetts: where everyone can afford a home in the communities they love; where no immigrant is afraid to walk down our streets; and where families can thrive,” he said. “This race has already shaken up the broken status quo. From Beacon Hill and beyond, we have put our State Senate on notice.”
The statement concludes, “Our work is not finished. We will fight on for the Massachusetts we deserve, because big dreams will never die.”
Senate President Karen Spilka released a statement on both the specific Suffolk and Middlesex District race, and the primary cycle more broadly. 
She congratulated those who won election, and said she wanted “to particularly congratulate Senators Will Brownsberger and Nick Collins on their victories. Will and Nick are deeply respected members of the Senate who have earned the trust of their colleagues through years of hard work, principled leadership and a commitment to the people they represent. I’m proud to call them colleagues and friends, and I’m grateful that they will continue bringing their experience, independence and leadership to the Senate.”
Spilka also congratulated Persis Yu, the one successful challenger who ousted a sitting senator during the primary, as well as two candidates who won open seats, Reps. Erika Uyterhoeven and Kate Lipper-Garabedian. 
She thanked Sen. Mike Rush, whom Yu ousted in her primary campaign waged from the left. 
“I want to thank my friend and colleague Senator Mike Rush for his many years of dedicated service to the Senate, to the people of his district, and our country. Mike has been a tireless advocate for veterans, working families and his communities, and an invaluable member of our leadership team. I am deeply grateful for his friendship, his service and everything he has contributed to this institution,” Spilka said. 
Her final message was for the Legislature to now move on from the primaries. 
“There was a great deal of time, money and political energy spent this year trying to remake the Senate,” Spilka said. “Voters had their say. I’m proud of the members of this Senate, and I think the results speak for themselves. Now it’s time to put the primary campaign politics behind us.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Former EPA officials warn of health risks from data center pollution
description: Former federal environmental officials are sounding an alarm in a new report about potential health impacts from data center pollution amidst what they see as a breakdown in oversight.
text:
An explosion of data center facilities, including the one pictured here in northeast Oregon on May 18, have been built along the Columbia River Gorge during the last few years. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Former federal environmental officials are sounding an alarm in a new report about potential health impacts from data center pollution amidst what they see as a breakdown in oversight. 
The Environmental Protection Network, a nonprofit organization made up of current and former Environmental Protection Agency staff and leadership, released its report Thursday on the hidden health costs of artificial intelligence data centers. 
The report said that as AI expansion drives demand for electricity to power the data centers, an increasingly weakening EPA is unprepared to manage the increase in pollution that comes with it.
“This massive AI buildout can have enormous consequences for America’s health,” Dr. Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and former EPA assistant administrator, said in a media briefing on the report’s release. “At the very same time, EPA is touting its efforts to weaken or reconsider safeguards designed to protect people from harmful pollution.”
The report cited health figures from a 2026 study by scientists at University of California Riverside and California Institute of Technology that estimated data center-related air pollution could impose roughly $11.7 billion to $20.9 billion in annual public-health costs by 2028. 
The research also estimated that, under a rapid-development scenario of AI data center expansion, pollution from power sources generating electricity for the centers would contribute to roughly 600,000 asthma cases and 1,300 premature deaths.
The Environmental Protection Network report paralleled the academic study with more than 30 different federal actions that the group says increase pollution-related health risks as data centers expand. The actions include narrowing environmental reviews for approved projects, moving to end citizen-led pollution lawsuits and changing the minimum public participation requirements in the process to grant pollution permits. 
“Public involvement in decision making is not just red tape. People are showing up at data center meetings because they want, and they deserve, a voice in the decisions that affect where they live and what they breathe,” said Walter Mugdan, a former EPA deputy regional administrator. Mugdan spent 48 years in his role working for the federal agency. 
“The government should be opening those doors, not closing them,” he added. 
The Environmental Protection Network’s report reiterated that its members don’t view increased health risks from data center pollution as an inevitable consequence of AI expansion. Before President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, “stronger pollution safeguards, planned fossil-fuel plant retirements and expanding cleaner power were on track to constrain additional pollution from rising demand,” the report states.
But when paired with current federal policies removing pollution safeguards and fast-tracking permitting for air and water quality control, it’s easier to “keep more-polluting sources of power online or add new ones while weakening many safeguards,” according to the report. 
“When you don’t have tough permitting or enforcement, you are not incentivizing people to do the right thing,” Goldman said.
The report calls on the federal government to restore pollution safeguards, such as requiring power plants that supply data centers with electricity to manage their pollution, properly permit and monitor on-site power generation at data centers and rebuild the EPA’s scaled-back enforcement division to ensure laws are followed. 
The Environmental Protection Network has calculated Trump administration staffing cuts across the EPA have affected roughly 25% of its workforce, which totaled more than 16,000 before January 2025.

title: Missouri Supreme Court finds Denny Hoskins “was in contempt” over congressional maps
description: The Missouri Supreme Court on Thursday found Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt for directing local election officials to use an illegal congressional map, but ultimately ruled he remedied the contempt by reversing his directive. The unusual proceedings Thursday were the first of their kind in living memory. The judges brought a statewide elected [[...]
text:
Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, right, speaks to reporters Thursday after the Missouri Supreme Court found Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, center, "was in contempt" for ordering use of an illegal congressional map. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)The Missouri Supreme Court on Thursday found Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt for directing local election officials to use an illegal congressional map, but ultimately ruled he remedied the contempt by reversing his directive.
The unusual proceedings Thursday were the first of their kind in living memory. The judges brought a statewide elected official in to answer for his actions that violated the court’s orders.
The court brought Hoskins in twice: In the morning to hear arguments on whether it should find him in contempt, and in the afternoon to find out what he had done in response.
Chief Justice W. Brent Powell delivered the verdict at the end of the afternoon hearing, finding that “the secretary was in contempt of its Sept. 3, 2026, order, enjoining him from the implementation, utilization, and mandating of the of the use of the congressional district districting map (passed in 2025) for the November 2026 general election.”
 By sending out an email Thursday afternoon to local election officials, and a public statement that the map drawn in 2022 would be used for this year’s elections, Powell said “the secretary has therefore purged himself of said contempt.”
The ruling comes just two days short of the anniversary of a state Senate vote that passed a redistricting map intended to tilt this year’s congressional election in the 5th District to Republicans. That vote triggered the events that brought Hoskins before the court on Thursday.
Missourians will see a referendum on the map as Proposition A on the Nov. 3 ballot, where a “yes” vote will be to keep the map and a “no” vote will be to reject it. And the election will be held in the districts previous used, which is expected to return six Republicans and two Democrats to the U.S. House of Representatives.
This story will be updated.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Weld County commissioners approve permit for Global AI data center
description: The Weld County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously Wednesday to allow the development of a new data center by an artificial intelligence infrastructure company. The 5-0 vote approved the zoning for a proposal from Global AI to create a 41-acre data center in an unincorporated area of the county near Windsor. It could become the […]
text:
Global AI is set to create a data center at the former Carestream Health property at 2000 Howard Smith Avenue W in Weld County. (Screenshot from Google Maps) The Weld County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously Wednesday to allow the development of a new data center by an artificial intelligence infrastructure company.
The 5-0 vote approved the zoning for a proposal from Global AI to create a 41-acre data center in an unincorporated area of the county near Windsor. It could become the biggest data center in the state. The decision came after a daylong hearing that included hours of public comment, mostly in opposition to the project.
“It is incompatible with future development. People do not want to live next to data centers,” said Marc Savela, the senior vice president of development at the Broe Real Estate Group. “This application ignores the fact that 600 acres of undeveloped land in the county immediately west to the site is planned and zoned for 2,000 residential units. Global AI has ignored our planned residential development. They have downplayed the impact of data centers.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Planning Manager Angela Snyder told commissioners that the county received over 400 written public comments about the proposal, with concerns ranging from water and electricity demand that could impact household use, environmental impact and worries about noise. People worried about Global AI’s ability to meet its need for electricity and water, though Global AI said Poudre Valley Rural Electric Association is prepared to deliver 35 megawatts of power and presented them a “will-serve” letter. The data center is expected to start at 27.5 megawatts during its first phase.
Local governments in Colorado enact moratoriums on data center development

“(The PVREA letter) doesn’t estimate or allocate the power that is needed, contains only a commitment to provide power for three years and it does not describe how that power can be physically delivered to the site,” attorney Hugh Gottschalk with Windsor Renewal said.
Global AI aims to have a capacity of 1 gigawitt in its network by 2029, according to the company’s website.
The board agreed a new data center was a proper reuse of the former Carestream Health site, which is already zoned for light industrial use. The county’s planning commission voted on Sept. 1 that the plan met the approval criteria, setting the stage for the commissioners to vote on the “Use by Special Review” permit required for projects with a bigger impact on the community.
“The community concerns have caused us to take the time to dig really deep into this topic,” Commissioner Lynette Peppler said, detailing how she overcame anxieties over water use, electricity consumption and noise levels through site visits and research. “I may very well have one of these as my next door neighbor. I live next to an industrial center. We have put these guidelines in place with citizens in mind.”
Global AI will have to use a closed-loop cooling system as a condition of the permit’s approval, and that initial water fill will be about 65,000 gallons with an annual top off of about 6,500 gallons. The company will also need to limit noise to already-established ambient levels around the site, and it will need to secure a bond to cover decommissioning costs.



Quotation







When you talk to anybody who develops aerospace or military applications, AI is absolutely essential in the way they move forward and do business. We want to be friendly to those uses.


– Scott James, chair of Weld County commissioners


David Foster, an attorney who represented Global AI, said the data center would operate at around 65 decibels and only exceed that in emergency situations that require the use of generators. A typical rock concert hits around 100 decibels.
Global AI bought the 438-acre property for about $15.6 million last December. It has eight buildings, and Global AI’s Chief Operating Officer Michael Cadigan said the first data hall could be operational later this year.
“When I toured the complex in Weld County, it reminded me immediately of our complex in New York — how well it was built, how the infrastructure was in place,” he said. “We know how to take that facility, which people have driven by for years, and bring it back to life in a responsible way.”
The approval comes as other local governments in Colorado enact moratoriums on data centers, and a few months after competing bills about the issue in the state Legislature died. Meanwhile, Colorado Springs is set to consider a major data center project during a hearing next week.
Global AI has one operational data center in New York and three others under contract. The company estimates that the new project will bring about 1,500 construction jobs and 200 long-term jobs to the county.
“I think this is a perfect place to put a use like this,” Scott James, chair of the county commissioners, said. “It repurposes an industrial facility that has been vacant for years. It will spur economic activity — granted, not to the level (Eastman Kodak) once held, but to a certain job level.”
“AI is necessary to what we do at this point moving forward in our society, whether we want to rage against it or not,” he said. “When you talk to anybody who develops aerospace or military applications, AI is absolutely essential in the way they move forward and do business. We want to be friendly to those uses.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Details of Oklahoma lawmaker’s alleged misconduct, recommended action to be made public later
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The House Rules Committee set a meeting date in two weeks to publicly discuss allegations of misconduct against an Oklahoma lawmaker for the first time since they came to light over a month ago.  The committee deliberated behind closed doors for about eight hours on Tuesday and five on Thursday about investigations […]
text:
Reps. Andy Fugate, D-Oklahoma City, left, and Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, right, speak to members of the media at the state Capitol on Sept. 10, 2026, after a closed-door meeting of the Rules Committee where they discussed allegations of a lawmaker's misconduct. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The House Rules Committee set a meeting date in two weeks to publicly discuss allegations of misconduct against an Oklahoma lawmaker for the first time since they came to light over a month ago. 
The committee deliberated behind closed doors for about eight hours on Tuesday and five on Thursday about investigations into Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, who House leadership said has been accused of “improper behavior” by House staff. 
Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, listens to the State of the State Address on Feb. 2, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
The details of the allegations or recommendations have not been made public, but are expected to be disclosed during the committee’s planned Sept. 24 meeting. 
Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, who chairs the committee, said the meeting date was set for two weeks from now because “that’s when we can get everybody together.” He said they were investigating Williams’ “workplace behavior.”
“After thorough discussion and consideration of the information presented to the committee, we have reached an agreement on recommendations to present to the (House) Speaker,” Osburn said. “Those recommendations will be taken up in an open meeting of the House Rules Committee on Sept. 24th at 9 a.m.”
Osburn did not answer other follow up questions from the media or say why the committee couldn’t publicly release the recommendations Thursday. 
He previously said a full House vote would be needed to take action on most recommendations, which could range from no action to expulsion. 
Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Oklahoma City, who is a member of the committee, said after Thursday’s meeting that “everyone brought their A-game.” 
“I would like to thank the Speaker for the hearings,” he said. “He took a bold step. He acted swiftly when he was first informed about these allegations. He took them very seriously.”
Fugate did not say what allegations against Williams were, but thanked the committee chair for promoting “open and honest discussion” in their review of the situation. 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, informed lawmakers in July that Williams was being investigated by a private, third party law firm following allegations of “improper behavior” toward chamber staff and that an internal HR investigation found “potential misuse of state resources.” 
He charged the Rules Committee with reviewing the findings of the investigations and taking any necessary action. Hilbert also suspended Williams from his committees and moved his office at the Capitol.
Williams previously told a KFOR reporter that he was told not to publicly discuss the allegations and that he didn’t remember what all the claims were, but said they weren’t sexual in nature. He has denied any wrongdoing.

description: It  looks like another round of health insurance premium increases for millions of Floridians who get their insurance through the federal health care makretplaces. text:
http://teekid.com/istockphoto/banner/banner3.jpgIt  looks like another round of health insurance premium increases for millions of Floridians who get their insurance through the federal health care makretplaces.
Twelve Affordable Care Act participating insurers submitted for rate increases in the coming year, data published by KFF show.
AmeriHealth Caritas Florida filed for the largest increase, 39.14%. By contrast, Centene Venture Co. Florida filed for the smallest increase, at 3.87%.
The rates, filed in the spring, haven’t yet been finalized. They are proposed changes. The Florida Office of Insurance Regulation will review and approve final rates for the plans.
With 12 carriers filing rates with the OIR for policy year 2027, Florida residents relying on the healthcare marketplace for their coverage will have fewer choices than they did this year.
A  comparison of OIR-posted information against the KFF data indicates that Ambetter Health of Florida Inc., Cigna Healthcare of Florida, Community Care Network, Molina Healthcare, and Sunshine State Health Plan Inc. will no longer offer plans in the Florida market.
However, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Florida, which didn’t participate in the healthcare marketplace this year, return for 2027.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Florida has led the nation in the number of people enrolling in “Obamacare” plans since they became available through the federal healthcare exchange.
The Sunshine State also lead the nation in the number of people who fell off Obamacare plans last year after enhanced premium tax credits that helped lower the costs of the polices expired. The subsidies were at the center of partisan impasse last year that led to a government shutdown.
An AP analysis of Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services data shows that 442,785 Florida residents who had health insurance coverage through an Obamacare plan in 2025 were uninsured in 2026.
While Florida saw the largest drop in terms of number of people, percentage-wise there was a 10.3% reduction in enrollment.
Ohio saw the largest dip in Obamacare enrollment between 2025 and 2026 at 32.4%.
Democratic senatorial candidate state Rep. Angie Nixon, has been criticizing her opponent, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, and Sen. Rick Scott while on the stump this week for their healthcare policies, including allowing the enhanced premium tax credits expire.

There are 276 insurers in 50 states and the District of Columbia participating in the healthcare marketplaces for policy year 2027, according to the KFF analysis.
KFF reports that the companies submitted premium changes for the 2027 policy year ranging from -1% to 54%.
Most of the carriers (63%) proposed changes of between 10% and 25%.
The KFF analysis measurers a premium increase as the enrollment-weighted average rate change across all of the policies within a state (bronze, silver, gold, and platinum plans).
Open enrollment for policy year 2027 coverage begins Nov. 1  and ends Dec. 15 for coverage effective Jan. 1, 2027.

name: VTDigger
title: Carbon credits are a lifeline for Vermont’s working forests
description:
As land costs rise and mill closures squeeze traditional revenue, carbon credit programs offer landowners a new way to keep working forests intact and in the family.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Carbon credits are a lifeline for Vermont’s working forests.
text:
This commentary is by Jessica Bakowski, the northeast regional forester for Chestnut Forest Carbon Works. 
As a professional forester living and working in northern Vermont, I’ve spent more than a decade helping landowners navigate the opportunities and challenges of long-term forest stewardship. Across New England, one question comes up repeatedly: How do we keep forests healthy and ensure they stay in the family for generations?
In Vermont, forests are more than a scenic backdrop. They support the state’s maple industry, protect clean water, provide wildlife habitat and fuel recreation and tourism economies central to many rural communities. Approximately 80% of Vermont’s forests are privately owned, placing landowners at the forefront of conservation and management.
Yet these forests face growing pressures. Rising land values, parcelization, second-home development and the complexities of transferring land to the next generation can make long-term ownership increasingly difficult. For many families, the challenge is compounded by the loss of regional mills and other market pressures that have reduced traditional revenue streams from working forests. As large forest tracts are divided into smaller parcels, keeping forests intact and actively managed becomes more challenging.
While there is no single solution, improved forest management carbon projects are emerging as a practical and complementary economic tool that can help landowners generate income while supporting long-term forest stewardship.
Climate-smart forestry is not a new concept in Vermont. For generations, landowners and foresters have managed northern hardwood forests with a long-term perspective, maintaining healthy sugar maple stands, protecting high-quality trees and promoting species diversity.
What is new is that carbon markets can now compensate landowners for many of these same practices.  

READ MORE

When landowners enroll in a carbon project, they commit to managing their forest in ways that increase their trees’ ability to store carbon through natural processes. In practice, this often means extending harvest rotations, retaining larger trees, maintaining healthy stocking levels and encouraging forest conditions that support productivity and resilience. Carbon projects also evaluate surrounding enrolled lands and regional harvest pressures to establish a baseline of likely forest management, helping quantify the additional climate benefits generated through these long-term commitments.
In Vermont’s northern hardwood forests, spruce-fir and mixed hardwood stands, these practices can deliver measurable climate benefits while supporting forest health. For many landowners, carbon projects provide an opportunity to be rewarded for conservation-focused management approaches that already reflect a working forest landscape. 
Owning forestland is rewarding, but it is not inexpensive. Property taxes, road maintenance, invasive species management and habitat improvements all require ongoing investment. At the same time, markets for lower-grade wood and pulpwood have become less predictable as mills have consolidated or closed across parts of the Northeast.
Carbon project income can help offset ownership costs and provide greater flexibility when making management decisions. It can also help families navigate succession planning challenges that might otherwise lead to subdivision or sale. For many Vermont forest owners, this additional source of revenue may help keep forests intact, reducing pressure to fragment land while supporting local ownership and active management.
Vermont’s forests are already experiencing the effects of changing conditions, including more intense storms, invasive pests such as emerald ash borer and hemlock woolly adelgid, and emerging threats like beech leaf disease.
Practices commonly supported through carbon projects, including longer harvest rotations, retention of larger trees and maintenance of species diversity, can help forests better withstand these challenges. Forests with a diversity of ages and species are generally better able to recover from disturbance and continue providing ecological and economic benefits over time.
One lesson I’ve learned throughout my career is that conservation works best when stewardship and economics support one another. While carbon projects are not the right fit for every property, they offer many Vermont landowners a practical way to align long-term forest management with financial sustainability. By supporting forest health, strengthening resilience and helping families keep land intact across generations, carbon projects can play an important role in ensuring Vermont’s working forests remain healthy, productive and locally owned for decades to come.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Carbon credits are a lifeline for Vermont’s working forests.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s US House candidates clash over Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions
description: The two candidates for South Dakota’s lone U.S. House seat expressed opposing views this week about President Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in voting.  Democratic nominee Nikki Gronli criticized Republican nominee Marty Jackley’s support for Trump’s actions. “This proposal flies in the face of our long tradition of running secure, accessible electi[...]
text:
South Dakota's 2026 nominees for U.S. House are Republican Marty Jackley, left, and Democrat Nikki Gronli. (Photos by South Dakota Searchlight)The two candidates for South Dakota’s lone U.S. House seat expressed opposing views this week about President Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in voting. 
Democratic nominee Nikki Gronli criticized Republican nominee Marty Jackley’s support for Trump’s actions.
“This proposal flies in the face of our long tradition of running secure, accessible elections, and our local election officials do an excellent job,” Gronli said in a news release. “They don’t need Marty Jackley helping Washington interfere with the way South Dakotans vote.”
Trump plan would bar millions of Americans from voting by mail, states tell Supreme Court

Gronli and Jackley, the state’s attorney general, are running for the seat being vacated by Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson. He ran unsuccessfully for the Republican nomination for governor in the June primary election.
Jackley, along with some other Republican attorneys general, has intervened in litigation to support a Trump executive order that gave rise to a Postal Service rule restricting mail-in voting. Among other things, the rule prohibits the Postal Service from delivering ballots to registered voters whose citizenship has not been verified by a Department of Homeland Security database. 
A federal judge has blocked the order as an unconstitutional intrusion into states’ management of elections, but the Trump administration is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn that ruling.
In response to South Dakota Searchlight questions about Gronli’s criticism, Jackley said in a statement that he is supporting Trump’s action to “prevent sending mail-in ballots to individuals who are not citizens or registered to vote.”
“I want all eligible Americans to be able to legally vote in American elections,” Jackley said, in part. “My opponent’s desire to send a ballot to someone not registered to vote opens the door to election fraud.” 
Advance voting for the Nov. 3 general election begins Sept. 18 in South Dakota, including mail-in voting and walk-in voting at local election offices.
