name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ACLU lawsuit seeks release of Hartford immigration court data
description: The ACLU-CT is arguing Americans should have the right to request and quickly receive certain immigration court data.
text:
The Connecticut chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union, or ACLU-CT, filed a federal lawsuit on Wednesday alleging that the Hartford immigration court is withholding access to “basic immigration court records.”
The lawsuit names U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and the chief immigration judge for the Hartford court, Angela Munson.
According to the suit, ACLU-CT requested all docket numbers and case captions — a line at the top of a court document that identifies basic information like the names of the parties involved — for May 2026 through July 2026. It also requested all “in absentia” removal orders, which are the orders of deportation made when people with pending immigration cases do not show up for court. The organization said it requested the information twice and did not receive a response.
The ACLU-CT claims in the legal complaint that such information should be available under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and should not require going through the Freedom of Information Act process to obtain.
The FOIA request process gives the government the right to withhold certain information for a variety of reasons. It can take a state or federal department months to comply with a request. Part of the purpose of the lawsuit, according to ACLU-CT, is to get such information contemporaneously to see what is happening inside the courts in close to real time, rather than waiting for months.
Dan Barrett, legal director for the ACLU-CT, said that while the public can attend court hearings and see the day’s docket, that is not a practical way for people to access that information and get a broad picture of what’s going on. For example, when people are being removed in absentia or to a third country, what are the details of their cases and why are they being removed? 
The lawsuit seeks a declaration from the United States District Court that “the Immigration Court is bound by the First Amendment right of public access,” and seeks to prohibit Blanche and Munson from blocking the ACLU’s records requests. 
Information such as full names is not normally provided via FOIA, according to Barrett. Such information is usually denied on the grounds of privacy.
A request for comment from the Department of Justice was not immediately returned.
The case has the potential to set legal precedent, which could have an impact elsewhere in the country, Barrett said.
The request, had it been satisfied, might have provided the ACLU with a comprehensive look at who is going through the immigration court system at a time when caseloads are growing astronomically. 
But release of the data could also raise a number of questions about privacy and safety, issues that have been top of mind for Connecticut officials. Late last year, state lawmakers passed a bill that prevents public agencies, including schools, from sharing an individual’s address, hours of work, public agency appointments or “any other information that provides the date, time or place where such individual may be located.” The bill was in response to federal officials’ requests for state-level data related to programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the potential for its use for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement action.
Also, some immigration cases involve people seeking asylum because they are being persecuted by a foreign government and releasing a person’s full name could be considered sensitive or even dangerous. 
Barrett said the group isn’t seeking for information about individuals in immigration court to be proactively published in a database, the way information for criminal cases can be accessed via online databases. He said rather that the ACLU-CT is arguing Americans should have the right to request and quickly receive such information without a FOIA request. 
He said that, as in a judicial court, anyone with concerns about their safety could move to seal relevant information. “Even better, a court rule could presumptively seal certain things automatically. Both the state and federal trial courts have such rules — for example, names of minors, and birthdates or SSNs of anyone.  Those rules would be just fine from the First Amendment’s perspective.”
Barrett said that he expected that should a ruling allow for access to such information, the immigration court will adopt a practice of automatically sealing the names of asylum applicants and other sensitive information.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on Tuesday tried to drive attention to the issue of in absentia orders by speaking with media after attending immigration court in Hartford. Blumenthal said he attended court to get a “snapshot of what seems to be purposeful chaos in the immigration court.”
Blumenthal said many people failed to appear for court on Monday, in some cases likely because they were not given adequate notice. If they fail to appear in court they can be ordered removed from the country “in absentia.”
“It is purposeful because it is due to lack of staff, reduction in numbers of judges, a system that is running amok and doing injustice,” he said. “And it is intentional injustice designed to deport as many people as possible as quickly as the system is able to do it, regardless of the merits of these cases.”
Currently, case-level immigration court information is available through the Executive Office for Immigration Review, a division of the Department of Justice that releases data regularly. While the releases do not include identifying information like the respondent’s name, the information released on the case itself is robust. These datasets include, among dozens of other fields, case outcome, respondent birth year, nationality and primary language, relief applied for, and if the most recent proceeding was an in absentia hearing.
This year, more than 99.8% of cases decided in Hartford with in absentia rulings have resulted in a removal order, according to immigration court data requested by the Deportation Data Project.
A CT Mirror analysis Hartford immigration court data found that both this year and especially this summer, a higher percentage of cases were closed in absentia, where the respondent did not show up to their final court date. This almost always end in a removal order, according to the analysis.
In May alone, respondents in more than 90% of cases closed that month did not show up to their court date. 
On the whole, fewer people are showing up to Hartford’s immigration court this year. From January to August 1, more than 79% of cases out of the court were marked in absentia at a final hearing. And 2025 saw the next-highest in absentia rate in at least 10 years, second to 2026, with 41% of respondents not showing up to their last court date in Hartford.
“All too often, we have focused on the detention of people, the seizure of people, which needs attention,” Blumenthal said, “but there’s also a kind of behind-the-scenes set of procedures here that also deserves attention. The basic infrastructure of the justice system is failing, and it is intentional and purposeful, designed to simply achieve deportations as quickly as possible, regardless of what evidence there may be to support people staying here.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Federal appeals court upholds Oklahoma HB 1775 but narrows its meaning
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A federal appeals court has upheld and limited the interpretation of a controversial Oklahoma law impacting public school teaching on race and gender. In a split decision Wednesday, the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals decided House Bill 1775 appropriately bars Oklahoma public schools from teaching certain discriminatory concepts as if they are[...]
text:
A classroom sits empty at Mayo Demonstration School in Tulsa Public Schools on April 8, 2024. The Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld an Oklahoma law banning certain race and gender concepts from being taught in public schools. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A federal appeals court has upheld and limited the interpretation of a controversial Oklahoma law impacting public school teaching on race and gender.
In a split decision Wednesday, the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals decided House Bill 1775 appropriately bars Oklahoma public schools from teaching certain discriminatory concepts as if they are facts. The decision overturned a 2024 preliminary injunction from a U.S. district judge in Oklahoma City federal court, who had blocked a few portions of the law for vagueness.
A group of Oklahoma students, teachers, college professors and activists who sued to overturn the 2021 law contended HB 1775 is overly vague and unconstitutionally censors classroom discussions. 
The law prohibits schools from requiring or making part of a course concepts such as one race being superior to another race, that individuals bear responsibility for past actions by others of their race or sex, and that students should feel discomfort or guilt over their race or sex.
Schools face a downgrade to their accreditation and teachers risk a certification penalty for violating HB 1775.
To violate the law, a teacher would have to present the banned concepts as fact, Tenth Circuit judges Gregory A. Phillips and Harris L. Hartz decided in their majority opinion.
“Apart from any prohibited racist or sexist editorializing, teachers remain free to instruct about historical or popular issues, and students remain free to draw their own conclusions,” Phillips wrote.
The third member of the three-judge appellate panel, Nancy L. Moritz, said the law should have been struck down “in full.” The majority opinion “impermissibly rewrites the statute” to clarify an unconstitutionally vague law, she wrote in her dissenting opinion.
The text of HB 1775 doesn’t specify that to violate the law educators must endorse a prohibited statement, Moritz wrote. Teachers could unintentionally make a banned concept part of a course “through discussion, by responding to questions, and in myriad other ways, any of which could violate the law,” she wrote.
Attorneys on both sides of the case celebrated the Tenth Circuit’s majority opinion.
The American Civil Liberties Union, representing the plaintiffs, said the judges’ narrow interpretation of the law means HB 1775 no longer impedes inclusive classroom discussions on race and gender.
“Oklahoma students deserve a nuanced education of race, gender, and American history,” ACLU of Oklahoma legal director Megan Lambert said. “This ruling narrowed Oklahoma’s censorship law out of existence by interpreting it to only prohibit educators from affirmatively encouraging discrimination.”
Megan Lambert, legal director for the ACLU of Oklahoma, speaks outside the William J. Holloway Jr. United States Courthouse in Oklahoma City after a federal court hearing Dec. 4, 2023, over House Bill 1775. Millwood High School teacher Anthony Crawford, left, and other plaintiffs join her. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/ Oklahoma Voice)
Attorney General Gentner Drummond, whose office defended the law, called the decision a first-in-the-nation appellate victory.
“This is a significant win for Oklahoma and affirms a simple principle: every Oklahoma student deserves to be treated as an individual, not defined or divided by race or sex,” he said. “Oklahoma teachers do important work every day, and the court has given them clarity to keep doing it well.”
With the Tenth Circuit decision on the preliminary injunction entered, the case now returns to Oklahoma City federal court.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Crime in Minnesota fell again in 2025
description: Crime in major categories continued to go down in 2025, according to a new report from the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. As in past years, crime is at a multi-decade low, reaching levels Minnesota hasn’t seen since the 1960s. That’s driven largely by a decrease in property crimes — which includes theft and, more rarely, […]
text:
Police block off a road in downtown Minneapolis after a police pursuit of a man on suspicion of homicide. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Crime in major categories continued to go down in 2025, according to a new report from the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension.
As in past years, crime is at a multi-decade low, reaching levels Minnesota hasn’t seen since the 1960s. That’s driven largely by a decrease in property crimes — which includes theft and, more rarely, arson — which are far more common than violent crime and make up the bulk of the crime rate.


Crime falls again in 2024

Violent crime has also been going down in recent years, getting closer to but not yet reaching pre-pandemic levels.
The drop in crime seems to have reduced the salience of the issue this election year, after crime dominated the conversation during the 2020 and 2022 election cycles. Both the pandemic spike in crime and police reform in the wake of the police murder of George Floyd were top of mind for many voters in those years.
Overall, Minnesota has a lower violent crime rate than the national average.
All eight index crimes — serious violent and property crimes that law enforcement agencies use to track crime over time — were lower in 2025 compared to 2024. Both violent crime and property crime dropped 12%.
Minnesota law enforcement reported 130 homicides in 2025, a steep drop from the 172 homicides in 2024. Most homicides were in Hennepin County, which had 70 homicides in 2025, also down from 89 homicides in 2024.


Robbery also dropped significantly, while aggravated assault had a more modest decline. Reports of rape decreased slightly in the state from 2,231 to 2,188 but increased slightly in the seven-county Twin Cities metro area.
In the property crime category, car thefts dropped significantly for a second year in a row; burglary, larceny and arson also went down.
Minnesota law enforcement agencies reported that their officers fired 326 shots in 21 use-of-force incidents in 2025, or 15 shots per incident, wounding 13 people and killing six. Officers accidentally discharged in three other incidents.
Of the 26 subjects of use-of-force by law enforcement, 12 were white, eight were Black, four were American Indian, and two were Asian. Of the 46 officers who used force, 43 were white, two were Asian, and one had race unreported.
In 2024, officers killed 11 people and wounded 11 others with guns.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Bevin appeals jail sentence to Kentucky Court of Appeals
description: Saying a judge has “slammed the door shut and thrown away the key,” a lawyer for former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin is asking the state Court of Appeals to order his immediate release from jail for contempt of court. Bevin, 59, was arrested Sept. 3 and lodged in the Jefferson County jail to serve a […]
text:
Former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin smiles at his arraignment in Jefferson County Court. Judge Angela Johnson sentenced him to 60 days in jail for contempt of court. (Pool photo by Matt Stone of the Louisville Courier-Journal)Saying a judge has “slammed the door shut and thrown away the key,” a lawyer for former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin is asking the state Court of Appeals to order his immediate release from jail for contempt of court.
Bevin, 59, was arrested Sept. 3 and lodged in the Jefferson County jail to serve a 60-day sentence for contempt for failing to produce financial documents a judge had ordered him to provide in an ongoing legal battle with his estranged, adopted son, Jonah Bevin.
Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson had sentenced him for contempt after finding he failed to release all documents she had ordered he produce as part of his divorce case with his ex-wife, Glenna, in which Jonah is seeking support.
Bevin also skipped a July 28 hearing the judge had ordered him to attend in person over the matter. The one-term Republican governor was arrested Thursday while working as an extra on a Christmas movie being filmed at a Bourbon County horse farm. 
Jonah, 19, has alleged the Bevins abandoned him at age 17 at a brutally abusive youth facility in Jamaica and is seeking support for living expenses and education. Jonah is one of four children the Bevins, who have nine children,  adopted from Ethiopia.
Glenna Bevin has testified in court that Jonah was aggressive and threatening as a teen and the couple sought multiple placements and treatment for him.
In sentencing Matt Bevin for contempt Friday, Johnson said he had ignored multiple court orders and opportunities to comply.
“You have done nothing to show the court that you are willing to act in good faith, and I cannot reward that with a reduced sentence or an alternative sentence or some form of relief for you, because you have shown this court that you are not going to do what you’re ordered to do because you don’t think that it should be this way,” she said.
Matt Bevin’s motion filed Sept. 9 by lawyer Jesse Mudd with the appeals court asks for emergency relief for him to be released from jail while it considers his appeal of the contempt finding and sentence.
Bevin already has produced over 1,000 pages of financial documents and, because the case involving his son’s claims for support has been submitted to the judge for a decision there is nothing further he can do to meet requirements of the court, it said.
His continued incarceration, it said, “amounts to nothing more than punishment for his past conduct.”
The appeals court had not ruled on Bevin’s petition by Thursday afternoon.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Sparks fly during town hall debate over property tax-cutting Amendment 3
description: A town hall discussion Wednesday night of the proposed constitutional amendment to reduce homestead property taxes sparked sharp exchanges between two Pinellas County Republicans. The conversation took place in Largo, the third largest city in Pinellas and fourth biggest in the Tampa Bay area with a population of more than 84,000.  City officials caution tha[...]
text:
Largo Fire Rescue members. (Photo via City of Largo's Facebook page)A town hall discussion Wednesday night of the proposed constitutional amendment to reduce homestead property taxes sparked sharp exchanges between two Pinellas County Republicans.
The conversation took place in Largo, the third largest city in Pinellas and fourth biggest in the Tampa Bay area with a population of more than 84,000.  City officials caution that if Amendment 3 passes in November, it would reduce the city’s budget by $10 million in its first year and more than $15 million by its second.
Local governments throughout Florida are conducting similar “community conversations” with the public ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. In other cases, county commissions are holding budget workshops on the potential financial effects if the proposal is approved. In all cases, those officials have to ensure that they are not advocating a policy position.
If Amendment 3 receives the 60% approval required for passage, the proposal would increase the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028, but the portion of property tax bills that pay for schools would be excluded from the increased exemption. The research arm of the Florida Legislature estimates it would reduce revenue by as much as $12 billion annually.
Participating Wednesday were former Pinellas Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes, a noted critic of the proposal, and sitting Pinellas House Rep. Berny Jacques, a strong supporter.
PInellas County Republican Rep. Berny Jacques in Tampa on Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)
Jacques was not originally slated to be there but was included after he wrote a letter to Largo Mayor Woody Brown complaining that including a prominent opponent like Brandes exclusively in a government meeting would give the appearance the city was electioneering on the taxpayer’s dime.
The meeting began with a detailed explanation by Largo officials — including Police Chief Mike Loux and Fire Chief Matt Carpenter — about how the amendment could harm city services. Then Jacques got his first crack at the mic, and he wasn’t forgiving, accusing city leaders of “using public safety as a scare tactic.”
“The evidence is clear that the city was prepared to use taxpayers to tell you, the taxpayer, that a tax cut is bad. And they would have gotten away with it if it wasn’t for a meddling state representative,” Jacques said, generating light applause from the audience.
“And something tells me that they’re still trying to do it, and this is evidenced by the fact that the leaders of City Hall brought forth the chiefs of the two most popular departments of the city to tell you that property taxes, if it’s cut, will somehow harm the things that we care about the most, which is public safety. As if there aren’t any other places where cuts can be had.”
Essential services
Florida House Republicans approved language during the legislative session that would have banned local governments from reducing funding for law enforcement, firefighters, and first responders below the level in either fiscal year 2025-26 or 2026-27, whichever was higher. However, the Senate never approved that proposal and it died during the session.
That’s in part why organizations representing law enforcement have come out in opposition to the measure. In July, the Fraternal Order of Police said Amendment 3 “creates far too much uncertainty about how local governments would continue to fund law enforcement, fire rescue, emergency medical services, and other critical public safety functions. Public safety should never become collateral damage with uncertain fiscal consequences.”
Brandes said  the state needs property tax reform, but argued that Amendment 3 is not the vehicle to get there. He maintains that if the measure becomes law, Florida homeowners will not get the tax cut they are being promised but will have to adapt to a tax shift.
“We’re already seeing this,” he said, noting that the City of St. Petersburg is already considering a special assessment to help pay for fire services that could offset property tax cuts. There is a strong possibility, he said, of new fees on stormwater management, utility charges, and other essential services.
Former Sen. Jeff Brandes addresses reporters ahead of a hearing on the proposed property tax Amendment 3 in the Leon County Courthouse on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
Florida’s Republican leadership in Tallahassee strongly supports the proposal. Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia has gone around the state over the past year calling out local governments for what he sees as “wasteful and excessive spending,” alleging their budgets have exceeded population growth and inflation.
Local officials like Largo City Manager John Curp insist inflation isn’t the best way to gauge the cost of providing certain basic services, citing a 25% increase in fuel prices and the cost of gear for firefighters going up by more than 50%.
Jacques emphasized that local government officials are overplaying how drastic the reductions to their budgets would be. He brought props, displaying a pie chart showing that of all the property taxes Largo takes in, 19% come from homestead taxes, and less than 4% of total revenues.
“They want to use our great men and women in public safety as the chief example, make an example of them, and unnecessarily cut them,“ he said. “That is a choice that they chose to make because they do not have to make it when 80% of funds left to fund critical government functions, public safety being at the top of it.”
‘That’s what makes us a great city’
Brandes interjected.
“So, in your mind, if we say police and fire is totally protected, and EMS is totally protected — all of that is totally protected — all of the cuts from somewhere else? Right? Is that what we’re saying?”
He went on to say that if public safety is taken off the table, then cuts must come from services that people enjoy about living in Largo.
“You love Largo because of the parks and the library and the recreation centers, right? That’s what makes us a great city,” he said, generating applause.
Largo Mayor Woody Brown argued the definition of “public safety” goes beyond police and fire to include the city’s wastewater treatment plant, street and stormwater crews, and building inspectors. The stuff that would be “easiest” to cut are the most popular, he added.
“These aren’t scare tactics — these are reality cuts,” he said.
“As Sen. Brandes said, we will survive, but we will not be the same city. Our residents appreciate our superior services. I mean, it’s in our motto, right? So, we provide superior services that instil community pride. We’d love to keep doing that. If this passes, it would be very difficult if not impossible to continue to service that motto.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Federal judge strikes down Kansas law offering in-state tuition rate to qualified immigrants
description: A federal judge in Kansas blocks use of a 2004 law enabling qualified immigrant students to pay in-state tuition rates at public colleges and universities.
text:
Ryan Kriegshauser, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Kansas, lauded the federal court decision blocking enforcement of a state law granting immigrant students the right to enroll at public colleges and universities at the in-state tuition rate. In this image from June 21, 2024, Kriegshauser addresses the State Objections Board. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A U.S. District Court judge issued an order forbidding enforcement of a bipartisan Kansas law adopted in 2004 that allowed certain immigrant students at public colleges and universities to pay in-state tuition rates rather than higher out-of-state rates.
Beneficiaries of the controversial state statute have been community college or university students who were brought to the United States as children, completed a high school education in Kansas and agreed to seek citizenship while pursing a degree in higher education.
The judge’s injunction takes effect immediately, but it was unclear how it would be implemented on individual campuses across Kansas.
The state law was challenged by the U.S. Department of Justice based on a premise the program violated federal immigration law, incentivized illegal immigration and unconstitutionally discriminated against U.S. citizens.
U.S. District Judge Holly Teeter, a nominee of President Donald Trump, issued a permanent injunction Wednesday night that relied on the Justice Department’s arguments to justify invalidation of the Kansas tuition program.
“The central problem here is that there are United States citizens and nationals who pay full nonresident tuition when an unlawfully present alien is eligible to pay a lower rate on the basis of residence,” the judge said in the decision.
Teeter said state statute was preempted by federal law “because it confers a postsecondary education benefit on an unlawfully present alien based on a state-defined residency conclusion without making that same benefit generally available to United States citizens and nationals regardless of their residence.”
Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach, a longstanding opponent of the tuition statute, collaborated with the DOJ on the legal challenge and jointly proposed a consent judgment blocking the law.
In defense of the state’s tuition statute, Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly sought to intervene and seek dismissal of the lawsuit.
Ryan Kriegshauser, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Kansas, said during a news conference Thursday that the court ruling meant Kansas couldn’t extend in-state tuition benefits to immigrant students without providing the same benefit to U.S. citizens.
“No longer will illegal aliens enjoy the benefit of lower in-state tuition in Kansas,” Kriegshauser said. “This decision has been a long time coming. In fact, I looked at this statute 20 years ago as a law student and a law clerk. It violated the supremacy clause then as it does now.”
Jessica Swonger, staff attorney with the ACLU of Kansas, said the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund and the ACLU of Kansas filed a motion in July to intervene on behalf of students impacted by U.S. v. Kansas.
“This is a disappointing denial of the rights of those most impacted by the current administration’s cruel crusade against students in Kansas to participate in a lawsuit that will directly impact their future,” Swonger said. “The court has allowed the Department of Justice, in collusion with Attorney General Kobach, to slam the door on hardworking Kansas students, even though Kansans have long supported providing all children in our state the opportunity to learn.”
In June, the DOJ filed its complaint against Kansas and endorsed a proposed consent decree to permanently forbid future use of the tuition law.
“Kansas’ unconstitutional and un-American laws should never have been passed in the first place and are prohibited by federal law,” said Brett Shumate, an assistant attorney general in the DOJ’s civil rights division. “The Department of Justice has won on this exact issue in Texas, Oklahoma, Kentucky and Nebraska, and we will take this fight to any states that fail to put American citizens first.”
During the 2026 session of the Kansas Legislature, the House and Senate passed Senate Bill 254 to prohibit people without authorization to be in the United States from receiving state and local public benefits, including in-state tuition at public colleges and universities.
Kelly vetoed the measure and denounced the bill as damaging to the state’s economy and to workforce development. The Republican-controlled Legislature failed to produce two-thirds majorities necessary to override the governor.
“There are many ways that we could, and should, work together to fix this country’s broken immigration system,” Kelly said when she filed the motion to intervene in the lawsuit. “In pursuing higher education, these young Kansans are a net-benefit to our entire state, gaining the education and training needed to be valuable members of our workforce and contribute to our economy.”
In February, Kobach issued a nonbinding legal opinion that concluded the tuition law known as KSA 76-731a conflicted with federal law.
“For years, Kansas universities have been violating federal law by giving in-state tuition rates to illegal aliens, while nonresident U.S. citizens have to pay much more in tuition,” Kobach said. “The governor tried to intervene in this case, because she wanted to continue giving in-state tuition benefits to illegal aliens. With this decision, the court rejected her illogical arguments, and once again, U.S. citizens will be treated better than illegal aliens by Kansas universities.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Conservative business group’s multi-PAC strategy flops as General Assembly incumbents prevail
description: In contrast to the stunning primary day upsets in which Democratic challengers dethroned Rhode Island’s governor and the mayors of Providence and Pawtucket, every sitting state lawmaker seeking reelection won Wednesday night. Incumbents typically hold an advantage, especially in Rhode Island, where the rigor of the job coupled with low pay and a dominant Dem[...]
text:
A concentration of campaign signs for Democratic candidates in Wednesday's primary are shown outside the Swift Community Center in East Greenwich. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)In contrast to the stunning primary day upsets in which Democratic challengers dethroned Rhode Island’s governor and the mayors of Providence and Pawtucket, every sitting state lawmaker seeking reelection won Wednesday night.
Incumbents typically hold an advantage, especially in Rhode Island, where the rigor of the job coupled with low pay and a dominant Democratic party suppresses competition. Nearly two-thirds of the 113 General Assembly seats featured a single candidate this election cycle, with just 13 sitting lawmakers — all Democrats — facing primary challengers (excluding open seat contests).
“It’s very hard to go against General Assembly leadership,” said John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island. “They put a lot of resources into protecting their members.”
But a new political group with an unconventional campaign finance strategy to unseat progressive lawmakers focused more attention on the few contested races by endorsing conservative-minded candidates. The League of RI Businesses champions gun rights, lower taxes and business-friendly policies, and backed a slate of challengers by circumventing the state law capping political action committee donations at $2,000 per candidate per year.
Yet The League’s 40 PAC strategy — one for every city and town plus a statewide organization — and open solicitation of anonymous donations failed to notch any wins on primary night. 
All seven of the Democratic challengers endorsed by The League in state legislative races lost, some defeated by a 50- or 60-point margin.
“Not only did we not win, we just got clobbered,” said Dave Levesque, co-founder of The League. “It’s an embarrassment.”
The problem, as Levesque sees it, is not with The League’s candidates, nor its strategy. Instead, he blamed the voters who sat out the primary despite voicing support for The League’s platform and candidates.
“The people on the left came out and voted,” Levesque said. “The people in the middle and the right didn’t.”
More than 19% of registered voters cast ballots across the state Wednesday, with the highest primary participation since at least 2018, according to preliminary turnout results from the Rhode Island Department of State. A breakdown by political party, and ideological factions within each, was not available. 
Progressive victories in the Providence mayoral and city council races, along with upsets of Pawtucket Mayor Don Grebien, a moderate Democrat, and Gov. Dan McKee, could suggest higher turnout among younger and more left-leaning voters. The League did not intervene in those races — focusing on state legislative seats only — but the more moderate candidates Levesque would have preferred lost anyway.
“That has nothing to do with us,” he said. “The left movement is just strong.”
But the victorious challengers — Helena Foulkes for governor, David Morales for Providence mayor and Adam Greenman for Pawtucket mayor — offer three very different ideologies and backgrounds. What they share, in Marion’s view, is a strong ground game rooted in hyperlocal issues like rent stabilization in Providence, and the Washington Bridge in the governor’s race.
“My big conclusion is that campaigns matter,” Marion said.
Shirley Testa of South Kingstown takes along her grandson Silas as she voted on Primary Day Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, at the South Kingstown Recreation Center in Wakefield. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
Money can’t buy everything 
Money may not be as important, evidenced by Smiley’s substantial spend against Morales in the Providence mayoral race.
While The League promised it could donate up to $1 million per candidate based on its 40 PAC cycle, no one actually got a seven figure boost — because donors didn’t come through. The League received just under $110,000 in donations across its PACs during the primary cycle, according to campaign finance reports.
Levesque estimated 1,000 individual donors contributed.
“You can’t make change on that few people,” he said.
And despite a heavy social media marketing campaign, The League’s messaging did not seem to break through with its target audience of conservative and moderate voters.
“I had people call me [on primary day] who didn’t know about The League,” Levesque said. “The average person isn’t paying attention to us.”



Quotation







Not only did we not win, we just got clobbered. It’s an embarrassment. 


– Dave Levesque, co-founder of The League of RI Businesses


Sen. Alana DiMario, a Narragansett Democrat who beat back League-endorsed challenger Mark Mesrobian in the Senate District 36 primary, offered a different take.
Many of the voters she spoke with during neighborhood door-knocking and campaign events had heard of The League. And their impression was not positive.
“People were aware of how much money was being pumped into my opponent’s campaign, and they did not like that,” she said. 
Campaign finance reports show The League funneled $10,500 into Mesrobian’s campaign leading into the primary. But the entrepreneur and Bonnet Shores Beach Club general manager also secured donations on his own, raising more than double what DiMario brought in during the three months that ended June 30. 
Mesrobian said he made “great inroads” as a first-time candidate and may try again in a future election cycle.
“It’s hard to understand what voters want,” Mesrobian said, adding that he will vote for DiMario in her unopposed general election bid on Nov. 3. 
While Mesrobian proved to be one of The League’s best independent fundraisers, the race for the Senate seat spanning North Kingstown and Narragansett was not even close. DiMario received nearly 72% of the vote, according to preliminary, unofficial results. Lopsided losses resulted for League races in Pawtucket’s Senate District 15, where incumbent Sen. Meghan Kallman led challenger Vanessa Lopez by 40 points; and House District 36 spanning parts of western Rhode Island, where Rep. Tina Spears of Charlestown beat challenger Leah Bosclair by more than 60 points. 
A few matchups were closer. Sen. Ryan Pearson of Cumberland won the Senate District 19 primary against League-backed challenger James Metivier by under 4 points, while Rep. Enrique Sanchez of Providence fended off Santos Javier for the House District 9 seat by a 5-point margin. Both are still outside the window that allows for recount requests. 
Sen. Dawn Euer, a Newport Democrat, secured a 35-point victory over another progressive candidate, Angela Lima, in Wednesday’s primary. Euer is now unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)
More incumbent wins 
Incumbents also prevailed in races outside The League’s scope of influence, though not all were the more progressive choice. Sen. Lori Urso defeated progressive challenger Gena Felix by nearly 20 points in the primary for Pawtucket’s District 8. In Senate District 13, spanning Newport and Jamestown, Sen. Dawn Euer notched a commanding 35-point victory over Angela Lima in a matchup between two progressives.
In several of the open seat races, the progressive choice prevailed, including Providence’s House District 7, where Working Families Party-backed candidate Amy Santiago defeated Providence Councilwoman Jo-Ann Ryan, and Warwick’s House District 22, where Zakary Pereira defeated charter school advocate Janie Lee Segui. In the open House District 32 in North Kingstown, Robert Craven Jr. defeated League-backed candidate Kevin Hoyle for the seat last held by Craven’s father.
But, in the three-way primary for the open seat representing North Kingstown’s House District 31, former Sen. Jim Sheehan got nearly twice as many votes as his progressive opponent, Matthew McCoy, and the more conservative leaning Thomas Menec. The matchup between moderate Democrats Brian Patrick Kennedy and challenger Stephen Moffitt for House District 38 in Westerly and Hopkinton also ended with a win for Kennedy, the senior ranking member of the chamber who has served since 1988.
Despite its lack of success with primary challengers this time around, Levesque said The League is not going away. The group is backing a dozen challengers in the Nov. 3 general election — mostly Republicans but a few independents. And there’s always the next election cycle.
But, the multi-PAC strategy might not be available in two years. Marion is planning to reintroduce legislation next session to close the loophole in state law by explicitly stating that connected PACs are subject to the $2,000 per candidate annual donation limit —- mirroring language in federal campaign finance laws. The bills failed to advance out of committee in both chambers in 2026.
“It’s not designed to protect incumbents, it’s designed to preserve the sanctity of contribution limits, which were really blown to shreds by the creation of a 40-PAC situation,” Marion said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Two Kenai dog walkers plead guilty in Alaska federal court to disrupting fur trapper
description: Two Soldotna residents have pleaded guilty to disrupting a legal fur trapping line in the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge after their dog was caught in a trap. Laura McIndoe and Trafford Evanoff had challenged a pair of citations issued by a Fish and Wildlife Service officer in February 2025 but abandoned their challenge shortly before […]
text:
Fall foliage is seen on Sept. 14, 2017 along the Kenai River in the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge. (Photo by Lisa Hupp/U.S. FIsh and WIldlife Service)Two Soldotna residents have pleaded guilty to disrupting a legal fur trapping line in the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge after their dog was caught in a trap.
Laura McIndoe and Trafford Evanoff had challenged a pair of citations issued by a Fish and Wildlife Service officer in February 2025 but abandoned their challenge shortly before it would have gone to trial. 
Conflicts between dog walkers and fur trappers are not unusual in Alaska, despite widespread efforts to prevent them, but federal court fights are rare, according to a search of U.S. District Court records.
McIndoe and Evanoff — her son — had been scheduled for trial in August, but both changed their “not guilty” pleas and agreed to pay small fines to settle the issue. 
According to the initial citations, a trapper called a Fish and Wildlife Service officer after McIndoe’s dog became caught in one of the trapper’s foothold traps and McIndoe became “very upset and cursed at him, telling him to stay away.”
“He said the woman told him that her sons were in their 30s and big men, and if they see him, they will kill him,” according to an affidavit signed by officer Shay Hurd. 
Two of the trapper’s other traps were destroyed, and the trap that snared the dog was lost. 
According to Hurd’s affidavit, the trapline was correctly marked and permitted.
The Beacon attempted to contact McIndoe and Evanoff through their listed attorneys on Tuesday morning but did not receive a response by Thursday morning.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Several on Saint Francis Hospital’s community board resign
description: The board resignations came after reports of serious patient safety and quality concerns at Saint Francis Hospital, owned by Trinity Health.
text:
Multiple members of a board overseeing Saint Francis Hospital have resigned, according to a spokesperson for the hospital’s parent company, Trinity Health of New England.
The resignations came after reports of serious patient safety and quality concerns at Saint Francis, including an incident in 2026 that left a patient dead.
Trinity Health of New England spokesperson Stephanie Valickis said in a statement that the resignations were from a locally-based body, known as the hospital’s “community board,” which plays a separate role from Trinity Health of New England’s governing board, which oversees all five hospitals in the system. 
Saint Francis Hospital’s community board “serves in an advisory capacity,” Valickis said. 
The chair of that board, John Kinney, who also served on Trinity Health of New England’s governing board, resigned from both positions.
Neither Kinney nor his fellow board members contacted for this story responded to requests for comment. Valickis did not respond to follow-up questions regarding how many board members resigned or their reasons for doing so.
In a statement shared by Valickis, Trinity Health of New England Board Chair Walter Harrison said, “My fellow board members and I have seen the Saint Francis team make real progress over the past several months. We remain confident in Saint Francis Hospital’s future and in its partnership with the leadership team.” 
Trinity Health of New England, which has three short-term acute care hospitals in Connecticut, is owned by Trinity Health, a $25 billion Michigan-based health system that touts itself as “one of the largest not-for-profit, faith-based healthcare systems in the nation.” The organization operates in 23 states and includes more than 90 hospitals across the country.
State Sen. Saud Anwar, D-South Windsor, said he’d spoken with several of the Saint Francis Hospital community board members and was told that an “overwhelming majority” of the board’s 11 members resigned during a meeting on Tuesday. 
Anwar said he understands they resigned over concerns that the parent company, Trinity Health, is not prepared to invest the resources to make necessary improvements to Saint Francis. (Valickis didn’t address reasons for the resignations in her comments to The Connecticut Mirror.)
“It is my understanding that they do trust the leadership of the hospital and the healthcare system in Connecticut, but they are extremely concerned that the leadership is only as good as the amount of funding and investment that Trinity provides,” Anwar said.
Anwar said he thinks the hospital’s characterization of the locally-based body as a “community board” is an attempt to downplay the significance of the resignations. He said he wasn’t aware of the hospital using that term in the past.
A March 2025 announcement from the hospital referred to the group as its “Board of Directors” and did not mention the term “community board.”
On Wednesday morning, a page on the health system’s website titled “Board of Directors” included a list of the board members for Trinity Health of New England Corp., as well as lists of locally-based “directors” and “trustees” for each individual hospital in the system. That page has since been updated to remove the lists for each individual hospital. 
Valickis did not respond to a question about why the page had been updated.
Saint Francis Hospital has in recent years struggled with serious shortcomings when it comes to patient care, records show.
Since January 2023, the hospital has been issued nine findings of “immediate jeopardy” — a situation in which the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services determines that the provider “has placed the health and safety of recipients in its care at risk for serious injury, serious harm, serious impairment, or death.” 
An immediate jeopardy, or “IJ,” is the most serious quality and safety finding CMS can issue to a hospital. In 2026 alone, Saint Francis has received three immediate jeopardy citations. 
The hospital entered into a consent order with the state in September 2024, committing to allow an independent consultant to assess its progress on staffing and safety. That consent order was still in effect as of last month.
The Connecticut Department of Public Health entered into another consent order with Saint Francis in July, which stated that it “remains concerned that prior remediation efforts have not resulted in sustained compliance across all cited areas.”
In recent months, Trinity Health of New England has acknowledged the problems at Saint Francis. In April, the health system replaced its president and CEO with Steven Hanks. Robert Roose was named interim president of Saint Francis Hospital and now serves as president of acute care for the system.
Hanks, who also leads Trinity Health New York, replaced former Trinity Health of New England president and CEO Montez Carter. Roose replaced Valerie Powell-Stafford at Saint Francis.
Both Hanks and Roose are physicians and longtime employees of Trinity Health. The pair signed a full-page ad that appeared in the Hartford Courant on a Sunday in July in which they acknowledged Saint Francis’ lagging performance and pledged to address the problems with safety and quality.
Valickis said in a statement that over $20 million has been spent in the past three months alone for capital investments in Saint Francis’s technology and equipment. During a tour of the hospital last month, Roose said Saint Francis could expect to receive investments from Trinity Health of “tens of millions of dollars every year over the course of the next several years.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Consumer Energy asks state regulators to delay decision on hydroelectric dam sale until November
description: Ahead of Thursday’s meeting of the Michigan Public Service Commission, one of the largest energy companies in the state submitted a notice asking the regulatory body to delay its ruling on whether to allow the sale of 13 hydroelectric dams across the state. Consumers Energy sent a notice to the commission on Tuesday asking the […]
text:
Foote Dam in Iosco County, one of 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Photo from Consumers Energy)Ahead of Thursday’s meeting of the Michigan Public Service Commission, one of the largest energy companies in the state submitted a notice asking the regulatory body to delay its ruling on whether to allow the sale of 13 hydroelectric dams across the state.
Consumers Energy sent a notice to the commission on Tuesday asking the commissioners to hold off on making a final determination at their Thursday meeting. The energy company said they were voluntarily extending the ruling deadline by 60 days, stating their belief that they could find a constructive solution to some of the concerns raised during case proceedings.
The item did not appear on the commission’s Thursday agenda. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In September 2025, Consumers Energy, announced that it planned to sell 13 hydroelectric dams located on the Au Sable, Manistee, Muskegon, Kalamazoo and Grand rivers to Confluence Hydro, a subsidiary of Hull Street Energy, a Maryland-based private equity firm.
While Consumers would sell the dams for a total of $13, Confluence Hydro agreed to provide the energy company with power from the dams through a 30-year power purchase agreement.
Supporters argue that if the dams are not sold, Consumers will be forced to decommission them, which would result in changes to the natural landscape that could harm local property values and recreational opportunities that support local businesses.
However, opponents have raised safety concerns around the decision to sell the dams to an out-of-state private equity firm.
Among those in opposition to the sale is Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who has pointed to the 2020 failure of the Edenville and Sanford Dams. A federal judge determined the dams’ owner, Lee Mueller, and his business, Boyce Hydro, were responsible for the failure and subsequent flooding. 
Attorney General Dana Nessel has also said that Mueller had “completely disregarded imminent threats to the safety and integrity of the dam.”
In a letter to the commission, Whitmer said the agreement between Consumers Energy and Confluence Hydro “does not provide sufficient safeguards to prevent these failures from happening again.” 
“The deal lacks firm, enforceable protections to ensure the dams will be properly maintained and safely retired when they are no longer economical to operate,” Whitmer wrote. “It does not require Hull Street Energy, the parent company, to cover all future repair, accident, environmental, and decommissioning costs, nor does it require adequately funded reserves to cover those expenses.”
While Consumers Energy promised to set aside $270 million to address unforeseen safety concerns, Whitmer said the recently proposed fund was “too little, too late, and too difficult to access.”
In an email to Michigan Advance, Consumers Energy Media Relations Specialist Brian Wheeler explained that the company believes it can address Whitmer’s concerns by engaging with the other groups participating in the case before the Public Service Commission.
“We plan to engage all the parties to the MPSC proceeding,” Wheeler said. “We look forward to constructive input. Any conditions attached to the final approval should be consistent with the transaction documents negotiated between Consumers Energy and Confluence. We believe there are opportunities for the parties to cooperatively address the governor’s concerns through conditions that are consistent with that goal.”
Map of the 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Graphic by Consumers Energy)
Confluence Hydro spokesperson Natalie Joubert said in a statement that the company is looking forward to “engaging in constructive dialogue with parties and working towards a resolution that supports the needs of communities, ratepayers and the state of Michigan.”
However, Consumers Energy’s request for collaboration was met with skepticism by some of the organizations opposing the sale.
The Environmental Law and Policy Center argued the commission should deny Consumers’ request and deny the sale at its Thursday meeting. The firm represents the Michigan Trout Unlimited, Michigan Steelhead and Salmon Fishermen’s Association, the Great Lakes Council of Fly Fishers International, Anglers of the Au Sable and the Michigan Hydro Relicensing Coalition.
“This is not a case in which the parties are fully and deeply engaged in ongoing negotiations that are close to resolution, and they jointly (not just Consumers Energy) want a little more time from the Commission in order to finalize a settlement,” Environmental Law and Policy Center Senior Associate Attorney Daniel Abrams wrote in response to the energy company’s notice. “That is just not the reality here, today, in this case.”
The Association of Businesses Advocating Tariff Equity, which also opposes the dam sale, told the commission it was “not aware of any potential ‘constructive solution’ or ‘opportunity to resolve the issues in this case cooperatively,’” and that Consumers had not given them any basis to believe there is one.
The Michigan Public Service commission did not include the dam sale on the agenda for its September meeting. Consumers Energy has asked the commission to issue its final decision on Nov. 9.
Commissioners greenlight natural gas rate increase, improved outage credits
While the commission did not discuss the hydroelectric dams, the commission voted to approve a $74.52 million natural gas rate increase for DTE Energy, which the commission said will support the company’s efforts to modernize its natural gas transmission and distribution system.
Commissioners also approved a virtual power plant program, allowing DTE to launch a two-year pilot program with residents of a net-zero community in Ann Arbor. DTE can draw power from the community’s battery storage systems to help meet energy demand during peak hours, while reimbursing residents $105 per kilowatt hour used.
Additionally, the commission increased the power outage credit energy consumers receive for lengthy or repeated power outages from $42 to $44. Customers can receive the credit if they experience more than six interruptions in 12 months. They are also eligible if they lose power for more than 16 hours under normal weather conditions, 48 hours under gray skies and 96 hours under catastrophic conditions.

text:
Fall fishing on the Madison River at sunrise. (Photo: NPS / Jacob W. Frank)Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks announced this week that daily fishing restrictions, commonly known as “hoot-owl restrictions,” have been lifted for portions of the Madison and Beaverhead rivers due to cooling water temperatures.
Restrictions are lifted for the Beaverhead River from Selway Bridge Fishing Access Site to the confluence with the Big Hole River and for the Madison River from the Warm Springs Boat Launch to the confluence with the Jefferson River.
These restrictions were implemented in July because of warm water temperatures.
Drought-related fishing closures remain in effect for portions of the Beaverhead and Big Hole rivers. To view current fishing restrictions and closures statewide, click here.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hinson doesn’t rule out Trump’s pledge of $5K to adults; calls for relief for families
description: Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ashley Hinson said Thursday she wants to look at all proposals aimed at improving affordability for working families, including recent comments from President Donald Trump to pay out $5,000 to U.S. adults.  Trump made the comments Wednesday night at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas and said the money would go […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson speaks with reporters Sept. 10, 2026 outside of a childcare center in Carlisle, Iowa. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ashley Hinson said Thursday she wants to look at all proposals aimed at improving affordability for working families, including recent comments from President Donald Trump to pay out $5,000 to U.S. adults. 
Trump made the comments Wednesday night at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas and said the money would go to “every adult” if Republicans maintain control of the House and the Senate following the upcoming election. 
“I never say what I’m going to support until I’ve had a chance to look at the details of it,” Hinson told reporters Thursday about the comments from the president. “But again, what I do support is making sure we’re providing real relief to hardworking families, like the middle-class tax cut bill, continuing to focus on reducing the regulatory burden and again driving down costs for everyone.” 
The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget said Thursday that the Trump plan to dole out checks was “fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious.” The committee estimates the plan would cost approximately $1.2 trillion and would “explode” the national deficit.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hinson, current U.S. representative for Iowa’s 2nd District, spoke outside Sprouts Early Learning Academy in Carlisle, following a tour and conversation with staff about making childcare more affordable and accessible.
Hinson, who is running for U.S. Senate, said there are lots of “overlapping regulations” when it comes to opening a childcare center that she would like to simplify. 
“If we want to increase the number of families that we have in this country, and certainly here in Iowa, we need access to affordable childcare,” Hinson said. 
Hinson has introduced legislation that would reauthorize the federal Child Care and Development Block Grant Act, which funds grants to states to help subsidize childcare for low-income working families. Hinson has also pushed for legislation that would expand childcare availability for families who work outside of a traditional 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. schedule.  
Hinson’s Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, has also listed lowering childcare costs as a policy priority. 
Hinson said tax reform from Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which eliminated taxes on tips and overtime, “helps a lot of people that are working in a facility just like this one.” Hinson said she wants to continue looking for places to protect the resources of working families so that if they get a check for $5,000 from the president, it can “go a lot further.”
“My whole focus is going to be on continuing to provide relief to middle-class families and working families, much like the people who are using this facility right here,” Hinson said. 
Trump has said he would campaign in 35 competitive races, ahead of the November election to help GOP candidates. The Cook Political Report has rated Hinson’s race against Turek for the open Senate seat as a “toss up.” 
Hinson said she has not spoken with the president about a potential trip to Iowa to support her, but she said she treats “every race like (she’s) 10 points down.” 
“Every race to me is competitive,” Hinson said. “I’m going out and earning Iowans’ votes, talking about what they need in their lives, and that is to make life more affordable for working families, life easier for our farmers who are feeding and fueling the world, and life certainly easier for our veterans as well.”
