name: Mississippi Today
title: Hinds County jail officials deny he was beaten. In a lawsuit, former inmate says he was left unable to walk or talk
description: Ife Myles, right, comforts her partner Deonte Shaw on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, in Jackson as they speak about Shaw's traumatic brain injury from a November 2025 attack in the Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond.
text:
Deonte Shaw remembers the late October day he arrived at the Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond. He remembers working in the kitchen, spending time with his cell mate and the white sheet that separated their cell from the crowded jail pod. 
What Shaw doesn’t remember is the beating. 
Denote Shaw wipes his eyes on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, in Jackson, as he listens to his partner recount how he suffered a traumatic brain injury at the Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond.  Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
On the night of Nov. 12, inmates attacked Shaw in his cell, according to hospital medical records Shaw provided Mississippi Today. Guards discovered Shaw the next morning, barely conscious and with bruises on his face. Hours passed before the infirmary sent Shaw to the emergency room, where he was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury and put on a ventilator.
His girlfriend, Ife Myles, didn’t know about the beating, and she wondered why he had stopped calling. She sought answers from the jail, but weeks went by before a friend told her in late December that Shaw had been severely injured.
On New Year’s Eve, after a week of frequent trips to Raymond, Myles got a call. “Bring a wheelchair,” a jailer told her. Shaw could go home. 
This summer, Shaw, 31, became the latest in dozens of people to sue Hinds County since 2015 when U.S. Justice Department officials declared conditions at the jail unconstitutional, including the failure to protect inmates from violence. His attorneys filed a complaint in U.S. District Court in Jackson – five days after inmates in Raymond stomped to death an 18-year-old, whose killing and last breaths were caught on video and shared on social media.
Lawsuit alleges widespread jail violence
The lawsuit alleges that Shaw’s rights were violated by the county’s failure to run a jail free from widespread violence and is demanding the county pay damages, including Shaw’s medical expenses. 
The couple wants accountability. But so far, Hinds County and the sheriff’s department have ignored public records requests from Shaw’s attorney that might explain Shaw’s injuries, including security videos.
In court filings, Jessica Malone, an attorney hired by the county, denies Shaw was beaten, instead alleging that he “suffered a medical emergency, was found unresponsive, administered Narcan and then provided with medical treatment.” Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones won’t comment on litigation, and Wendell France, the Maryland-based court-appointed receiver currently overseeing the detention center, is barred by the federal court from making statements to the media.
Medical records reviewed by Mississippi Today mention that Shaw had ingested drugs – something Shaw denies – but describe his “mechanism of injury” as assault. According to the medical report, the only drug in Shaw’s system was benzodiazepine, which paramedics gave him before he was admitted to the University of Mississippi Medical Center.
Myles, 35, cried when she recounted the moment she finally laid eyes on Shaw. Shaw cried, too.
“It’s not me, like how I used to be,” Shaw said. 
Ife Myles, right, sits with her partner Deonte Shaw at Khalaf and Nguyen Law Firm on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, in Jackson. The couple spoke about a lawsuit against Hinds County after Shaw suffered a traumatic brain injury in November 2025 while being held at the county’s detention center in Raymond. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The couple met six years ago when Shaw worked as a cook at Waffle House. Shaw took Myles’ order – a cheesesteak melt and a bowl of grits, then asked for her phone number. He came over for her birthday, Myles said, “and he never left.” 
The alleged beating couldn’t break their bond. Myles took Shaw to physical therapy, bathed him and fed him. 
Now she’s helping Shaw prepare for the day he might have to testify in court. 
Traffic stop leads to jail
Shaw had just paid $1,000 for a used car when Capitol Police pulled him over on Oct. 24 on a traffic stop. Shaw knew he was going to jail. Months earlier, a Hinds County Circuit Court judge had issued a bench warrant after he skipped drug court. 
At Raymond, Shaw called Myles as often as he could. Myles tried to cheer him up by showing off her new red hair. That conversation was on the afternoon of Nov. 12, hours before Shaw says he was beaten.
Then Shaw went silent.
By Thanksgiving, Myles was concerned. She called an official with the Hinds County drug court who told her that Shaw might be at the state mental hospital, where a judge had ordered him to undergo rehab. But the hospital told Myles that Shaw wasn’t there. 
“I got depressed,” Myles said. “I was like, did he run away?” 
On Dec. 20, Myles heard from her legal husband, who she had separated from years earlier. He was also in jail. He knew Shaw, and the two men had chosen to be cell mates for safety reasons. Her estranged husband told her he saw Shaw being beaten. 
The next day, a friend whose boyfriend was also in jail gave her similar news. 
Using a friend’s phone, Myles began recording herself calling the jail. On recordings shared with Mississippi Today, voices from both sides of the conversation were audible.
On one phone call, Myles spoke to a man who introduced himself as a jail supervisor. Myles explained that she hadn’t heard from Shaw in over a month and was considering reporting him missing after learning he had been “severely beaten.”
“OK, I don’t know who told you all that,” the supervisor said on the recording. “Shaw is good.” 
But when Myles asked which zone Shaw was in, the supervisor responded that he couldn’t say. “That’s violating the HIPAA,” he said, referring to the federal law meant to protect sensitive health information. 
“Jail is public record!” Myles yelled into the phone. 
After days of driving to Raymond, Myles finally got confirmation of what she’d suspected. On Dec. 29, a jail captain told her Shaw was in the infirmary. But she was not allowed to see him.
On New Year’s Eve, a Hinds County judge signed Shaw’s release. Later that day, Myles received the call that she could get Shaw from jail.
She brought a wheelchair as instructed. She borrowed it from a neighbor. She wasn’t told why she’d need one.
A tear rolls down Deonte Shaw’s face on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, in Jackson, as he recounts how he suffered abuse during his time at the Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
As she was driving, Myles’ phone rang. A man identified himself as the jail administrator and told Myles that a “doctor report” showed Shaw had taken drugs, passed out, hit his head and had a stroke in the hospital, according to another recording reviewed by Mississippi Today. 
Myles said she knew it was a lie. The caller invited her to speak with an investigator.
Inside the waiting room, Myles’ heart raced. Then the door opened. 
“The first thing I saw was his feet,” she said. “He didn’t have his shoes on.” 
Shaw was slumped in a wheelchair, she recalled. He was drooling, his left arm curled on his chest. His hair was overgrown, and he smelled. 
Myles fell to her knees. Shaw opened his eyes. “He started to kiss my forehead,” Myles said. “And I said, ‘He knows it’s me.’” 
Regaining independence
Myles keeps videos and images in a folder she refers to as life after disaster. 
Unsettled by the jail’s assertion that Shaw wasn’t beaten, Myles knew she needed to document everything.
She has pictures of Shaw at rehab as he learned to walk again. She has videos of Shaw bedridden, struggling to eat and thrashing his skinny legs – signs, Myles said, that he was trying to get stronger. She has recordings of him using muffled, angry and urgent sounds while trying to communicate with her and his children.
“Leave me alone,” Shaw says in one video, slurring his words. 
By February, he had regained some independence. One day, Myles said he rolled out of bed, stood up and began to walk on his own. Soon, he was staying up all night listening to music, sounding out the words to his favorite songs from Memphis rappers like BEO Lil Kenny. 
Now the next grueling step: seeking justice.
Through connections she’d made years ago at a legal clinic, Myles found Shaw a pair of attorneys – Jad Khalaf and his law partner, Ammie Nguyen. 
Khalaf said he’s read reports from a federal monitor – dating back 10 years –  detailing conditions at the Hinds County jail and was struck by the sluggish progress in securing the safety of inmates. 
“All the while, more people are dying or being severely beaten,” he said. “It’s ridiculous.” 
Khalaf said he’s seen Shaw make a remarkable recovery since their first meeting earlier this year. 
“He didn’t say much,” Khalaf said. “He barely could walk.”
Because he has trouble speaking, Shaw is still a man of few words. He still has seizures. His kids still ask, “What’s wrong with Daddy?” 
Shaw worries he’ll never fully recover.
“I still can’t run,” he said, but then added he won’t stop trying.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: In rare move, SCC orders three in-person hearings for NextEra-Dominion merger case
description: The State Corporation Commission has ordered additional chances for the public to officially testify in the case to approve or reject the proposed $67 billion NextEra-Dominion merger, Virginia regulators said Thursday. In addition to the three days for telephonic testimony already planned at the beginning of the case, the commissioners mandated three in-pers[...]
text:
Virginia State Corporation Commission members have ordered three opportunities for the public to have their say about the proposed NextEra-Dominion merger, the first to kick off Nov. 5. In this September 2, 2025 photo, commissions hear testimony in Richmond on a different case. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The State Corporation Commission has ordered additional chances for the public to officially testify in the case to approve or reject the proposed $67 billion NextEra-Dominion merger, Virginia regulators said Thursday.
In addition to the three days for telephonic testimony already planned at the beginning of the case, the commissioners mandated three in-person hearings across Dominion’s Virginia coverage area.
Clock starts for state regulators to review proposed Dominion-NextEra merger

This will allow additional opportunities for residents to weigh in on the merger that could create the largest regulated utility in the world, as the public and state lawmakers heighten their scrutiny of the deal.
The first of the three in-person meetings will be held on the evening of Nov. 5 inside the SCC’s courtroom in Richmond. The dates and locations of the other two meetings have yet to be determined.  
“Over the last few years, the Commission has endeavored to increase accessibility to its proceedings,” Commissioner Samuel Towell wrote in the order.
It is not unprecedented for the commission to host hearings outside of the Richmond courtrooms. Those typically happen for cases such as transmission lines or compressor stations, however, which would mostly impact one locality. 
But the magnitude of the merger and vigorous public engagement in the case has prompted the SCC to take this unusual step.
“There is no identified remote locus most impacted by this proceeding; the entire Dominion service territory is affected. Further, the approval or denial of the application does not uniquely alter the physical character of any particular community,” Towell wrote. “This is not a case that, under normal circumstances, would warrant remote, in-person hearings. But this is not a normal case.”
The three public testimony periods to be held via telephone are scheduled on the morning of Nov. 5 as well as Nov. 9 and 10. Due to time constraints, the public is encouraged to submit written testimony, by Nov. 9.
Towell noted that commissioners weigh in-person testimony equally with telephone or written testimonies. 
“A statement made in person at a remote location is given no more (or less) weight than a statement provided telephonically or in writing.”
The merger of the two major utility companies has garnered significant national attention and prompted action from state lawmakers.
Va. House speaker details ‘concerns’ about NextEra-Dominion merger in letter to state regulators

Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi launched a statewide listening tour about the proposed deal and House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, sent a letter to SCC Chair Kelsey Bagot — a former NextEra attorney who has declined to recuse herself from the case — detailing his concerns and suggestions about the merger.
Lawmakers also requested that Gov. Abigail Spanberger call a special session to allow the General Assembly a chance to pass legislation that would allow the merger case’s six-month review period to be extended. 
Spanberger said late last week she would not convene a special legislative session over the merger, pointing out that she has already taken an unprecedented step by filing to intervene in the case.
A timeline of the schedule for the merger case can be found on the SCC website.

title: North Dakota sees first West Nile death in 2026
description: North Dakota has recorded its first death from the mosquito-borne West Nile virus in 2026.  The North Dakota Health and Human Services said in a news release Thursday that the person who died was over 60 years old and lived in southwest North Dakota.  People ages 60 and older, those with underlying health conditions and […]
text:
A member of Cass County Vector Control shows mosquito larvae in a testing cup. (Photo provided by Cass County Vector Control)North Dakota has recorded its first death from the mosquito-borne West Nile virus in 2026. 
The North Dakota Health and Human Services said in a news release Thursday that the person who died was over 60 years old and lived in southwest North Dakota. 
People ages 60 and older, those with underlying health conditions and those who take medications that suppress the immune system are at greatest risk of developing a severe illness, the health agency said
As of Wednesday, 25 human West Nile virus cases have been reported in 14 North Dakota counties. Fourteen people have been hospitalized. 
In 2025, North Dakota had 86 cases and two West Nile virus-related deaths. 
West Nile virus transmission usually peaks in late summer in North Dakota. As the year progresses, people may be inclined to skip mosquito protection, the agency said. 
There is no vaccine or specific treatment for the virus, so preventing mosquito bites is the best way to reduce the risk of infection. The agency recommends using repellents, wearing clothing that covers arms and legs and limiting outdoor activity after dusk and before dawn. 
People should also eliminate stagnant water and keep lawns trimmed to eliminate breeding areas. 
Most people infected with West Nile virus have no symptoms or only mild symptoms, such as fever and headache, the agency said. In more severe cases, the virus can cause high fever, severe headache, stiff neck and altered mental state. People with symptoms should see a healthcare provider immediately. 
For more information, visit hhs.nd.gov/wnv.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming’s high court hears arguments over years-long Casper Mountain gravel pit controversy
description:
Both the state and the prospective miner are under intense public criticism for their roles in the matter that spawned two cases before the Wyoming Supreme Court.
The post Wyoming’s high court hears arguments over years-long Casper Mountain gravel pit controversy appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A controversial gravel mining operation proposed on state land at the base of Casper Mountain remains in legal limbo after Wyoming’s top court heard oral arguments Wednesday regarding one of two cases before it.
Attorneys representing the State Board of Land Commissioners and Casper-based Prism Logistics defended their opposing positions and fielded dozens of questions during the roughly hour-long proceeding. Both parties are under intense public criticism for their roles in the matter — the state board for blindsiding neighboring homeowners and Natrona County officials by approving, without public notice or directly reviewing the applications, the mining leases, and Prism for doggedly pursuing the project in the face of fierce public opposition.
Under public pressure, the state board — composed of Gov. Mark Gordon, Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, Secretary of State Chuck Gray, Treasurer Curt Meier and Auditor Kristi Racines — attempted to undo the panel’s initial lease approval by denying Prism when several leases came up for renewal last year.
That spawned a lawsuit by Prism and a subsequent Natrona County District Court ruling in January siding with the gravel miner. The state appealed to the Wyoming Supreme Court.


Though Prism met at least one of four qualifying terms for a statutory “exclusive right” to renew, the state board was not legally bound to oblige, Wyoming Assistant Attorney General Kate Gamble told the five justices Wednesday. Instead, the board was operating within its constitutional and statutorial authority to decide renewing the leases was “inappropriate and inconsistent with the board’s land management goals,” which can evolve.
“The state is not advocating that the board have unbridled discretion,” Gamble said. “But what the state is suggesting is that under the Constitution and under [state statute] Title 36, the board clearly has a fiduciary duty to manage state lands for the trust beneficiary’s best interest.”
Cheyenne-based attorney Deborah Roden, representing Prism, countered that a broad level of discretion clearly applies when the state board first considers whether to approve a lease application but not when it comes to renewals.
“In order to deny a lease renewal application, the board would have to find that none of the four conditions have been met,” Roden said. Despite parallel legal wrangling with the Natrona County Board of Commissioners that helped create a “regulatory deadlock,” Roden added, “Prism was proceeding in good faith to develop the lands.”


What are state trust lands?
Upon granting statehood in 1890, the federal government bestowed some 4.2 million acres of “state trust lands” to Wyoming, and it now manages about 3.4 million acres of trust land. The Wyoming Constitution prescribes that the primary use of those lands, which are scattered throughout the state in a checkerboard pattern, is to generate revenue to support public schools.The Office of State Lands and Investments commonly leases those lands — often referred to as “school sections” — for grazing and industrial development such as mining and oil and gas drilling.


The court will issue a written opinion at a later date, Chief Justice Lynne Boomgaarden said.
The controversy
Nearby homeowners object to the mine’s industrial traffic through the rural neighborhood, along with potential impacts to shallow aquifers and residential water wells, as well as the likely loss of public recreation on the state lands where the mine will operate. They formed the Casper Mountain Preservation Alliance and gathered more than 20,000 signatures from residents throughout the county in opposition. Casper Mountain and the surrounding lands are a popular recreation spot.




Click to enlarge: This map depicts state land parcels targeted for gravel mining. (Casper Mountain Preservation Alliance)
Despite the public outcry, Prism Logistics Manager Kyle True said he believes the actual impacts will be far less than predicted.
“As long as we are diligent and lawful about our development procedures, which of course we plan to be — and we will be well regulated by the [Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality] — we look forward to responsibly mining that resource close to town,” True told WyoFile after Wednesday’s oral arguments. “It’s my hope that we will bring down the cost of gravel and gravel-related products in the Casper area over time, because construction and housing have become real problems for many Americans.”
Though one neighbor believes the high court’s review should result in a legal affirmation of the state’s decision to not renew the leases, the situation highlights how state laws, county zoning authority and the reality of evolving public land values sometimes don’t align to meet the will of the people, said Carolyn Griffith, who lives near the proposed mine and chairs the Casper Mountain Preservation Alliance that opposes the project.
Cyclists gather for a riding event on state lands at the base of Casper Mountain. (Carolyn Griffith)
“I think we, as citizens, all expect our government officials — whether that be legislators to local leaders to employees — we expect them all to do their due diligence,” Griffith told WyoFile. “When pieces of that fail, it affects all of us. And this issue here is big right now in Casper, but it could happen anywhere in this state.”
Meanwhile, the high court postponed oral arguments until October in a related case regarding the proposed gravel mine. 
Prism filed a petition for judicial review in October 2024 regarding an action by the Natrona County Board of Commissioners. After the state issued leases to Prism, and after public outcry, the county rezoned the area to a previous designation that would prohibit the mining activity — an action that the State Board of Land Commissioners mentioned in deciding whether to renew Prism’s leases.
The lawsuit resulted in another Natrona County District Court ruling in January that state land leases are not subject to county land use regulations.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Coe College to lower tuition for better clarity on actual cost of education
description: Coe College is cutting the cost of its tuition by nearly half with the goal of showing prospective students a more clear picture of what they’ll be paying and reducing uncertainty of the cost of a college education. The Cedar Rapids private college announced in a news release it will reduce tuition by 45% to […]
text:
Coe College will reduce its tuition by 45% in the 2027-2028 academic year to provide more clarity on what students will actually pay. (Photo courtesy of Coe College)Coe College is cutting the cost of its tuition by nearly half with the goal of showing prospective students a more clear picture of what they’ll be paying and reducing uncertainty of the cost of a college education.
The Cedar Rapids private college announced in a news release it will reduce tuition by 45% to $31,850 for the next academic year starting in 2027. Part of “Clearly Coe,” an initiative to showcase the value of an education from the institution, the reduction brings the starting direct cost of attending Coe with other fees, food and boarding to around $45,000.
Coe College President David Hayes said in the release the initiative will ensure that student investment “yields the highest potential return” as well as providing more clarity for those looking at potential colleges.
“We want to eliminate friction from the college decision,” Hayes said in the release. “We are empowering students and families to prioritize factors like excellence, opportunity and career success rather than price tags.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the release, with the reduction Coe College’s direct costs will fall underneath the average pre-aid cost of $57,000 at competing private institutions. This change comes in addition to the college’s Iowa Ready Initiative, which caps Iowa resident student direct costs at $25,560 to keep it within 10% of the average direct costs of an Iowa public university education.
Rather than using the traditional model of setting tuition high then offsetting it with grants and scholarships, the release stated Coe’s model will start at $45,000 for tuition, fees, housing and dining then subtract how much a student has received in merit scholarships, federal aid through the FAFSA and any funds from loans or work study programs.
Both new and returning students will see the tuition change, the release stated, and financial aid officials will provide projections with updated costs and aid offers for those coming back to campus next fall. Coe College is following other private institutions’ lead in switching up their tuition model, the release stated, like Graceland University and Simpson College, and the college hopes it will provide an easier comparison for prospective students.
“We want to help students focus on the factors that set Coe apart,” said Josh Kite, interim vice president for enrollment, in the release. “Guaranteed hands-on experiences, one-on-one faculty connections and comprehensive student support make Coe a great value.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico congressional delegation asks Google, Apple to commit to keeping state’s name on maps
description: New Mexico’s congressional delegation on Thursday called upon major tech companies Apple and Google to commit to ensuring New Mexico retains its name on the companies’ maps. The push follows Donald Trump's proposal to rename the state 'New America.'
text:
President Donald Trump on Sept. 6, 2026, posted on Truth Social images and text that proposed renaming New Mexico, prompting immediate pushback from Democratic officials. (Screenshot image)New Mexico’s congressional delegation on Thursday called upon major tech companies Apple and Google to commit to ensuring New Mexico retains its name on the companies’ maps.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The letter to Apple CEO John Ternus and Google CEO Sundar Pichai follows President Donald Trump’s social media posts on Sunday that first showed New Mexico’s name altered on a map to be “New America” and then later expressed enthusiasm for such a change by writing: “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!”
New Mexico state and federal officials swiftly rebuked Trump’s post, with U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), who leads the Thursday letter, writing on social media that, “It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be. Just like how you’ll always be a sinvergüenza and corrupt.”
Last year Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America) by executive order and, more recently, renamed Lake Ontario (Lake America) by the same mechanism.
The letter, signed by the rest of the delegation, all Democrats — U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich and U.S. Reps. Melanie Stansbury, Teresa Leger Fernández and Gabe Vasquez — notes that Trump lacks the authority to rename the state, which can only be done through a state constitutional amendment.
The letter notes, however, that Apple and Google updated their maps to reflect Trump’s new names for Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.
“This is disappointing but unsurprising,” the letter says. “Both of your companies have significant business interests before the federal government. These include antitrust enforcement, tariffs, regulation of artificial intelligence and online platforms, and federal contracting opportunities.”
The letter also notes the $24.5 million Google paid to settle Trump’s lawsuit over his YouTube suspension following the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, and both companies’ corporate donations to Trump’s ballroom project.
“Because of this history, we ask each of you to publicly commit that Apple Maps and Google Maps will continue to identify the State of New Mexico as New Mexico, regardless of what the President posts on social media, what executive order he attempts to issue, or what pressure he puts on your companies,” the letter says, and asks for that commitment by Sept. 19.
New Mexico’s “name has belonged to the people of New Mexico since before the United States existed,” the letter concludes. “It should not become a political football to be negotiated between an unhinged President and two of the most powerful technology companies in the world.”
Source NM has requests for comment into both Google and Apple and will update this story as necessary.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. grocery store owner’s son: Federal agents demand he ‘get out of the way’
description: A Tuesday encounter between apparent federal agents and Latino Pittsburgh’s signature grocery store brought renewed tensions Wednesday, scaring customers but bringing out advocates for immigrants.
text:
Staff members from Casa San José put up “know your rights” flyers and information on Pittsburgh's Latino support network outside of Las Palmas grocery store and taqueria, Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Beechview. The organization has been very busy with the region's Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking and Haitian communities. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)
This article first appeared on Pittsburgh’s Public Source and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
Joey Berumen paced up and down Broadway Avenue outside Las Palmas grocery store Wednesday around lunch time under a blistering late-summer sun. He held a walkie-talkie while he glanced around the road. He was looking for signs of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
Workers at the independent grocery store and adjoining taco stand were on edge Wednesday after agents they believe to be with ICE appeared outside the store twice in 24 hours. Employees say business is down, with community members deterred from shopping by the federal agents.
Joey Berumen, who grew up working in his father’s Las Palmas grocery store, looks toward Broadway Avenue as he takes a call outside of the taqueria while on his security shift at the store and restaurant on Sept. 9, in Beechview.  (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)
Workers with Casa San José were on the block earlier, taping up Spanish language posters with information on legal rights and other resources. Four or five legal observers from Frontline Dignity, which responds to support immigrants amid news of ICE activity, milled around the Las Palmas taco stand throughout the late morning.
Immigration enforcement appears to have increased in Beechview, a hub of Pittsburgh’s Latino population. An agent confronted Berumen Tuesday, and agents returned Wednesday morning, he said.
The ramped-up activity here is part of a nationwide ICE crackdown aimed at making good on one of President Donald Trump’s core campaign promises: to dramatically increase the number of people deported from the United States. In a statement in response to Public Source’s questions, ICE spokesperson Jason Koontz said the agency’s Beechview presence reflects “everyday” enforcement operations across the country.
“Citizens and legal residents should find reassurance in the presence of trained law enforcement officers removing criminals and illegal aliens from their streets,” he said.
Under Trump, he said, “if you enter the country illegally or violate your lawful status, you will face consequences. … We will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you.”




A sign barring ICE agents from entering unless they have a valid judicial warrant hangs in the entryway at Las Palmas. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)




“We got together and said you know what, we’re going to keep an eye out,” said Berumen, who said he is the store owner’s son. Employees now work in shifts keeping watch on the street from open until close.
He said business is “nothing compared” to before ICE enforcement increased, “and it will be [low] until this stops.”
Across the street, an employee standing outside the restaurant La Cocina de Betty said “not a lot of people come” when there is news that ICE is around the area. “I want our customers to be safe,” she said, with the aid of a translation app, adding that customers can order from the restaurant through apps if they don’t feel comfortable going out. She asked not to be named.
Monica Ruiz, executive director of Casa San Jose, said ICE’s scrutiny of businesses like Las Palmas is harmful to the community.
Monica Ruiz, executive director of Casa San José, takes a call as she surveys activity by Las Palmas grocery store and taqueria on Sept. 9, in Beechview. Ruiz was on her way to pick up a child who got sick at school, because the child’s parent was afraid to pick them up for fear of interaction with ICE. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)
“Do you think this establishment doesn’t pay taxes? Of course they do,” Ruiz said. “That money pays for the T train, it pays for the roads, it pays for the schools. How is this good?”
She said her organization recently had to cancel a class that helps new mothers read to their children because participants were too afraid to attend.
Berumen said ICE’s attention toward his business took on a personal nature when agents returned Wednesday. He said one referred to him by name, despite him never introducing himself.
“He said, ‘I’m here, Joey, get out of the way, Joey,’ … There’s no reason to intimidate us. We’re not going to close down. We’re going to stay strong together.”
Charlie Wolfson is the local government reporter for Pittsburgh’s Public Source. He can be reached at charlie@publicsource.org.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico childcare providers struggle as demand, waitlists increase
description: Last year, New Mexico became the first state to offer universal childcare, but one year after Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham unveiled the program, childcare center business leaders say they’re struggling to meet increasing demands and are concerned about long-term sustainability. The program currently has 47,000 enrollees, with Early Childcare Education and Car[...]
text:
From left to right: Child care business owners Ray Jaramillo, Daisy Lira and Angela Garcia share their struggles with the Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee on Sep. 9, 2026. (Photo by: Leah Romero/Source NM)Last year, New Mexico became the first state to offer universal childcare, but one year after Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham unveiled the program, childcare center business leaders say they’re struggling to meet increasing demands and are concerned about long-term sustainability.
The program currently has 47,000 enrollees, with Early Childcare Education and Care officials estimating the number will increase to 58,000 children in the coming year. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Daisy Lira, founder of early childcare center The Hive Education, in Sunland Park, told state lawmakers on Wednesday they aren’t thinking enough about how to support providers to meet that increasing demand.
“A provider can’t simply add another classroom because demand increases,” she said during a Las Cruces hearing at the Legislature’s Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee. “They have to hire qualified staff. They need equipment and supplies. They need insurance.”
The childcare business leaders on Wednesday proposed lawmakers consider amending the rules governing the program to ease reporting requirements for providers and have reimbursement rates — essentially payments providers receive from the state — keep pace with current costs and inflation. They also said the state needs to streamline its funding mechanisms across different agencies and sources.
That same day, the ECECD addressed one of the concerns that childcare providers had — a proposed mandate that childcare businesses, if taking the reimbursement, would put 57% of their revenue toward wages for teachers and administration. 
In an updated policy, the ECECD lowered the mandate to 50% and expanded the eligible employees to assistants, cooks and other workers to ease the strain on childcare businesses.
Childcare leaders also cited rising business insurance costs as a challenge. 
“We have public funding available, families waiting for care and providers willing to create more slots. But if that provider cannot obtain the coverage needed to operate, those seats or slots never get created,” Ray Jaramillo, director of Alpha School for Young Children in Las Cruces, told lawmakers.
Jaramillo proposed lawmakers help childcare businesses create a “captive insurance company,” one controlled by its members, to help address rising costs, but faced immediate pushback. 
“If you, as a private industry, want to create an insurance pool, more power to you,” state Rep. Tara Lujan (D-Santa Fe) said, “but for us to come on board and say we need to help you solve that problem—I don’t see that as the function of the state.”
State Rep. Marian Matthews (D-Albuquerque) noted that the childcare providers must have a voice during universal childcare discussions to deliver long term results. “We’re going to have people leave the business because of these problems, which to me seem to be process problems and could absolutely be solved with some guidelines,” she said.
Some state Republican lawmakers, like Sen. Crystal Brantley (R-Elephant Butte), said that the universal childcare program is an “attempt to create some sort of lasting legacy for leadership” and that the program was rolled out “without addressing all concerns.”
But the childcare providers were clear they want universal childcare to succeed. “But for it to succeed long term, we have to protect: quality for children, access for families, and sustainability for the providers who keep the doors open. That’s how we build something that lasts here in New Mexico,” Jaramillo said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Asheville leaders make it illegal to collect rent when housing is unsafe
description: Asheville has joined Durham and a handful of other municipalities across North Carolina in making it illegal for landlords to collect rent on a property the city has deemed unsafe. The Asheville City County unanimously approved an amendment to the city’s housing code on Tuesday to give tenants more protection against landlords who don’t make […]
text:
An Evergreen Ridge Apartment in Asheville, N.C. Residents complain about mold and poor maintenance. (Photo: Asheville Area Tenant Union) Asheville has joined Durham and a handful of other municipalities across North Carolina in making it illegal for landlords to collect rent on a property the city has deemed unsafe.
The Asheville City County unanimously approved an amendment to the city’s housing code on Tuesday to give tenants more protection against landlords who don’t make critical repairs to rental units after receiving notices of violations from the city.
City ordinances list 18 criteria under which a rental unit can be ruled unsafe. The lack of hot water, a heating system or smoke detector are among the violations that would qualify a rental property as unsafe.
The amendment would be triggered if a landlord fails to make needed repairs after receiving a notice of violation.
Asheville Mayor Esther Mannheimer (Photo: City of Asheville)
On Tuesday, Mayor Esther Mannheimer cautioned that state law does not allow tenants to withhold rent payments before being granted a judicial right to do so. They  could, however, receive refunds if complaints are not resolved.
Mannheimer acknowledged the challenges the city faces between what state law permits in such circumstances and the amendment the council was asked to consider.
“I think it’s important that we send a signal that we’re not supportive of any landlord that would require rent payment for what is essentially uninhabitable rental property,” Mannheimer said. “This is kind of our only vehicle to do that, because the state does preempt us from taking greater action.” 
Organizers with the Asheville Area Tenants Union (AATU) started pushing for the amendment about 10 months ago after Durham residents successfully lobbied their city council to adopt a similar amendment. 
The union lobbied the council under the banner of “No Room for Slumlords.” 
Success in Durham has other tenant groups eyeing housing code changes

“When we watched Durham do that, we decided that was a fight we needed to have in Asheville,” said Rachel Wyse, an AATU organizer and lifelong Asheville resident. 
Wyse said Asheville has a shortage of affordable housing like many cities and large towns across the state. Rentals that are affordable, she said, are often poorly maintained.
“The people who live in these kinds of spaces are elders on Social Security fixed income, disabled folks on disability fixed income, and then poor people who are service workers who make a lot less than a living wage, and we don’t have anywhere to go,” Wyse said. “These sorts of apartments are the last stop before homelessness.”
Property owners and landlords appeared largely in support of the amendment during Tuesday’s council meeting, but were concerned about what Matt Allen, director of government affairs for the Realtor’s Association, called a “rush to push” the amendment through.
“This could have been an opportunity for responsive rental owners, property managers and tenant advocate groups to come together and craft something that holds bad actors accountable, while also ensuring that unintended and potentially negative consequences for owners and tenants alike are considered and addressed,” Allen said. 
In addition to Asheville and Durham, Charlotte, Pineville and Pittsboro have similar ordinances in place.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: State treasurer to provide upfront cash for storm-hit communities
description: State Treasurer Daniel Elliott is making $50 million available immediately for communities hit hard by last month’s wind and flooding damage. Cities, towns, counties, townships, schools, libraries and municipal utilities with damage to public infrastructure or facilities from a natural disaster can apply for up to $1 million. A disaster declaration is not re[...]
text:
Indiana Treasurer Daniel Elliott, speaking, is flanked by Jonathan Whitham, Gary Mayor Eddie Melton, state Rep. Danny Lopez and Connersville Mayor Chad Frank, from left to right, at a Statehouse press conference on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)State Treasurer Daniel Elliott is making $50 million available immediately for communities hit hard by last month’s wind and flooding damage.
Cities, towns, counties, townships, schools, libraries and municipal utilities with damage to public infrastructure or facilities from a natural disaster can apply for up to $1 million. A disaster declaration is not required to apply.
“As I’ve had the opportunity to go to some of these communities, see some of the difficulties that these local leaders are dealing with, these folks who are working hard on the ground, talking to them on the phone, going to their locations, seeing people living in tents, I realized that as treasurer, I need to do something,” Elliott said. 
He chairs the Indiana Bond Bank, which regularly lends money to Indiana governments for infrastructure projects at a discounted interest rate.
“Disaster relief funding takes time to arrive, and repairs to roads, utilities and public buildings often cannot wait,” a news release on the new program said. “RAPID lets an Indiana community begin that work now and repay as its insurance proceeds and recovery funding come in.”
RAPID stands for Recovery Advance Program for Infrastructure Damage.
The storms that began Aug. 11 caused severe flooding in many communities in central and eastern Indiana and pushed the White River to record-high levels as it flowed into Indianapolis. Northwest Indiana incurred widespread wind damage, including more than 350,000 power outages in the area.
A pile of debris in Connersville left from early August flooding and storms. (Photo from Gov. Mike Braun’s Flickr)
President Donald Trump granted a major disaster declaration for 21 Indiana counties, which allows individuals and local governments to seek aid. But that aid takes time to be delivered.
“This program covers a gap that has been a challenge for states and continues to be a challenge for every other state … by filling that gap between the time of the disaster and when that money starts to flow in these communities,” said Jonathan Whitham, executive director of the Indiana Department of Homeland Security. “Not every community can front the cash to begin that recovery process.”
That’s where the new program comes in.
It can be used for an array of needs, including debris removal and cleanup, damage assessment, repairs and replacement. Some specific examples given at Thursday’s press conference included repairing roads, replacing wastewater equipment ruined by being underwater and removing trees and debris from roads and sidewalks.
“Our community came together and cleaned up about 15,000 cubic yards of debris. We wanted to get it off the streets. We did not want people to look at everything they had lost, sitting out in the pile, rotting away, mold setting in, the smell, and then everything they had loved just disappear,” said Connersville Mayor Chad Frank.
He estimated the wastewater facility alone had suffered $5 million in damage.
Elliott said he can ask the Indiana Bond Bond Bank board for additional money if it is needed.
Whitham said the program will be a permanent way to help local governments hit by disasters. That leaves state disaster funds, paid for by a fireworks tax, to be directed to individual Hoosiers in need.
The money — including a low 2% interest rate — can be repaid with federal or state recovery funding, long-term financing, local funds or a combination.
Applications are due at least two weeks before the intended closing date of the loan. The next deadline is Sept. 16 for a Sept. 30 closing.

name: Missouri Independent
title: US Supreme Court again blocks use of Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map
description: The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked a federal judge’s order requiring Missouri to use a gerrymandered congressional map in November, putting the state back on course to conduct the election using districts drawn in 2022. In a one-page order, the court granted an emergency request from a political action committee called People Not Politicians […]
text:
Supreme Court Associate Justice Brett Kavanaugh attends the State of the Union address during a Joint Session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 24 in Washington, DC. (Win McNamee/Getty Images).The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked a federal judge’s order requiring Missouri to use a gerrymandered congressional map in November, putting the state back on course to conduct the election using districts drawn in 2022.
In a one-page order, the court granted an emergency request from a political action committee called People Not Politicians and its executive director, Richard von Glahn, to stay a temporary restraining order issued Tuesday by Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark in St. Louis.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles emergency matters from Missouri, referred the request to the full court. The unsigned order did not disclose the vote or explain the court’s reasoning, and no justice publicly dissented.
The ruling is the latest turn in a legal fight that has bounced between the Missouri Supreme Court, a federal district judge, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and the U.S. Supreme Court in the span of a week.
Its immediate effect is to revive a unanimous Missouri Supreme Court ruling from Sept. 3 that found the gerrymandered 2025 congressional map never took effect because it was suspended by a valid referendum petition.
The state court ordered Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to place the referendum on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition A and conduct this year’s congressional election using the map adopted in 2022.
Republican lawmakers approved the new map during a 2025 special session called by Gov. Mike Kehoe. The plan was designed to make the Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District, represented by Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, more favorable to Republicans.
People Not Politicians gathered more than 300,000 signatures seeking a statewide vote on the plan.
Hoskins rejected the referendum petition on Aug. 4, the day of Missouri’s primary, citing constitutional objections raised by Attorney General Catherine Hanaway. The Missouri Supreme Court concluded last week that the petition was legal, sufficient and timely and that the 2022 map remained the only congressional map in effect.
Hoskins and Hanaway immediately sought emergency relief from the U.S. Supreme Court. Kavanaugh rejected that request Tuesday without referring it to the full court.
Missouri Supreme Court blocks gerrymandered congressional map, orders referendum vote

Minutes later, however, Clark issued a 14-day temporary restraining order in a separate federal lawsuit filed by Republican candidates and voters. Clark ordered Missouri to use the 2025 map in November, concluding that changing district lines after candidates had been nominated in the August primary could violate voters’ federal constitutional rights.
Clark wrote that voters moved into different districts would be forced to choose among candidates they had no opportunity to help nominate and that switching maps could disrupt the election.
People Not Politicians appealed. The 8th Circuit declined Wednesday to stay Clark’s order, sending the group back to Kavanaugh with an emergency application.
The group argued that Clark lacked authority to issue the order without convening a three-judge court, as federal law generally requires for constitutional challenges involving congressional apportionment. It also argued that the federal court had improperly interfered with a state court’s interpretation of Missouri law just weeks before an election.
Missouri and Hoskins opposed the stay, joined by the U.S. solicitor general. They argued that People Not Politicians lacked standing to pursue the appeal and that forcing the state to change maps again would cause severe election-administration problems.
Hoskins told the court that election authorities were already preparing ballots using the 2025 map and warned that switching back to the 2022 districts could jeopardize the Sept. 19 deadline for sending ballots to military and overseas voters.
The U.S. Supreme Court granted the stay anyway.
Thursday’s order does not resolve the underlying federal lawsuit or explain whether the justices agreed with People Not Politicians on standing, the three-judge court requirement or the merits of Clark’s constitutional analysis.
Instead, the court ordered Clark’s ruling stayed while the appeal proceeds in the 8th Circuit and, if necessary, through a petition asking the U.S. Supreme Court to hear the case. If the justices ultimately refuse to hear the case, the stay ends automatically.
For now, however, the order removes the federal ruling that had directly conflicted with the Missouri Supreme Court.
That means election officials are once again under an order to use the 2022 congressional districts in November.
The ruling came the same morning Hoskins was scheduled to appear before the Missouri Supreme Court to answer allegations that he violated its Sept. 3 order by directing election officials to implement the 2025 map.
The dispute has left local election authorities racing against the calendar. Some counties paused work on congressional ballots while others prepared the portions of ballots unaffected by the map fight, waiting for courts to settle which districts should be used.
Under the Missouri Supreme Court ruling now back in effect, voters will decide Proposition A in November. If voters reject the 2025 map, the 2022 districts remain in place. If they approve it, the new map can take effect after the election.
For this election, at least for now, Missouri is back to the old lines.
This story will be updated.

name: VTDigger
title: 5 things we’re watching in Vermont’s general election
description:
From perhaps the closest governor's race in years to a fight over control of the Legislature, here's what VTDigger is watching as Vermonters head to the polls this fall. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  5 things we’re watching in Vermont’s general election.
text:
People enjoy the view from the top of the golden dome during a tour at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Thursday, May 15, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Election Day is on the horizon. There’s no presidential race on the ballot, but all of Vermont’s state and county-level offices, our lone U.S. House seat and two other ballot items are up for Vermonters to vote on.
VTDigger is watching the most important contests and votes this election cycle, and we’re here to tell you what to keep an eye on. 
Nov. 3 is Election Day. Here are five stories we’ll be watching:

The most exciting race for governor in years — probably
A lieutenant governor race with candidates who’ve had (or have) the job
“Rural Vermont Rising:” What impact will the movement have?
How national politics could impact the balance of power in Montpelier
Two constitutional amendments: collective bargaining and equal rights

Can Janoo do it?
For years, the question has not really been whether Republican Gov. Phil Scott would win — it was how much he’d win by. In the last two elections, he got a majority of votes in every city and town in the state, and his 2024 margin of victory was his largest ever.
Now seeking a sixth term, Scott is up against a challenger who could well give him the biggest run for his money yet: Amanda Janoo. The progressive Democrat rode to victory in August’s primary on a wave of voters’ discontent with the status quo and by promising bold changes like universal primary care funded by taxing the rich. Scott, meanwhile, is calling for new tax cuts and limiting state spending.
Janoo, an economist, has raised far more money at this stage of the race than any Scott challenger since 2020. And she did so after entering state politics earlier this year with virtually no name recognition and having never run for office before.
One poll found Scott’s job approval rating at its lowest level on record, though another still ranks him as the most popular governor in the country, an accolade he’s had for years straight. He remains popular with many Democrats, especially moderate ones, who appreciate his willingness to push back on the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and efforts to curtail mail-in voting.
The question is whether Janoo can build an even broader coalition than she did in the Democratic primary, in just a matter of months, to oust him.
Two redos for No. 2
While Janoo’s name will be new to many voters, both candidates for the state’s second-highest office may be more familiar. Incumbent Lt. Gov. John Rodgers, a Republican, is running for a second term. His Democratic opponent is Molly Gray, who served one term as lieutenant governor from 2021-23. Gray left her post to run, unsuccessfully, for a seat in Congress.
In Vermont, lieutenant governor is a job with few day-to-day responsibilities beyond presiding over the state Senate. But it does come with a bully pulpit to advocate for legislation and key issues the office-holder cares about. 
The race has interesting political lines. Rodgers served for years in the state Legislature as a Democrat, but switched his party label to Republican to run for lieutenant governor in 2024. He said at the time the party had grown too far to the left for his taste. Gray is no staunch progressive, though she is differentiating herself as a more vocal critic of President Trump’s administration than Rodgers and is touting her advocacy for refugees since leaving office. 
Rodgers has been aligning himself closely with Gov. Scott’s messaging in campaign materials this year. How well the governor does this year could well determine how well Rodgers does, too. 
Both lieutenant governor candidates are playing up their rural credentials on the campaign trail. Gray was born in the Orange County town of Newbury though now lives in Burlington. Rodgers lives on his family farm in Glover, a town in the Northeast Kingdom where he grew up.
The power of rural Vermont
Expect a lot of talk on the campaign trail about Vermont’s rural communities and the issues that are most pressing there. It’s no doubt a response to the backlash that Democratic leaders in the Legislature faced earlier this year over land use regulations, especially a 2024 law known as Act 181. 
The grassroots movement that led to significant repeals of some land use measures has coalesced into a group called “Rural Vermont Rising.” The group’s most visible demonstration was on the Statehouse steps in March to protest changes passed in Act 181 that were set to take effect this year. 
That push worked, but it remains to be seen how the new movement could have an impact at the ballot box. Since the end of the legislative session in June, Rural Vermont Rising has grown but also become more diffuse — rallying around specific land use and affordability issues in communities across Vermont.
The group does not fit neatly into partisan politics, though Republicans have been eager to align themselves with it, top among them Gov. Scott and Lt. Gov. Rodgers. 
Majority rules?
Democrats have controlled a majority of seats in the Vermont House and Senate for years. They held a supermajority in both chambers after the 2022 election and used it to repeatedly override vetoes from Gov. Scott. Then, Republicans made historic gains in the 2024 election — dismantling those supermajorities and undoing some legislation Democrats had passed.
This year, of course, Democrats will be looking to win back the seats they lost. They have reasons to be confident: it’s a midterm election, and at least at the national level, the party in power tends to struggle in the midterms. President Donald Trump is digging in his heels on an unpopular trade fight with Vermont’s northern neighbor and biggest trading partner, Canada, while also continuing to wage an unpopular war against Iran.
Vermont Republicans are confident that voters will care more at the ballot box about local issues like increases in their property tax bills, their pointed messaging on which helped win them so many new state legislative seats two years ago, as did a boost from Gov. Scott’s coattails. Even if they pick up more seats this fall, though, winning majority control of either chamber would be a big lift.
Their best chance is in the Senate, where the party now holds 13 seats to Democrats’ and the Vermont Progressive Party’s 17-member caucus. GOP senators seem to know this: They held a press event on the Statehouse steps over the summer to outline the legislation they’d advance if they had control, including changes to tax and bail policies.
Labor rights, equal rights
It’s not every year that Vermonters get to vote on changes to the state’s Constitution. This year, there are two up for consideration. 
The first would codify employees’ right to join a union and collectively bargain with their employers. It’s known as Proposal 3. Supporters say the amendment would prevent Vermont from passing laws in the future that prohibit employers and labor unions from making union membership a condition of employment, known as “right to work” laws. These laws are on the books in a majority of states.
The other measure, Proposal 4, would add a passage to the Constitution guaranteeing equal protection under the law for all people, regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or nationality. 
If this one passes, Vermont would join a majority of other states in having a version of what’s known as an equal rights amendment. It’s something advocates have been pushing to add to the U.S. Constitution for more than a century.
We’ll be watching these races, and others, as Election Day approaches. Follow our ongoing coverage and check out VTDigger’s election guide, where you can look up the candidates on your ballot, find out how to vote by mail and explore the biggest races across Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  5 things we’re watching in Vermont’s general election.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Three Alaska fishers plead guilty after being accused of deliberately scuttling boats
description: Three southeast Alaska commercial fishers accused of deliberately sinking their boats are now pleading guilty. John Fisher of Sitka, Joseph Poling of Petersburg and Tony Vanveen of Sitka have each signed plea deals, according to documents filed with the U.S. District Court in the District of Alaska. The three were initially charged earlier this year […]
text:
Boats in Sitka's Crescent Harbor are seen on a clear winter day in 2024. (Photo by Meghan Chamberlain/U.S. Forest Service)Three southeast Alaska commercial fishers accused of deliberately sinking their boats are now pleading guilty.
John Fisher of Sitka, Joseph Poling of Petersburg and Tony Vanveen of Sitka have each signed plea deals, according to documents filed with the U.S. District Court in the District of Alaska.
The three were initially charged earlier this year by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Anchorage. Despite similar details, the cases are not linked.
Fisher, whose plea deal was finalized on Aug. 27, was sentenced to 1 month in prison and one year on supervised release. 
According to court documents, Fisher deliberately scuttled the fishing vessel Igloo near Sitka in March 2025 and admitted doing so to the U.S. Coast Guard.
“The navigable waters of Southeast Alaska are especially precious to the communities who depend on them,” said a sentencing memorandum signed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jack Schmidt. “Illegally scuttling vessels creates risk to the environment and can create a hazard to navigation if done carelessly.”
By phone, Schmidt said it appeared as if Fisher was trying to dispose of his boat but forgot about the boat’s EPIRB — the emergency beacon that automatically deploys and messages the Coast Guard if a boat sinks.
When the Coast Guard contacted Fisher, he admitted sinking the Igloo.
Alaska has a chronic problem with abandoned and derelict vessels; maintaining boats is expensive, and disposing of an unseaworthy boat is also expensive. 
The Alaska Department of Natural Resources has a list of more than 400 abandoned boats on state land and waters.
Poling pleaded guilty on Aug. 7 and is scheduled to have his sentence imposed Oct. 29. The Anchorage U.S. Attorney’s office is recommending a fine of $6,000 and five years of probation for sinking the fishing vessel Leeward in Thomas Bay, northeast of Petersburg.
Tony Vanveen entered his guilty plea on July 27 and is scheduled to have his sentence imposed on Oct. 29 as well. Prosecutors are recommending 30 days in prison and one year of supervised release for sinking the motor vessel O’Kisutch in late September or early October 2025.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ICE arrests SCSU athlete at Tweed airport
authors: Thomas Breen, Paul Bass and Dereen Shirnekhi | New Haven Independent
description: Federal immigration agents arrested a Southern Connecticut State University SCSU basketball player at Tweed New Haven Airport on Friday.
text:
Federal immigration agents arrested a Southern Connecticut State University basketball player at Tweed New Haven Airport on Friday — as ICE has established an authorized presence at the Morris Cove regional airport.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that arrest in an email comment sent to the Independent on Tuesday.
“On September 4, at the Tweed New Haven Airport, ICE arrested Deng Deng, an illegal alien from South Sudan,” the DHS spokesperson wrote. “He legally entered the U.S. and illegally overstayed, violating the immigration laws of our country. All of his claims will be heard by an immigration judge and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law.”
A photo provided to the Independent shows that Deng was arrested while wearing a grey, long-sleeved Southern Connecticut State University shirt. Deng’s Instagram account and an article on NJ Hoops indicate that Deng attended high school in New Jersey before starting at SCSU this year. His Facebook account indicates that he is originally from the city of Aweil in South Sudan.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s online detainee locator, meanwhile, shows that Deng is currently being held at the Wyatt Detention Center in Rhode Island.
Federal court records also show that Deng, represented by local attorneys Glenn Formica and Steven Strom, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on Friday. On that same day, U.S. Judge Vernon Oliver issued an order preventing Deng from being transferred to any ICE detention facility beyond 150 miles of the Connecticut border. Deng’s case was then transferred from the District of Connecticut to the District of Massachusetts on Wednesday.
”We are aware that one of our students was detained by immigration authorities over the holiday weekend while traveling off campus,” SCSU spokesperson Jason Edwards told the Independent in an email comment Wednesday. “The university is in contact with the student and those supporting them and is assisting where appropriate. Our priority remains the student’s safety and well-being.”
All of this comes as ICE agents now have access credentials to a part of the airport parking lot reserved for law enforcement.
An Avports spokesperson told the Independent that the airport followed federal law in giving agents access credentials. He cited Section 49 CFR § 1542.209(m)(1), which states that “airport operators ‘must authorize’ unescorted access for qualifying government employees, including law enforcement officers, as long as a background check was part of the employment process. Access and credentialing remain subject to the airport’s TSA-approved security program and other applicable security requirements.”
“Airport credentials document access privileges; federal law establishes an officer’s enforcement authority,” said the spokesperson, who said ICE agents had access to the parking area reserved for law enforcement.
In a separate comment, that same spokesperson wrote, “Tweed-New Haven Airport, like all public-use airports, is subject to federal law enforcement agencies and has no visibility into or influence over enforcement activity.”
Kica Matos, who lives in New Haven and serves as president of the National Immigration Law Center, said the incident revealed that ICE apparently “has unfettered access to the entirety of Tweed Airport, and there is active coordination and complicity between the airport and ICE.” She cited activists’ photos and video of agents wearing Tweed access badges and parking in a staff lot.
“The idea that people are being detained and arrested at the Tweed Airport should be repulsive to anybody who lives in our community. We don’t want ICE here. We want them gone. It’s instilling fear across communities irrespective of immigration status,” Matos said.
Meanwhile, Anne Watkins from the New Haven Immigrants Coalition told the Independent that two community members were detained at Tweed and one at Hartford’s Bradley Airport last week.
“New Haven immigrants and others are in solidarity with Deng Deng,” Watkins said. “They [ICE] are actively at Tweed. They are parking in the Tweed parking lots, sometimes in illegal parking spaces. They have applied for and received Tweed badges. We are curious about what decisions Tweed is making to give them the kind of access that they have.”
Watkins also said that federal agents “were aggressive with legal observers and rapid responders,” and that the New Haven Police Department “threatened to cite legal observers on the ground who were trying to ensure the protection of the constitutional rights of the residents who were detained.”
“Every place, every public place is a hunting ground for ICE,” Unidad Latina en Accion lead organizer John Lugo told the Independent on Wednesday. “They’re going to increase their presence, we need to be aware about that, and we need to be careful as a community.”
In a Wednesday afternoon phone interview, Mayor Justin Elicker told the Independent that he spoke with SCSU President Sandra Bulmer on Friday about Deng’s arrest, which he described as “just awful.”
He also said that he met on Tuesday via Zoom with various Avports officials who told him the same thing they told the Independent about the airport being required to give authorized federal agents access to the airport. “We’re looking into confirming that that is true,” Elicker said.
And, in response to Watkins’ critique of city police officers’ conduct, he said that the city is currently reviewing New Haven Police Department body camera footage to see if officers interacted appropriately with activists on the scene. “We clearly want to facilitate people protesting and expressing their opinions on things,” Elicker said. People cannot, however, do such things as “block the entrance and exit to the airport and obstruct the airport from functioning.”
Elicker stressed that city police “do not coordinate with ICE,” and that there is always an officer at the airport — usually in the arrivals area. “That officer is responsible for public safety.”
Deng’s arrest comes amid a surge in ICE detentions across Connecticut and the country in recent weeks, including at airports. It also comes several months after ICE made an off-campus arrest of a SCSU nursing student on March 31. That arrest prompted a campus rally, a GoFundMe fundraiser, and concerted efforts by local activists and lawyers to secure her release on bond in May.
This story was first published Sept. 9, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Black children in SC are more likely to be detained than their white peers, report finds
description: The American Civil Liberties Union report also encouraged the state to stop locking up teens for breaking laws that apply only to minors.
text:
The Department of Juvenile Justice's detention building near Broad River Road. (File photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina locks up Black children at a higher rate than white children, found a report from a civil rights group released Wednesday.
The American Civil Liberties Union’s report, which drew from public records, came amid a push from legislators to crack down on violent crime among youth and improve conditions at the state Department of Juvenile Justice, where complaints about overcrowding and violence have persisted for years.
“Vulnerable youth are suffering through a crisis in the South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice, and our state owes them a chance at real healing and rehabilitation,” said Jace Woodrum, head of the state’s ACLU chapter, in a statement.
“We are calling on the state legislature to address the dangers and inequities exposed in this report,” Woodrum continued. “These children can’t wait another year for justice.”
Legislators’ efforts will continue this year, said Rep. Brandon Cox, a Republican from Goose Creek who led a six-member bipartisan committee tasked with tackling youth crime rates. The panel’s existence suggests an appetite among legislators to tackle the problem in the coming session, he said.
The ACLU is also suing the state agency over alleged mistreatment of youth and uninhabitable conditions. The report is not part of the lawsuit, which is ongoing, but instead meant to fill in the gaps left when DJJ stopped publishing regular reports about the number of youth housed in its facilities and the charges they faced, according to the ACLU.
A spokeswoman for DJJ did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
Racial disparities
Since 2017, the first year the ACLU included in its report, the number of youth under the age of 18 held in DJJ facilities has dropped from a daily average of 400 to 271.
Roughly three-quarters of those children are Black, the ACLU found. The report doesn’t include disparities in arrest rates or explain the reasons for the disparity.
A decade ago, in 2016, 64% of children detained were Black, and 31% were white, the group found. About 28% of youth statewide are Black, according to the report.
More than 25K SC teens committed crimes last year. Legislators are looking for solutions.

The reason for the disparity remains unclear, according to the report. However, the number of Black children detained compared with white children likely begins with which youth local law enforcement officers are stopping and arresting, which can lead to a referral to DJJ, the report reads.
“You can come and sit in our courtrooms here in Charleston County and watch the cases that are being brought before the family court, and it’s Black child after Black child after Black child after Black child,” public defense attorney Tamara Coppinger Green said in the report.
Figuring out for certain what’s driving that disparity will be key to resolving it, Cox told the Daily Gazette.
Cox wants to take a more comprehensive look at what leads children and teenagers to getting locked up. Legislators and advocates have pointed to a series of socioeconomic factors as reasons youth might commit crimes.
In 2023, 44% of Black children lived in two-parent homes, compared with 76% of white children and 67% of Hispanic children, according to the SC Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention. Black children in the state are also more likely to live in poverty, with 32% in households below the poverty line in 2023, compared to 10% of white children, according to United Health Foundation’s national data.
Addressing overlooked problems, such as child nutrition and excessive screen time, might help steer more teenagers on the right paths, Cox said. Getting to the root of the issue is important because getting out of the legal system can prove difficult for children once they’ve gotten in trouble once, he said.
“My goal is to keep children out of that system,” Cox said. “All children.”
Several of the ACLU’s proposals for improving the system include diversion programs, such as requiring family counseling before a child is sent to DJJ for non-violent offenses or encouraging community-based programs that teach children problem-solving skills. Legislators proposed bills that would do that, though none became law this year.
Status offenses
Generally, the rate of crime among children and teenagers has decreased over the past two decades, the report found. In 2005, 2,489 youth received referrals to DJJ for violent offenses. By 2025, that had fallen to 1,149.
Of the total referrals last year, roughly 14% were cited for status offenses, which are only illegal until a child turns 18. Running away, skipping school and “incorrigibility,” which means failing to listen to their parents, are all offenses that can land a youth in legal trouble.
So can loitering in a billiards hall and sneaking into an R-rated movie, though those offenses aren’t enforced. Legislators this year repealed a portion of the law banning pinball for minors, which also went unenforced.
Legislators tasked with curbing juvenile violence in SC start with teens already charged

South Carolina is the only state that locks up youth on status offenses alone, according to the ACLU.
Legislators have talked for years about eliminating status offenses, though no comprehensive bill has made it over the finish line. The effort to legalize pinball for youth took a decade of proposals to become law.
That should be a top priority for legislators when it comes to addressing crime among youth, Cox said.
“Being in the DJJ facilities, it’s pretty sad when you see a kid who skipped multiple days of school sitting next to someone who’s been accused of adult homicide,” Cox said.
‘Further traumatized’
The report was intended to take the place of regular reports the Department of Juvenile Justice stopped publishing years ago. Those featured data about its detention and evaluations centers, including how many children were housed there and what offenses they were charged with committing.
Police officers, solicitors and school officials can refer youth to DJJ for certain offenses. During the 2024-2025 fiscal year, DJJ received nearly 12,700 referrals for children as young as 5 years old, according to the report.
The agency can either release the child back to a parent or guardian or keep them in a detention center while waiting for their day in court. South Carolina has two state-run detention centers, one in Columbia and one in Greenville, as well as a youth wing at the Charleston County jail.
SC juvenile justice changeups add capacity to reduce overcrowding, violence

The agency has an estimated 356 beds, though the children housed are often not distributed evenly across buildings, meaning the detention center can remain overcrowded while evaluation facilities have beds to spare.
Once a judge has found a child delinquent, that child is evaluated and committed to DJJ to serve out the length of their sentence, which can be a set amount of time or until the youth’s 22nd birthday.
Overcrowding and general conditions for youth have improved in recent years, the report acknowledged. DJJ opened an Upstate detention center in June 2025 to increase capacity, and a treatment center for youth with mental health needs started accepting patients in March.
Still, the ACLU raised concerns about continued violence and maintenance issues at DJJ’s detention centers.
In 2025, DJJ reported nearly 850 instances of physical violence, 170 incidents described as “sexual in nature,” and 27 near fatalities. The report did not include any more details on those incidents.
Youth were reported as restrained 62 times and put in isolation 36 times that year, according to the report. That suggests an environment that punishes teens rather than rehabilitating them, the ACLU wrote.
“Traumatized children that have had, most likely, a high number of adverse childhood experiences, end up in systems where they’re further traumatized, where they’re not getting help, and also where they’re exposed to other youth with violent proclivities,” said Aleksandra Chauhan, an attorney who represented youth in court, in the report.
