name: Mississippi Today
title: Proposed changes could gut Head Start, but Mississippi’s early education programs protect some children
description: Pailan Brown participates in a coloring exercise at Franklin Head Start in Bude, Miss., Thursday, March 31, 2022.
text:
The Trump administration wants to slash federal regulations for Head Start, an anti-poverty program that has long been considered a gold standard in early childhood education. Advocates say it could drastically impact about 18,000 children served by the program in Mississippi, while researchers say that Mississippi’s state-funded, high-quality early education programs protect some Head Start centers from the changes.
Among the biggest proposed changes are removing the regulatory requirements that govern class ratios, which means class sizes could double in Mississippi, and eliminating wraparound health services, such as medical and dental screenings, for children in poverty. Trump administration officials said the changes would cut red tape and serve more students while minimizing bureaucracy for Head Start providers across the country. 
Critics say the changes would undermine the mission of Head Start, which has historically served the nation’s most vulnerable children. They also say it’s not clear that the administration would reinvest into the program the $2.2 billion it estimates saving from the proposed changes. 
The federal proposals aren’t yet final. The public can leave comments about the changes until Oct. 6. Hundreds have already weighed in, and the Trump administration must review the feedback before finalizing the changes. 
It’s hard to say how the overhaul could take shape in Mississippi, one of the nation’s poorest states. Nearly a quarter of 4-year-olds are enrolled in the program, according to an analysis by Mississippi First, an education policy organization that advocates for expanding charter school options and pre-kindergarten programs. 
Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District has one of the nation’s highest numbers of funded Head Start slots, third only to districts covering Chicago and New York City. Democratic U.S. Congressman Bennie Thompson, who represents that district, said the program needs strengthening, not weakening. 
“Head Start was created to give children from low-income families a fair shot at success. If we lower standards for things like teacher-to-student ratios, we risk giving children who already face the greatest challenges fewer resources and less support,” Thompson said in an email to Mississippi Today. 
Nita Norphlet-Thompson, executive director of the Mississippi Head Start Association, asks herself one guiding question about regulations: Are they good for children? 
The proposed regulations don’t pass her test, she said, especially when it comes to increasing the number of children teachers must be responsible for. 
“I don’t see how that’s going to improve outcomes and how that’s going to be good for children and families,” Norphlet-Thompson said. 
Bigger classes, less attention
Eloise McClinton, chair of the National Head Start Association board of directors, works in Holly Springs and oversees 21 childcare centers in 14 counties across north Mississippi. It’s already difficult to hire new teachers, she said, but if more students are put into classrooms, “everybody will be quitting.” 
It will be impossible to uphold the same standards under those conditions, she said. 
“If you take all of these things away from Head Start, then Head Start will not be Head Start as it was intended to be,” McClinton said. “It will affect the whole state of Mississippi.”
The proposed regulations default to state childcare standards for teacher-student ratios. In Mississippi, that would mean one Head Start caregiver would be responsible for nine toddlers instead of four. 
The Trump administration says the lower ratios can help Head Starts serve more students. But Micayla Tatum, a Mississippi First researcher who studies early education policy, said it would reduce education quality and safety.
Tatum worries that getting less individualized attention from teachers would hurt children’s development. 
Ikendra Fox gives Jamorion King a high-five during class at Franklin Head Start in Bude, Miss., Thursday, March 31, 2022.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Those interactions are really important at that age,” she said. “The more interactions you have, it helps you develop speech.”
Head Start programs will also no longer be required to conduct certain screenings, such as ensuring a family has ongoing medical care or insurance, that children are vaccinated and that they’ve seen a pediatrician and dentist. These services are essential components of the Head Start program to Biz Harris, executive director of the Mississippi Early Learning Alliance, which focuses on strengthening the state’s early childhood ecosystem.
With the proposed changes, centers could keep previous Head Start standards, said Alex Adams, assistant secretary of the Administration for Children and Families at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. “We trust these local programs to make good decisions.”
In theory, that might be true, said Elizabeth Pufall Jones, the director of preparation and work environment programs at the Center for the Study of Child Care Employment at the University of California at Berkeley. But it remains to be seen if centers will receive federal funding to provide more than the bare minimum once the higher standards are written out of the regulations, she said. 
Tatum shares Pufall Jones’ concerns. She said she believes there’s a good chance local grantees will follow the regulation shifts, especially if it leads to less paperwork. 
Head Start has long been an outlier within the climate of what many have called a childcare crisis. Childcare in the U.S. is unaffordable, according to standards from Health and Human Services, and is often subpar and sometimes dangerous. The Head Start program’s rules are stricter than those governing other childcare options, because the program was designed to give disadvantaged children “a head start in life,” Pufall Jones explained. 
More than 60 years after Head Start’s inception, that could all change. 
Expanding state early learning programs
Mississippi can push back against the proposed changes, researchers say. 
Mississippi’s state-funded early learning programs are highly rated by the National Institute for Early Education Research. One example is Mississippi’s early learning collaboratives, which create education partnerships between K-12 public schools, childcare centers and Head Start centers. The collaboratives, or ELCs, enroll 20% of the state’s 4-year-olds. 
Head Start centers that partner with the collaboratives will be insulated from the federal changes because they have to follow the state program’s rigorous standards. 
“Our state is very wedded to the thought of high quality pre-K programs,” Tatum said. “A good way to counter this deregulation happening at the federal level is to get more Head Starts into ELCs.”
Amid potentially wide-ranging changes, now may be the perfect time to expand those programs, said Steven Barnett, who leads NIEER. But that requires political will and resources. 
“I think the state has been moving in that direction, but you can’t just wave a magic wand and invent the teachers and the classrooms you need,” Barnett said. “Mississippi has been moving fast. Whether they can move faster, I don’t know.” 
Barnett said state leaders should consider how to supplement the ELC program and encourage Head Starts to join with the collaboratives.
Mississippi First, Tatum’s organization, found 14 school districts interested in joining the collaboratives this year — but there wasn’t state funding to expand the program. 
House Education Vice Chairman Kent McCarty, a Republican from Hattiesburg, has long advocated for increased funding for ELCs. He plans to once again introduce a bill to boost funding next session.
“This is obviously a huge priority for me,” he said. “I’ve been pushing for the last few years for universal availability to every student. These changes establish an even greater need for that.”
A ripple effect
Childcare centers, schools and Head Start agencies comprise Mississippi’s early learning ecosystem. 
“There is always going to be a ripple effect because our systems are running parallel to each other,” she said. “Whatever happens with Head Start will ripple in some way through ELCs, childcare centers and our early childhood system as a whole.”
For example, she said, if Head Starts are able to serve more families, childcare centers could lose students and money.
Under the proposed regulations, Head Start programs can also have shorter days. That could make it difficult for working parents to find additional childcare, Harris of the Mississippi Early Learning Alliance said. 
“If you only have to pay for three hours of childcare instead of five, think about the cost savings there,” Harris said. “It’s potentially the difference between keeping you in the workforce or not.”
Already, more than 6,000 Mississippi families remain on a waitlist for childcare vouchers, or coupons that make childcare more affordable. If families can’t get the childcare they need at Head Start centers, that waitlist might grow.
Harris said Mississippi needs Head Start. The program addresses children’s health and kindergarten readiness. It enables their parents to go to work. 
“I’m not sure we can overstate the ways this program is supporting some of our children most at risk of not thriving,” she said. 
At best, Harris said, the new regulations won’t tank the program, but they will drain an already burdened system.
McClinton in north Mississippi fears the worst-case scenario.
“Just because you have written it on paper that you’re gonna have that billions of dollars in savings and get to serve more children doesn’t mean that it will actually come back into the program.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: State doles out millions of dollars for flood and fire-related repairs
description: An infusion of state aid will help restore a Spokane landfill ravaged by last month’s Old Trails Fire and reconstruct a Chelan County road washed out by last winter’s historic flooding. The Washington State Public Works Board has approved $7.45 million in loans and grants for local governments in Chelan, Franklin, Grays Harbor, King, Lewis, […]
text:
Flood waters in Chelan County during December 2025.  The state Public Works Board has approved funding to rebuild part of a road washed out when the Stehekin River overflowed its banks. (Photo courtesy of the Department of Commerce)An infusion of state aid will help restore a Spokane landfill ravaged by last month’s Old Trails Fire and reconstruct a Chelan County road washed out by last winter’s historic flooding.
The Washington State Public Works Board has approved $7.45 million in loans and grants for local governments in Chelan, Franklin, Grays Harbor, King, Lewis, Spokane and Walla Walla counties. The money will be spent on emergency projects including repairs to and restoration of essential services.
Of the total, $2 million is for three emergency projects in eastern Washington and $5.45 million will assist four Washington communities dealing with damage from the flooding.
“Public works infrastructure is the backbone of every community across Washington state,” Vince McGowan, chair of the 13-member panel, said in a statement. The board, he said, “is proud to be a small part of disaster recovery by getting recovery funds in the hands of the communities that need them as quickly and efficiently as possible.”
The city of Spokane is getting a $1 million loan for emergency work at the Northside Landfill where electrical service and roughly three-quarters of the vegetation cover were damaged by the Old Trails Fire. That blaze is one of three Spokane-area fires that damaged or destroyed more than 800 structures. Money will be spent to restore vegetation and electrical power serving landfill-gas systems.
Also on the east side of the state, the city of Connell, Franklin County, is getting a $612,000 loan and $108,000 grant to repair the city’s damaged wastewater treatment lagoons and the city of Waitsburg in Walla Walla County received a $255,000 loan and $45,000 grant to fix a failed sewer pipe. The sewer line is a major collector for the city and its failure would lead to widespread sewer back-ups, according to the state Department of Commerce.
Four communities are getting help with infrastructure wrecked by the atmospheric river that hit the state in December.

The cities of Kent, in King County, and Hoquiam, in Grays Harbor County, were each awarded $2 million.
In Kent, it will go toward work on a low-lying section of South 259th Street where the Green River overflowed its banks and water reached emergency flood barriers erected along the roadway.
Hoquiam will use its funding to repair a segment of Broadway Avenue  along the Hoquiam River that is on the verge of catastrophic failure due to damage caused by king tides and heavy runoff, according to the release.
Chelan County was awarded $750,000 for reconstruction of a 400-foot stretch of Company Creek Road which was washed out by severe flooding of the Stehekin River.  Floodwaters reached their highest level since record-keeping began more than a century ago, destroying a levee that had protected downstream private and public facilities, according to the state Department of Commerce.
“Failure to complete the project will likely result in significant loss of property and life as well as loss of public access to the western end of the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area,” Mike Kaputa, director of the Chelan County Department of Natural Resources, wrote in the county’s funding application.
The city of Chehalis, Lewis County, received $700,000 to repair and reopen the Exhibitor Avenue Bridge. It was closed to traffic in June due to structural and safety concerns caused by the flooding.
The funding approved by the board on Sept. 4 came from two buckets. Money for the eastern Washington communities came from an emergency fund maintained by the board. It is open until the money is given out. There is $5.1 million left for the current budget cycle.
Funding for the flood-related damages comes from a special $10 million appropriation by the Legislature to the board earlier this year.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Montclair State University has extraordinary responsibility overseeing NJ PBS
description: Montclair State University has a great opportunity and an extraordinary responsibility as the new operator of NJ PBS.
text:
Students walk on the Montclair State University campus. The school is embarking on a new role as operator of NJ PBS. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
New Jersey has long had an unusual problem for a state of nearly 10 million people: We live in the shadow of two of the largest media markets in the country, yet neither is primarily responsible for covering us.
New York looks east across the Hudson. Philadelphia looks west across the Delaware. In between are 564 municipalities, hundreds of school districts, a state government in Trenton, and millions of residents whose daily lives are shaped by decisions that rarely make the evening news in either neighboring city.
The Center for Cooperative Media has described this as a structural problem for New Jersey journalism. Our position between New York and Philadelphia siphons away advertising revenue, audience attention, and journalistic talent.
Last month, New Jersey took an intriguing step toward addressing that problem.
Montclair State University announced that it will acquire NJ Spotlight News, the statewide policy and government news organization founded in 2010. The acquisition from the WNET Group includes the NJ Spotlight News name, its website, and an archive of more than 26,000 articles. Founding editor John Mooney has been retained to help lead the transition.
By itself, preserving a respected New Jersey newsroom would be significant. But this acquisition comes barely a month after Montclair State assumed operation of NJ PBS, the state’s public television network.
Taken together, these developments have created something considerably more consequential.
A New Jersey public university now sits at the intersection of statewide public television, public-policy journalism, journalism education, and a network of hundreds of local news organizations.
Montclair State has an opportunity to build something New Jersey desperately needs: a genuine statewide civic-information institution.
We frequently speak about universities as civic institutions. We tell students that higher education prepares citizens, strengthens communities, and contributes to democracy. Those claims can sometimes feel abstract.
Montclair State now has the chance to make them tangible.
The university enters this role with an asset few universities could replicate. Its Center for Cooperative Media already coordinates the NJ News Commons, connecting more than 300 local news and information providers across New Jersey. The university therefore has the potential to connect statewide reporting with local outlets, public television, students, faculty and communities across the state.
But that opportunity comes with an equally extraordinary responsibility.
For this experiment to work, Montclair State must protect the independence of the journalists now operating under its institutional umbrella, including when their reporting becomes uncomfortable for the school itself.
A public university is hardly a neutral observer in New Jersey politics. Its leadership deals with state appropriations, elected officials, unions, employees, students, donors, and competing public interests. Universities experience protests, personnel controversies, budget disputes, and questions about how public money is spent.
Eventually, one of those stories will involve Montclair State.
When that day comes, the real test of this arrangement will begin.
Could an NJ Spotlight News reporter aggressively investigate the university president’s administration? Could NJ PBS scrutinize Montclair’s finances or employment practices? Could journalists pursue a story that embarrasses the institution housing their newsroom or creates problems for university leaders in Trenton?
The answer has to be yes.
Fortunately, Montclair appears to recognize this tension. When the state selected the university to operate NJ PBS, Montclair State committed to a code of journalism ethics, an independent ethics committee with external appointments, and a community advisory board. As a public university, it is also subject to New Jersey’s Open Public Records Act.
Those safeguards should now become central to the NJ Spotlight News transition.
They should be strong enough that editorial decisions cannot be quietly influenced by university administrators, political officials, or institutional priorities. The ethics committee should have meaningful independence. The public should understand how complaints about editorial interference can be raised. Journalists should know that scrutinizing their institutional home will be protected rather than merely tolerated.
This matters because the greatest danger here is also what makes the experiment so promising: Montclair State is becoming powerful within New Jersey’s civic-information ecosystem.
That power should be welcomed, but accompanied by transparency and accountability.
There is a larger lesson here for higher education, too.
At a moment when universities are frequently asked to justify their civic value, Montclair State may be developing a compelling answer. A public university can educate students while also helping citizens understand the institutions governing their communities. It can prepare future journalists while sustaining journalism in the present. It can convene communities while providing them with the information necessary to govern themselves.
That is a more meaningful contribution to democracy than another campus statement about the importance of civic engagement.
New Jersey should want this experiment to succeed.
But success should ultimately be measured by something more demanding than whether NJ PBS remains on the air or whether NJ Spotlight’s archive remains online.
Years from now, New Jerseyans should be able to look to this institution and find rigorous reporting about their governor, Legislature, schools, towns, public agencies and universities.
Including Montclair State.
If Montclair can build a newsroom strong enough to hold even itself accountable, New Jersey will have gained something far more important than a new owner for a news organization.
It will have gained civic infrastructure.
Alejandro J. Ramos is the founder and executive director of the Ramos Research Institute, a New Jersey-based nonpartisan research organization focused on democracy, civic education, media literacy, and public leadership. He is a doctoral student at Vanderbilt University, holds an M.P.A. from Cornell University’s Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Inside the network helping NJ immigrants during mass deportation effort
description: A patchwork of advocates, officials, and faith leaders has aided immigrants in the last 20 months as President Trump has cracked down on illegal immigration.
text:
Pierre Delaforcade of Montclair holds a sign while flashing the peace sign outside the Delaney Hall immigrant jail in Newark on Nov. 6, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
This is the third in a three-part series examining President Donald Trump’s mass deportation effort and its effect on New Jersey.
New Jersey has become a key battleground in the national fight over President Donald Trump’s efforts of mass detention and deportation.
The Garden State is home to two detention centers, including one of the East Coast’s largest, with a third proposed in a warehouse in Roxbury. But it’s also home to a patchwork of advocates, officials, and faith leaders who are finding ways to respond to a crisis with no clear end. 
These aren’t people who are in danger of deportation themselves, but are living with the consequences of this moment in different ways. Their roles are different — some hold institutional power, others operate entirely outside of it — but they’re all navigating new ways to help migrants living under direct threat. 
Jorge Torres of the National Day Laborers Organizing Network at an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse, Freehold, Friday, March 27, 2025. (Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Jorge Torres of the National Day Laborers Organizing Network at an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Asma Elhuni of Resistencia en Acción NJ speaks at an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Protestors attend an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rachel Peace speaks during an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A mother talks about how her son was taken from work by ICE during an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Jorge Torres of the National Day Laborers Organizing Network carries a banner at an Ice Out rally and protest at the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
At 16 years old, Jorge Torres left Ecuador with his family for the U.S. to chase the promise that has drawn immigrants to America for generations.
He overstayed his visa, ended up working in factories and fast food restaurants, and navigated nearly nine years without legal papers. His father gave him clear, simple instructions: Don’t tell anyone about your status, don’t speak Spanish, and don’t talk to the police.
He eventually gained citizenship through marriage. And now, at 41, he is a prolific immigration organizer in central Jersey. He settled in New Jersey in the early 1980s, founding what was then called Unidad Latina en Accion New Jersey, now known as Resistencia en Accion. 
He’s also the director for the National Day Laborer Organizing Network and runs a rapid response operation that has grown in response to the escalating raids under Trump’s second term. 
The exhausting work is always personal to Torres. 
“I know what it is to live under that pressure firsthand,” Torres said in an interview in Spanish. “I have family members who are still undocumented.”
He has been calling for the abolition of ICE since he started his movement, then a radical stance even in progressive circles. While other nonprofits focused on policy wins like labor protections, driver’s license access, and wage theft legislation (policies he supports), he was focused on closing detention centers and defunding enforcement.
He remembers being treated like “the strange one in the room.” But he no longer feels that way; he feels vindicated and equally upset at the outcome. 
Since 2025, Torres has helped build the ICE Out of New Jersey coalition, drawing on years of relationships with other grassroots organizations across the state, including CATA, New Labor, and Cosecha. The rapid response network stretches from Mercer County to Essex County. 
When a raid is reported, the call goes into a coordinated group chat, the location gets checked against a statewide map, and trained volunteers — of which there are hundreds — are dispatched to the spot. He said that often, responders show up after ICE is already gone, but the volunteers serve other purposes, like tracking what’s happening, connecting families to legal help, and confirming that someone in the community is paying attention. 
He’s also built out independent Spanish-language media, including his own radio show, because he said mainstream outlets were not challenging enough of Trump’s messaging. 
“Only the people can save the people,” he said. “No politician is going to think about us without us. That’s why I keep doing this and finding new ways to bring attention to what is happening.” 
Kathy O’Leary with Pax Christi shows the state of a supplies tent she operates next to Delaney Hall, the Newark immigrant detention center, on June 1. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Every week, hundreds of people make their way to Newark to stand for hours on line outside of Delaney Hall, one of the largest immigration detention centers on the East Coast. Some of them make their first stop at a folding table near the entrance, where Kathy O’Leary hands out donated clothes. 
Delaney Hall, which opened its doors in May 2025 and has regularly housed over 1,000 detainees at any given time, enforces a strict dress code. Ripped jeans, open-toed shoes, graphic tees, leggings are all reasons desperate visitors have been turned away by unforgiving guards. So O’Leary, who has done immigration advocacy in New Jersey for nearly two decades, keeps a supply of clean shirts and guard-approved pants on hand for anyone who shows up.
She started doing it last June after a woman who had driven four hours from Boston to visit her detained father was denied entry for ripped jeans. The visitor looked for a volunteer about the same size as her and switched pants in the parking lot to get inside. 
O’Leary said she knows the dress code isn’t a safety measure, but a mechanism of attrition. 
“We understood that getting people in to see their loved ones was an act of resistance. The system is set up so that people inside give up hope and sign voluntary departure forms and leave the country,” she said. “Having a visit from a loved one gives people the strength to keep fighting.” 
Delaney Hall almost immediately became a flashpoint in the immigration enforcement debate upon its opening. Hundreds of protests have been held outside. Democratic politicians are regularly there to hold press conferences, calling attention to pastors and restaurant owners who have been arrested by ICE. The Newark mayor was arrested outside the gates, which led to the felony indictment of a congresswoman accused of assaulting agents during the arrest.
The unrest escalated sharply in late May of this year, when 300 detainees inside said they launched a month-long hunger and labor strike over abysmal conditions: moldy food, abuse by guards, and a severe lack of medical attention. It prompted massive protests outside the facility, and clashes between demonstrators and ICE agents armed with batons and pepper spray.  
New Jersey State Police temporarily took command of the area before Newark police assumed control and Baraka imposed a nightly curfew; several protesters were arrested in the days that followed. That unrest also touched the visitation lines O’Leary spends her afternoons working. The curfew narrowed the hours families had to wait in line for a visit and required detainees to submit a list of approved visitors, more obstacles layered onto a dress code that advocates believe is meant to turn visitors away.
While she’s skeptical of politicians using Delaney Hall as a backdrop for press events, O’Leary has been there regularly, about four to five times a week, since the jail opened. She keeps track of the buses that drop off detainees, and takes an informal count of visitors on the line snaking around the front lot, where industrial trucks zoom past on Doreamus Avenue. Weeknights can see 200 visitors, and on weekends, she’s counted over 300, she said. She noted that the facility has been moving detainees between units and transferring others out on buses. 
“We have lists of people in dire need of medical care. People are getting off the buses on crutches, people who are blind, people who are supposed to be getting chemotherapy, people who shouldn’t be in there under any circumstances,” she said. “To just use it as a backdrop for a political campaign doesn’t help anyone but themselves. There’s work that needs to get done.” 
While immigration enforcement has escalated under Trump, she dismisses the notion that it’s only his fault. She started this work as a pregnant woman over 20 years ago after hearing a story of a woman who had been taken in a raid from her apartment while breastfeeding her youngest child, forcing the infant to be weaned. That mother spent months in detention before being deported. 
Her advocacy has shifted from legislation and policy to helping people who are inside the jail and pushing for individual releases, along with overarching calls to close immigration detention across the country. 
“This system wasn’t built by Trump. You can trace it back to at least Clinton. All the Democrats have lined up almost as quickly as Republicans to give more money to ICE over all these years,” she said. 
She laments that the facility won’t close any time soon. She plans to return next week, and the week after, with more clothes at the folding tables.
Monmouth County Prosecutor Raymond S. Santiago, only the second Latino to hold that office in the county, speaks during an interview on March 4. (Photo courtesy of Thomas P. Costello/Asbury Park Press)
Raymond Santiago’s earliest memories are of large family gatherings. Eating roasted pig at barbecues, the aroma of gandules and pernil filling the air as relatives crowded together in his childhood home in Santurce, just outside of San Juan, Puerto Rico.
He lived there until he was 5, eventually moving to Brooklyn with his father, from Ponce, and his mom, from New York. He says he grew up carrying those roots with him. He took his own children back to see his small childhood home years later, to ensure they understood where their family came from. 
He didn’t grow up expecting to become a prosecutor. And he didn’t expect that the job would one day require him to consider whether his last name would make him a target. 
“Having the surname Santiago doesn’t help me at all,” he said with a chuckle.
He said he’s weighed avoiding international travel, and carries his passport more often than he used to. 
Santiago is the Monmouth County prosecutor — only the second Latino in the state to hold that office in its roughly 200-year history — nominated by then-Gov. Phil Murphy in 2022. He has been a public defender, a private criminal defense attorney, and most relevant to this moment, an immigration lawyer. He knows the difference between a U-visa and a T-visa, and he’s witnessed what happens when someone’s work authorization lapses because their employer has retaliated. 
He said that knowledge has become an animating force of his tenure in office as the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement has intensified across New Jersey, and the country. Santiago says the most profound change he’s witnessed in Monmouth County is the silence. 
There’s a growing reluctance among immigrant residents to come forward as victims or witnesses in criminal cases, he said. And criminals who have long preyed on migrants because they know their targets fear the police are taking advantage. Domestic abusers use immigration status as a weapon. 
Even people who may have trusted local law enforcement just two years ago are pulling back, he noted. 
“I don’t want people suffering in silence,” he said. “Who’s suffering in silence that I can’t help because they won’t come forward?” 
He says part of his role as prosecutor is to build trust between Monmouth County residents and local police. He’s held community events to explain that visas are available to victims of crime who lack legal status and how they offer a pathway to remain in the country in exchange for cooperating with police.
He launched We Are Monmouth, an initiative that brings together faith leaders, community activists, and local police chiefs. He attends town halls on immigration, and supports know-your-rights meetings hosted by immigrant advocates. He has re-briefed every police agency in the county on the state’s policy that largely bars local cooperation with federal immigrant agents.
A version of that directive, originally issued as an attorney general’s order in 2018, was signed into law by Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill earlier this year. Santiago had testified in support at the Statehouse, stressing the importance of codifying the policy into law. The law bars local officers from asking about immigration status, participating in civil immigration enforcement, or detaining people on ICE’s behalf in many circumstances.
For Santiago, he says it’s a legal shield and a practical tool. He bristles at the suggestion that it handicaps law enforcement, as other prosecutors have alleged. 
“The ability for law enforcement to do their jobs in keeping communities safe involves being able to have trust with the community itself,” he said. “If that deteriorates, it’ll be very difficult for us to keep the streets safe.” 
He said he’s petrified of the chaos surrounding immigration that has unfolded across the country and whether it could ever come to Monmouth County. He says he’s optimistic about a fresh administration in Trenton, and is confident that the state’s legal framework is on strong footing. But he’s also honest and clear-eyed about the damage already done, comparing the erosion of trust to the years it took to rebuild relationships with communities after the racial reckoning of 2020. 
“What we’re seeing here is so much more profound in such a short time,” Santiago said. “I’m truly concerned with how we repair the damage that’s being done.” 
Pastor Pete Ahn in the Metro Community Church offices in Englewood on April 3. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Pastor Peter Ahn founded the Metro Community Church in Englewood 22 years ago on a simple premise: people shouldn’t gather around strength and achievement, but around vulnerability, struggle, and shared pain.
He said the church, where the congregation is about 75% Asian, draws people who feel like they don’t fit anywhere else. And when the Trump administration launched its crackdown on immigrants, that instinct to shelter the vulnerable was put to the test.
Some Latino families who attended Metro regularly stopped showing up on Sundays, too scared to leave their homes. Now, Ahn and his staff developed what he calls an “ICE drill,” a protocol for what the congregation would do if federal agents show up during a service. 
His staff includes a Guatemalan pastor who holds a green card and constantly wakes up fearing it will be the day he gets unlawfully deported. Ahn wanted to bring him on a mission speaking trip to Argentina this fall, and asked lawyers whether it was safe. They said no — he might not make it back into the U.S. 
“That’s the climate we’ve been living in,” Ahn said. “It’s not just the undocumented community. It’s people who are here legally too. They’re afraid to travel. They’re afraid they’re not going to be able to get back to their families.” 
Ahn is Korean-American, the son of immigrants who came to America in the 1970s when South Korea was among the poorest nations in the world. He was born malnourished, and when doctors told his parents the medicine he needed to survive didn’t exist there, they moved to New York when he was 3 months old. He later moved to Bergen County, home to over 100,000 Koreans. 
He said the story of his own family’s immigration isn’t so distant from the stories of the immigrants sitting in his church pews. They all came here to chase safety and dreams, and that drives his work. 
But Ahn acknowledged that it doesn’t always land with everyone in the congregation. He’s made the case that welcoming immigrants isn’t a political act, but a spiritual one, pointing to biblical stories like Joseph and Mary fleeing to Egypt when Jesus was an infant. He’s recognized that many members don’t hear it that way.
People have left his church over these sermons in the past. When he was vocal about Trayvon Martin’s killing over a decade ago, a churchgoer wrote him a letter saying he committed a sin from the pulpit, and he lost generous donors. But Ahn said he had no choice but to continue, and the congregation emerged stronger for it, because people who stayed built something powerful. 
Most Korean American congregations in Bergen County are silent on what’s happening to their immigrant neighbors, he said, in part because it doesn’t touch their community directly. He finds that disappointing, and theologically indefensible. 
“The gospel is about fighting injustice,” he said. “There’s a political aspect to it, and for some reason, a lot of churches just really believe in this idea of separation of church and state, so a lot of churches stay silent on it. It’s tragic.” 
Ahn said he’s still learning lessons. Earlier this year, a family who lacked legal status left his congregation and quietly moved back to their home country because they feared they’d be separated from their children. Ahn questions whether the church did enough to help them, and he thinks the answer is no — he got too focused on running the church. 
“Who cares about a budget? We should have done whatever we could to support that family, even financially. If it means our church goes into debt, I think that’s a beautiful thing for us to do,” he said. 
Now, Metro has begun paying for immigration attorneys for congregation members who can’t afford representation, and has helped people complete asylum applications. He wants to do more, like offer housing and deeper legal support. He wants to open his home to Latino families for dinner, even though he doesn’t speak Spanish. 
“We’re on a journey. We’re not amazing at this. We’re growing,” he said. “And I dropped the ball, but I think I have a second chance at doing better now.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: It’s time to fix Missouri’s charter school funding system
description: The title of this column may give some readers a sense of déjà vu. After all, it was only a few years ago that Missouri legislators tried to close the longstanding funding gap between the state’s charter and traditional public schools by passing House Bill 1552, which boosted funding for charters by nearly $4,000 per […]
text:
Students work in a classroom  in Salt Lake City in 2024. As AI use in schools grows, more lawmakers and districts aim to put guidelines in place (Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch).The title of this column may give some readers a sense of déjà vu.
After all, it was only a few years ago that Missouri legislators tried to close the longstanding funding gap between the state’s charter and traditional public schools by passing House Bill 1552, which boosted funding for charters by nearly $4,000 per pupil.
That was a big win for charters – public schools that are run by non-profits rather than the government. As we document in a new study, the extra money allowed charter schools to hire more teachers and support staff and appears to have boosted teacher experience and students’ year-to-year growth in math.
Yet, despite HB 1552’s passage, our analysis shows that Missouri’s charter schools still receive about roughly 20 percent – or about $5,500 – less in total revenue per pupil than traditional public schools in the same city.
Importantly, this gap is not attributable to differences in the number of low-income students, English learners, or special education students – all groups that are typically associated with more funding. Nor is it attributable to post-pandemic differences in emergency funding from the federal government.
Rather, the biggest reason for its persistence is that traditional school districts have little to no legal obligation to share the local revenues they receive with charters, which now educate nearly half of Kansas City and St. Louis students.
Missouri’s school finance system is designed to provide public schools with a mix of local and state revenues, in addition to federal payments. However, because they aren’t taxing bodies, charters don’t receive local property tax revenue. And because enrollment in traditional public schools is declining, local funding per district pupil is increasing.
Consequently, the state must make ever larger payments to charters just to keep pace with districts like SLPS and KCPS.When HB 1552 was passed, the anticipated cost was $2,400 to $2,700 per pupil. The real cost is double that amount – and rising.
Essentially, every local tax dollar that goes to traditional public schools in Missouri’s two big cities is now matched by a state dollar that goes to charters. Simple arithmetic implies that the state’s “match rate” will increase if, as has been the case, the share of students who enroll in charters rises and the same local dollars are divided between ever fewer district students.
That’s unsustainable, given the state of Missouri’s finances.
It’s also unfair. After all, schools should be funded based on the number of students they serve, even if that means schools that are serving fewer students get less money. And of course, kids in charter schools should have the same resources and opportunities as students in traditional public schools.
As far as we can tell, only one solution accomplishes all those things simultaneously: Insist that all schools get their fair share of state and local revenues by pooling those funds. Treat every student as equally worthy of public investment. Let public dollars follow kids to the public schools of their families’ choosing.

title: As state officials pursue route change for Idaho Centennial Trail, here’s how to give your feedback
description: The Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation Board is seeking to change a section of the Idaho Centennial Trail’s official route to improve hikers’ safety and avoid a dangerous creek crossing, state officials announced Sept. 3.  The Idaho Centennial Trail, or ICT for short, is a more than 900-mile trail that crosses the entire state […]
text:
The Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation is changing a section of the Idaho Centennial Trail to improve hikers' safety and avoid a dangerous creek crossing, state officials said. (File photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation)The Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation Board is seeking to change a section of the Idaho Centennial Trail’s official route to improve hikers’ safety and avoid a dangerous creek crossing, state officials announced Sept. 3. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Idaho Centennial Trail, or ICT for short, is a more than 900-mile trail that crosses the entire state of Idaho, from the desert at the Idaho-Nevada border, all the way up to the Canadian border. Along the route, the trail passes through some of the most wild, scenic and remote places in Idaho, including the Frank Church-River of No Return Wilderness, the Sawtooth Wilderness and the Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness.
Although a few people complete the Idaho Centennial Trail as a thru-hike in a single, months-long push, the trail is broken up into segments and utilizes other, existing trails to allow different users the opportunity to enjoy smaller sections of the trail without having to navigate the entire trail.
The new route change involves adding about nine miles to the Idaho Centennial Trail to avoid an unabridged crossing of Big Creek in the Salmon-Challis National Forest. 
Rather than forcing hikers and backpackers to ford Big Creek, the new route will follow Milk Creek Trail 064 and Monumental Creek Trail 005 to allow hikers to safely cross Big Creek at a bridge near the junction with Monumental Creek, Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation officials said.
The purple line indicates the route of the Idaho Centennial Trail, which offers an East Alternative and a West Alternative to give users options for navigating wilderness areas and the Sawtooth Mountain Range. (Map courtesy of the Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation)
“A longer trail isn’t always a better trail, but in this case, the additional miles provide a significant safety benefit,” Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation Director Susan Buxton said in a written statement. “By routing the Idaho Centennial Trail across an existing bridge, we can help ensure that more people can experience this incredible section of the ICT without having to take on a potentially dangerous creek crossing.”
The official route for the Idaho Continental Trail was approved in 1990 by the Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation Board, which has the authority to change routes on the trail in partnership with land managers and the public. 
Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation officials said their counterparts with the Salmon-Challis National Forest support the change, and they are opening a 30-day public comment period about the route change. 
To offer public comment, send an email to Hailey Husband, the Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation’s nonmotorized trails coordinator, at hailey.husband@idpr.idaho.gov or call 208-514-2419.

title: Woman rallies for her daughters, other victims of violent crimes
description:
The founder of MMIR 307 is asking Wyoming’s Department of Corrections not to allow one of the men convicted in her daughter's murder into a community corrections program. 
The post Woman rallies for her daughters, other victims of violent crimes appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—You can find Nicole Wagon outside the courthouse in a huddle with a victim’s family members, handing out advice about what comes next in their loved one’s court case.
Sometimes, she’s the voice on the line on a frantic call when a child goes missing or sharing a missing-person poster template, the best way to communicate with authorities – whatever a family might need in those crucial moments.
A missing and murdered Indigenous advocate, Wagon is the founder of MMIR 307, and she never knows what the day will bring in her fight for justice. Some days she’s fighting for her own family.
Wagon recently sat down and penned a letter to state Department of Corrections officials, urging them not to place one of the men convicted in her daughter’s murder into a community corrections program. Last spring, she successfully lobbied against his release on parole.
He’s one of four convicted in her daughter Jocelyn Watt’s murder, and Wagon knows there will be more parole hearings, more letters.
Juggling her broader advocacy work with her family’s fight for justice isn’t always easy, but Wagon says each step is one of healing.
“With your own experience, I think people should help others, and I’ve already gone through those storms. Now with the parole hearing, it feels like it’s never going to stop. But through each one, I truly believe you heal with yourself. Every walk, every march, every letter, it’s a healing,” she said. “It’s so easy to get lost within the grief and the sorrow, but who else is going to be able to advocate for them?”
Thrust into the fight
In January 2019, Jocelyn and her partner, Rudy Perez, were murdered in their Riverton home. Just a year later, in 2020, Wagon’s other daughter, Jade, was found dead on the Wind River Indian Reservation weeks after being reported missing.
Wagon had to wait years for answers in Jocelyn’s case — four people were arrested in late 2021 in connection with her death. She’s still waiting for justice for Jade.
In the wake of her daughter’s deaths, Wagon said she realized there was little help out there for victims and their families.
She put it simply: “There was nothing.”

Jade Wagon (Courtesy)

As Wagon navigated the criminal justice system herself, she also began rallying for change as an advocate. She was invited to and joined the Wyoming MMIP Task Force, which began studying the issue of Missing and Murdered Indigenous People in Wyoming and pursuing structural changes.
In 2021, when Gabrielle Petito went missing and sparked a nationwide media frenzy, Wagon’s daughters’ stories bore a striking dichotomy: Missing and murdered Indigenous people’s cases rarely gain as much attention.
Wagon has testified before the state Legislature, national committees, task forces and leaders across the country, pushing for structural change. She’s helped usher in the Ashanti Alert system, an emergency alert used to locate missing and endangered people over the age of 17 who don’t qualify for Amber Alerts. 
Her testimony helped pass a slew of law enforcement reforms in 2024 aimed at improving how missing persons cases are handled and reported by Wyoming law enforcement agencies. And she was integral in bringing victim advocate services to the Bureau of Indian Affairs office on the Wind River Reservation.
“Every year that passes, you try to make it better,” she said on justice system reforms.
Much of Wagon’s work happens during those late-night, frantic phone calls, parents searching for their lost kids, families suffering in the wake of losing a loved one. She watches local criminal cases closely, shows up at court hearings and helps families navigate what they can do to become advocates for their loved ones and themselves.
“I know how important it is to be involved with the criminal justice system, even if it sometimes feels overwhelming. But to stay focused on the issue and get justice for your child, the momma bear comes up in you,” she said.
Jocelyn’s case
On Jan. 4, 2019, Watt and Perez were shot and killed inside Watt’s home in Riverton during a robbery. Two years later, Brandon Monroe was arrested and later sentenced to two life prison sentences. His accomplices, Bryce Teran, Patrick SunRhodes and Korbin Headley, were also convicted for their roles that night.
Teran is the first to come up for parole and now for a bid to be housed at a more relaxed Wyoming facility.
Teran was the driver the night of the double homicide, and police used his cellphone data to pinpoint his location at the scene; he later cooperated in the investigation. He pleaded no contest to aiding and abetting burglary and was sentenced to 8-10 years with credit for just under two years in jail.

Jocelyn Watt (Courtesy)

Wagon, in writing to the Wyoming Community Corrections Placement Board, said she was opposed to his placement in a community corrections setting.
“I have already stood before the court and asked for the maximum sentence for Mr. Teran. I did so because two people were murdered in their own home, and because the consequences of those actions did not end when the police finally identified the people responsible,” she wrote. “They continue every single day.”
Jocelyn had a life, a special smile, a family, hopes and dreams. And she had people who loved her, Wagon shared.
“She was not simply a victim in a case file,” Wagon said. “She was my child.”
Teran was the only adult convicted in Jocelyn’s murder, and for nearly two years, he stayed silent about what happened, Wagon told the board. 
“For nearly two years, we had to live with the uncertainty of not knowing who had done this to our loved ones. The community felt unsafe. People wondered who could have committed such a terrible crime and whether those responsible were still around us,” she continued. “Those were two years of grief, fear, unanswered questions and wondering whether justice would ever come.”
The Placement Board will determine whether Teran can be placed in a community setting, where he would be allowed to work in the community and potentially be released on furloughs.
Wagon said she couldn’t support that.
“When I hear the words ‘community corrections,’ I think about the community that was left traumatized by what happened to Jocelyn and Rudy. I think about the families who still live with their absence,” Wagon wrote. “How do we make our communities feel safe again when people who played a role in such a devastating crime are returned to the community before completing their sentence? … There is often discussion about rehabilitation, second chances and helping someone build a better life. I believe people can change, and I believe people can seek redemption. But accountability must remain part of that process.”
Jocelyn, Wagon told the board, deserves to be remembered for the life she lived, not the way she died. 
“I ask the Community Corrections Board to look beyond Mr. Teran’s desire to return to the community and remember the people who can never return to theirs,” she said.
A sacred balance
Wagon now raises Jade’s son and daughter as her own as she juggles her advocacy work and her own continued fight for justice for Jocelyn and Jade.
“For me, it’s harder to watch my kids, what they went through,” she said of the two youngsters.
As she sat down to pen her letter to the parole board this spring, and now to the corrections board, she said she leaned on tradition, burning green cedar, then reading and refining, then reading again, to get her statement just right.
“I see [Jade’s] spirit through my grandkids, their mannerisms,” she said. “It just gives me joy.”
Wagon believes it’s the children who are sacred, and she often tells families lost in new grief to focus on them as a light in the darkness. Having her own grandchildren who needed her, she said, is what got her through the darkest days after the losses of her daughters.
“I need my grandkids as much as they need me,” she said. Knowing they are safe, protected, “That gives me comfort.”
Wagon expects to hear the ruling from the Community Corrections Board on Sept. 14.

title: The Wyoming agriculture industry’s outsized influence and consumption
description:
Data doesn’t back up the state’s image as an agrarian powerhouse, writes Dagny Signorelli.
The post The Wyoming agriculture industry’s outsized influence and consumption appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

Agriculture is routinely invoked as one of the foundations of Wyoming’s economy, particularly when decisions involve public lands and access, water or wildlife. But if an industry is truly an economic “backbone,” the data should support that assertion. It should account for a substantial share of employment, wages and economic production.
Agriculture does none of those things.
The most recent annual employment data from the Wyoming Department of Workforce Services show that the entire private agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector supported almost exactly 1% of Wyoming employment.

Beef cattle ranching and farming, the industry arguably most synonymous with the Cowboy State, accounted for just 0.6% of 2025 statewide employment.
The wage numbers also fail to surpass 1% of Wyoming’s overall wages. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting generated approximately 0.74% of Wyoming wages. Average annual pay in the agriculture sector was $46,709, well below the state average of $63,511. In 2024, the entire agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector — which combines livestock grazing on public and private lands, farming, and guiding and outfitting business — generated just 1.5% of state gross domestic product. 

That was not an anomalous year. Looking back through the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis data, agriculture has produced a small fraction of Wyoming’s total economic output for decades.

For comparison, the mining industry (which includes oil and gas) generated approximately $6.9 billion of the $51 billion Wyoming GDP in 2024, more than 10 times the value added by agriculture. Construction generated approximately $3.2 billion.
Perhaps more revealing is outdoor recreation.
In 2024, the Bureau of Economic Analysis calculated that outdoor recreation generated 4.5% of state GDP, more than three times the economic contribution of crop and animal production, and supported 16,545 jobs.
The contrast becomes even more striking when economic footprint is compared with physical footprint.
The University of Wyoming Extension identifies irrigated agriculture as Wyoming’s largest consumptive water use by far. Its statewide water analysis estimates that irrigated agriculture accounts for 80 to 85% of all consumptive water use (water removed from the available supply and not returned to the hydrologic system) in Wyoming. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s 2023 Irrigation and Water Management Survey found that about 87% of Wyoming’s irrigated acreage was devoted to alfalfa, other hay, or pasture, forage and grazing resources used to support livestock production.

USDA’s 2024 Wyoming agricultural statistics report estimates that the state’s agricultural exports were worth $409.6 million, equivalent to about 21.5% of total farm cash receipts.
The much larger numbers commonly cited for agriculture measure something different. The familiar $1.6 billion figure cited in the news represents gross agricultural sales, not value added, while University of Wyoming’s $2.5 billion ‘economic impact’ estimate also includes spending by suppliers and households. Those ripple effects occur in every industry, which is why economic impact totals should not be compared directly with GDP.
This complicates a political argument Wyoming residents hear constantly: that extraordinary public accommodation of agriculture is necessary because ranching is indispensable to Wyoming’s economy, or because Wyoming agriculture is necessary to “feed America.” Wyoming’s outsized resource commitment does not translate into outsized cattle production: The state produced just 1.2% of the nation’s cattle and calves by weight in 2025, while Wisconsin produced nearly three times as much.
Agriculture is a small part of Wyoming’s modern economy, but an enormous consumer of its natural resources. Ranching interests are routinely given extraordinary weight in debates over public lands, water allocation, large carnivore management, wildlife habitat and federal land policy. If Wyoming is going to make consequential choices about finite public resources, those choices should proportionately reflect the scale of each sector’s economic benefits and costs, not an inherited and outdated assumption of agricultural dominance.

title: Wilderness advocates delay removal of tree ‘Yellowstone Forest Reserve’ surveyors inscribed in 1893
description: Public opposition will slow plans to remove and display a section of a dead Shoshone National Forest tree that surveyors mapping Yellowstone Forest Reserve boundaries inscribed 133 years ago. The dead Engelmann spruce still stands about 28 miles from the nearest trailhead in the Washakie Wilderness. Plans to recover the artifact via helicopter have been unde[...]
text:
Phillip M. Gallaher led the survey crew that inscribed this tree in the modern-day Shoshone National Forest in October 1893. Some 132 years later, lawmakers and archaeologists want to recover the historic artifact from the backcountry. (Courtesy photo)Public opposition will slow plans to remove and display a section of a dead Shoshone National Forest tree that surveyors mapping Yellowstone Forest Reserve boundaries inscribed 133 years ago.

The dead Engelmann spruce still stands about 28 miles from the nearest trailhead in the Washakie Wilderness. Plans to recover the artifact via helicopter have been underway for years, and there’s even a place in the Wyoming State Museum to display it.
But as plans advanced, federal land managers did not loop in the general public nor advocacy groups whose mission it is to uphold the Wilderness Act. When they ultimately learned about the project, advocates publicly objected — and let Shoshone National Forest Supervisor Ken Coffin know it.
“I got probably somewhere around 200 emails from people from across the country who had legitimate concerns about the project because it’s in the wilderness,” Coffin told WyoFile. “Admittedly, we worked with the folks who believe that the removal is an appropriate thing to do —  I happen to be in that camp — but we didn’t really work with the other side. I thought they had a point.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
 Tree removal would require use of helicopter, mechanical equipment in designated wilderness, where it’s not allowed

Concerns about the tree removal emanated from Wilderness Watch, a Missoula, Montana-based advocacy group that seeks to preserve and steward lands and rivers in the National Wilderness Preservation System. In mid-August, Katie Bilodeau, the group’s legislative director and policy analyst, wrote a blog post encouraging folks to send the Shoshone National Forest their thoughts about the tree removal plan.
Readers wrote in droves contesting the plan, which required a “minimum requirements analysis” because the tree removal would require use of a helicopter and other mechanical equipment in designated wilderness, where it’s not normally allowed.
The Yellowstone Timber Land Reserve, pictured here, was passed by Congress in March 1891. (Map courtesy of the General Land Office, 1892)
“It would have also included at least four helicopter landings in the wilderness,” Bilodeau told WyoFile. “Wilderness is a place where nature should govern. We shouldn’t be so eager to jump in with our tools, because we can radically alter things pretty quickly.”
After hearing from Bilodeau and others, Coffin paused the project. As a result, the beetle-killed tree will not leave the remote reaches of the southern Absaroka Mountains in 2026.
And it might stay in the 9,100-foot-high basin permanently. The Shoshone National Forest is in talks with Wyoming State Parks about using a 3D scan to create a replica of the inscribed tree instead of displaying the real thing in Cheyenne.
“If we walk away from that meeting feeling like that [3D scan] serves our purpose,” Coffin said, “then it’s possible that we would not remove the tree.”
If project proponents, led by Wyoming State Parks, aren’t appeased by that plan, then the Shoshone National Forest would resume its approval process for removing the tree.
 Tree’s historical significance is clear

The tree in question has been researched by historian Lawrence Todd, a Colorado State University emeritus professor who lives in Meeteetsee. Surveyors inscribed the spruce on Oct. 3, 1893, while mapping the Yellowstone Forest Reserve, which is the forebear to the Shoshone National Forest. The mapping party, led by Phillip M. Gallaher, took shelter near the tree during a snowstorm that slowed their surveying and carved their names into its trunk “probably out of boredom, more than anything else,” Todd told WyoFile in early 2024.
Phillip Gallaher, surveyor. (Photo courtesy of Lawrence Todd)
Its historic value is clear. The tree was inscribed just 21 years after Yellowstone National Park’s establishment and three years after Wyoming gained statehood, and it’s a reminder of Americans’ early efforts to “reserve” some forests rather than harvest them all. The 1.2 million-acre forest reserve designated in 1891, was the first piece of land set aside for inclusion in what would eventually become the National Forest System.
A century and three decades later, the tree was standing dead. In 2024, Wyoming lawmakers debated setting aside some funding to recover the inscribed section and temporarily put it on display at the Wyoming State Museum in Cheyenne. Long-term, the plan is to put the tree section at the Buffalo Bill Center of the West Museum in Cody.
The first attempt at funding died, but Wyoming State Parks secured a $25,000 allocation during the Legislature’s 2025 session, plus another chunk of money through a state grant program to celebrate the American sesquicentennial anniversary.
State Parks Director Dave Glenn told WyoFile on Tuesday he agrees with Coffin’s decision to “slow roll” the project to “make sure everybody’s supportive” of it. And Glenn’s open to 3D printing a hologram of the tree — he’s seen the scans and said they turned out really well.
Still, Glenn prefers that the tree be removed from the wilderness so it doesn’t topple over and rot.
“From our perspective, we’d still like to get the tree [out of] there, just because it’s so historic,” Glenn said. “That history is going to go away. It’s going to fall down and be gone.”
Bilodeau at Wilderness Watch, meanwhile, has shared gratitude for Coffin pausing the project. On Tuesday, she wrote another blog piece commending that decision and thanking her members for writing to the national forest.
“Y’all saved the survey tree,” she wrote. “While trees don’t have as many lives as cats do, they do have a meaningful second life when they die and become snags, spending years giving back to the ecosystem that had given them life… Removing this ‘deceased’ tree would have devalued this tree’s second life as a snag.”
While it remains to be seen if wilderness advocates will succeed at permanently preventing the survey tree’s removal, it would not be the first time their advocacy has shaped or slowed projects planned in designated wilderness in Wyoming. In 2017, the Bridger-Teton National Forest caught an earful about its plans to helicopter in a new Yellowstone River bridge at Hawks Rest, though the bridge was ultimately replaced four years later.
Plans to stock naturally fishless Mystery Lake in the Teton Wilderness also were scrapped in 2016 as a result of concerns shared by wilderness proponents.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: ACLU claims Memphis Safe Task Force harassing plaintiff
description: Memphis Safe Task Force agents are continuing to harass and intimidate people who record their activities, according to a new federal court filing by the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU and legal team for Memphis resident Hunter Demster filed a declaration on his behalf Wednesday, claiming the task force is retaliating against him for […]
text:
In a lawsuit filed on his behalf by the ACLU, Hunter Demster, photographed in Nov. 2025, alleges federal agents with the Memphis Safe Task Force have harassed and intimidated him for recording their activities. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Memphis Safe Task Force agents are continuing to harass and intimidate people who record their activities, according to a new federal court filing by the American Civil Liberties Union.
The ACLU and legal team for Memphis resident Hunter Demster filed a declaration on his behalf Wednesday, claiming the task force is retaliating against him for recording immigration and law enforcement activity. The filing, which is backed up by video, claims task force agents also “abused” Tennessee’s Halo Law by tackling and arresting Demster as he recorded them arresting a man in late August. 
The law makes it illegal for a person to get within 25 feet of an officer after being ordered to stop approaching or to retreat. The filing claims officers moved toward Demster as he recorded them Aug. 26, creating a “moving wall,” which he said in a video violated his First Amendment rights.
The filing also says task force agents went to Demster’s home on Aug. 30 and Sept. 3 and took pictures or shot video of him at the residence. 



Quotation







The task force has tried to punish and intimidate me for exercising my First Amendment rights, but I will not let them chill my speech.


– Hunter Demster


A federal court is slated to hear arguments Sept. 23 on the lawsuit filed by Demster and other plaintiffs who are seeking a preliminary injunction to prevent the task force from retaliating against them as they record and observe immigration and law enforcement activities. In addition to the request for an injunction, the legal team filed multiple declarations about agents threatening to arrest Memphis residents, intimidating them with vehicles, making illegal traffic stops and watching their homes after they recorded task force actions.
“The task force has tried to punish and intimidate me for exercising my First Amendment rights, but I will not let them chill my speech,” Demster said in a release. “It is not only concerning, it is also deeply frightening how their retaliation has escalated — all because I show the world what’s going on in Memphis.”
The new filing points toward three incidents, the first in late August when he observed task force agents on a Memphis sidewalk and started shooting video. Agents approached him even though he wasn’t interfering with them and yelled “25 feet,” referring to the Halo Law, and moving toward him, according to the filing. When Demster asserted his right to stay there even as one agent said he “extended the scene” by walking toward him, agents took him to the ground, restrained his legs and handcuffed him.
During the arrest, ACLU of Tennessee legal director Lucas Cameron-Vaughn, arrived and was threatened with arrest after being ordered to retreat when he tried to speak with Demster, according to the filing. Demster was ultimately released at the scene.
Another incident took place Aug. 30 at Demster’s home where task force agents gathered across the street and took pictures of him and video of his house after he approached them. 
Task force agents parked outside his home again on Sept. 3, the filing says. When Demster asked if he could help them, one of them said no, and when he started videotaping the vehicle, a person inside the SUV stuck a phone out the window and took pictures and video of Demster, according to the filing.
“Task force agents should not be staking out our clients’ homes simply for recording their activities in public,” Scarlet Kim, senior staff attorney with ACLU’s Speech, Privacy and Technology Project, said in the release. “Nor should they abuse the Halo Law to interfere with our clients’ First Amendment right to record.”
The task force of 31 state, local and federal agencies started aggressively patrolling Memphis in September 2025 at the order of President Donald Trump and Gov. Bill Lee, conducting traffic stops and immigration sweeps, in addition to serving large numbers of arrest warrants. Lee sent the Tennessee National Guard to participate in the task force as well.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: After year of upheaval, Martin community members launch Grassroots Soybean Festival
description: MARTIN, Tenn. — Dozens of children jumped in joy Tuesday night as fire trucks, scouting troops and floats from local businesses rolled down the streets of Martin, flinging candy toward families gathered on the downtown sidewalks. The parade marked the start of a week-long Soybean Festival that’s been a tradition in Martin since 1994. This […]
text:
Parade participants kick off the Tennessee Soybean Festival in Martin, Tennessee, on Sept. 8, 2026. The community banded together to put the annual festival on. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)


Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee LookoutMARTIN, Tenn. — Dozens of children jumped in joy Tuesday night as fire trucks, scouting troops and floats from local businesses rolled down the streets of Martin, flinging candy toward families gathered on the downtown sidewalks.
The parade marked the start of a week-long Soybean Festival that’s been a tradition in Martin since 1994. This year, it’s also a form of victory march for community members who logged thousands of volunteer hours over the last three months to keep that tradition alive, creating a grassroots version of the festival from scratch. 
The Tennessee Soybean Festival Committee announced the official festival’s cancellation in May, citing the city’s recent financial challenges. It was a painful blow to a community already stinging from the indictment of former Mayor Randal Brundige, Economic and Community Development Director Bradley Thompson and Brundige’s daughter, Natalie — all charged in November with official misconduct and the combined theft of more than $450,000 in public funds since 2015.
Their court cases are ongoing, and in the meantime, the city is under orders from the state’s comptroller to build up its anemic cash reserves and pay down its debts. In June, the Martin Mayor and Board of Aldermen unanimously approved the addition of a city manager, an appointed position that will be responsible for managing day-to-day operations and additional oversight.
John Sellers, owner of Martin’s Coffee and Bakery, said the festival’s cancellation caused him a level of frustration he’d never felt before. He believed that the celebration could go on, though on a smaller, more locally focused scale, without the ticketed big-name musical acts and carnival rides that joined the festival in recent years.








Rita Barrett enjoys cotton candy while watching the Tennessee Soybean Festival Parade in Martin, Tennessee. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









University of Tennessee-Martin cheerleaders fire up the crowd during Wednesday's Soybean Festival parade. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Crowds of Martin residents lined the streets while waiting for the parade to begin. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Among the floats rolling through the streets of Martin, Tennessee for the annual Tennessee Soybean Festival was one from Rural King featuring a giant inflatable chicken. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






Within hours, Sellers and other community members mobilized, sketching out their own plans for Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival. 
When they were unable to get the Tennessee Soybean Festival Committee’s help with administrative logistics, they formed their own entity, created a board, and secured permits and insurance. Mayor David Belote — the city’s former vice mayor who was scrutinized but ultimately appointed to the role after Brundige’s resignation  — helped outline what Sellers and others would need to bring the event to life.
The group raised $115,000 through sponsorships and partnerships with businesses, including $25,000 from the Tennessee Department of Agriculture and $30,000 from Martin’s tourism fund, which is fed by a specially designated hotel tax. Simmons Bank chipped in to sponsor the parade.
About 90 days later, Sellers sat in a folding chair in front of his storefront wearing a “Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival” T-shirt, watching nearly 50 groups march in the parade. Participants included campaigns for mayoral candidates David Bell and Kent Kelso, who are vying for votes in November.
Rick Hughey and his wife, Jessica, set up to watch the parade from the sidewalk in front of Martin’s Coffee and Bakery about an hour before it began. They both graduated from the University of Tennessee at Martin, and Rick Hughey lived in the town of 11,000 his whole life before moving to nearby Southport. He said the turmoil of the last year did bruise public trust, but “it’s on its way back.”
Rick and Tina Hughey met as students at the University of Tennessee-Martin. Rick Hughey said recent political turmoil roiled the city but public trust is returning. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Steven Tucker moved to Martin from Wisconsin in 2021 to join family members there, and has attended the festival every year since.
“We really like the people, and there’s a feeling of camaraderie with everyone,” Tucker said. While it may be scaled back this year, Tucker pointed out that people were still lined up on the sidewalks to watch the parade.
Angela Anderson was one of those people, there to watch two of her grandchildren participate with their karate and dance groups. 
Debbie Carden, a resident of nearby Gleason, watched as her 3-year-old grandson Brynson Massey jumped up and down as tractors and other heavy equipment rolled past. 
“He loves all things farm-related,” she said.
“They’ve done a really good job,” Carden said. “The community pulled together to put together a really nice week for everyone. Everybody’s happy that people stepped up.”








Two parade participates represented pork and corn as part of Tennessee's agricultural tradition. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Plenty of political candidates used the parade as an opportunity for soft campaigning. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Chantal Gipson of Outlaw Exotic Pets with her pet raccoon, Crunch. Gipson's truck carried two other of her raccoons, one of which is albino. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






On Thursday, 20 faith institutions will participate in the festival’s Faith and Family night, which will feature a free petting zoo and inflatable jump park for children. The first 1,000 attendees will receive a free meal thanks to partnerships with Tosh Farms, Martin Stockyards and Walmart. Vendors, food trucks, and performances from local musicians will stretch through Saturday night.
Any profits left over after the festival concludes will be donated to the local fire department to help fill a funding gap for needed breathing apparatus upgrades, Sellers said.
“It’s really showing what we can do when everyone comes together and does their part,” he said. 
One of Sellers’ favorite folktales is “Stone Soup,” a tale about hungry travelers who bring a village together by convincing them to contribute ingredients to a soup made from water and stones.
“It really reflects that here, because everybody bringing what they have makes something greater … it has been amazing to witness it,” Sellers said.
