name: Alabama Reflector
title: To prevent veterans’ suicides, advocates seek to expand safe storage with gun retailers
description: Alabama veteran suicide prevention advocates are recruiting firearm retailers to a program that allows veterans who feel at risk of taking their lives to safely store their guns with a gun shop. Statewide, 14 gun retailers in 10 counties have agreed to participate in the program. The organization expects to have gun safes placed in […]
text:
Supporters plant 150 flags in honor of veterans who died by suicide in 2024 at an event in Montgomery, Alabama on Sept. 9, 2026. Advocates who spoke at the event  said they are actively recruiting gun shops that can serve as locations where veterans can voluntarily surrender their firearms until they are no longer concerned that they are at risk of suicide. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Alabama veteran suicide prevention advocates are recruiting firearm retailers to a program that allows veterans who feel at risk of taking their lives to safely store their guns with a gun shop.
Statewide, 14 gun retailers in 10 counties have agreed to participate in the program. The organization expects to have gun safes placed in those stores by the end of the month.
“Two per county would be the ultimate goal,” said Jason Smith, founder and chair of S.A.F.E.R. Together, an initiative whose mission is prevent suicides among veterans. “Let’s say 67 counties, at least one. If we reach 67, and we have got coverage throughout the state, that is the ultimate goal.”

If you or someone you know is in a crisis, call, text or chat the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. For a list of Crisis Centers in Alabama, visit the Alabama Department of Mental Health’s website. If you need help with grief and loss, the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention offers advice and resources. You can also call the National SAMHSA Helpline, 1-800-662-HELP, with services in English and Spanish, toll free 24/7.

Smith made the appeal as the Alabama Department of Veterans Affairs Wednesday began the Operation We Remember campaign, an initiative to honor veterans in the state who have lost their lives to suicide. Staff laid down 150 flags to remember the veterans who died by suicide in 2024.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the Alabama Department of Public Health, the suicide rate was 20.1 per 100,000 people in 2021 for Alabama, but it was 35.4 per 100,000 for veterans in that year.
According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, veterans often have high risk factors for suicide, including financial struggles like unemployment or homelessness; pain or trauma from service, or difficulties adjusting to life outside the military.
“When you transition to the civilian world, you don’t put on a uniform, you don’t have anybody telling you what to do next, where to go, what time to be there, what to eat,” said Sandra Lucas, deputy commissioner of Alabama Department of Veterans Affairs. “Now you are left in a spot you are not trained for, and you don’t know what that mission set is. And a lot of times that can be overwhelming, especially if other life triggers come into play.”
In 2024, Alabama ranked fourth for firearm mortality at 23.7 deaths per 100,000 total population, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, trailing only Mississippi, New Mexico and Alaska.
According to the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, 73% of suicides in Alabama in 2024 involved a firearm, and 48% of all firearm deaths that year were suicides.
Smith said that the organization expects to meet a goal of signing up 20 firearm retailers by the end of the year. He wants to convince more gun shops to participate in the program, particularly in places with high rates of people who commit suicides. He is actively looking for gun shops in Tuscaloosa, Mobile County and Calhoun County.
According to data from the National Institutes of Health, Calhoun County has the fourth highest rate of suicide in Alabama with 22.9 suicide-related deaths per 100,000 total population between 2020 and 2024. The highest was Cleburne County at 31 deaths per 100,000 total population.
In 2025, the Alabama Legislature passed  SB 40, sponsored by Sen. Keith Kelley, R-Anniston, that allows individuals that own a gun to enter into agreement to have the owner of a gun shop take possession of the firearm and keep it for an agreed amount of time before returning it.
The legislation protects the gun shop owner from legal liability after the person returns the firearm to the individual who surrendered it.
“I am asking Alabama’s gun dealers to step up and help us save lives,” Kelley said in a statement Wednesday. “These are people who understand firearms, they understand responsible gun ownership, and they are in a position to provide a safe place when someone says, ‘I need some time away from my gun.’”

title: Payday lender Advance Financial closes several dozen Tennessee stores
description: Nashville-based payday lender Advance Financial closed over 40 of its storefront locations Wednesday. At its peak in 2021, Advance had 105 locations, but over the past few years it has reduced that number and now operates under 30 stores, according to the company’s website listing its current locations.  Cullen Earnest, senior vice president of public […]
text:
An Advance Financial store in Sparta, Tennessee is one of the stores that was not closed as part of the company's restructuring. (Stacy Kranitz for ProPublica)Nashville-based payday lender Advance Financial closed over 40 of its storefront locations Wednesday.
At its peak in 2021, Advance had 105 locations, but over the past few years it has reduced that number and now operates under 30 stores, according to the company’s website listing its current locations. 
Cullen Earnest, senior vice president of public policy at Advance Financial, said the company is restructuring and consolidating some stores because its “long-time retail customers learned to do business online during COVID and never went back.”
Advance Financial is one of the largest political spenders in Tennessee state politics. 
An Advance Financial in Nashville, Tennessee was boarded up and closed as of Wednesday, September 9, 2026. (Photo: Adam Friedman/Tennessee Lookout)
The company’s owners, Michael and Tina Hodges, were behind a 2014 law that created a new type of payday loan with a 279.5% annual interest rate, called a Flex Loan.
The Flex Loan removed many of the consumer protections that existed for other high-interest debt and sidestepped federal regulations at the time.
An investigation by the Lookout and ProPublica found that while Advance claimed its loans would be better for Tennesseans, it has used a provision in the new law to sue 110,000 borrowers in the decade since the Flex Loan’s passage.  
Borrowers have described how the company encourages them to keep borrowing, tearing a hole in the law’s safety net. The company also aggressively pursues outstanding debt using the court to garnish wages even from borrowers who have often paid back their loans multiple times over.
Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, sponsored the Flex Loan law and helped pass it in 2014. This was before he had the top job in the state House. 
This lender said its loans would help Tennesseans. It has sued more than 110,000 of them.

Sexton’s campaign and political action committee have received more than $105,000 from the company, making it one of the largest contributors to him over the past decade. He is also an ally of the company’s owners, fighting in 2021 to protect their gambling company. In 2026, he appointed John Cheadle, Advance’s debt collection lawyer whose firm has sued thousands of Tennesseans, to the Nashville Airport Authority Board. 
Earnest previously told the Lookout that the company has an A+ rating from the Better Business Bureau. He added that the Tennessee Department of Financial Institutions has received just 91 complaints about flexible credit lenders since 2020, representing less than 0.001% of all new flex loan agreements, and that this data reflects the satisfaction of the vast majority of Advance’s customers.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: If you care about Idaho’s Priest Lake, you have to care about the Coolin Wetlands
description: I spent more than 40 years as a professional biologist working to preserve, protect, perpetuate and manage Idaho’s fish and wildlife – over two thirds of that in the Idaho Panhandle. In retirement, I serve as president of the Idaho Panhandle Chapter of Trout Unlimited, part of one of the nation’s most respected conservation organizations. […]
text:
Priest Lake is located in North Idaho's Bonner County. (Photo by Getty Images)I spent more than 40 years as a professional biologist working to preserve, protect, perpetuate and manage Idaho’s fish and wildlife – over two thirds of that in the Idaho Panhandle. 
In retirement, I serve as president of the Idaho Panhandle Chapter of Trout Unlimited, part of one of the nation’s most respected conservation organizations. In both roles, a central focus has been to ensure fish, wildlife, and the habitats they depend on, and especially high value habitats like Priest Lake, continue to flourish for the enjoyment and benefit of the people of Idaho. 
For three decades I’ve worked with land  management and regulatory agencies, industry, NGOs, and the public to help ensure Priest Lake maintains its status as a crown jewel of Idaho. 
I’ve seen a lot of projects in that time. Like others, I’ve learned to recognize those where someone decided it was easier to ask for forgiveness than permission. What’s happened to the Coolin Wetlands is one of the most egregious examples I’ve seen. 
The Coolin Wetlands are a 65-acre peat bog on the south shore of Priest Lake, one of only 13 Class 1 wetlands in the entire state of Idaho. That classification means near pristine condition. It means the system is functioning at full ecological capacity. The Idaho Department of Fish and Game has identified this area as among the top 50 most important wetland habitats in the state. 
These are not ordinary acres. They’re a filtration system, a carbon sink, and support essential and critical habitat for wetland species, and fish species that depend on the cold, clean water Priest Lake is known for. 
Priest Lake is a gem. People from across Idaho and beyond come here because it remains one of the few truly pristine lakes left. That’s because of the wetlands, uplands and riparian systems that surround it, systems like the Coolin Wetlands that humbly do the work of keeping the water clean. From a water quality standpoint, the importance of  large, intact wetland areas in close proximity to a lake like this cannot be overstated. 
Bull trout, listed as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act, rely on Priest Lake as critical habitat. Westslope Cutthroat Trout, a species that nearly disappeared in Priest Lake, have made a meaningful comeback over the past three decades because of conservation efforts and the regulatory systems put in place to protect their habitat. 
I’ve been fortunate to watch that comeback happen. I know what it took, and I know how quickly it can unravel when the systems protecting habitat and water quality are compromised. 
During my career, projects like this – proposals to fill or develop sensitive wetlands in proximity to critical fish habitat – were exactly what we worked to avoid and/or mitigate. 
Not to obstruct development for its own sake, but to find outcomes that maintain fish and wildlife habitat. However, where habitats are high functioning and unique, such as the Coolin Wetlands, the science is unambiguous: you cannot fill a high-value peat bog and expect the surrounding ecosystem to absorb that loss. 
Once it’s gone, it’s gone. No mitigation credit, no restoration project, no amount of money can bring it back. 
A developer acquired three large parcels, encompassing the Coolin Wetlands, along the south shore of Priest Lake in 2021 and moved to develop them, filing 54 quitclaim deeds in a single day to manufacture 26 waterfront lots without triggering any public review. He then submitted two additional land division applications, each kept just under the threshold that would require full subdivision scrutiny. 
Bonner County’s own attorney acknowledged on the record that the developer was gaming the system. The county approved the applications anyway. 
In July, the Idaho Supreme Court unanimously ruled that this scheme cannot stand and reaffirmed that decision at the end of August following an appeal. The court held that the developer’s applications, filed simultaneously for contiguous land under common ownership, function as a single subdivision and must face full public review. 
It’s the right call. The public process exists for exactly this kind of situation. 
Now the case returns to district court. Bonner County faces a choice: accept the Supreme Court’s ruling and let the process move forward, or spend taxpayer money continuing to defend a position their own attorney conceded was indefensible. I hope they choose wisely. 
Perhaps the developer would consider shifting gears and donate or sell the property to a land trust or conservancy … a win-win outcome. But gaming the permitting system to avoid public review and then putting heavy equipment to use on site, while the court case is still pending? That’s asking for forgiveness rather than permission. 
In my experience, when someone operates that way with a resource this sensitive, the damage is rarely undone. 
Priest Lake is one of Idaho’s most treasured resources. The Coolin Wetlands are part of what makes it that way. The wetlands and the lake they protect are worth more than the legal fees. 
For those great many of us who value Priest Lake, let’s not be willing to watch them disappear without saying something.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama community college enrollment nears 100,000 for-credit students
description: Alabama’s community colleges are on track to enroll over 100,000 students in for-credit courses this fall despite barriers, according to data presented to the system’s board of trustees Wednesday morning. Neil Scott, vice chancellor for student success for the Alabama Community College System (ACCS), said there are 99,083 students enrolled in for-credit cour[...]
text:
Members of the Alabama Community College System Board of Trustees as seen Aug. 12, 2026. Enrollment for fall 2026 is likely to pass 100,000 for-credit students, according to data presented to the board Wednesday. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s community colleges are on track to enroll over 100,000 students in for-credit courses this fall despite barriers, according to data presented to the system’s board of trustees Wednesday morning.
Neil Scott, vice chancellor for student success for the Alabama Community College System (ACCS), said there are 99,083 students enrolled in for-credit courses for the Fall 2026 semester as of Tuesday, a 1.9% increase over the final Fall 2025 headcount. 
“We still have time to register more students, so I’m really crossing my fingers for 100,000. We’re hearing colleges talk about still having some more dual enrollment students that they’re working on getting registered,” he said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Scott said students are enrolled in almost 834,000 credit hours, a 2.7% increase over the final Fall 2025 credit hour production. 
Community college enrollment in Alabama has grown at a faster rate than the national average in previous years, but Scott said it is likely slowing this year due to a new identity verification software colleges had to implement for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) application.
“This has been a little bit of a challenging year from an enrollment standpoint. There have been some environmental things that our colleges have had to weather,” Scott said. “There’s a lot of talk right now coming out of Washington D.C. and certainly out of Montgomery related to application fraud, financial aid fraud, and people taking advantage of resources like Pell Grant with bad intentions. And so we saw that challenge.”
According to Higher Ed Dive, students are still enrolling in community colleges more than public or private four-year universities, but the rate is slowing. Community colleges nationwide saw a 4.6% enrollment increase from Spring 2023 to 2024; a 5.2% increase from Spring 2024 to 2025; and a 3.1% increase from Spring 2025 to 2026. 
The FAFSA identity verification software was introduced in April, so colleges may not see the impact of the new software until this semester. 
“As with any new application software, any new barriers for students to enroll, that is something that our colleges have embraced,” Scott said. “We’re curious to see what impact that might have on enrollment.”
ACCS Chancellor Jimmy Baker said in an interview after the meeting that high enrollment proves the quality of a community college education.
“There was a time when the community college system was not viewed as being quality, and I think that’s old stories,” Baker said. “We’ve got good management across the system that is giving people a good buy for their work, and they know that. That’s the genesis for increasing enrollment – it’s worth going to pay your money to get an education, or training.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Data shows big jump in WV voters choosing no-party ballot in closed Republican May primary
description: In a stress test for West Virginia Republicans’ return to a closed primary, new data shows fewer Republicans came out to vote in the May primary election compared to the 2022 primary.
text:
A sign marks a Kanawha County polling place during an election. (Photo by Lori Kersey| West Virginia Watch)In a stress test for West Virginia Republicans’ return to a closed primary, new data shows fewer Republicans came out to vote in the May primary election compared to the 2022 primary.
Despite an education push from the state GOP ahead of Election Day, non-affiliated voter registration in 2026 climbed by 13% since the last mid-term primary in 2022. More than 21,000 residents selected a no party ballot, a 74% increase from 2022.
The Secretary of State’s office released comprehensive data Wednesday on May’s primary, which was an unusual election in terms of big spending to influence state-level races in the midterm. Gov. Patrick Morrisey also involved himself, backing a number of incumbents and challengers to lawmakers in his own Republican party. 
Voters also faced a closed Republican primary for the first time since the 1980s. Privately, some Republicans surmised that the closed primary impacted the Supreme Court races because unaffiliated voters could take out their frustrations in the statewide judicial races available on every ballot.
Independents joined Democratic voters in rejecting Morrisey’s picks for the West Virginia Supreme Court, opting to elect Bill Flanigan and H.L. “Kirk” Kirkpatrick to the state’s highest court.
The Secretary of State’s office compared May’s voting data to 2022 since it was the last midterm election cycle.
West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner
 
“Election administration is one of the most important responsibilities of my office, and my team works closely with all 55 county clerks to ensure every eligible voter has the opportunity to participate and that every ballot is secured and counted accurately,” Secretary of State Kris Warner said in a statement. “West Virginians deserve elections that are safe, secure, transparent, and fair. This report reflects our commitment to delivering exactly that.”
Near the close of registration for the primary election, West Virginia had 1,198,036 registered voters eligible to cast a ballot. Of them, 21.03% of all eligible voters participated in the primary election. The majority of voters participated in-person. 
Republican voter registrations continued to climb since 2022, but there was a 22% decrease in the number of Republican ballots cast in May.
The number of Democratic registered voters fell by 17% in this same time period, but the party reported a slight increase in the number of ballots cast in May.
Of the 252,008 ballots cast, 126,365 were Republican ballots and 104,028 were Democratic. 
The Secretary of State’s Office also shared that the highest rate of reports of issues at the polls involved missing, incomplete or unclear polling place signage. The second highest number of complaints involved the closed primary election requirements
The May primary also marked the first implementation of a new voter identification law that strictly required voters to have a photo ID like a driver’s license, passport or a resident identification card to vote in-person. State lawmakers eliminated 11 formerly accepted identification options, like Medicaid cards and utility bills, in a 2025 measure.
The mid-term general election is Nov. 3 in West Virginia. All 100 House of Delegates seats are on the ballot along with Senate seats, Congressional seats and a constitutional amendment regarding citizenship and voting rights. 
The last day to register to vote is Oct. 13.

title: What just happened to mail balloting?
description: We can all be forgiven for not keeping up with the rapidly changing legal activity surrounding mail balloting. There has been so much. Complex changes have been proposed by the Trump Administration so near to the midterm elections that the changes themselves don’t seem to be the point. Instead, confusion and disenfranchisement are so predictable that electio[...]
text:
A U.S. Postal Service whistleblower in a report published Sept. 1, 2026, alleged that USPS rushed the development of electronic tools to comply with a Trump administration policy placing new restrictions on mail-in voting. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)We can all be forgiven for not keeping up with the rapidly changing legal activity surrounding mail balloting. There has been so much. Complex changes have been proposed by the Trump Administration so near to the midterm elections that the changes themselves don’t seem to be the point. Instead, confusion and disenfranchisement are so predictable that election chaos must be the true intended objective. Voters in West Virginia need to be prepared.
The whole thing started with an Executive Order issued by Trump in March 2026. The Order inserted the federal government into state procedures for absentee and other mail balloting, claiming that federal intervention is necessary to maintain election integrity. Nevermind that there is virtually no evidence of fraud in mail balloting and Trump himself votes this way. 
The Order directed the Postal Service to issue a rule on handling mail ballots. A proposed rule was issued on March 19, 2026. That rule required state election officials to provide the USPS in advance with the names and addresses of voters to whom they would mail a ballot, along with sample outbound and return ballot envelopes for approval. State election officials would be required to certify that any mail ballots they provide to voters will comply with the procedures in the rule. If a state failed to certify, the USPS would not carry that state’s ballots through the mail.
The lower court challenge
The Executive Order and the USPS rule were immediately challenged as unconstitutional by 23 states in one case and a group of organizations led by The League of Women Voters in a second. They argued that the Constitution’s Elections Clause and the separation of powers doctrine deprive the president and the USPS of any power to regulate elections. They also argued that Congress has not delegated the USPS any power to create by rule a new category of non-mailable material. But the merits of these arguments have not yet been decided. 
Most of the recent legal wrangling has been about whether the USPS rule should go into effect before its constitutionality is finally determined. The federal district judge where the challenge was brought preliminarily ruled that the whole scheme is unconstitutional. She ordered the USPS to cease any further implementation, but only as to the November midterm elections, and only in the 23 plaintiff states. West Virginia was not one of them. The government sought a stay in the Court of Appeals pending the appeal, but this was denied.
In the Supreme Court
Only the question of the stay, not of constitutionality, went to the Supreme Court. The government’s sole argument was that when the states filed their action they had not been harmed, and therefore had no standing to sue, because there was no final USPS rule in place. A split Supreme Court agreed with the government in a ruling on August 24, 2026. 
Blinking reality, the Supreme Court’s majority said that with no final USPS rule in place, the states were inflicting harm on themselves by incurring planning costs that may not be necessary. The Court dismissed the states’ fear that their own election officials would be prosecuted. To demonstrate how wasteful and diversionary this Supreme Court ruling was, the USPS’s final rule – making real and immediate all the states’ concerns — was published by the USPS several days before the Supreme Court’s Aug. 24 ruling. Surely the Court was aware this was about to happen.
Justice Jackson’s dissent should grab the attention of every American. Here is part of what she said:
Taking its eye off the ball, the majority misses the government’s actual objective: to secure our imprimatur for its effort to foment chaos ahead of the November elections.
Rather than swallow the government’s gamesmanship whole, the court should have given this empty, strategic, and bad-faith stay bid the swift rejection it deserves.
The USPS final rule back in the lower courts
The final USPS rule differs only slightly from the proposed rule. Crucially, the agency will not deliver mail ballots in states that do not share voter data with the federal agency. Additionally, the USPS would use new software to screen every envelope for compliance with the new standards before accepting ballots into its system. This review would include checking that the recipient was enrolled with the Postal Service to receive a mail ballot and that the ballot envelope meets certain specifications.
Immediately after it was published, the final rule was challenged again by the same states and nonprofit groups as before. On Sept. 4, 2026, the district court judge once again found the whole scheme unconstitutional and issued a preliminary injunction barring the USPS from taking further steps to implement the final rule. That injunction applies nationwide. 
The Trump Administration quickly appealed the Sept. 4 district court injunction directly to the Supreme Court. This is a highly unusual procedure that bypasses the Court of Appeals. It is unclear how quickly the appeal will be resolved.
A whistleblower exposes the Trump administration’s defiance
Whether the Trump Administration will comply is questionable, because its response so far has been to defy the courts. On Aug. 31, 2026, a whistleblower report detailed how the USPS rushed to implement the new software for scanning ballot envelopes, despite being under injunction from two courts not to do so. 
The whistleblower detailed how the untested batch-scanning system can disenfranchise thousands of mail voters. When ballots are submitted to USPS in large-volume batches, if any one ballot in the batch cannot be verified or scanned for some reason, all ballots in that batch will be rejected.
The potential effect of mail ballot chaos
Voters and election officials around the country are expressing confusion and worry that their mail ballots will not be counted. If the USPS refuses to carry mail ballots from entire states or if large batches of ballots are mishandled by its new procedures, voter disenfranchisement will be widespread. Nearly 47 million voters in 2024, or roughly 30% of the electorate, voted by mail.
Eight states automatically send mail ballots to all active registered voters before Election Day: California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington. In 29 states, any voter can request and submit a mail ballot without providing a reason, and 13 others, including West Virginia, grant absentee ballot requests for reasons approved by statute.
There is an obvious incentive for the Trump Administration to interfere with mail balloting. Thirty-seven percent of Democrats reported voting by mail in 2024, compared to 24% of Republicans. 
Where things stand in West Virginia
The situation in this dispute changes almost daily. But for now, the USPS rule and the cloud over mail balloting it created are stopped nationwide until further notice. In West Virginia, that means the familiar rules for absentee voting still apply.  
Beginning Sept. 18, county clerks will mail absentee ballots to those voters who have already applied. Thereafter, the clerks will promptly mail ballots to new applicants who qualify. The deadline to apply for an absentee ballot is Oct. 29. The completed ballot must be postmarked by Nov. 3, 2026.
It seems likely that the drama is not over. Hold onto your hats.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Economic development is a top priority in Lexington
description: Lexington’s government and its economic development partners work on economic development every day to ensure there are good-paying jobs for our residents, and to keep our quality of life high for everyone. For me, it’s a top priority – it’s my job to ensure our economy continues to thrive. Our investments in economic development have […]
text:
Lexington Mayor Linda Gorton speaks to trainees at the workforce development center in Davis Park. (Photo courtesy LFUCG)Lexington’s government and its economic development partners work on economic development every day to ensure there are good-paying jobs for our residents, and to keep our quality of life high for everyone. For me, it’s a top priority – it’s my job to ensure our economy continues to thrive.
Our investments in economic development have helped put money in the pockets of our residents. Between 2020 and 2024, economic growth helped raise the median household income by nearly $11,000. Per capita personal income increased during the same period by over $13,000.
One reason for our strong economic strength is our workforce. Labor Day is the perfect time to celebrate the members of our strong, growing workforce, the economy they help us build, the high quality of life they help us maintain, and the bright future they help us create.
 Over the past year we have had more people working in our county than at any time in our history. Over the past six years, our workforce has grown by over 12 percent, from 154,856 in July 2020, to 173,944 in July 2026.
The strength and the quality of  the Lexington workforce has helped our community attract new businesses to town, including the recent addition of BOS Innovation System, with its focus on industrial automation and robotics. BOS opened its North American Headquarters in Lexington earlier this month, bringing 111 new full-time jobs to the community.
Because of the strong skills and hard work of our residents, the GDP in Lexington increased by $7.7 billion, or 36%, between 2020 and 2024.
Lexington’s government helps develop our workforce by investing in workforce development training for all skill levels. 
In 2025, Lexington opened its workforce development center in Davis Park. The center provides our workforce team and its partners with a dedicated space for job training programming. This year, Lexington will spend over $400,000 to provide people with the job skills they need, and our economy needs, to succeed.  
Workforce training helps us grow the economy by ensuring our employers have a skilled workforce they can rely on. Our investment in workforce training helps people at all income levels. Since 2015, the percentage of the population below the poverty line has decreased by nearly 4%, dropping from 18.9% to 14.9%. We still have work to do, but we’ve made progress.
Lexington also grows its economy by investing in new businesses. The Lexington JOBS Fund, a unique local incentive program, has assisted more than two dozen companies, such as the highly successful Lexington-based Space Tango. Our support of Space Tango and other companies has resulted in the creation of 300 jobs. Currently, there is approximately $1.83 million still available in this fund.
We also developed the Lexington Public Infrastructure Fund to spur economic growth by assisting developers with the public infrastructure portion of their projects, as long as new job creation is part of the project. Recently, we invested in the Railyard on Delaware Avenue, assisting a developer who is creating jobs, as well as affordable housing.  This project was also assisted by funds from the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet. Over $5 million has been awarded to this fund, with $1.6 million still available.
Growing a strong economy also means planning for the future – we  need good jobs for our children and our grandchildren.
Our new Legacy Business Park will be complete later this year and is projected to be home to more than 1,000 workers, and over $100 million in payroll when it is fully built out.
We have also worked with the City of Berea, and the Madison and Scott County governments to establish the Central Kentucky Business Park Authority. The Authority is developing the 300-acre Triple Crown Business Park that began construction in May.
Thanks to $20 million from the Kentucky General Assembly, we are purchasing an additional 700+ acre site for job creation, as well. Once completed, the revenues from the Authority will be split evenly among the three counties, allowing us to invest more in public safety, job creation and quality of life programs for our residents.
The Lexington economy, one of the most diverse in the country, is built on a strong workforce, attracting new businesses, investing in local businesses, and looking to the future. 
Kevin Atkins is Chief Development Officer in Lexington.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Reports say ICE detention is growing in KY but records, details remain unclear, advocates say
description: The number of federal immigration detainees in Kentucky jails is growing dramatically, but the public knows less and less about them, including whether or not they have criminal records, according to new reports on federal efforts to deport more people.
text:
From left to right, U.S. Reps. Delia Ramirez, Gwen Moore and Morgan McGarvey go to a Northern Kentucky jail to see conditions for people being held by ICE in August. (Photo provided by U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey's office)The number of federal immigration detainees in Kentucky jails is growing dramatically, but the public knows less and less about them, including whether or not they have criminal records, according to new reports on federal efforts to deport more people. 
Some information on U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainees in Kentucky jails is hard to find, a new report from the League of Women Voters of Kentucky says. 
The League’s analysis found a few online rosters at Kentucky jails that house federal immigration detainees are unclear on the local crimes charged or status of the detainee. Three do not list people who are in ICE custody. 
“Kentucky jails belong to us, the people of Kentucky, so we should know how immigrants are being treated,” wrote League President Jennifer Jackson in a letter about the report. “The people held there are human beings, so Kentuckians should insist on their human rights.”
The League, a group that has been tracking ICE data statewide for a few months, also said in the latest analysis a dozen jails across Kentucky are being paid to house ICE detainees and most do not have a criminal conviction; more than 60 jails in the state have voluntarily placed ICE holds on people arrested locally; most jails that provide ICE custody are overcrowded because of federal roles; and two jails and more than 50 law enforcement agencies have partnerships with ICE. 
In November, about 12 local police agencies and three jails in Kentucky had partnerships with ICE under 287(g) agreements. Two bills were filed in the 2026 legislative session to direct Kentucky State Police or local law enforcement agencies to enter such ICE agreements, but they did not get floor votes. 
According to data from Relevant Research, Kentucky jails are housing about 1,200 people for ICE as of July. 
Last week, progressive think tank Kentucky Center for Economic Policy said in an analysis that arrests through the 287(g) agreements have grown in recent months. In November 2025, there was one arrest in Kentucky through the agreement program. In July 2026, there were 70. 
After its report, the League of Women Voters sent letters to leaders in counties with the greatest participation in ICE detention: Boone, Bourbon, Campbell, Christian, Daviess, Fayette, Grayson, Hopkins, Jefferson, Kenton, Laurel, Oldham and Woodford. Among the group’s requests were providing more fully transparent inmate lists and evidence about the treatment of detainees. 
The full analysis said jails in Bourbon, Boone, Grayson, Hopkins, Laurel and Oldham counties include ICE detainees in their roster listings. Those people can be identified by an immigration charge listed or that the arresting officer or agency is listed as ICE, Immigration or the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. 
The League said Campbell, Christian and Kenton counties do not list people there in ICE custody. Daviess County “appears to include people in ICE custody in its public roster, but not in a way that makes that status clear, as it may include people arrested by other federal agents, like U.S. Marshals. Fayette and Woodford counties’ “approaches are unclear to the League.”
Matt Mudd, a spokesperson for Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg, said Louisville Metro Department of Corrections “does not house individuals who are in ICE custody,” but it does honor detainer requests from ICE to hold people 48 hours beyond their scheduled release for local offenses. The American Civil Liberties Union of Kentucky criticized the practice in August, saying it reviewed data that showed a nearly 300% increase in the average number of monthly detainer requests since the city’s policy change last year. Mudd said the cost for the holds “is negligible, and LMDC has not increased its budget to accommodate these holds.”
“To protect individual information, names of those subject to an ICE detainer are not released. Furthermore, information related to immigration detainers is subject to confidentiality requirements of federal law. The individual’s attorney may request additional information in person with proper identification while in person at LMDC,” Mudd added. “However, all local charges for individuals in custody at LMDC are available on a searchable public website that shows all allowable information.”
Mudd also referred to the state law governing conditions for jails, such as the requirement to provide inmates three nutritious meals a day to inmates and health and mental health evaluations and treatment.
ICE detention in Kentucky has made headlines in recent months. U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, a Democrat who represents Kentucky’s 3rd Congressional District, joined two of his House colleagues to visit the Campbell County jail in July to review conditions for ICE detainees there. 
“Trump and Republicans in Congress gave ICE billions in taxpayer money to target and terrorize immigrants in our communities,” McGarvey said in a Wednesday statement to the Kentucky Lantern. “At a bare minimum, we as taxpayers deserve transparency about where our neighbors are being taken and how they’re being treated.”
McGarvey joined family members of a Louisville woman, Sarafinah Bukirwa, who was detained by ICE in calling for better medical care for her while she was in the Grayson County Detention Center in July. Bukirwa, who has sickle cell anemia, was not getting all of her medications, her brother said, but the jailer denied the claim. Bukirwa was later released in August by a federal judge and after her family paid her bond. 
Nationwide, more than 30 people have died in ICE custody since October and the fatality rate for ICE custody has reached a 22-year high in the opening months of the fiscal year.

title: Va. health dept. updates food allergen list, food establishment guidance
description: Sesame has now been added to the state’s major food allergen list, the Virginia Department of Health announced along with several regulation updates and revamped guidance for food establishments that will go into effect on Thursday.  The ingredient joins fin fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, milk, peanuts, soy, wheat and eggs as items that restaurants,[...]
text:
Virginia Department of Health offices in Richmond. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for The Virginia Mercury)Sesame has now been added to the state’s major food allergen list, the Virginia Department of Health announced along with several regulation updates and revamped guidance for food establishments that will go into effect on Thursday. 
The ingredient joins fin fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, milk, peanuts, soy, wheat and eggs as items that restaurants, food trucks and other food vendors must disclose in packaged and unpacked items on their menus for consumers’ awareness. 
Businesses are not required to reprint existing menus and can offer a standalone handout or a QR code so customers can access the information. 
The protocols stem from the most recent food code update from the United States Food and Drug Administration — a mandate last revised in 2022. 
Brookie Crawford, a communications manager with VDH, explained that implementing FDA food code updates takes time because they “must go through an executive branch review and then to the General Assembly.”
Virginia’s last food code update was in 2021 and aligned with the 2017 FDA Food Code. The federal code is updated every four years. 
Beyond adopting the latest federal guidance, VDH is also in the process of implementing new state laws that build on food safety protocols. 
House Bill 373 by Del. Marty Martinez, D-Loudoun and Senate Bill 248 by Sen. Kannan Srinivasan, D-Loudoun, will require VDH to post guidance in multiple languages on its website for restaurant staff who encounter customers with food allergies.
The measure will also require restaurants to post signage or update menus to include the phrase “if you have a food allergy, please notify us” in multiple languages. 
When implemented, VDH will provide a sign that establishments can use, though they can also create their own sign. 
Additionally, SB 183 by Sen. Angelia Williams Graves, D-Norfolk, is meant to enhance transparency about food safety for people with allergies or sensitivities that order carry-out of delivery items. 
The law directs the state health board to promote regulations requiring restaurants that alter or substitute food due to consumer-identified food allergies or sensitivities to place an identifying marker on items that have been altered. 
Though the legislation officially became law on July 1, implementing the requirements from the state lawmakers will take time and VDH anticipates the new regulations taking effect in 2027. 
“Agency staff are actively working on proposed regulations and will be convening a public stakeholder group of industry and public representatives shortly to gather feedback on language,” Crawford said.

title: Feds float ending tax-exempt status for private universities that have race-based policies
description: The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service have formally proposed revoking tax-exempt status from private educational institutions that use race-based policies in admissions, scholarships, or other programs, arguing that they constitute discrimination. Some schools offer admission, scholarships or other assistance to historically di[...]
text:
The Treasury Building in Washington, D.C. The U.S. Treasury and the IRS have proposed revoking federal tax-exempt status from private educational institutions that use race-based policies in admissions, scholarships or other programs. (Photo by Getty Images)The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service have formally proposed revoking tax-exempt status from private educational institutions that use race-based policies in admissions, scholarships, or other programs, arguing that they constitute discrimination.
Some schools offer admission, scholarships or other assistance to historically disadvantaged groups and minorities who were locked out of educational opportunities in previous decades. 
But last year, the federal government told colleges to stop using race in admissions, scholarships, and other programs, or risk losing federal funding. The proposed rule goes further, threatening to pull private schools’ federal tax-exemption (501(c)(3)) status.
Feds to Virginia schools: End race-based policies or risk losing funds

The proposal aligns with broader efforts by President Donald Trump’s administration to eliminate race-based considerations in education. If found in violation, institutions’ financial stability and student support could be at risk.
It’s the latest development stemming from the Supreme Court’s June 2023 decision that effectively ended affirmative action in higher education by striking down race-conscious admissions policies at Harvard University and the University of North Carolina. 
Under the proposal, private institutions receiving the tax exemption would follow a ban on racial discrimination affecting an estimated 18,000 private educational institutions, from K–12 schools through colleges and trade schools. 
The rules would cover admissions, athletics, financial aid, scholarships, educational programs, and other school-supported activities. 
“Private educational institutions that promote discriminatory practices will no longer be afforded the benefits of federal tax-exempt status,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano in a Sept. 3 statement, adding that the proposed regulations put institutions on “notice” and schools that engage in racial discrimination should “expect to lose that status.”
Under the proposal, the changes would remove older IRS provisions that allow certain race-based preferences, which Treasury and the IRS say conflict with Supreme Court precedent.
The proposal states that religious schools could retain their religious missions and select students based on genuine religious affiliation, consistent with federal law.
Schools could also still support disadvantaged students using race-neutral factors such as income, geography, first-generation status, hardship, military-family status, or academic achievement.
The proposed rules would apply to tax years beginning on or after May 31, 2027, giving schools time to revise their policies.
Chris Peace, president of the Council of Independent Colleges in Virginia, said the 28 nonprofit private colleges represented in the group practice and promote discrimination-free educational environments. 
He added that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 already prohibits intentional discrimination based on race, color, or national origin.
“All of our institutions took seriously the federal government’s requests and did sort of internal inventories on … all relevant programs or other student opportunities to ensure that … they were in compliance with the federal law and federal interpretations of law,” Peace said by phone.
“At the end of the day, we’re going to remain compliant with federal law and expectations,” he said.
The public comment period for these proposed regulations remains open until Nov. 3, with potential publication by late May 2027.
Comments can be submitted through the eRulemaking Portal at www.regulations.gov (indicate IRS and REG-119986-25). 
Comments may also be submitted by paper to: CC:PA:01:PR (REG-119986-25), Room 5503, Internal Revenue Service, P.O. Box 7604, Ben Franklin Station, Washington, DC 20044.

name: VTDigger
title: Affordable housing project falls apart over infrastructure gaps in Highgate
description:
The lack of basic infrastructure like water and sewer lines has impeded housing development in many rural towns across Vermont. But the cancellation of a publicly-funded affordable housing project is highly unusual. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Affordable housing project falls apart over infrastructure gaps in Highgate.
text:
A rendering of the Highgate Village Housing project. Image courtesy of Cathedral Square/gbA Architecture
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
Plans to build 30 new subsidized senior apartments in the Franklin County town of Highgate have come to a halt. 
Affordable housing developer Cathedral Square and town officials called off the project after the town determined it could not provide a public water source for the apartments. The lack of basic infrastructure like water and sewer lines has impeded housing development in many rural towns across Vermont. But the cancellation of a publicly-funded affordable housing project is highly unusual.
Sharon Bousquet, a former town administrator for Highgate who helped shepherd along plans for the development three years ago, said the housing could have provided a way for older residents to remain in Highgate as they age – and brought in tens of thousands of dollars in new tax revenue.
“It was an opportunity of a lifetime for the town of Highgate,” Bousquet said. “It’s so sad.”
The Highgate Village Housing project was intended to be a cornerstone of a larger, years-long effort to revitalize the Canadian border town’s village core. Town officials hoped to build out a new municipal sewer system and a library. When a property at the center of town came up for sale, the town purchased it, and later brought in Cathedral Square as a nonprofit developer to construct apartments for adults aged 55 and over.
The wastewater plan has since hit a snag. It is still moving forward, but town officials are now considering pursuing a line of credit to make up a gap in funding, according to the Saint Albans Messenger. Back when plans for the housing development got underway in late 2023, town officials believed the wastewater system was on track to be completed in time to support the apartments, Bousquet said.
The town also thought a well serving the nearby Highgate Sports Arena could provide water for the apartments. 
But a feasibility study concluded in late 2025 that connecting to the sports arena well wasn’t viable, in part because of state rules regulating land use near public water systems. Other options – including extending water access from the Franklin County State Airport or the local elementary school, or drilling a new well – faced similar permitting hurdles or proved prohibitively expensive. 
Town officials and Cathedral Square looked to a new state financing tool, the Community and Housing Infrastructure Program, to help fund the water supply for the apartments, but determined it wouldn’t provide enough money. State officials have yet to approve their first CHIP loan.
The town ultimately decided that it couldn’t provide public water within the strict timeframe that Cathedral Square required, said current Town Administrator A.J. Johnson.
“We were all running on good assumptions, good expectations,” said Cindy Reid, director of real estate development at Cathedral Square. “If I knew then what I knew now, we would do more due diligence straight off on the water supply.”
Cathedral Square had already lined up $17 million to build the apartments, much of that public funding with swiftly-approaching deadlines. The nonprofit sunk $124,000 that it won’t get back on design and planning work, Reid said. She expects the bulk of the remaining funding will get redirected to other housing projects in the state.
The project’s largest single source of funding – about $9.7 million – came from highly-competitive federal tax credits awarded by the Vermont Housing Finance Agency earlier this year.
VHFA is currently figuring out how to go about re-awarding the credits so the state doesn’t lose them before they expire, said Executive Director Maura Collins. 
“It is commonplace in Vermont for there to be a lot of pressure to award projects funding when there are gaps in the development plan, whether that be not fully-approved permits or zoning needing to be changed, or, infrastructure being missing,” Collins said. 
In the future, the agency plans to grant funding awards later in the development process – once more uncertainties in the building plan have been ironed out, she said.
Reid and Bousquet, the former town administrator, both pointed to frequent turnover in town leadership as another factor in the housing project’s demise.
If the town is able to create a public water source in the future, Cathedral Square would consider reviving the project, Reid said.
“We’d be interested in coming back and looking at it, because it is an underserved area, it’s a growing elderly population, and we would love to support seniors aging in place in Highgate,” Reid said.

Former Indiana Govs. Mike Pence (left) and Mitch Daniels chat during an event on Tuesday, August 6, 2024. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Former two-term governor, Purdue University president and possible presidential contender Mitch Daniels’ new book — “Impatience is a Virtue: A Life Where the Buck Stops” — hits shelves Sept. 15.
“From the White House to the boardroom of Eli Lilly and Company to Indiana’s Governor’s Office to the presidency of Purdue, Daniels has brought transformative change to America’s public, private and nonprofit sectors,” a release from Lyons Press said. “Along the way, Daniels reflects on an incredible American story, how the Harley-Davidson riding grandson of a Syrian immigrant became one of the nation’s most admired leaders.”
We received an advance copy and gathered some key thoughts from the 505-page book.
On accepting a job in the Reagan White House: “The chance to work in the White House, especially that White House, proved irresistible. By late 1984, Ronald Reagan had done more than merely win another election; he had revived the American economy, and even more important, the American spirit. He had elevated and validated principles of ordered liberty that I had come to embrace, and was implementing them effectively in legislative and executive action. He had ushered in a conservative Camelot, as exciting and hopeful in its way as the Kennedy era had seemed to American liberals. I didn’t want to miss a chance to be part of it, directly.”
On President George W. Bush’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003: “Two decades after history has reached negative judgment about the decision to invade Iraq, I don’t dispute that conclusion, nor can I say whether the information on which it was based was sufficient or credible, as I was never privy to it. I do, on the other hand, reject the slander that President Bush knowingly lied to justify invading Iraq and deposing Saddam. The George Bush I came to know was precluded by his upbringing and his faith from doing such a thing. He may have let his anger at the murder of thousands of his countrymen cloud his judgment. He may have felt that if Saddam did in fact have WMDs, the consequences were so horrible that he could not run the risk. But in the moment of decision, I accept that he believed he had good reason to act as he did.”
On leaving D.C. to run for governor in 2003: “Not wishing to be charged for an extra weekend, I’d returned the rental furniture during the day. I slept on the rug in the small living room. On Saturday morning, I strapped my few belongings on the luggage rack of my two-seater convertible, stuffed the rest into the little trunk and passenger seat, and rolled out of the garage for the 600-mile drive home … I was now off the government payroll, but something made me wait a few more minutes until I crossed the boundary line from D.C. into Maryland. Picked up the phone and called Bill Oesterle. ‘Okay, big boy, you win. I’ll give you a month to get things ready. It’s a go.’ And off we went on the ride of a lifetime.”
When Democrats gained control of the Indiana House in 2007: “At his weekly press availability, (House Speaker B. Patrick Bauer) had told the reporters that I’d only be here two more years. Irritating as that was, I had a growing feeling that he was probably right. Looking back, this may have been the lowest period of the entire eight years. Ominous polls, the loss of the House, negative press stories, and frequent editorial sniping combined to put me in a fantastic mood. I lashed out privately at journalists like Matt Tully, allies like Luke Kelly, and apparently even those closest to me.”
On biting his lip: “I almost always managed to behave myself publicly. I can remember at one point telling press that my only health risk was bleeding to death from biting my lips so hard. When I did pop off in public, I always seemed to get the short end of the media stick. Our opponents would could say virtually anything about me and have it treated as good sport, but heaven forbid that I reply in kind, as in the ‘carbombed’ episode.”
On a 2010 Republican landslide: “As a purely political matter, 2010 completed the reshaping of the state’s electoral map that our 2004 win had launched. Very few Democrat officeholders were left in Southern Indiana; even local offices turned over to a similar degree as the legislative rout. The win ushered in an era of ‘trifecta government’ (one-party control of the governorship and both legislative houses) that continues to this day. However welcome when it’s your side that enjoys that status, it is at best a mixed blessing in terms of the quality of campaigns and government governance over the long term.“
Mitch Daniels’ campaign RV is now housed by the Indiana State Museum for possible future exhibits. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
On not running for president in 2012: “None of those calculations mattered when it became clear that Cheri and the four girls hated the idea and were petrified at the prospect. I tested their attitude at various intervals and made sure they understood how impressive the support was and how reasonable the prospects of success, and how many people I would be letting down by ducking. Nothing made a dent in their fear or opposition, as I put in my notes. All the planets were aligned, but the sun around which I revolve (the family) was not. So that was that. As I said to disappointed acquaintances later, there’s one sentence a father has no answer for. ‘Daddy, please don’t.'”
On RFRA: “In view of the many precedents for Indiana’s (Religious Freedom Restoration Act), I thought the uproar would subside. It was just one of those many occasions when I was dead wrong. The attacks on the bill escalated, and I watched sympathetically as Governor Pence was filleted by ABC commentator George Stephanopoulos on his Sunday talk show. Asked the same question six separate times, Mike floundered badly, trying to assert that the bill would not permit discrimination against gays. Certainly, one reason the issue erupted in Indiana and not in all the previous venues was the evolution of public attitudes about homosexuality, and there were nuances in the Indiana bill that opponents claimed differentiated it from other RFRAs. But I have no doubt that a contributing factor in the disaster that befell Governor Pence was the way in which he celebrated his temporary victory.”
On Donald Trump choosing Mike Pence as his running mate in 2016: “The tandem had no personal relationship but a persuasive political rationale. Mike had a reassuringly traditional conservative record to balance Trump’s new, more populist brand of Republicanism. His choice to run for governor had panned out perfectly. He had added an executive credential to his long and admirable legislative record. Whatever the media or Indiana public opinion said about his performance was of no importance now. Mike was a good fit for a national ticket back in the arenas, which he was best suited and most comfortable.”
On not running for U.S. Senate in 2023: “Some at the time may have imagined that the shot-across-the-bow threat from (David) McIntosh’s group had intimidated me out of running. That would be backward. If I had any real interest in the Senate, taking on that sort of politics would have been an incentive, not a deterrent. And we would have won. A survey at the time showed me with high recognition and favorable ratings, which by then must have had as much to do with our work at Purdue as my time in elected office. Meanwhile, no one outside his district had any idea who Jim Banks was.”
(Compiled by Niki Kelly)

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Employers highlight childcare solutions, pan tax credit risks
description: Indiana officials are increasingly looking to employers for help tackling the state's childcare shortage, but a tax credit remains unused.
text:
Toys are scattered along a shelf at Shepherd Community Center's Minnie Hartmann Neighborhood Childcare facility on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)As Indiana officials increasingly look to employers for help tackling the state’s childcare shortage, some gathered Wednesday to tout their internal solutions — and warn of a key risk in a years-old but unused tax credit.
The Indianapolis Airport Authority, which employs about 500 people operating several public airports and a heliport in central Indiana, seized on childcare as one fix for a demographic problem.
In 2019, half the municipal corporation’s workforce was set to reach retirement age within just five years. Their successors would be in their thirties and forties, and would have different needs, like childcare for their young kids.
But turnover was high, at 30%, and those leaving reported being unable to find affordable or high-quality care, said Rachel Stevens, senior director of human resources.
The airport authority now reimburses up to $10,000 in after-school care, summer camps and more for each child annually.
Stevens said turnover has dropped to under 10%.
Rachel Stevens, senior director of human resources at the Indianapolis Airport Authority. (Courtesy photo)
“We are hardly losing anybody, and we’re certainly not losing anybody because they’ve got family issues going on that we haven’t been able to help them address,” she said, noting the airport authority also offers reimbursements for elder care. 
Stevens spoke at a daylong childcare summit hosted by the Indiana Chamber of Commerce that also explored cheaper and pricier solutions.
Healthcare system Parkview Health has a staff of 18,000 working throughout northeast Indiana and northwest Ohio. It found that many exiting employees didn’t have a next job. Instead, they were leaving to take care of family.
But staff retention is key for Parkview, said Kristen Ruble, a well-being manager. It’s challenging to recruit from outside the state, and local talent can choose between the three different healthcare systems competing for their labor.
Parkview selected childcare “as one of those ways” to retain staff, with backup care being the biggest lift, according to Ruble.
“We are all day, all night,” she said. Most employees had childcare secured for their planned hours, but struggled when they had to pick up shifts last-minute. 
“We partnered locally with our childcare facilities — those that had capacity in order to take backup care — and so then we were able to market that to our employees,” Ruble said. “… And in addition to that, backup care is expensive because you don’t know that you need it right away. So we decided to take a step forward and say we would subsidize that for you.”
Others have gone further. Cummins, an engine manufacturer with 70,000 employees worldwide, has its own childcare facilities for staff, said John Havenaar, the company’s vice president of total rewards.
One site in Columbus, Indiana serves between 100 and 150 children daily. But demand is closer to 1,500 seats, Havenaar said.
“There’s definitely an interest, I think, in expanding our … brick and mortar facilities,” he said. “We’re looking at those things now.”
The panel walked through different solutions based on a company’s resources and employee needs.
Stevens said airport authority leaders “don’t want to get into the childcare business,” for instance, after concluding that was “beyond” the best interests of the organization and its staff.
Report: state loses out on $4.2B annually due to child care shortage

Panelists highlighted flexibility as a low-budget item, like allowing a parent to work remotely instead of take the day off when caring for a child too sick to attend school.
Parkview also participates in Tri-Share+, a regional initiative splitting the cost of childcare between certain employers, limited-income families and economic development grant funds held at the Northeast Indiana Early Childhood Coalition.
The healthcare system additionally offers employees money back for positive lifestyle habits — and matches the amount spent on childcare — while an internal social network allows employees to share babysitters, Ruble said.
‘Risks’ in state’s tax credit
Gov. Mike Braun has repeatedly called on businesses to do their part after he secured approval for a $200 million infusion to a government-run voucher program for low-income children.
“Every business in this state ought to be interested in that, if they’re complaining about not having the workforce,” he told reporters after visiting a childcare facility in July. “… They should be interested, again, in paying for a good portion of it, and that’s why we’re going to try to offer them incentives to get involved broadly across the state.”
In March, he signed into law House Enrolled Act 1177, which expanded eligibility for Indiana’s employer child care tax credit to small businesses with up to 500 employees and broadened what spending is eligible for the credit beyond the establishment of new facilities.
Employers can get a credit for up to half their qualified spending on licensed childcare for their employees’ children, up to $100,000 per firm annually. But there’s a statewide cap of $2.5 million.
The changes were retroactive to the beginning of the year. The tax credit was first available in the 2024 taxable year, but has never been used, according to the Department of Revenue.
Department of Revenue Tax Policy Director Collin Davis (Courtesy photo)
Sen. Kyle Walker, R-Lawrence, authored the credit.
“Until it was changed … it wasn’t as attractive, and I think now there’s just still an awareness issue,” he told reporters Wednesday.
Summit attendees repeatedly questioned what would happen if the cap is hit.
“That’s kind of the way that credits work when there’s a global cap,” Department of Revenue Tax Policy Director Collin Davis replied. “If you make an expenditure and (when) you file your return, you’re 26th in line and 25 people have claimed the maximum amount, you’re kind of out of luck.”
He said the agency processes credits in the order the tax returns are received, “which makes it all the more important to tax plan ahead of time and get the return in.”
But because the credit has never been claimed, there’s little information to go off. Davis said the risk businesses would be hit by the cap this upcoming tax year after making qualifying expenditures was unknown.
Stakeholders pressed for ways to track how much has been claimed as they consider childcare investments.
There’s no dashboard available, but the Department of Revenue is keeping tabs on the credit — and is “evaluating options for making this information more accessible,” according to the agency.
Camille Blunt, the chamber’s vice president of government affairs, urged the business community to take action and demonstrate to lawmakers if there’s any need for change.
“We’re not utilizing it, so we don’t have a good case or a basis for increasing that amount,” she said. “Once we do have that, … we’ll have a better story to tell.”
