name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Upcoming textile exhibit to offer ‘a personal connection’ to the crew of the Hunley submarine
description: "Textiles from the Deep: Findings from the H.L. Hunley Submarine" opens Oct.3 at The Charleston Museum
text:
The preserved H.L. Hunley Submarine is on display at the Friends of the Hunley museum and Clemson University's Warren Lasch Conservation Center in North Charleston. (Photo courtesy of Friends of the Hunley)CHARLESTON — A silk bandana worn around a crew member’s neck. A boot that still bears the footprint of the man who wore it. And a brass oil can with oil still inside.
These are among items recovered and preserved from the Confederate submarine, the H.L. Hunley, which was lost at sea for more than a century. It’s an exhibit more than 25 years in the making, with the articles of clothing and bits of cloth worn by members of the eight-man crew going on display for the first time at The Charleston Museum next month.
A before photo of a neckerchief recovered from the Hunley submarine. (Photo courtesy of Friends of the Hunley)An after photo of a neckerchief recovered from the Hunley submarine. (Photo courtesy of Friends of the Hunley)A before photo of a shoe recovered from the Hunley submarine. (Photo courtesy of Friends of the Hunley)An after photo of a shoe recovered from the Hunley submarine. (Photo courtesy of Friends of the Hunley)
“History can feel distant until something brings you closer to the people who lived it,” said Kellen Butler, executive director of the Friends of the Hunley nonprofit. “These remnants of clothing do just that, offering a remarkably personal connection to the men of the Hunley.”
The exhibit, “Textiles from the Deep: Findings from the H.L. Hunley Submarine,” opens Oct.3, remaining on display through April 4.
Funding from the non-profit friends group and the state-appointed South Carolina Hunley Commission paid for the exhibit, Butler said.
The Hunley’s history
The Hunley made history as the world’s first attack submarine on Feb. 17, 1864, when the all-volunteer crew boarded the ship and used it to sink the USS Housatonic, one of the Union’s mightiest naval blockade ships, off the coast of Charleston.
But after completing its mission, the Hunley mysteriously disappeared. It remained missing until 1995, when novelist and underwater explorer Clive Cussler found the shipwreck 4 miles off the coast of Sullivan’s Island after 15 years of hunting.
Another five years of ownership and funding fights ensued, led by former state Sens. Glenn McConnell and Ernie Passailaigue, of Charleston, and former U.S. Sen. Fritz Hollings, D-S.C.
South Carolina and the federal government eventually reached an agreement to keep the Hunley in the Palmetto State. Under the agreement, the United States retains title, but South Carolina gets custody.
In August 2000, crews finally hoisted the sub from the ocean floor and transported it to Clemson University’s Warren Lasch Conservation Center at the former Charleston Naval Base in North Charleston, where it remains submerged in a chemical bath for preservation.
Excavation of the Hunley’s interior began in 2001, with the remains of the crew buried at Magnolia Cemetery. Working with the Friends of the Hunley, Clemson scientists spent the next 25 years preserving the ship’s contents.
“They didn’t take a lot of things because they thought they had a mission to go out and come back,” Butler said of the crew. “They weren’t planning on staying.”
A preservation challenge
To restore the clothing and other textiles, the scientists meticulously cleaned each item while it was submerged in water before freeze drying the various cloth — silk, wool, cashmere and cotton. There are also personal items, including a wallet and a mustache comb.
A researcher at Clemson University’s Warren Lasch Conservation Center works to preserve a piece of textile recovered from the Hunley submarine. (Photo courtesy of Friends of the Hunley)
“Conserving textiles in marine environments is quite a feat. The fact that we can now preserve, study, and share them is an extraordinary opportunity,” said Virginia Theerman, curator of historic textiles at The Charleston Museum.
The Friends of the Hunley so far have been unable to display the items at their North Charleston museum due to a lack of humidity controls, Butler said. More than a century in salt water also damaged much of the clothing.
But Theerman, of The Charleston Museum, and Johanna Rivera-Diaz, a conservator at Clemson’s Warren Lasch Conservation Center, have put their collective scientific and historical expertise together to build a more complete picture of what the crew might have been wearing the night they went out.
What visitors will see
In the museum exhibit, visitors will see the pieces of recovered textiles next to mannequins dressed in matching historic garments from the time period.
“Clothes can be a way of really humanizing something that seems very distant and far away,” Theerman said. “These were men who were possibly scared, who were seeking valor, who had many many motivations for the actions that they took, and so reminding ourselves that every action taken by someone in history is also an action that we can imagine putting ourselves into, and really rediscovering what that might have felt like.”
An acrylic reproduction of the Hunley, showing the size of the crew cabin and position of tools, stands on the other side of the museum’s u-shaped gallery.
One of the original slings used to pull the Hunley out of the Atlantic Ocean and a jumpsuit from the volunteer team that worked to excavate the ship is also on display. And throughout the exhibit is the story of enslaved people who worked on the Hunley, sinking and raising it several times during test runs in the harbor, as well as those who made gunpowder at Ashley Ferry Nitre Works.
All together, Theerman said, the exhibit puts a new lens on a story that captured global attention for decades.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: TikTok wants state’s suit dismissed, responds to state ban on minor social media use
description: TikTok wants to scroll past Florida’s claim it isn’t complying with the state’s social media ban for minors, seeking to dismiss a lawsuit Attorney General James Uthmeier brought earlier this summer. The state’s suit must be dismissed because the 2024 law, HB 3, banning Floridians under age 14 from using social media apps, and requiring […]
text:
Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on June 15, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Uthmeier's office)TikTok wants to scroll past Florida’s claim it isn’t complying with the state’s social media ban for minors, seeking to dismiss a lawsuit Attorney General James Uthmeier brought earlier this summer.
The state’s suit must be dismissed because the 2024 law, HB 3, banning Floridians under age 14 from using social media apps, and requiring parental consent for those age 14 and 15, is vague and infringes on the First Amendment, TikTok argued.
“As applied to TikTok, HB3 shrinks the audiences of willing listeners to whom Defendants may speak, and silences the very minors the law purports to protect,” it wrote in a 52-page response to the state’s suit filed in a state trial court in St. Lucie County.
“And under HB3, the only way to avoid that unconstitutional result is to succumb to another — to cease offering a ‘social media platform,’ thereby abandoning a suite of expressive publishing features and TikTok’s chosen mode of expression,” it continued.
In June, Uthmeier filed the suit seeking monetary damages and a declaration that the social media company is a public nuisance. 
The 2024 law, tied up in court initially, took force in November 2025. It requires social media companies to prohibit children 13 and younger from using any app containing addictive features such as endless scrolling, push notifications, auto-play videos, and live-streaming. The law requires parental consent for users aged 14 and 15. 
Attorney general will now ‘aggressively enforce’ social media ban on minors

This is the first lawsuit the state has pursued against a company for not following the law since it started being “aggressively” enforced.
TikTok used its response to call into question the state’s prescription for companies to deliver on the law’s demands. It’s not clear, the company argued, how the state would like parental consent to be obtained, pointing out it has received no guidance about the “vague” statute. The company says it requires users under 18 to obtain parental permission before using the platform.
“Is that contractual provision sufficient? If not, what else might be required? A checked box on the TikTok sign-up page? A digital waiver? A notarized affidavit? HB3 provides no answer — it thus fails to provide ‘fair notice’ of what platforms must do to avoid liability for allowing 14- and 15-year-olds to hold accounts,” TikTok attorneys wrote. 
Uthmeier alleged TikTok is a public nuisance under statute and common law. The company argues that the law “burdens the First Amendment rights of Defendants and minor TikTok users in Florida in a way that is not appropriately tailored to a compelling or significant government interest.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The legal brief continues: “By forcing Defendants to abandon their chosen mode of expression in order to reach 13-, 14-, and 15-year-olds, and now seeking to hold Defendants liable for allegedly failing to do so, HB3 impermissibly burdens TikTok’s editorial discretion and compels it to speak in a materially different — and less effective — way.”
The document adds:
“Stripped of its rhetoric, the Complaint asks this Court to substitute the State’s editorial preferences for Defendants’ own — deciding how a dynamic platform containing billions of user-generated videos should be rated, what it should say about itself, which Floridians may speak on it, and how their speech should be arranged.”
The state seeks monetary damages to a degree Uthmeier feels could amount to “potentially billions.”
“When an enforcing authority seeks disgorgement through [the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act], it must allege, and ultimately prove, actual damages. The state has not alleged actual damages,” TikTok wrote, adding that actual damages “do not include consequential damages, nominal damages, speculative losses, or compensation for subjective feelings of disappointment.’”
Why us?
In a response to the Phoenix in June, TikTok said it had notified users under age 14 that their accounts would be suspended and that it was continuing to update the platform in response to the 2024 law. 
“TikTok already prohibits children younger than 13 years old from using the main TikTok platform,” the company wrote in the court filing.
The state claimed TikTok’s description of itself in the app store as having “infrequent/mild” sexual content and nudity constitutes an unfair business practice. 
“Courts have consistently recognized that age rating, content rating, and analogous evaluative classifications do not communicate objectively verifiable facts,” TikTok responded in its filing. “Instead, they reflect inherently subjective judgements that depend on context, perspective, and community standards.”
The law targets specific features of social media channels as in violation of this law, including infinite scrolling, autoplay, and livestreaming. 
“On many television channels and streaming services, the programming is 24/7, viewers can click to the next channel in an endless loop, and programming ‘auto-plays’ from one to the next. Yet, HB3 targets only ‘social media platform[s],’ not television,” TikTok argued. 
Uthmeier investigates
Uthmeier was appointed to his position in early 2025 by Gov. Ron DeSantis. He has been a central figure in the controversy over Hope Florida Foundation and works part-time as a professor at the University of Florida College of Law.
He faces his first election in just under two months.
Since being appointed, Uthmeier has used the power of his office to announce several headline-grabbing investigations targeting:

The “climate cartel” for alleged violation of the state’s consumer-protection or antitrust laws.
The NFL for alleged violation of the state’s Florida’s Civil Rights Act for attempting to diversify its team leadership.
Lorex, a Canadian company that sells home security cameras, often used to monitor cribs, pets, babysitters, and doorbells, for alleged ties to the Chinese government. The subpoenas were part of Uthmeier’s “consumer protection investigation into possible foreign spying risks,” according to a news release.

Uthmeier has not, however, used the power of his office to do what other Florida AGs have done: intervene in proposed public utility rate hikes before Florida’s Public Service Commission.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Teachers are omitting a big part of financial literacy
description: Financial literacy cannot exist without tax literacy, and how we teach taxes to the next generation shouldn’t start and end with what happens on April 15.
text:
Connecticut parents and students are gearing up for a new school year, and this fall brings a welcome addition to classrooms in the state and in many others nationwide. Personal finance courses, long an afterthought in the classroom, are now a graduation requirement or legislated for implementation in 30 states, including Connecticut (starting with 2027 graduates under S.B. 1165).
This is good news if done well, but a crucial component is often missing from or mistaught in these courses: taxes. You wouldn’t hand a 16-year-old the keys to a car and expect them to know how to drive. We shouldn’t expect the next generation to fully grasp financial literacy without a basic understanding of taxes either.
Right now, most Americans don’t understand how the tax code works. According to a poll conducted by TaxEDU, a majority of respondents do not have a basic understanding of common tax concepts. Sixty-four percent of respondents couldn’t correctly identify the difference between a credit and a deduction. Fifty-two percent were unaware of how tax brackets work. Most believed that a bigger tax refund was a good thing.
These misunderstandings aren’t just filing-season headaches. They create real financial consequences across a person’s entire career, overall financial planning, and major life decisions, like moving to a new city or starting a family. Scroll any social media feed, and you’ll read story after story of people turning down promotions out of fear that they’d lose more of their paycheck by entering a higher tax bracket. When we’re not teaching people the basics of when and how we’re taxed, it lets fear do the decision-making at the cost of advancement and opportunity.
Even when tax is taught alongside personal finance, the lessons tend to start and end with sitting students down with a pencil and a W-2, skipping to step 20 without even identifying the basics of what taxes are and how they work. That’s like handing your teenager a screwdriver and asking them to build a transmission.
Financial literacy cannot exist without tax literacy. Taxes touch your paychecks and your Amazon purchases. Taxes play a role in the roads you drive on, the schools you learn at, and in your savings for college, a mortgage, and retirement. Their impacts range from inconsequential to substantial, but either way, they’re real.
And just like every financial decision you make has trade-offs, so does every tax —and it goes far beyond filing. Students with blue-collar parents have probably heard about the no-tax-on-overtime provision that was signed into law last year. But do they know that this exemption expires in three years? Or that its price tag is adding to the national debt?
Or consider students in one of the nearly dozen states that have tried to repeal property taxes this year. Do they know that zeroing out the property tax in a place like Florida could lead to sales taxes rising up to 20 percent just to fill the revenue gap? Or that rural counties would have to increase taxes higher than cities without property taxes in place?
Taxes and the policy decisions that drive them don’t happen in a vacuum, and how we teach taxes to the next generation shouldn’t start and end with what happens on April 15.
We need to shift the focus, to help students and teachers alike understand how our government is financed and what role we play as taxpayers in that system. States like Connecticut deserve kudos for finally prioritizing financial literacy. But before students can drive off into the sunset of being financially sound, they need to understand the nuts and bolts of the taxes that influence almost every financial decision they’ll make.
Zoe Callaway is Vice President of Education at the Tax Foundation.

title: At midterm convention, Trump pledges cash to voters if Republicans hold Congress
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump headlined the first night of the first Republican midterm convention Wednesday, seeking to rally his base ahead of the November elections and dangling a “Trump dividend” to voters if his party retains control of both congressional chambers.While the Republican National Committee’s two-day event — dubbed a “Trump-a-palooza” by party Chair Joe Gruters — aimed to bolster support for major candidates, some vulnerable Republicans were notably absent.Still, speaker after speaker, including Republican lawmakers, Cabinet members and people billed by the RNC as “everyday Americans,” filled five hours before Trump took the stage and promised, “Vote Republican and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come.”“There’ll be nothing like it,” Trump said during a nearly two-hour keynote address in which he touted the “greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”The event at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, which did not include voting delegates, is the first major-party midterm convention since Democrats’ convention in 1982. Democrats also held convention-like conferences following the 1974 and 1978 elections.The GOP convention comes amid sagging poll numbers for Trump as his war with Iran drags on and voters worry about inflation driven by increasing energy costs and tariffs.Financial incentiveTrump acknowledged political challenges without attributing them to the unpopular parts of his agenda.“For some reason, when a president wins, even if he's really a good president or a great president — there aren't too many of them — they don't win the midterms, and nobody quite knows why,” he said. “We've got to change that because we have something going that's so good we can't let that string be broken. So I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot.”Trump said if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate, he would pay out $5,000 “to every adult.”“The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America. We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money,” he said.This is not the first time Trump has promised to send checks. The president said in November 2025 he would send $2,000 to Americans from tariff revenue that he falsely said would reach “trillions” of dollars. Those payments never materialized and Trump’s emergency tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court. The government is now on the hook for refunding American businesses that paid the import taxes.Trump announced he’ll be campaigning for nearly three dozen Republican candidates in competitive races over the next 55 days.“We can win every one of those races, but I'm going to go to every one of those states for congressmen and for senators,” he said.Collins, Sullivan absentIn perhaps the night’s most surprising turn, Democratic Sen. John Fetterman made an appearance in a video praising fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick, a Republican, and vowing to work with Trump to shore up the steel industry. But two of those most vulnerable Republican senators were missing from the more than three dozen speakers Wednesday night.Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Dan Sullivan of Alaska, both locked in tough reelection bids, reportedly declined to attend. Neither Collins’ nor Sullivan’s campaigns or Senate offices replied to States Newsroom’s requests for comment.Sullivan’s campaign posted several images and videos of the senator in Alaska Wednesday.Collins posted a message of support for the New England Patriots on her X feed as the RNC event was in full swing. The made-for-TV political gathering aired the same night as the NFL’s season kick-off between the Patriots and Seattle Seahawks.An analysis by CNBC on Wednesday found fewer than half of Republican candidates in the most competitive congressional districts were slated for speaking roles during the two-day event. Crowd boos ThuneBut many Trump allies running for reelection spoke, and U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, sat in a row with Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet members.Attendees cheered when Trump said Johnson “will go down as the greatest speaker of the House in the history of our country.”But a chorus of “boos” erupted when the president asked where Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota was in the crowd.“No, no,” Trump responded to the booing. “John is working hard. He's got great opposition.” Thune and Trump have been at odds about the Senate taking up a strict election bill that would require voters to provide a birth certificate or passport to register to vote, among other provisions.Unlike other Republican leaders from both chambers, Thune was not scheduled to speak at the convention.An individual close to Thune told States Newsroom the majority leader is in Dallas and wanted to give other Republicans an opportunity to speak.‘We’re so glad you’re here’Several Trump allies, even those facing tight or toss-up races, spoke in praise of the president while stumping for their own candidacies.Former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, running for an open Senate seat in North Carolina, and Sen. John Husted, fighting to keep his seat in a special Ohio election, praised Trump for passing tax cuts. The North Carolina seat is rated “lean Democrat,” by the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, and the Ohio seat rated a “toss up.”While both Whatley and Husted mentioned their opponents and former President Joe Biden more times than they did Trump, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for U.S. Senate, did not shy away from lauding the president.“We’re so glad you’re here,” said Paxton, who unseated longtime Sen. John Cornyn in a Republican primary after receiving Trump’s endorsement.“The press, the courts, and the establishment all tried to take President Trump down, but he's won every single time. He's delivered more for this country than anyone before, secured victories for America that no other president could, and always stood up for Texas,” Paxton said.Attendees waved “Keep the Majority” signs and chanted “USA” while House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., railed against Democrats, and said “We will not let the Marxists, communists and anarchists destroy it.”“This historic midterm convention is rallying Republicans at the perfect time because so much is on the line this November,” said House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, a Louisiana Republican.‘A party for Donald Trump’Democrats panned the event as an expensive celebration for the president.“While Republicans spend millions of dollars throwing a party for Donald Trump, Democrats are spending our time and resources doing the work that wins elections: Talking to voters, registering new ones, organizing communities, and fighting for every vote,” Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said in a statement Wednesday.“The difference is stark,” he continued. “As Republican candidates worship an unpopular president, Democrats are going on offense and staying focused on lowering costs, making life more affordable, and delivering for working families.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Baltimore City Community College leader defends school against audit
description: The president of Baltimore City Community College defended the school against a recent state audit that found management problems and the potential payment of financial aid to nonexistent "ghost students," but lawmakers appeared unimpressed.
text:
Baltimore City Community College's downtown location. (File photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The president of Baltimore City Community College defended the school against a recent state audit that found management problems and the potential payment of financial aid to nonexistent “ghost students,” but said Wednesday that improvements remain a work in progress.
“The audit at this point, is served to assist to validate the state of college for the new day, and we’ve been working for that new day,” said BCCC President and CEO Debra McCurdy in testimony to the legislature’s Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee.
“These findings can be taken care of. They can be fixed so that we can demonstrate continuous improvement in operation at the institution,” she said.
But state lawmakers appeared unimpressed with the progress. And Legislative Auditor Brian Tanen, noting some repeat violations in this summer’s audit from an audit in 2022, rated the latest audit of the school “unsatisfactory.”
Baltimore City Community College President and CEO Debra McCurdy, center, testified before the General Assembly’s Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The state audit, released in June by Tanen’s office, found that the college apparently awarded $264,000 in financial aid to 145 potentially fictitious or “ghost students,” and didn’t adhere to procurement laws. It also said the school could not account for more than 20,000 missing items such as laptops and other computer equipment, worth a total of about $20 million.
In terms of the AI-generated fake students identified in the audit, McCurdy said that is a national concern that’s not just happening at the community college.
McCurdy, who became president of the school in 2019, attributed some of the challenges to a vacancy rate that exceeds 25% for BCCC positions.
McCurdy said new leadership has been hired to help get the school back on track, some of whom sat beside her Wednesday. McCurdy said the new staff came to the college after the publication of a 2022 audit.
Committee co-chair Del. Jared Solomon (D-Montgomery) read a portion of the 2022 audit, which said the school planned to invest in new software to keep track of its inventory. But the 2026 audit said the school couldn’t account for more than 20,000 missing items such as laptops and other computer equipment totaling about $20 million.
“With all due respect … this response is almost verbatim to what you’re telling us today. How long should we expect to give you grace that this is going to be fixed?” Solomon asked. “And again, where are those 20,000 items? How many of them are lost?”
The school’s controller, Eileen Waitsman, said most of the unaccounted-for items “were older assets” with a net value of less than $40,000.
“They were not located, and so that’s why they were identified as missing,” Waitsman said.
Del. Steve Johnson (D-Harford) asked why the school doesn’t conduct competitive bids and keeps track of any documentation.
Del. Steve Johnson (D-Harford) questioned officials with Baltimore City Community College about a recent audit of the college. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Anna Lansaw, executive director of procurement and auxiliary services at the college, said the school was awarded statutory delegation in July 2021 to operate “under our own purview. A lot of the procurements that are conducted are conducted in inter-cooperative government purchases that are excluded from a formal procurement process.”
Lansaw challenged the audit finding that the school did not have formal contracts.
“Even though we did not do a formalized executed contract, we did do purchase orders because these are only one-year agreements,” Lansaw said.
“You understand how this could attract scrutiny on a pretty huge level. That’s why we have the questions today,” Johnson said.
“Yes sir,” said Lansaw, who added future grant-funded contracts will include formal, written agreements.
The audit committee’s meeting comes slightly more than two weeks after the community college’s faculty ratified its first-ever contract.
Faculty members, represented by United Academics of Maryland Local 6628, an affiliate of American Federation of Teachers-Maryland, voted unanimously on the contract that includes a 3.25% raise and a $1,000 bonus in the first year. It also establishes wage increases of at least 8.25% over the three-year contract, “clearer criteria for promotion, and critical protections, including a successorship agreement that ensures faculty keep their union in the event of a merger or reduction in force.”

description: Just 264 votes separated moderate Aaron Guckian from MAGA candidate Elaine Pelino in the GOP gubernatorial primary as of 10:30 p.m. Wednesday, one of few races still too close to call. Guckian led Pelino by 1.1 percentage points according to preliminary and unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Results from ballots cast […]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidates Aaron Guckian, left, and Elaine Pelino, right. (Left photo by Michael Salerno; right photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)Just 264 votes separated moderate Aaron Guckian from MAGA candidate Elaine Pelino in the GOP gubernatorial primary as of 10:30 p.m. Wednesday, one of few races still too close to call.
Guckian led Pelino by 1.1 percentage points according to preliminary and unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Results from ballots cast on Wednesday in Little Compton, Portsmouth, Providence, and Warwick were still incomplete, along with some mail ballots.
A self-described “compassionate conservative,” Guckian, 50, offered a more tempered version of Republican ideology compared to Pelino’s outspoken Trumpian views. Guckian also has modest name recognition in Rhode Island, having worked as an aide for former Gov. Don Carcieri and ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor in 2022.
Pelino, by contrast, was a political newcomer. Yet, the 72-year-old led retired comedian led Guckian in multiple public polls leading up to the primary. Her campaign, run primarily through social media, espoused a clear Trump agenda, warning that the state’s leftward progression was veering into “socialism.”
Guckian, who won the Rhode Island GOP’s endorsement, emphasized his ability to work across the political aisle, including in his former job as executive director of the Rhode Island Dental Association. 
While voting at the Swift Community Center in East Greenwich Wednesday morning, Guckian argued with a poll worker who prevented him from taking a photo of his daughter Emma, 18, while she voted for the first time. Ballot selfies are allowed in Rhode Island as long as other voters’ ballots are not shown. Guckian did not immediately respond to requests for comment Wednesday afternoon. 
The same poll worker also demanded that a Rhode Island Current photographer delete a photo she had just taken of a line of voters checking in at the Swift Community Center. Rhode Island Current did not delete the photo and left the building. The poll worker came outside and apologized to the photographer.
The primary winner will face Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, and independents Ken Block, Jay Gotra, and C.D. Reynolds in the Nov. 3 general election. 
Laura Paton contributed to this story.

text:
Vic Mellor, right, defeated Dr. Stephen Skoly, left, in the Republican primary for Rhode Island's 2nd Congressional District seat. (Contributed photos)Warwick businessman Vic Mellor will face Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner in November after defeating Dr. Stephen Skoly in the Republican primary for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District Wednesday.
Mellor captured just over 58% of the vote, compared with Skoly’s 42%, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections.
Mellor, a 56-year-old entrepreneur and former Marine who moved back to Rhode Island last year after several decades living in Florida, prevailed over the Rhode Island Republican Party’s endorsed candidate. Mellor participated in the Jan. 6, 2021, march on the U.S. Capitol, describing the event as “a peaceful exercise of free speech rights, emphasizing his stance on grassroots activism and the right to protest government actions” on his campaign website.
On that date, a mob of President Donald Trump’s supporters attacked U.S. Capitol Police officers, pushed through barricades and disrupted a joint session of Congress where the results of the presidential election of 2020 were being certified as lawmakers fled. 
Forty two minutes after the polls closed, Magaziner announced he would hold an 11:30 a.m. press conference Thursday outside the State House with police officers who fought to defend the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6. Magaziner’s press release called Mellor a “rioter.”
Magaziner will be joined by Harry Dunn, who served as a U.S. Capitol Police officer for over 15 years, and Daniel Hodges, a D.C. Metropolitan Police Department Officer since 2014, and a Virginia National Guard veteran. Hodges was attacked by the mob as captured on video. 
Mellor and Skoly met for only one debate, which was recorded at WJAR NBC10 the Friday afternoon before Labor Day weekend. Mellor’s campaign was buoyed by a plentiful amount of self-financing which he poured into his campaign. Mellor reported more than $3 million in receipts through Aug. 20, including $2.175 million in loans and more than $735,000 in contributions from Mellor himself, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Skoly, a 70-year-old East Greenwich oral and maxillofacial surgeon, reported about $225,000 in total receipts over the election cycle, according to his most recent filing as of Aug. 20.
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: Rhode Island Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos clinches second term, defeating four primary challengers
description: Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos held on to her seat, defeating four Democratic primary challengers Wednesday night with 37% of the votes just before 9 p.m., according to preliminary, unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. The Democratic incumbent’s victory comes as her gubernatorial counterpart, Gov. Dan McKee, was trounced in his reelection bid[...]
text:
Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos checks in to vote at her polling site at Webster Avenue School in Providence to vote in Wednesday's primary. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos held on to her seat, defeating four Democratic primary challengers Wednesday night with 37% of the votes just before 9 p.m., according to preliminary, unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections.
The Democratic incumbent’s victory comes as her gubernatorial counterpart, Gov. Dan McKee, was trounced in his reelection bid against challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes. Matos’ win was not assured, having been outfundraised by many of her Democratic challengers and polling neck-and-neck with one of them, former Newport mayor and current councilor Xay Khamsyvoravong just two weeks ago.
Trailing Matos by more than 10 points as of 9 p.m., Khamsyvoravong conceded the race, congratulating Matos in a statement provided by text message Wednesday night.
Matos’ campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment. 
Matos, 52, is the state’s first Afro-Latina lieutenant governor.
She was McKee’s pick for the No. 2 spot in state government after he ascended to the governor’s seat in 2021. But their relationship frayed as each official faced their own set of scandals. For Matos, that included fake signatures on her nomination papers during the 2023 Democratic primary for Rhode Island’s 1st Congressional District, which ended with criminal charges and probationary sentences for two of her campaign workers. Matos was never charged, and maintained her innocence.
Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor Xay Khamsyvoravong shakes hands with South Kingstown voter Chris Diorio outside the South Kingstown Recreation Center on Wednesday morning, Sept 9, 2026. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
More recently, last week, Matos’ campaign came under fire from Khamsyvoravong, marking the first sparks in an otherwise quiet and congenial primary. Khamsyvoravong denounced Matos’ campaign for a $100,000 advertising spend by a “dark money super PAC.” The Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association spent money on mailers and radio ads on Matos’ behalf in the final days before the primary. Khamsyvoravong’s campaign said the association has accepted money from corporate interests, including Amazon and Northrop Grumman, which have ties to “ICE detention and enforcement infrastructure.”
Matos’ campaign defended the PAC donations, which were not accepted in her own campaign account, but made on her behalf. A first-generation immigrant who moved to Rhode Island from the Dominican Republic at age 20, Matos has been outspoken about the need for protections for immigrants while denouncing federal enforcement tactics. 
Matos drew support from unions and advocacy and municipal groups, reflecting her work as lieutenant governor and prior tenure on the Providence City Council, where she served from 2011 to 2021, leaving as council president. She did not place any TV ads, the only Democratic candidate other than Ponaganset High School teacher Ross McCurdy not to use traditional broadcast messaging in her campaign. 
Khamsyvoravong, the son of Laotian refugees, would have been the first Asian American elected to the seat in Rhode Island.
Matos’ incumbency did not translate to a campaign cash advantage. Khamsyvoravong outraised the incumbent lieutenant governor by more than triple during the campaign cycle, outspending her by even more.
The former Newport city mayor, and current member of the city council, Khamsyvoravong, 42, leveraged political ties that transcended the City by the Sea, receiving endorsements from local Democratic party leaders, Attorney General Peter Neronha and U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo, among others.
The primary also featured Providence City Councilor Sue AnderBois, who received 17% of votes; former R.I. Sen. Cindy Coyne of Barrington with 13% of primary votes;  and McCurdy at just under 6% of votes as of 9 p.m.
Matos will face Republican John Loughlin in the November general election.

description: Former state cannabis regulator Kim Ahern on Wednesday won the Democratic nomination to be Rhode Island’s next attorney attorney general, defeating three other candidates including the chosen successor of the outgoing AG. Ahern received 37% of the vote in the Democratic primary, according to preliminary, unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elec[...]
text:
Kim Ahern, Democratic candidate for attorney general, holds her daughter Parker, 2, as she votes at Laurelmead Senior Living in Providence on Wednesday morning, Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Former state cannabis regulator Kim Ahern on Wednesday won the Democratic nomination to be Rhode Island’s next attorney attorney general, defeating three other candidates including the chosen successor of the outgoing AG.
Ahern received 37% of the vote in the Democratic primary, according to preliminary, unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Hoffmann, a former policy director and senior counsel in Attorney General Peter Neronha’s office who won the term-limited incumbent endorsement, received 33%.
Rep. Joe Solomon Jr. of Warwick received 20% and Rep. Jason Knight of Barrington, received 10.4%.
If elected in November, Ahern will be only the second woman to serve as Rhode Island attorney general. Republican Arlene Violet was the first, serving from 1985 to 1987.
Ahern served nine years as a special assistant AG under three attorneys general: Neronha, Peter Kilmartin, and Patrick Lynch. Her campaign notes she prosecuted more than 1,000 cases as a member of the office’s Special Victims Unit. 
She then went on to serve as deputy counsel for former Gov. Gina Raimondo and went on to become the deputy chief of staff for Gov. Dan McKee.
Ahern most recently served as the head of the three-member Cannabis Control Commission, a position she held since the panel’s inception by the state in 2023. Hoffmann has critiqued Ahern’s tenure as a cannabis regulator, using social media to promote how no new retail shops have been licensed since recreational weed was legalized in the General Assembly in 2022.
Democratic candidate for attorney general Keith Hoffmann, right, watches election returns with his wife Rachel during his campaigns watch party at The Guild in Pawtucket on Sept. 9 ,2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Hoffmann maintained a significant financial edge in the crowded race, raising over $1.5 million since launching his campaign last August. That included $760,000 in loans to his own campaign.
Ahern in the closing days of the race loaned herself $295,000, which her campaign said was needed to respond to Hoffmann’s paid attacks.
Solomon, who was first elected to the House in 2014, sought to capitalize on his more moderate profile and relied primarily on his support from police and firefighter unions. Polls consistently ranked him third.
Knight, a U.S. Navy veteran and former state prosecutor who now works as a criminal-defense attorney, tried to emphasize his credentials as a “progressive fighter” thanks to his tenure in the state’s House of Representatives.
Ahern will face Republican Alan Gordon, who ran unopposed in the GOP race for the office, in the Nov. 3 general election.
Democratic attorney general candidate Jason Knight, left, meets Providence resident Justin Taymes and his duck, Dawn, outside Vartan Gregorian Elementary School on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. Noelia Martinez sits on a motorcycle nearby. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)

title: Alaska gubernatorial candidates participate in first forum since a post-primary ballot shuffle
description: Three of the four remaining Alaska gubernatorial candidates discussed subjects ranging from the hard numbers that quantify the state’s fiscal challenges to more esoteric topics like quality of life on Tuesday in their first face-to-face meeting since a post-primary shakeup changed the field. Former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, and former A[...]
text:
Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, a Republican candidate for governor, listens to a question at a Sept. 9. 2026, forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. Next to him, from left, are former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins, a Democrat, and former Attorney General Treg Taylor, a Repub.ican. The three, along with Republican Bernadette Wilson, who did not attend the event, are facing off in the general election. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Three of the four remaining Alaska gubernatorial candidates discussed subjects ranging from the hard numbers that quantify the state’s fiscal challenges to more esoteric topics like quality of life on Tuesday in their first face-to-face meeting since a post-primary shakeup changed the field.
Former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, and former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Attorney General Treg Taylor, both Republicans, pitched their visions for state leadership at a candidate forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club.
It was a friendly audience for him and Taylor, Bronson noted at the event, held at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage.
“I’m assuming most folks in the room, except for maybe the media, are Republicans,” Bronson said.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

It was the first post-primary forum for Taylor, who moved from the fifth to fourth spot on the open ballot after Democrat Tom Begich withdrew from the race. Among the 17 gubernatorial candidates in the open primary, Kreiss-Tomkins finished first, with 22.5% of the vote. Begich, a former state senator, finished second with 20.8% but pulled out of the race at the end of August and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins.
Taylor joked about the rapid changes to the election field — he was removed from the ballot at the end of August because of financial reporting problems but then placed back on the ballot when Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom reversed her disqualification decision.
“I’m back!” he said in his opening statement. “Surprised nobody out there has a neck brace on.  I certainly needed one for a little bit there, but it’s great to be back.”
Not attending was Bernadette Wilson, the top-ranked Republican with 10% of the primary election vote, putting her in third place among the 17 contenders in the primary and second among the four candidates advancing to the general election.
Bronson, who finished the primary just behind Wilson with 8.1% of the vote, aimed some veiled criticism at her, nonetheless.
One barb came during a discussion about the Alaska Permanent Fund dividend.
“Some people will tell you that you can cut your way to a full PFD. You can’t do it. It’s not mathematically possible,” he said.
Wilson has argued that state government should be drastically reduced and that the annual dividend payout should revert to its older and more generous form. That would not be possible, even if every state worker were fired, Bronson said.
 

Former Attorney General Treg Taylor speaks at a Sept. 8, 2026, gubernatorial candidate forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“Anyone who tells you it is has no idea what they’re talking about,” he said.
Kreiss-Tomkins’ criticism during the forum was aimed at outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican.
He said his plans for working with Republicans and independents as well as Democrats contrasted with what he characterized as a combative, highly partisan and unproductive approach taken by the current governor.
“If you have liked the last eight years of governance in the state of Alaska, you should not support us. If you want change, if you want a different approach to government in the state of Alaska, a problem-solving approach, a bipartisan approach, you should consider supporting me and Zac,” he said, referring to his running mate, Anchorage Assembly member Zac Johnson.
Variety of issues
The forum covered a wide range of issues, including fiscal topics, education, the proposed North Slope liquified natural gas pipeline, Cook Inlet natural gas needs, fishing, public employee pensions and data centers.
A key difference between Kreiss-Tomkins and the two Republicans at the forum concerns the use of public money for students’ education. Kreiss-Thomkins said he supports varied educational options that give students and families choices — including neighborhood schools, charters schools, correspondence schools — but he emphasized that public education money should go only to public schools.
“If parents want to educate their children in a private or parochial school, by all means, that should be their right, but I don’t think public money should pay for that education,” he said.
Taylor, an advocate of vouchers that can be used to pay for private schools, said parents should be able to use state funding to provide whatever they consider to be the best educational choice for their children.
“I, for one, am fully on board with a constitutional amendment that allows the money to follow the child,” he said. “The only way our education system gets better is if there’s competition, and there has to be viable competition.”
As the state attorney general, Taylor defended the Dunleavy administration’s policy of providing homeschool funding for students attending private schools. The issue continues to play out in the courts.
Bronson articulated a position on school choice similar to that of Taylor, including support for a constitutional amendment.
Under the approach he would take, “the money goes in the kid’s backpack and wherever the parent says the kid goes, the money goes with them figuratively,” he said.
 

Former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins speaks at a Sept. 8, 2026, gubernatorial candidate forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Both Kreiss-Tomkins and Bronson said the deterioration of public education in Alaska is an important factor in the state’s loss of working-age adults and its 13 consecutive years of net outmigration, with more people leaving Alaska than moving in.
For Kreiss-Tomkins, education shortcomings are at or near the top of the list of factors that feed the demographic trend.
“A lot of the people who are leaving the state are people in my generation,” he said. “Key reasons they’re leaving: They’ve lost confidence in the quality of schools in Alaska.”
Bronson agreed with Kreiss-Tomkins that Alaska’s educational system has deteriorated and that the poor quality is a big factor in the state’s negative demographic trend.
But Taylor said the key to reversing the loss of working-age adults was to expand resource extraction industries. More economic activity through resource development would draw more working-age people to Alaska and keep more here, he said.
“We haven’t fully embraced the idea that we are a resource state, in my opinion,” he said.
Other differences on display concerned labor issues.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he would have signed a bill passed by lawmakers, House Bill 78, that would have restored a defined-benefit plan for public employees. To save money, the state switched two decades ago to a defined-contribution pension system. But lawmakers supporting House Bill 78 concluded that the change made working in Alaska less attractive. Dunleavy vetoed that bill, and lawmakers fell short when they tried to override the veto.
Taylor said he opposed the bill and agreed with Dunleavy’s veto and considers defined-benefit pensions to be bad for the economy.
“People with pensions do not generate generational wealth,” he said. “They mean nothing to their children. They work all those years and have nothing to give to their children.”
Pensions, unlike 401(k) retirement accounts, do not transfer to heirs. But people who receive pensions can invest them in ways that benefit their heirs.
Bronson said he would not have allowed House Bill 78 to become law, either. He said it is possible for the state to support defined-benefit pensions, but that would require management by an outside financial adviser.
 

Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson listens to discussion at a Sept. 8, 2026, gubernatorial candidate forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	In addition to support of a return to defined benefits for certain state employees, Kreiss-Tomkins said he supports the law passed through citizen initiative in 2024 that raised the state’s minimum wage and mandated paid sick leave, though added that he is open to modifications if they are needed.
“I think it’s important for the state of Alaska to stand up for people who are otherwise really going to struggle to make ends meet,” he said.
Taylor said he opposed the law, and considers it government intrusion that dampens business opportunities. “I’ve heard over and over and over again from small business owners being suffocated by that new law and the requirements for that new law,” he said.
Bronson was not specific about his position on the new law, but he agreed with Taylor’s statements about government regulation.
The candidates also discussed the idea of data centers in Alaska. The idea of large-scale data centers is controversial because of potential stresses on local energy and water supplies, as well as possible disruptions to neighborhoods.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he supported a moratorium on data centers until the legislature approves a bill to regulate them and ensure that they fit with Alaska’s needs.
Bronson said data centers are inevitable because of the use of artificial intelligence in industry, the military and other spheres. They should be properly regulated, he said, but the state and nation should not delay their development because China and other competitors have already embraced them.
“AI is coming. It’s here. You’re not going to stop it,” he said. “You can be mad. I know the buggy whip manufacturers are still mad from 120 years ago when we got rid of the horse and moved to that thing called an automobile.”
Taylor stated a position similar to that expressed by Bronson.
“It’s reality in our lives,” he said.  Alaska could heed lessons from other states and regions where data centers have been built, he said. “We’ve seen where it works right. Now, it’s really loud where it doesn’t work right, so we know what works.”
The Last Frontier Republican Club recorded the forum. It is one of dozens scheduled this fall for gubernatorial, U.S. Senate and U.S. House candidates.
Former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, and former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, a Republican, chat before the start of a Sept. 8. 2026, gubernatorial candidate forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

title: A landslide victory and a potential new chapter for Rhode Island’s capital city
description: Providence voters handed a decisive win to progressive Rep. David Morales over the capital city’s pragmatic incumbent Brett Smiley in Wednesday’s Democratic mayoral primary. Morales captured 57% of the vote to Smiley’s 43% after polls closed at 8 p.m. according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. The 27-year-old democratic sociali[...]
text:
State Rep. David Morales defeated Providence Mayor Brett Smiley in Wednesday's Democratic primary. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Providence voters handed a decisive win to progressive Rep. David Morales over the capital city’s pragmatic incumbent Brett Smiley in Wednesday’s Democratic mayoral primary.
Morales captured 57% of the vote to Smiley’s 43% after polls closed at 8 p.m. according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections.
The 27-year-old democratic socialist will face Republican Dave Talan, 77, in the Nov. 3 general election. The Providence electorate is solidly Democratic, with 55% of the city’s voters registered as Democrats. 
Voter turnout in Providence reached 31%, according to the Secretary of State’s voter turnout tracker. 
The central theme of Morales’s campaign had been that Providence can no longer endure the status quo when it comes to housing affordability in the capital city. Smiley, 47, campaigned on his record as a calm and steady steward of city management.
The contest unfurled alongside a schism over the Democratic party’s direction and ethos — a similar context which helped propel New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to success last November. Morales embraced more fully the leftist strains of Democratic electoral politics, acquiring the endorsements of U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna of California. The Morales campaign even held a Brooklyn fundraiser in July to gather the support of well-connected progressives there, some of whom were also in Mamdani’s camp. The New York City mayor never, however, endorsed Morales.   
Smiley argued Morales’ idealistic approach was ill suited to the intricacies of running the capital city. The mayor has opposed rent control policies, arguing they are impractical and do not address the root causes of the housing shortage. He frequently criticized the Providence City Council’s specific variant of rent pricing regulation as “a bad version of a bad policy.” 
Morales’ campaign tried to attract a younger and more diverse voter bloc in response. Providence is a relatively young, diverse and renter-heavy city, per Census Bureau estimates, which put its population of 195,000 at about 45.3% Hispanic or Latino, 33.5% foreign-born, and only 11.6% aged 65 or older. Only 41.4% of occupied housing units are owner-occupied in the city.   
Both candidates were optimistic earlier Wednesday as they crisscrossed Providence, chatting and meeting with voters in the final hours of the hotly contested race.
Morales cast his vote bright and early when polls opened at 7 a.m. at Pleasant View Elementary School. He spent the rest of day darting to and from polling places, even those on the East Side — traditionally seen as a stronghold of Smiley supporters. But the area now had a troop of supporters for Morales and his City Council allies a little over a block away from Smiley’s own polling place.
Smiley cast his ballot shortly after 8:30 a.m. at the Fox Point Boys & Girls Club, where he was accompanied by his husband Jim DeRentis. In a pretty much empty gymnasium, the two men fed their ballots into the machine with reporters and poll workers looking on.  
Providence Mayor Brett Smiley votes at Fox Point Boys & Girls Club in Providence at around 8 a.m. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
“This has always been in the hands of the voters, and this is not about me. This is about the city,” Smiley said outside his polling place Wednesday morning. 
Around noon at Vartan Gregorian Elementary School, right down the street from Smiley’s polling site, Morales donned one of his characteristically colorful suits to meet up with supporters and thank voters for turning out. 
After 11 months of campaigning, Morales said he was excited with how voters were responding to him in the election’s final moments.
“What’s at stake is the question of whether or not we can continue to call the city we love home,” Morales said.
In the final laps toward the primary, from Aug. 12 through Sept. 1, Smiley’s campaign spent about 7.6 times what Morales’ campaign did. 
The mayor’s most recent campaign filing reported spending $652,537 while raising about $159,794 from individuals and political action committees. Smiley entered the campaign’s final week with $61,086 in cash after this spending spree, down from more than $555,000 at the beginning of the reporting period and smaller even than Morales’ campaign coffers in the final stretch. 
Morales’ filing for the same period shows he spent $85,789, with about $73,046 incoming contributions from individuals and PACs. He entered the primary’s concluding week with $96,490 on hand.   
In addition to differences in political philosophy, Morales and Smiley demonstrated different approaches to campaign spending. Smiley lavished hundreds of thousands of dollars into television advertising while Morales largely relied on digital outreach, mailers and lots of knocking on doors. An August analysis of campaign finance filings by The Providence Eye found Morales had received contributions from 3,241 unique donors since June 2025, compared with 1,231 for Smiley. The median contribution to Morales was $27, compared with $500 for Smiley.  
Morales also entered Wednesday with a coalition of progressive organizations, labor unions and tenant advocates behind him — a broad progressive front which sought to win not only the mayor’s office but enough City Council seats to advance a shared governing agenda, with housing a shared desire.
In a memo released Wednesday, the Rhode Island Working Families Party called the Providence races its first major push into municipal politics in the state. WFP said it spent $52,000 reaching more than 25,000 Providence voters through digital video advertising in English and Spanish and voter texts, targeting younger voters in particular.

title: Fetterman continues GOP flirtation, appears in surprise video to midterm convention
text: Democratic U.S. Sen. John Fetterman made a surprise video appearance Wednesday at the GOP convention in Dallas, praising Republican Sen. Dave McCormick while vowing the pair of Pennsylvanians would continue working with President Donald Trump to “defend the steel way of life right here in the Steel Valley.” The brief, pre-recorded appearance, which wasn’t advertised on the convention’s schedule, showed a deepening rift between Fetterman and mainstream Democrats. The video boosted speculation that Fetterman could switch parties.“Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said in the video, where he stood in front of a U.S. Steel mill in Braddock, Pennsylvania, roughly 10 miles outside Pittsburgh. Fetterman also distanced himself from a wave of progressive Democrats, some affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, who have won primaries this year.“I’m always going to stand with America,” he said. “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life.”In addition to a more ideological divide with Democrats over issues such as Fetterman’s strong support for Israel amid the continuing war in Gaza, Fetterman has taken heat from former aides who told The Wall Street Journal that he is indifferent toward his job.Wednesday’s video introduced McCormick before the GOP senator took the convention stage. Fetterman lauded McCormick as “the kind of senator that gets the job done” and is “going to fight for Pennsylvania.” “I have this opportunity to introduce this great American, a great senator, and yes, he’s in a different party, but I’m proud to count him as my great friend,” he added. Dems mock videoDemocratic members of Congress criticized Fetterman’s cameo at the convention.“A year ago I labeled John Fetterman ‘Trump’s favorite Democrat,’” U.S. Rep. Brendan Boyle, a Pennsylvania Democrat, posted to social media. “Tonight, he yet again proves why.”Delaware Democratic U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride compared Trump’s presidency to a historic disaster.“Being a Democratic politician who decides to speak at Trump’s midterm convention is like boarding the Titanic after it hit the iceberg,” she wrote.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Foulkes wins Democratic gubernatorial primary, marking historic loss for McKee
description: This story will be updated Gov. Dan McKee won’t be in office to see through his promised “day of reckoning” over the Washington Bridge closure, after losing his reelection bid to Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes on Wednesday, according to preliminary, unofficial results.  Foulkes had 62% of votes, compared with McKee’s 38%, with more than […]
text:
Former CVS executive Helena Buonanno Foulkes bested incumbent Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee in Wednesday's Democratic primary. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)This story will be updated
Gov. Dan McKee won’t be in office to see through his promised “day of reckoning” over the Washington Bridge closure, after losing his reelection bid to Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes on Wednesday, according to preliminary, unofficial results. 
Foulkes had 62% of votes, compared with McKee’s 38%, with more than half of votes reported as of 8:20 p.m. The Associated Press called the race for Foulkes.
The upset marks the first time in Rhode Island a Democratic incumbent governor has lost a reelection bid in the primary since 1994, and the first nationwide since 2018. But, it’s hardly a surprise. After losing to McKee by three percentage points in a four-way 2022 primary, Foulkes mounted a formidable comeback this year, maintaining a commanding lead in public polling,a sizable campaign cash advantage and a laundry list of endorsements from local party officials.
Change was the common refrain of Foulkes’ campaign. A former CVS executive who never held elected office — or even ran for one before 2022 — the 62-year-old Providence resident presented herself as an alternative to a status quo she characterized as ineffective. The late 2023 closure of the Washington Bridge offered a cornerstone for her argument against what she termed McKee’s “incompetence.”
The 75-year-old incumbent governor’s favorability plunged, and never recovered, after the westbound highway abruptly shut down, with voters across party lines dissatisfied with the lack of communication and transparency on the bridge’s existing condition along with the rising cost to rebuild it. Congestion continues to frustrate drivers, too, with a broken down concrete truck tying up traffic on the eastbound bridge — serving both directions in the interim — for part of Tuesday morning. 
McKee’s campaign fended off criticism by turning the spotlight back on Foulkes, reprising attacks made in the 2022 gubernatorial primary cycle about her role in the opioid crisis as former president of CVS Pharmacy.
Personal feuding overshadowed the campaign, though the rivals are not far apart on policy. Both supported a millionaire’s tax, while putting affordable housing, economic development and protecting Rhode Island from the Trump administration at the forefront of their campaigns. 
Representing either end of the baby boomer generation, neither candidate offered an obvious ideological fit with the younger, progressive contingent of Rhode Island voters. However, public polling showed younger and more progressive voters favoring Foulkes, while McKee’s support skewed toward older, blue-collar voters.
Gov. Dan McKee shows off his ‘I Voted’ sticker to a television journalist after voting Wednesday morning, Sept. 9, 2026, at Bear Hill Village in Cumberland. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Seeking to tap into his labor base, which included both state teachers unions, McKee framed himself as a man of the people shaped by his early life in the Cumberland clubhouse of the Boys & Girls Clubs, which his late father helped to start. McKee’s political ascent began as a Cumberland Town Council member in 1992, later rising to mayor. He was elected lieutenant governor in 2014, filling the governor’s seat after then-Gov. Gina Raimondo was tapped as U.S. Commerce Secretary in March 2021.
Yet, his roots were not strong enough to win the endorsement of the Cumberland Democratic Town Committee, nor Town Mayor Jeff Mutter, who both backed Foulkes. McKee also failed to win the endorsement of the Rhode Island Democratic Party and the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, which both did not back either candidate — a rare move when an incumbent is on the ballot.
As Foulkes supporters celebrated her win Wednesday night, a more somber scene unfolded a mile and a half west at Maria’s Cucina on Federal Hill, where McKee supporters gathered for a results watch party. 
But when McKee, who infamously told a campaign staffer four years ago to hang up when Foulkes called to concede, made his own concession call to Foulkes on Wednesday night, she took the call.
Foulkes will face the Republican primary victor, and three independent candidates — Ken Block, Jay Gotra and C.D. Reynolds — in the Nov. 3 general election.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

title: US Sen. Jack Reed secures easy victory for Democratic nomination in bid for sixth term
description: U.S. Sen. Jack Reed on Wednesday secured the Democratic nomination to pursue a sixth term in office, defeating two long-shot progressive challengers in Rhode Island’s primary. Reed, 76, secured roughly 76% among Democratic primary voters, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Connor Burbridge, a 31-year-old elder care work[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed speaks to Head Start advocates and workers inside the Park Square Children’s Center in  Woonsocket on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)U.S. Sen. Jack Reed on Wednesday secured the Democratic nomination to pursue a sixth term in office, defeating two long-shot progressive challengers in Rhode Island’s primary.
Reed, 76, secured roughly 76% among Democratic primary voters, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Connor Burbridge, a 31-year-old elder care worker, received 14% of votes. Dr. Luis Daniel Muñoz, a medical school graduate who has worked as a technology consultant, came in third place with 9.8%
There was little doubt Reed, a former U.S. Army paratrooper who was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996, would lose his primary bid. Every public poll of the race showed Rhode Island’s senior senator comfortably ahead of his two opponents with little name recognition.
Reed promoted his experience and results as the top reasons voters should give him another six years on Capitol Hill, emphasizing the federal money he’s brought back to Rhode Island for investments in affordable housing and infrastructure.
But in an election year where progressive insurgencies elsewhere in the country have led to establishment defeats, both of Reed’s opponents saw an opportunity..
Burbridge, a former battalion human resources officer in the Army Reserve, argued the state needed a more confrontational, progressive senator, rather than another establishment Democrat to take on the Trump administration.
Muñoz similarly cast himself as a progressive outsider, arguing his background in healthcare, technology and community organizing had prepared him to take on the federal issues shaping Rhode Islanders’ lives.
Both Democratic challengers criticized Reed’s support for Israel, which the senator defended while blaming Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for causing “great harm” to the Middle East ally’s standing.
Neither progressive campaign drew the broad backing from grassroots groups seen in other successful insurgencies like the Democratic Socialists of America, though Burbridge did win endorsements from a handful of current and former elected officials and organizations.
Burbridge conceded the race at 8:18 p.m.
“Let’s be honest: this was never supposed to be an easy race,” Burbridge said in a statement. “I was a political outsider with very little money, very little institutional support, and essentially no political experience. We were up against a 30-year incumbent and an entire political establishment that told Rhode Islanders, in one way or another, that this was not our time.”
Reed will face Republican Ray McKay, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, and independent Michael Bahry in the Nov. 3 general election.

title: Officials tout population growth, larger tax base, other benefits of data centers in North Dakota
description: Data centers grow communities’ property tax base, add more people to the local population and are an opportunity for North Dakota’s energy resources, according to a panel discussion Wednesday at the Lignite Energy Council’s annual conference. Rainbow Energy Center CEO Stacy Tschider, Applied Digital Director of Local & Regional Affairs Dave Nehring and Ellen[...]
text:
From left, Rainbow Energy Center CEO Stacy Tschider, Applied Digital Director of Local & Regional Affairs Dave Nehring and Ellendale Mayor Don Flaherty discuss data centers with moderator Retha Mattern at the Lignite Energy Council's annual conference on Sept. 9, 2026, in Bismarck, N.D. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Data centers grow communities’ property tax base, add more people to the local population and are an opportunity for North Dakota’s energy resources, according to a panel discussion Wednesday at the Lignite Energy Council’s annual conference.
Rainbow Energy Center CEO Stacy Tschider, Applied Digital Director of Local & Regional Affairs Dave Nehring and Ellendale Mayor Don Flaherty discussed benefits, best practices and misconceptions they see related to data centers, which have generated intense public scrutiny.
Data centers, which are huge facilities housing computers to handle financial transactions, email, artificial intelligence and other purposes, have drawn growing pushback from critics related to their size, noise, proximity to homes, water usage and other factors. 
The panelists cited the city of Ellendale’s experience with Applied Digital, a company that built a data center campus near the small town. The mayor said Applied Digital will ultimately bring in 300 to 350 full-time data center employees, many living in Ellendale or commuting from outside. He predicted a population growth of 400 to 600 people over the next five years for the city of about 1,100 people.
He acknowledged strains from the project on the small town but encouraged communities to get to know new residents, to become “good Ellendalites” in his town’s case.
“We have to befriend them, get to know them, build relationships with them, welcome them to our community, not as a threat but as someone who is going to strengthen our community,” Flaherty said. 
North Dakota town serves as an example of the promise and perils of data centers for South Dakota

The city of Ellendale annexed Applied Digital’s property in early 2025. At the end of that year, the city’s taxable value was $3.5 million, expected to ultimately grow more than tenfold over the next several years, the mayor said.
“That is a huge shift,” he said. The city is able to freeze utility rates and create special assessment “holidays” covered by the city’s general fund – indirect ways to help people save money, the mayor said.
Applied Digital feels “as though we should pay our property taxes just like any other industrial user, and help prop up the communities that we’re in,” said Nehring, a former state lawmaker. 
Applied Digital is projected to be the largest property taxpayer in North Dakota by 2028 or 2029, at more than $25 million a year, he said. The company has data centers or planned projects in or near Ellendale, Harwood, Jamestown and Oliver County.
Data centers and local communities should work together as a partnership between government and business, Nehring and the Ellendale mayor said. 
“I don’t see them as a corporate giant that tells us what to do. I don’t think that they see us as a small, little community that is backwater and going to listen and hang on their every word,” Flaherty said.
Community town halls have been “contentious” at times, but they foster open honest, “fact-based” discussion, Nehring said. 
Data center nondisclosure bill dies in North Dakota Senate vote

“I think what we’re building west of Center is going to be a pretty phenomenal thing for Oliver County,” he added.
Data centers are job creators and present an opportunity for North Dakota’s coal, gas and all energy resources within the state, Tschider said. The No. 1 consideration in where to build a data center is power, Nehring said. 
Tschider said, “For us, we should be laying out the red carpet. We shouldn’t be fighting the data centers. We should be welcoming them to our communities,” he said. Rainbow owns Coal Creek Station, the largest coal-fired power plant in North Dakota.
Tschider and Nehring hit back at criticisms about data centers’ water usage and noise. Nehring said misinformation and disinformation comes from social media users. 
The Ellendale mayor said he’s been accused online of “dancing with the devil” because of his community’s data center relationship.
“That’s the biggest joke in the world. This is a partnership, and it’s a purposeful partnership,” Flaherty said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.
