title: Audit: Minnesota often fails to inspect assisted living facilities on time
description: A Minnesota assisted living facility was able to score average ratings from the state on resident health, safety and staffing, despite five separate incidents in two years that led to one resident death and four hospitalizations. That’s because the Minnesota Department of Human Services doesn’t factor in serious maltreatment incidents when publishing an assi[...]
text:
Deputy Legislative Auditor Jodi Munson Rodriguez and Legislative Auditor Judy Randall present a report to a joint hearing of the House education finance and children and families committees on Feb. 8, 2023. Randall's office presented a report on assisted living facilities Wednesday. (Photo by Catherine Davis/House Information Services)A Minnesota assisted living facility was able to score average ratings from the state on resident health, safety and staffing, despite five separate incidents in two years that led to one resident death and four hospitalizations.
That’s because the Minnesota Department of Human Services doesn’t factor in serious maltreatment incidents when publishing an assisted living facility “report card” rating, according to a new report from the Office of the Legislative Auditor.
The legislative auditor, a nonpartisan watchdog in the legislative branch, evaluated the licensing process for the over 2,000 assisted living facilities that provide housing and medical services to seniors and disabled adults in Minnesota and also found the state is frequently late on its routine inspections of assisted living facilities.
“We have basically a simple recommendation that the department comply with the statutorily required timelines for assisted living facility inspections,” said David Kirchner, the manager for the evaluation, during a Wednesday presentation to legislators.
Minnesota established licensing for assisted living facilities in 2021 following a string of maltreatment investigations — becoming the last state to do so, KARE 11 reported at the time.
Assisted living facilities, state-regulated businesses sometimes referred to as “group homes,” can look like converted single-family homes with just a handful of residents, or large buildings that can serve sometimes hundreds of people. They differ from nursing homes, which are meant for people with higher medical needs and have to meet federal standards. The distinction in use is sometimes blurry, though, with seniors increasingly opting into assisted living homes over nursing homes, the Star Tribune reported.
Regulating assisted living facilities is complex: the state’s health department is responsible for licensing, while the human services department is responsible for paying facilities that have clients on Medicaid. A third regulatory body oversees licensing individual assisted living facility directors.


The Office of the Legislative Auditor found that, for the most part, the state “did a good job processing licensing applications.”
But it also found that health department inspectors completed their first two-year round of routine inspections a year late.
Health department leaders explained in a response to the report that the delay was caused in part by an unexpectedly high number of applications and many of its nurses being reassigned during COVID. Auditors noted that inspections have sped up since then, though in the latest data from the first half of 2025, still less than a third of inspections were completed by the statutory deadline.
Health department inspectors also investigate facilities that have complaints of neglect or abuse, and the health department regularly publishes substantiated maltreatment complaints. A recent MPR News investigation found that some assisted living facilities faced minimal consequences in cases of substantiated maltreatment.



How licensing has affected the amount of maltreatment in facilities was out of the scope of the new report, Kirchner said, though auditors did find that substantiated cases of maltreatment don’t hurt a facility’s rating.
Ratings of facilities have been published in report cards by the Department of Human Services since 2024 and are meant to help people find quality providers for themselves or their loved ones. Maltreatment findings are listed in the report card separately from a facility’s rating out of five stars.
Department of Human Services Temporary Commissioner John Connolly said that a facility’s rating “ideally would reflect” maltreatment findings, and that developing a system that properly incorporates maltreatment in the same scale as the existing rating system is doable but would take time.
Medicaid spending on assisted living facilities was around $1.1 billion in the 2024 fiscal year, according to the report. For context, that same year, Minnesota spent $18.5 billion on its entire Medicaid program.
Reports of Medicaid fraud and, by extension, the ongoing state-federal fight over federal Medicaid funding, have centered on 14 services deemed vulnerable to fraud, waste and abuse by the state. That list does not include assisted living services, called “customized living” in the state’s Medicaid program.
Still, auditors highlighted a possible “risk for incorrect payments”: DHS doesn’t check a facility’s maximum capacity when paying claims. Auditors cited one facility which had a licensed capacity of six residents but was paid for 18 residents during a single month in 2024.
Echoing a much-used sentiment in official communications, Department of Health Deputy Commissioner Wendy Underwood said at the Wednesday presentation: “Fighting fraud is everyone’s job at our agency.”

title: Federal judge blocks Vermont AG’s probe of ‘Planet Hank’ AI video
description:
The ruling tested Vermont’s first attempt to enforce its new synthetic-media law, finding that a controversial AI-generated video was protected political satire.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Federal judge blocks Vermont AG’s probe of ‘Planet Hank’ AI video.
text:
U.S. District Court Judge William Sessions speaks at the Vermont Statehouse in September 2018. File photo by Mike Dougherty/VTDigger

A political satire video was “ridiculous” enough to be protected speech, a federal judge ruled, blocking Vermont’s first attempt to enforce its new AI-media law.
“The Court considers this video to have a ridiculous nature and finds that Vermont’s interest in protecting and preserving the integrity of the electoral process and related fraud is lower when the threat faced is an unrealistic, satirical video,” Senior U.S. District Judge William K. Sessions III wrote in a decision issued Tuesday.
The preliminary injunction marks the first major court test of Act 75, enacted in March to regulate deceptive AI-generated election material. Although the ruling applies only to one video and does not resolve a broader challenge to the law, it raises questions about how Vermont can regulate synthetic political media without infringing on constitutionally protected satire.
Sessions ordered Attorney General Charity Clark’s office not to enforce a civil investigative demand against Hank Poitras, who posts videos and political commentary under the name “Planet Hank,” or take other enforcement action against him based on a video he uploaded to several social media platforms entitled “Mark Helps Vermont Take Out The Trash,” generated using artificial intelligence.
Sessions found that Poitras was likely to prove Clark’s investigation violated his First Amendment rights. The judge also found that the video appeared to qualify for Act 75’s exemption for satire and parody.
The law requires certain synthetic media that injures a political candidate’s reputation and is published within 90 days of an election to include a disclaimer identifying it as digitally manipulated or generated. Poitras posted his video without a disclaimer two months before Vermont’s Aug. 11 primary, which fell within the timespan that requires such a disclosure.
But Sessions concluded that the video’s voice-over, the “unnatural appearances” of the people depicted and the events of the video all contributed to an unmistakably satirical character.
Sen. Brian Collamore, R-Rutland, who sponsored the legislation in the Vermont Senate, said Sessions’ ruling reflected lawmakers’ intent.
“One of the provisions was an exemption to the law if it was clearly satirical,” Collamore said, adding that he thought most reasonable people would consider Poitras’ video satirical. “It did not have to have identification as AI generated.”
Poitras posted the video on June 7. It uses AI-generated likenesses of U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., and then-Republican U.S. House candidate Mark Coester.
In the video, Coester criticizes Balint’s campaign and policies before using an excavator to lift her into a trash bin outside the Vermont Statehouse.
“Help fight back against evil,” a narrator says. “Help Vermont take out the trash.”
Five days later, the attorney general’s office notified Poitras that it was investigating whether the video violated Act 75. The office offered to close the investigation at the time if Poitras brought the video into compliance with the law by adding a disclosure, according to court documents.
Poitras instead sued Clark on July 8, contending that the demand that he alter his video under the threat of civil or criminal penalties violated his First Amendment rights.
Coester, who later lost the Republican primary to Gerald Malloy, said in an interview Wednesday that the investigation was unjustified even though the video also could have reflected poorly on him.
“It’s just really sad that it’s the citizens that pay the price for legislation that’s unconstitutional in the first place,” Coester said. “This has cost a high price for people to defend against something they never should have been prosecuted on, something that was clearly satire.”
Poitras’ lawsuit challenges Act 75 more broadly, alleging five First Amendment violations and one violation of the 14th Amendment. Sessions’ preliminary injunction is considerably narrower: It applies only to the June 7 video and the attorney general’s resulting investigative demand.
Lauren Jandl, Clark’s chief of staff, said the office was reviewing the decision and “determining next steps.”
“The Attorney General’s Office supported the synthetic media disclosure law because transparency and the integrity of elections are critical,” Jandl wrote in an email.
Poitras and his attorneys intend to seek a permanent injunction preventing Clark from enforcing Act 75 against Poitras and others, Poitras’ attorney Brady Toensing said.
“This preliminary injunction is an important victory for our fundamental right to make fun of politicians in this country,” Toensing wrote in an email.

title: Mental health professionals highlight errors in Nebraska assessment for developmentally disabled
description: LINCOLN — Just over a year after Nebraska launched a new system to assess Nebraskans with intellectual and developmental disabilities seeking Medicaid assistance, a group of parents gathered to inform state officials about the negative impacts the change has had on their families. Mental health professionals Carol Salber and Tori Sorensen, who are both paren[...]
text:
Tony Green, director of the Division of Developmental Disabilities in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, at a meeting of the Nebraska Olmstead Advisory Committee. Dec. 19, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Just over a year after Nebraska launched a new system to assess Nebraskans with intellectual and developmental disabilities seeking Medicaid assistance, a group of parents gathered to inform state officials about the negative impacts the change has had on their families.
Mental health professionals Carol Salber and Tori Sorensen, who are both parents of participants in the system, gave a presentation Wednesday to Nebraska’s Developmental Disabilities Advisory Committee that noted multiple flaws in the state’s interRAI tool.
The interRAI system determines the level of publicly assisted care, services and funding for Nebraskans with developmental disability waivers. Salber and Sorensen’s presentation identified seven errors in how the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services calculates what each participant receives, which they claimed could dramatically shift the funding and services doled out.
InterRAI uses a Case Mix Index chart to help measure what funding tier a participant should land in based on the complexity of their circumstance. Sorensen said Nebraska officials made several typos copying the Case Mix Index, and some of those errors impact both funding and eligibility of services for participants.
One example in their presentation claimed that the errors could result in a participant receiving nearly $68,000 that they don’t need, while a different participant who is in need would lose out on that same amount.
“If the interRAI is wrong, then I have even more questions about it being a valid test,” Sorensen said. “If Nebraska is wrong, then we need to fix it. Because certain individuals are getting less funding, significantly less funding, just because of a typo.”
DHHS spokesman Jeff Powell said the department would review the concerns shared at Wednesday’s meeting. He noted that assessments that result in a reduced funding tier automatically undergo a secondary review, and he said assessments can be corrected and rescored when concerns are identified.
“DHHS will continue to monitor the system and use the independent review to identify any areas where improvements may be needed,” Powell said in an email.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Sorensen and Salber listed multiple other issues with interRAI, including that the state’s transition to the system altered the funding of 46% of continued participants. According to their presentation, 17% of participants saw their funding decrease by at least one tier.
Salber said this change has resulted in participants with significantly different needs being categorized in the same funding tiers. She gave an example of a participant who took the children’s version of the interRAI assessment and was placed in a basic funding tier. The following year, the same participant completed the adult interRAI assessment and was placed in the advanced tier, despite having no major health changes.
One of the biggest flaws noted at Wednesday’s meeting was that the interRAI system lowered the funding of participants who live at home with their loved ones. Salber said this is considered “informal support” and is used to justify reduced aid.
Multiple parents testified Wednesday that their children’s funding tiers dropped because of this factor, though all said their needs are severe enough to require higher support.
Nancy Enstrom, a 74-year-old mother from Dodge County, said she has kept her 51-year-old daughter alive by caring for her at home, although doctors had told her she wouldn’t survive past infancy. Her daughter’s funding tier decreased after the switch to interRAI, and Enstrom said she was told by state officials that her daughter would be in the advanced tier if she didn’t live at home.
Enstrom said she is suing the state to restore the previous level of support.
“You will not be the people that ruin my daughter’s life,” Enstrom said.
Enstrom said her husband works 80-90 hours a week so she can stay home and care for their daughter. She said she hasn’t made a penny off the aid they have received from the state.
Kathy Rohloff, a mother whose 15-year-old son fell two funding tiers in the switch to interRAI, argued that parents who care for their disabled children at home are more cost-effective for the state. She estimated that housing the same participants at a state institution would be roughly four times more expensive than allowing parents to care for them.
Enstrom agreed, estimating that parents like her and Rohloff have saved Nebraska millions of dollars over the years. Rohloff said parents don’t want to walk away from their children, but argued that the new system encourages that.
DHHS officials announced in August that they hired an outside contractor to review interRAI usage. Tony Green, DHHS Division of Disability and Aging director, said he doesn’t anticipate receiving the report until next spring.
Mike Browne, vice chair of the committee, asked if DHHS could halt making reductions in funding until after the report. He said he viewed some of the concerns expressed Wednesday as a fairness issue.
“I see a real potential problem, because it looks like you’re dividing into two classes,” Browne said.
Green disagreed with Browne’s perspective, saying regardless of a participant’s guardians, the same review happens for each participant. He said DHHS would not pause its implementation of interRAI, as it would create a budget concern to continue funding increases under the system while pausing any reductions.

title: Alaska continues rollout of Rural Health Transformation Program awards
description: Alaska Department of Health officials announced a fifth round of federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding awards on Friday. The latest awards for $25.8 million bring the total to more than $207 million to date. The funding is aimed at bolstering Alaska’s rural health system. The latest round of awards will go to 32 projects […]
text:
The Providence Kodiak Island Medical Center, Kodiak's main hospital, is seen on Feb. 2, 2024. The hospital facility is owned by the Kodiak Island Borough who was awarded $3.8 million in September 2026 to update the hospital's climate control system. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska Department of Health officials announced a fifth round of federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding awards on Friday. The latest awards for $25.8 million bring the total to more than $207 million to date.
The funding is aimed at bolstering Alaska’s rural health system. The latest round of awards will go to 32 projects focused on improving health access, nutrition, telehealth services, healthcare infrastructure, workforce development and more. 
Alaska was awarded $272 million in federal funding under the program this year, with the remaining roughly $65 million expected to be awarded in the coming weeks, ahead of a federal deadline of October 30.
Congress created the Rural Health Transformation Program last year as part of the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act to offset the fallout from the bill’s nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid spending cuts over the next decade — particularly in rural communities. The $50 billion in program funding is set to be allocated over the next five years, until 2030. Alaska is one of the largest recipients and is slated to receive roughly $1.3 billion.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The department received nearly 1,800 project proposals and narrowed down a list of more than 400 projects in June from healthcare entities including hospitals, clinics, Tribal health organizations, as well as state agencies, local governments and school districts. 
Among the list of projects in the latest round of awards published Friday, several awards have been granted to local governments. Those include $435,000 to the City of Kenai Fire Department for modernizing emergency services; $3.8 million to the Kodiak Island Borough for updating its hospital’s climate control system; and two awards of nearly $750,000 to the Matanuska-Susitna Borough for upgrading emergency services and mobile medical care. 
The Wrangell Public School District is set to receive over $608,000 for a new virtual-reality based program for middle and high school students learning about healthcare sciences and careers in nursing, emergency medicine, behavioral health, dentistry and community health.
Tribal governments, tribally-led entities and health consortiums were among the awardees. Grants include $4.8 million to the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium for expanding access to pharmacy care; $323,000 to the Cook Inlet Tribal Council to expand behavioral health services; and $219,000 to the Norton Sound Health Corporation for upgrading maternal and neonatal care equipment. 
The Native Village of Chenega was awarded over $242,000 to begin planning and designing a new clinic to serve the Prince William Sound community. 
New technology upgrades are a focus of many proposals that received awards. 
The passenger and cargo service air carrier, Ryan Air, was awarded $4.1 million for a proposal to deploy “autonomous cargo drones and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft” to deliver prescriptions and transport patients and healthcare providers in the Bethel and Dillingham regions, according to an award summary. 
“This project addresses the near-total lack of reliable, affordable pharmaceutical access and medical transport in remote Alaska Native villages, where geography, weather, and the absence of road infrastructure create life-threatening gaps in basic healthcare,” the company wrote in its proposal. 
The Alaska Commercial Company, a privately-owned grocery chain, was awarded $1.8 million to build containerized hydroponic mini-farms for growing fresh produce year-round in four unidentified communities in rural Alaska.
“We intend to use compact indoor growing systems to address the unreliable supply of fresh fruits and vegetables in remote communities across Western, Northern, and Southeast Alaska. All communities in this project are not on the road system,” the company wrote. 
The state health department awarded its own Division of Public Health $300,000 for information technology upgrades to improve coordinated care for high-risk youth, and over $452,000 was awarded to its Division of Public Assistance to implement a healthy food waiver program for recipients of the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program, or SNAP.
The new waiver program would allow Alaska to restrict the purchase of certain non-nutritious foods with SNAP benefits, including soda and candy.
However, healthy foods waivers are a subject of legal dispute with the Trump administration: A federal judge ruled in June that the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which oversees the waiver program, overstepped its legal authority in allowing five states to ban the purchase of certain foods, vacating the waiver programs in those states. The USDA filed an appeal in federal court last month. 
Officials with the Division of Public Assistance said in a statement Wednesday that Alaska was not a part of the litigation and so the new waiver program “remains under development.” They said the division is working with the USDA’s Department of Food and Nutrition Administration and will “and proceed with applicable federal requirements and federal guidance.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Board of Education censures teacher, parent in alleged corporal punishment case
description: A mother, also a licensed teacher, is accused of child abuse, but years later the state Board of Education decides on censure instead of license revocation.
text:
Kansas State Board of Education member Debby Potter, of Garden Plain, helps defeat a recommendation that a mother, also a licensed teacher, should lose her state education credential because of allegations she spanked her son with a belt outside a Wichita child care center. In this image from July 8, 2025, Potter speaks to colleagues on the Board of Education in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas State Board of Education rejected conclusions of child abuse investigators, a professional practice commission and attorneys with the Department of Education to protect the teaching license of a mother accused of physically abusing her son.
The incident prompting regulatory intervention occurred in December 2022 at the Child Development Center on McConnell Air Force Base in Wichita. The center’s staff called the mother, who held a Kansas teaching license since 2020, to the school because her preschool-age son was throwing objects at a teacher. Educators testified the mother — unidentified because of redaction of state documents chronicling the case — watched video of the child’s conduct before declaring, “You’re going to learn how to act in the car.”
The boy, witnesses said, started to cry and repeatedly screamed that he didn’t want to go to the vehicle. The mother took him to and from the car three times that day, but during the second trip, Child Development Center teachers said, they observed the mother retrieve something that looked like a belt. School personnel said they saw the mother raising and lowering her arm inside the vehicle as if she was smacking the child. An assistant director of the Child Development Center said she saw the boy return to school rubbing his buttocks and thigh.
School staff called 911 and cooperated with a McConnell AFB criminal investigation in which military documents indicated the boy disclosed his father used a belt and his mother used sticks on him.
The Kansas Department for Children and Families opened an inquiry. The mother, public records say, denied physically disciplining the boy, but she maintained she had the right to punish the child within reason. DCF temporarily removed all children from the household. The mother’s name was added to the state’s child abuse registry, but after three years her name was expunged from the roster in May.
DCF documents say “the child’s body was hit with a belt as a form of discipline and injuries were inflicted as a result.” Based on the agency’s substantiation of abuse, the state Professional Practices Commission conducted an evidentiary hearing in April. Christy Ziegler, of the commission, said the majority of the commission agreed evidence showed the minor was abused. The commission voted 6-1 to recommend the State Board of Education revoke the mother’s license to teach in Kansas.
The mother responded with a letter to the State Board of Education last month arguing revocation would be inappropriate because of lack of proof. She said Child Development Center personnel were mistaken when they assumed she was hitting the boy with a belt rather than “talking with my son while moving my hands.” She wrote in the letter that her son was examined the day of the incident, Dec. 27, 2022, by McConnell medical personnel who reported finding “no markings, abrasions or bruising” on his body.
In addition, the mother said, she subsequently completed anger management and parent counseling courses and had “learned from my rehabilitation.”
On Tuesday, the State Board of Education voted 7-3 to reduce the proposed license revocation to a written censure. That censure document would be attached to the mother’s licensing file. The State Board of Education had the option of revocation, censure and suspension or to dismiss the case entirely.
Censure was supported by board members Beryl Ann New of Topeka, Connie O’Brien of Tonganoxie, Michelle Dombrosky of Olathe, Dennis Hershberger of Hutchinson, Debby Potter of Garden Plain, Betty Arnold of Wichita and Jim Porter of Fredonia. Voting against the censure motion were Cathy Hopkins of Hays, Melanie Haas of Overland Park and Danny Zeck of Leavenworth.
Potter, who objected to the child-abuse determination made by DCF, said there was no law forbidding a parent from engaging in corporal punishment.
“That’s not illegal if she did spank with a belt,” Potter said. “That’s not an illegal thing.”
Under common law in Kansas, a parent or guardian could use a degree of physical force to discipline a child. State statute draws a line at inflicting cruel and inhuman corporal punishment for people younger than 18.
Hopkins, who serves as chair of the State Board of Education, said the mother at the center of the case chose not to formally appeal the Professional Practices Commission’s decision. Instead, the mother simply asked the State Board of Education to reject the complaint seeking revocation of the teaching license.
“This person did not appeal the decision of the PPC. That is a factor we all need to take into account,” Hopkins said.
Meanwhile, Potter accused Hopkins and the State Board of Education’s general counsel of failing to deliver to her correspondence related to the case of alleged child abuse.
“Our mail is going through the chair and general counsel gatekeeping,” Potter said. “I am very, very frustrated by this.”
Hopkins answered the claim from Potter by pointing to procedures and regulations guiding the State Board of Education. At that point, Hopkins’ microphone went dead. The livestream of the meeting suggested Hopkins continued to speak for 50 seconds, but her thoughts were lost on the viewing public.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Zinke to introduce landscape-scale conservation, recreation plan
description: For more than two decades, a coalition of conservation organizations, sportsmen’s groups, business owners and individuals have sought ways to expand protections and recreation opportunities around the Seeley-Swan and Blackfoot River valleys in western Montana.  Wednesday, Montana U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke announced his intention to introduce legislation in Congre[...]
text:
Montana U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke speaks at a press conference announcing the launch of the bipartisan Public Lands Caucus, while Montana Rep. Troy Downing listens. (Courtesy photo)For more than two decades, a coalition of conservation organizations, sportsmen’s groups, business owners and individuals have sought ways to expand protections and recreation opportunities around the Seeley-Swan and Blackfoot River valleys in western Montana. 
Wednesday, Montana U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke announced his intention to introduce legislation in Congress combining multiple proposals into a single “landscape-scale plan” of “multiple use.”
Dubbed the “A River Runs Through It Act,” the legislation includes adding the first new protected wilderness in 14 years, supporting timber harvest, reducing wildfire risks and opening additional recreation opportunities. 
“This is what locally led conservation looks like,” Zinke said in a statement. “We can put people to work in the woods, support our timber industry, reduce wildfire risk, and keep our forests healthy while protecting public access and conserving the iconic places we cherish. This proposal was built by the people who live, work, hunt and recreate in the Blackfoot, and after decades of work they found a way forward that keeps this landscape working for everybody.”
The A River Runs Through It Act, named for the Norman Maclean novel that drew national attention to Montana and its natural beauty, combines two large-scale proposals that have been workshopped and considered in various legislative forms over the years – the Blackfoot Clearwater Stewardship Proposal and the Lincoln Prosperity Proposal. 
Members of the steering committee that helped craft the proposal include retired foresters form the Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation and Pyramid Mountain Lumber — a local timber mill in the rural Seeley Lake community that closed in 2024  —local outfitters, ranchers and guides, and state and national conservation organizations. 
More than 430,000 acres of land near the Clearwater and Blackfoot rivers are included in the act with five priority focus areas. 
A key piece of the legislation is the inclusion of nearly 100,000 acres of Forest Service land to the Bob Marshall and Scapegoat wilderness areas, the creation of new wilderness on Nevada Mountain, and the release of approximately 23,000 acres of Wilderness Study areas, opening them up to timber harvest and other management practices. . 
Zach Angstead, government affairs specialist with Wild Montana, said the organization has been part of the two collaborative proposals for more than 20 years. 
“Seeing this work come together in the A River Runs Through It Act is a remarkable achievement. The legislation would protect iconic landscapes, expand recreation access, strengthen forest restoration, support rural economies, and resolve long-standing wilderness study area designations,” Zangstead said in a press statement. “This proposal was built the Montana way: By sitting down together, working through differences, and finding common ground for a place we all love. Now it is up to Congress to recognize how special this hard-won agreement is and pass this locally driven legislation.”
Additional goals of the bill focus on forest management and recreation opportunities. 
Across roughly 180,000 acres, six “forest restoration areas” are designated to improve the health of the forest. Those actions include timber harvest, thinning, vegetation management, prescribed fire and stream restoration.  
Additional fuel reduction and forest restoration projects west of Lincoln will aim to reduce wildfire risks to homes and infrastructure, and provide more flexibility in forest management choices.  
“This proposal reflects Montana values of being good stewards to the land and working together with broad partners to get more accomplished,” said Gordy Sanders, a retired forester with Pyramid Mountain Lumber. “Our forests and rural communities need a vibrant forest products industry, and the focus on restoration in the Blackfoot Valley will help sustain the health of both.”
Six newly designated recreation areas, totaling roughly 60,000 acres, will secure permanent winter access for snowmobiles, add additional mountain biking routes, and create a connected off-highway vehicle trail loop that is more than 70 miles long. 
The bill also “maintains and expands opportunities for hunting, fishing, hiking, horseback riding, mountain biking, snowmobiling, and off-highway vehicle use,” according to Zinke’s office, and will create new and improved trail connections. 
“For motorized recreationists in the upper-Blackfoot Valley, the A River Runs Through It Act provides huge benefits. It will permanently protect important ATV and snowmobile access and authorize construction of several new trail connections,” said Russ Ehnes, president of the Great Falls Trail Bike Riders Association. “Whether you’re looking for a day-ride with your family or a multi-day backcountry loop riding experience, this bill will improve the quality of the experience for many.”
Zinke’s bill, likely to be one of his last before he retires from Congress at the end of the year, drew praise from elected officials throughout the region as well, with commissioners from Missoula, Lewis and Clark, and Powell counties adding statements of support. 
The bill “strikes that balance” between the timber and recreation industries, Powell County Commissioner Bill Hooker said, and gives residents more certainty about the future of these lands. 
The supporting organizations and individuals all highlighted the process that created the proposal, as opposed to legislation being crafted in Washington, D.C. 
“The A River Runs Through It Act is a perfect example of people, communities and partnerships shaping the future of the Blackfoot Valley,” said Jim Stone of Rolling Stone Ranch. “We are building a stewardship ethic for working lands that will sustain generations and allow many people to enjoy and prosper.”
 Getting it done

Versions of this legislation — namely of the Blackfoot Clearwater Stewardship Act, one part of the new legislation — have gone before Congress time and time again, without much traction. 
In 2010, former Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Tester first introduced the Blackfoot Clearwater Stewardship Act as part of a larger recreation and jobs focused legislative package. 
Subsequent attempts to pass the legislation in combination or as a standalone bill didn’t make much headway in Senate committees. A 2021 version failed to pass committee when it was opposed by Republican U.S. Sen. Steve Daines, who wanted to see it paired with his own bill that would release additional wilderness study designations in the state. 
A version Tester introduced in 2023 passed out of committee, but stalled out on the Senate floor. 
Last year, Zinke introduced the Greater Yellowstone Recreation Enhancement and Tourism Act, also supported by a coalition of sportsmen and conservation organizations, which would add nearly 100 miles of the Gallatin and Madison rivers to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System.
That bill was referred to committee on Aug. 1, 2025 but has not moved any further through the legislative process since then. 
A spokesperson for Zinke did not respond to questions from the Daily Montanan about a timeline for moving the A River Runs Through It Act through committee or what would make this process different from prior bills that stalled out. 
Angstead, with Wild Montana, said next steps include getting the rest of Montana’s all-Republican delegation on board and the coalition has collected letters of support from counties and local governments asking for federal support to pass the legislation before the end of the Congressional term. . 
“We have three months so it’s going to be a sprint, but I think everyone from Congressman Zinke’s office, to Wild Montana, and the whole coalition is going to do what we can to move this forward,” Angstead said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Senators rally to Brownsberger as recount begins in tight race
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: The results of this week's recount will settle who wins the district – a longtime incumbent and the third-most powerful Democrat in the Senate, or a challenger with the backing of political rival Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.
text:
STATE SEN. WILLIAM BROWNSBERGER paced the recount floor of Boston City Hall on Wednesday, never stopping for longer than a minute. 
Crossed arms, weaving his way through the tables where election workers carefully sifted through hundreds of ballots while poll watchers loomed over their shoulders, the incumbent senator whose political career may be on the line closely watched the tallies.
Watertown and Boston on Wednesday were recounting the ballots cast in the nail-biting Suffolk & Middlesex District Senate race. Thursday recounts in Belmont and Cambridge will complete the district.
By the first unofficial count, challenger Daniel Lander pulled ahead of Brownsberger by three votes out of nearly 25,000 cast. Later counts showed Brownsberger in the lead by just over two dozen. The results of this week’s recount will settle who wins the district – a longtime incumbent and the third-most powerful Democrat in the Senate, or a challenger with the backing of political rival Boston Mayor Michelle Wu. 
Brownsberger did not show up to Boston City Hall alone Wednesday. He was joined by a show of support from his fellow senators.
Eleven senators were at City Hall throughout the day Wednesday: State Sens. Sal DiDomenico of Everett, Michael Rodrigues of Westport, William Driscoll of Milton, Joan Lovely of Salem, Jake Oliveira of Ludlow, Robyn Kennedy of Worcester, Adam Gomez of Springfield, John Cronin of Fitchburg, Pavel Payano of Lawrence, John Velis of Westfield, and Brendan Crighton of Lynn. Some got there early in the morning, sporting casual clothes and drinking the Dunkin’ coffee provided for volunteers, while Brownsberger paced in his suit.
Most of the present senators served as poll watchers for Brownsberger’s campaign.
Rep. Steve Owens of Watertown also watched the election count on Brownsberger’s behalf, as did a number of staff members for Senate President Karen Spilka and other Senate staffers.
Former Boston City Councilor Frank Baker, a Wu adversary, was a poll watcher for the Brownsberger campaign, and current Councilor Ed Flynn observed from the sidelines. 
“It’s almost a caucus in the Senate here as volunteers because my opponent doesn’t have a grassroots operation,” Lander said in an interview, on the side of the recount floor. As opposed to Brownsberger, Lander mainly watched the event from a banister overlooking the floor where election workers tallied ballots. 
“Personally, I believe that there’s a lot of business that is undone on Beacon Hill right now that would be a perfectly good use of the first Wednesday after Labor Day to get done,” he said. “Things like getting phones out of our high schools, things like building more affordable housing, expanding the public transportation system, but again and again, Senate leadership is unwilling to work on that.”
Included in the poll watchers for Lander’s campaign were some top Wu allies.
Though the recount started around 1 p.m., election workers and poll watchers began arriving at City Hall around 8 a.m., they said, some grumbling about the early hour and then long wait for the action to start.  
Rodrigues, chair of the powerful Senate Ways and Means Committee, told the News Service he left his house in Westport at 6:30 a.m. to make it to Boston City Hall.
As the recount was about to get underway, Lander recount attorney John Gannon, who has worked on local recounts as well as the 2000 Bush vs. Gore recount in Florida, asked if “out of respect” for the city election workers, they should be aware of a deadline for the day. 
“We believe we’re going to finish today, just keep going,” the election official replied. 
Gannon and Brownsberger’s recount attorney, Dennis Newman, who also worked on the 2000 recount in Florida, both circled the recount floor along with the incumbent senator. 
There were a handful of disputes.
Brownsberger often flagged Newman down to investigate a possible question, and Gannon raised his hand to get the attention of election officials when there was an issue at some of the tables. 
Around 2:50 p.m., most of the tables were done counting. Those recounting for Wards 21 and 22, covering parts of Allston, Brighton, and Fenway were the last remaining.

title: Vermont Conversation: ‘We are the patriots fighting for democracy.’ AG Charity Clark on suing Trump and winning $92.7M from Meta
description:

Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘We are the patriots fighting for democracy.’ AG Charity Clark on suing Trump and winnin[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark speaks during a press conference highlighting gun safety efforts in Vermont in Burlington in April 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark has had a busy summer. Since late June, she has sued the Trump administration an average of twice per week. That brings to 67 the number of lawsuits — as of midday Wednesday — she has filed or joined against President Donald Trump since January 2025. They include lawsuits defending birthright citizenship and challenging cuts to medical research funding, the dismantling of the Department of Education, voting restrictions and tariffs.
Clark said her office has prevailed in 92% of the suits, including both final decisions and preliminary injunctions. Many of these decisions are being appealed, but “getting that initial win is hugely helpful in all the work that we are doing battling the unconstitutional and illegal acts of the federal government right now,” Clark told me.
In August, the attorney general announced a landmark settlement of $92.7 million with the social media company Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, for designing its programs to addict young people and harm their mental health. The settlement resulted from a lawsuit involving 47 other states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories. Meta agreed to limit the time that teenagers can spend on its platforms and impose age restrictions.
“I really think this is the dawn of a new era for social media,” Clark said.
Clark, 51, won election as Vermont’s attorney general in 2022, the first woman to do so. She graduated from the University of Vermont, then worked as a policy analyst in the office of Gov. Howard Dean. She later graduated from the Boston College School of Law and worked as an assistant attorney general and later as chief of staff to her predecessor, TJ Donovan. In April, she was named Woman of the Year by the Boston College Women’s Law Coalition. She is currently running for a third term as attorney general.
In a recent lawsuit, Clark joined 24 other state attorneys general challenging a new rule by the U.S. Postal Service that would grant it the authority to regulate mail-in voting. 
“This is such an egregious attempt to overtake the state’s prerogatives with voting and elections. But more importantly, it is so wildly impractical,” said Clark, adding that it would take years to implement.

READ MORE

“I can’t imagine that the United States Supreme Court is going to say, ‘Yeah, we’ll just do this and disenfranchise so many of these voters.’ I mean, it would be pandemonium if they did this.”
Clark said that despite the Trump administration’s ongoing attempts to overturn longstanding legal precedents, “I believe in America.”
“We will keep exercising our rights under the Constitution and standing up for our country,” she said. “We are the patriots fighting for democracy and our Constitution, and we’re going to keep doing it until this administration is gone. And we’re going to keep doing it whatever the next administration is who comes in in 2028.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah housing market remains among most expensive in U.S., with 91% of renters priced out
description: The latest pulse reading on Utah’s housing market is out — and it shows home ownership remains out of reach for many Utahns, especially first-time homebuyers.  Despite some slight fluctuations in early 2026, Utah is still among the nation’s top 10 most expensive states for single-family homes with a median price of $559,900. Utah’s median […]
text:
New homes are under construction in Spanish Fork on Tuesday, July 16, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The latest pulse reading on Utah’s housing market is out — and it shows home ownership remains out of reach for many Utahns, especially first-time homebuyers. 
Despite some slight fluctuations in early 2026, Utah is still among the nation’s top 10 most expensive states for single-family homes with a median price of $559,900.
Utah’s median sale price across all housing types increased from $500,000 in the first quarter of 2025 to $520,000 in the first quarter of 2026 — requiring an annual income of nearly $150,000 to buy, according to a new report released Wednesday by University of Utah housing researchers. 
While many current homeowners are incentivized to stay locked into their current mortgages with low pandemic-era interest rates and are gaining wealth through equity — first-time homebuyers have it much harder. 

The estimated monthly payment on a median-priced home hit a high of $3,725 in 2025 before dipping slightly to $3,669 in early 2026 — but that’s still more than $1,200 above monthly payments in 2021. 
A vast majority of Utah renters — a striking 91% — can’t afford that mortgage payment. And less than 5% of homes sold last year were affordable to renters earning the median salary of $64,000. 
 As mortgage rates remain elevated and aren’t expected to budge any time soon, researchers predict Utah’s tight housing market and its affordability problems will continue to persist — and if nothing changes, get worse. 
The state’s population is expected to balloon to more than 4 million in 2035, which researchers say will require an additional 280,000 housing units. Of those, about 61,500 will need to be for new owners and renters aged 35 and younger, 120,000 for those aged 35 to 64, and about 98,000 for those 65 and older. 
“While the path to homeownership appears bleak for many potential first-time buyers, opportunities exist with the right housing options,” the report says.
The report’s authors, Dejan Eskic and Moira Dillow with the University of Utah’s Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute, discussed their findings during a panel discussion at the Thomas S. Monson Center in Salt Lake City on Wednesday. 
They and other panelists including Steve Waldrip, senior housing adviser for Gov. Spencer Cox, Springville City Administrator Troy Fitzgerald and Steven Bond, founder and CEO of the nonprofit HomeOwnership4U discussed the report’s warnings and what should be done to solve Utah’s stubborn housing crisis. 
They agreed that there’s an appetite for smaller single-family homes on smaller lots — rather than homes with huge footprints. Utah is among states with the largest homes for sale in the country, with an average of more than 2,400 square feet, the Deseret News recently reported. 
Utah’s household size is shrinking, Dillow said, projected to go from about 2.9 persons per household today to about 2.6 in the next 10 years. 
“What this really means is that even with the same population growth, a decrease in household size increases housing demand in the next decade by 11%,” she said. “Smaller homes are OK because our household size is shrinking as we age. And those are both new words for Utah.” 
What Utah lawmakers did — and didn’t — do for housing in 2025

Eskic, also the chief economist for the Salt Lake Board of Realtors, and Bond said Utah’s average home square footage is high compared to other states. 
“We’re the largest by square footage per home by a large degree,” Bond said. “We’ve built big homes since we’ve had big families. But we now have a strain on household size, and it’s time to think about … smaller homes on smaller footprints to make it more attainable.”
The Utah Legislature in recent years has moved to create more tools cities can use to incentivize developers to build smaller “starter homes,” stopping short of sweeping mandates. 
But Fitzgerald said as Springville has made zoning changes and tried to encourage developers to build smaller homes, they haven’t bit. He said Springville has more than 2,000 lots available for development now with lot sizes that are 3,000 square feet or less, but “very few of them are coming out of the ground.”
“They don’t want them,” Fitzgerald said of developers. “We’ve approved a zoning code that requires smaller houses on these smaller lots. Every single builder is coming back and asking our council to change them and increase the size of the home … presumably because that’s what the market is asking for. And that’s an incredible problem.” 
When looking at the numbers included in the housing report released Wednesday, Waldrip said it’s “hard not to be a little bit depressed.”
“I’m sitting here going, ‘What have I been doing for the last couple of years?’” he said. 
The bottom line, he said, is “we need a lot of homes,” even as Utah faces “land constraints” in between the Great Salt Lake and the mountains. 
“So (we need) smaller homes on smaller lots,” he said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: AG candidate Nate Willems calls for greater accountability of Iowa polluters
description: Democratic candidate for Iowa attorney general Nate Willems said Wednesday that “bullying does not work” on him and he won’t be pulling ads targeting current Attorney General Brenna Bird in relation to an Iowa pollution case.  Willems’ campaign has been threatened with a lawsuit from biofuel producer POET, after the campaign released an ad criticizing […]
text:
Nate Willems, a Democratic candidate for Iowa attorney general said Sept. 9, 2026 he will not pull ads related to a pollution settlement in Iowa, despite threats of a lawsuit against him. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Democratic candidate for Iowa attorney general Nate Willems said Wednesday that “bullying does not work” on him and he won’t be pulling ads targeting current Attorney General Brenna Bird in relation to an Iowa pollution case. 
Willems’ campaign has been threatened with a lawsuit from biofuel producer POET, after the campaign released an ad criticizing Bird for not pursuing further damages after it was discovered in 2024 that the plant had been releasing excessive amounts pollutants that can cause cancer and other health issues.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bird has said she did not pursue further damages because the case was not referred to her office by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources. 
“The Iowa DNR assessed the statutory maximum fine, which was paid, and the matter was not referred to the Attorney General’s office for any further action,” Bird’s campaign spokesperson said in a statement. “Attorney General Brenna Bird will continue to hold corporate actors accountable according to the law, not politics.”
Willems argued the state’s legal office has the independent authority to take further action in such cases, regardless of whether the DNR refers the case.
“That’s not a good excuse,” Willems said. “The office just did not do its job in this POET instance.” 
The case at hand involves a POET-owned biorefinery in Shell Rock that Iowa DNR discovered had likely been emitting air pollutants in excess of permitted limits for several years. DNR levied its maximum administrative fine of $10,000 on the company, which was also required to pay nearly $43,000 in fees to the state for underreporting pollution.
Willems’ political ad “Shell Rock” features a family in the area who say they felt “betrayed” by the situation and the lack of further action from the attorney general’s office. The ad does not name POET as the company, though it does show aerial footage of the plant. The ad also highlights contributions from POET CEO Jeff Broin to Bird’s campaign.
POET’s legal team, in a letter to the Willems campaign threatening legal action, said the ad gives the impression that “POET knowingly concealed information about dangerous emissions from the public and bribed a state official to avoid any penalties.” 
“That implication, which was intentionally made by the Campaign, is 100% false,” the letter to the Willems campaign reads. 
A letter from counsel representing the Willems campaign said it would not pull the ad and held that the “statements at issue are substantially true,” citing reports from DNR. 
“The ad is accurate; every fact in it is true,” Willems said at a news conference Wednesday. “And I’ll say the other part directly because I think Iowans need to hear this out loud: bullying does not work on me.” 
The letter from POET said the company “inherited” the issue from the previous owner and that once it discovered the issue, it shut down the system and fixed the emissions issue. 
Willems said an individual who drives a car recklessly and causes an accident cannot blame the accident on the previous owner of the car, “so why should it be different for a multibillion-dollar corporation that pollutes our air?” 
While the letter threatening lawsuit from POET argues that voters should “not trust someone who does not bother to investigate and learn the truth with an Office that depends on investigating and learning the truth,” Willems said the ad was not about POET or its CEO, but about Bird’s record and choices.
“What happened in Shell Rock is not the exception – it is a pattern for Brenna Bird,” Willems said. “In corporate pollution incidents across the state, she routinely lets them off easy.” 
Bird has been criticized for settlements in pollution cases DNR referred to her about a massive fish kill in the East Nishnabotna River and repeated wastewater discharges from a meatpacking facility in Postville. 
Willems said if elected to the role, he would work with DNR to “pursue real penalties” in pollution cases, publish an annual report on pollution incidents referred to the office and their outcomes and notify residents in applicable areas when a pollution settlement has been reached. 
Willems said he would also refuse to accept contributions from companies, or their executives, if they are being investigated or have been found guilty of polluting Iowa’s landscape. 
“I will never back down when the health and safety of Iowa families is on the line, not from this company, not from their lawyers, not from anybody,” Willems said.

name: VTDigger
title: A bear in the yard isn’t a crisis, it’s Tuesday
description:
Newcomers and social media are turning ordinary bear sightings into “incidents.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A bear in the yard isn’t a crisis, it’s Tuesday.
text:
This commentary is by Carol Winfield, a zoologist, naturalist and wildlife educator and rehabilitator who lives in Vermont.
I am writing to beg the Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department not to extend bear season into the time when these animals are metabolically slowing down and denning up for the winter. 
No true sportsman should ever consider allowing such an abhorrent practice as to kill a bear in its den, and extending the season into mid-December makes that more likely, not less. Other states, including Minnesota and Colorado, ban the practice, unlike Vermont. The Fish & Wildlife board has now proposed banning the killing of a sow bear with cubs, but there are no guarantees it will pass.
Multiple studies have found that extending the season does not necessarily reduce interactions with humans. One reason for the sharp increase in human-bear interactions is the increase in the human population, especially in rural areas. And some of this increase is from folks who did not grow up out in the country. They get a little more anxious about wildlife than Vermonters, and so they “warn” everybody when they see a bear. Social reporting amplifies this. When I was a kid, we saw bears and deer and foxes and thought, “Well, that’s cool,” and then went about our day. Now everyone can report to the whole world within seconds everything that happened in their lives, including seeing a bear, or their neighbor’s new car, or the soup they made for dinner.
As kids growing up in rural Vermont, we all knew that wildlife would get into your garbage if you didn’t secure it, and so we did secure it. No big deal, nothing newsworthy. And if we got careless and found our garbage strewn all over the lawn the next morning, we cussed, cleaned it up and were more careful next time. We didn’t report an “incident.”
By the Fish & Wildlife Department’s own admission in its media releases, it really does not know what the carrying capacity for bears is in our state. The department’s harvest-based population model is seriously flawed and likely inaccurate, as it does not reliably account for many factors affecting a wild population. So how can they possibly assert that there are too many? Is increasing the number of animals killed a measure to placate the fears of a very small number of people in the population?
Humans have traditionally treated other species abominably. But over the years, we’ve evolved somewhat and seen the error of our ways. Cockfighting, dogfighting and bullfighting are all banned in most civilized countries. Even in Britain, the great and glorious tradition of foxhunting with horses and hounds has now been discontinued.

READ MORE

Yet Vermont still allows hounding and trapping. Only around 18 states allow the chasing of bears with hounds. More than 85 other countries have banned steel-jaw traps, as have seven states in the U.S.
It is time to evolve and recognize that some of these so-called traditions are archaic and cruel and no longer necessary, and to ban them as the travesties they truly are. We cannot continue to allow wanton cruelty to animals by a few humans who call themselves sportsmen but seem to have no concept of the term. Honest, ethical hunters, who stalk their game and bring it down in the quickest and most humane way they possibly can, should also protest these abhorrent practices of chasing, tormenting and terrifying a wild creature with vicious dogs. 
Any decent, honest hunter should also condemn the practices of baiting and of setting steel traps indiscriminately to catch any creature that has the misfortune to wander by.
“Tradition” is a warm, fuzzy word that goes well with family gatherings for holidays. But that word is distorted when used to justify cruel, sadistic, outdated practices.

name: Mississippi Today
title: US appeals court considers effort to restrict the most common abortion method
description: Boxes of the drug mifepristone sit on a shelf at the West Alabama Women's Center in Tuscaloosa, Ala., March 16, 2022.
text:
A panel of federal judges heard arguments Wednesday over whether prescribing rules should be tightened for a key drug used in the most common abortion method in the United States, one of several ongoing efforts to restrict abortion access four years after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed states to decide the issue.
The case before the New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals is one of three making its way through the courts as abortion opponents try to block providers in states where abortion is legal from sending drugs for medication abortions into states where it is not.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration also says it’s reviewing the rules and could call for a change — and that the agency process should take precedence over court action.
It comes in a midterm election year in which President Donald Trump’s anti-abortion supporters are frustrated that a legal workaround to abortion bans remains. At the same time, most voters favor legal abortion access in most cases.
It will be up to the Supreme Court to sort out
At least 3 in 5 U.S. abortions are now obtained using a two-drug combination. At issue before the appeals court is just one: mifepristone.
Wednesday’s arguments were part of a case brought by Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and Rosalie Markezich, who says she was coerced into taking abortion pills. A survey conducted for the Society of Family Planning, which supports legal abortion access, estimates that between 770 and 900 women in Louisiana obtained abortions each month in 2025 by using pills prescribed online or by doctors or nurse practitioners in other states that have “shield laws” intended to protect those prescribers.
The three judges hearing the case are two nominated by Democratic presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden and one nominated by Republican George W. Bush.
Three other three-judge panels on the 5th Circuit — one in this case and two in an earlier one — and two district courts have already agreed that rules for prescribing mifepristone are too loose.
But the Supreme Court unanimously rejected an effort to roll back availability in 2024 — not because of the core legal argument, but because the court found the anti-abortion groups who brought the challenge didn’t have legal standing to make it.
On Wednesday, lawyers for the FDA and mifepristone manufacturers argued that Louisiana also lacks legal standing. One of the judges, Stephen Higginson, questioned whether the FDA’s role is a reason pills are flowing into Louisiana. “Those are state shield laws,” he said. “The government has nothing to do with the shield laws.”
Benjamin Aguinaga, Louisiana’s solicitor general, said the state is impacted, though, because some women who use the pills seek treatment for complications and, he said, perhaps half also have state-funded Medicaid health coverage.
Another ruling from the 5th Circuit would not immediately change the landscape because the Supreme Court has also blocked changes to the prescribing rules until it sees the case again. Even if the FDA makes changes without court approval, such an action would surely be challenged.
Other GOP state officials are also challenging the FDA’s rules. The attorneys general of Florida and Texas have filed one lawsuit and the top government lawyers of Idaho, Kansas and Missouri have another. Separately, Louisiana and Texas have attacked shield laws by bringing criminal and civil cases against some out-of-state providers.
Meanwhile, over the past year, federal judges in Hawaii and Virginia found that current FDA rules for mifepristone prescribing are too restrictive.
Abortion methods have changed since Roe was overturned
Abortion pills were already widely used before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in the 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization case that allowed states to enforce abortion bans.
Currently, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy. Another four do so after about the first six weeks, before many women realize they’re pregnant.
Opponents say the shield laws in some Democratic-controlled states, along with the rules allowing mifepristone to be mailed to patients, have undermined the bans.
“This case is going to have a huge impact,” said Gabriella McIntyre, legal counsel at Alliance Defending Freedom, which is representing Murrill and the other plaintiff in the case. “The promise of the Dobbs decision was that states would be able to decide on their own how to regulate abortion.”
A lawyer for mifepristone maker Danco Laboratories, though, told judges Wednesday that the 2023 rules were not intended to do so.
Abortion rights advocates also believe major consequences would arise if Louisiana eventually prevails. “They’re asking to restore an in-person requirement for every person across the country to access this medication regardless of whether they live in a state with strong legal protection for abortion access,” said Amanda Allen, executive director of the Abortion Coalition for Telemedicine.
The political situation is tricky for Trump
Anti-abortion groups who want to rein in pill access have been Trump’s key supporters.
Abortion opponents have called on the FDA to settle the lawsuit with Louisiana and roll back prescribing rules to how they were before telehealth prescriptions were allowed. They also want the administration to enforce an 1873 “anti-vice” law to bar mailing the pills.
Some states, including Mississippi and Texas, have adopted laws with civil or criminal penalties for those who prescribe abortion pills.
READ MORE: This medication saved a Mississippi lawmaker’s fertility. Her colleagues criminalized it
But on state ballot questions and in public opinion polls, voters have generally supported legal abortion access in most cases.
The administration has been mostly quiet through the legal battles, even though the FDA, whose scientists have repeatedly found mifepristone to be safe and effective, is the defendant in the cases.
The FDA says it’s studying mifepristone’s safety and reviewing prescribing rules around the drug. But Trump’s latest nominee to head the agency, Dr. Heidi Overton, the deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, has publicly criticized the agency for relaxing its prescribing rules for the drug — the most recent change coming in 2023.
One judge ordered the agency to provide a status update by Oct. 7, less than a month before the midterm elections in which control of Congress is in play. It’s not clear how detailed an update might be — or when the full study could be completed.
Prescribers are preparing to shift which drug they ship
Even if mifepristone access is curtailed, advocates say it won’t end access to abortion pills.
The most common regimen for pills in the U.S. is a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol. Misoprostol, which is commonly used to treat stomach ulcers and has never been formally approved for abortion, can cause abortions on its own. According to the FDA label on mifepristone, the combination completes medical abortion 97.4% of the time. Some studies have found misoprostol’s individual effectiveness at around 80% or higher.
Organizations that prescribe abortion pills by telehealth for women who are in states with bans say they would shift to sending misoprostol alone if mifepristone could be dispensed only at medical clinics rather than at pharmacies and through the mail.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Bobby Charles pushes back against sister’s criticisms as she endorses his gubernatorial opponent
description: Drawing on her own experience of being sexually abused as a child, Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles’ sister, Anita Charles, criticized his record on abortion at a Wednesday press conference in Portland. She also publicly opposed his education policy, divisive rhetoric and alignment with President Donald Trump, listing all of them as reasons she[...]
text:
Bobby Charles at a Portland press conference in response to his sister's public criticisms (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Drawing on her own experience of being sexually abused as a child, Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles’ sister, Anita Charles, criticized his record on abortion at a Wednesday press conference in Portland. She also publicly opposed his education policy, divisive rhetoric and alignment with President Donald Trump, listing all of them as reasons she supports his opponent, Democrat Hannah Pingree. 
At the press conference, the educator from Lewiston said her brother’s campaign has been built on “denigrating others and targeting Mainers with mean-spirited rhetoric that aims to incite fear and hatred towards vulnerable groups.”
An hour later at his own press conference a block away, Charles expressed sorrow at his sister’s abuse, detailing how it impacted the family. He disagreed that either his remarks or his abortion and education policies were harmful, but softened some stances, such as conceding that abortions should be permissible in cases of rape.
The family conflict is playing out two months before the election, earning Pingree an unexpected supporter as she leads in the polls and fundraising. 
Anita Charles’ criticisms of her brother were first made public through an op-ed in the Portland Press Herald, where she cited many of the same issues. 
“Bobby and I have never agreed politically, but we have tried to maintain civil discourse,” she said at the press conference. “But now Bobby has placed divisive and often false rhetoric at the center of his campaign, and I can no longer remain silent.”
She also detailed experiencing sexual assault, saying her experience did not make her brother more sympathetic toward supporting women’s bodily autonomy. 
Bobby Charles’ sister, Anita Charles, at a press conference criticizing her brother’s political stances and campaign rhetoric. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
“Bobby has known about this for about 50 years, yet Bobby has never stood up for the right of a woman or a girl to her own body,” she said, pointing to the Republican candidate’s record of opposing abortion.
“His stance against abortion rights, even in the case of rape, despite his knowledge of what I, his younger sister, experienced, would have gone against my health and well-being in ways that are truly morally reprehensible,” she added.
Charles, joined by his daughter Sophia, said he was still negatively impacted by what happened to his sister, but that it was “her story to tell.” He said her experience had made him focus on ensuring that perpetrators of sexual assault were adequately punished.
He also acknowledged that their political disagreements and the timing of the upcoming elections may have been the motivation behind her coming forward with her story.
 
“We happen to be in the middle of a gubernatorial race, and she’s a big supporter, I guess, of Janet Mills’ policies. I’m not a big supporter of Janet Mills’ policies,” the Republican nominee said. “Maybe there was some value she thought in bringing this stuff to the foreground. It’s painful for all of us, but … now we’re discussing an issue of enormous importance to far more Mainers than people know.”
Charles also denied his sister’s claim that he was entirely anti-choice, saying while he does not support abortion, he would be in favor of an exception for rape.
“I don’t believe in late term abortion, I don’t think the public should be paying for abortions,” he said. “But it’s not my big issue. And to be honest, that kind of a situation is so horrifying that, of course, there are exceptions.”
Planned Parenthood endorses Pingree, says rivals can’t be trusted on abortion rights

Anita Charles also pointed to her brother’s association with former U.S. House Speaker Dennis Hastert — who was convicted for financial offenses related to the sexual abuse of teenage boys — as further proof of him not speaking out against sexual assault perpetrators. 
Charles did not deny being associated with Hastert, but clarified that it was well before any allegations of child sexual assault against him came to light.
“I think it’s monstrous, and I think people against whom these charges are proven need to go to prison and stay there forever,” he said. “And frankly, that’s what I wished had happened to the individual who hurt my sister.”
Education record
Anita Charles, a lifelong educator, also condemned her brother’s stance on education, saying his approach undermines the hard work educators put in and the progress Maine schools have been making. She claimed the Republican candidate has not set foot in a public school since he was 18, contrasting that with her lifelong experience in the field.
“I am a heart surgeon for education, and Bobby wants to come in and play the kids’ version of Operation with a mini pair of tweezers,” she said. “It’s insulting and it’s harmful to our families, children, and youth, and to our teachers and other school personnel.”
Bobby Charles previously told Maine Morning Star that his biggest educational priorities are supporting teachers and making sure Maine can improve academic outcomes, but he has also publicly blamed current challenges schools are facing on “woke indoctrination” in classrooms, and has proposed that schools end equity-based initiatives and return to traditional learning models.
Maine’s gubernatorial candidates agree on education challenges, but not solutions

“He has no understanding of what standards exist in our schools, or what professional development and licensure teachers have, or what administrators do,” Anita Charles said. “His budget and his education plan would decimate our public schools.”
Charles denied his sister’s statements, saying he had initially sought her input on education policy when he first announced his run. But he also emphasized the importance of national assessments that have shown Maine test scores reached an all-time low in 2024, for which he blamed the Mills administration.
“I understand the need for emotional learning,” he said. “But it’s not that simple. I am a true believer in getting education back on track.”
Past rhetoric
Bobby Charles first rose to prominence amid a crowded field in the Republican gubernatorial primaries for his attacks against Democratic Rep. Deqa Dhalac from South Portland, calling her a “radical Somalia-first” state representative. He has also supported widespread immigration enforcement in Maine, which has largely targeted people without criminal records and said immigrants are to blame for a large share of Medicaid fraud in the state.
He has also spoken against Maine’s inclusive transgender student policy, advocating for the state to comply with the federal government’s anti-trans stance and require students to use bathrooms and play on sports teams aligned with their sex assigned at birth as opposed to gender identity. 
Anita Charles denounced his statements, saying, “Sadly, Bobby campaigns against his own extended family, with members who represent diversity across race, gender orientation, and gender expression, religion, country of origin, and more. 
“These family members feel unsafe through the rhetoric that Bobby promotes,” she added.
“I love my sister, but that’s not what’s happening,” he responded. “I would never campaign against any extended family member on any of those bases.” 
“If someone’s defined themselves as transgender, or what the medical profession had previously called, I think, gender dysphoria, they have my ultimate compassion,” he added. “The same is true of country of origin.”
