name: Virginia Mercury
title: Voters could move Congress to revisit H.R. 1 healthcare overhaul, Kaine and McClellan say
description: During a roundtable discussion at Feed More, a food bank in Henrico County Wednesday, U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said he believed there’s a growing chance Congress could adjust or undo Medicaid changes the Republican-controlled legislature enacted last summer — with or without flipping Congress to Democratic control.  It would still be a long shot, […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., and U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Richmond, speak with the media following a roundtable discussion on federal healthcare and housing policy  in Henrico County on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)During a roundtable discussion at Feed More, a food bank in Henrico County Wednesday, U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said he believed there’s a growing chance Congress could adjust or undo Medicaid changes the Republican-controlled legislature enacted last summer — with or without flipping Congress to Democratic control. 
It would still be a long shot, he and  U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Richmond, noted. But since H.R. 1 passed, every member of Congress has spent time in their districts hearing from their constituents, as voters name healthcare a chief concern.
Some Republicans — including Virginia U.S. Reps. Jennifer Kiggans and Rob Wittman — voiced opposition to the changes last summer before ultimately voting for the federal spending bill. 
“The magnitude of these cuts is really becoming manifest right now,” Kaine said. “We probably could have had three or four votes a year ago. People have been home during recess, talking to their healthcare providers. We might have now, you know, 10 or a dozen. We need about a dozen Republican votes to do that.”
With forthcoming additional eligibility factors and processes, an estimated 300,000 Virginians are expected to lose Medicaid, while 125,000 Virginians have already lost their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits. The federal programs have for decades helped people nationwide access health insurance and provided assistance buying groceries. 
Virginia’s health secretary Marvin Figueroa, who also attended the roundtable, said that H.R. 1 “by design” was intended to make people lose their benefits. 
He explained that as the top public health official in the state, he’s responsible for helping blunt the impact.
He and others in Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration plans to ensure state and local agencies comply with additional workloads. State lawmakers approved funding to boost those efforts and prevent eligible people from losing their benefits. 
Congress had also failed to renew expired tax credits that helped offset costs for people who buy their insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace. 
Roughly 94,000 Virginians have dropped their coverage amid spiking premiums. Some may be eligible this November to tap into part of a $150 million state-level subsidy that state legislators earmarked in the current budget. 
As the bill made its way through the nation’s legislature the Rural Health Transformation Fund also emerged as a compromise to offset impacts in existing healthcare deserts. 
Over the past year a handful of Virginia hospitals have trimmed services and clinics have closed, all citing H.R.1 as a factor. Thirteen rural hospitals have also been flagged as vulnerable to cuts or closure by a state report.
Kaine and Figueroa said Wednesday that the fund —  totaling $10 billion, with  $189 million earmarked for Virginia —  is not enough money to fill the healthcare holes that H.R. 1 will create, but it can still help. 
More than reading headlines or connecting with providers in their states and districts, McClellan reiterated that elected leaders are hearing concerns and calls to action directly from people they represent. 
“They’re hearing from their constituents the impact that this is having, and their constituents are demanding action too,” she said. 
Richmond Mayor Danny Avula also participated in the roundtable panel, focusing his remarks on another top concern for voters: housing. He and the elected leaders discussed federal tools to support expanding housing access for Richmonders, Virginians and Americans.
Richmond Mayor Danny Avula participates in a roundtable discussion on health, housing and public services in Henrico County on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
“The tariffs are killing us, the cost of labor is killing us,” Avula said. “It just takes so much more public subsidy to get housing costs down.” 
Congress celebrated a bipartisan win this summer with the passage of the 21st Century Road To Housing Act, Avula noted, but implored Kaine and McClellan to  ensure funding for grants within the federal policy actually get appropriated. 
All seats in the  U.S. House of Representatives are up for election this fall, along with half of the U.S. Senate. Analysts and polls have identified voters’ view of affordability and healthcare as key issues that could tip the balance of partisan power in both chambers. 
Early voting begins Sep. 18 and Election Day is Nov.3.

name: Source New Mexico
title: NM US Sen. Heinrich tours Albuquerque Food Farmacy to tout fruits and vegetables as medicine
description: U.S. Sen Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Wednesday helped volunteers at an Albuquerque health clinic distribute bags of fresh produce to food-insecure patients, part of an effort to highlight a “food is medicine” bill he has co-sponsored in the Senate.
text:
U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Sept. 9, 2026, visited Presbyterian Healthcare Services’ Food Farmacy, which provides patients with bags of fresh produce. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Sen Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Wednesday helped volunteers at an Albuquerque health clinic distribute bags of fresh produce to food-insecure patients, part of an effort to highlight a “food is medicine” bill he has co-sponsored in the Senate. 
Presbyterian Healthcare Services distributes roughly 10-pound bags of fresh fruits and vegetables to approximately 1,000 of its patients each week. The program, which first launched in 2018, seeks to improve access to healthy food and nutrition education and thereby stave off chronic diseases linked to poor diet. 
But the program relies almost entirely on funding from Presbyterian or donations, Leigh Caswell, Presbyterian’s vice president of community health and equity, told Source NM on Wednesday at the company’s Community Health Resource Center in Albuquerque. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Providing healthy food to patients “is a healthcare intervention, but it’s not a thing that’s billable,” she said. “You’re not able to charge Medicaid for it or Medicare. It’s just not part of how healthcare is financed.”
The “Accountable Produce is Medicine Act of 2026,” which Heinrich co-sponsored early last month, seeks to change that. The bill, which has Republican sponsors in both the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate, would require the federal Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation to conduct a five-year study on whether paying public funds for nutrition assistance programs like Presbyterian’s Food Farmacy improves outcomes for patients with chronic diseases. 
The study will evaluate patients’ weights, blood pressure and blood glucose measurements, along with other factors, according to the bill text. 
Versions of the bill in both legislative chambers currently await consideration in committees, Heinrich spokesperson Luis Soriano told Source NM. 
Presbyterian’s program enrolls patients who describe being food insecure in patient screenings, Caswell said, including not having enough money to pay for groceries. At the Albuquerque clinic Heinrich visited, approximately 160 patients arrive in vehicles every Wednesday and accept brown bags full of fruits and vegetables from volunteers. 
Heinrich — after handing a patient a bag with pears, okra, peaches and other items Wednesday — told Source NM that he visited Presbyterian’s Food Farmacy to see a model he says demonstrates a food system that supports both local farmers and public health more broadly. 
“I think this program, from a healthcare point of view, just proves out how valuable a fresh fruit and vegetable kind of diet is for the population, and we should learn from that when we’re setting things like farm policy and writing a new Farm Bill,” he said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Josh Turek calls for lifting income cap on Social Security to sustain program
description: Social Security advocates joined Rep. Josh Turek Wednesday to speak with older adults about the U.S. Senate candidate’s commitments to preserving and expanding government systems that many Americans rely on for medical expenses and income. Turek, campaigning for the state’s open Senate seat, told senior living center Scottish Rite Park residents that where h[...]
text:
Former Social Security Administration Commissioner Martin O’Malley, left, Social Security Works PAC President Jon Bauman and Rep. Josh Turek speak to older adults at Scottish Rite Park on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Social Security advocates joined Rep. Josh Turek Wednesday to speak with older adults about the U.S. Senate candidate’s commitments to preserving and expanding government systems that many Americans rely on for medical expenses and income.
Turek, campaigning for the state’s open Senate seat, told senior living center Scottish Rite Park residents that where his opponent, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, has voted to cut Social Security, Medicaid and other programs, he would instead push for further supporting the programs. Former Social Security Administration Commissioner Martin O’Malley and Social Security Works PAC President Jon Bauman voiced their support for Turek, saying Social Security is one of the areas where Turek and Hinson differ the most.
“Ashley Hinson has damaged Social Security, she voted to cut it,” O’Malley told reporters after the discussion. “Josh Turek will vote to improve it, improve benefits, and strengthen it for the long term.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Max Richtman, president and CEO of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, also joined the group to throw the organization’s endorsement behind Turek. More than 12,450 people are members of the organization, Richtman said, and former U.S. senator and advisory board chairman Tom Harkin gave his “gold standard” recommendation for the endorsement.
Hinson has a low scorecard when it comes to voting on the issues important to seniors, the group stated, with Richtman and Bauman saying their organizations have both scored her votes. Bauman said a scorecard from the Alliance for Retired Americans found that “nine times out of every 10, she votes wrong for … Iowa seniors.”
This includes voting for cuts to the Social Security Administration by as much as $452 million, O’Malley said, as well as supporting Medicaid cuts and allowing DOGE to drive out 1 in 5 Social Security employees. Iowans and people across the U.S. now have a harder time seeking help from the agency when they need it, the group said, and a Social Security office in Decorah had to close due to lack of staff.
According to a June press release from Hinson, the office reopened this summer. Since Hinson took national office, Turek said as many as 842 “healthcare entities” have closed across Iowa.
“This is in a state with a healthcare crisis, a mental health crisis, and a cancer crisis. Voting to cut healthcare (means) the downstream effects are … less services, less supports, less facilities. This is fundamentally wrong,” Turek said. “I give each and every Iowa senior my pledge — I will do everything I can to protect Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security, and expand it to all of you.”
Hinson Campaign Communications Director Billy Fuerst said in an email Hinson has gone on the record in the Cedar Rapids Gazette opposing raising the retirement age, and voted in favor of both the Working Families Tax Cuts and the Social Security Fairness Act.
The July 2024 vote included a 4% decrease to staffing funding at Washington, D.C., and Baltimore Social Security Administration offices, the email stated, and no cuts to offices interacting with seniors or to benefits were included in the bill.
“Ashley Hinson has never and will never cut a penny from Social Security – she is fighting to protect it for Iowa seniors. That’s the truth no matter how desperate Josh Turek gets,” Fuerst said in an emailed statement.
Eliminating the cap on Social Security is the best option to ensure the program’s solvency in the future, Turek said. He said it’s “ridiculous” that regular Americans have to pay into Social Security year-round while the country’s wealthiest, like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, don’t have to pay any more past the $184,500 cap once they’ve met it, which happens early on each year.
Each of the officials speaking with seniors Wednesday supported the removal of income caps for Social Security taxes and the idea that millionaires and billionaires should pay more into Social Security to ensure their fellow Americans can pay their bills. If the cap was removed, O’Malley said the administration’s ability to pay out benefits through Social Security would extend past 2090.
There are other areas where people would benefit from caps, Turek said, including on insulin costs, which he sponsored a bill for in the Iowa Legislature, and on medical insurance costs within Medicare. He said he also supports negotiated drug costs and taking an “all of the above” approach to lowering costs associated with longtime care for aging or disabled Iowans.
“Two of the biggest issues we’re facing right now in the country (are) wealth divide and tax avoidance, and unfortunately, you’ve got folks like Ashley Hinson that have been up there and voted for cuts to health care, food assistance, Social Security Administration, just to give more tax breaks to these billionaires,” Turek said. “I want to fight for the people, not the billionaires.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont’s first general-election attack ad links Fazio to Trump and ICE
description: Gov. Ned Lamont linked Republican challenger Ryan Fazio to President Donald Trump’s crackdown on undocumented migrants.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont linked Republican challenger Ryan Fazio to President Donald Trump’s crackdown on undocumented migrants with an ad featuring a Black minister decrying racial profiling by immigration agents and Fazio’s vote against a law intended to make schools and churches off limits to ICE.
The ad, released Wednesday by the Democratic governor’s reelection campaign, is the first attacking Fazio by name, and it comes days after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agents raised their profile in Connecticut with arrests of migrant parents at school bus stop in Danbury.
“Members of my congregation are fearful of going outside because of these ICE agents. They’re stopping individuals based on the color of their skin,” Senior Pastor   Lindsay Curtis of Grace Baptist Church in Norwalk says in the ad. 
“Thankfully, Gov. Lamont stepped in. He signed a law barring ICE agents from our churches and our schools,” Curtis says. “But Ryan Fazio sided with Trump to allow ICE into our schools and our houses of worship. I really can’t imagine him being governor. That is too extreme for Connecticut.”
The ad is referring to a law passed in 2026 with a provision aimed at ICE that defines  schools, hospitals, courthouses and places of worship as “protected areas” where law enforcement cannot make an arrest without a judicial warrant. Fazio, a state senator, and every other Republican opposed the bill, as did a few Democrats.


“I think it is very striking that the very first commercial ad in the general election campaign of a man who’s been in office for eight years is lying about his opponent rather than defending his own record or talking about his agenda for a potential third term,” Fazio said.
Given that Fazio voted against the measure referenced in the ad and filed a bill in 2025 to repeal revisions of the Trust Act passed in 2019, how is the ad a lie?
“First of all, because the governor well knows that nothing, no law or policy passed at the state level constitutionally affects federal policy,” Fazio said. “So it’s constitutionally a lie for anyone who’s taken fifth grade civics. Plus, I wonder if he would label as ‘extreme’ the Democratic members of the legislature who voted no on that legislation.”
Lamont said the 2026 bill establishing protected areas was an important statement of intent by Connecticut.
“Generally speaking, they’ve respected our purpose. And generally speaking, we work with them when it comes to a case of a serious criminal,” Lamont said.
The measure, Senate Bill 397, passed on votes of 24-10 in the Senate and 91-53 in the House. No Democrat in the Senate opposed the bill. In the House, four Democrats joined all 49 Republicans in opposition.
Fazio, who was elected to the Senate in a special election in 2021, said he would have voted for the original Trust Act, which passed the General Assembly unanimously in 2013 during the Obama administration.
Democrats say the original bill and revisions passed in 2019 during the first Trump administration were intended to ensure an undocumented immigrant would feel safe reporting a crime or seeking aid from police without fear of being turned over to ICE. 
Fazio said the revisions hampered local authorities from cooperating with ICE, and he favored repealing them.
“I think that the governor was wrong and radical in tying the hands of state and federal law enforcement in communicating with federal authorities in the case of people who are here illegally, who have been convicted of Class C, D and E felonies like manslaughter and sexual abuse,” Fazio said.
Fazio on Wednesday repeated a claim he made on Facebook in January that the 2019 revisions had kept the state from holding an undocumented immigrant for ICE. The man and his wife pleaded guilty to risk of injury and other charges related to the death of their two year-old son, Liam Rivera.
“All the Trust Act says is we don’t want our state police and local police resources to be engaged in federal immigration enforcement,” he said.  
Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, co-chair of the Judiciary Committee, said nothing in the Trust Act or its revisions prevents ICE from arresting and deporting anyone.

name: Michigan Advance
title: After backlash, Whitmer says EGLE must consider Michigan Supreme Court ruling on Line 5 permits
description: When the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy issued a set of permits for the Line 5 tunnel project in July, opponents of the pipeline called it a betrayal — with some laying the blame at Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s feet. Now, both Whitmer and EGLE are pushing a harder line against Enbridge Energy […]
text:
The Mackinac Bridge in the Straits of Mackinac, May 27, 2024 | Susan J. DemasWhen the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy issued a set of permits for the Line 5 tunnel project in July, opponents of the pipeline called it a betrayal — with some laying the blame at Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s feet.
Now, both Whitmer and EGLE are pushing a harder line against Enbridge Energy as the state’s regulators gear up to re-examine the potential environmental impacts of building the tunnel project, which Enbridge has said would serve to protect the dual pipelines from the type of disaster Whitmer has warned about throughout her career.
The re-examination of the project and its impacts is the product of the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision in late July to toss the Michigan Public Service Commission’s approval of the tunnel project. The high court in a nearly unanimous decision found that the state did not properly examine the environmental harms that might arise from extending the pipeline’s lifespan.
On Wednesday, Whitmer’s office released a statement saying EGLE must examine how the Supreme Court ruling affects its own permitting decisions. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The governor also sent a letter to Enbridge CEO Gregory Ebel, demanding the company stop treating the tunnel project as its only alternative to the dual pipelines, noting that multiple energy supply chain experts had concluded that the market can adapt to a Line 5 shutdown without significant supply shortages or price spikes.
“I am calling on Enbridge to pursue an alternative to both the existing dual pipelines and the tunnel, and to begin that work now,” Whitmer wrote. “Develop a planned, orderly transition that protects Michigan families and businesses and gets oil out of the Straits far sooner. That alternative may not preserve Enbridge’s current market share or be as profitable for your shareholders. But those are not reasons to expose the Great Lakes to another decade of unthinkable risk.”
During her 2018 campaign, Whitmer pledged to take action against the pipeline, which stretches for 4.5 miles through the straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet.
However, with fewer than six months left in her tenure as governor, anti-Line 5 advocates argued that Whitmer had softened her stance against the pipeline.
Great Lakes tribal nations and environmental advocates have pushed for a shut down to the pipeline for years over concerns that the pipeline could rupture and contaminate the lakes with crude oil.
Following an anchor strike in 2018 which dented the pipeline in three places, Enbridge reached an agreement with the state, led by Republican Gov. Rick Snyder, to build a utility tunnel to house a new section of the pipeline and permanently shut down the dual pipeline currently operating on the lakebed.
In order to move forward with the construction of the tunnel, Enbridge needs permits from multiple regulatory agencies. While it has received the approval of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the Michigan Supreme Court’s recent action overturned the permit granted by the Michigan Public Service Commission.
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy emphasized that the company already has an agreement with the state to build the tunnel. 
“Without years of litigation and political intervention, this project would be moving toward completion,” Duffy said.
He noted Enbridge would “continue to stand ready to meet with the Governor to look at ways that protect Michigan’s natural resources while ensuring the continued safe operation of critical energy infrastructure.”
In a statement shared alongside Whitmer’s Wednesday announcement, EGLE Director Phil Roos said the agency had completed a review of the cultural and environmental impacts of the tunnel project and an analysis of alternatives under the scope set by law. That said, given the Supreme Court’s decision, EGLE’s permit may need further review, Roos said.
“Until all those legal questions are resolved, conditions in EGLE’s permit prevent construction of the tunnel entrance from moving forward,” Roos said.
Protest signs at a rally agains Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline in Lansing on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo By Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Whitmer’s office, in Wednesday’s news release, said the state is reviewing its options for proceeding in a manner consistent with the Supreme Court’s decision and Michigan law.
Nichole Keway Biber, the Michigan Water Justice Organizer for Clean Water Action and a tribal citizen of the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, told the Advance on Wednesday that Whitmer’s announcement is a sign that pressure from the people and established law can work in concert to make a difference.
Emily Woodcock, Michigan director for Clean Water Action, also said the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision effectively requires the state to consider the Michigan Environmental Protection Act and the public trust doctrine — the idea that certain natural resources and features like the Great Lakes are preserved for public use — in all its environmental permitting decisions.
“That is so important, not just for the Line 5 fight, but for every single fight moving forward,” Woodcock said. “That is like a game changer for our work.”
David Gover, a managing attorney for the Native American Rights Fund representing the Bay Mills Indian Community, thanked Roos and the governor for hearing the tribal nations and communities opposed to the project alongside the court’s decision.
“EGLE should have never issued these permits and the recent Michigan Supreme Court decision confirms that,” Gover said. “It is imperative that all permitting agencies take the time to review and fully understand the impacts on Tribal Treaty-protected resources, as there is no denying the harm this proposed project would cause to cultural resources, the environment, and the impacted Treaty resources. The Straits of Mackinac are a sacred space, and should be protected from permanent destruction by oil pipelines running through the Straits.”
The Anishinaabe consider the Straits of Mackinac the site of creation, with the EGLE permit noting this “project will have adverse effects on known historic and cultural resources, including their destruction and/or removal These resources are unique and highly significant to the Anishinaabek communities, as well as the State of Michigan.”
The permit requires Enbridge to “mitigate the loss of historic, archaeological, and cultural resources,” a condition Gover previously said would force tribal citizens to unearth their buried ancestors.
In a previous statement to the Advance, Enbridge said past site surveys found no confirmed tribal ancestral burial grounds within the proposed construction areas, but their process “fully accounts for the possibility of discoveries.”
Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle said the state’s announcement is an important step, but emphasized that Michigan needs to listen to tribal nations.
“Our treaty rights are not an afterthought, and our voices should not only be heard when it is convenient,” Gravelle said in a statement. “The Straits are our homeland, not a corridor for a foreign oil company. We do not own the Great Lakes. We are borrowing them from future generations, and it is our responsibility to return them whole. That means moving beyond Line 5 and toward safer alternatives that do not gamble with the heart of the Great Lakes.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Thousands of South Dakota habitat license plates do nothing for habitat, due to two-part process
description: Thousands of South Dakota drivers who have habitat conservation license plates have not actually made a financial contribution to protect habitat for wildlife. That’s because unlike some other states, where drivers’ habitat contributions are collected during license-plate transactions, South Dakota dispenses the plates and then asks drivers to separately don[...]
text:
A meadowlark habitat decal is affixed to a South Dakota habitat conservation license plate. The optional decal purchase is what helps to fund habitat conservation, and some people don't take the extra step. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Thousands of South Dakota drivers who have habitat conservation license plates have not actually made a financial contribution to protect habitat for wildlife.
That’s because unlike some other states, where drivers’ habitat contributions are collected during license-plate transactions, South Dakota dispenses the plates and then asks drivers to separately donate to habitat conservation later by ordering habitat-themed decals and affixing them to the plates.
Some drivers don’t follow through with the optional purchase of the decals. As a result, the state has sold 8,484 more sets of habitat plates than decals, according to data from the state Department of Game, Fish and Parks running from March 2025, when the plates first became available, through last month. That equates to about $415,000 in potential funding for habitat that’s not being collected.
Meanwhile, the state has sold 4,626 sets of decals, generating about $230,000 for habitat conservation.
Jeff Olson is a Black Hills Sportsmen Club board member, co-president of Black Hills Flyfishers, a board member of the South Dakota Wildlife Federation, and a former state Game, Fish and Parks commissioner. He is happy the state started a plate program that puts money toward habitat conservation.
“Yet, I have a hard time understanding why we would require people to purchase these things separately,” Olson said. “It doesn’t make sense.”
Olson said he has a friend who has plates with no decals who told Olson “it is too complicated and people just give up.”
How the process works
South Dakota habitat plates feature a special design with a field of grass and a blue sky, and the phrase “Habitat Conservation” across the bottom. The plate number is offset to the right, allowing space for the optional decal to be affixed on the left.
The plates cost $10 beyond the price of a standard vehicle registration, which covers the cost to make the special plates. Habitat plates are valid for three years.


Drivers can obtain plates in person at their county treasurer’s office or through the mail. Either way, the state Department of Revenue says, drivers are given written notice of the opportunity to separately purchase the habitat decals from the state Department of Game, Fish and Parks.
A set of decals costs $50 — or $30 for motorcycles and all-terrain vehicles — and can be purchased on the Game, Fish and Parks website. The department uses the decal proceeds for habitat conservation work on public and private lands, for projects such as planting native grasses and trees, and doing prescribed burning to control invasive species. Drivers can choose from four decal designs, which the state describes as emblems: a deer, a meadowlark, a pasque flower (the state flower), or a pheasant.
Why is it this way?
Lawmakers authorized the program two years ago, and the state implemented it in March 2025.
Kendra Baucom, a spokesperson for the state Department of Revenue, which works with counties to manage vehicle licensing and registration, told South Dakota Searchlight in a statement that the two-step process is legally necessary due to language in the state constitution.


The decades-old language in Article 11, Section 8 says vehicle license and registration fees “shall be used exclusively for the maintenance, construction and supervision of highways and bridges of this state.”
Baucom said “it would be unconstitutional to tie the sale of the emblems to the sale of the plates, then use the proceeds for habitat conservation purposes.”
“While it might not be convenient to purchase the emblems separately, that is how we can both follow the constitution and provide support for habitat conservation,” Baucom added.
How other states handle habitat plates
Other states have figured out how to streamline the process.
In Minnesota, the purchase of a habitat plate includes a minimum $30 contribution to the state’s Critical Habitat Program at the time of the plate purchase. No additional decal is required. The state’s Department of Public Safety receives the $30 contribution and passes it along to the habitat program fund. The $30 contribution is made annually when drivers renew their registration.
Iowa has a natural resources plate program, which includes a $45 contribution to the program at the time of the plate purchase and annual $25 renewals, with no extra decal purchase required. After the money is deposited into a road tax fund, the state treasurer credits an equivalent amount to the Iowa Resources Enhancement and Protection Fund, used for habitat and wildlife programs.
Searchlight asked South Dakota’s Department of Revenue why it can’t follow the example of those other states.
“Every state constitution is different,” Baucom replied.
Policymakers react
The disconnect between plate sales and decal sales in South Dakota disappoints the two lawmakers who served as primary sponsors of the authorizing legislation in the state House and Senate.
Erin Tobin of Winner, who was serving as a Republican state senator at the time but is no longer in the Legislature, said state officials should revisit the program to determine whether there is a better way to structure the purchases.
“I’m still really proud of this program,” Tobin said. “It gives people who don’t hunt and fish, but care about habitat, an opportunity to participate in the state’s conservation work as well.”
Hunters and anglers contribute to habitat conservation through fees included in the price of their hunting and fishing licenses, and with taxes on equipment.
The House sponsor, Rep. Jessica Bahmuller, R-Alexandria, said South Dakotans would be more likely to complete the decal transaction if they could purchase the plates and decals together. She hopes to address that if she wins reelection in November, she said.
Game, Fish and Parks Commission Chairwoman Stephanie Rissler said the plates themselves, even without decals, provide a benefit.
“Whether someone chooses to display the emblem or not, the plate itself still helps promote the importance of habitat conservation across South Dakota,” Rissler wrote in a statement to Searchlight.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV to give $2.4M in Rural Health funds to expand Ascend to healthcare professionals
description: HURRICANE, W.Va. – The state of West Virginia will allocate $2.4 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds to expand the Ascend program to recruit healthcare workers throughout the state, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Wednesday.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey (center) speaks during an announcement that the state will give $2.4 million in federal Rural Health Transformation funds to expand Ascend West Virginia to recruit healthcare professionals. Beside Morrisey are Alys Smith, wife of Marshall University Pres. Brad Smith, and Michael Benson, president of WVU. (Photo courtesy Morrisey's Office via Flickr)HURRICANE, W.Va. – The state of West Virginia will allocate $2.4 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds to expand the Ascend program to recruit healthcare workers throughout the state, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Wednesday.
“We are moving quickly to put these historic resources to work improving healthcare outcomes for West Virginians,” Morrisey said in a news release. “That starts with making sure our communities have the doctors, nurses, and other healthcare professionals they need. By strengthening our healthcare workforce, we can improve access to care, help West Virginians live healthier lives, and get more people healthy and back to work.”
The initiative aims to recruit 125 licensed healthcare professionals to rural parts of the state in the first year. 
Marshall University President Brad Smith and wife Alys Smith spearheaded the Ascend West Virginia program in 2021 to recruit remote workers to West Virginia with financial assistance and programming. The program has since expanded to attract teachers and military veterans to the state. 
Ascend West Virginia is operated by West Virginia University, which will partner on Ascend Health with WVU Medicine, Marshall University, Marshall Health, Vandalia Health, the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine and the state Department of Tourism. 
The money will be used for three programs: Ascend West Virginia Healthcare, First Ascent Healthcare and a third pilot program, said Danny Twilley, WVU’s assistant vice president of economic, community and asset development.
Ascend West Virginia Healthcare aims to attract out-of-state health care professionals into six areas of the state: the Greenbrier Valley, the greater Elkins region, the New River Gorge, the Charleston area, the Eastern Panhandle or the greater Morgantown area, he said.
First Ascent Healthcare will target graduates of Marshall, WVU and the School of Osteopathic Medicine to live in any of those six areas or in Huntington, Twilley said. The new pilot program will provide opportunities for healthcare professionals to live anywhere in the state, Twilley said. 
The 125 medical professionals will comprise the “full gamut” of licensed healthcare professionals, from social workers and mental health providers to physician assistants, nurse practitioners, nurses and physicians, said Beth Hammers, vice dean for administration at the Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine at Marshall University. 
Twilley said the program will work to fill critical positions within the Marshall Health Network, WVU Medicine and Vandalia Health. 
“They’ll know that better than we will,” Twilley said. “And so that’s where we’re going to identify, and we’re going to learn a lot in year one about exactly the type of individual that will be applying, the positions that they are applying for, and the locations in which they’re going to live.”
In a statement Wednesday, state health secretary Arvin Singh said he’s excited to partner with Ascend. 
“Ascend WV’s expertise in relocation and workforce integration makes them an ideal partner to help healthcare professionals and their families establish roots in West Virginia communities,” he said. “Through this initiative, we aim to build a stronger, more resilient healthcare workforce across the state.”
The Rural Health Transformation Program, funded by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, aims to “transform the existing rural health care infrastructure and build sustainable health care systems that expand access, enhance quality of care, and improve outcomes for patients,” according to CMS.
The program was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law last summer. 
The law made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending in the United States. The five-year program awarded $199 million to West Virginia in its first year. 
Morrisey announced last week the program would award $2.4 million to expand three workplace health programs in the state.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Local partnerships with ICE result in record number of immigration arrests in Oklahoma
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma law enforcement agencies’ partnerships with federal immigration forces have resulted in the arrests of over 1,800 people, the majority of whom have no criminal history, records show. Of the over 1,800 immigration-related arrests made in Oklahoma from January through July with these partnerships, fewer than 20% of arrestees had any cr[...]
text:
An Oklahoma Highway Patrol vehicle is pictured. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma law enforcement agencies’ partnerships with federal immigration forces have resulted in the arrests of over 1,800 people, the majority of whom have no criminal history, records show.
Of the over 1,800 immigration-related arrests made in Oklahoma from January through July with these partnerships, fewer than 20% of arrestees had any criminal conviction, according to an analysis of data published by the Deportation Data Project, which gathers and processes arrest data provided by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Patrol, and other federal agencies through Freedom of Information Act requests. 
Only five of those detained this year had previously been convicted of a violent crime, the analysis found. 
The arrests were made through 287(g) partnerships, which allow state and local officers to be credentialed under ICE and carry out some aspects of federal immigration enforcement.
In all of 2025, officials made about 1,200 immigration-related arrests in Oklahoma through 287(g). In 2024, they made just under 500, according to the dataset. 
The increased immigration enforcement efforts in Oklahoma come as the Trump administration has pressed for increased immigration enforcement efforts. The number of 287(g) partnerships nationwide have increased from 135 agreements to 2,466 since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, according to Homeland Security. 
Supporters have said that the efforts are targeted at ensuring violent criminals are not in the country, but Oklahoma’s arrests mirror the national trend of ICE arresting a record high number of people without criminal histories this summer.
Of those arrested through Oklahoma’s 287(g) partnerships, over 1,600 had no criminal conviction, according to the dataset from the Deportation Data Project. About 200 had a previous conviction for nonviolent crimes. 
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson in a statement disputed the Deportation Data Project findings and said it is “cherry picked” to “peddle a false narrative.” The spokesperson also said neither Homeland Security nor ICE have reviewed the project or its results. 
The spokesperson said many of those counted as “non-criminals” have a “rap sheet,” but just not in the U.S. 
“Further, every single one of these individuals committed a crime when they came into this country illegally,” the spokesperson said. “ICE enforces the law as written. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S.— full stop.” 
Violating immigration law is generally a civil offense in the United States.
Top immigration officials, such as Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have recently said criminal records are not important and people will be deported regardless for violating U.S. immigration law. 
Over 110 Oklahoma law enforcement agencies have entered into 287(g) partnerships with ICE, according to the federal agency. 
Among those is the Oklahoma Highway Patrol.
Sarah Stewart, a spokesperson for the Highway Patrol, said in a statement that the partnership with ICE allows troopers to take action during their normal course of duties when they encounter people who are unlawfully present in the U.S.
“Our responsibility does not begin only after someone has committed a violent offense,” she said. “Our responsibility is to enforce the law, address violations when we encounter them, and work with the appropriate agency when an individual falls under that agency’s jurisdiction.”
Since the beginning of 2026, the Oklahoma Highway Patrol has taken 141 people into custody for immigration violations across four “Operation Guardian” events, according to data provided by the Oklahoma Highway Patrol. More than 60 were operating commercial vehicles. 
Operation Guardian targets commercial drivers utilizing Oklahoma’s highways in an effort to arrest motorists in Oklahoma without legal immigration status.
This year’s Operation Guardian enforcements took place Jan. 14 in Kay County, March 25 in the Panhandle, May 13 across multiple locations, and June 17 in Backham and Sequoyah counties, according to a Highway Patrol spokesperson. 
Previous Operation Guardian events have targeted major ports of entry to Oklahoma. Operations in 2025 resulted in at least 200 people being detained for immigration violations, according to previous reports from the Highway Patrol. 
The Oklahoma Highway Patrol is concerned about “unvetted and inadequately trained” commercial drivers on Oklahoma roads, especially if they have difficulty understanding English road signs, Stewart said. 
“These concerns are not about where someone comes from,” she said in a statement. “They are about whether someone operating a commercial vehicle on Oklahoma highways has been properly vetted, properly trained, properly licensed, capable of safely operating that vehicle, and has the proper intentions.”

title: NC Supreme Court weighs whether state can pursue TikTok lawsuit
description: Millions of North Carolinians routinely download and use TikTok for entertainment, news and advertising. But its popularity in the state doesn’t mean that ByteDance, TikTok’s parent company, should be tried here, attorneys for the social media giant argued Wednesday before the North Carolina Supreme Court. The case stems from an October 2024 lawsuit filed by[...]
text:
The North Carolina Supreme Court heard arguments Sept. 9, 2026 on whether a case against TikTok should be heard in state court. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Millions of North Carolinians routinely download and use TikTok for entertainment, news and advertising. But its popularity in the state doesn’t mean that ByteDance, TikTok’s parent company, should be tried here, attorneys for the social media giant argued Wednesday before the North Carolina Supreme Court.
The case stems from an October 2024 lawsuit filed by then-Attorney General Josh Stein in which a bipartisan group of attorneys general sued ByteDance for designing the app to addict young kids with its features and deceiving parents that it had safety guidelines in place to protect kids. Attorney General Jeff Jackson is now pursuing the case against TikTok.
A bipartisan group of attorneys general sued ByteDance in 2024 for allegedly designing the app to addict young kids with its features. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Wednesday’s hearing focused less on the allegations of harm and more on jurisdiction.
TikTok attorney Jon Hacker argued that North Carolina courts don’t have jurisdiction over TikTok and ByteDance in this matter because the product’s design features were not “purposefully directed” toward the state of North Carolina.
“TikTok did not design the challenged features in North Carolina or tailor them in any way for North Carolina users,” Hacker said. “TikTok likewise did not make the allegedly deceptive statements in the state of North Carolina, or target them specifically to anyone in North Carolina.”
Hacker told the high court that the claims made by North Carolina’s attorney general relate to its nationwide business model.
But a North Carolina business court has already disagreed with that argument. In an August 2025 ruling, Superior Court Judge Adam Conrad rejected a motion by TikTok to dismiss the case.
“Unlike a general web search, TikTok use is neither a one-and-done transaction nor a one-sided inquiry from a user,” wrote Conrad in that opinion. “ByteDance regularly sends communications into North Carolina (through push notifications to users’ phones, for example) and retrieves data from in-state users (including personal data that ByteDance monetizes via targeted third-party advertisements). What results is a two-way exchange of information across state borders on a massive scale.”
Hacker told the Supreme Cour the fact that an international platform is accessible to users in a given state isn’t enough to give that state jurisdiction over the platform. North Carolina should be suing in California where TikTok has headquarters and where the design or conduct allegedly occurred, Hacker told the justices.
NC Associate Justice Allison Riggs questions TikTok attorney Jon Hacker. (Photo: NC Supreme Court video)
Associate Justice Richard Dietz noted that most websites collect cookies these days, but the court would need to weigh how TikTok handled the information it collected and look at “that spectrum of that interaction.”
Dietz then offered a hypothetical.
“For example, if you had someone in California and they targeted a million people here in North Carolina and called them on a phone with this fraud scheme, and defrauded them all, would you agree that our attorney general could sue for unfair and deceptive trade practices here in North Carolina?” asked Dietz.
Hacker said a phone call was a physical intrusion into the state. By contrast,  TikTok was “sending a signal into the ether” and inviting people to reach out from their jurisdictions to join the platform.
Associate Justice Allison Riggs questioned how the defendants could be viewed as indifferent to their subscribers’ residency when they invited the state’s PTA president to an event that promoted TikTok as a safe platform for minors, and sent PR materials about its safety to North Carolina parents via the PTA.
Hacker told the court that it was part of a national program.
State Special Deputy Attorney General Josh Abram argued that ByteDance was trying to muddy the waters and misrepresent the case.
“ByteDance has millions of contracts with North Carolina that let it harvest users’ data, cultivate addictive relationships with our children, and then serve them geo-targeted ads,” Abram said.
Meta to pay North Carolina up to $645 million in landmark settlement

He argued TikTok relied on massive marketing campaigns using both local and national channels, and reminded the court that a business court had agreed with the state on this issue.
“This case is about ByteDance’s conduct that impacts North Carolina. North Carolinians download TikTok, they use it here, and they are harmed here,” Abram told the justices.
It’s unclear when the N.C. Supreme Court will decide whether the case against TikTok and ByteDance should be heard in state court, or when that trial could potentially take place.
Wednesday’s hearing comes just days after Meta, the owner of Instagram and Facebook, agreed to pay North Carolina up to $645 million to settle a lawsuit that Meta designed its apps to hook children and collect data while the company downplayed the risks to parents.

title: Trump administration aims to exclude many noncitizens from the census
text: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration wants to overhaul the U.S. census to exclude noncitizens who don’t have a green card from the country’s next population count in 2030, according to a Wednesday notice in the Federal Register. The document, which will officially be published Thursday, could mean major changes for how millions in federal funding is allocated to states, as well as affect the population numbers for determining the number of U.S. House members in each state. The House is made up of 435 lawmakers apportioned among congressional districts in the 50 states.The move is likely to face legal challenges, as the changes run counter to the U.S. Constitution’s 14th Amendment that directs representatives in Congress to be appointed based on the “whole number of persons in each State,” excluding Native Americans “not taxed.” The amendment language does not specify immigration status. The states handled immigration enforcement until the federal government took over in 1882 with the passage of the Chinese Exclusion Act. The proposed changes would exclude any noncitizens who do not have lawful permanent residence, or a green card, which could result in millions being excluded from the population count. That would include immigrants in the country without legal authorization, those with some form of temporary legal status, refugees and asylum seekers. The unauthorized immigrant population — that includes noncitizens who have some form of limited legal status — has grown to more than 15.8 million since mid-2024.The Trump administration argues that noncitizens who are not green card holders should be kept out of the census count because “they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a ‘usual residence’ in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States,” according to the document. The proposal also calls for removing several questions pertaining to sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, and suggests adding a question relating to citizenship, which President Donald Trump has pushed to include since his first term. But the Supreme Court in 2019 kept the question off the 2020 census. The Trump administration wants those demographic questions removed from the census because the survey “should be colorblind and should not be distorted in any way by questions about immaterial personal characteristics, such as race,” the proposal says.The census has collected information about race and ethnicity since 1790, the first survey count in the U.S.Public comment will last for 30 days after the document is officially published Thursday.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Police Chief calls Tasia Fortune’s death a homicide but says investigators are still awaiting autopsy report
description: A makeshift memorial for Tasia Fortune is seen in the backyard of a vacant home in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. According to authorities, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a vacant home Monday, Aug. 3, 2026.
text:
The Jackson Police Department is investigating the death of a 29-year-old woman found hanging from a tree in west Jackson last month as a homicide, Chief RaShall Brackney told the City Council during its Tuesday meeting.
Brackney said an autopsy on the woman, Tasia Fortune, was completed four weeks ago.
“To date, we have not received the outcomes of that autopsy,” Brackney told Jackson City Council members. 
“However, the Jackson Police Department has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide until we hear otherwise from the medical examiner’s office,” she said.
Brackney’s statements were in response to Councilman Kenneth Stokes and a letter from Fortune’s mother, who lamented the lack of information about her daughter’s death and what she said was the lack of communication from investigators.
“I’m not sure what you can do, but if you need me to present I will travel to Jackson so my voice is heard. I will attend anything I need to attend,”  Christy Spivey, who lives in Kentucky, wrote in her letter, which was read out loud during the meeting.
Brackney said that investigators have been in constant contact with Spivey and her estranged husband. 
In early August, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree behind a vacant house at the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in a mostly Black neighborhood in west Jackson. The manner in which she was found – a Black woman hanging in a place with a history of racial terror lynchings – drew national attention.
Authorities have identified a person of interest, who was arrested on an unrelated gun charge.
Stokes, who shared the letter, said, “Hanging is an ugly, ugly part of our past that we never ever want to come back again.”
Spivey previously told Mississippi Today that she believes her daughter was killed but was not the victim of a hate crime. She insisted Fortune was not suicidal.
Stokes previously wrote to the U.S. Attorney Baxter Kruger, and U.S. Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, both Mississippi Republicans, requesting federal assistance in the case. He also called for answers at a press conference outside City Hall on Sunday.

title: Sweet talk won’t stop Burlington’s drug dealers
description:
A recovering addict says compassion without consequences just prolongs the nightmare on Burlington's streets.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Sweet talk won’t stop Burlington’s drug dealers.
text:
Dear Editor,
My wife and I purchased a home in Burlington to be near family who live here. I thank Charlie Smith for his insightful, balanced observations in a recent commentary published by VTDigger. As a sober alcoholic and former drug abuser, I can attest to the fact that some Burlington public officials are only facilitating the living nightmare that too many areas of the city have become. 
As a practicing lawyer, I know firsthand that drug dealing is organized crime run by career criminals who cannot be sweet-talked or social-worked. Re-funding the police and supporting them with vigorous prosecution are essential to combat such organized crime. 
Drug addicts frequently steal and may commit violent acts to feed the compulsion that afflicts them. Clean needles do not help them get clean and sober. I got clean and sober only when — to paraphrase the first of Alcoholics Anonymous’s 12 steps — I hit bottom and was forced to admit I was powerless over drugs and alcohol and that my life had become unmanageable. 

READ MORE

Although I was lucky enough to reach that point while I still had a home and family, I have personally known many fellow addicts for whom that required incarceration.
Michael PillBurlington, Vt.

Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate, were invited to participate, but the debate has now been canceled since both candidates did not accept the invitation. (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Broadcasters Association Foundation has canceled its gubernatorial candidate debate planned for this month. 
The organization first announced that it planned to host an October debate between the Republican and Democratic nominees in April. It has hosted debates in the Wisconsin gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races since 1990.
Both Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate, and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate, were invited to participate, but the debate has now been canceled since both candidates did not accept the invitation. Tiffany has said he was only agreeing to one debate because it is “sufficient” for the race.
“Based on legal precedent, for the foundation to air a debate, multiple candidates must participate. Two invitations were sent and both had to be accepted in order to have a debate,” WBA said in a statement. “That did not happen.”
Tiffany told conservative radio host Dan O’Donnell on Tuesday that he would likely only participate in one debate. 
“I had no time. There was lots of negotiations going on behind the scenes,” Tiffany said. “One debate is sufficient to be able to cover the issues that need to be covered.” 
According to WBAY, Crowley was planning to participate in the debate and said in a statement that he looked forward to “continuing the Wisconsin Broadcasters Association’s more than 30-year tradition of putting candidates directly before voters statewide.”
Both candidates have agreed to an Oct. 21 debate hosted by WISN-12. It will be moderated by WISN-12 reporters Matt Smith and Gerron Jordan and will cover topics including cost of living, taxes, immigration enforcement, data centers and election security.
Tiffany said that he watched how the reporters conducted the Democratic primary debate as well as others over his career in politics. 
“I think they are very fair and they set up for what appears to be a good [debate],” Tiffany said. “It’s only going to take one debate to get the information out there for the people of Wisconsin… I just always look for fairness in reporters.”
“We look forward to debating Congressman Tiffany on October 21 and speaking directly with Wisconsinites about why David Crowley is the right choice to deliver for working families and serve as a governor for all Wisconsinites,” the Crowley campaign said.

title: Scott Green to step down as University of Idaho president
description: This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 9, 2026. University of Idaho President C. Scott Green will retire on June 30. Green made the announcement during the president’s “state of the university” address Wednesday — an annual event that took a sudden and emotional turn. Addressing the campus community at his alma mater, […]
text:
University of Idaho President Scott Green presides over the 2022 commencement ceremony at the school's Moscow campus. (Photo courtesy of the University of Idaho)This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 9, 2026.
University of Idaho President C. Scott Green will retire on June 30.
Green made the announcement during the president’s “state of the university” address Wednesday — an annual event that took a sudden and emotional turn.
Addressing the campus community at his alma mater, Green recounted success stories from his seven-year tenure, including advances in enrollment, research and athletics. He also reflected on the challenges of leading the U of I through a global pandemic and in the aftermath of the November 2022 off-campus murders of four students.
“We truly were at our best when the Vandal family and the Moscow community needed us,” said Green, fighting back tears.
“We love you, Scott,” one member of the audience said aloud, before the room rose in a standing ovation.
Green’s departure marks a transition at the state’s land-grant university, and sets the stage for another high-profile job search. The State Board of Education — which doubles as the U of I’s Board of Regents — recently filled the president’s vacancy at Boise State University, after a tumultuous and largely closed-door 16-month search.
 University president: ‘We accomplished more than most thought possible’

A former U of I student body president, Green returned to Moscow in July of 2019, leaving New York City and a top management position with Hogan Lovells, an international law firm.
Green said he came back, in part, to bring some stability to the president’s office — a revolving door at the helm of a university established before Idaho’s statehood itself. During Wednesday’s speech, Green noted that his tenure marks the longest of any U of I president since Richard Gibb.
Gibb was president while Green was a U of I undergrad.
Green graduated in 1984.
Green also discussed several milestones from his presidency.
By spring 2020, the U of I had covered $40 million in operating losses, a shortfall inherited by Green. Enrollment rebounded from a pandemic-era lull (last fall, the U of I welcomed its second-largest freshman class in history.) In 2025, the U of I received top-tier R1 research status from the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education, the first Idaho university to reach this threshold. Later that year, the U of I wrapped up a $500 million capital campaign.
“We accomplished more than most thought possible,” Green said.
On Wednesday, Green also relitigated one of his high-profile initiatives, a failed bid to purchase the University of Phoenix, a massive for-profit online university with a national footprint and tarnished reputation.
The State Board gave the Phoenix deal the green light in 2023, after a series of closed-door discussions. The 2024 Legislature balked at the bid — with some lawmakers grumbling that they had been cut out of the process. The U of I and Phoenix broke off negotiations in June 2025.
Green said the purchase — with an overall price tag of $685 million — would have landed Idaho an asset that has since gone on the public market for $1.1 billion.
“History has already shown (this) was one of the greatest financial opportunities the state of Idaho will ever see,” Green said Wednesday.

name: WyoFile
title: ACLU to appeal immigration case against Laramie County sheriff to Wyoming Supreme Court
description:
A Laramie County judge dismissed the case last month over lack of standing. But the question of whether the sheriff exceeded his authority when he entered the ICE contracts is unresolved, the judge says. 
The post ACLU to appeal immigration case against Laramie County sheriff to Wyoming Supreme Court appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The American Civil Liberties Union will appeal its immigration case against Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak to the Wyoming Supreme Court after a judge dismissed the matter last month.  
The timing of the appeal is still up in the air, a Wyoming ACLU spokesperson told WyoFile. 
Kozak said the group should instead drop the matter.
“The public has already put this frivolous [lawsuit] in the past; the ACLU should do the same,” Kozak said in a text message. “We will continue our mission to impact drug, sex, and labor trafficking.” 
The lawsuit alleges Kozak broke the law when he partnered with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement without Laramie County commissioners’ approval. Laramie County District Judge Robin Cooley struck down the lawsuit in August, stating in her dismissal order that the plaintiffs lacked standing because they didn’t demonstrate direct harm from the actions they were challenging in court. 
“We’re disappointed that the court found that our plaintiffs lacked standing and dismissed our lawsuit challenging Laramie County’s contracts with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” Wyoming ACLU Executive Director Libby Skarin said in a statement to WyoFile. “We respectfully disagree with the court’s decision, and we intend to seek an appeal at the Wyoming Supreme Court.” 
While Cooley dismissed the lawsuit, she noted that the question of whether Kozak exceeded his legal authority when he entered the agreements without commissioners’ approval is still unresolved. 
“The commissioners are not party to this action and have not asserted any resulting injury,” Cooley’s decision states. “Although plaintiffs allege concrete harms arising from immigration enforcement, they have not alleged a particularized injury arising from the alleged infringement of the commissioners’ authority. Accordingly, the underlying question of defendant Kozak’s authority and statutory authority remain unresolved.”
Wyoming ACLU attorney Andrew Malone and Cheyenne attorney Elizabeth Lance filed the lawsuit in May on behalf of a local barbershop, a nonprofit advocacy group and a church that said they had suffered as a result of Kozak’s 287(g) contracts, which are named after section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and allow local and state law enforcement to perform some immigration enforcement under ICE’s oversight. 
The Laramie County Sheriff’s Office is one of two law enforcement agencies in Wyoming — the other being the Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Office — that has signed all three voluntary immigration enforcement agreements that ICE offers. The most controversial of the three types, the Task Force Model, was phased out during the Obama administration following documented civil rights violations but resurrected in 2025 under Trump. 
The ACLU has pushed back against 287(g) agreements across the country, bringing legal challenges against these immigration enforcement partnerships in other states like Minnesota and Pennsylvania. 
Malone, the Wyoming ACLU attorney, previously said the organization may file lawsuits against other Wyoming law enforcement agencies with 287(g) contracts, depending on the outcomes of this case. Skarin reiterated that the group’s effort to push against these partnerships isn’t over. 
“The ACLU of Wyoming will continue to push back against 287(g) agreements and efforts to unlawfully use local resources, such as jails and law enforcement officials, to facilitate mass detention and deportation in Wyoming,” she stated. 
The Laramie County commissioners didn’t immediately respond to WyoFile’s inquiry about the case.

A page on the South Dakota Governor's Office of Economic Development website in September 2026. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Board of Economic Development approved a total of $1.4 million in state assistance for four projects through the SD Works, Economic Development Partnership, and Local Infrastructure Improvement programs, according to a news release Wednesday from the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.
The board approved a $597,275 SD Works loan for IR LLC to support construction of a new location for Rev It Up Espresso in Sturgis. The new facility will allow the locally owned coffee business to expand from its kiosk operations into a permanent storefront with a sit-down cafe, drive-through service, on-site coffee roasting, and an expanded food and merchandise offering. Rev It Up Espresso began in an 8-by-12-foot trailer and has since grown to three kiosks throughout Sturgis.
