The board also approved a $320,000 SD Works loan for JBHM LLC to support construction of a new facility for Elwood Family Dental Care in Yankton. The expansion will allow the practice to add a second dentist and operate five days per week. The project is expected to grow the practice from eight to 16 full-time equivalent positions.
A $10,000 Economic Development Partnership Program grant was awarded to Sioux Metro Growth Alliance to support its Leadership Sioux Metro Regional Economic Development Training Initiative. The program will provide training in areas including business retention and attraction, site readiness, housing and development, workforce, development finance, and regional collaboration.
The board approved a $500,000 Local Infrastructure Improvement Program grant for Clear Lake Area Development to support construction of a water tank and pump station. The infrastructure will strengthen the water system serving the Clear Lake community and provide the water supply and fire protection necessary to support an expansion by the company Tech Ord, which produces detonating and explosive components and materials for the military.
The SD Works, Economic Development Partnership, and Local Infrastructure Improvement programs provide financing and grants that support business growth, economic development capacity, and infrastructure investments. They are available to businesses and organizations that meet program requirements established in state law and by board policy.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. elections chief: ‘Nothing has changed’ following Trump mail-in ballot order
description: Secretary Al Schmidt assured voters that President Donald Trump's mail-in ballot order doesn't change anything this midterm election.
text:
Poll workers wait for voters at the Saltsburg Borough Building in Saltsburg, Indiana County on Election Day May 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Amid a national legal battle over the use of mail-in voting ahead of this year’s midterm elections, Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt said Wednesday that Pennsylvanians should be confident in the state’s election process and security.
“The Department of State remains committed to ensuring another free, fair, safe and secure election this November, and fighting any unlawful federal overreach into our elections,” Schmidt continued. “Despite the federal government’s attempts, and while we recognize that litigation is ongoing, nothing has changed about Pennsylvania’s mail ballot voting laws.”
Each of the state’s 67 counties oversees elections in their jurisdiction, he added, including preparing, proofing, printing and mailing ballots. Some ballots for overseas and military voters have already been mailed. 
 
Schmidt also asked eligible Pennsylvanians to consider being a poll worker, noting that the state needs roughly 45,000 people to staff more than 9,000 polling places across the state. Many counties are still working to secure and train all the staff they’ll need before Election Day.


Nearly two million Pennsylvanians used mail-in ballots in 2024, compared to 5 million others who voted in person. President Donald Trump, who votes by mail, continued his attack on the popular method ahead of a critical midterm election and directed the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting — a move that some argue usurps Constitutional, congressional and state authority.
A federal judge paused the ruling while litigation continues, giving the U.S. Supreme Court time to weigh in. However, a whistleblower revealed last week that the federal agency is moving forward with developing the tools to comply with Trump’s order. 
The “new and onerous” requirements, including unique barcodes on ballot envelopes, “add nothing to election integrity,” Schmidt said. “The currently blocked USPS action is not lawful, and the Shapiro administration will challenge any such efforts that seeks to prevent eligible voters from voting, whether in person or by mail.” 
More on the 2026 election
Earlier this summer, Schmidt rebutted a U.S. Department of Homeland Security claim that the state had upwards of 14,000 noncitizens registered to vote, emphasizing that noncitizen voting is “extremely rare.” He said the agency had yet to provide “any written or detailed description of the methodology they used to support its claims.”
Last week, two noncitizens were charged with voting in Pennsylvania’s 2024 election out of the millions of ballots cast. Many of these cases typically happen because of software malfunctions or administrative errors at state agencies, according to Votebeat. 
Some Trump administration officials have “left open the possibility of troops or officers being at the polls,” according to CNN, including ICE. That would be prohibited by both state and federal laws, Schmidt added, with Pennsylvania Election Code limiting officers from being within 100 feet of a polling place unless they are voting, serving a warrant or preventing distributions that interfere with voting. 
Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt shares an election update ahead of the 2026 midterms on Sept. 9, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
“Let me be clear: my office expects everyone working in, voting in or observing polling places to follow the law,” continued Schmidt. “Voters should rest assured that their state and local election officials will not tolerate voter intimidation or election interference of any kind.”
Schmidt, a Republican and former Philadelphia city commissioner, was attacked by Trump online following his 2020 loss. Schmidt later testified before Congress about the Trump campaign’s false claims about voter fraud in that election. 
“As an election official with 15 years of experience in county and state election administration, I can say with the utmost confidence that Pennsylvania’s elections are safe and secure, but the potential spread of misinformation and disinformation about elections is one of my biggest concerns,” said Schmidt. “There are unfortunately bad faith actors who spread disinformation in the hope of suppressing voter turnout and undermining public confidence in our electoral system.” 
He instead urged voters to trust official sources, such as their county offices and the Pennsylvania Department of State. 
The state agency is scheduled to provide weekly updates up until the Nov. 3 election and Schmidt said there would be a dashboard published after counties begin mailing ballots. 
Voters can request a mail-in ballot at their local county office until Oct. 27. Ballots must be returned by 8 p.m. on Election Day.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmaker accuses election opponent’s employee of harassing her at events
description: New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva (D-Las Cruces) on Tuesday accused her Republican opponent and the GOP’s leader in the state House of Representatives of failing to intervene to stop a campaign employee from harassing her and her husband at recent public events.
text:
New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva (D-Chaparral) on Sept. 8, 2026, issued a public statement accusing her Republican opponent’s employee of harassing her. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva (D-Las Cruces) on Tuesday accused her Republican opponent and the GOP’s leader in the state House of Representatives of failing to intervene to stop a campaign employee from harassing her and her husband at recent public events. 
Silva, who is running for re-election to a second term representing House District 53 in southern New Mexico against Republican Ben Luna, Jr., recounted in a social media post Tuesday “aggressive” encounters with Adalberto Rodriguez, whom Luna employed to help with his campaign at least until recently. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to Silva, at several public events between April and July, Rodriguez approached her and her husband, journalist Heath Haussamen, while brandishing a tripod and a phone or camera and filming. Rodriguez can be seen on several videos Silva provided calling the lawmaker “baby” or “princess” and repeatedly insulting Haussamen as he tries to intervene.
In one instance July 13 at a Chaparral community meeting at the Becky McKnight Community center, Rodriguez repeatedly thrust the tripod in Haussamen’s direction while making kissing noises at him, according to video Haussamen captured and that Silva published Tuesday. 
Silva and Haussamen filed a police report in late July regarding Rodriguez’s behavior, which she described as “disruptive, offensive and dangerous in its escalation.” Silva also said she reached out to House Speaker Rep. Javier Martinez (D-Albuquerque), whom she said then spoke with House Minority Floor Leader Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) regarding the matter, urging her to intervene.
Martinez told Source NM on Tuesday that Silva called him roughly two months ago regarding Rodriguez’s behavior, which he found troubling following his own experience as a target.
Martinez was one of several Democratic officials whose houses were shot at by failed Republican candidate Solomon Peña several years ago. Peña was subsequently sentenced to 80 years in prison.
Martinez said he reached out to Armstrong several times to see if she could help de-escalate the situation, but she only responded once, saying that Rodriguez did not work for Luna.
“It was not followed up on, unfortunately, and of course, myself being a victim of political violence, this is not something I take lightly for anyone, not just Democrats,” Martinez said.
New Mexico lawmakers last year began a special legislative session by denouncing what they described as a rise in political violence in the state and elsewhere. Last year alone included a case of arson at the state Republican party headquarters and bomb threats at the homes of Santa Fe Democrats Senate Majority Leader Peter Wirth and House Majority Floor Leader Reena Szczepanski.
In the social media post Tuesday, Silva said Armstrong’s inaction prompted her to both hire private security for future events and also issue a public statement.
“I wish my opponent and Leader Armstrong would commit to keeping campaign workers from acting inappropriately. It’s clear I can’t trust them to do that,” she said. “So, with candidate forums and other public events coming up, I’m sharing this publicly…in the hopes that bringing this situation into the light will help ensure everyone’s safety.”
Armstrong did not respond to Source NM’s call seeking comment Tuesday. 
Luna told Source NM on Tuesday that he only employed Rodriguez briefly as a canvasser for the campaign but fired him in July. He said he decided to end Rodriguez’s employment both because of the conduct he saw on videos but also because Rodriguez did not meet a quota for outreach to potential voters. 
“He was hired for canvassing, and wasn’t meeting his quota, and he became uncontrollable in a sense of behavior,” Luna said. 
Luna said he’s reached out to several other Republican candidates in New Mexico who have hired Rodriguez in some capacity to tell them about Rodriguez’s misbehavior. He declined to say which other candidates are currently employing Rodriguez or in what capacity. 
Rodriguez posted at least two of the videos to social media accounts he controls called “The Border Gazette,” which has 75,000 Instagram followers. 
Rodriguez, reached by phone, told Source NM on Tuesday that he had “deleted the video,” though he did not specify which video, and declined to comment further on the allegations. 
Silva told Source NM on Tuesday that the sheriff’s office decided not to press charges. The sheriff’s office did not respond to Source NM’s inquiry about the status of the case as of publication time Wednesday.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Affordable Care Act insurance costs to rise steeply again in WA
description: A quarter million Washingtonians who get their insurance through the state’s exchange under the Affordable Care Act face another year of double-digit rate increases.  Health insurance rates will rise an average of 22.2% starting Jan. 1, Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer announced Wednesday. This comes after thousands dropped coverage due to the expiration[...]
text:
(Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)A quarter million Washingtonians who get their insurance through the state’s exchange under the Affordable Care Act face another year of double-digit rate increases. 
Health insurance rates will rise an average of 22.2% starting Jan. 1, Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer announced Wednesday. This comes after thousands dropped coverage due to the expiration of federal tax credits, the debate over which led to a lengthy government shutdown last fall. 
This insurance option is meant for people not covered through their work or government programs like Medicaid or Medicare, like those who are self-employed or retired early. Small businesses with fewer than 50 employees also use the Washington Health Benefit Exchange, for their workers. About 250,000 people are enrolled this year in the exchange.
Thirteen insurers had requested an average 22.4% rate hike for 2027, which Kuderer is required to approve if the increase is actuarially justified. Premiums rose 21% this year, partly due to the end of the tax credits, which began during the COVID pandemic. 
The 2027 hike is mainly due to rising costs of healthcare and enrollees’ more robust needs, Kuderer said.
“This is, unfortunately, a reflection of the increasing cost of care,” Kuderer said in a statement. “Families shouldn’t experience sticker shock every year when shopping for health insurance, but these pressures are likely to continue without changes that slow health care spending, improve affordability and keep more people covered.”
Insurance companies cited a few reasons for the steep increase. For one, the end of the tax credits makes coverage less affordable, meaning healthier people who need less care dropped their insurance. This raises the costs for those who stay on their health plans.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Other issues leading to the rate hike include health care organizations charging more for services and prescription drugs and members using more of these services, according to Kuderer’s office. 
Jim Freeburg, executive director of the Patient Coalition of Washington, said the increases will have “real consequences for the Washington families and small businesses that purchase their coverage through the Exchange.”
“It’s going to cost my wife and I over $36,000 to cover ourselves and our two girls and that’s simply unfair for the coverage we’d get,” Freeburg said in an email.
The rates are used to determine monthly premiums.
On the low end, the 16,000 members on Regence BlueShield plans will see an average 6.7% increase. For the more than 40,000 people on Kaiser Foundation Health Plan of Washington it will be around 14.1%. Community Health Plan of Washington, with nearly 37,000 enrollees, was approved for a 30.5% hike while the 98,000 covered by the Coordinated Care Corporation face a more than 25% jump.
The Washington Health Benefit Exchange Board is set to certify the rates at its Thursday meeting. Open enrollment opens Nov. 1, and lasts until Jan. 15.
One other insurer not on the exchange, Asuris Northwest Health, is awaiting an approved rate change for its roughly 800 enrollees in Washington. It requested a 14.9% increase.
Enrollment in the exchange this year is down roughly 36,500 from 2025, a nearly 13% reduction, the biggest falloff since the marketplace launched in 2013. State officials had feared an even larger dropoff when the tax credits went away.
Rural counties saw some of the steepest declines, but the state’s own premium assistance, known as Cascade Care Savings, helped avert some of the more dire notions of the drops in coverage.
Those most likely to drop their coverage were young and lower-income. Many of those no longer covered could’ve found insurance elsewhere, like joining a family member’s plan or getting employer-sponsored coverage.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: GOP legislators renew call for major CT tax relief
description: GOP lawmakers renewed its call for major tax relief, but Democrats say Republicans would weaken efforts to shrink CT's big pension debt.
text:
Minority Republicans in the General Assembly renewed their call Wednesday to slash state income taxes and offer other relief to middle-class households struggling with Connecticut’s high cost of living.
But Republicans didn’t pitch major spending cuts to pay for the relief. Instead it likely would be covered by the huge budget surpluses state government has forced since 2017 to shrink its hefty pension debt, a task that’s far from over.
The linchpin of the plan involves income tax rate cuts that would save individuals earning less than $100,000 and couples below $200,000 a collective $975 million annually starting in 2028.
The GOP also pitched: a sales tax exemption for prepared meals sold in supermarkets; a one-year, retail gasoline tax holiday; and elimination of the public benefits charge on consumer electric bills.
“Connecticut’s trajectory is going in the wrong direction,” House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, said during a midmorning press conference at the Legislative Office Building in Hartford. “We continue to see other states thrive while Connecticut’s cost of living continues to rise. And the crisis doesn’t seem to have an end in sight.”
The Senate’s Republican leader, Stephen Harding of Brookfield, said this stems from decades of almost uninterrupted Democratic control of the General Assembly.
“Democrats have controlled this building and have done nothing but raise costs, raise taxes, and make the state more unaffordable by the day,” he said.
But the majority quickly fired back that the Republican claim is both false and misleading.
Gov. Ned Lamont and his fellow Democrats in the legislature enacted one of the largest tax cuts in state history in 2022 and 2023, including the first reduction in state income tax rates since the mid-1990s.
Income tax changes alone saved most middle-income filers about $300 to $400 per year. Democrats also ordered a 13-month gasoline tax holiday during this period.
“The Connecticut GOP would love to distract you from the fact that Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have been doing their best to drive the American economy into a ditch for the last two years,” Ian Clarke, spokesman for the state Democratic Party, said Wednesday, referring to federal cuts expected to strip $1.1 billion from healthcare and food assistance programs by 2034. “This is typical political theater.”
But Republicans say the tax relief Lamont and Democratic legislators have authored was far too modest, given the context.
Sen. Ryan Fazio, the Greenwich Republican who is challenging Lamont for governor this year, said other taxes and fees have crept up to offset those tax breaks and make Connecticut more unaffordable, including:

A 0.5% payroll deduction was ordered to finance a Paid Family and Medical Leave program in 2019.


A 1% sales tax surcharge was placed on restaurant food and other prepared meals.


A highway use tax on large, non-farm, commercial vehicles.

Fazio also noted Connecticut, which already has some of the highest electricity rates in the nation, has seen them rise higher in recent years.
The Republican plan would waive the sales tax surcharge and base 6.35% rate on prepared meals available in grocery stores.
The public benefits charge, which supports various state-mandated environmental, social and grid-management initiatives, would be repealed, saving ratepayers an estimated $30 per month. The Republicans did not outline how they would preserve these programs if the charge is removed.
The 25-cents-per-gallon retail tax on regular gasoline would be waived for 12 months starting next July.
Republicans also pledged to offer incentives to cities and towns to offer homestead exemptions, protections that can prevent credit card companies and other creditors from forcing debtors to sell their homes to cover their obligations. The GOP also would help businesses form association health plans to reduce insurance premium costs for their employees.
“These are real efforts to lead and to solve the problems facing our families every day, to make this state affordable and to make this economy work for everybody,” Fazio said.
But Lamont campaign spokeswoman Lauren Gray said “while Ryan Fazio was busy taking credit for ideas he didn’t come up with and making pie-in-the-sky promises, Governor Lamont was busy actually working with Treasurer Russell to strengthen Connecticut’s pension funds,” referring to reforms that have greatly improved pension investment earnings in recent years.
Gray added that Lamont also has supported or launched other initiatives to help working families, including the state’s debt-free community college program and more than $700 million reserved for a new endowment to expand affordable childcare.
Democrats also have questioned the Republican tax-cutting plan, arguing it would chip away at the big state surpluses Lamont has used since 2020 to pay down more than $11 billion in state pension debt. Connecticut still owes more than $30 billion in this area, making it one of the most indebted states, per capita, in the nation.
But Candelora countered the Democrats live by a double standard. Democrats have weakened surpluses to provide average annual raises of 4.5% for most state employees since 2022 — that outstrips most private-sector compensation — while blocking GOP efforts to curb Medicaid benefits for undocumented residents.
“It really is a matter of priority,” Candelora said. “Are you serious about fixing the affordability issue or not?”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Denny Hoskins asks federal judge to block Missouri Supreme Court contempt hearing
description: Secretary of State Denny Hoskins asked a federal judge Wednesday to block the Missouri Supreme Court from holding a contempt hearing over his decision to implement a congressional map the state court barred him from using. The Missouri Supreme Court issued an unusual late-night order Tuesday demanding that Hoskins appear in person to explain why […]
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, left, is asking a federal judge to block an order for him to answer contempt charges before the Missouri Supreme Court. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)Secretary of State Denny Hoskins asked a federal judge Wednesday to block the Missouri Supreme Court from holding a contempt hearing over his decision to implement a congressional map the state court barred him from using.
The Missouri Supreme Court issued an unusual late-night order Tuesday demanding that Hoskins appear in person to explain why he isn’t following its injunction on the congressional district map that will govern the Nov. 3 elections. The order gave Hoskins until noon Wednesday to respond in writing and set his hearing for 10 a.m. Thursday.
Hoskins filed his response just a few minutes after the deadline and, at the same time, filed a request to Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark of the U.S. Eastern Missouri District Court for an order blocking the state Supreme Court hearing.
“This court should bar the Missouri Supreme Court’s attempt to punish Secretary Hoskins for complying with this court’s order,” Lou Capozzi of the attorney general’s office wrote on Hoskins’ behalf. 
The state Supreme Court order to Hoskins capped a day of conflicting actions over which congressional map Missouri must use in November. 
When Tuesday began, the Missouri Supreme Court’s order meant  the legislation creating the map would be on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition A. If a majority of Missourians vote “no,” the map would be defeated and would not become law.
Along with sending voters the referendum sought by the political action committee People Not Politicians, the state Supreme Court also issued an injunction directing Hoskins not to use the gerrymandered 2025 map for the November elections.
Instead, the map that would govern congressional elections is the one drawn by lawmakers in 2022 and used the last two cycles. 
Hoskins appealed that ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court, where Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied it without comment. 
Minutes after Kavanaugh acted, Clark issued a temporary restraining order in a separate federal lawsuit filed by U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, state Sen. Rick Brattin and two voters. Clark’s order seemingly contradicted the state Supreme Court by blocking Hoskins from “implementing, using, publishing, distributing, or mandating the use of any congressional district map other than the (2025) map” in November. 
Using that decision as the controlling authority, Hoskins directed local election officials to use the 2025 map because Clark’s order “takes precedence over the Missouri Supreme Court’s order.”
That brought People Not Politicians back to the state Supreme Court, asking that Hoskins be held in contempt for failing to follow the court’s order not to use the 2025 map. Chief Justice Brent Powell responded by demanding that Hoskins appear to explain why his email to local election officials “is not an affirmative violation of this court’s injunction” and why he thinks “this court’s injunction is not still in full force and effect.”
In the request to Clark for an order blocking the Thursday hearing, Hoskins blames Richard von Glahn, director of People Not Politicians, for his position stuck between two courts.
“Von Glahn’s motion is a blatant attempt to frustrate this court’s order,” Capozzi wrote. “Indeed, Von Glahn proclaimed that the Missouri Supreme Court should ‘make clear that regardless of other orders (except from the United States Supreme Court) the Missouri Secretary of State must comply with [the Missouri Supreme Court’s] injunction…Remarkably, the Missouri Supreme Court is taking Von Glahn’s motion very seriously.”
Clark did not rule immediately. He set a 5 p.m. Wednesday deadline for People Not Politicians to file a response to the request to stop the Thursday state court hearing.
And People Not Politicians is seeking to overturn Clark’s decision by seeking review from the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals.
In the response to the Missouri Supreme Court, Capozzi argues that the state’s jurisdiction over Hoskins ended when Clark issued his ruling. 
“This court’s order can no longer compel the secretary,” Capozzi wrote.
Clark’s decision came just before the deadline for fixing the ballots for November and was the operative decision, Capozzi wrote. 
“So long as the district court’s order stands, the secretary must obey it,” he wrote.
The two cases argue unrelated points of law and therefore do not overlap, Capozzi wrote.
“The court must not,” he wrote, “take the radical step of holding the secretary of state in contempt for following a federal court order.”
This story will be updated.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Coalition launches campaign opposing constitutional amendment on taxes
description: A coalition of Iowa organizations launched a campaign Wednesday opposing the Nov. 3 ballot issue that will ask Iowa voters whether to amend the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority vote of lawmakers to raise state personal and corporate income taxes. Fair Taxes for Iowa’s Future, which includes labor unions, progressive nonprofits and others,[...]
text:
A coalition of Iowa organizations is launching an educational campaign opposing a proposed constitutional amendment that would require a two-thirds vote of Iowa lawmakers to raise personal or corporate income taxes. (Photo by Getty Images)A coalition of Iowa organizations launched a campaign Wednesday opposing the Nov. 3 ballot issue that will ask Iowa voters whether to amend the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority vote of lawmakers to raise state personal and corporate income taxes.
Fair Taxes for Iowa’s Future, which includes labor unions, progressive nonprofits and others, is planning an informational campaign opposing Amendment 1.

Coalition members
Members of the Fair Taxes for Iowa’s Future coalition include AAUW of Iowa; AFSCME Council 61; Common Good Iowa; Iowa Federation of Labor AFL-CIO; Iowa Hunger Coalition; Iowa State Education Association; League of Women Voters of Iowa; National Association of Social Workers, Iowa Chapter; and Progress Iowa.

Anne Discher, executive director of Common Good Iowa, said people’s first impression of a law making it harder raise taxes tends to be favorable. But, she said, “When you actually talk to people about the tradeoffs that are required, the equation gets a lot more complicated. The more we talk to people about this amendment, the less people like it.”
Members of the coalition said Wednesday that requiring a supermajority of lawmakers to raise income taxes would lead to cuts in services Iowans depend on and other revenue increases that disproportionately affect lower-income families.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Amendment One doesn’t cut anyone’s taxes. It just makes it permanently harder to fix what’s broken, and our schools are what gets cut first,” Joshua Brown, representing Iowa State Education Association, said.
Coalition representatives said during a news conference that Iowa’s budget is already strained by years of tax cuts that have largely benefited the wealthiest Iowans and led to a second year of billion-dollar budget deficits offset by spending from reserve funds.
Kylie Spies, senior policy advocate for Common Good Iowa, cited the elimination of state taxes on inheritance and retirement income and multiple cuts in personal and corporate income tax rates leading to the current 3.8% flat-rate income tax. “An estimated two-thirds of the benefits of that income tax change went to the top 20% of income earners,” Spies said.
Coalition members said states that have enacted supermajority requirements for tax increases tend to look to alternative revenue sources – especially sales taxes. “Sales tax is the most regressive form of taxation. The bottom 20% of income earners pay six times more of their income in sales tax than the top 1% It’s also one of the primary sources of state general fund revenue,” Spies said.
Iowans for Tax Relief launched a campaign in July to promote the amendment, saying a majority of Iowans support making it harder to raise taxes. The group argued the amendment would not prevent tax increases but require a stronger consensus.
Discher said Fair Taxes for Iowa’s Future will likely not raise as much money for its campaign as backers of the amendment will. She said the current plan includes yard signs and potentially digital advertising.
But she said the group was hopeful based on the results of a vote in Missouri last month that soundly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that would have phased out the income tax and limited other taxes.
A poll released in August found that likely Iowa voters are sharply divided over the proposed amendment – but nearly a third remain undecided. The Suffolk University Political Research Center poll, released Aug. 26, found roughly 33% of likely Iowa voters planned to vote “yes” on Amendment 1, while 36% planned to vote against the amendment. An additional 30% said they were still undecided, while 1% refused to answer the question.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: As North Carolina summers get hotter, the Festival for the Eno is changing
description: For nearly five decades, the Festival for the Eno has brought thousands of people to the banks of the Eno River around the Fourth of July. But the organization behind the festival says increasingly extreme heat and unpredictable weather have forced it to rethink when and how the fundraising event is held.  The Eno River […]
text:
A Sunny Paperhand Puppet Parade at the Festival for the Eno. (Photo: Fred Myers/ Eno River Association)For nearly five decades, the Festival for the Eno has brought thousands of people to the banks of the Eno River around the Fourth of July. But the organization behind the festival says increasingly extreme heat and unpredictable weather have forced it to rethink when and how the fundraising event is held. 
The Eno River Association — an organization working to conserve the Eno River Basin — did not hold its traditional festival this past July. Instead, it will celebrate its 60th anniversary on Saturday with a fall benefit concert and free community event in downtown Durham. 
When the festival returns to the riverbanks, likely in 2027, it will be held in the spring or the fall. 
The decision followed an internal review of the festival that began after Executive Director Ryan Fehrman joined the organization last year. He said the association was already confronting rising costs, with its 2025 festival budget of nearly $400,000. 
But the group also had growing concerns about the risks of holding a large outdoor event during the hottest part of the year. 
“We’re an environmental organization. We talk about climate change,” Fehrman said. “I think it’s important to note that this is not some phenomenon like the Northern Lights that we know exists, but we never see.” 
He said the festival relies on roughly 650 volunteers to run the event, about two-thirds of whom are seniors, and he was concerned that they could suffer injuries from the heat. 
Climate change making allergy season longer in North Carolina, new study says

Those concerns come as North Carolina’s climate continues to warm. Average temperatures have increased in all four seasons across the state, according to a report from the North Carolina Institute for Climate Studies. 
The North Carolina State Climate Office says June, July and August are the months when high heat is most common across the state, while May and September see fewer days of extreme heat. 
But the risks aren’t just limited to extreme heat. Fehrman pointed to heavier rain events, hurricanes, wildfire smoke and drought as examples of climate-related conditions that have already affected the state. 
Tropical Storm Chantal, which struck the Triangle the day after last year’s festival, reinforced those concerns. The storm caused flooding and thousands of power outages around the Eno River and affected West Point on the Eno, the festival’s longtime home. 
The bridge over Bolin Creek in Chapel Hill. At the height of the storm, water topped the bridge, one resident said, and pushed a dumpster in the middle of the street. (Photo: Lisa Sorg/Inside Climate News)
The festival’s traditional location is also undergoing accessibility project improvements that could have conflicted with the July event, giving the association another reason to reconsider its schedule. 
For this year, the result is a smaller event that includes a seated benefit concert, with a separate free community gathering planned outside the Carolina Theater. 
The association is still working on plans for the festival’s return. Fehrman said the group is awaiting a signed agreement before announcing details, but said attendees can expect cooler weather. 
He said the decision wasn’t easy, but it was necessary, and more organizers need to find sustainable ways to plan around climate change. 
“For anyone who’s doing events outdoors in the summer in North Carolina, if you’re not thinking about ways to mitigate risk, ways to ensure the health and wellness of staff, volunteers and attendees, I think you’re doing yourself a disservice,” he said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: A Louisiana sex offender’s surgical castration sentence might never happen
description: A convicted sex offender from Assumption Parish is believed to be the first person in the U.S. sentenced to undergo surgical castration without their consent, but the lawmaker who pushed for the severe punishment to be made available said it’s unlikely to ever take place
text:
Stock photo by Motortion/Getty ImagesA convicted sex offender from Assumption Parish is believed to be the first person in the U.S. sentenced to undergo surgical castration without their consent, but the lawmaker who pushed for the severe punishment to be made available said it’s unlikely to ever take place. 
The state corrections department has also confirmed its not currently staffed to handle the procedure. 
Carrol Ray Clark (Assumption Parish Sheriff’s Office photo)
Carrol Ray Clark, 51, of Bayou L’Ourse pleaded guilty last week to second-degree rape, two counts of indecent behavior with a juvenile and two counts of possessing child pornography. He agreed to a 35-year prison sentence and to undergo surgical castration, according to District Attorney Ricky Babin’s office.
Clark’s charges stemmed from a 2024 investigation based on a tip that he had received and distributed online child pornography. Police interviewed people living in the same home as Clark and determined he had sexual contact with a young girl at the residence on multiple occasions.
A Sept. 1 post on the X account of Attorney General Liz Murrill, whose office started the investigation, celebrated Clark’s conviction and sentence.
“Louisiana justice served on another child rapist,” the post reads, followed by emojis of a fleur de lis and a pair of scissors.

Breaking: Louisiana justice served on another child rapist
Great job by DA Ricky Babin on the prosecution, my agents and the ICAC Task Force on the arrest, and Judge Jason Verdigets for imposing the sentence. pic.twitter.com/Ld1faoUlAH
— Attorney General Liz Murrill (@AGLizMurrill) September 1, 2026

Louisiana is the only state where surgical castration is a sentencing option for convicted sex offenders, whose testicles or ovaries are removed in the procedure. The law was approved in 2024 and only applies only to cases with victims younger than 13. 
A spokesperson for the Louisiana Department of Corrections, which is tasked with administering surgical castration under the law, confirmed it has never carried out the punishment.
Tyler Cavalier, Babin’s chief of staff and chief investigator, said in an interview that Clark’s sentence is the first time the new law is being used, and he anticipated the procedure would not occur immediately. It’s too early to declare that it will never take place, he added.  
“I think it’s going to take some time for the kinks to be worked out,” Cavalier said.
Chemical castration, a reversible procedure administered through intravenous drugs, has been a punishment option for sex offenders in Louisiana since 2008. Cavalier said judges in his jurisdiction have included chemical castration in two recent sex offender convictions, though he added that neither sentence has been carried out. 
In a chemical castration sentence, defendants can opt instead for surgical castration, but the timeline for carrying it out is vague. Both the 2008 and 2024 laws call for the punishment to be administered “not later than one week prior to the defendant’s release from prison.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Brad Cascio, an assistant district attorney in the 23rd Judicial District, wants such sentences carried out sooner rather than later. In April 2024, he secured a guilty plea from Glenn Sullivan Sr. for multiple counts of second-degree rape involving a 14-year-old girl in Livingston Parish. Sullivan, now age 56, was sentenced to 50 years in prison and chose the surgical option when a judge ordered his chemical castration. 
Cascio, who’s a candidate for the DA’s join in the Nov. 3 election, said in an interview the Sullivan case was the first time a sex offender has consented to surgical castration in Louisiana. Since then, he has obtained more convictions for sex offenders who have been sentenced to chemical castration, though he could only say it’s been “less than a dozen” when asked for a number.
Cascio said he wasn’t aware the 2008 chemical castration law existed until the Sullivan case two years ago.  
“To be honest with you. I kind of stumbled across it, and I went to my boss and I said, ‘Do you mind if I start doing this?’ and he didn’t tell me no,” Cascio said.
Nine other states allow chemical castration, according to research from the National Council of State Legislatures. Some of these states offer surgery as an option to the drugs, but there are no sources that track whether anyone has made that choice or if it’s been executed.
The Louisiana Department of Corrections said it has no records of chemical castration being administered in the state.
State Rep. Delisha Boyd, D-New Orleans, shaped the 2024 surgical castration law and said in a text message Thursday that Clark’s procedure “will likely never happen” because of provisions in the statute. 
It calls for a court-appointed medical expert to determine whether the offender is “an appropriate candidate” but doesn’t define what meets that standard. If the person chooses not to go through with the surgery, they can be sent back to prison for three to five years.
“[Clark] can simply refuse to have it done and [serve] a few more years of his sentence,” Boyd said.
Parole and early release are not available to persons convicted of second-degree rape in Louisiana, which means Clark would be at least 86 years old before he can get out of state prison.
Clark’s public defender, Phil Maples, did not respond to phone messages.
Cascio said the onus is on the Louisiana Department of Corrections to carry out surgical castration sentences that district attorneys and law enforcement work hard to obtain. 
“This is no different than if you have an inmate that has appendicitis and has to have his appendix removed,” he said.   
Falon Brown, press secretary for the corrections department, said via email there’s no one on staff or under contract with the agency to perform surgical castrations.
The attorney general’s office has not responded to an email, calls or texts asking whether Murrill was aware the state is currently not staffed to carry out a surgical castration.
Should state officials move to employ a surgeon, they could encounter moral objections. The American Medical Association officially opposes chemical castration. While it has no policy specific to surgical castration, the AMA approves of doctors performing court-ordered procedures “only if the procedure being mandated is therapeutically efficacious and is therefore undoubtedly not a form of punishment or solely a mechanism of social control.”
Castration as a punitive measure has drawn criticism from criminal defense lawyers who argue it violates the Eighth Amendment prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment.   
Lisa Wayne, executive director of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, said in an email the consent aspects of Louisiana’s castration laws also raise ethical concerns. There is also no proof that castration acts as a deterrent to sex offenders, she added.  
“There is no solid evidence that castration outperforms existing options. It is untested and politically driven, punitive punishment, rather than evidence-based,” Wayne said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Secretary of state candidate Ballard calls for increased Indiana poll worker training
description: The greatest risk to secure voting in Indiana is a lack of sufficient training for county election workers, secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard said in proposing a standardized statewide training program.
text:
Secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard speaks during an Indiana Statehouse news conference on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The greatest risk to secure voting in Indiana is a lack of sufficient training for county election workers, secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard said Wednesday in proposing a standardized statewide training program.
The former Republican Indianapolis mayor, who is running under the Lincoln Party banner, argued that the frequent GOP rhetoric on election security overlooked the challenges faced by county clerk offices and poll workers.
Ballard released a campaign proposal calling for the secretary of state’s office, which oversees statewide election policy, to begin a hands-on clerk training workshop and develop standardized procedures for all 92 counties to follow.
Many county clerks now turn to those from other counties to figure out election process problems, Ballard said.
“This is what election security actually looks like, making sure the people running an election know how to run it the same way in all 92 counties,” Ballard said during a Statehouse news conference. “Not slogans, not talking points, but ensuring that the people conducting our elections have the training, the support that they need and that they deserve.”
Indiana secretary of state hopefuls clash over voting rules, office audit

Republican candidate Max Engling frequently cites issues such as ensuring only U.S. citizens are allowed to vote as a top priority if he wins the November election.
Engling said he has been meeting with clerks and other county officials about what election assistance they need from the state.
“Greg Ballard is proposing yet another top-down, one-size-fits-all program, without identifying how it will be funded or showing how he will work with the officials who actually administer the elections,” Engling’s campaign said in a statement. “Our clerks deserve a partner who wants to serve alongside them — not someone who wants to run to a microphone every time they come up with an idea.”
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh said in a statement that he supported “any effort to address the unmet needs of our hardworking county clerks.”
“If I’m elected, I look forward to collaborating with the bipartisan Election Division and the Association of County Clerks to make sure we address training needs in a way that’s both efficient and secure,” Bayh said.
Ballard said he believed the cost of his proposal could likely be largely paid for through the secretary of state office’s current budget. He maintained, however, that the state has never funded a certification program for poll workers that was first called for in a 2005 law.
The lack of sufficient training can lead to problems such as the potential mishandling of ballots that led to a legal fight in a state Senate Republican primary race with a three-vote margin, Ballard said.
The Indiana Supreme Court is set to hear arguments Thursday in that ballot dispute between Sen. Spencer Deery of West Lafayette and challenger Paula Copenhaver.
Ballard blamed that dispute on “procedural election mistakes that never should have happened. That’s what it looks like if this goes wrong.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: UConn withdraws plans for golf practice facility, looks to new location
description: UConn is withdrawing plans for a golf practice facility at a Mansfield location locals have been protesting over environmental concerns.
text:
The University of Connecticut is withdrawing plans for a golf practice facility at a location in Mansfield that locals have been protesting for months over environmental concerns, according to a notice posted by Connecticut’s Council on Environmental Quality on Tuesday.
The university will instead look at an alternative site on its Depot Campus.
“It’s a big relief,” said Quin Harper, a local resident concerned about stormwater and pesticide runoff.
His parents’ home suffered constant water damage after trees were removed from a nearby property in 2001. Harper and other locals worried the same would happen at the proposed golf site in Mansfield.
“Whatever it was that tipped the scale and made them reconsider a different location, we’re all very glad that it happened,” he said.
“We all hope that however it proceeds, it’s done with the same kind of environmental concerns in mind.”
What is UConn building and what’s the controversy?  
UConn is looking to build a new golf practice facility for its men’s team. The site will be smaller than a golf course and will not be open to the public.
The university initially proposed building the facility on top of a hill on the corner of Storrs Road and East Road. The site is currently home to a collection of dwarf conifer trees once studied by university researchers.
Construction would have involved “selective tree clearing,” according to the university. But local residents and protestors said tree clearing could lead to potential stormwater and pesticide runoff into residential wells and the Fenton River.
“We’re getting heavier rains, they’re coming in these massive deluges, flooding, that’ll go into people’s wells. It’ll have soil runoff. It’ll take the chemicals from the grass and put it into the streams. There’s no way that it makes sense,” said Phoebe Godfrey, a professor-in-residence of sociology at UConn, who took part in a protest at the university campus in April.
The notice did not specify why the project was not moving forward at its original location, but stated the cancellation was “unrelated to the environmental review requirements of the Connecticut Environmental Policy Act (CEPA).”
The university is now looking to build the project on its Depot Campus, located approximately 5 miles away from the original site in Mansfield.
Updated information on UConn’s website states the original site “remains viable for future developments,” but the Depot Campus site is “a better candidate at this time.” Four buildings on Depot campus, which are already in poor condition, are scheduled to be demolished in early 2027. The new site also has direct access to UConn utilities and requires less clearing work.
The proposed building will be approximately 6,000 square feet with office space, lockers, restrooms, showers, equipment storage and repair space, a team room, indoor putting and simulation areas, according to a new scoping notice published by the Council on Environmental Quality.
The facility will take up approximately 6.5 acres of land.
Learn more
Written comments from the public will be accepted until Oct. 9. Requests for a public scoping meeting must be made by Sept. 18. Comments and requests should be sent to: Ian Dann, Sr. Project Manager, University Planning, Design & Construction at ian.dann@uconn.edu.
This story was first published Sept. 9, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss felony charge against former Mesquite police chief
description: A preliminary hearing is scheduled Nov. 4 in the criminal case against former Mesquite Police Chief MaQuade Chesley, who is accused of one felony count of secretly recording a conversation in Mesquite City Hall.  Chesley is the second public official prosecuted by Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson for the alleged offense in the last […]
text:
(Photo courtesy of Travel Nevada/Sydney Martinez)A preliminary hearing is scheduled Nov. 4 in the criminal case against former Mesquite Police Chief MaQuade Chesley, who is accused of one felony count of secretly recording a conversation in Mesquite City Hall. 
Chesley is the second public official prosecuted by Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson for the alleged offense in the last year. 
Henderson City Councilwoman Carrie Cox, who is seeking reelection, faces trial in October for allegedly recording her colleague and others at City Hall. 
Chesley’s attorney, Tony Sgro, argued in July that the law his client is charged with violating is vague and antiquated in an age of smart phone ubiquity. 
Pro Tem Judge Christopher Laurent ruled Wednesday that the law “is not unconstitutionally vague” and that a judge’s order in a civil case involving Chesley and his former employer, the city, could not be mentioned at the preliminary hearing.  
In that case, Clark County District Judge Nadia Krall stated  that Chesley’s recording was not criminal, and that the city’s accusation against him amounted to “bad faith and harassment” on the city’s part, and “an ongoing pattern of bad faith defenses.” 
She found the accusations “are contrary to the facts” and that Mesquite “fabricated false charges… to relieve themselves of the due process obligations under the law.” 
Chesley is suing the city for wrongful termination. 
Deputy District Attorney Austin Beaumont argued that Krall’s ruling is inadmissible in the criminal case. Beaumont is currently campaigning for a seat on the Clark County District Court. 
Mesquite officials initially asked the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Dept. to refer a criminal charge against Chesley to the D.A., but police declined, according to court documents.  
The city pursued the investigation of Chesley on its own when the former chief’s lawsuit against the city for wrongful termination “gained traction,” according to Sgro.
The city is already on the hook for a $1.425 million settlement with Chesley approved by the council in April to resolve wrongful termination cases he filed with the state Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and in District Court.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Enjoy the wins, LSU fans, as college sports crumbles before our eyes
description: Part of me really enjoyed the beatdown LSU administered Saturday night to Clemson at Tiger Stadium, unquestionably cementing the venue’s status as the real “Death Valley.” But even the lopsided outcome won’t shake the funk I’ve felt since well before the season opener.  My typical enthusiasm for the start of the college football season is […]
text:
Clouds pass over Tiger Stadium on Monday, March 20, 2023, on LSU’s campus in Baton Rouge (Matthew Perschall/Louisiana Illuminator)Part of me really enjoyed the beatdown LSU administered Saturday night to Clemson at Tiger Stadium, unquestionably cementing the venue’s status as the real “Death Valley.” But even the lopsided outcome won’t shake the funk I’ve felt since well before the season opener. 
My typical enthusiasm for the start of the college football season is tempered by its most prominent programs’ headlong leap into an out-of-control arms race. Making matters worse is LSU coach Lane Kiffin’s insistence that two former players who flirted with the pro ranks are worth LSU hurtling deeper into the black hole, though he decided late Tuesday to finalize the Tigers’ roster without them. 
Let’s set aside for now whether the 42 athletes seeking a fifth year of college eligibility have any grounds for the lawsuit they’ve filed in Louisiana. I think the question before the state court is a legitimate one, though the answer won’t resolve the bigger issue. 
Let’s also not pretend that college sports was a pristine landscape prior to name, image and likeness deals or revenue-sharing. Maybe there weren’t any millionaires on the field, but you can’t ignore decades of players benefiting from benevolent boosters eager to provide new cars, mortgage payments, no-show jobs and hundred-dollar handshakes.
Most troublesome to me is that elected officials, including Louisiana’s leadership, have entered the fray with a sense of righteousness that risks further legitimizing an apparatus likely to implode college athletics as we know it.
Attorney General Liz Murrill filed a brief in support of the athletes trying to rejoin their college teams, citing a “broken” system and its arbitrary NCAA policy decision.
It’s not that Murrill doesn’t have good points here. It’s that she and Gov. Jeff Landry shouldn’t have inserted themselves into the debate in the first place. Their involvement serves only to politicize an already murky matter that won’t find clarity at the state level.
Landry’s support for Kiffin during the controversy — “Don’t hate the player, hate the game” — is hardly constructive. It’s an implicit endorsement that no matter how fault-ridden the system might be, LSU should seek every avenue possible to gain a competitive edge.
But the attorney general is no longer on the sidelines, and the governor has just one degree of separation. After filing a federal lawsuit against LSU and its board last week, the Southeastern Conference replaced the defendants Tuesday with Murrill, Kiffin, athletics director Verge Ausberry and the individual members of the LSU Board of Supervisors who Landry appointed or reconfirmed. 
In a nutshell, the SEC claims Murrill and LSU’s leadership are conspiring to subvert its authority to enforce league rules that bar pro athletes. The 16 presidents from its member schools are scheduled to meet Thursday for a possible vote on whether LSU should remain part of the SEC, according to the federal court filing. 
In an interview Tuesday with Matt Moscona of ESPN Radio-Baton Rouge, Murrill said the amended lawsuit is an attempt from the SEC to prevent her and LSU from blocking Thursday’s vote — something the attorney general said she and the university have no intent on doing.
Exhibits in the amended filing submitted Tuesday to the U.S. District Court for Northern Alabama include posts from Murrill’s social media accounts in which she states her support of the player plaintiffs in the Louisiana case and calls the SEC’s lawsuit “garbage & frivolous.”
“Defendant Murrill’s actions were taken in active concert with the other Defendants and in furtherance of a coordinated effort by Louisiana state actors, including the Governor and officials at LSU, to override the SEC’s governance of its own association,” the SEC’s attorneys wrote in the filing. 
Reading between those lines, I see the Southeastern Conference trying to establish authority over a rising member institution and its outlaw coach who are intent on forging their own path in the college sports landscape. The NCAA is growing more obsolete by the second, if it isn’t already there, and the SEC wants to have a prominent say-so in the new system that takes shape. The conference can’t do that if LSU has a voice as loud or louder at the table. 
The chance that LSU actually gets the boot from its peers, who all relish the Fighting Tigers’ hefty contributions to their bottom line, is about as good as Dabo Swinney winning Coach of the Year honors. But should a vote actually take place, it would be yet another sign that the current iteration of college sports is not long for this world. 
History shows the Southeastern Conference and commissioner Greg Sankey can’t claim the high ground in this argument. The league has previously allowed former pro athletes to compete at its member schools, conflicting directly with the stance it’s taken against LSU.
My hope is that LSU fans and their SEC rivals recognize no winner will emerge from this showdown over the long term, save for the lawyers involved. Now that the attorney general is a party to the federal case, public dollars will pay for her defense.  
There are nearly 60 lawsuits with some 450 former college players seeking eligibility, and they are all part of the mess that won’t disappear even once decisions are made in the cases.
The Tigers’ dominance on the field and Kiffin’s loose cannon antics might provide a nice distraction in the coming months, but let’s not be lulled into believing they aren’t evidence of a structure with a severely compromised foundation.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Donalds, Luna to speak at ‘multi-millionaire-palooza’ in Dallas Wednesday
description: Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters says tonight’s first midterm Republican convention in Dallas has one mission: to defy history and grow Republican majorities in both the House and Senate in November. The Sarasota Republican, officially still representing Florida’s 22nd District in the state Senate, became the RNC chair a year ago and leads[...]
text:
GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna displayed her tickets to the Dallas Republican convention on her X account.Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters says tonight’s first midterm Republican convention in Dallas has one mission: to defy history and grow Republican majorities in both the House and Senate in November.
The Sarasota Republican, officially still representing Florida’s 22nd District in the state Senate, became the RNC chair a year ago and leads a party that could suffer major general election losses, in the House in particular.
The late summer GOP get-together comes as the United States is seven months into an unpopular war with Iran, with gas prices rising again, and oil topping $100 per barrel as of Tuesday. That development has contributed to President Donald Trump’s approval ratings dropping sharply in recent months.
Additionally, historically a president’s party can suffer electorally in midterm elections. In the 20 midterm elections since the end of World War II in 1945, the president’s party has lost seats in 18 of them (the exceptions were in 1998 and 2002).
Pinellas County U.S. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna is scheduled to appear in the first hour. A close ally of the president, Luna is running for a third term against retired Army brigadier general and attorney Leela Gray.
The other Florida Republican scheduled to speak Wednesday night is Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds, who in early 2025 received Trump’s backing to succeed Ron DeSantis.  He is scheduled to speak in primetime, shortly after 8 p.m. Eastern time. Donalds will discuss “Red State Success vs. Blue State Failure,” according to the program overview provided by the RNC.
Donalds played down his appearance during the convention in a brief interview with the Phoenix last weekend, acknowledging he would speak but adding, “I’ve got to get back to Florida.”
Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried blasted the two Republicans, saying in a virtual press call Wednesday that the GOP was throwing Trump a “’multimillion-dollar-palooza’ to celebrate his historically unpopular agenda. And Byron Donalds and Anna Paulina Luna are going to be the life of the party.”
“Instead of fighting for a more affordable Florida, Donalds and Luna are jetting off to Texas to celebrate themselves and Trump. For what? Because Donalds and Luna have voted for Trump’s unaffordability agenda every step of the way,” Fried said.
She specifically referred, she said, to votes the two have cast to protect the president’s tariffs from congressional oversight and the war in Iran.
“Donalds and Luna might be able to pop some champagne and worship the president, causing prices to skyrocket, but Floridians? We’re fed up,” Fried added.
Another Floridian will speak in Dallas Wednesday — Mary Alice Hazen, listed in the GOP program as an “Everyday American, Retiree and Senior Tax-Relief Beneficiary.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire voters have spoken. So what did they say?
description: In many ways, the results of Tuesday’s primary elections in New Hampshire played out as same old, same old. On the Democratic side, the establishment candidates in this purple state ended up winning in both congressional races, as well as the U.S. Senate nomination battle. However much Stefany Shaheen, Maggie Goodlander, and Chris Pappas might […]
text:
A voter fills out a ballot  at Manchester Memorial High School, the poll location for Manchester Ward 8, during the primary election on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin) In many ways, the results of Tuesday’s primary elections in New Hampshire played out as same old, same old.
On the Democratic side, the establishment candidates in this purple state ended up winning in both congressional races, as well as the U.S. Senate nomination battle. However much Stefany Shaheen, Maggie Goodlander, and Chris Pappas might claim the progressive mantle when it suits them politically, these are not disrupters by any stretch. They are politicians who like to play it down the middle and keep their heads down, which isn’t particularly inspiring but it is practical. And you can’t argue with Tuesday’s results. 
Still, the Pappas and Goodlander votes in favor of the anti-immigrant (and anti-due process) Laken Riley Act continue to draw the ire of the party’s frustrated left, and Pappas’ recent “present” vote on an amendment to strip Israel of billions in aid was not exactly a profile in courage. But that kind of fence-sitting does put him in good U.S. Senate company. Sens. Maggie Hassan and Jeanne Shaheen also voted in favor of the Laken Riley Act, and they abandoned their stand to protect the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and they joined Republicans in confirming some particularly inept Cabinet characters.
To that point, maybe nobody could have foreseen just how disastrous Kristi Noem’s time at the helm of Homeland Security would be, but two longtime New Hampshire political players like Shaheen and Hassan should have picked up on at least one big clue. Anyone who has New Hampshire’s own Corey Lewandowski whispering in her ear is a solid bet to be problematic, but Shaheen and Hassan greenlighted her anyway. 
I suppose that’s just the maddening way it goes when your delegation feels compelled to offer the benefit of the doubt to an administration that has never earned it.
And that leads me to the part of Tuesday that didn’t feel like the same old story. Three progressive candidates — Carleigh Beriont in the 1st District, Paige Beauchemin in the 2nd District, and Karishma Manzur on the Senate side — succeeded in making splashes. None were close to winning, which is the official story of the day, but what each of them overcame was significant. With very little name recognition when they launched, and comparatively very little money to spend, here’s the share of the vote each won, as of midday Wednesday: Beriont, 22%; Beauchemin, 18%; and Manzur, 33%.
In the end, these were not quixotic efforts. They were messages, and they will only grow louder in the second half of this current presidential administration. The question is, will the Democratic establishment still listen now that the left flank is back on the electoral sidelines?
There were messages sent on the right, too, but more by the candidates themselves than the voters. In the 1st District, eventual winner Anthony DiLorenzo was routinely targeted by his competitors for what they perceived as a too-empathetic view (gasp!) of immigrants. Lily Tang Williams, who won the 2nd District nomination easily, is leaning more into fiscal conservatism this time around rather than the heartless, pugilistic blueprint her party has followed for the past decade. And John Sununu showed absolutely no interest in running against main challenger Scott Brown, perhaps predicting that any race with Donald Trump as a third wheel could only have negative consequences come November.
In fact, Sununu kept his head so low for so long during the Republican primary that I sometimes wondered if he had dropped out and neglected to tell anyone. But then I would see four or five of his robotic anti-Pappas ads in a row and realize he’s just really uncomfortable running on the right. And I suppose that’s to his credit. 
Whatever concerns voters may have about the harmful Trump administration policies Sununu, Williams, and DiLorenzo might support should they join the Republican congressional hive mind — and those concerns are fully warranted — there is good news for everyone who is tired of all the chaos: All three seem to be more interested in being wonky than provocative. 
Baby steps, people. Baby steps.
The most important takeaway from Tuesday, though, has nothing to do with the political personalities. No matter how much of a carnival politics becomes, and no matter how hard the barkers work to redirect people to their sideshows, the domestic needs of the people don’t really change very much from year to year.
They want affordable healthcare and good wages. They want job security and a chance at home ownership. They want fair taxation and access to affordable childcare. They want clean air and water, and they don’t want to end every month in the red because of the inescapable costs of electricity, gasoline, and food. 
They want a future they can believe in, and not just for themselves but for their children, their neighbors, their communities.
In short, they want their leaders in Washington and Concord to understand who they work for — even after the final ballot is counted.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Angie Nixon says there are ‘$10 million reasons’ to oppose Ashley Moody
description: ST. PETERSBURG — Three weeks after her double-digit victory in the Florida Democratic U.S. Senate primary, Angie Nixon is making her case to general election voters by linking GOP incumbent Ashley Moody to Donald Trump, saying she “rubber-stamps everything he does.” The Jacksonville state representative is also referencing Moody’s involvement in the Hope Flo[...]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon speaking at the Bethel Community Baptist Church in St. Petersburg on Sept.8, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)ST. PETERSBURG — Three weeks after her double-digit victory in the Florida Democratic U.S. Senate primary, Angie Nixon is making her case to general election voters by linking GOP incumbent Ashley Moody to Donald Trump, saying she “rubber-stamps everything he does.”
The Jacksonville state representative is also referencing Moody’s involvement in the Hope Florida saga.
The recently leaked grand jury report revealed that while no indictments resulted from an investigation led by State Attorney Jack Campbell in Leon County, the panel found that the DeSantis administration “misappropriated” $10 million of taxpayer money in 2024, and that Moody as the state’s attorney general was aware of those plans to divert those funds to the Hope Florida Foundation and authorized her former chief deputy to sign the settlement agreement.
Speaking at the Bethel Community Baptist Church in South St. Petersburg Tuesday night, Nixon said “two scammers” represent Florida in the U.S. Senate, noting that Rick Scott once ran a healthcare company that was hit with at that time the largest Medicare fraud fine in U.S. history.
“And now we have one who’s unelected who her reward for stealing $10 million dollars from medically needy kids and unhealthy children was to be appointed to this U.S. Senate by scamming,” she said.
She added that there are “$10 million reasons why y’all don’t need to vote for Ashley Moody.”
Spectrum News asked Moody in an interview broadcast Monday night whether, had she known in 2024 what she knows now, would she have signed off on the $10 million settlement agreement?
“I can tell you, as attorney general we fought hard to protect Floridians,” she said. “Make sure that we were protecting communities. Make sure that we were protecting citizens. That is why I have been endorsed by 64 of our 67 sheriffs. Republican, independent, and Democrat.  And every police organization. I will keep doing my job and doing it well with the interests of Floridians in mind.”
Health care cuts
Acknowledging her presence in a place of worship, Nixon said it was “not holy to steal $10 million,” nor was it a good thing to “end healthcare for over 440,000 people here in the state of Florida” — a reference to an Associated Press report that about 440,000 Floridians dropped Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage this year — more than any other state — after Republicans in Congress including Moody let enhanced federal subsidies expire in January as part of Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025.
Nixon said she spoke earlier Tuesday with a pediatrician at Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital in St. Petersburg and learned that close to 70% of the hospital’s funding comes from Medicaid. “Which was cut by y’all’s President Donald Trump. Because he cut that funding because he wanted to give his billionaire friends and family a tax break.”
The “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by nearly $1 trillion over the next decade.
“And now, because of him, there are going to be children in this area and surrounding counties that are going to die,” Nixon said, “because they have to cut programs because of something that the guy in the White House did.”
Nixon’s agenda also includes supporting Medicare for All, a cornerstone of the progressive wing of the Democratic Party — as well as with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which she joined in June.
“Universal healthcare would save over a trillion dollars if we were to pass it,” Nixon said. “Don’t take my word over it, take the Yale study that just came out last month. It would also save over 114,000 lives.”
That study she referenced is a new report led by researchers at the Yale School of Public Health — not yet peer reviewed — positing that a single-payer universal health care system “could save more than 100,000 lives a year, and still cost $1 trillion less than the system it would replace.”
Nixon criticized the financial cost of the conflict with Iran; called for raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour; and assailed the Trump administration’s mass deportation program.
No debate?
In her interview with Spectrum News, Moody said that, like vanquished Democratic Senate opponent Alex Vindman, she doesn’t intend to debate Nixon this fall.
“I am running against a self-proclaimed socialist who, when has been given a stage, likes to quote the Communist Manifesto and, very disturbingly, cop-killers,”Moody said. “I can tell you, as the wife of a law enforcement officer, I am not going to give attention or a stage to that. There is no reason that we would want to shine a light or any police organization would want us to shine a light on something like that.”
Moody has previously expressed her outrage that Nixon has cited quotations from Assata Shakur. She was a member of the Black Panther Party and later the Black Liberation Army convicted in 1977 of the first-degree murder of a New Jersey state trooper, and who later escaped from prison to live in Cuba until she died in 2025.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Community, scientist disputes Oklahoma water agency finding that dams not to blame
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – There is no link between the construction of two dams and declining water levels at a lake west of Oklahoma City, according to the findings of a report released by a state agency tasked with managing water.  The reduction in water levels at Cedar Lake is more likely caused by a drop […]
text:
A water level marker at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – There is no link between the construction of two dams and declining water levels at a lake west of Oklahoma City, according to the findings of a report released by a state agency tasked with managing water. 
The reduction in water levels at Cedar Lake is more likely caused by a drop in aquifer levels related to homeowners’ domestic wells, according to the Oklahoma Water Resources Board’s 69-page report, which was distributed to some lawmakers and others.
But residents of the lakefront community located about 45 miles west of Oklahoma City and an independent hydrologist dispute the Water Resource Board’s findings. They said the agency’s report is riddled with inaccuracies and not based on science.
The agency, which is tasked with policing Oklahoma’s water resources, released the report to lawmakers amid heightened scrutiny over how it has handled a yearlong fight over two unpermitted dams erected upstream of the nearly 400-person community. 
Residents blame a dam erected in 2019 on a tributary feeding Cedar Lake for slowly causing water levels to drop and drying up their wells. They said that the agency has slow played their complaint because the dams are tied to a politically connected family.  
Some residents believe the water board’s reluctance to force the dams to be removed or to release water is because the property is connected to V. Glenn Coffee, a former powerful state senator and former Oklahoma Secretary of State, who serves as a legal consultant to the State Senate Republican Caucus.
The Water Resources Board did not respond to a request to make the author of the report or someone familiar with it available for an interview. The report does not say who authored it.
The agency’s report states that evaporation losses will outpace streamflow and runoff during drought.
Low lake levels will continue with or without the smaller dams upstream, the report said.
Carol Becker, an independent hydrologist  who reviewed the agency’s report, said she questions some of the conclusions.
Becker, who has about 35 years experience in water quality and resource management, said the Water Resources Board appeared to use wells in a different watershed to reach some of its conclusions.  
While the report says water flowing into Cedar Lake can be estimated using nearby stream gauges, Becker said there are no nearby gauges.
Becker evaluated the Cedar Lake water level earlier this year after residents asked for  an independent expert opinion.
She found that two of the upstream dams are capturing almost 40% of the watershed runoff, which would normally recharge Cedar Lake.  Cedar Lake then recharges the aquifer located below it. That aquifer feeds the water wells that residents rely on, she said. 
While Becker found that several factors can influence water levels at Cedar Lake, including household water use, land-cover changes, and climate, Becker said the two dams are the primary cause of the lake’s water drop.
“The evidence shows that they have little to no measurable effect compared with the dam impoundments, which remain the primary cause of declining water levels in the watershed,” according to Becker’s report.
Don Machacek has had property at the lake for about four years. He said there were no problems with Cedar Lake water levels and wells until the dams were built. He said the Oklahoma Water Resources Board report is “laughable” and not based on facts or science.
He said while Cedar Lake is going down, water being held behind the dams and in other lakes has not dropped.
“If it was anyone else… just the common man off the streets, rancher, farmer, what not, those dams would have been taken down,” Machacek said.
Cedar Lake residents are getting the “good old boy” treatment from the agency, he said.
Mark Sullivan, who owns property at Cedar Lake, said he believes the Oklahoma Water Resources Board governing body, composed of nine gubernatorial appointees, has gotten bad advice from agency staff.
In July, Cedar Lake residents went to an Oklahoma Water Resources Board meeting where the governing board was being asked to consider an agreement to allow the dams to remain in place while Coffee seeks a permit.
The governing board postponed consideration of the consent order until its Sept. 15 meeting after angry residents voiced their opposition.
