title: Michigan Department of Corrections to add over 800 high-security beds, 30 accessible rooms
description: The Michigan Department of Corrections is adding 870 high-security beds to its correctional facilities across the state, as well as upgrading an additional 30 rooms to meet increased accessibility needs, the department said Tuesday. Two state prisons — Oaks Correctional Facility and St. Louis Correctional Facility — will have one entire new high-security uni[...]
text:
Department of Corrections | Susan J. DemasThe Michigan Department of Corrections is adding 870 high-security beds to its correctional facilities across the state, as well as upgrading an additional 30 rooms to meet increased accessibility needs, the department said Tuesday.
Two state prisons — Oaks Correctional Facility and St. Louis Correctional Facility — will have one entire new high-security unit built at the two facilities, which is targeted to be completed by 2030. That will establish over 400 new Level IV and Level V/Segregation beds, the highest security levels in the MDOC classification system. Oaks Correctional Facility is located near Manistee, while St. Louis Correctional Facility is located in Gratiot County. 
Oaks Correctional Facility will also convert several units to higher-security beds, as will Macomb Correctional Facility, and Richard A. Handlon Correctional Facility in Ionia will convert a general population unit to a Protective Housing Unit, all of which are expected to be completed by the end of 2026. Bellamy Creek Correctional Facility, also in Ionia, which is undergoing an Americans with Disabilities Act accessibility project, will have 30 rooms upgraded to meet accessibility needs by the end of January 2027. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“When we have the right housing to support individuals throughout their course of incarceration, we create safer facilities for staff and increase the success of those housed there,” Department of Corrections Director Heidi Washington said in a news release. “Our population is always changing and the transitions happening right now will deliver immediate improvements in how we operate. At the same time, our new investments in high‑security infrastructure will ensure that, moving forward, we will be providing the most advanced and effective correctional environment available within these new units.”
Byron Osborn, president of the Michigan Corrections Organization, which represents all state corrections officers in Michigan, said in an interview with the Michigan Advance that the changes were a step in the right direction. 
However, Osborn, who is a correctional officer himself in the Upper Peninsula, expressed concern on the timeline proposed for those added high-security beds, saying that the timeline of over three years for the new high-security units was “not immediate help for us.”
“We are not pleased with the delays that are going to occur, because these problems are persisting,” he said. “We’ve got prisoners getting seriously assaulted, staff getting assaulted, prisoner homicides happening somewhat regularly now, and the need for these Level V beds, single cell beds is more of an immediate need.”
Osborn’s organization has repeatedly asserted that the state does not have enough high-security prisons to house all of the prisoners who are classified as high-security prisoners, and that fact has led to increased violence both by prisoners against corrections officers, as well as between prisoners. 
“We’ve got all of these prisoners who normally, if the prison system was operating correctly, would be housed in a higher security level due to their misconduct reports and their bad behavior,” he said in an interview prior to the MDOC announcement. “That’s why you see, when we report on a lot of these staff assaults and even some of the prisoner assaults, we’re saying some of these assaults, in most cases, most of them would not be occurring if the department didn’t have a security classification problem. These guys would be in single man cells at level five, where they can’t assault anybody.”
However, Osborn also expressed some skepticism about the feasibility of the new changes, especially in the wake of significant staffing shortages at a number of facilities throughout the state. 
St. Louis Correctional Facility, for example, has about a 14.5% staff vacancy rate according to data from the department. Osborn noted that the department has not yet explained to the union how they plan to provide staff for the additional high-security beds at St. Louis Correctional Facility, or SLF, and Oaks Correctional Facility.
“Already, SLF is facing a pretty significant staffing shortage,” he said. “So if you add another level 4 or 5 housing unit, that’s another 4 or 5 assignments per shift that they’ve got to fill.”
Meanwhile, Citizens for Prison Reform, an advocacy group for incarcerated people in Michigan, highlighted the importance of improvements to accessibility and safety. The group also raised questions about the changes being made.
“Alongside adding hundreds of higher security beds, what is being done to address the underlying issues contributing to the increased need for this type of housing in the first place?” The group posted on Facebook in response to the announcement from the department. “Adequate staffing, expanded and consistent access to educational and rehabilitative programming, medical and mental health care, substance use treatment, trauma informed practices, appropriate classification, and support for family connection and reunification can all play a role in creating safer prisons.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Doctors ask state for hearing on new proposed vaccine rule
description: Florida physicians want a formal hearing on the DeSantis administration’s latest effort to weaken vaccine requirements for Florida schoolchildren. The Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians on Wednesday sent notice to the Department of Health requesting a rule hearing on a proposal to make it easier for parents to opt out of vaccinating […]
text:
The Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians wants a rulemaking workshop on a proposal to make it easier for parents not to vaccinate their children. (Photo by Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)Florida physicians want a formal hearing on the DeSantis administration’s latest effort to weaken vaccine requirements for Florida schoolchildren.

The Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians on Wednesday sent notice to the Department of Health requesting a rule hearing on a proposal to make it easier for parents to opt out of vaccinating their school-aged children.
“The Chapter requests that the Department take note of its interest in this issue and to accept this correspondence as part of the official record,” Jacksonville health care attorney Christopher Nuland wrote to the DOH on behalf of the association and its 10,000 members.
“Numerous scientifically vetted studies have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of these immunizations, while the Chapter is unaware of any substantial competent evidence that would indicate otherwise.”
Nuland included in his letter an American College of Physicians position paper on vaccines issued more than a decade ago. In it, the association supports mandatory childhood vaccinations and opposes expansion of opt-out provisions such as the one Florida seeks.


“Support for eliminating existing exemptions, except for medical reasons, from immunization laws was among the policy recommendations adopted last weekend at the summer meeting ofthe Board of Regents of the American College of Physicians (ACP),” Dr. Wayne J. Riley, president of ACP, said in a written statement at the time.
“Allowing exemptions based on non-medical reasons poses a risk both to the unvaccinated person and to public health,” he added. “Intentionally unvaccinated individuals can pose a danger to the public, especially to individuals who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons.”


The American College of Physicians is the largest medical specialty organization, according to its website. Members include 143,000 internal medicine physicians, specialists who diagnose, treat, and care for adults.
The DeSantis administration published the proposed rule changes last month, one day after Republican gubernatorial hopeful Byron Donalds, appearing on Face the Nation, said he’d like to “study and really engage it” before deciding whether to repeal statutory vaccine requirements for schools.


The DOH did not immediately respond to the Florida Phoenix’s request for comment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Legal requirements
For entry and attendance in Florida schools, childcare facilities, and family daycare homes, state law requires children to be immunized for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, tetanus, and “other communicable diseases as determined by rules of the Department of Health.”
Under that authority, the DOH has required through regulation that children also be immunized for haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.
Exemptions are allowed for valid medical reasons and religious reasons only.
The proposed rule contains a trio of changes:

It eliminates vaccine mandates that aren’t required by law.
It proposes changes to the religious exemption form to allow opt-outs for parents and guardians who maintain immunizations conflict with their “sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s).”
It allows parents to opt out of their children’s information being put into SHOTS, the State Health Online Tracking System, a free statewide online immunization registry used to track and manage vaccine records.


DeSantis will be governor for four more months. He has  repeatedly said he wants to pass this policy before his term limit forces him to leave Tallahassee.

His first tried last year, appearing with Ladapo in a press conference to announce he wanted to eliminate all vaccine mandates from Florida statutes.
To that end, the DOH published notice of proposed rulemaking, the first step in the lengthy rulemaking process designed for public input, which, therefore, can take months to complete.
The administration was asked to hold a public hearing on the proposed changes, and did.
In addition to trying to push the changes administratively, the governor lobbied the Legislature to pass the policy. But it refused.
With the clock ticking, now the DeSantis administration is refocusing its efforts on changing policy through rule.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Supreme Court sets Sept. 30 arguments over validity of K-12, collegiate sports ballot measure
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court decided Tuesday to expedite and hear oral arguments in a lawsuit seeking to disqualify a ballot measure that would cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the Nebraska Constitution. Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke signed a one-page order Tuesday afternoon indicating the high court would hear the challenge Sept. 30.[...]
text:
Attorney Daniel Gutman argues before the Nebraska Supreme Court. From left on the bench are Justices Jason Bergevin, Jonathan Papik, William Cassel (not pictured), Jeffrey Funke (chief justice), Stephanie Stacy and John Freudenberg. At right is Gage County District Judge Rick Schreiner, who is rounding out the court due to a temporary vacancy. Dec. 3, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court decided Tuesday to expedite and hear oral arguments in a lawsuit seeking to disqualify a ballot measure that would cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the Nebraska Constitution.
Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke signed a one-page order Tuesday afternoon indicating the high court would hear the challenge Sept. 30. The justices initially decided Sept. 1 not to take up the case, so the challenging Lincoln voter, Cara Ullman, refiled her challenge before Lancaster County District Judge Lori Maret. 
Maret ruled against Ullman and all arguments from her attorneys on Tuesday.
Lancaster County judge dismisses challenge to Nebraska K-12, collegiate sports ballot measure

Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen must certify the Nov. 3 general election ballot by Friday, so the measure will appear on the ballot regardless. However, the appeal, if successful, could invalidate the vote in November.
The first certified ballots of the year must be sent to military and overseas voters by Sept. 18.
Ullman’s main contention is that the Fairness for Girls campaign lacked detail in some specific petition language, known as an “object statement,” so she signed a petition to place the measure on the general election ballot without fully knowing what it would do.
Maret disagreed and said the statement was “certainly brief,” but state law only requires that the statement be “concise.”
The Supreme Court will give supporters and opponents 10 minutes per side. Aligned parties must share argument time. Ullman’s attorneys were ordered to submit a brief by Sept. 15, while attorneys for Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen and the campaign must submit a brief by Sept. 22. Any reply from Ullman, if she has one, is due Sept. 25.
The sponsors for the ballot measure are University of Nebraska Regent Rob Schafer, former state Sen. Julie Slama of Dunbar and Nebraska Family Alliance’s Elizabeth Nunnally.
The Fairness for Girls proposal would make permanent part of a 2025 state law requiring public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state playing against those schools, to designate sports and athletic teams as male, female or coed. Male students couldn’t play on female-only teams.
The ballot measure would not define “sex” in the constitution. State law defines sex as whether someone “naturally has, had, will or would have, but for a congenital anomaly or intentional or unintentional disruption, the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports and utilizes” either eggs (female) or sperm (male) for fertilization.
Also Sept. 30, the high court will hear oral arguments in an appeal from the Republican National Committee and two Lancaster County voters over the constitutionality of a state law that allows U.S. citizens who have never resided in Nebraska but have a parent registered to vote in one Nebraska county to register in that county. Lancaster County District Judge Ryan Post upheld the validity of that state law Aug. 12.

name: VTDigger
title: Elizabeth Weir Toor
description:
Beth was a brilliant scientist, mother, wife, dog lover (particularly Irish and Gordon Setters), passionate supporter of women’s choice and voting rights, and an activist for clean air.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Elizabeth Weir Toor.
text:
Born: 07/20/1927
Edmonton, Alberta
Died: 08/24/2026
Middlebury, Vermont
Details of service:

Elizabeth Weir Toor died at age 99 on August 24, 2026 in Middlebury.
Beth was a brilliant scientist, mother, wife, dog lover (particularly Irish and Gordon Setters), passionate supporter of women’s choice and voting rights and an activist for clean air. She was an enthusiastic follower of women’s tennis, enjoyed a martini at the end of the workday, and loved her cigarettes, chocolates and mystery novels. She spoke her mind, did not suffer fools gladly and carried Kleenex in every pocket. In her younger days, she had flame-red hair and wore bright red lipstick with wild jewelry.
Beth was born and raised in Edmonton, Alberta. Her mother taught French at a women’s college, while her father was the first dean of the law school at the University of Alberta. Beth remembered that her father “gave me the idea that I could be anything I wanted to be when I grew up,” making sure she was given the same opportunities as her brothers. She passed that same philosophy on to her own children.
Beth was interested in science from an early age and started college at age 16. She studied at Stanford and the University of Alberta, graduating with a degree in chemistry. Although many colleges did not accept women into graduate programs in science, she was admitted into the PhD program at Northwestern University. While there, she met Herb Toor in a Mathematical Methods in Physics class. From this classically nerdy beginning they spent over 60 years together.
After graduating with a PhD, Beth took a postdoctoral research position with Kathleen Lonsdale at University College, London, where she used X-ray diffraction to study the structure of macromolecules. Her research project failed, as she was attempting analysis that the technology of the time could not support, but she took heart that years later another researcher using more modern technology did very similar work and received a Nobel prize for it. (When asked whether she had any regrets in life, her response was “not getting the Nobel prize in Chemistry.”) She and Herb had a memorable time in England, returning with a strong belief in the virtues of central heating. Herb then began a faculty position at Carnegie Tech (later Carnegie Mellon) in Pittsburgh, while Beth took a research position in the Metallurgy Department, as Carnegie at the time would not hire women for faculty positions in science or engineering.
Herb and Beth, always adventurous, spent a sabbatical year in India with three young children, where Herb worked with UNICEF to start up a new engineering school. Beth and Herb made lifelong friends there, and their time in India made a deep impression.
Beth worked part-time at the U. S. Bureau of Mines when the children were young. She also became very active in local politics, working with the League of Women Voters and with the Group Against Smog and Pollution (GASP). She played a key role in the successful campaign to stop construction of a destructive beltway around Pittsburgh. Later, she returned to full-time work doing research in a lab at Carnegie Mellon on such diverse topics as gallstones and coal slurries.
Beth was a lover of fiber art: an accomplished seamstress, knitter, and weaver, who gifted many people with her intricate creations. She devoted many hours to the Weaver’s Guild of Pittsburgh and leaves an extensive collection of works.
The family took extended summer trips to Beth’s brother’s cabin at the base of Mount Robson in British Columbia, often with a whole pack of nieces, nephews, and dogs. Beth and Herb were hikers and backpacked extensively in the Canadian Rockies. On one memorable trip — the 100-mile North Boundary trail — Beth came down with kidney stones and was evacuated on horseback. She corrected the doctor who told her this was the worst pain one could suffer, pointing out that childbirth involves larger items than kidney stones. Upon returning from the backcountry, Beth and Herb were delighted to learn that Richard Nixon had resigned.
In 2008, after retiring, Beth and Herb bucked the norm of retiring south and instead moved north to Vermont, where they were near both their daughter and a son’s summer home. The family enjoyed many holidays and summer vacations together on Lake Champlain.
Beth was a brilliant, beautiful, creative and independent woman who made an impression on all who knew her. She will be deeply missed. She leaves behind her three children, Helen Toor, John Toor and his wife Margaret, Will Toor and his wife Mariella, grandchildren Milo, Maren, Cead, Nicky and Misha, and many nieces and nephews of multiple generations.
The family would like to thank the wonderful staff at the Residence at Otter Creek for their kindness and care for Beth over the many years she lived there, especially during her time in assisted living, as well as the hospice team at Addison County Home Health & Hospice, and the amazing Dr. Laura Weylman.
In lieu of flowers, the family suggests donations to Planned Parenthood of Western Pennsylvania, the Group Against Smog and Pollution (GASP) in Pittsburgh, or the caregivers at the Residence at Otter Creek (made out to the Residents’ Appreciation Fund, care of Sasha Keck, 350 Lodge Road, Middlebury Vermont 05753). A celebration of Beth’s life will be held next summer around what would have been her 100th birthday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Elizabeth Weir Toor.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: A heart of stone: Barton County couple revive 126-year-old barn with help of state grant
description: BARTON COUNTY — It was a parched, sunbaked afternoon in the rolling hills of rural northeastern Barton County. The wind whistled through the scrubby trees and rustled the waving grass. With few modern-day landmarks around, the scene resembled the time in 1900 when James L. Homolka and his brother Joseph Homolka used brawn, skill and […]
text:
Jim and Katie Homolka display the oversized $25,000 check they received for participating in the Kansas Department of Commerce’s Tourism Office Barn Adaptation and Restoration Needs grant program. The funds help with the restoration of their limestone barn built in 1900 in northeastern Barton County. (Dale Hogg for Kansas Reflector)BARTON COUNTY — It was a parched, sunbaked afternoon in the rolling hills of rural northeastern Barton County.
The wind whistled through the scrubby trees and rustled the waving grass.
With few modern-day landmarks around, the scene resembled the time in 1900 when James L. Homolka and his brother Joseph Homolka used brawn, skill and determination to chisel a massive barn out of the native golden limestone.
Despite a fire in 1930, that barn still stands as James L.’s grandson Jim and his wife, Katie, breathe new life and purpose into it. The couple received one of six barn restoration grants from the Kansas Department of Commerce’s Tourism Office to complete its resuscitation with eyes on developing an events space.
“It’s been a lot,” Katie said of the passion project, noting they added a lot of personal investment in the project. “We put a lot of heart into it.”
Kansas introduced the Barn Adaptation and Restoration Needs — or BARN — grant as a one-time program in 2024, doling out $100,000, said commerce spokesman Patrick Lowry.
He said the program was “well-received” but that “there are no immediate plans to revive the grant.” It was closed because of a lack of future funding, he said.
According to state tourism officials, the program launched in May 2024 to support and expand Kansas agritourism by converting underutilized or vacant historic barns into new business venues. Designed to rescue agricultural structures from demolition or collapse, the program aimed to drive rural economic growth while creating new travel destinations for visitors.
In September 2024, state officials announced the grant recipients, who collectively provided more than $200,000 in matching funds to support the restoration work.
In addition to the Homolkas’ farm, other recipients included Sunshine Whiskey and Ranch in Osage County, which received the maximum award of $25,000; Cattle Cartel Merchandise in Russell County, awarded $22,000; Wendlin Vines in Leavenworth County, awarded $15,000; the Barn at Richmond in Anderson County, awarded $9,000; and Red’s Corn Maze and Pumpkin Patch in Logan County, awarded $4,000.
Looking at their property and all of its possibilities, Kate said it is a shame the program wasn’t renewed to help similar sites.
“It’s very sad that a lot of history is going to be lost,” she said.
 
Bringing it back to life
Back 126 years ago, those brothers thought they might as well do something with the limestone since the ubiquitous rock made doing just about every farming task darn tough in the age of horse-drawn implements and hand tools.

This sign denotes the name of Jim and Katie Homolka’s Scorched Stone Farm in northeastern Barton County. The name comes from the fire that gutted the limestone barn and charred the stone walls. (Dale Hogg for Kansas Reflector)

Their will was as hard as that stone, and that hewn barn rose from the plains — until the fire in 1930, caused by farmhands carelessly smoking during wheat harvest, gutted the wooden interior.
Jim and Katie, who now own the property, last month celebrated the resurrected barn on what is now known as Scorched Stone Farm, a name derived from those blazes that left reddish scars on the still-solid walls.
The couple received the grant in August 2024 and had two years to finish the work. The $25,000 was one of six projects statewide sharing the $100,000 awarded.
“We had already spent a lot of money out there,” Katie said. “This allowed us to finish it. Preserving that history is important to us.”
These were matching grants, so the Homolkas had to put up $25,000 of their money for the renovation effort.
The Homolkas have lived on the family homeplace since 1985, inheriting it in 2002. But the family has roots on the land since it homesteaded there in the latter half of the 19th century.
The wooden interior was rebuilt after the fires as the barn remained in service. But the Homolkas envisioned a different future for the historic structure.
They removed the grain and feed bins and the livestock stalls. And they replaced the dirt floor with concrete, added insulation, relocated the staircase to the loft and upgraded the electricity to the building. Installing air conditioning and renovating the loft remain on the list.
The exterior walls of the barn and house are more than two feet thick. There are two layers of one-foot limestone blocks with a layer of crushed limestone in between.
Although providing some insulating properties, Jim said those walls offer only some relief from the hot Kansas summers and the cold Kansas winters.
 
More than just a barn
The Homolka brothers also built a limestone house on the homestead, which, after some modifications, is home to the Homolkas, a smokehouse, a cellar and other outbuildings, all of which stand to this day.
But it remains a working farm.
“I came in and there was a calf laying there (on the new floor) all of a sudden,” Katie said. “That was my son Josh doing that.”
Josh Homolka left coaching football at Northern Illinois University to help farm when his dad fell while working cattle and impaled himself on a fence post. Although Jim continues to farm some, his son runs the operation.
Josh raises award-winning Wagyu beef on the 1,000-acre property, while continuing his love of coaching as the head football coach at Ellsworth High School.
But the barn is for more than bovines.
In 2018, Katie, a retired teacher, started raising wildflowers, which now add colorful exclamation points around the golden stone buildings. She and her daughter-in-law Jessica hold flower-decorating workshops and make floral arrangements for weddings.
 
Shown is the refurbished interior of Jim and Katie Homolka’s barn in northeastern Barton County. Although it is now an event space instead of a home for livestock, cattle have been found on the new concrete floor. (Dale Hogg for Kansas Reflector)
How they did it
In turn-of-the-century Kansas, particularly across this mostly treeless central Post Rock region that straddles Barton, Ellsworth, Russell and Rush counties, harvesting limestone for barns, homes and fence posts depended almost entirely on manual labor, Jim said. Quarrying occurred mainly during late fall and winter, when farm chores subsided and internal moisture made the stone easier to manipulate.
Jim said his grandad and grandad’s brother quarried the stone on their property and hauled it to the building site with horses and a buckboard wagon. He still has that wagon.
“They had all the tools,” Jim said. “But we lost them in the fire.”
Workers began by clearing topsoil and dirt from exposed ledges using horse-drawn scrapers, shovels and pickaxes to uncover the limestone seam, a layer roughly 8 to 12 inches thick. Using handheld star drills or hand-cranked augers, they drilled a straight line of holes along the ledge. The holes were filled with water and the winter freeze caused the blocks to break free.
Once fractured, workers pried the slabs free with long iron crowbars. The freshly cut limestone contained ground moisture known as quarry sap, leaving the rock soft enough to shape with chisels, stone axes and handsaws.
Exposed to sun and air, the sap evaporated, allowing calcium carbonate within the stone to harden into a durable, weather-resistant finish.
 
What’s next
On this late-summer afternoon, the sun baked the storied structure. But, the wind whistling through the open doors provided some relief.
Standing in the remodeled space, the Homolkas are content with the progress, but there is still a restlessness. They see so much more potential.
“We are looking at possibly expanding the barn into more of an event space,” Katie said.
While they have hosted a couple of small events, anything more formal is down the road.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Hudson residents join lawsuit against town over ICE detention center zoning
description: The town of Hudson has refused for months to take any steps to review and enforce its zoning code as it applies to a planned immigration detention center there, say the plaintiffs in a lawsuit seeking to block the facility — and three Hudson residents are now joining them. Wendy Homstad, Caden Grosshans and Emily […]
text:
The dormant Hudson Correctional Facility is pictured on Sept. 4, 2025. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The town of Hudson has refused for months to take any steps to review and enforce its zoning code as it applies to a planned immigration detention center there, say the plaintiffs in a lawsuit seeking to block the facility — and three Hudson residents are now joining them.
Wendy Homstad, Caden Grosshans and Emily Shanks, all residents of Hudson, were added as plaintiffs alongside Weld County resident Janet Carlson and the nonprofit Together Colorado, in an amended complaint filed Tuesday in state court, the group said. Carlson is a neighbor of the dormant prison known as the Big Horn Correctional Facility, which operated as a private prison for the Alaska Department of Corrections from 2009 until 2013, but her property is not within town limits.
The GEO Group, a private prison company, has announced a five-year contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reopen the facility as a 1,200-bed immigration detention center. But the lawsuit, filed in July against the town of Hudson, its town council, its planning commission and Planning Director Jennifer Woods, alleges that a conditional use permit for the site, approved by voters in 2008, is now void after more than 12 years of vacancy.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’ve gone to meeting after meeting, and I’ve watched my neighbors do the same, and every time the answer is the same: it’s not our problem,” Shanks said in a statement Wednesday. “I’m not asking Hudson to take a side in a national debate. I’m asking Hudson to follow its own rules, the same rules it would make anybody else follow.”
Hudson officials have maintained that the town “does not have authority to approve or deny federal use of this private facility.”
Faith group, Weld County resident sue Hudson over ICE detention center zoning issue

Attorneys for the town filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit last month, arguing the plaintiffs lack standing to bring the case. Together Colorado “lacks any connection to the Town,” they argued, while Carlson “lacks a direct connection to the Town,” and the injuries both plaintiffs claimed in the initial complaint were “presently speculative and cannot be determined until a remote time in the future.”
The amended complaint, however, points to Hudson’s own estimates, in its Water Supply Master Plan, that the reopened facility’s water consumption could reach 230 acre-feet annually, nearly doubling the town’s average water use over the last 20 years.
“The reopening of the (Big Horn Correctional Facility) will reintroduce demands that the Town has not anticipated for some time,” the plan says.
“Once the (facility) reopens, Hudson no longer can use the (Colorado-Big Thompson Project water) dedicated for the prison to meet other water demands within Town,” it continues. “This drives the need for Hudson to immediately shift its approach to use other water resources to meet its water demands.”
Other concerns cited by town residents in the new complaint relate to a projected increase in 911 calls, a trend observed in other rural ICE detention centers run by GEO, and the risk of public health emergencies like the tuberculosis case state officials have been barred from investigating at GEO’s facility in Aurora.
“After hearing about deaths and disease outbreaks in other detention centers, including a tuberculosis outbreak at the GEO-operated facility in Aurora, Plaintiffs Homstad and Grosshans have also grown concerned about the public health risks posed by the Facility, which could spread to the community through Facility staff and visitors, and the strain on the Town’s limited emergency services infrastructure,” the complaint reads.
Despite months of residents raising concerns about the facility through public comment periods and other official channels, town officials have declined to formally explain their position, review the alleged violation, “adopt an official code revision, or issue a conditional use permit” for the facility, the suit alleges.
“Hudson has had every opportunity to sit down, answer questions, and follow the process laid out in its own code,” said David Seligman, executive director of Towards Justice, the progressive legal advocacy group representing the plaintiffs. “Instead it has chosen silence, and now litigation.”
Demonstrators protest against potential new immigrant detention centers in Colorado outside the Hudson Correctional Facility on Sept. 13, 2025. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Immigration advocates and Colorado Democrats have been staunchly opposed to the Hudson facility’s potential use as an ICE detention center since last year. The Aurora facility, which has long been the target of criticism from activists over allegations of inhumane conditions and dehumanizing treatment, is Colorado’s only currently operational ICE detention center.
GEO seeks to intervene
In his second term, President Donald Trump has pledged to carry out the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history,” aiming to remove all of the estimated 12 million immigrants in the country without permanent legal status, regardless of how long they have been in the country, the legal status of their family members or whether they have criminal records.
Together with CoreCivic, another large private-prison company, The GEO Group is expected to be the prime beneficiary of a multibillion-dollar windfall for expanded immigration detention services authorized by Republicans’ 2025 spending and tax cut law. Last year, GEO chairman George Zoley spoke during an earnings call about the “attractive opportunity for investors” presented by “the unprecedented growth opportunities we anticipate will materialize over the balance of this year and next year.”
Attorneys for GEO moved to intervene in the case last month so that the company “can seek dismissal of this lawsuit and, if necessary, defend its substantial interest in performing its contracts with the property owner and ICE.”
The plaintiffs say their case only concerns the town of Hudson’s application of its zoning laws. They’re seeking a court order requiring town officials to comply with the “relevant procedures for amending the Land Development Code and/or granting or amending a conditional use permit.”
“This case concerns only the Town’s own authority and duties under the LDC — not the validity, meaning, or performance of any contract to which GEO is a party,” the plaintiffs in an Aug. 31 filing said. “GEO’s efforts to intervene in this matter will do nothing other than needlessly complicate this litigation.”

New nominations[...]
text:
The entrance to the Maine Department of Corrections in Augusta. Feb. 25, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Commissioner of the Maine Department of Corrections Randall Liberty is retiring on Oct. 1 after seven years in the post and more than four decades of corrections, military and law enforcement service. 
Deputy Commissioner Anthony Cantillo will become acting commissioner until an official replacement is nominated, likely by the next governor. New nominations require confirmation by the Maine Legislature. 
During his time as commissioner, Liberty implemented the “Maine Model of Corrections,” praised as one of the country’s most restorative programs focused on rehabilitation, human dignity and community reintegration. 
“Only in Maine, and only in America, could a young corrections officer once assigned to guard his own father in a county jail go on to lead transformational change across corrections systems around the world,” Gov. Janet Mills said of Liberty, who had done so during his first job as a part-time patrolman for the Fairfield Police Department and Somerset County Jail. 
Commissioner of the Maine Department of Corrections Randall Liberty. (Courtesy of the Office of Governor Janet Mills)
Mills nominated Liberty to serve as commissioner shortly after she was first elected in 2018. 
“I am deeply grateful to every department employee whose dedication made this work possible, and to Governor Mills for her steadfast trust and support as we’ve worked to redefine what corrections can look like,” Liberty said in a statement Wednesday. 
During interviews with Maine Morning Star, people incarcerated in Maine have praised the improvements Liberty made during his tenure, such as allowing people to engage in remote work and obtain degrees while in prison. However, incarcerated Mainers and prison reform advocates are also continuing to raise alarm about the ways they see the system falling short, such as a longstanding loophole in prison disciplinary policy that allows for punishment regardless of guilt and a lack of independent oversight of Maine prisons. 
Liberty had also previously served as warden of the Maine State Prison and before that for more than 26 years in the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office, including nine as the elected sheriff. Liberty served in the military for 24 years, including 21 in the Army National Guard and Army Reserves.

title: Salvadorans await word on protected status as midnight deadline approaches
text: WASHINGTON —  Temporary protected status for 170,000 Salvadorans is set to expire at midnight Wednesday, but the Department of Homeland Security said protections will remain in place until the Trump administration makes a decision to extend or terminate El Salvador’s designation, in place since 2001.“An announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time,” a DHS spokesperson said in an email to States Newsroom. “Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”Based on the temporary protected status statute, if a determination to extend or terminate a country’s protections is not made by the government by the expiration of the deadline, then TPS is automatically extended for six months.If the Trump administration does make a determination to end protections, then Salvadorans will have 60 days to leave the United States.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has not indicated his plans for El Salvador’s temporary legal protections. Additionally, there is no notice in Wednesday’s Federal Register or a preview of Thursday's edition regarding TPS for El Salvador. On Tuesday, White House border czar Tom Homan said the decision would be up to Mullin, but added that El Salvador is now much safer than when its previous designation was made in 2001. If TPS is terminated for nationals for El Salvador, they will be the latest large group of immigrants to lose their legal status in the country as President Donald Trump has sought to dismantle the program Congress created for people who hail from countries deemed too dangerous for return. The Supreme Court has accelerated that move. The court’s conservative majority this summer determined that the TPS statute does not allow decisions on country designations, terminations and extensions to be subject to judicial review. Before the start of the second Trump administration, 17 countries had TPS, totaling to about 1.3 million immigrants with legal status. Now, if TPS for El Salvador ends, only three countries will remain: Lebanon, Sudan and Ukraine. TPS is granted to nationals who hail from a country experiencing a natural disaster, violence, or other extreme circumstances, allowing them to remain in the U.S. and obtain work permits that last for six-to-18-month cycles. Each renewal process requires a TPS holder to go through a background check and pay hundreds of dollars in fees as well as undergo other vetting.  If TPS ends for El Salvador, it could stymie the country's economy, where more than a quarter of its gross domestic product relies on money sent back to the country from Salvadorans in the U.S., known as remittances. El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, also has a close relationship with the Trump administration, ranging from accepting deportees that are not Salvadoran into his country to visiting the president at the White House.In 2019, Bukele asked the first Trump administration to extend TPS protections, not because El Salvador was unsafe, but because the end of designation would break apart families in the U.S. Bukele has not made any recent public calls for the Trump administration to continue TPS for Salvadorans.

name: WyoFile
title: Star Plunge future murky after inspectors find ‘significant’ concerns at Thermopolis water park
description:
After settling with former owner of the Hot Springs State Park pools, Wyoming officials debate how to proceed with historic Thermopolis property.
The post Star Plunge future murky after inspectors find ‘significant’ concerns at Thermopolis water park appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After Wyoming State Parks settled with the former owner of the popular Star Plunge hot springs facility in August for $1.8 million, inspectors discovered gas leaks, sagging beams and “significant problems with the pools,” Wyoming State Parks Deputy Director Nick Neylon told lawmakers Tuesday. 
The findings throw a wrench into the state’s plans for the Hot Springs State Park pools and water slides in Thermopolis, Neylon told the Legislature’s Joint Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee. 
“We’re at the point now where we need to decide whether we want to continue to put money into this facility that is in really poor shape, or do we want to just build something new, something first class for the people of Wyoming and the people of Thermopolis,” Neylon said. 
It’s the latest twist for the embattled Star Plunge, a mineral-springs-fed destination of pools, tubs and slides that has been closed to the public for nearly two years while a lawsuit filed by former owner Roland Luehne against the state was argued in court.
The Star Plunge in Hot Springs State Park has been a soaking destination for decades. The family that has run it since 1975 sued Wyoming in 2024 after the state selected a new operator through a request-for-proposals process. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
Wyoming and Luehne reached a settlement in August that concluded all litigation and stipulated the state reimburse Luehne’s company $1.8 million for capital investment and ongoing business concerns at the facility. 
The agency reached a similar settlement with a second concessionaire in the state park, Big Springs Spa, Inc., which operated the Hot Springs Hotel. The state agreed to pay the company $1.2 million.
The settlements resulted from Wyoming State Parks’ years-long effort to update and modernize the park’s aging facilities. Critics have accused the state of attempting to Disney-fy the park and warn that the efforts will price out many loyal patrons. Supporters say improvements at Wyoming’s most popular state park are long overdue. 
When the state announced the Star Plunge settlement, Neylon said the facility could soon reopen to the public. 
Now, however, the agency is not so sure, he said Tuesday. The parks department is waiting for inspection reports on the facility’s electric system before it makes a determination on what to do next, he said. 
“We’re going to take a look at that electrical report when we get it and move forward from there,” Neylon said. 
Replacement dispute 
The spring-fed mineral waters of Star Plunge and Hot Springs State Park have been a destination for residents and visitors for centuries. Native Americans visited the waters, which they prized for their healing qualities, long before white settlers. The original 1-square-mile park was established through a treaty.
The public park, which sits on the banks of the Bighorn River, features playgrounds, a boardwalk over mineral terraces, multi-use trails and aquatic facilities along with numerous buildings.
Visitors walk the boardwalk at Hot Springs State Park, as seen from across the Bighorn River in May 2024. The dome of the Teepee aquatic center and white roof of the Star Plunge are visible. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
As landlord, Wyoming holds concessionaire agreements with park operators. That includes the Star Plunge and Teepee aquatic facilities and two hotels. All four were built decades ago and are in various stages of aging. Wyoming also operates a state bathhouse, which is free and open to the public per the treaty language.
The Luehne family had operated the Star Plunge since 1975, when Wolfgang and Christine Luehne bought it and took over a 50-year concessionaire lease. Their son, Roland, bought it from them in 2012.
In 2024, Wyoming State Parks selected Wyoming Hot Springs LLC to take over running Star Plunge after requesting proposals from interested operators. The company’s primary representative, Mark Begich, a former U.S. senator from Alaska, also purchased the nearby Tepee Pools in late 2023. Hot Springs LLC’s application laid out plans for significant upgrades and renovations. 
The state’s selection promised to effectively evict the Luehne family from Star Plunge. Luehne had been operating on a string of short-term management agreements since 2008.

Owner Roland Luehne in the Star Plunge aquatic facility in March 2026, more than a year after the pools closed to the public due to a legal dispute with the state of Wyoming. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)

Luehne contested the process in a pair of lawsuits filed by his company, C&W Enterprises. They accused Wyoming State Parks of exceeding its authority and violating regulations. Luehne argued the state was attempting to dislodge him without fairly compensating him for the improvements. 
The Star Plunge closed in early 2025 after Luehne’s most recent management agreement expired. 
The state, meanwhile, defended its process in court filings and statements. The court dismissed Luehne’s first lawsuit, and the second one, over compensation, was set for an October trial.
In the spring, lawmakers earmarked $3 million in the budget bill for “concessionaire remedies” at Hot Springs State Park and mandated the state appraise the businesses. 
That led to this summer’s settlements. 
Good news, bad news
During an agency update before the travel committee Tuesday, Neylon started with what he described as the good news. 
“As of today, we own the Star Plunge,” he said, and “we’ve come to an agreement with the owner of the Hot Springs Hotel, the former Days Inn.”
With the litigation over, “we are able to move forward developing these properties with a new concessionaire, like we’ve always hoped that we could, that’s the exciting part of the news,” he said. 
Swimmers in the Star Plunge’s indoor pool area on Jan. 10, 2025. The facility could close to the public amid pending sale negotiations and litigation. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
But the infrastructure problems pose new questions about how best to proceed with the historic facility.
The state now owns a hotel and a “facility that’s kind of falling apart,” said Co-Chair Sen. Bill Landen, R-Casper. “If you could get all the resources you needed, what is the vision there?”
Wyoming State Parks has been “disappointed” with the quality of three of the four Hot Springs State Park concessionaire properties for some time, Neylon said: the Star Plunge and Teepee pools and the Hot Springs Hotel. 
“We’re now in a position where one concessionaire can operate all three of those for us,” Neylon said, referring to Begich’s Wyoming Hot Springs LLC. 
“This is a company that has developed quality facilities in other parts of the country, and is interested in coming here and spending a considerable amount of money to renovate and potentially expand the hotel and to do something with the water park situation at Hot Springs.” 
The state has yet to finalize what that “something” is, Neyon added.
“We know that there will be something new there,” he said. “We’re just not sure where it will be. Will both locations continue to have a water park where the Teepee is and where the Star Plunge is? Maybe, but maybe not. That’s going to be part of that negotiation and discussion that we have with the concessionaire.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Mainers’ grand bargain
description: As the only Senate Republican representing a state that has voted three times against President Donald Trump, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins is once again amplifying her power as a chief appropriator who delivers outsized earmarks for the state. She has also positioned herself as a bulwark, protecting Mainers from Trump’s dramatic cuts to government programs […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine tours the Maine Energy Marketers Association Technical Education Center in Brunswick on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)As the only Senate Republican representing a state that has voted three times against President Donald Trump, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins is once again amplifying her power as a chief appropriator who delivers outsized earmarks for the state.
She has also positioned herself as a bulwark, protecting Mainers from Trump’s dramatic cuts to government programs as well as his fierce cruelty towards political opponents and vulnerable populations.
As she seeks re-election, Collins is arguing that her presence in the U.S. Senate protects her constituents from a regime that she supports 95% of the time and when Mainers head to the polls in November, they are largely voting on whether her seniority and the privileges and protections it affords the state is worth the cost to the rest of the nation.
Collins as protector
“I focus on results, not rhetoric,” Collins told Maine Morning Star in an interview last year when asked about calls for her to more publicly challenge some of the actions of the White House, touting the success she’s had behind the scenes.
“Because I have these relationships with the president’s Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and with Cabinet members, I have been able to restore funding that was in jeopardy,” Collins said.  
Collins used that influence as Maine became a frequent target of Trump’s second administration after Gov. Janet Mills’ heated exchange with the president over the state’s transgender protections.
For example, Collins said she consulted with the Trump administration to restore the U.S. Department of Agriculture grants to the University of Maine, renegotiate the Maine Sea Grant, and reverse the cancellation of a decades-old program that allows parents to register their newborns for a Social Security number while at hospitals. 
She also took credit for the end of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge in January.
“I have been urging Secretary Noem and others in the Administration to get ICE to reconsider its approach to immigration enforcement in the state,” she wrote on X on Jan. 29. “I appreciate the Secretary’s willingness to listen to and consider my recommendations and her personal attention to the situation in Maine.”
The Press Herald later reported that beginning on Jan. 22 federal authorities were planning to leave the state because of a pending snowstorm. And in the months that followed, federal agents continued to arrest and deport Maine residents, the vast majority of whom had no criminal record, though in a less confrontational manner.
Collins as appropriator
Collins’ influence as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee is cited by many of her supporters as the main reason for their vote, particularly when it comes to securing funding for the state.
As the Morning Star previously reported, Collins has secured more than $1 billion for Maine since 2022, when Congress reinstated earmarks. During the most recent cycle, Maine received the second highest allocation of federal funding per capita in the country, securing $460 million for roughly 200 projects across the state. 
Though Collins’ congressional colleagues, including U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, who is a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, also secured millions in funding, many projects are attached to Collins and publicized by her office.
During the latest congressional recess, Collins visited a childcare center in Bangor, a defense manufacturer in Biddeford, a bridge dedication in Millinocket, a lobster pound in St. George, as well as a crisis care center and affordable housing development in Calais. She christened the launch of a 3D-printed boat at the University of Maine and signed a truss for the new Kenduskeag Public Library — all to tout investments that she requested or secured in recent years.
The senator works hard for the people of Maine and her team makes sure we know it.
And that pork does come at a cost. Under Republican rule, Congress and the White House have taken an ax to spending on healthcare and social programs that predominantly support vulnerable populations, which is already having a ripple effect on state budgets, including Maine’s. 
Collins as moderate
Collins has frequently brandished her reputation as the most bipartisan senator to distance herself from the more disgraceful actions of her party.
Supporters like to characterize the senator as a “thorn in the president’s side,” with one letter to the editor using the example of her opposition to Todd Blanche, Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer. But like many of Collins’ opposing votes, it did not stop him from being confirmed as attorney general.
The Bangor Daily News’ recent analysis of times Collins cast the deciding vote found that, even though she does break from her party more than any other senator, it very rarely results in an outcome that’s in the Democrats’ favor, and among the 56 times she did, roughly half were before the first Trump administration. The analysis also weighs each vote equally, and so fails to account for the significance or impact of the legislation passed or blocked by Collins. 
Which leads me to her very high profile 2018 vote in support of Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the U.S. Supreme Court, which she has said she does not regret, despite it ultimately leading to the repeal of the federal right to an abortion. That act had a devastating impact on women’s health, rights, access to reproductive care, and economic opportunities across the country. Democrats won’t stop talking about that vote in relation to Collins because it was a time she could have wielded her power in defense of issues she purports to care about, but chose not to.
Perhaps if the impact was closer to home, if Maine residents weren’t protected by the state’s strong abortion protections, Collins would feel differently.
The solidarity vote
Troy Jackson, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, joins protesters at a July 14 demonstration outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough, days after federal agents killed a man in Biddeford, Maine. (Photo by Jackson for Senate campaign)
Ultimately, Collins is banking on Maine’s swing voters opting for what they see as local interest — money for firetrucks, a direct line to Cabinet members when the state is under threat — over Democrats winning control of the Senate, which would significantly curtail Trump’s agenda. 
And while it is an understandable impulse in this moment of precariousness and scarcity, it stands in contrast with a wider view of mutual caring and support that extends beyond the boundaries of Maine. 
Solidarity is the notion that you are not just fighting for your own betterment, but others’ as well, and only by joining together in a struggle can you build enough power to win. In local parlance, a rising tide lifts all boats.
Collins’ opponent, Troy Jackson, has made this idea his personal motto (and campaign merch). As part of his Solidarity Forever tour, the Democratic nominee is currently driving around the state in a minivan with those words affixed to the exterior, frequently donning t-shirts amplifying the call long associated with the labor movement.
For Jackson — who came to politics by helping lead a blockade near the Maine-Quebec border to stop logging companies from hiring cheaper labor and depressing wages and who spent 20 years in the Maine Legislature working to pass stronger labor protections, increase access to childcare and lower drug costs — solidarity is “a lifestyle, not a slogan.”
“I learned a long time ago that working people can win fights that nobody expects us to win when we stand together and when the people we elect remember whose side they’re supposed to be on,” Jackson told the audience at the annual Southern Maine Labor Council’s Labor Day event in Portland on Monday.
Maine voters, particularly the 40,000 or so who have previously backed Collins but not Trump, will in many ways be deciding on how they want to approach the remainder of his presidency — whether that is linking arms and demanding change for everyone or capitalizing on power and access in the hope of shielding the state. 
But whether it is measles or skyrocketing oil prices or foreign corruption or unregulated AI or fascist extremism (the list goes on!), the threats of this presidency know no bounds.

title: Pillen faces blowback on Nebraska immigration stance, releases ‘Pillen Playbook 2.0’ platform
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen is facing pushback from the challengers to his reelection bid over his immigration stance as a new Flatwater Free Press investigation states his family ag operation has long hired undocumented laborers. The Flatwater report, released Wednesday in partnership with The New York Times, states Pillen’s hog business has employed[...]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, right, hosts a general election kickoff event where he confirmed he is sticking with his running mate, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, for another four years on Aug. 25, 2026, in Lincoln. To Pillen's right are first lady Suzanne Pillen, Kelly and Kelly's wife Susie. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen is facing pushback from the challengers to his reelection bid over his immigration stance as a new Flatwater Free Press investigation states his family ag operation has long hired undocumented laborers.
The Flatwater report, released Wednesday in partnership with The New York Times, states Pillen’s hog business has employed migrant workers for more than a decade, some of whom are in the country legally and others who are not. The Flatwater story says it confirmed the reporting with state and federal court records and interviews with more than 40 current and former employees, prosecutors, immigration lawyers and community organizers.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen speaks with state Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte (obscured) at a general election kickoff event where he confirmed he is sticking with his running mate, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, for another four years on Aug. 25, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The challengers to Pillen’s reelection each argued Wednesday that the investigation shows Pillen plays by “his own set of rules.”
Hours after the investigation was released, Pillen’s campaign released “Pillen Playbook 2.0,” an updated policy wishlist. It’s a play on Pillen’s having been a defensive back for the Huskers in the 1970s. 
The memo mentions immigration once, with no specifics: “Eliminate state taxpayer benefits for illegals.”
Pillen and family company respond
According to Flatwater, Pillen Family Farms and an official spokesperson for Pillen said neither the company nor the governor “knowingly hired an illegal immigrant.”
Laura Strimple, Pillen’s spokesperson, told Flatwater the governor “went above and beyond the legal requirements to verify the immigration status of his employees” and that he “has the strongest immigration record in Nebraska history.”
Nearly one year ago, at Pillen’s direction, the director of the Nebraska Department of Correctional Services signed a contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to convert a state prison in McCook into a new ICE holding facility. Pillen and federal officials dubbed the rebranded Work Ethic Camp the “Cornhusker Clink.”
“We want President Trump to know that Nebraska is supportive and grateful for his ongoing, critical work with Secretary (Kristi) Noem to arrest and deport criminal, illegal aliens,” Pillen said in an Aug. 19, 2025, statement when he announced the Nebraska-ICE partnership.
Nebraska Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, left, looks to his running mate, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, as he speaks at a general election kickoff event after confirming Kelly will be staying on the Pillen-Kelly ticket for another four-year term on Aug. 25, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Pillen and Corrections Director Rob Jeffreys also fought back against a lawsuit, mostly from McCook residents, challenging their authority to convert the prison without legislative approval. A judge upheld Pillen’s discretion. Advocates are appealing to the Nebraska Court of Appeals.
At a campaign event in late August in Lincoln, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, a longtime prosecutor who is Pillen’s homeland security adviser, did not reference the McCook facility but did praise Pillen for twice deploying Nebraska National Guard soldiers to the U.S.-Mexico border
“We found some great Nebraska soldiers who were willing to do that, and it was very helpful to that overall effort to do and give us what we’ve got today: a border where people aren’t climbing over those fences every five minutes like they were years ago,” Kelly said at the time.
Pillen’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday on the Flatwater-NYT investigation.
‘His own set of rules’
Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, Pillen’s Democratic opponent this fall, said the Flatwater investigation outlines Pillen’s “latest con.” She asserted, as she has before, that Pillen has been “enriching himself and his friends since day one, and this falls right into the pattern.”
“When the cameras are off, the rules don’t seem to apply to him,” Walz said in a statement. “He’s built a career holding other people to standards he won’t keep himself. When it’s his farm, his business, his bottom line — suddenly the rules have a lot more flexibility.”
Walz said she would be a governor “who actually is what they say they are.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, bottom left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, bottom right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, top left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First Party, top right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, who is running for governor as the America First Party nominee, said in a social media post Wednesday that he read the “disturbing” story but is “not at all surprised. This is exactly who Governor Jim Pillen is.”
“He plays by his own set of rules while holding the rest of the state to a different standard. If this is how he has run his business for decades, how has he been running the state the last 3.5 years?” Lindstrom wrote.
Lindstrom ran against Pillen for the GOP nomination in 2022. He later switched to nonpartisan earlier this year before switching to the America First Party to revive his gubernatorial bid.
Rick Beard, who is the gubernatorial nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, said that if people are “actually serious” about border control, then corporate owners and leadership need to be held criminally accountable for their illegal practices.
“Making them accountable removes the engine creating unauthorized workforces in the first place,” Beard said in an email to the Nebraska Examiner. “Our culture of excusing corporate crimes while calling those crimes a necessity to do business has to end. No one is above the law in the state of Nebraska.”
‘Pillen Playbook 2.0’
Walz and Lindstrom have each released their own platforms. Walz’s is “Lynne’s Commitment to Nebraskans,” and Lindstrom’s is the “Nebraska Doctrine.” Beard, while he does not have a set policy document, has called for a state-run medical cannabis program, among other priorities.
Among the new items in Pillen’s “Playbook 2.0” released Wednesday:

Lower property insurance rates.
Stop hedge funds from buying up Nebraska homes.
Eliminate toxins in food and water.
Protect the Ogallala aquifer.
Protect the integrity of elections and reform the “broken ballot petition process.”
Counter aggression from the Chinese Communist Party and other foreign adversaries.
Ensure all third graders can read at grade level.
Reform K-12 funding to have the state take on more of the burden of educating children.
Expand trade opportunities for agricultural products.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen speaks with reporters after hosting a kickoff event where he confirmed he is sticking with his running mate, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, for another four years on Aug. 25, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
As with policy platforms released by other gubernatorial candidates this year, Pillen’s campaign does not state exactly how he would achieve or fund the ideas in his “playbook.”
Said Pillen: “The new Pillen Playbook is about my commitment to the people of our state: making Nebraska more affordable, defending the values that make our state extraordinary, investing in our kids and workforce and protecting the land, water and communities we are proud to call home.”
Beard, responding to Pillen’s policy platform, described the updated Pillen platform as “all hat and no cattle.” Beard said his proposals, to grow Nebraska’s own food and produce new revenue with cannabis and industrial hemp, would clean Nebraska’s soil and provide new rural opportunities.
Lindstrom said in a text that “what’s most striking” about the document “is what’s missing.”
“There’s no mention of Nebraska’s budget crisis, the hundreds of millions of dollars in shortfalls or any accountability for the decisions made over the last three and a half years that helped put us here,” Lindstrom said. “Nebraskans don’t need a recycled playbook of promises. They deserve an honest assessment of where we are today and a real plan to fix it.”
Walz had no immediate comment on the “Pillen Playbook 2.0.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico’s plan to reduce wildfire risk currently ‘nowhere near enough’
description: New Mexico Forester Laura McCarthy has a six-point plan for the state, which she recently presented to legislators, mitigate wildfire risk.
text:
State Forester Laura McCarthy on Sept. 8, 2026, previewed legislation for New Mexico lawmakers to help mitigate the state's wildfire risk. Above: Crews work on mulching burned trees in the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire burn scar on Feb. 1, 2023. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico’s top forest administrator on Tuesday warned legislators that the state is behind on wildfire risk reduction goals, and provided six possible bills ahead of the next legislative session that could improve planned targets.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state’s Forest Action Plan aims to treat 125,000 acres a year by thinning and prescribed burns to meet a 1.7 million acres decade-long target to improve forest health and wildfire resilience.
In the past year, however, only 22,000 acres were treated, State Forester Laura McCarthy told state lawmakers during an Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee meeting in Las Cruces, making New Mexico “way below where we need to be.”
The poor treatment rates, according to McCarthy, stem from forest landowners and contractors lacking the necessary capital for tree thinning. Landowners need money to pay tree thinning contractors upfront before being reimbursed through federal and state programs. The contractors need the money to buy the machinery and equipment. 
The state also lacks sufficient workforce for tree thinning and burns, and has high transportation costs to move the wood, McCarthy added.
McCarthy, flanked by ecological economists and investors, put forth a six-point plan to address the poor risk reduction rates while also promoting a “biomass economy.” 
In order to address these issues, McCarthy and ecological economists outlined legislation they hope lawmakers will consider in next year’s session. 
Those bills would: provide loan guarantees to landowners and contractors; finance companies building biomass infrastructure; create cooperative wood yards; grant funding for biomass research; create procurement preferences for state construction and purchasing; and establish a data initiative to update statewide wildfire risk analysis and mapping. 
State Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas) noted that the proposed solutions did not address workforce shortages that hinder wildfire risk-reduction efforts.
The presenters said that they’ve been relying on the Wildfire Resilience Training Center at Luna Community College to train the future wildfire workforce, but that they “don’t want to get people trained and then not have jobs for them.” They added that another bill to build up the workforce would be necessary.
“We’re not going to get there overnight,” McCarthy said. “If we can only get from 12,000 acres a year to 22,000 in the seven years that I’ve been State forester, that tells me we need a different approach.”

text:
Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee for Maine's 2nd Congressional District, held a press conference in Bangor Thursday to commemorate the 61st anniversary of Medicaid and Medicare. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)Democratic congressional candidate Matt Dunlap challenged Republican Paul LePage to four debates on Wednesday.
Dunlap has received and accepted invitations from WMTW for Oct. 1 and WABI on Oct. 15, according to his campaign. Overall, he has proposed debates be held in Bangor, Lewiston, the Downeast region and up north. 
LePage spokesperson Brent Littlefield said the campaign issued a memo to “organizations and news outlets requesting debates” months ago. “We are evaluating and will announce our schedule,” Littlefield said, not specifying when but confirming that the Republican will debate. 
Dunlap and LePage are vying for Maine’s 2nd District seat to replace Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, who is not seeking reelection. 
Dunlap criticized LePage, former governor of Maine, for not holding town halls and declining events such as the Maine Medical Association candidate forum earlier this month.
“If you’re not willing to answer tough questions, you have no business running for Congress or any other office,” Dunlap said in a statement Wednesday. 
Meanwhile, Littlefield took aim at Dunlap’s record when pressed on LePage’s debate attendance. 
“Governor LePage will absolutely debate Dunlap who failed the auditor exam multiple times, was forced to leave office, and who let welfare fraud perpetuate on his watch,” Littlefield said in a statement.
In 2021, Dunlap stepped down as state auditor after he failed to pass two accounting tests, preventing him from securing a key certification within the eligibility window. Jacob Norton filled the position, but also resigned shortly after he failed to get his auditing certification. Dunlap passed the exams after his 2021 resignation, and returned as state auditor in 2022. 
Maine is facing heightened federal scrutiny over allegations of improper billing and fraud within MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program. Dunlap had flagged several potential problems during his annual review of Maine’s compliance with various federal programs.
Disagreements over debates are not unique to this race. Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson have been sparring over dates and format.

text:
In her first campaign ad for the general election, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree highlights her record as Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives. (Photo is a screenshot from the campaign ad)This story will be updated
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree released her first TV ad of the general election on Wednesday, becoming the first candidate to go on air.
The ad highlights her record as Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives where she fought prescription drug companies to lower prices, and promises to build on that experience to make housing and health insurance more affordable. 
“As governor, I’ll take on the tough fights to bring down costs for you,” she says in the ad. “Tax out-of-state homeowners to reduce property taxes for Mainers, and create a public insurance option to lower premiums.”
Since she announced her campaign last year, Pingree has run on promises to deliver affordability, leaning on her legislative and executive branch experience. Before she announced her run for governor, Pingree led Gov. Janet Mills’ Office of Policy Innovation and the Future, where she worked on housing issues, addressed energy efficiency and climate challenges and introduced workforce initiatives to strengthen Maine’s economy. 
“This ad is about being honest with people: times are tough, and it’s going to take a governor who’s tough enough to take on the powerful interests driving up costs,” Pingree said in a statement.
Her campaign has reserved $1.8 million to buy eight weeks of broadcast television and cable advertising before the Nov. 3 election. That’s more than the combined total raised by her two opponents, according to the latest available campaign finance data published in late July. 
As of July 14, Pingree had raised more than $3 million. Republican Bobby Charles had raised $1.3 million, and independent Rick Bennett raised just more than $780,000, according to Maine Ethics Commission data released in July.
Pingree’s campaign said her campaign has been “fueled by strong grassroots support, high volunteer engagement, and a growing list of endorsements from elected leaders, health care experts, and community advocates across Maine.” 
Three public polls have shown Pingree leading the gubernatorial candidate field.
Bennett said Pingree’s record of working on affordable housing and energy in Maine has not yielded results. 
“Mainers should be skeptical of an ad that celebrates a record on affordability — because the person in it is the one who ran Maine’s housing and energy policy for the last six years,” he said. 
“Failure does not earn her a promotion.”

title: Dubois County man gets probation after guilty plea in lieutenant governor threat case
description: A Dubois County man accused of sending threatening messages to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith was sentenced Tuesday to nearly a year of probation after pleading guilty to felony intimidation. Joshua Wasson, 25, of Jasper, pleaded guilty in Dubois Circuit Court to one Level 6 felony count of intimidation and misdemeanor charges of possessing marijuana and […]
text:
Threatening messages directed at Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith led to a criminal case that ended concluded months later with three convictions and a probation sentence for Jasper resident Joshua Wasson. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A Dubois County man accused of sending threatening messages to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith was sentenced Tuesday to nearly a year of probation after pleading guilty to felony intimidation.
Joshua Wasson, 25, of Jasper, pleaded guilty in Dubois Circuit Court to one Level 6 felony count of intimidation and misdemeanor charges of possessing marijuana and paraphernalia. A second felony intimidation charge and a misdemeanor harassment charge were dismissed under the plea agreement.
Joshua Wasson, of Jasper, was sentenced Sept. 8, 2026, to 364 days of supervised probation after pleading guilty to felony intimidation and two misdemeanors in a case involving threats against Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith. (Photo provided by Indiana State Police)
Judge Nathan A. Verkamp sentenced Wasson to 544 days on the intimidation count, suspending 364 days to supervised probation. The court awarded 90 days of credit for time served and another 90 days of good time credit, satisfying the 180-day unsuspended portion.
Wasson also received concurrent sentences of 180 days for marijuana possession and 60 days for paraphernalia possession. Court records show both misdemeanor sentences already completed.
The probation order bars Wasson from direct or indirect contact with Beckwith and requires him to complete anger management counseling within six months. He must also undergo substance abuse and mental health assessments and complete any recommended treatment.
If Wasson completes probation without any revocations, he can petition the court to reduce the intimidation conviction to a Class A misdemeanor. That change would require court approval.
“I am thankful that the defendant, Mr. Wasson, was brought to justice in this case,” Beckwith said in a statement to the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “I would also like to thank the Indiana State Police and Dubois County Prosecutor Beth Schroeder for their work. This was an important case because it shows that people cannot make serious violent threats from behind a keyboard and expect no consequences. I believe Mr. Wasson will now get the help he needs during his supervised probation.”
The case began April 30, when Indiana State Police arrested Wasson after investigating social media posts and messages directed at Beckwith. Police said investigators interviewed Wasson at his workplace and found suspected marijuana and paraphernalia while retrieving items from his vehicle.
Beckwith said at the time that the messages began in March and escalated before the arrest.
Court records show Wasson began GPS-monitored pretrial home detention May 1. The court lifted that requirement July 28, when a written plea agreement was filed, but kept his other release conditions in place.
