name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Burgin city council member walks out to stop a vote for a proposed data center project
description: BURGIN, Ky. — A city council member for a small Mercer County community walked out of a meeting Tuesday evening, stopping a vote that could have restarted efforts to annex land for a proposed hyperscale data center, a project that’s been under local scrutiny for months.  During a special meeting at the city’s fire department, […]
text:
Some attendees of the Burgin city council meeting brought lawn chairs to sit inside the engine bay. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)BURGIN, Ky. — A city council member for a small Mercer County community walked out of a meeting Tuesday evening, stopping a vote that could have restarted efforts to annex land for a proposed hyperscale data center, a project that’s been under local scrutiny for months. 
During a special meeting at the city’s fire department, the Burgin city council lost a quorum to be able to conduct business and subsequently ended their meeting after council member Melinda Wofford abruptly walked out of the door of the department’s engine bay.
Melinda Wofford walked out of the meeting, which prevented a vote that could have advanced consideration of a proposed data center project. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
“You can’t do business without a quorum,” Wofford told the Kentucky Lantern while standing in a gravel lot near the building after the meeting had ended.
Wofford told the Lantern she walked out on purpose but didn’t expand on her reasoning for walking out. 
More than a hundred people packed into the engine bay, some of them wearing blue shirts for the community group “We Are Mercer County” that has voiced strong concerns about the potential project. After the meeting, a few attendees thanked Wofford for walking out. 
The council was set to vote on whether to direct the city attorney to draft an ordinance — to potentially be voted on in the future — that would annex several parcels of land north of the city where developer Panattoni Data Centers wants to build a hyperscale data center with a potentially massive power demand. It would have been the second time the city of about 1,000 people had considered annexing the proposed data center site. 
Two chairs for Burgin city council members sit empty as the council can’t proceed with business. Wofford had walked out a moment prior. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Zoé Strecker, one of a number of Mercer County residents who spoke against the proposed project during a public comment portion of the meeting, told the council the data center industry was “extractive” and echoed a range of environmental concerns residents had on noise and air quality impacts. 
“There is every reason not to rush. We are clearly a target. Why? Because the land is inexpensive, the power is nearby and cheap, and the local government is eager for an increase in tax base. But we are not interested in being sacrificed,” Strecker said. 
Brock Tomlinson, a senior vice president for Panattoni Data Centers, also spoke to the council in favor of the project, saying the company has “listened closely to the residents in Burgin and Mercer County.” He cited potential tens of millions of dollars in local tax revenue, speaking over heckling from the members who accused him of lying. 
He also referenced an executive order from Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear that seeks to mitigate the impacts of hyperscale data centers looking to locate in the state.
“Gov. Beshear has been clear that Kentucky residents should be protected and should not pay the costs,” Tomlinson said. “We agree with the governor in that stance.” 
A lost quorum
While Wofford’s walkout triggered the loss of a quorum, it was also made possible because of a recusal of a council member and the absence of another. 
Travis Irvine, another city council member for the community of about 1,000 people, recused himself from the vote because of a potential conflict of interest he saw as an employee of the local school district. The school superintendent and school board for Burgin Independent School, which serves about 500 students, have advocated for the proposed data center because of a potential windfall of tax revenue for the school district and city. Irvine had also left the building. 
Irvine’s recusal, combined with Wofford suddenly walking out and the absence of council member Kevin Wallce, meant the council didn’t have enough members to continue the meeting. 
“That’s her choice,” said Burgin Mayor Joe Monroe to reporters after the meeting. “I have to stand up for Travis because he recused himself all along. And he stood his ground, and she stood hers.” 
Earlier in the meeting, Monroe made the tie-breaking vote to give a first reading, or initial consideration, of another ordinance that would have Burgin join the Mercer County government and the county seat of Harrodsburg on a joint planning and zoning commission and a board of adjustment. 
Burgin does not have planning and zoning regulations and could adopt regulations as a part of the joint commission. The crowd, some of them sitting in lawn chairs, stood up and cheered after Monroe made the tie-breaking vote. 
Monroe told reporters he thought it was a “big mistake” for the city to annex any property without planning and zoning because “they can pretty much do as they please.” 
He said joining the joint planning and zoning commission was the only way to have more control over annexed property. Wofford had joined him in that vote, saying she wouldn’t approve any annexation of property until the city had planning and zoning rules in place. 
The Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission voted in July to advance data center zoning regulations that restrict where large data centers projects can be located and also require a developer to prepare an environmental impact statement and create a benefits agreement with the community. 
A county’s data center moratorium doesn’t include a small city considering huge project

In August, the Mercer County Fiscal Court had also passed a temporary pause on data center construction — which doesn’t apply to Burgin because the city doesn’t have planning and zoning — until the fiscal court can pass those regulations into law. 
On Tuesday, the fiscal court also gave a first reading of the commission’s data center regulations. Republican Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele said wanted to have the meeting where the second reading of the regulations happens to be at a “place that we can have more room” for more people to attend. 
Mary DeLima, 65, and her dog Bo wait for the Burgin city council meeting to start on Tuesday. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Monroe told reporters that Burgin adopting planning and zoning regulations doesn’t “kill” the proposed data center project but “makes things a little bit harder.” 
“You got to see what the public wants. Is there a possibility of a chance to make some money out of it for the city in taxes? Yes, there always is, but you still have to listen,” Monroe said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Public defender challenging incumbent in Clark County Dept. 21
description: Clark County District Judge Tara Clark Newberry, who is wrapping up her first term on the bench, faces a challenge in November from longtime Deputy Public Defender Alex Hubert. Hubert, who says his job as a public defender “is 85% social worker, 15% lawyer,” says he chose to run against someone with whom he “would […]
text:
Tara Clark Newberry and Alex Hubert (Campaign photos)Clark County District Judge Tara Clark Newberry, who is wrapping up her first term on the bench, faces a challenge in November from longtime Deputy Public Defender Alex Hubert.
Hubert, who says his job as a public defender “is 85% social worker, 15% lawyer,” says he chose to run against someone with whom he “would have the most contrast.”
Clark Newberry served as a police officer for eight years – a position she says gave her a “qualified, informed and exceptionally well-rounded” view of the legal system. “I spent most of my law enforcement career engaging the community and trying to improve community relations and making the world a better place.”
She also served as a civil attorney before her election to the bench in 2020, and represented plaintiffs and defendants before the Nevada Supreme Court and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.
She credits her work in disability services at the University of Cincinnati with giving her an appreciation of “how differing life experiences impact interactions with the legal system.” 
Clark Newberry attended the California Western School of Law and was admitted to the Nevada Bar in 2007. 
In 2022, she was named the presiding judge over civil cases, and the task of clearing the backlog of cases accumulating since the pandemic fell to her. 
She says she was “the catalyst” in forming the medical malpractice court, “which helped us dig out of COVID much faster.” Malpractice cases, which rely on a handful of specialty attorneys, present a “logistics” issue, she says, and are known to cause “a bottleneck.”  
Her next charge is to “figure out what do we do with this monstrous caseload increase of the past three years” that she attributes to artificial intelligence. 
Clark County’s civil caseload increased from 21,000 in 2023 to more than 25,000 in 2025, and is projected to top that this year, she says. 
Business technology, such as AI, “when used ethically, increases productivity,” she observes, and is an increasingly popular means of composing legal filings, especially for pro se litigants. “It enhances our access to justice because there are folks that cannot afford attorneys. We do have to figure out how to deal with it in an ethical way,”
Courts across the U.S. are being buried in briefs authored by Chat GPT and other platforms. Some include erroneous interpretations, botched facts, and fake legal citations.  
Clark Newberry compares the phenomenon to the advent of online resources in the 1990s. “If you don’t use the tool correctly, you’re going to make mistakes.”
Clark Newberry had a 68% retention rating from attorneys participating in the Las Vegas Review Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 evaluation. 
“There’s always going to be folks that you make unhappy, but no one’s perfect, and everyone can improve. And so I see it as an opportunity to improve and find ways to educate yourself, learn, and do better.” 
Clark Newberry is endorsed by SEIU Nevada; Laborers 872; Southern Nevada Building Trades Union; Ironworkers Local 433; and the Clark County Marshals. 
She has raised just under $390,000, which is ten times what she raised in her first campaign. The 2020 campaign season, in which she came in second to Jacob Reynolds in the primary and went on to win the general, was largely sidelined by the pandemic, she notes. 
“I had no idea what kind of fundraising apparatus I’d be going up against,” says her opponent Hubert, adding he was “very naive in that regard.” He has raised just under $13,000 and has just under $7,000 on hand.
Hubert has been a Clark County public defender for almost two decades. “The reality is that we’re 85% social worker and 15% lawyer.” 
The challenge of a public defender, he says, is cutting through the mental health issues and/or addictions that are landing clients in trouble, and then finding help. 
Diversion programs for defendants in Clark County, he notes, “are better than they used to be. The frustration is these programs exist, but they always have funding problems.”
He says he chose to run against Clark Newberry because he finds her approach to justice to be “heavy-handed” with little room for nuance.  
Hubert says he’s not concerned about appearing to be a “public defender masquerading as a judge. As a public defender, my job is to be a zealous advocate. As a judge, my job would be to strive for neutrality.”
Hubert’s endorsements include Veterans in Politics International; Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada (PLAN); Hispanics in Politics; AFL-CIO; Culinary Local 226; Teamsters Local 631; and, IATSE Local 720. 
Hubert grew up in Los Angeles, where his father headed up the psychiatric ward for the Veterans Hospital. He received his law degree from Arizona State University and passed the bar exam in that state before moving to Las Vegas, where he volunteered at a civil law firm while waiting to take the Nevada bar exam.  His experience, however, is largely in criminal law. 
“Everyone has a learning curve,” he observes. “It’s part of the challenge.”

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.

 Catching Our Eye

• The Toledo Blade. The Toledo Blade reports, “Possible final edition of Blade announced; company explores sale.”
Block Communications has announced its intention to explore a sale of The Blade’s assets, which, if unsuccessful, will result in the final edition of the newspaper being published Dec. 31.
• Annie get your gun. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford reports, “A new film unveils the hidden history of iconic Ohio sharpshooter Annie Oakley.”
Most people know Annie Oakley for her incredible sharpshooting skills: hitting dimes in midair and splitting playing cards with her trusty .22-caliber rifle.
But a new documentary goes beyond those famous feats and takes a closer look at the life of the Darke County native — and the women who have spent decades piecing together her story.
“North Star” tells Oakley’s story, while also spotlighting the Garst Museum researchers who have kept her legacy alive: Brenda Arnett, Karen Besecker and Nancy Stump.
• Other states. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “Ohio US senators target other states licensing some immigrant drivers.”
Ohio’s two U.S. senators, Bernie Moreno and Jon Husted, want federal government intervention to block other states from issuing driver’s licenses to immigrants living in the U.S. without legal authorization.
• Roy Cohn and Trump. In The New York Times, Carlos Lozada writes, “Trump’s Only Teacher.”
At this point in the Trumpian arc, we’re all too familiar with the president’s methods: Deny everything; apologize for nothing. Hog the spotlight. Counterattack, counterpunch, countersue. Always declare victory, even when you lose (especially when you lose). Resentment sells. Nativism sells. Cruelty, if not yet normal, becomes the norm. Rules and traditions are for suckers; everyone is, if not corrupt, at least corruptible. These are President Trump’s instincts, yes. But before they were his, they were Roy Cohn’s.
Kai Bird’s new book, “American Scoundrel,” written with Susan Goldmark (Bird’s wife and chief researcher), is a biography of Cohn, the sinister 20th-century lawyer who served as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy when the junior senator from Wisconsin was Red Scaring America and as lawyer to Trump when the young real estate developer was deflecting allegations of discrimination against prospective Black tenants. “American Scoundrel” is very much a how-we-got-here book, showing how Cohn’s guile, paranoia and shamelessness guided McCarthy, rubbed off on Trump and stuck fast to America.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Developer of Delta data center announces ‘revolutionary’ tech to turn natural gas into water
description: Creekstone Energy, the company behind a huge data center campus being built near Delta in Millard County, has announced that it’s in the process of patenting a “revolutionary technology” that can turn natural gas into water.  The new technology — which the developer said can capture water vapor from the exhaust of Creekstone’s own natural-gas-powered […]
text:
Construction crews work to build the first phase of a natural gas connection at the site of a data center project near Delta, Utah. (Photo courtesy of Creekstone Energy)Creekstone Energy, the company behind a huge data center campus being built near Delta in Millard County, has announced that it’s in the process of patenting a “revolutionary technology” that can turn natural gas into water. 
The new technology — which the developer said can capture water vapor from the exhaust of Creekstone’s own natural-gas-powered electricity generation and convert it into water — has been named GIGAWATER, which the company said is the “centerpiece” of its Project Oasis initiative at the Delta Gigasite campus. 
“We at Creekstone Energy, we don’t believe Utah should have to choose between economic growth and responsible water stewardship,” the company’s founder and CEO Ray Conley told reporters in an embargoed virtual briefing last week, ahead of Wednesday’s announcement. 
Ray Conley, founder and CEO of Creekstone Energy, a company working to build the largest data center campus in the world near Delta, Utah. (Photo courtesy of Creekstone Energy)
“Because Creekstone’s focused on building the largest data center campus in the world, that comes to the forefront very immediately,” Conley said. “We think that the data centers have to be designed for the places where they’re built. And because we’re building in Delta, in the arid West, it’s not just about minimizing local water demand from the beginning, which we’ve been focused on. But how do we innovate and how do we recognize ways to do this better?”
So Conley said Creekstone has “filed for a patent on a new technology that creates water,” designed to capture water vapor that’s created when natural gas is combusted to create electricity. 
“To confirm the science holds at scale,” the company said in a news release Wednesday, Creekstone Energy has signed a research agreement with the University of Utah’s Energy & Geoscience Institute “to independently verify the technology.” 
Though the company is likely several years away from generating water at a large scale, Conley said he wanted to announce it now, as the University of Utah prepares to start its research, because “I felt that it’s important for people to understand that data centers — at least some of us in the industry — are trying to push innovation forward to benefit the environment.”
“It’s something that can actually benefit Utah and not simply be a drain on resources,” he said.
As controversy over data centers have swept across the country, the majority of ire in Utah hasn’t been focused on the project near Delta, but rather on a different data center campus proposed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary in Box Elder County, in northern Utah. Amid intense backlash, the project area has been scaled back from 40,000 acres to 20,000 acres. 
About 200 miles south of Box Elder County in a rural area, the Delta Gigasite is already under construction after five years of planning. There, Creekstone says it’s working to build the largest data center campus in the world meant to “enable leadership in the race to AI superintelligence,” according to its website. 
Creekstone owns 1,143 acres near Delta, but the project’s footprint will also span across 30,000 acres owned by the Utah Trust Lands Administration that are under lease for solar, which the company says will generate the majority of the campus’ energy needs. Agreements have also already been struck to build a pipeline to bring natural gas from Wyoming to Utah.
O’Leary agrees to cut Stratos data center area in half following letter from Utah Senate president

At full build out, Creekstone says the campus will have more than 10 gigawatts of electrical capacity — more than double what the entire state of Utah currently consumes. 
In April, the Utah Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity awarded Creekstone Energy a post-performance tax incentive for its Millard County project. In exchange for the creation of 106 jobs with wages totaling $33 million over 20 years (averaging an annual salary of about $162,148 each), the company was awarded a 50% tax credit. 
That post-performance refundable tax credit will save the company about $172 million in taxes over 20 years. That equates to a cost of about $1.6 million per job over the lifetime of the deal. 
According to an April news release issued by the Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity announcing the deal, Creekstone Energy is expected to invest more than $17 billion in Utah over the next two decades and generate more than $334 million in new state revenue.
Developer expects to create ‘vastly more’ water than it uses
Creekstone promises an “essentially waterless operation” with a dry cooling system that works like a car radiator, not a swamp cooler — and that it will only use water for bathrooms and drinking. 
With its patent-pending technology, the company expects the data center campus to generate more water than what the Delta Gigasite “itself will ever consume.” 
“Vastly more,” Conley told reporters. 
With about 2.1 gigawatts expected to be generated from natural gas (compared to 6 gigawatts from solar and 1.8 gigawatts from the Intermountain Power Project, a power plant near Delta), Conley said Project Oasis is expected to generate 4,000 acre-feet of water per year. That’s equal to about 1.3 billion gallons, or enough to cover a football field one foot deep 4,000 times.
Creekstone Energy is working to build what could be the largest data center campus near Delta, Utah. (at the site of a data center project near Delta, Utah. (Diagram courtesy of Creekstone Energy)
“Now, that’s just a projection,” Conley said, “based on the chemistry and the physics of what we’ve done. But we recognized early on that even though we did our own engineering analysis, which was needed to put this together for the patent and to put into operation, having independent validation was really important.”

That’s why he said they’re working with the University of Utah’s Energy & Geoscience Institute “to independently test our model, our assumptions, and help us really determine how that system can perform at scale.” 
Conley, however, said he’s “pretty confident” the technology will pan out, hoping to build a working pilot program near Creekstone’s construction site “to validate that it works,” and then the University of Utah’s research will determine “what would be needed to take it to commercial scale performance.” 
He expects the university’s results to come next summer. Then after about two years, he said the company will “know if it makes sense to go ahead and scale it up.” 
“The science behind Project Oasis is promising,” Milind Deo, the principal investigator with the University of Utah’s Energy & Geoscience Institute, said in a prepared statement included in Wednesday’s news release. 
Deo said the institute is “committed to rigorous, independent verification, moving from theory and math through computer modeling and, ultimately, to physical demonstration.”
“If the results bear out, this could change the way the data center industry thinks about water,” Deo said.
A diagram depicts the power generation and water capture process that Creekstone Energy’s patent-pending technology that it was can create water from natural gas combustion. (Diagram courtesy of Creekstone Energy)
How does the new tech work?
Creekstone’s news release described the new technology as a process that turns “exhaust into water.” 
“When natural gas is burned to generate power, the exhaust it produces contains water vapor,” the company said. “GIGAWATER captures that exhaust, cools it through a regenerative rock-bed system, and converts the vapor into usable water, collected on site. It doesn’t drain Utah’s water supply. It adds to it.” 
Conley — who holds degrees in aeronautics and astronautics from MIT, according to his website — developed the new technology’s underlying model himself, Creekstone’s news release said. 
When explaining how it works, Conley compared it to condensed water that drips out of an idling vehicle’s tailpipe. 
“That’s actually condensed water in the tailpipe from the combustion process,” he said. “What we’ve done is figured out how to do that same process, only at a very large scale in the desert, to capture the water byproduct of combustion when we’re burning natural gas to make electricity.” 
Conley believes the new water could potentially be used for a variety of purposes: irrigation, agriculture, geothermal energy cycles, and potentially — if it’s filtered — potable water. 
“We believe that there’s a good chance the water, with at least a little bit of filtration, would be potable because there’s no bad chemicals that are in it. You know, you’re just literally precipitating the water out,” he said. “It will likely have a higher degree of acidity just because of how water interacts with rocks and that kind of thing. In which case, it would have some applications for agricultural use.” 
Construction crews completed an access road for the site of a data center project near Delta, Utah. (Photo courtesy of Creekstone Energy)
He added the company will need to do more testing to figure out what it could be used for and “how much processing and filtering we would have to do to make it drinkable.”
“But the goal doesn’t have to be (to) make it drinkable at the end of the day, because there’s plenty of other uses you can use for it,” he said. 
As for the natural gas emissions, Conley said the company is following federal standards and working with the Department of Environmental Quality on air permits. 
“In our case, we are expecting to be considered a small (emissions) source,” he said.

He said one of the campus’ biggest emissions will be nitrous oxide. But rather than having a smokestack, he said the company is testing and evaluating whether they can put it underground and “how much of those nitrous oxides and other types of chemicals react with the rock and the other stuff we’re putting in there to minimize that emission.” 
“That’s part of what Utah is looking at and what we’re trying to make sure, that it’s not only compliant with what the air quality standards are, but hopefully exceed those by a fair bit,” Conley said. 
An unprecedented question for Utah lawmakers
If Creekstone’s Project Oasis works, it could pose an interesting and unprecedented issue for Utah lawmakers to grapple with: What happens when a company starts generating more water than it needs? Will it own it? Sell it? Who gets to decide the terms? 
“That’s a really good question,” Conley said. “Well, we are paying for all the inputs. We pay for the gas, and we pay for the machinery that creates it.”
But he also acknowledged that water is a “unique” issue in drought-stricken Utah, noting he’s heard a joke that “the water that’s in your body, somehow Utah has a right to. Which I don’t think is actually true, but whatever.”
“I am not an expert on water law, and I’m sure people will have opinions on that,” Conley said. “But I think it’s a good problem to have because we’ll have created the resource.” 
So if Project Oasis becomes flush with water it doesn’t need and could potentially sell, Conley said he doesn’t know how the discussion will play out “because there is no precedent, right?”
Bill to force data centers to publicly disclose water use advances

“It’s not like we’re doing something that’s been done before. And so it leaves an open question,” he said. “Those are things that are really matters of law. … We can follow, like, what I would think would be right. But, you know, if lawmakers have a different opinion, then they get a say in that, right?” 
Conley added that if policy makers “make a decision that would deprive the economic value of it, then that would obviously impact whether or not it would be worth the effort of doing it, too.”
“So there’s always a give and take between commercial interests and how you make those decisions,” he said. 
Given that Creekstone is investing money to make the project possible, however, Conley said it’s not likely that the company would give away the water it generates for free. 
Utah lawmaker says project could create new standards for data centers
Rep. Jill Koford, R-Ogden, issued a prepared statement included in Creekstone’s news release Wednesday saying she hopes Project Oasis could set a new standard for how the data center industry operates as a whole. 
“What Creekstone is doing with Project Oasis goes well beyond compliance,” she said. “This is exactly what it looks like when Utah businesses, our universities, and state leaders work together to meet a challenge head-on. I hope it sets the standard for how the entire industry operates.”
Koford successfully sponsored legislation earlier this year to require data centers to disclose how much water they use.
Conley said Creekstone is building GIGAWATER “because we don’t think Utah should have to choose between hosting this industry and protecting its water.”
“We hope it becomes the model for how data centers are built across every arid climate where water is precious,” he said.

title: Hazardous waste management company hit with $1M Washington state fine
description: A national waste management company faces over $1 million in Washington state fines for alleged mishandling of used oil, solvents and other toxic materials.  Last week, the state Department of Ecology fined Crystal Clean $1.04 million after its Lakewood location was found to have violated multiple state laws. It’s the highest penalty Ecology has imposed […]
text:
(Photo by SteveDF/Getty Images)A national waste management company faces over $1 million in Washington state fines for alleged mishandling of used oil, solvents and other toxic materials. 
Last week, the state Department of Ecology fined Crystal Clean $1.04 million after its Lakewood location was found to have violated multiple state laws. It’s the highest penalty Ecology has imposed on a single company so far this year. 
Over two years, Ecology found violations that included more than 120 examples of inaccurate or misleading documents and shipments sent to unauthorized facilities. The department also said the company improperly stored hazardous waste.
Businesses often use waste service providers like Crystal Clean to transport hazardous waste to facilities permitted to properly dispose of it. The process requires businesses to track waste from “cradle to grave.” That requirement was broken based on Ecology’s findings that Crystal Clean altered shipping documents without notifying its customers. 
“If you ship an important package, you expect the delivery service to know where it is, handle it properly and deliver it to the right location,” said Katrina Lassiter, manager of Ecology’s hazardous waste program. “Hazardous waste isn’t being managed correctly or safely if we don’t know where it’s going for disposal.” 
Ecology also cited Crystal Clean for presenting itself as a designated facility for dangerous waste when it did not have a permit. 
“We intend to appeal the penalty assessment, but we do also intend to fully cooperate with the department,” said Crystal Clean CEO Brian Recatto. 
Assuming the company appeals, the state’s Pollution Control Hearings Board will handle the case.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: The SC Arts Commission should fund art, not police ideas
description: The Greenville Gay Men’s Chorus and Proud Mary Theatre Company, two LGBTQ-related arts organizations in the Upstate, had been recommended for South Carolina Arts Commission grants through the agency’s normal review process. The agency’s governing board approved grants for more than 170 other organizations. But commissioners singled out these two and postpone[...]
text:
The Greenville Gay Men's Chorus, founded in 2011, consists of more than 35 tenors and basses "dedicated to artistic excellence, meaningful collaboration, and the power of choral music to build community and connection," according to the group's website. (Photo courtesy of Nakeshia Shannon)The Greenville Gay Men’s Chorus and Proud Mary Theatre Company, two LGBTQ-related arts organizations in the Upstate, had been recommended for South Carolina Arts Commission grants through the agency’s normal review process.
The agency’s governing board approved grants for more than 170 other organizations. But commissioners singled out these two and postponed their grants until they can make another case for their artistic merit.
Why? The answer appears to have less to do with the quality of their art than with the ideas commissioners believe the organizations represent.
That should concern anyone who believes an arts commission ought to promote the arts rather than police the ideas expressed through them.
South Carolina law says that state arts policy should encourage and assist the arts “rather than limiting the freedom of artistic expression that is essential for the well-being of the arts.”
That language is bold and inspiring. It specifically tells the state to encourage artistic expression rather than limit it.
It is difficult to imagine a more direct statement of what an arts commission is supposed to do — and what it is not supposed to do.
The commission’s recent resolution says it may require grant recipients to certify that no Arts Commission money will be used for “expression that promotes an ideology.”
That raises a rather obvious question: What, exactly, is ideology?
If it means that art expresses ideas about the world, human beings and how we ought to live, then virtually all serious art becomes “ideological.”
Consider some of the greatest works in the Western artistic tradition.
Mozart’s “Requiem” expresses a profoundly Christian understanding of death, judgment, sin, mercy and redemption. So do Handel’s “Messiah,” Verdi’s “Requiem,” and Mahler’s “Resurrection Symphony.”
Walk through any museum filled with Old Master paintings. Michelangelo, Caravaggio and Rembrandt created works expressing ideas about God, humanity, suffering, salvation and the sacred.
Would we say that a symphony orchestra should not receive a state arts grant because the music it performs promotes “the ideology of the sacred”?
The Q-word and the angry, divisive state of SC politics

Of course not.
There is a perfectly sensible reason: The government supports the art because it is artistically meritorious, not because it agrees with the theology expressed in it.
The same principle applies across the artistic spectrum.
Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 expresses a vision of universal brotherhood. “Les Misérables” explores poverty, justice, mercy and redemption.
Great art routinely asks us to think about what is right and wrong, beautiful and ugly, just and unjust, sacred and profane.
Indeed, what makes much great art great is precisely that it means something — often something profound.
If expressing ideas makes a work “ideological,” then virtually every serious arts organization in South Carolina would have to defend itself for expressing ideas that make us think.
And that is why the question before the Arts Commission shouldn’t be whether it approves of the ideas associated with the Gay Men’s Chorus of Greenville or Proud Mary Theatre Company.
The question should be much simpler: Is the art good?
The commission’s own grant-review process answered that question in the affirmative.

Proud Mary Theatre Company actors perform in “The Book of Merman” comedy in August. (Photo courtesy of Proud Mary Theatre Company)

According to published reports, the organizations were among those recommended for funding ($13,050 for the chorus, less than $4,000 for the theatre company) before commissioners intervened.
Both organizations have also received Arts Commission grants in the past, without an apparent concern over ideology.
An arts grant is not an endorsement of everything an organization believes. It is an investment in the state’s cultural life.
South Carolina is enriched by having a broad range of artistic organizations — orchestras and theater companies, dance troupes and museums, gospel choirs and chamber ensembles, traditional artists and artists who challenge traditional ideas.
We don’t make our culture stronger by narrowing that range.
There is also a larger American principle at stake. We are a nation built on freedom of speech and artistic expression. Those freedoms aren’t reserved for ideas that happen to be popular with the people holding political power.
Government doesn’t have to agree with an artist to recognize the artist’s right to create.
As someone who has watched the South Carolina Arts Commission for three decades, I have seen it stay above the culture wars that have increasingly poisoned our public life.
That has been one of the commission’s strengths — and one of the reasons its current course is so disappointing.
The Arts Commission has an important role in South Carolina’s civic life precisely because it has generally resisted turning the arts into another battlefield in our culture wars.
Its current course is a departure from that tradition — and a reminder of why the commission’s independence matters.
The state should judge art on its merits and leave the ideas to the artists and their audiences.
The Greenville Gay Men’s Chorus, founded in 2011, consists of more than 35 tenors and basses. (Photo courtesy of Nakeshia Shannon)

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan rabbis push El-Sayed to change  rhetoric on Israel, ensure safety of Jewish community
description: The road ahead for Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed remains lined with speedbumps and fences to be mended, particularly with members of Michigan’s Jewish community who don’t like his rhetoric on Israel. A new coalition of Jewish clergy and synagogue lay leaders in Michigan launched a new group Tuesday  and called on El-Sayed to […]
text:
Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed at an election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. The Democratic primary for U.S. Senate was too close to call at the time he spoke. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)The road ahead for Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed remains lined with speedbumps and fences to be mended, particularly with members of Michigan’s Jewish community who don’t like his rhetoric on Israel.
A new coalition of Jewish clergy and synagogue lay leaders in Michigan launched a new group Tuesday  and called on El-Sayed to affirm “baseline community needs” — among them being a commitment to their safety, respect for their identities, political participation and self determination.
The coalition, Nonnegotiable Michigan, says it represents 40,000 Jewish voters in the state and characterized its demands of El-Sayed as “an invitation” to address urgent needs from Michigan’s Jewish community if he expects their votes in the Nov. 3. general election.
“Protecting the human dignity of every individual is a fundamental Jewish mandate,” the group said in a launch statement. “That is why American Jews helped build the movements at the forefront of the progressive coalition. Our community has been a relentless force standing up to the assaults on history, science, healthcare, inclusion, voting rights, abortion access, immigrant justice, climate action, LGBTQ equality and the rule of law itself.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The group is asking Jews across Michigan to sign a petition calling on El-Sayed to commit to a list of principles, including:

Jewish safety, including the safety of Zionist Jews, is nonnegotiable;
The right of Jews to define their own identities is nonnegotiable;
Jewish sovereignty in Israel is nonnegotiable;
The full participation of Jews, including Zionist Jews, in American political life is nonnegotiable; and
An affirmative vision for a better future for the Middle East is nonnegotiable.

El-Sayed is invested in making inroads, his campaign says
El-Sayed has been highly critical of the United States’ relationship with Israel — particularly the nation’s war against Hamas in Gaza. Groups including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, Doctors Without Borders and an independent United Nations body contend that Israel’s actions have amounted to a genocide against the Palestinian people.
El-Sayed also made the American Israel Public Affairs Committee a key target during his August primary race against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), which spent heavily on Stevens’ behalf due to her pro-Israel stance. AIPAC said it planned to spend big against El-Sayed again in the general election and in support of his opponent, former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake, who is also pro-Israel. However, Republicans have asked AIPAC to back off of funding Rogers in the general election, citing their involvement as potentially politically toxic.
The Democratic nominee’s rhetoric about Israel has some Jews in Michigan feeling fearful and threatened as antisemitism rises across the nation, fueled in part by a growing opposition to  Israel’s military actions, and have said they no longer feel safe or welcome in the Democratic Party. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel was among Jewish elected officials who said that she would be skipping the party’s summer nominating convention after its spring convention ended with many Jewish Democrats saying they were harassed by pro-Palestinian delegates and attendees. 
Over the last few weeks, one of the sharpest voices in that movement has been Rabbi Asher Lopatin, leader of the Kehillat Etz Chayim congregation in Huntington Woods. Lopatin is also the Jewish Federation of Greater Ann Arbor’s director of community relations.
U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers speaks at a “Democrats for Rogers” event in Detroit, Mich on Aug. 20, 2026 (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
In late August, Lopatin joined Rogers’ effort to court disaffected Democrats to support his campaign. By proxy, that also included a push to attract Jewish voters to join his Democrats for Rogers coalition.
It has been incumbent on El-Sayed to mend those broken ties with the Democratic Jewish community, El-Sayed’s campaign said Tuesday. Over the past few weeks, El-Sayed has been in regular communication with Jewish leaders across Michigan, focusing on party unity and building a strong coalition to beat Rogers in the fall.
Some of that work has included closed-door meetings with prominent Jewish organizations, at both the state and national level, and conversations directly with rabbis.
In one of his earliest press conferences as the Democratic nominee, El-Sayed reaffirmed his commitment to protecting Jewish Michiganders as the state’s next senator.
“To all of my sisters and brothers of the Jewish faith … I want you to know that my commitment to Jewish safety is the same as the commitment I have to the safety of my own daughters,” El-Sayed said then. “I stand in solidarity with my sisters and brothers, and we can condemn antisemitism and at the same time we can be talking about how to bring people together.”
Concerns over El-Sayed still linger with the Jewish community
Nonnegotiable Michigan’s founding leaders include Rabbi Aaron Starr, spiritual leader of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield and president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis, and Rabbi Josh Whinston, a leading progressive Reform rabbi at Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor. The list also includes nine other rabbis and congregation leaders.
In a press conference Tuesday afternoon, Whinston, who defined himself as leaning left politically, said that he has had multiple conversations with El-Sayed and has valued those talks.
“I’m somebody who cares deeply about the future of the Palestinian people and their their ability for self-determination, and I also care deeply about about Israeli Jews, Israelis in general, their ability to continue to have self determination and to defend themselves, and as well Jewish safety primarily here in Michigan,” Whinston said. “That is of the utmost importance to me, as one might imagine, the safety of my community and making sure that the kind of rhetoric that we hear from our elected officials, and from those seeking our vote, do not put the Jewish community in harm’s way. That is a primary concern of mine, as it should be for everyone.”



Quotation







I want to help him figure out a way to continue to move the needle in ways that will be meaningful for the Jewish community and would have real effect on any potential policy that he’s a part of when he’s elected to the Senate. I think he’s trying to figure it out, but he hasn’t figured it out yet.


– Rabbi Josh Whinston, a leading progressive Reform rabbi at Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor


Whinston said he appreciated and accepted El-Sayed’s apology over his remarks on the Temple Israel attack, in which El-Sayed condemned the violent attack on a West Bloomfield temple, but also said that “hurt people hurt people,” referring to the attacker, whose brother was identified by the Israeli government as a Hezbollah leader killed in an Israeli airstrike.
The concern was that El-Sayed had suggested that the violence at the temple “could be understood through the lens of Israeli actions,” said Temple Israel Rabbi Jen Lader in an op-ed published by The Free Press. Ladder also called El-Sayed’s remark offensive.
During an annual, pre-Michigan Democratic Convention meeting of the Michigan Jewish Democratic Caucus, known as their Summer Simcha and held in the weeks following the August primary,, El-Sayed formally apologized for those remarks.
In his conversations with Whinston, specifically, the rabbi said it was apparent that El-Sayed was trying to figure out a way forward.
“I want to help him figure out a way to continue to move the needle in ways that will be meaningful for the Jewish community and would have real effect on any potential policy that he’s a part of when he’s elected to the Senate,” Whinston said. “I think he’s trying to figure it out, but he hasn’t figured it out yet.”
Still, Whinston said that apology hadn’t gone far enough, and much more work needed to be done by El-Sayed and his campaign.
Starr said El-Sayed is trying to  bridge a gap with the Jewish community, but his previous rhetoric cut deeply.
“We hope that there will be another bridge between where he is now and where he can go in the future,” Starr said. “Frankly, I hope that Dr. El-Sayed, if he is elected to be our senator, or if Congressman Rogers is elected to be our senator, that they will stand up and that they will condemn violent rhetoric against the Jewish people, violent rhetoric against Israel and its right to exist. That’s what we’re asking for. We’re asking for someone to step up and be an ally, to work toward safety and security and a better life for all Michiganders, including Jewish Michiganders.”
In response to Tuesday’s news conference, Rogers campaign spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet said that El-Sayed, who Rogers’ campaign has taken to calling a “conman,” was attempting to “flip flop his past crazy town comments,” and that the attempt was falling on deaf ears with some Democrats.
“Try all he wants to run from his extreme stances on everything from Israel/Gaza, to abolishing prisons and putting boys in girls’ sports, he’s not fooling anyone,” Brouillet told Michigan Advance.
El-Sayed’s campaign, in turn, said it will continue the work it has been doing, which has also included joining Congregation T’chiyah in Ferndale on multiple occasions for Shabbat services and Passover Seder to sitting down with Jewish Democratic leaders and interfaith clergy for candid roundtable conversations.

name: Mississippi Today
title: New thrift store aims to fill retail void left by closure of Family Dollar in south Jackson
description: Niyah Sessom discusses the massive amount of clothing to be sorted once renovations are complete at the Mega Thrift store, located on Terry  Road in south Jackson, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026.
text:
For most of the summer, the former Family Dollar on Terry Road in south Jackson has sat vacant, leaving people in the community with fewer convenient options for everyday necessities. 
Family Dollar’s shutdown in May is part of a recurrent theme of business closures in the capital city in recent years, with south and west Jackson hit the hardest. 
Now, over 41,000 pounds of clothing fill the store’s back room, visible through the glass doors of the storefront.
George Roethemeyer, left, and Niyah Sessom talk of renovations inside the the soon-to-open Mega Thrift store, located on Terry Road in south Jackson, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The mountain of clothing is part of what Niyah Sessom and George Roethemeyer have been working toward — a new secondhand goods store named Mega Thrift.
The store will sit adjacent to Roses, a regional discount store, in the Roses Plaza in southwest Jackson. Owned by Nashville-based Brookwood Capital Advisors, the plaza has undergone renovations the past two years. 
According to company founder Ben Hamd, $900,000 has been put into the plaza and the July opening of the Roses. The parking lot also hosts a flea market on weekends — an effort to turn the space into a community hub, Hamd said.
Renovations are currently underway to prepare Mega Thrift for an opening no later than Oct. 1, according to Roethemeyer, who serves as the store’s property manager. To keep the community informed of their progress, the store posts “A Day in the Life” videos on social media. 
“You’re really seeing a sense of community emerge online, and I think that’s going to translate to a real world community where people want to get involved with something like this,” Hamd said.
The store’s pricing model is what stands out. Most items are marked below $5, with clothing costing customers $1.79. Those who donate items get a 50% discount on their next purchase.
“We don’t cherry-pick our inventory,” Sessom said. “So whatever we get, we put out there.” 
After Family Dollar closed its doors, Hamd said Brookwood Capital attempted to lease the building to grocery chains, but was unsuccessful.
The Mega Thrift store, right, in the former Family Dollar store, is adjacent to the new Roses Discount Store on Terry Road, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, in south Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“In a perfect world I would have loved to put a grocery store, because I think it’s needed in southwest Jackson,” Hamd said. “But this is the next best thing.”
The lack of options continues to leave south and west Jacksonians without access to food unless they travel to other local communities. 
“Even though it’s a thrift store, it could be the beginning for other types of stores,” said Johnny Byrd, the vice president of the Association of South Jackson Neighborhoods. 
He said the new thrift shop could help keep “bad actors” out of the area.
Ward 7 City Councilmember Kevin Parkinson and Ward 6 Councilmember Lashia Brown-Thomas, who represent swaths of south Jackson, have voiced their frustrations about the recurrent closures in the area, telling Mississippi Today in May that they had met with several groups who were planning projects in the area. 
Parkinson said the area still has potential for development as residents want to support more local businesses. 
“They’re tired of going to Byram,” Parkinson said. “They want Jackson options and I think they deserve Jackson options.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Laurene Powell Jobs and Darren Walker are keynote speakers for Mississippi Today 10th anniversary event
description: Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, and Darren Walker, president and CEO of Anonymous Content and former president of the Ford Foundation, will headline Mississippi Today's 10th Anniversary Celebration on Oct. 7 in Jackson.
text:
Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, and Darren Walker, president and CEO of Anonymous Content and former president of the Ford Foundation, will headline Mississippi Today’s 10th Anniversary Celebration on Oct. 7 in Jackson.
Bill Bynum, founding CEO of HOPE and a national leader in community development, will moderate the conversation between two of the nation’s most influential voices in philanthropy, storytelling and social impact. The nonprofit newsroom is marking a decade of mission-driven reporting and launching its next chapter serving communities across the state.
The celebration is part of a two-day anniversary event that includes Mississippi Today’s second annual “All In on Mississippi” summit on Oct. 8 beginning at 1 p.m. at the Two Mississippi Museums. 
“Mississippi Today was founded on the belief that independent, nonprofit journalism could strengthen our state,” said Emily Wagster Pettus, editor-in-chief of Mississippi Today. “We’re honored to welcome two global leaders whose work reflects that same belief — that informed communities, powerful storytelling and bold ideas can create meaningful change.”
A conversation on storytelling, democracy and the future
Powell Jobs and Walker will appear together during the Mississippi Today 10th anniversary event in conversation with Bynum, exploring the role of storytelling and journalism in strengthening democracy and expanding opportunity.
Their discussion will frame an evening celebrating the impact of independent journalism while looking ahead to the challenges and opportunities facing communities across Mississippi and the South.
About Laurene Powell Jobs
Laurene Powell Jobs is the founder and president of Emerson Collective, a company that combines venture investing and philanthropy to address some of the most consequential challenges in education, economic mobility, immigration and energy.
She founded the Waverley Street Foundation to support community-driven climate solutions and College Track to help students become the first in their families to graduate from college, with continued support as they begin their careers. She also co-founded the XQ Institute to drive innovation in high school education.
She is the lead investor and board chair of The Atlantic, board chair of College Track and a member of the Ford Foundation board.
About Darren Walker
Darren Walker brings decades of leadership across philanthropy, finance and the arts. Currently, he serves as president and CEO of Anonymous Content, leading the company’s next phase of growth — overseeing its management and commercial business, guiding its international partnerships, and shaping a global strategy across film, television, and emerging media. 
Prior to Anonymous, Walker served as president of the Ford Foundation for more than 10 years, which followed leadership roles at Rockefeller Foundation, the Abyssinian Development Corporation and senior  positions across international law and finance. 
He is president of the board of the National Gallery of Art and advises some of the world’s most prominent organizations on governance, strategy and leadership. Additional board service includes the Ralph Lauren Corporation, the Obama Foundation, Bloomberg L.P., the Clooney Foundation for Justice, the Waverley Street Foundation, the Perelman Performing Arts Center and Art Bridges. 
A trusted connector across business and culture, Walker has long championed artists and storytellers worldwide. His move into media reflects a belief that great storytelling not only shapes culture but defines it.
Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration
Taking place at the Two Mississippi Museums on Wednesday, Oct. 7, the celebration will honor a decade of public service journalism through an evening of conversation, music, storytelling and immersive experiences that showcase the newsroom’s work.
Guests will hear firsthand accounts of the newsroom’s impact while getting a look at Mississippi Today’s vision for the future. The celebration is made possible through sponsorship from Carol and John Palmer, Collaborative Solutions LLC and The McMullan O’Connor Fund. 
‘All In on Mississippi’ summit
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Mississippi Today will host the second annual “All In on Mississippi” summit, focused on innovative solutions, economic opportunity and community impact.
Presented with support from JPMorgan Chase, the Foundation for the Mid South, Centuri, Butler Snow and Brown Bottling Group, the summit will bring together leaders from business, education, workforce development, philanthropy and journalism for forward-looking conversations about Mississippi’s future.
Featured sessions include:

Boots on the Ground: Mississippi Industry, AI and the Future of Work.
A New Era for Apprenticeship Programs in Mississippi.
The Literacy Launching Point and What Comes Next.
Mississippi on the National Stage.

Additional speakers and agenda details will be announced in the coming weeks.
Tickets and sponsorships
Celebration tickets begin at $150, with additional options including premium seating, tables and sponsorship packages.
Tickets for the “All In on Mississippi” summit are $25.
Organizations interested in sponsorship opportunities can contact sponsorships@mississippitoday.org.
Registration, sponsorship information and the latest event updates are available at summit.mississippitoday.org.
Editor’s note: Emerson Collective is a funder of Mississippi Today. Donors to Mississippi Today have no influence or control over editorial decisions.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska state employees union enters negotiation phase for next two-year contract
description: LINCOLN — On the eve of new negotiations beginning for their next two-year contract, members of the largest union representing Nebraska state employees gathered near the state Capitol to share what terms they’re seeking. The Nebraska Association of Public Employees, known to many as NAPE/AFSCME, will begin contract negotiations Wednesday with state officials[...]
text:
Justin Hubly, executive director of the Nebraska Association of Public Employees, speaks at a rally Sept. 8, 2026 celebrating the start of new contract negotiations. Behind him (from left to right) are members of the NAPE negotiation team Madeline Kettler, Brandon Brown and Melissa Schmid. (Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — On the eve of new negotiations beginning for their next two-year contract, members of the largest union representing Nebraska state employees gathered near the state Capitol to share what terms they’re seeking.
The Nebraska Association of Public Employees, known to many as NAPE/AFSCME, will begin contract negotiations Wednesday with state officials to set the terms of the next two-year labor contract, which runs from July 1, 2027-June 30, 2029. The negotiations phase typically lasts through December, though NAPE Executive Director Justin Hubly said their members will be at the table for as long as it takes to reach an agreement.
Members said their top goal is to secure wage increases that keep up with inflation. Hubly said they are hoping to track wages with the Consumer Price Index, which he estimated would amount to about 3%-4% increases per year.
Last year, NAPE officials reached an agreement with Gov. Jim Pillen’s negotiators to provide raises between 6.5% and 19% over the next two years. Coming off that, along with the state’s continuing budget deficit, Hubly said meeting that goal would be challenging, though he’s optimistic.
“They will try to balance the budget on our backs if we don’t continue to negotiate,” Hubly said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Hubly and other NAPE members said negotiators will need to get creative to balance the state’s financial strain and their requests. Madeline Kettler, communications specialist for Nebraska’s Department of Veterans’ Affairs, raised the idea of promoting remote work as a way of limiting physical office space — referencing an ongoing dispute between Pillen’s office and the union.
Kettler also highlighted issues with high turnover among state employees, estimating the annual rate to be just under 20%. She said the state could save money by replacing retirees with entry-level workers, but argued that competitive salaries are needed to recruit young workers.
At least 61 employees left Nebraska Department of Economic Development within 15 months

Kettler pushed for benefits such as paid maternity leave for all new parents. NAPE’s current contract offers six weeks of paid maternity leave for eligible mothers under the Family and Medical Leave Act, which was just added in the latest round of negotiations.
In addition to wage increases, Hubly said NAPE’s next priority is stabilizing health insurance costs for members. Brandon Brown, senior agent for the Nebraska Department of Revenue, said health insurance premiums have risen nearly 25% over two years, cutting into employee salaries.
Hubly said state employees’ current health care plan guarantees a minimum level of coverage, which means costs can spike in years with catastrophic claims. He said this is why premiums have risen, and it prompted NAPE members to consider if there should be changes to the coverage plans the state offers.
“Maybe there is a time and a place to change coverage in order to help control costs,” Hubly said. “But we want to voice it now. We don’t want to just leave that to the governor to choose.”
