name: New Jersey Monitor
title: For many here illegally, self-deportation is only option
description: To avoid being deported to a country they've never lived in, some immigrants are self-deporting. Voluntary departures are skyrocketing under President Trump.
text:
Julie Moreno, a volunteer with American Families United, with her dog Topo Chico in her Newark home on April 9, 2026. Moreno's husband, Nef Juarez, self-deported to Mexico last year in October. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
This is the second in a three-part series examining President Donald Trump’s mass deportation effort and its effect on New Jersey.
Julie Moreno knew the night Donald Trump won the 2024 election that her husband would have to leave the country.
“I almost quite literally had a nervous breakdown,” she said. “All this rhetoric, all of the clear organization they put in place for more detention, more deportation. It was obvious this was going to be a totally hyper-charged administration 2.0.”
Ten months after the inauguration, her husband, Nef Juarez, boarded a plane to Mexico, a country he hadn’t been to since he moved to the U.S. more than two decades prior. 
Their story has become an increasingly common one across New Jersey and the nation, as families agonize over whether to wait out the Trump administration’s enforcement surge, hide in the shadows, or leave on their own terms before U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement decides to come for them. 
Juarez arrived from Puebla, Mexico, in 2000, while in his 20s. By 2008, he met Moreno and fell in love. Moreno, a Newark resident and advocate working with mixed-status families, married Juarez in City Hall in Manhattan in 2017, during Trump’s first term.
Juarez had no criminal record, no encounters with ICE during his time in America, and no deportation order, Moreno said during an interview in her Newark apartment. But under immigration laws dating back to 1996, his path to legal status was effectively blocked, having entered the country illegally without authorization. That triggers what’s referred to as an inadmissibility bar, which prevented him from applying for a marriage-based visa.
The couple had tried three separate times to obtain status for Juarez before learning he was ineligible for a consular appointment. They lived in a legal limbo they learned to navigate, Moreno said. They worked and resided in New Jersey, largely without fear, and his status was just a reality of their lives, she added. 
But Moreno, 47, stressed that Trump’s second term felt different from his first. She pointed to Project 2025 and the shift in aggressive language surrounding enforcement, detention, and deportation. 
“It became obvious that they had the structure to actually do what they talked about the first time,” she said. “Families like ours, we became scared.” 
What accelerated the decision for Juarez to leave was the news that federal officials weighed repurposing Fort Dix as an immigration detention center. That hasn’t happened, but the plan would add 3,000 beds to the enforcement infrastructure in New Jersey. And Delaney Hall in Newark had just opened its doors as a migrant jail after years of being shuttered. 
“That was a huge red flag,” she said. “We saw exactly what this was going to be. It was a nightmare, really.” 
In October, Juarez boarded a plane to Mexico, leaving his life — and his wife — behind. 
A photo from 2017 of Julie Moreno, a volunteer with American Families United, and her husband, Nef Juarez, who self-deported to Mexico in October 2025. (Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Moreno works with American Families United, a national nonprofit organization representing U.S. citizens in mixed-status marriages, an estimated 1.5 million households across the country. The organization is pushing for the passage of the American Families United Act, a bill in Congress that would create a waiver process allowing couples like Moreno and Juarez to petition for relief from inadmissibility bars on a case-by-case basis. It has not moved forward.
Experts and advocates note that people who opt for voluntary departure are not necessarily doing so because they want to leave. Some have legal avenues to remain in the U.S., but dismal detention conditions and the steep uphill battle of finding legal representation for court proceedings have pushed them toward departure. 
The Vera Institute of Justice found that monthly voluntary departures surged from a few hundred at the end of the Biden administration to over 9,000 in a single month by March 2026. In all, immigration judges issued over 80,000 voluntary departure orders between January 2025 and March 2026 — a 600% jump from the final 15 months of the Biden administration, according to Vera Institute data reviewed by the Washington Post. And that doesn’t include people like Juarez who decided to leave before getting involved in the judicial system. 
More than 70% of people granted voluntary departure under Trump’s second term were being held in immigration detention when they requested to leave, the data showed, and Vera researchers have said the rise is happening alongside, not instead of, formal removal orders, meaning people facing deportation orders have even slimmer chances that they’ll stay in the U.S. 
New Jersey-specific figures are not publicly available, and ICE did not provide those numbers. 
According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, more than 2 million immigrants without legal status have voluntarily self-deported since Trump took office in January 2025. 
Trump administration officials claim over 100,000 have used a federal app on the DHS website to do so, although the department has not released data to substantiate that figure, and outside researchers have repeatedly challenged it. A Brookings Institution report said the department’s numbers “should not be considered a serious source,” and separate reporting by The Atlantic and ProPublica found the verifiable count of app-assisted departures was far lower, in the tens of thousands.
Homeland Security officials have repeatedly responded to questions about its detention and deportation effort by saying “being in detention is a choice.”
“We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said. “We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”
Rep. Rob Menendez speaks outside of Delaney Hall on Dec. 23, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08) makes regular visits, both announced and unannounced, to Delaney Hall and meets with detainees inside. Menendez, a co-sponsor of the American Families United Act, said some of them are forced into signing self-deportation orders without understanding what they’re reading. 
He said it’s all part of the Trump administration’s tactics: Scare people who are woven into the fabric of New Jersey’s communities into self-deporting or put them in a jail that “breaks them.” 
“What they are doing in there is trying to create conditions where people are so demoralized, they sign voluntary departure papers to not have to be in there anymore,” he said in May. “I think what they’re trying to do inside is they’re trying to break people, so people give up.” 
ICE did not respond to questions about how many people detained at Delaney Hall have self-deported, or to Menendez’s characterization that people are being coerced into signing these forms. 
Moreno explained that her husband made his choice knowingly, without being put into detention. It was one of the hardest choices they ever had to make, she said, and it weighs on her constantly as she walks through the empty apartment she shares now with two dogs and a cat. 
“That life of ours is dead and gone,” she said with pain in her voice. “We know there’s no going back on that decision.” 
A photo from 2017 of Julie Moreno, a volunteer with American Families United, and her husband, Nef Juarez. (Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
The transition has been difficult in ways she couldn’t anticipate. He shouldered much of the daily tasks in their life: running errands, picking up prescriptions, carrying the load of the small business of packaging and importing boxing gloves that they built together. He also did construction work. And now, with him thousands of miles away, she said, depression made ordinary tasks feel heavy, and she described the months after his departure as drowning.
“Everything felt like it was dragging me down, stuff both small and big,” Moreno said. “The life we expected to have, the life that we were working towards, I’m holding on by my teeth trying to keep things together now.”
In March, she visited him in Mexico for a family wedding. Seeing him eased fears that time apart would erode what they had built, and she said she wants to relocate to Mexico after her nephew graduates high school. 
She said Juarez’s family was relieved to have him home, and he’s shared months with his elderly mother they may not have otherwise spent together — a silver lining. But the distance between them remains, she stressed. 
“I miss him, but it felt like not one single day had passed. We’re really tight still,” she said. They have plans for a road trip when she visits again in the summer to find a spot for their next home. She smiles at the thought of seeing him again. 
But for now, she keeps advocating — even louder than when Juarez was here, she says, because there’s nothing left to protect by staying quiet. She talks to other families in American Families United who are making similar calculations, quietly researching what documents they may need and scoping out regions of Mexico for where they’ll land.
“People are not necessarily naming dates, but they really, seriously are making their plans to leave,” she said.
This story was produced as part of the Center for Cooperative Media at Montclair State University’s 2025 NJ News Commons Investigative Reporting Initiative, and supported with funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri schools deserve better than a single letter grade
description: As the parent of a public education student and a parent organizer, I am concerned about the governor’s proposed A-F School Grading Framework that requires the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education  to implement a plan that will assign a single letter grade to our public schools and districts. The current plan to calculate this […]
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024 (Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch).As the parent of a public education student and a parent organizer, I am concerned about the governor’s proposed A-F School Grading Framework that requires the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education  to implement a plan that will assign a single letter grade to our public schools and districts.
The current plan to calculate this letter grade is mostly based on the Missouri Assessment Program tests taken by public education students in the spring.
The use of the A-F framework is flawed and will not improve student outcomes. A low grade won’t result in the school or district receiving any additional state funding for reading intervention or math programs and it won’t raise teacher pay to attract and retain quality teachers.
Multiple states that previously adopted letter grade systems halted their programs. A district court ruling and multiple studies found the scorecard systems did not accurately reflect the performance of the school.
Under the A-F framework, only public and charter schools get a letter grade. Private schools, including those that receive our tax dollars through private school vouchers, won’t receive one and they aren’t even required to take MAP tests. If this framework is truly an effective way to measure school success, it should apply to all schools in Missouri that receive public education funding dollars to allow for a more accurate comparison.
A low letter grade impacts more than just the school itself and should concern any group interested in the public perception of a community. People consider the success of a school district when deciding where to raise a family or start a business. The letter grade will become a representation of the community as a whole.
A single letter grade ignores the hard work of public school educators by measuring success solely based on their student’s performance on a single standardized test. Most importantly, this one test doesn’t reflect a student’s knowledge, curiosity, problem solving, creativity, kindness, or future success.
This framework is deeply flawed and should not be implemented because of the harm it will cause our kids, our teachers and our communities. Questions from school districts and community group questions have gone unanswered because the planned implementation is being rushed.
Missouri school districts cannot afford a rushed framework implementation that results in an inaccurate grading system. I urge the State Board of Education to pause the fall preview.

name: WyoFile
title: Amid national backlash, Wyomingites fight Flock while police defend surveillance cameras
authors: By Maya Shimizu Harris, Charles Farmer, Jeannette Boner and Danielle Wilson
description:
Glenrock, Green River and other communities question use of license plate readers over lack of transparency, cost to taxpayers and risk of unreasonable search and seizure. 
The post Amid national backlash, Wyomingites fight Flock while police defend surveillance cameras appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The police chief turned his table to face a standing-room-only gallery in Glenrock’s aging town hall. With the Glenrock Town Council behind him, Police Chief Colter Felton sat for more than an hour explaining Flock cameras to an audience that alternated between concerned and agitated.
“To be clear, I am not in any way suggesting that any member of our town government or our law enforcement here is planning to misuse this program,” Rolling Hills resident Tim Cain told the council. “But evidence shows that the potential for harm across the country … outweighs the potential for good.”
The revelation that the Glenrock Police Department operates five Flock Falcon 2.2 model cameras — four in Glenrock, and one in neighboring Rolling Hills, which Glenrock police patrol — has ignited a furor among residents of this small, central Wyoming community.
Public anxiety over automated license plate reader technology and government surveillance has spilled over from city hall onto city streets in Wyoming and nationally. Cameras from Flock Safety, an Atlanta-based company, have particularly drawn attention. 
A Flock Safety Automated License Plate Reader camera on the east side of Glenrock was installed two years ago. (Charles Farmer/Douglas Budget)
Flock’s system uses artificial intelligence to monitor and photograph passing vehicles. That information is uploaded to a central system that participating law enforcement agencies can search — though Glenrock and Jackson limit data sharing. There are now roughly 120,000 Flock cameras operating in every state but Alaska, and more than 7,000 law enforcement agencies use the technology, according to the New York Times. If you’ve been driving any notable amount over the past few years, chances are your car’s been recorded by the system.
In southwestern Wyoming, what began as a debate over federal grant funding and data privacy in Green River morphed into viral social media speculation and property damage in neighboring Rock Springs. On the other side of the state, Cheyenne police have embraced the cameras while the Laramie County sheriff has avoided them due to concerns about violating the U.S. Constitution’s Fourth Amendment, which protects against unlawful searches. 
Some Wyoming law enforcement agencies view the technology as a vital tool to help catch fleeing suspects, locate runaways and track stolen vehicles. But vocal contingents of residents argue the systems represent an unconstitutional expansion of public surveillance.
The value of surveillance
In Glenrock, the cameras have been in place for two years after being added during a council budget session, which many residents now see as a sleight-of-hand maneuver to install them. Nearby Rolling Hills uses a single camera, which the council there considered during a regular session that drew a handful of opponents who spoke against installing the camera to monitor the community of about 400 people. The cameras cost $15,000 per year, or $3,000 per device, although the first year was a touch over $19,000 with installation costs.
Glenrock’s particular model of cameras takes pictures day and night, but doesn’t record vehicle speeds or video. The driver’s face isn’t visible through the windshield. According to Chief Felton, the cameras can search for details such as “red Ford Focus with bumper stickers,” but not, say, “Trump sticker” or “Biden sticker.” 
While Glenrock has a more basic model, Flock also sells cameras that can record video or take more detailed pan, tilt and zoom shots, according to the company’s website. 
During the Aug. 25 meeting, local residents detailed their concerns, occasionally interrupting the speaker as they expressed fears about a lack of oversight, uncertainty over Flock as a company and the security of photos stored for 30 days at a time. They questioned whether this type of surveillance violates their civil liberties. 
At the individual level, one car passing a camera isn’t valuable. But when that same car passes multiple cameras at different locations and times, and they’re all communicating through Flock’s network, a savvy investigator can piece together a path of travel for a car without leaving their office, and, notably, without a warrant. 
The potential benefits have spurred some tribes to allow license plate readers on reservations to enhance public safety in the face of officer staffing shortages and patchy enforcement due to complex, overlapping jurisdictions.  
License plate reader cameras are in use on the Fort Peck Reservation in northeastern Montana, American Indian Movement Montana co-Director Lance Fourstar said. “I can remember a couple years ago, before the cameras were installed, we were having fentanyl overdoses like every day. And that stopped. The methamphetamine [use has] quieted down quite a bit. And we’ve used those cameras to save people that are being trafficked — all the way down in southern California.”
Fourstar said AIM and other activists vetted these license plate readers “so that they wouldn’t be abused by their law enforcement or governments towards our people and our exercising of freedom of speech.” 


A Flock Safety license plate reader is seen along a public road, Oct. 16, 2025, in Houston. (AP Photo/David Goldman, File)

Local data, national reach
Flock’s product is data. When an agency participates in the national Flock network — Glenrock does not, according to Felton — it is logged into a searchable database that any officer with access can use to retrieve data, regardless of their location. To search, a unique case number and reason are required, such as “grand larceny” or another type of crime. In the last 30 days as of this writing, Glenrock’s cameras have identified 16,897 vehicles. Police have made seven searches during the same period.
Law enforcement have other means for obtaining pictures of cars and license plates on public roads — an investigator could go to a local bank, for example, and ask to see security cameras, and if the private business gives permission, the investigator has access without a warrant. 
But the network and amalgamation of this information that Flock provides is unique and has been found to sometimes lack adequate guardrails to protect against abuse. An officer in South Florida, for instance, used the system to search a woman he met on the set of a television show, using the system to track her, pull her over and ask her out. He was later arrested. The Washington Post has identified at least 50 incidents of officers using the system for stalking purposes.
Glenrock police don’t share Flock data with the federal government or other law enforcement without an explicit request, Felton has stressed both in interviews and to the public. 
Flock gives agencies the option to opt out of certain features, and in some cases, it’s as simple as flipping an off switch in the settings menu. There are options for immigration and abortion investigations, among others. Felton showed those two switches were turned off during his demonstration with the Douglas Budget.
Since Flock’s contract states that the company doesn’t own any of the data, the onus falls on law enforcement and local regulations to securely store and disseminate that information. In the case of Glenrock, that oversight falls to Felton.
Councilmember Judi Colling, who is running against incumbent Mayor Bruce Roumell in November, has concerns with the system.
“I think a publicly registered vehicle on a public road does not have the right to privacy that some people believe,” Colling said. “However, when you add in the possibility of misuse and abuse by public officials, that’s a real concern, and that is something we need to look into. Until I am convinced that the guardrails are in place to protect people from possible misuse and abuse, I have to say I am opposed to the usage.”
The council, as well as Felton, were open to more oversight of the system.
“I don’t have any problem with auditing,” Mayor Roumell said. “I think if somebody’s going to audit it, it should be another outside law enforcement agency, somebody outside the county. It’s not just going to be an independent somebody off the street that doesn’t know what they’re looking at.”
Glenrock’s contract is up for renewal this fall.
Surveillance tech stirs up Sweetwater County
In Green River, controversy over the cameras culminated when the southwestern Wyoming community’s city council considered a $112,000 state homeland security grant. The 100% federally funded grant would have allowed the Green River Police Department to acquire automated license plate readers manufactured by Motorola.
Green River Police Chief Shaun Sturlaugson tried to assure residents in the community of 11,000 people that police would use the cameras reactively rather than proactively. During a city council meeting, the chief clarified that officers would not use the cameras for routine traffic enforcement like identifying expired registrations, but rather to receive automated alerts when a vehicle tied to a national crime database or missing child rolled into town. He added that data retained in Motorola’s cloud system would be automatically scrubbed in under 30 days.
Despite the chief’s assurances, residents packed council chambers to express deep distrust over private vendor data storage, potential Fourth Amendment violations and setting a precedent of monitoring law-abiding citizens.
Green River Police Chief Shaun Sturlaugson speaks about potential automated license plate readers during the July 7 city council meeting. (Screenshot)
Among those who spoke was Dennis Laughlin, a local business owner and vice chair of the Wyoming Libertarian Party. Laughlin commended police but urged caution introducing surveillance infrastructure.
“Green River PD, you guys … I really have never felt safer,” Laughlin told the mayor and council. “That being said … I think maybe the fact that nobody has gotten up here and been like, ‘Yeah, let’s do this,’ maybe think against doing this.”
Laughlin praised the public for thoroughly researching the potential legal and privacy pitfalls associated with private software vendors like Motorola. He urged the council to examine how software architecture and third-party data distribution function before committing the town to automated surveillance systems.
Ultimately, the Green River City Council voted 6-1 to reject the grant agreement, forfeiting the federal dollars. Councilman Gary Killpack cast the sole “Yes” vote, arguing that neighboring jurisdictions already use the cameras and that rejecting the grant limits local law enforcement’s investigative capabilities without eliminating tracking elsewhere.
While Green River turned down the technology, rumors regarding surveillance swirled in its larger neighbor, Rock Springs. 
As online rumors escalated, vandals tampered with and damaged city property. The city and the police department responded with a statement clarifying what technology has been installed and warning against destroying municipal infrastructure. Rock Springs police do not use Flock cameras, and the damaged equipment turned out to be solar panels installed by the city’s streets department to power streetlights. A private business installed the downtown cameras several years ago after art pieces were stolen or damaged.
While police acknowledged they could not prove vandalism resulted from the online posts, officials called the timing “concerning enough that we want to address it.” Officials cautioned residents against letting unverified social media speculation drive public action, pointing out the false assumptions can result in costly damage.
“Those solar panels and other components are there for a reason,” the city stated, noting repairs strain public funds and disrupt community services. 
While acknowledging privacy and surveillance are legitimate topics for public debate, officials urged residents to base those conversations on facts.
Growing regional debate
Amid the growing statewide debate, municipal leaders in cities like Cheyenne and Jackson have embraced Flock cameras as essential “lead generators” for criminal investigations.
License plate-reading cameras have operated in Jackson for several years, helping police investigate crimes while generating persistent questions about surveillance, data sharing and federal access. 
The Jackson Town Council voted 3-2 in 2023 to spend $184,800 to purchase and install 30 Flock cameras. Subsequent town reports have described 28 cameras operating around the northwest Wyoming city.
At the time, supporters said the cameras could deter crime, locate stolen vehicles and reduce the time officers spend searching for vehicles connected to investigations. The Jackson council has since renewed the agreement at a cost of nearly $90,000 annually.
A Flock camera, pointing north, scans each license plate that passes from a light pole along North Cache Street in Jackson on Sept. 8, 2026. (Kathryn Ziesig/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
In 2023, Jackson Councilman Arne Jorgensen voted against installing Flock, questioning the cost and whether the technology could eventually be used to track women traveling across state lines for abortions. He has since been elected mayor and voted in favor of renewing Flock’s contract after assurances Jackson has a contract and policies in place to limit how the data may be accessed and used. 
“Can we trust Flock? I don’t know,” Councilor Jonathan Schechter said at the town’s June meeting, where residents continued to raise concerns about surveillance. “Can we trust them any more than any other company that is going to be vulnerable? I don’t know.”
Police say the cameras are used in cases involving stolen vehicles, hit-and-runs, missing people, welfare checks and other incidents involving cars. Jackson Police Lt. Russ Ruschill previously told the Jackson Hole News&Guide that Flock is “another tool, like a records system or a patrol car, that helps us move faster on cases and keep families safe.”
Under Jackson’s policy, camera data must be automatically deleted after no more than 90 days. Police permanently retain an audit trail documenting searches, including when a query was conducted and what information was accessed. 
Jackson’s policies do not make the local data broadly searchable by other communities. Outside agencies must provide Police Chief Michelle Weber with a case number and supporting documentation before receiving access. Only the chief is authorized to release the information. Weber previously said Jackson had received about 15 outside requests, and none came from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or were abortion related.
Cheyenne police embrace Flock, sheriff doesn’t
The Cheyenne Police Department received city council approval in 2024 to enter a contract with Flock. The 23 cameras installed on major roads throughout the community cost the city of Cheyenne $146,300 over its two-year contract. The city is using American Rescue Plan Act funds to pay for the cameras.  





Click to enlarge: A screenshot shared by the Cheyenne Police Department shows an example of an image taken by a Flock camera of a passing department vehicle, highlighting the vehicle’s license plate. (Cheyenne Police Department)

The department also has additional automated license plate reading cameras that aren’t affiliated with Flock. These cameras are used for parking enforcement only, according to the department’s spokesperson. The agency has two parking vehicles with four total license plate cameras between them, as well as seven license plate cameras at the entrances and exits of city parking garages. These cameras are operated through the department’s parking vendor, Passport. Images from the cameras are automatically deleted after 90 days, according to the department’s spokesperson. 
The Cheyenne Police Department actually experimented with the use of license plate-reading cameras as far back as 2014, Cheyenne Police Chief Mark Francisco said during a March public meeting on Flock cameras. “It was a successful trial, but it was expensive back then,” Francisco said. “The technology was expensive, and the storage was really expensive, so it just kind of went away.” 
Francisco has described Cheyenne’s Flock system as a “lead generator” that helps solve crimes. Over the past 30 days, the cameras collected 223,424 unique plate reads, according to the Cheyenne Police Department’s Flock Transparency Portal. Cheyenne police searched the camera data 218 times and found 607 “hotlist hits” — license plate readings related to stolen vehicles, warrants or Amber Alerts. 
“Really, it’s every day we are using this technology to help solve crimes in Cheyenne,” Capt. David Janes said during the March meeting. “It’s one of those very, very common things because most people who are committing crimes and victimizing others are using vehicles to get there.”
The data helped Cheyenne police track down a sex offender who had stolen a truck from the Cody area, Janes said. Law enforcement didn’t know the license plate number of the stolen truck, but they knew it was a white Ford Ranger with a rusted top. An officer was able to narrow down camera images using that information. Even then, he had to scroll for “hours and hours and hours until he saw the picture of the white Ford Ranger with the rust on the top,” Janes said. The officer got the license plate number from a Flock camera image and used that to check for other times the truck had passed Flock cameras. Officers found that the suspect was in Fort Collins. “So they were able to go down there, find him and arrest him.” 
A three-page policy governs the Cheyenne Police Department’s use of its cameras. According to the policy, all database searches have to be associated with “an official law enforcement investigation,” and must be attached to a case number and explanation of the search’s purpose. Only trained personnel can use the equipment and databases. The data is wiped after 30 days, except for data that’s used for “evidentiary or legal purposes.” 
Cheyenne Police Department Chief Mark Francisco speaks to a room of local residents about Flock cameras at a community meeting March 11, 2026, at the Public Safety Center. (Ivy Secrest/Wyoming Tribune Eagle)
Laramie County has been a hotspot for immigration enforcement in Wyoming since the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office signed agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to enforce immigration laws. The partnership has raised concerns that the Cheyenne Police Department’s surveillance data could be used for immigration enforcement. 
The data can be shared with “law enforcement or prosecutorial agencies for official purposes,” the Cheyenne Police Department’s policy states. Agencies with signed memorandums of understanding and Flock access “may request data through the Flock system.” But Francisco told community members at the March meeting that the department doesn’t share data with ICE. “There’s really only two that we share, and I believe one was a postal service, and one was some air force base. I don’t recall the name off the top of my head, but we do not share with ICE. We use these for criminal enforcement, not civil,” he said. 
According to the department’s spokesperson, the Cheyenne Police Department hasn’t received a request from ICE to share data. 
A community member asked why there wasn’t more transparency “right at the get-go,” when the police department and city council were considering purchasing the cameras. The city council approved the contract in a “consent agenda,” meaning it was grouped with other decisions voted on all at once. 
At the time, the city was trying to decide how to spend leftover pandemic relief money, which had to be used by the end of 2024, Francisco said. “We were really under the gun, and as we worked with the mayor and city staff, I’m like, ‘I got an idea,’” the chief explained. “So literally, we had no time to do much other than get it through the system.” 
But “hindsight being 20-20,” Francisco said the department should have alerted the public that the police department and city were considering the cameras. “I take responsibility for that,” Francisco said. “These things in my world have been ubiquitous. They’re everywhere. I would have expected the citizens of Cheyenne to maybe be surprised they weren’t already here, just because they’re everywhere.” 
The city council will have to decide by February whether to renew the Flock contract.  
The Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, meanwhile, didn’t adopt Flock cameras after the company approached the agency asking if it would deploy them throughout the county. 
“Now, do I believe that there is a use for license plate readers in certain high crime areas, or if you have a big problem with auto theft? Yes, on a limited basis, yes, I do agree with that,” Sheriff Brian Kozak said in a video. 
But, noting that Flock camera systems are connected by AI, and that they can search other vehicle characteristics like color, type and bumper stickers, Kozak said he was concerned that the cameras could bring up Fourth Amendment issues. 
“For that reason, we did not deploy any cameras in unincorporated Laramie County, and I have no plan to deploy them in the future,” Kozak said. 
— Sarah Elmquist Squires of WyoToday Media contributed to this report.
The post Amid national backlash, Wyomingites fight Flock while police defend surveillance cameras appeared first on WyoFile .

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Auditor finds state nursing home inspections are often delayed
description: State auditors found that health department inspectors are lagging in their inspections of nursing homes, potentially endangering residents.
text:
State auditors found that health department inspectors are lagging in their inspections of nursing homes, potentially endangering residents. (Getty Images)Staffing levels at many New Jersey nursing homes remain inadequate and state inspections are frequently delayed, weaknesses that increase the risk to residents, a new state audit warns.
State Auditor David Kaschak released a report Tuesday based on his office’s audit of the Department of Health’s work between July 1, 2022, and March 31 of this year. The department oversees New Jersey’s 350 nursing homes, conducting at least 500 inspections and responding to at least 1,000 complaints annually.
Kaschak’s report calls the health department’s oversight of nursing homes “adequate” while noting that it has not been able to comply with state or federal regulations on the number of minimum nursing home inspections. Federal and state regulations require each nursing home to be inspected at least every 15 months, while the statewide average for all inspections must be under 12 months.
“We found the division is falling significantly short of meeting the required time frames,” Kaschak said.
Auditors found that, as of February, state inspectors were checking nursing homes every 20 months on average. More than a quarter of the facilities had not been inspected in at least two years.
In addition, more than 80% of the division’s inspections resulting from nursing home complaints were delayed, according to the report. One incident that should have triggered a facility visit within three days took 215 days for the team to examine.
Delays are a result of a COVID-19 era backlog, hiring freezes, and a loss of staff — there are now eight inspection teams, instead of 12 — and the June expiration of a contract with a company that served as a backstop for state inspectors, the auditors found.
“Without expanding the division’s current resources, an even greater strain will be put on existing staff to try and complete the necessary inspections,” Kaschak said.
State officials have faced ongoing criticism for their oversight of nursing homes during the COVID-19 pandemic, which spread rapidly in congregate housing facilities, especially among vulnerable and elderly residents at high risk for infection.
A report commissioned by former Gov. Phil Murphy identified multiple weaknesses and recommended the state strengthen its control over these facilities.
Neil Eicher, a deputy health commissioner, said staffing challenges, the lingering impact of the pandemic, and federal government closures and funding interruptions have delayed inspections. Surveys are prioritized for facilities that haven’t been recently reviewed or have complaints or poor outcomes in the past, he said.
“The Department remains committed to strengthening oversight and accountability, addressing identified gaps, and prioritizing resources based on resident health and safety” while supporting compliance with federal requirements, Eicher wrote in a response included in the report.
Andy Aronson, president and CEO of the Health Care Association of New Jersey, which represents nursing facilities, said the survey backlog will be reduced by a new, risk-based federal inspection model set to take effect this fall that will allow the state to target facilities that are most in need.
“Skilled nursing facilities in New Jersey provide an extremely high quality of care and are subject to the most rigorous inspection system of provider type in the health care system,” Aronson told the New Jersey Monitor.
New Jersey adopted a host of changes designed to strengthen state oversight of nursing homes in the wake of the pandemic, including a novel law that dictates staffing levels. Industry leaders, including the Health Care Association, sued the state claiming the mandate is unconstitutional and impossible to meet, given what they say are ongoing staffing shortages. That lawsuit is ongoing.
State auditors also found this problem continues. Five of the 11 facilities they visited and checked had staffing levels that did not meet the requirement, according to the report.
In addition, auditors found nearly a quarter of the nursing home complaints were improperly classified, contributing to inspection delays. Even when nursing home management raised a concern, it could take the state more than a year to inspect.

title: Wyoming becomes 50th state to join maternal care alliance
description:
Participation was announced at inaugural maternal care summit in Laramie, where health and policy experts gathered to discuss closing care gaps for moms and babies. 
The post Wyoming becomes 50th state to join maternal care alliance appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LARAMIE—When Wyoming recently joined the Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health — a nationwide initiative to support best practices that make births safer and improve maternal health outcomes — it was the 50th state to do so. 
However late to the party the state is, participants of Wyoming’s inaugural Maternal Health Summit used the news as a point of celebration to kick off the event last week at the University of Wyoming. With an issue as challenging and complex as maternal healthcare gaps in this rural state, every step counts, Rural Health Institute Director Laura Gilbert said. 
Alliance participation “represents an exciting opportunity for Wyoming to be part of a national commitment to eliminating preventable maternal mortality and severe maternal morbidity,” Gilbert told the audience. By quilting together solutions like this one, Wyoming will create a stronger system for mothers and babies, she said. 
“The focus of this summit is really to focus on our strengths … to learn about and build on those strengths,” she said. 
Margot Carr, center, talks about how she developed a neonatal nurse practitioner program at Ivinson Memorial Hospital, where she is manager of oncology. Erin McKinney and facilitator Joia Crear-Perry also sat on the panel during Wyoming’s inaugural Maternal Health Summit in Laramie Sept. 2-3. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Other strengths the summit zeroed in on were Wyoming’s first and only nationally accredited freestanding birth center in Cheyenne and a new partnership spearheaded by Ivinson Memorial Hospital that brings specialized neonatal and pediatric care to Laramie. Presenters explained strategies at Cheyenne Regional Hospital for creating a medical plan when an infant is identified as prenatally exposed to substances, and told the audience that Wyoming boasts one of the country’s lowest cesarean section rates. 
It was impossible to talk about Wyoming’s maternal health landscape without mentioning its weaknesses, however. The vast and sparsely populated state is dominated by census-designated frontier areas where harsh weather can make long drives perilous; recruitment obstacles result in workforce shortages; and low patient volume creates financial challenges at hospitals.  
Other factors are compounding those challenges: 
The number of births in Wyoming declined every year from 2019-2023. Since 2022, four Wyoming hospitals have closed labor and delivery wards, leaving 16 birthing hospitals for a state spanning 97,000 square miles. Wyoming has zero pediatric intensive units. Rural babies are at higher risk of low birth weight and adverse outcomes. More than 75% of pregnancy-related deaths in Wyoming between 2018-2023 were determined to be preventable. Wyoming’s percentage of induced vaginal births has grown more than 10% between 2016 and 2026 to 43%, higher than the national average.
Quality maternal health leads to strong families and thriving communities, said UW College of Health Sciences Dean Patrick Hardigan. 
“But let’s be real about the ground we’re standing on,” he said. “In a rural frontier state like ours … overcoming these hurdles isn’t something any single organization can accomplish by themselves. It takes all of us crossing disciplines, breaking down silos and building real bridges between our communities and the government.”
Low-hanging fruit
Three years after a WyoFile investigation revealed severe gaps in Wyoming’s maternity care system, deficiencies remain for women seeking prenatal, delivery and postpartum care and resources in the Equality State. Despite lengthy legislative study and statewide concern, Wyoming’s maternity care issues have actually worsened in areas like Natrona County, where the number of practicing obstetricians has gone from six to two.
When a 2025 Wyoming Women’s Action Network white paper concluded that Wyoming lags behind others in embracing and implementing solutions, it specifically highlighted the fact that Wyoming was the only state not participating in the maternal health alliance. 
That was something reproductive health researcher Gaby Alvarado recognized pretty quickly when she was researching her new home state this spring. Alvarado joined the University of Wyoming’s Rural Health Institute in March with a focus on supporting maternal health efforts in the state through a federal grant. 
Joining the alliance, she said, “felt like low-hanging fruit.”
With a green light from the health department, Alvarado said, the Rural Health Institute spearheaded the effort for Wyoming to join, which was approved in August. As a participating state, Wyoming will have access to resources for improving maternal outcomes related to substance use, severe hypertension and hemorrhaging, among others.

Participants at the inaugural Wyoming Maternal Health Summit on Sept. 2-3 in Laramie came from more than a dozen states. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)

Alvarado organized the Laramie summit, which drew obstetricians, healthcare lobbyists, policymakers and more for two days of workshops and presentations. Though Wyoming’s maternity care gaps are significant, she said, she did not want summit participants to be mired in doom and gloom. 
“I feel like public health framing is really deficit oriented,” Alvarado told WyoFile. “We wanted to also focus on strengths … what are people in Wyoming doing that is scalable and effective?”
In that vein, participants talked about Medicaid expansion opportunities, strategies for better implementing doulas and effective mental health screening. 
The summit also served as the launch of Momentum Wyoming, a new maternal health effort under the Rural Health Institute designed to survive beyond the five-year federal grant. 
Action items
One theme that emerged is that efforts to improve maternal healthcare in Wyoming are often disconnected, resulting in siloing and a lack of shared knowledge about existing resources or initiatives. 
“It’s rooms like this that can change that,” Wyoming Medical Society Executive Director Sheila Bush said in a closing panel. However, she noted, agreeing on a unified vision will be crucial to success. 
“We have to figure out what cake we’re baking when we’re looking at maternal health in the state,” she said. “I still don’t think we have a vision of what we want maternity care to look like.”  
Wyoming midwife Heidi Stearns checks an infant after a home birth. (Teal Barmore Photography)
Healthcare experts and policymakers have been mulling strategies for patching up the state’s maternity care gaps for years, including legislative studies. Those discussions have touched on everything from tort reform to workforce incentives.
This year, Wyoming has a meaningful opportunity to bolster maternity care thanks to $205 million in federal Rural Health Transformation funds. An advisory panel earmarked more than $8 million specifically for labor and delivery initiatives, and other initiatives aimed at hospitals and telehealth are also expected to improve maternity care access. 
For Wyoming Rep. Mike Yin, D-Jackson, who sits on the Legislature’s labor and health committee, the summit was valuable for better understanding how maternity care gaps affect people on the ground.
“For me, I think it highlights that we still have a lot to do,” Yin said.

title: What happened to Trump’s deporting the ‘worst of the worst’?
description:
Carlos Montes was a Cheyenne barber before he was stopped for a broken taillight. He was soon deported to Nicaragua, writes columnist Kerry Drake 
The post What happened to Trump’s deporting the ‘worst of the worst’? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Driving with a broken taillight should not result in a man losing his job, then being secretly taken away from his family and deported to a country where his life is in danger.

Opinion

But it did end that way for Carlos Montes of Cheyenne, despite not having a criminal record and doing everything he could to become a legal citizen of the United States. 
Montes is by no stretch of the imagination the “worst of the worst,” the type of person President Donald Trump told Americans he would remove through his mass deportation plan. He repeatedly made that promise during his campaign in 2024, and it’s what he claims his administration has accomplished.
Trump specifically talked about murderers, rapists, kidnappers, drug dealers, gangs, child predators and terrorists who cause communities to live in fear. 
But his immigration policies directly led to Laramie County law enforcement stopping a Wyoming barber for a minor traffic violation, moving Montes to deportation facilities in other states and whisking him off to Nicaragua. 
His pregnant partner and 5-year-old son, with him during the traffic stop, watched helplessly while Montes was taken into custody. Authorities told them nothing about what would happen next. More than a week later, they learned what transpired from Oil City News, which in partnership with WyoFile, sought to learn what happened.
It took another two weeks for his distraught family to be able to talk to Montes on the phone.
I don’t believe 70% of Wyoming voters who wanted to send Trump back to the White House thought someone like Montes — who was no danger to the community — would receive such harsh punishment.
Why would anyone want to see a young boy and a woman about to give birth suffer like this, and take away the man they love?
Montes entered the U.S. when migrants from Nicaragua had temporary protected status, because staying in their native country put their lives in jeopardy. Trump signed an order terminating that status a year ago.
Barbershop owners Drew Weston and his wife Andrea Shipley hired Montes in April 2025. The couple told reporters he was trying to legally obtain U.S. citizenship, had a naturalization number and was working through the process with the Wyoming Attorney General’s Office.
“I know that he has done so much paperwork to even be here and get his [barber’s] license, that he’s a guy who will do what he needs to do the legal way,” said Weston. “So for this to pop up and then to be treated like this, oh my God.”
Montes is representative of those who are being deported in our names. About 70% of suspects detained by ICE from the beginning of Trump’s second term through this past July did not have a criminal conviction.
ICE considers anyone a criminal who has a conviction, whether it is a serious felony or a minor violation punishable by a fine, like fishing without a license or not keeping a dog on a leash.
Or driving with a taillight out.
This tragic series of events began on Nov. 26, when a deputy pulled Montes’ vehicle over in south Cheyenne for the alleged taillight violation.
The deputy discovered that Montes did not possess a driver’s license or proof of insurance — both misdemeanors that weren’t adjudicated by a court. The sheriff’s office notified ICE of the charges under an agreement Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak signed with the federal agency.
ICE took custody of Montes and transported him to an Aurora, Colorado, detention center. Then he was sent to a county correctional facility in Natchez, Mississippi. On Dec. 5 his family used an ICE online tracker to learn about that last move, but it was too late. A day earlier, Montes was deported to Nicaragua.
Last week Laramie County District Judge Robin Cooley dismissed a lawsuit filed by Montes’ former employer, Drew’s Barbershop, and two other plaintiffs who alleged that the sheriff illegally signed three agreements with ICE. 
The parties contended the Laramie County Board of Commissioners has the authority to enter into such agreements, not the sheriff. The lawsuit was tossed because the judge ruled plaintiffs did not have standing and could not prove economic injuries arose from ICE activities.
In January, Montes was reunited with his family when they traveled to Nicaragua to live with him and his parents. But what Montes wants is to be able to return to Cheyenne, where he built a good life by working hard to support his family and making many friends.
Such a reunion won’t be possible for between five and 10 years because of paperwork he signed while in custody, Montes told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle. He said being stuck in a single cell with many other immigration detainees left him unable to sleep, and one day he was asked if he wanted to “get out.”
Montes speaks some English but isn’t proficient enough to understand legal documents without a translator’s assistance. Believing he would be going back to Wyoming, he signed paperwork that said he was self-deporting.
ICE wants us to believe Montes signed the document willingly. Sure, why wouldn’t a man who loves Wyoming and his job want to go back to a country where his political beliefs put his life in jeopardy? Why would he want to sign something that ultimately forced his young family to leave home?
If you believe that ICE had a good reason to keep Montes isolated from his family until long after he landed in Nicaragua, you’ll likely automatically put him in the “worst of the worst” category. 
According to a polling analysis by Newsweek released on Labor Day, Wyoming gives Trump the highest net job performance rating in the country. His approval rating here is 15% higher than the percentage of Wyomingites who disapprove.
But at the beginning of Trump’s second term, Wyoming had high hopes for the president. He had a net +47 approval rating.
There are myriad reasons Trump’s favorability has fallen by 25 points here in the past 20 months. The most commonly cited nationally are the poor economy and the disastrous war against Iran.
But the failure of the president’s mass deportation policy is no doubt a factor. In communities across the country, there are injustices like what Carlos Montes suffered. 
People take notice of that. It’s one reason why Trump’s crusade to build more ICE jails have fallen flat.
I think most Wyomingites pay attention to what’s happening elsewhere. The most recent immigration horror was in Springfield, Ohio’s Haitian community, when the promising future of 20-year-old honor student Pierre Damas Bel ended when he apparently committed suicide after being forced to wear a humiliating ankle monitor that led to him being bullied.
Bel committed no crime. Like Montes, he and his family were given temporary protected status, which allowed about 330,000 Haitians to live and work in the U.S.
The Trump administration ended that protection in July, and ICE fitted Bel, who’d been a cadet in his high school’s J.R.O.T.C. program, and many other Haitians with ankle monitors. The agency said it was an alternative to being detained; the monitors enabled authorities to locate migrants who fail to comply with orders to report to court hearings or ICE check-ins.
This “humane” approach led to Bel’s Instagram post that explained he was “carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience.”
Bel made a video call to his father, telling him that he was not feeling well mentally because of the bullying. Three hours later, police notified his dad that Bel had walked into oncoming highway traffic and was struck by a truck, killing him.
I believe some day the tragedies surrounding this massive mistake to use undocumented workers as pawns in political games will end. But until then, how many good people will we lose?
The post What happened to Trump’s deporting the ‘worst of the worst’? appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: After budget cuts, Idaho plans to maintain low government spending, state official says
description: Idaho state government agencies’ budget requests for the next fiscal year are now publicly available.  The requests, which are online on the Division of Financial Management’s website, are for Idaho’s fiscal year 2028, which starts July 1, 2027.  On the heels of a 2026 Idaho legislative session marked by budget cuts after years of state […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho state government agencies’ budget requests for the next fiscal year are now publicly available. 
The requests, which are online on the Division of Financial Management’s website, are for Idaho’s fiscal year 2028, which starts July 1, 2027. 
After ‘tight budget year,’ Idaho ends fiscal year with positive cash balance

On the heels of a 2026 Idaho legislative session marked by budget cuts after years of state tax cuts, the requests outline the state’s strategy of continuing to operate state agencies and public programs with less funding, according to the governor’s budget chief, Lori Wolff.
In a media briefing last week, Wolff told reporters that non-discretionary funding for Medicaid, state prisons and public schools is eating up most of a recent projection of increased revenue.
“We were very tight on our bottom line before, so it doesn’t give us a whole lot of room,” Wolff told reporters.
“That really quickly takes up most of the increase in our revenue,” she said. “So, our focus this year is going to be on keeping those budgets at where we set them last year.”
In May, she wrote a memo to state agencies instructing them to only submit barebones budgets, and that the next budget year was not the time to start restoring budget cuts. 
The budget request for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare — the state’s largest government agency that runs Medicaid and other public assistance programs — is the only budget plan that hasn’t been published yet, the governor’s spokesperson, Emily Callihan, said in a statement. She said officials expect to post the agency’s budget request Tuesday.

The requests are one of the first major steps in the process to fund state government. 
In January, Idaho Gov. Brad Little typically releases his own proposed state budget. Then the Idaho Legislature, which meets during the first few months of the calendar year, considers budget requests by state agencies and the governor as lawmakers draft budget bills. 
In recent years, Idaho’s powerful budget-setting committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, has shifted to a different budgeting process that splits agency budgets into barebones funding and new spending.
The 2027 Idaho legislative session is set to start in January.

title: ACLU claims Memphis Safe Task Force harassing plaintiff
description: Memphis Safe Task Force agents are continuing to harass and intimidate people who record their activities, according to a new federal court filing by the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU and legal team for Memphis resident Hunter Demster filed a declaration on his behalf Wednesday, claiming the task force is retaliating against him for […]
text:
In a lawsuit filed on his behalf by the ACLU, Hunter Demster, photographed in Nov. 2025, alleges federal agents with the Memphis Safe Task Force have harassed and intimidated him for recording their activities. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Memphis Safe Task Force agents are continuing to harass and intimidate people who record their activities, according to a new federal court filing by the American Civil Liberties Union.
The ACLU and legal team for Memphis resident Hunter Demster filed a declaration on his behalf Wednesday, claiming the task force is retaliating against him for recording immigration and law enforcement activity. The filing, which is backed up by video, claims task force agents also “abused” Tennessee’s Halo Law by tackling and arresting Demster as he recorded them arresting a man in late August. 
The law makes it illegal for a person to get within 25 feet of an officer after being ordered to stop approaching or to retreat. The filing claims officers moved toward Demster as he recorded them Aug. 26, creating a “moving wall,” which he said in a video violated his First Amendment rights.
The filing also says task force agents went to Demster’s home on Aug. 30 and Sept. 3 and took pictures or shot video of him at the residence. 



Quotation







The task force has tried to punish and intimidate me for exercising my First Amendment rights, but I will not let them chill my speech.


– Hunter Demster


A federal court is slated to hear arguments Sept. 23 on the lawsuit filed by Demster and other plaintiffs who are seeking a preliminary injunction to prevent the task force from retaliating against them as they record and observe immigration and law enforcement activities. In addition to the request for an injunction, the legal team filed multiple declarations about agents threatening to arrest Memphis residents, intimidating them with vehicles, making illegal traffic stops and watching their homes after they recorded task force actions.
“The task force has tried to punish and intimidate me for exercising my First Amendment rights, but I will not let them chill my speech,” Demster said in a release. “It is not only concerning, it is also deeply frightening how their retaliation has escalated — all because I show the world what’s going on in Memphis.”
The new filing points toward three incidents, the first in late August when he observed task force agents on a Memphis sidewalk and started shooting video. Agents approached him even though he wasn’t interfering with them and yelled “25 feet,” referring to the Halo Law, and moving toward him, according to the filing. When Demster asserted his right to stay there even as one agent said he “extended the scene” by walking toward him, agents took him to the ground, restrained his legs and handcuffed him.
During the arrest, ACLU of Tennessee legal director Lucas Cameron-Vaughn, arrived and was threatened with arrest after being ordered to retreat when he tried to speak with Demster, according to the filing. Demster was ultimately released at the scene.
Another incident took place Aug. 30 at Demster’s home where task force agents gathered across the street and took pictures of him and video of his house after he approached them. 
Task force agents parked outside his home again on Sept. 3, the filing says. When Demster asked if he could help them, one of them said no, and when he started videotaping the vehicle, a person inside the SUV stuck a phone out the window and took pictures and video of Demster, according to the filing.
“Task force agents should not be staking out our clients’ homes simply for recording their activities in public,” Scarlet Kim, senior staff attorney with ACLU’s Speech, Privacy and Technology Project, said in the release. “Nor should they abuse the Halo Law to interfere with our clients’ First Amendment right to record.”
The task force of 31 state, local and federal agencies started aggressively patrolling Memphis in September 2025 at the order of President Donald Trump and Gov. Bill Lee, conducting traffic stops and immigration sweeps, in addition to serving large numbers of arrest warrants. Lee sent the Tennessee National Guard to participate in the task force as well.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Department of Corrections: Staffing efforts show concern with prison violence
description: Attorneys for the Alabama Department of Corrections and the state last week filed a motion for summary judgment in a long-running federal lawsuit over violence in Alabama’s correctional facilities, around the same time as the U.S. Department of Justice. Bill Lunsford, an attorney representing the state, argued that the state had worked to address staffing […[...]
text:
An officer is seen in the yard of Holman Correctional Facility in Atmore, Alabama on Oct. 22, 2019. The Alabama Department of Corrections is seeking summary judgment in a long-running lawsuit over violence in state prisons, arguing its efforts to increase staffing show a commitment to addressing the problem. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)Attorneys for the Alabama Department of Corrections and the state last week filed a motion for summary judgment in a long-running federal lawsuit over violence in Alabama’s correctional facilities, around the same time as the U.S. Department of Justice.
Bill Lunsford, an attorney representing the state, argued that the state had worked to address staffing issues and safety within Alabama prisons, “belying any claim that the state has historically acted with indifference or continues to act with any level of indifference on these issues.”
Lunsford said in the motion that the state reviewed its current staffing levels and worked to expand recruitment and retention, executed the policies that it had in place for use of force through “training, investigation, discipline, and criminal referral” and developed a system to classify people in its custody that included screening, risk assessment, regular review and where staff would house people in their custody.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A message seeking comment was sent to the U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday.
Alabama prisons have suffered from violence and overcrowding for decades. The U.S. Department of Justice sued the state in 2020 after a series of reports detailing physical and sexual assaults of inmates, saying conditions in state prisons violated inmates’ Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office filed a motion for summary judgment of its own last Wednesday, asking U.S. District Judge Harold D Mooty III to rule that the ADOC failed to protect people in prison from physical violence, sexual violence and excessive force by correctional staff and failed to provide safe conditions for people while incarcerated.
The 260-page filing provided a litany of incidents in arguing that violence within the prisons was unconstitutionally high and that the ADOC did not do anything to address the issues. The motion also accused correctional staff of routinely using excessively force and said leadership in the department was “deliberately indifferent to the serious risk of substantial harm.”
Lunsford wrote in his motion last week that the state ‘responded reasonably” to the threats of violence and could not be found to have shown deliberate indifference.
ADOC and Alabama, Lunsford argued, had an inmate classification system and tried to address staffing issues outlined in the DOJ’s charges.
“In the face of a persistent and ongoing national correctional staffing shortage readily acknowledged by Plaintiff’s retained experts, the state invested hundreds of millions of dollars and countless hours of time from members of ADOC’s leadership focused solely upon the recruitment and retention of correctional officers,” the motion states.
And because of that, “ADOC’s correctional staffing numbers increased substantially and continue to do so. ADOC reconsidered, revised, and improved its policies with the intent of improving officer training, performance, and outcomes within its prison system.”
In the most recent quarterly report, ADOC had about 1,400 correctional officers on staff at the end of February, about 200 more than they had at the same time in 2025.
At a legislative budget meeting in 2024, former Commissioner John Hamm said there are 2,400 budgeted correctional security positions across all the facilities, and that 365 were vacant at the time.
Lunsford wrote that the agency launched an advertising campaign and hosted numerous events to boost recruitment. The motion states that in 2020, ADOC hosted “14 hiring events with 849 total attendees.” In 2021, ADOC hosted 17 events with more than 400 attendees.
The motion stated full-time staff at Bibb Correctional Facility increased from 74.5 to more than 136 from 2022 to 2024, an increase of almost 90%, according to the motion.
The increases at other facilities were more modest. At Donaldson Correctional Facility, correctional staff went from 122 FTE to about 150 FTE. In other facilities, staff declined. At Easterling Correctional Facility, it went from 76.5 FTE to 65 FTE from 2022 to 2024.
The motion also states that the ADOC had policies in place to address allegations of excessive use of force and that staff followed the procedures.
“As of June 5, 2023, correctional staff received training at ADOC’s APOSTC Academy, which consisted of a 400-hour written curriculum that included use of force,” the motion states.
Lunsford included a graphic in the motion that indicated that the number of reported excessive use of force complaints declined, going from 2,213 in 2020 to about 1,000 in 2023.
