name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: More Wisconsin communities are dropping Flock
description: Stevens Point, Winnebago County, Fond du Lac County and Sheboygan are among the Wisconsin communities that have recently moved away from Flock license plate reader cameras. On Tuesday, city staff in Stevens Point began covering the cameras while local elected leaders determine whether they can cancel their Flock contract altogether.  Meanwhile Sheboygan brok[...]
text:
A Flock camera on the Lac Courte Orielles Reservation in SawYer County. (Photo by Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)Stevens Point, Winnebago County, Fond du Lac County and Sheboygan are among the Wisconsin communities that have recently moved away from Flock license plate reader cameras. On Tuesday, city staff in Stevens Point began covering the cameras while local elected leaders determine whether they can cancel their Flock contract altogether. 
Meanwhile Sheboygan broke ties with Flock after the company reportedly attempted to sell the city back traffic data it was unaware the multi-billion dollar surveillance company was even collecting. Flock cameras capture images of vehicles and their license plates on the roadways. Law enforcement officers can search the data to see where a vehicle has traveled. 
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Investigative reporting has shown that the cameras can also recognize human features. Over 5,000 agencies had Flock contracts in late 2025, creating a network of tens of thousands of cameras that can be queried simultaneously. Police often say that the technology has been invaluable in solving crimes including carjackings, kidnappings, homicide, drug trafficking and gun violence. The cameras are also used for less serious reasons such as for traffic enforcement and in policing evictions. 
“Reports are surfacing all over the country about the system being misused by municipal and state employees who have access to the data,” said Stevens Point Mayor Mike Wiza in a press release late last week. 
A few of those cases have played out in Wisconsin courts, police departments and sheriff’s offices. Four officers across Wisconsin have been charged with misconduct in public office and other offenses for misusing Flock cameras. 
Josue Ayala of the Milwaukee Police Department (MPD) was given a year of probation and avoided jail time earlier this year after misusing Flock. Cristian Morales of the Menasha Police Department was sentenced to six months in jail and three years probation for a similar infraction. In Kenosha County, former sheriff’s deputy Frank McGrath was charged with misconduct in public office last month for misuse of the surveillance technology. In July, Milwaukee police detective Tehrangi Chapman — who worked the internal affairs investigation into Ayala’s Flock misuse — was charged with misusing the system to track someone he had been monitoring since 2019, years before Flock came to Milwaukee. Chapman and McGrath are still going through court proceedings. 
Ayala, Morales and McGrath all used Flock to monitor their current or former romantic partners. The exact relationship Chapman has to the people he allegedly monitored is not mentioned in available court records. McGrath used Flock and a squad car tracking system called Polaris to monitor his girlfriend, who was also a Kenosha County Sheriff’s deputy. Chapman allegedly employed both Flock cameras and car-mounted GPS trackers. McGrath was caught after a supervisor noticed some suspicious Flock searches in an audit, while Ayala and Chapman were both reported to police by the victims themselves. 
People fill up a Milwaukee Fire and Police Commission meeting to call for an end to Flock in the city. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Numerous other officers have been investigated or charged with misusing Flock around the country. In Racine County, the district attorney admitted that a few unnamed officers have been investigated for their use of Flock cameras. 
The rash of misuse is not the only thing motivating local communities to drop Flock. When the city of Verona decided to cover its cameras in February, Mayor Diaz said that while the community trusted its police department, it no longer trusted Flock Safety. At that time the first cases of misconduct were beginning to emerge in Wisconsin, and many people had expressed fears about how the federal government — especially immigration enforcement — could leverage local Flock networks for its own priorities. Trust was also broken in Oshkosh months later, after the police chief learned that the cameras could create heatmaps of vehicle movements, contrary to what a company representative had said. 
The sheriffs and police departments in Fond du Lac County recently announced they will cancel their contracts because out of state agencies had used open records requests to obtain audit data the sheriff said was confidential and in some cases linked with ongoing investigations. Journalists and other citizens nationwide had begun requesting Flock audit data from local police departments to learn how the cameras were being used. 
In 2025, a Wisconsin Examiner analysis showed that at least 221 law enforcement agencies were using Flock in Wisconsin. Many of the searches used vague search terms such as “investigation,” “suspicious,” or non-law-enforcement terms such as “cooch,” or single characters such as “.” or “s”. Some of these vague search terms have appeared in confirmed misconduct cases. Officers in other parts of the country have also  used Flock for controversial reasons, such as tracking women suspected of traveling out of state to get an abortion. 
A police officer uses the Flock Safety license plate reader system. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)
Flock Safety has struggled to adapt to canceled contracts and misconduct investigations. Although the company has released new features including requiring case numbers when searching the database, fixed options for search terms, and the ability to flag suspicious searches, it has also worked to hide information in the audit data such as officers’ names. Flock Safety has claimed that people have used the audit data to identify undercover officers. However, the information which Flock is making harder to view is also the very information that allowed citizens and journalists to detect instances of misconduct.
Winnebago County, Neenah, Menasha, and Chetek have each canceled a Flock contract, are considering it or have covered up their cameras. In Chetek, the police chief responded to public criticism of Flock cameras by threatening to run background checks on citizens who disagreed with his use of the cameras. Other Wisconsin communities including Kaukauna, Sturgeon Bay, Appleton, Dane County, Stoughton and Manitowoc which have also canceled their Flock contracts. 
Other communities have chosen to heighten oversight of their Flock cameras In Milwaukee, County Executive David Crowley asked that all Flock operations on county property be paused until new transparency and oversight measures could be developed. 
Milwaukee County Sup. Justin Bielinski, who is also chairman of the Committee on Judiciary, Law Enforcement, and General Services, has also called on the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office to disable its Flock network. “Residents should not have to wait for another disclosure before we act,” said Bielinksi. “Even if you have confidence in the Sheriff’s Department’s use of Flock, the question remains: do we trust Flock itself with this information?”
A Flock camera outside of Washington Park in Milwaukee. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
The Milwaukee Police Department has restricted its Flock network from other local agencies, limited access to the system to supervisors only, and launched a new Flock transparency portal. The portal notes that data captured by Flock cameras in Milwaukee is only retained for seven days, and that there were 983 “search sessions” over the last 30 days. It also keeps track of the number of “hot list hits” over the last 30 days. Hot lists are lists of vehicles which law enforcement have flagged in the system. When a camera sees the flagged vehicle, a notification goes out to police in the area. The Milwaukee police transparency portal  does not track the number of vehicles detected, unlike a transparency portal released by the Green Bay Police Department.
“This effort underscores the commitments MPD has made in partnership with the Mayor to establish appropriate guardrails for the use of this technology while providing greater public understanding of how Flock [Automatic License Plate Reader] technology is used to support public safety,” the Milwaukee department said in a press release. “MPD remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the responsible use of technology. Through this new resource, MPD is continuing its efforts to provide the public with meaningful information about the tools we use to support the safety of the Milwaukee community.”
People in the community continue to push back against the cameras. Last Thursday, dozens of residents filled a Fire and Police Commission meeting to capacity in Milwaukee. An overflow room was opened to accommodate all the people who showed up to testify, unanimously rejecting Flock and calling for the city to cancel its contract. Speakers argued that Flock is a form of indiscriminate mass surveillance which can and has been used in abusive ways by police. Many of the speakers expressed deep frustration with the commission, city government and police, saying that they’d called for an end to Flock for months only to see some of their fears realized. 
Napoleon Jones holds a picture of his vehicle in captured by Flock. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Napoleon Jones, 32, was one of those people. Although Jones is from Sussex, he came to the Milwaukee FPC meeting to describe his  experience of Flock surveillance. Jones, a Navy veteran, was stopped by a Waukesha County Sheriff’s deputy after filming a traffic stop. Jones was arrested and taken to jail, only to be released without charges. When he filed a complaint about the deputy’s conduct, according to a federal lawsuit, Jones became the target of a  Flock search by that deputy, who was  directed by his supervisor to conduct the searches. 
“When I first found out I was just super surprised,” Jones told the Examiner. “I never thought it would happen to me. And when I found out and I got the records and seen how many different searches there were, I was at a loss of words because it’s hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of searches and the network is so big on these Flock cameras.” Jones added that “I drive all around. If this guy really wanted to put together a timeline of where I’m at, or who I know, or whose house I’m at, he could have done it.”
He added, “I drive past these things all the time. Everyone does.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio farmers need help after tariffs, foreign competition bring big struggles
description: Ohio farmers are making hard decisions to pay the bills, and bearing the brunt of criticisms about food-borne illnesses in the produce aisle. They are demanding to be heard by Congress and the Trump administration as tariffs dig into struggling farmers’ bank accounts, and partisanship threatens the Farm Bill, legislation that had bipartisan support for […]
text:
A tractor sits on a Chris Gibbs' Shelby County farm. (Photo courtesy of Chris Gibbs)Ohio farmers are making hard decisions to pay the bills, and bearing the brunt of criticisms about food-borne illnesses in the produce aisle.
They are demanding to be heard by Congress and the Trump administration as tariffs dig into struggling farmers’ bank accounts, and partisanship threatens the Farm Bill, legislation that had bipartisan support for decades before the One Big Beautiful Bill Act changed things.
Meanwhile, consumers are having trouble choosing at the grocery stores after recalls of lettuce, other produce, and even some types of meat.
“Of course, farmers always get the black eye at the end of the day when that sort of stuff happens,” said Joe Logan, a beef farmer in Northeast Ohio, and president of the Ohio Farmers Union.
Logan and others in the union are concerned about the cuts that have been made within the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which could have prevented some of the illnesses, or at least helped the country respond to contaminations like cyclosporiasis.
Logan specifically pointed to cuts made to the Agricultural Food Safety Inspection Service, and the fact that the government backed off of a law that required country-of-origin listings on cuts of beef, pork, and ground beef back in 2016.
“It was not very long ago that we would know not only the pathogen, we would know the source, because we would have surveillance in the system, and there’s a reason we do these things,” Logan said. “The USDA is being kicked around, and mismanagement is the reason.”
There are currently 17 active alerts listed on the USDA’s website, which includes recalls and public health alerts. Ten of them are listed as Class 1, the highest priority for recalls.
Cows graze in a field.(Photo courtesy of Chris Gibbs)
While product contamination is listed for several recalls and public health alerts, seven are listed as import violations, or “produced without benefit of inspection.”
Beef farmers like Logan are also facing struggles as the Trump administration attempts to push back against tariff-induced price increases by importing beef from other countries.
Trade conflicts with China and Canada are also causing issues. According to Logan, two-thirds of livestock grown in Canada is sent to the U.S.
“It really puts us in a tough place,” Logan said.
As a fifth-generation farmer who’s seen his share of ups and downs in the marketplace, Logan said in his first year as a beef farmer (transitioning from dairy cattle), beef prices were “solid all year.”
“It was kind of gratifying to think about maybe making a little money, and maybe expanding our herd,” he said.
Those hopes were dimmed after the announcement that Trump planned to import beef from outside the U.S., hampering an opportunity for Logan to become more profitable.
He said the choice to broaden the market as Trump tries to soften the blow of tariff prices on the American consumer sends a disappointing message to farmers.
“The clear signal that it sends to cattle producers is that you can not trust this administration to come up with (policies) that are going to give us a stable enough marketplace for us to be confident about expanding our herd,” Logan said.
Tariff prices are hitting farmers in many ways, from competition, to parts and materials. While preparing for corn season, Shelby County farmer Chris Gibbs replaced a drive chain on his planter, and noticed the parts number for the company on one side, and “made in China” on the other.
“I don’t care where it comes from, but what I knew at that exact moment is that I paid tariff on that doggone thing,” Gibbs said.
Even without tariffs in the discussion, farmers are looking for some level of predictability from the government, as participants in an industry that lives and dies by weather conditions and good crop years.
When there are droughts or low commodity prices, farmers have a knack for figuring it out.
“You do it, you move money around, you dig nickels out of the couch, you put off buying capital assets,” Gibbs said. “You make do.”
But the recent changes from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and a Farm Bill that has been limping along without a full renewal since 2018 have created a “cash-flow working capital crisis in agriculture,” according to Gibbs.
That crisis revolves less around large corporation farms and more on those that actually grow the food for Americans, according to Logan.
“We have a livestock-centric policy right now that leaves the people that actually produce food that people eat kind of out in the cold, in terms of agricultural policy and subsidy support,” Logan said.
In December of last year, Gibbs headed to his supplier to pick up inputs like fertilizer and seed, and realized he couldn’t afford them because of the cost of production.
“I didn’t have the money,” Gibbs said. “I had the crops in the bin (ready to sell), but I was unwilling to sell them just to buy my inputs.”
The price of nitrogen-based fertilizer, used on crops like wheat, had already gone up. Then the Iran war began and the global oil market had a direct impact on local farmer costs.
“The oil drilling process in the Middle East creates gas, and that gas is what’s used to make nitrogen fertilizer,” Gibbs said. “It’s a worldwide market, so what happens there affects me.”
As the war continued, prices for the fertilizer doubled, even as commodities stayed at the same price.
Gibbs said he went into his supplier “dejected and almost embarrassed.” It was something the supplier had seen from many of his customers.
“He told me that’s the same story throughout the area,” Gibbs said.
Both Gibbs and Logan are hoping government officials will hear their concerns and bring back funding for the Farm Bill and long-established supports that have faded away through budget cuts and staff losses.
The Farm Bill is usually a bipartisan effort that combines the nutrition supports needed predominantly in urban areas of the country with the agricultural supports needed in rural areas.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act changed the priorities, leaning away from nutrition assistance, like SNAP, supported by urban constituencies, and more toward rural districts.
That means fading bipartisan support, and less support from farmers as well.
“What Congress has hooked farmers’ wagon to is that now agriculture is dependent on one party, and that’s a dangerous place to be,” said Gibbs, who used to be chair of the Shelby County Republican Party and is now chair of the Shelby County Democratic Party.

Combining his role as Ohio farmer and former county executive director for the USDA’s Farm Service Agency, Gibbs joined a July letter to the heads of the congressional agriculture committees, which was actually a follow-up to letter sent in February, urging action to counteract Trump administration decisions.
“In the five months since many of us wrote to share our concerns, the pressures facing farmers and ranchers have intensified dramatically in ways that jeopardize the entire U.S. ag economy – now and in the future,” the letter stated.
The group of more than 40 former farmers, academics, and agriculture leaders asked that the committees reflect on the increases in fuel and fertilizer costs, the stalling of agricultural exports, and increasing amount of farm bankruptcies.
They also decried the “widespread use of tariffs as a trade policy,” saying it “continues to be a disaster for American agriculture.”
“The outcome of these new tariffs will damage U.S. ag exports and our competitiveness in the world and increase costs to Americans,” the letter stated.
“The various handshake deals secured by this administration do not come close to offsetting the instability and loss of markets caused by this haphazard trade policy.”
Gibbs said neither congressional committee has responded to the letter.

title: Ohio State University, three other Ohio universities receive an ‘F’ in latest free speech rankings
description: The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression gave four Ohio colleges and universities a failing grade on their 2027 College Free Speech rankings.    The survey ranked 261 colleges and universities after receiving responses from nearly 63,000 students who were surveyed via College Pulse from Jan. 2 through June 3. 13 Ohio colleges and universities were[...]
text:
On the campus of The Ohio State University in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for the Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original story.)The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression gave four Ohio colleges and universities a failing grade on their 2027 College Free Speech rankings.   
The survey ranked 261 colleges and universities after receiving responses from nearly 63,000 students who were surveyed via College Pulse from Jan. 2 through June 3. 13 
Ohio colleges and universities were ranked between No. 64 and 237. 
Half of students surveyed nationwide said the Israeli–Palestinian conflict was difficult to openly discuss on campus. 
Slightly less than half (46%) of students said President Donald Trump was hard to openly talk about on campus. 44% of students said right-wing activist Charlie Kirk who was killed last September while speaking at Utah Valley University, 43% said abortion, 38% said immigration, and 38% said transgender rights were difficult to openly discuss on campus. 
This is the seventh consecutive year FIRE has done this survey, which now gives universities letter grades. Slightly less than half of universities surveyed — 121 out of 261 — received a failing grade for their campus speech climate. 
Only 24 universities received a C or better. 
FIRE summed up 12 parts to come up with an overall score for each college or university: comfort expressing ideas, self-censorship, disruptive conduct, administrative support, openness,  political tolerance, the Chicago statement, institutional neutrality, FIRE’s spotlight rating and various speech controversies on campus.
The University of Chicago received the highest ranking with an overall score of 81.42 and a B- grade. New York University got the lowest ranking with an overall score of 44.97 and an F grade. 
Here’s where Ohio colleges and universities ranked on FIRE’s list:
64. Wright State University — 64.82 overall score — D climate grade — 153 students surveyed. 
76. Kenyon College — 63.57 overall score — D climate grade — 151 students surveyed. 
77. Miami University — 63.56 overall score — D climate grade — 294 students surveyed. 
80. Bowling Green State University — 63.38 overall score — D climate grade — 291 students surveyed. 
88. Denison University — 62.98 overall score — D climate grade — 176 students surveyed. 
91. University of Toledo — 62.86 overall score — D climate grade — 155 students surveyed. 
101. Ohio University — 62.27 overall score — D- climate grade — 307 students surveyed. 
108. University of Cincinnati — 61.84 overall score — D- climate grade — 284 students surveyed. 
121. Case Western Reserve University — 60.47 overall score — D- climate grade — 288 students surveyed. 
174. Ohio State University — 58.18 overall score — F climate grade — 333 students surveyed. 
189. Kent State University — 57.65 overall score — F climate grade — 338 students surveyed. 
194. Oberlin College — 57.19 overall score — F climate grade — 86 students surveyed. 
237. University of Dayton — 53.75 overall score — F climate grade — 275 students surveyed.
Case Western had the biggest positive change and was ranked No. 163 on last year’s survey. 
Ohio State had the biggest negative change and was ranked No. 124 on last year’s survey. Ohio State banned chalking on campus last summer and all dorm decor in the common areas must be Ohio State-specific.
Ohio Senate Bill 1 took effect last summer that bans diversity efforts, regulates classroom discussion, prohibits faculty strikes, creates post-tenure reviews, puts diversity scholarships at risk, and creates a retrenchment provision that blocks unions from negotiating on tenure, among other things.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Remembering Flight 93 through the lens of healing
description: From 2001 to 2009, I was one of a handful of caretakers of the Flight 93 crash site in Somerset County, Pennsylvania.
text:
Hemlock trees in the woods that are part of the Flight 93 crash site. They were with marked spray-paint by searchers in the days and weeks after the crash. This photo is from sometime in 2006. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert)The parking lot was dotted with just a handful of cars on this comfortable August morning. It was the first week of school for many families, so visitors were a bit more sparse than usual.
After a two-hour drive from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, to this secluded spot in Somerset County, it was nice to stretch my legs and feel the sun on my face. I had nearly forgotten how windy it can be out here. 
My brain sort of went on autopilot as my body started to slowly move forward, past the education center and a small group of tourists milling around, and onto a black granite walkway. Every few steps, I’d glance at an engraving in the pathway — marking the time and location of a terrible event that preceded what I’d see when the walkway simply ends.



Passing through two towering concrete walls, my eyes were focused on the overlook ahead. The expanse of fields of tall grasses, trees and flowers disappeared from view. I reached the end and stood in front of a waist-high glass window, marked with the phrase: “A common field one day. A field of honor forever.”
I was back at the Flight 93 National Memorial.
Instinctively, I glanced up at the blue sky. “It would have passed right over my head,” I thought as I looked out at the green field. A boulder marked the approximate area where United Flight 93 met the earth at more than 560 mph on Sept. 11, 2001. Forty innocent passengers and crew as well as four al-Qaida terrorists lost their lives there.
It was peaceful now. The sound of birds, crickets and cicadas merged as the wind picked up again. The grass had recently been mowed, and 60-foot-tall hemlock trees still stood around the area that’s come to be known as the “bowl.”
Has it really been 25 years since that horrible day?
The crash of United Flight 93 is marked by a boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The rebellion 
Perhaps the story of Flight 93 has faded over the last quarter century, so it might be a good time to pause for a refresher.
The cross-country flight was headed from Newark, New Jersey, to San Francisco when it was delayed on the runway for about 25 crucial minutes. Takeoff occurred about four minutes before the first jetliner struck the World Trade Center in New York. 
Once in the sky, the four al-Qaida terrorists took control of the plane somewhere over northeast Ohio. Because of the late takeoff, passengers and crew members were able to gather invaluable information through 37 phone calls to loved ones about the attacks in New York and at the Pentagon outside of Washington, D.C., and what was likely their fate too. 
So, they came together to try to retake the hijacked jetliner and protect innocent people on the ground. Investigators believe the intended target was the U.S. Capitol, but when faced with the uprising, the terrorists chose to bring the plane down amid the struggle for control of the cockpit. 
After strikes on the symbols of America’s financial and military strength, al-Qaida designed the fourth blow to destroy the very seat of democracy. 
Thanks to the actions of 40 people who found courage amid the most terrifying experience of their lives, the terrorists failed in the final act of their attack. 
Aerial view of the United Flight 93 crash site and temporary memorial is seen July 26, 2002 near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Roger Kerekes/Getty Images)
A caretaker
This was my first visit to the memorial in Stonycreek Township since the remembrance event to mark the 20th anniversary of the attacks in 2021. I’m not sure why I haven’t been back. Life has a way of just churning along, I guess. 
I was a visitor now, experiencing this out-of-the way field like any other person who found themselves drawn to it. I couldn’t help leaning over to someone who was asking their friend or partner a question and answering it for them.
“Yes. They did recover the black box.”
Force of habit. 
You see, from 2001 to 2009, I was one of a handful of caretakers of this area that became known around the world on that horrible Tuesday morning. Some of the land that was considered an essential part of the crash site had been in my family for more than seven decades. It’s not talked about much, but there were at least five other private property owners in the same situation. 
Back in the 1930s, my grandfather purchased about 200 acres just outside Shanksville and near Lambertsville. It eventually was whittled down to 163 acres after he and my father built several cabins and sold off pieces of land here and there. (My grandfather also worked on building the Pentagon during World War II, but that’s another story.) My father handed it off to me in the 1990s.
I never thought much about it (except when the property tax bill came), until that day in September. 
The crash of United Flight 93 is marked by a boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
‘Those are trees are ours’
Like most journalists, Sept. 11 was a blur of trying to make sense of the senseless and calmly conveying what we knew to listeners, readers and viewers (while barely holding it together).

May that lesson never be forgotten.

text:
A protestor carries a sign during a demonstration against the cancellation of student visas. (States Newsroom file photo.)With attention deservedly focused on the Department of Homeland Security’s increased use of violence to detain, deport, and in some cases, kill immigrants for the assumed crime of driving while Latino, the Trump administration continues to roll out rules and regulations that will seriously impact the nation’s economic future and our future as a nation of immigrants. 
Changes to rules regarding international student visas as well as barring the admission of those who might potentially apply for government benefits in the future are literally guaranteed to undercut the country’s future growth. 
And why are these rules deemed necessary? For no other reason than to advance the anti-immigrant nativism long maintained by President Trump and his xenophobic counselor, Stephen Miller. 
Take the case of international students. 
International students have historically brought significant benefits to higher education institutions, by subsidizing the tuition paid by domestic students while adding global diversity and understanding to thousands of campuses. 
And they have contributed to the overall U.S. economy. 
According to the International Trade Administration of the Department of Commerce, international students added a combined $42.9 billion to the economy in the 2024-2025 school year and supported more than 355,000 jobs across the country. 
Up until now, international students on F-visas were allowed to continue their studies until the completion of their programs, as long as they remained in status. 
But new rules would allow international students a fixed period of no longer than 4 years to complete their degrees, while also prohibiting graduate students from changing majors, transferring, or completing additional degrees in different fields. 
According to the Education Data Initiative, completion of a doctorate, for example, can range from 5 to 11 years, and the average time to complete a bachelor’s degree is closer to 5 years. 
Once their time is up, students would have a maximum of 30 days to find a job, leave, or be subject to deportation. 
The decline in international students, which the new rules virtually guarantee, are bound to hit Ohio with a vengeance. 
Ohio currently enrolls just under 36,000 international students, a figure which already reflects a decline of nearly 3,000 students from just a year ago. 
Enrollment declines at Cleveland State University, for example, are expected to cost the school an estimated $11.5 million in lost tuition revenue this year alone. 
For a state whose international students contribute an estimated $1.3 billion a year to the overall economy, and support almost 11,000 jobs, the loss of even more foreign students is a self-imposed wound that provides no understandable benefit. 
As Marcello Fantoni, Kent State’s vice president of global education remarked, “There is damage done there, and it will take a long time to be fixed. A long time.”  
The same is true with the new rules published on July 20 regarding what is known as the “public charge ground of inadmissibility.” 
The new procedures, which lack clear standards or measures, allow the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to block the entry of otherwise legal immigrants who they think — again, without a clear standard of evaluation — could apply for government benefits at some point in the undefined future.
 And these include benefits as modest as taking part in a school’s free lunch program. To be clear, the rules aren’t about preventing noncitizens, including green card holders, from accessing benefits: those prohibitions are already on the books. The new rules are about allowing federal immigration services to ban low-income, legal immigrants.
As with the changes to international student visas, this new rule will cost the economy dearly. 
According the to the libertarian Cato Institute, the population most likely to be hamstrung by these revisions contributed $2.8 trillion more to the U.S. economy from 1994 to 2023 than they received in benefits or other costs. 
In Ohio, in 2023, immigrants earned $27.3 billion and paid $7.3 billion in state taxes. Although it is difficult to calculate how much of that will be lost with the new regulations in place, the loses — and there will be losses — are once again self-imposed injuries generated solely because of this administration’s well-documented animosity to immigrants, particularly low-income immigrants of color. 
As they rampage through Trump’s second presidency, neither he nor his enablers see any reason to disguise this. We have become all too familiar with Trump’s denigration of “shithole” countries, or his repeated insistence that immigrants are “poisoning the blood of our country.” 
Commenting on the Supreme Court’s recent decision to block asylum seekers at the border, Stephen Miller crowed “America’s doors are [now] closed fully to asylum seekers.” 
He could have said the same for refugees. Of a ceiling of 7,500 refugees permitted for FY 2026, a historical low, all but three of the 6,668 accepted were white South Africans. When the administration added an additional 10,000 slots this past May, all were reserved for white South Africans. 
As fans cheered for the U.S. men’s national soccer team in the World Cup, it was not lost on many how well the team actually represented today’s America. Of the 26 players, nearly half have dual citizenship; 6 were foreign born, and 5 others were born to immigrant parents.
 And yet a DHS social media post sought to drum up support for the U.S. at the World Cup by calling on fans to “DEFEND THE HOMELAND: One Nation. One Homeland. One Team,” a slogan frighteningly reminiscent of the Nazi’s “Ein Volk, Ein Reich, Ein Führer” (One People, One Nation, One Leader). 
As the administration continues to use both violence and rule-making to make immigrants’ lives intolerable and to slam shut the door shut to most future immigration, its measures are both economically self-destructive and a refusal to accept that we are, in fact, a country of many different people, all yearning to breathe free.

title: Shaheen defeats Sullivan to win Democratic nomination in 1st Congressional District
description: The once wide-open Democratic primary in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District has come to its conclusion.  Stefany Shaheen, a former Portsmouth city councilor and the daughter of U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, won the Democratic nomination for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. Wednesday. In a clos[...]
text:
Stefany Shaheen edged Maura Sullivan to win the Democratic nomination in the 1st Congressional District. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)The once wide-open Democratic primary in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District has come to its conclusion. 
Stefany Shaheen, a former Portsmouth city councilor and the daughter of U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, won the Democratic nomination for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. Wednesday.
In a close battle, Shaheen defeated fellow center-left candidate Maura Sullivan, a veteran and former Obama administration official. With 88% of the vote counted when the race was called, Shaheen led Sullivan 37.2% to 34.9%. Progressive Carleigh Beroint, a union organizer and chair of the Hampton Select Board, placed third in the race with 22% of the vote. 
There were six other Democratic candidates in the crowded field, although some left the race ahead of voting day. Christian Urrutia, a human rights attorney and veteran, dropped out and endorsed Shaheen over the weekend. Heath Howard, a state representative, dropped out last month and endorsed Beriont, the remaining progressive candidate. 
On the campaign trail, Shaheen battled with Sullivan over campaign finance, healthcare, and corporate and foreign endorsements.
She will try to keep the office blue as current officeholder, four-term U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, passed up a reelection bid to run for U.S. Senate. Shaheen will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo, a Portsmouth businessman, in November’s general election.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A guiding principle: respect the rule of law
description: The bottom line is simple: if you don’t like the laws, work to change them, but don’t break them, and don’t ignore them.
text:
I speak to a principle that has guided my generation of Americans since childhood: the rule of law is the foundation of a stable and civil society. Without it, we do not have order, fairness, or trust, we have anarchy.
I was raised to believe that laws exist to create social civility, and that if you disagree with a law, there is a peaceful, democratic process to petition for change. That is the strength of our system. What concerns me today is the growing willingness of Democratic elected officials to selectively enforce the very laws they made and swore to uphold.

Warren Levy

Let’s be clear: you break the law the moment you violate a statute, whether you steal a candy bar or steal a cash register. The severity may differ, but the principle does not. And if you knowingly hide or shield someone who committed either offense, you are aiding and abetting unlawful conduct. The law does not excuse selective enforcement.
The same principle applies to immigration. Federal law distinguishes between civil violations and criminal violations, but it does not give elected officials the authority to ignore statutes they personally disagree with. When officials obstruct enforcement, direct subordinates to disregard legal obligations, or provide protection from lawful process, they undermine the rule of law itself.
The bottom line is simple: if you don’t like the laws, work to change them, but don’t break them, and don’t ignore them. Our system depends on leaders who respect the laws they make. When enforcement becomes optional, accountability disappears, and public trust erodes.
Immigration and ICE enforcement are extremely volatile issues. That’s exactly why leaders must be careful and responsible in how they speak. Our mayor represents all residents, and should not inflame tensions or encourage division, especially on issues where emotions already run high. Freedom of speech matters, but so does responsible leadership.
I urge our mayor and state elected officials to work to repeal the Trust Act and reaffirm their commitment to consistent, impartial enforcement of the law. That is how we preserve civic order, protect democratic legitimacy, and maintain the public’s confidence in its institutions.
Warren Levy lives in Danbury.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Dear Fairfield, have you met AI?
description: I am not suggesting we replace our elected officials with robots.  (Although it may have crossed my mind.) I am suggesting we give  the humans some better tools.
text:
I recently started looking into what Fairfield is spending on the various camera technologies. One number stopped me in my tracks. 
I could have sent another unanswered email to the first selectwoman or my district RTM members but then I thought, if we are willing to spend millions on technology because we are told it will make Fairfield safe, what else can technology do for Fairfield?
After sitting through enough RTM meetings, I kept finding myself thinking the same thing: this  isn’t working.  Not because the people sitting there are not capable of doing their jobs. I just kept thinking there has to be a more efficient way to do this. 
Mind you I watch the meetings from the comfort of my couch and can’t imagine sitting there for several hours in chairs that look like mini torture chambers. (You know the kind … chairs that are intentionally uncomfortable so people don’t get too comfortable.)
There are questions. A  lot of questions. People have limited time to speak. Rules have to be looked up, questions get repeated. Some questions do not even get answered until later. Someone has to keep track of everything that happened so everyone can figure out what happened after the meeting.
If we are willing to invest that kind of money in technology to make government better at public safety, why aren’t we asking what technology could make the government itself work better? That is when that RTM meeting thought came back to me. Maybe the problem isn’t the people sitting around the table. Maybe the process needs an upgrade.
And then I had a thought…. AI.
Wait, hear me out!
Before anyone panics, no, I am not suggesting we replace our elected officials with robots.  (Although, depending on the meeting, it may have crossed my mind.) I am suggesting we give  the humans some better tools. The more I thought about it, the more I realized AI could potentially handle a lot of the administrative work that makes meetings and email responses cumbersome while leaving the actual decisions exactly where they belong, with people.
Then I started to think about how much Fairfield is already willing to spend on technology. That got my attention. Truth be told, I don’t have any insight into if Fairfield is already using AI.  But my observation is if they are using AI there is an opportunity to expand that technology to help town government do what they are designed to do — serve its residents.
I know this isn’t just some futuristic idea because I have already seen it work at my own job.
I recently had AI listen to a meeting to create a summary of the discussion, organize meeting notes and assign action items.  Did I have to go back and correct a few things? Absolutely, AI isn’t perfect and that’s exactly why a human still needs to review the work. 
But what would have normally taken me 30 minutes to gather all the info from my notes and create a summary with an action list was done in a fraction of a time. I reviewed it, made the necessary corrections copied and pasted it into an email and sent it to a distribution list of stakeholders. And it did not stop there. I had AI create a calendar  follow up with people responsible for action items. 
Suddenly I was the smartest person in the room.  And that never happens.
That got me thinking, why couldn’t local government use AI much the same way? Not to make decisions — just to take out some of the repetitive administrative work.
I have heard plenty of complaints from fellow residents who say the First Selectwoman’s office and the RTM aren’t responsive to emails. I don’t know what happens on the other side of that inbox, although I have had the same experience. Perhaps the town staff are overwhelmed by the volume of emails and everything else they are responsible for. Imagine 250 email questions coming in about speed cameras, another 500 about Flock and Axon cameras and let’s add 700 complaints about the various cameras.
AI goes to work: Congratulations! You have a camera issue!
It could sort the 1,450 emails into categories: questions, complaints, requests for information and issues requiring a staff response. Then the staff can tell AI to identify the most frequently asked questions and provide each sender with information on where it can be found.  Instead of one person trying to work through 1.450 emails, that person has  an organized summary of what information residents need. And if 200 people are asking the same question? It’s not because residents are unreasonable. Maybe the information simply isn’t readily available or what is available does not fully answer the question. And now you have a root cause and a fix.
And then something more important happens. Residents get what they deserve, a response from the people they elected to represent them. AI does not replace that response. It helps make sure the people responsible for giving it actually have the time and information to do it. That is not replacing government. That’s making government more responsive with technology.
If we are going to spend millions embracing technology, maybe we should let some of that technology make government easier for the people who work there – and the residents who have to deal with it. Instead of the old adage you can’t fight city hall, let’s use AI so residents and city hall work together.
So, Fairfield…..have you met AI?
P.S. I had AI edit this document so I could remove all the sarcasm, emotion and anything else that may have made this unnecessarily entertaining. 
Leslie Jezior lives in Fairfield.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Officials demand answers after violent ICE confrontation with Frederick protesters
description: Elected officials were demanding answers Tuesday after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement confrontation with protesters in Frederick turned violent over the weekend. So were protesters, who want to know why ICE was there in the first place.
text:
An ICE agent raises a baton to strike a protester Friday outside a house in Frederick. (Screenshot from of Hagerstown Rapid Response video).Elected officials were demanding answers Tuesday after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement confrontation with protesters in Frederick turned violent over the weekend.
And they weren’t the only ones.
“People were legitimately scared and pretty much terrorized by ICE for two full days before things escalated on Friday night. If you didn’t take anybody into custody, why did you even show up?” asked Tatiana Santos, a member of Indivisible Frederick Forward who witnessed some of what happened in the Tasker’s Chance neighborhood Friday night.
Protesters turned up Thursday after they learned that ICE agents were in the neighborhood, apparently staking out a house.
On Friday, after blocking the street, protesters could be seen locking arms and going to the house as a human barrier, according to video of the incident provided by Hagerstown Rapid Response.
At that point, the video shows ICE agents moving in, grabbing and pushing the protesters, with at least one agent hitting a person on the ground with a baton, the scene illuminated by the headlights and police lights of ICE vehicles on the scene.
Lacking federal funds, local groups press to continue legal aid for immigrant children

“It felt like they [ICE agents] were just terrorizing people. You don’t get brutal with people. It’s inhumane,” Soolah Kemp said Tuesday. She was a member of the Hagerstown group that showed up to support residents in the Frederick neighborhood.
Santos and Kemp called on the Maryland Attorney General’s Office  to investigate what happened, but the office declined to comment Tuesday.
Representatives with ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond Tuesday to requests for comment.
Jennifer Gerlock, manager of public affairs with the city of Frederick, said in an email Tuesday the city isn’t aware of any arrests made by federal authorities during the incicent. Frederick Police, who were called to the scene at 9 p.m. Friday in response to “escalating tensions between protesters and federal agents,” did not make any arrests at the scene, Gerlock said.
“FPD was not notified in advance of the federal law enforcement operation and was not involved in its planning or execution,” Gerlock said. “Our officers’ role was to maintain public safety, protect life and property, and help prevent further escalation between those gathered and the federal agents conducting the operation.”
Gerlock continued: “Officers worked to ensure that individuals could lawfully exercise their constitutional rights while also helping to prevent actions that could lead to physical confrontations or arrests. FPD was not there to assist ICE in carrying out its federal enforcement operation.”
Gov. Wes Moore (D), asked Tuesday about the Frederick incident, said his office was monitoring the situation throughout the Labor Day weekend. But he expressed concerns about “this latest iteration of ICE,” which he said is larger than the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Agency and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

“While I know that there are still things that are being investigated right now, it’s a continuation of the challenge that we have with this latest iteration of ICE,” he said. “The … continued problem that I have with how these actions are being used and utilized — not with our communities, but just in and to our communities — is something that I continue to have very real challenge and very real issues with.”
Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-6th), whose district includes Frederick, said the confrontation is “deeply concerning.”
“I am especially disturbed by reports that ICE agents used force against Frederick residents,” McClain Delaney said in a statement. “These allegations demand immediate answers and a full, transparent investigation.”
Del. Kris Fair (D-Frederick), whose district includes the Tasker’s Chance neighborhood but wasn’t present when ICE was there Friday, hopes an investigation by state and federal officials will occur to determine if anyone’s civil rights were violated, especially after he watched video footage of the “erratic behavior” of ICE agents.
“We continue to watch the brutalization of our communities by overly aggressive law enforcement power structures,” Fair said. “I’m hoping that our society as a whole can look at this situation truly, deeply, and reflectively, and ask itself if this is the kind of society that we want to live in where law enforcement goes in without any regard for public safety and escalates a situation which was otherwise non-existent prior to Thursday.”
He said Congress has “the power of the purse string here. ICE answers to them. They need to utilize their unilateral power that they have to rein in these out-of-control federal agents.”

title: DiLorenzo secures GOP nomination in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District
description: Portsmouth car dealer Anthony DiLorenzo won the GOP nomination for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District Tuesday. The Associated Press called the race at 8 p.m. Tuesday night. DiLorenzo will try to replace Rep. Chris Pappas, who gave up the seat to run for the Senate, and become the first Republican from New Hampshire elected to […]
text:
Anthony DiLorenzo speaks to supporters in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after winning the Republican nomination for New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District in the Sept. 8, 2026, primary. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Portsmouth car dealer Anthony DiLorenzo won the GOP nomination for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District Tuesday.
The Associated Press called the race at 8 p.m. Tuesday night. DiLorenzo will try to replace Rep. Chris Pappas, who gave up the seat to run for the Senate, and become the first Republican from New Hampshire elected to Congress in over a decade. At the time his victory was called, the Democratic nominee was unclear. 
DiLorenzo, 62, beat out a crowded GOP field in which candidates often struggled to differentiate themselves. With 39% of votes counted, DiLorenzo captured roughly 51% of the electorate and 13,110 votes, per the Associated Press. He beat out Hollie Noveletsky, a Newfields businesswoman who earned 27% (7,485 votes) of the vote, and state Rep. Brian Cole, who represents Manchester in the State House and earned 14.1% of the vote (3,978 votes).
DiLorenzo earned President Donald Trump’s endorsement in the race but at times tried to balance the more conservative values of his party with centrist policy proposals. He weathered attacks from opponents who tried to cast him as insufficiently conservative throughout the race.
DiLorenzo owns over a dozen car dealerships and has cast himself as a pragmatic businessman who will use his business acumen to solve problems in Congress.
Before Pappas won the seat in 2018, it had flipped hands between Democrat Carol Shea Porter and Republican Frank Guinta four times. However, Pappas was able to hold the district through three straight elections, leading spectators to wonder whether voters in the district had soured on the GOP or whether Pappas was a uniquely strong candidate.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: From climate change to the economy to healthcare, NH voters seek solutions with their ballots
authors: William Skipworth, Molly Rains, Maya Mitchell, Ethan DeWitt
description: Scott Thompson, a retired mechanic from Epsom, usually doesn’t vote in midterm elections, but after a GOP candidate for state representative showed up at his door he decided to make plans to vote on Tuesday. “Josh Shapiro Jr. actually came to my house on a 98-degree day to talk to me,” Thompson, 59, said as […]
text:
Supporters hold signs for their preferred candidate in Wolfeboro during the Sept. 8, 2026, primary election. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Scott Thompson, a retired mechanic from Epsom, usually doesn’t vote in midterm elections, but after a GOP candidate for state representative showed up at his door he decided to make plans to vote on Tuesday.
“Josh Shapiro Jr. actually came to my house on a 98-degree day to talk to me,” Thompson, 59, said as he left the polls. “He made an effort more than I’d seen anybody else. I normally only vote in the presidential elections, but I thought: He’s going to make an effort; I’ll make an effort. So I looked at his website to see what he stood for.”
After agreeing with his stances, Thompson decided that Shapiro earned his vote. As a Republican, he also voted for John Sununu for U.S. Senate and Gov. Kelly Ayotte for reelection.
Thompson was among those who showed up at the polls throughout New Hampshire Tuesday to vote in primary elections. Bulletin reporters fanned out across the state to hear from voters about what motivated them to come out, how different candidates earned their votes, and how they feel about the state of democracy in the Granite State.
In Concord, Susan Burkhardt voted in the Democratic congressional races but was torn between the progressives she agreed with more on policy and the centrists she felt had better chances in the general election. In the end, she picked one of each: She chose newcomer progressive Karishma Manzur over establishment centrist Chris Pappas for Senate, but incumbent U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander over her progressive challenger, Paige Beauchemin.
“Pappas has never been my favorite,” she said. 
Burkhardt believes Pappas, who currently represents the eastern half of the state in the U.S. House of Representatives but is asking voters for a promotion to the Senate, is “pretty conservative for a Democrat.”
At the top of the list for reasons Burkhardt voted against Pappas was his support for Israel. Pappas has long supported military aid to the Middle Eastern country. However, as Americans nationwide have soured on Israel amid its multi-front wars and an increasing number of independent experts concluding its military is committing genocide against the Palestinian people, he’s moderated his stance. At AIPAC’s 2026 Congressional Summit in February, Pappas enthusiastically called himself “a strong supporter of the bipartisan U.S.-Israel relationship, which is a cornerstone of our national security policy,” but in July, he voted “present” — neither for nor against — on a measure that would’ve restricted weapons sales to Israel. He told the Bulletin he wanted “a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.”
Burkhardt is unsure whether Manzur could win in November, but “it’s at least a message to the Democratic establishment here in New Hampshire, which is pretty stuck, that people are looking for something else.”
In the 1st Congressional District, Burkhardt wanted to vote for Beauchemin, currently a state representative from Nashua, but was worried she would lose in a general election to a Republican, which she felt would be the worst outcome.
Downballot, Burkhardt voted for Jason Quinno, a young candidate for state representative who knocked on her door.
“(We) could use some youth,” she said. “The New Hampshire Legislature is so white and so old.”
Supporters for various candidates stand outside Manchester Memorial High School with signs to greet voters. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
In Warner, Sarah Hansen, a farmer and Democrat, cast her ballot with concerns about data centers, climate change, and “getting money out of politics” on her mind, she said on Tuesday morning. But the topic that informed her choices the most, she said, was healthcare.
“I fall in a wage gap that’s just above qualifying for Medicaid and very well below being able to afford health insurance, given that (President Donald) Trump has taken away our subsidies,” she said. “Not having health insurance, in my occupation — not even just in my occupation, but just as a person living in the world, is quite scary.”
In the New Hampshire Senate primary, Hansen said she voted for Manzur, in large part because Manzur has said she wants to see a single-payer Medicare for All health insurance system. 
Hansen said her peers, including other young adults like herself, faced similar challenges. 
“I think there’s a lot of people in my community, of my age, who are not making enough to pay rent, to pay a mortgage, to pay for health insurance, who are just this kind of, like, in-between class who’s being completely forgotten,” she said.
Hansen added that she liked Manzur’s commitment to not accepting funds from corporate PACs and super PACs.
Both Manzur and Pappas have made campaign finance a cornerstone of their campaigns.
Though voters often agreed with Hansen that they wanted to see change in the healthcare system, they were divided on what that might look like. 
Bradford independent Marcia Moyer said she was voting in opposition to the expansion of public healthcare, with the goal of preventing Democratic Socialist-aligned candidates from gaining ground. Moyer voted in the Republican Senate primary, casting a ballot for Sununu. 
Moyer said she had seen family members suffer in the Canadian public healthcare system, including her parents.
“I have concerns that healthcare is not working in the U.S., but it’s not going to be fixed by more government,” she said. 
Candidate signs adorn a sidewalk outside a polling place at Oyster River High School in Durham, Sept 8, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Kaitlyn Gennaro recently moved to Manchester from Florida because of New Hampshire’s moderate political leanings. As an independent, she decided to vote in the Republican primary because she leans to the right economically, despite aligning with the Democratic Party on social issues. 
Gennaro said she wanted to vote for candidates who were not “MAGA-related,” leading her to vote for Sununu for U.S. Senate and Lindsey Anderson, a business and technology leader from Moultonborough, for the 1st Congressional District. She expects Anderson to “not go very far.”
“It’s very important in these midterm elections that we elect the leaders who can help Washington to make laws that are not only going to benefit New Hampshire, but are going to benefit the United States overall,” she said. “I will definitely have to read more about Chris Pappas. So I guess that’s up in the air until November.”
Some of Manzur’s supporters said they were drawn to her progressive, left-leaning stances.
Caldwell Lowell, of Durham, voted for Manzur after being impressed with her opposition to corporate fundraising. “I really appreciated the willingness to stand up and say, ‘I’m not doing this for corporate interests, I’m doing it for the people of New Hampshire,’” he said.
Lowell mentioned Manzur’s science background as a plus: “Having a Ph.D., going to Berkeley, I see a lot of experience in education and wisdom,” he said.
Those credentials were important to University of New Hampshire student Morgan Pritchett, too, who showed up Tuesday for her second-ever voting experience after the 2024 presidential election. As a biological science student herself, Pritchett was heartened by the representation Manzur could have brought to female scientists, and she liked Manzur’s positions. “She had a pretty strong stance about climate activism, (and) I really liked her pitch about education,” Pritchett, referring to Manzur’s policies in favor of transitioning the country toward clean energy and providing universal childcare and public higher education. 
Todd Massicote, an Exeter Democrat, said he voted for Manzur to stand up for scientists and help reverse cuts to grant funding and penalties for colleges and universities in Trump’s second term. “A lot of academia is hurting for funding. They’re laying people off. We’re losing researchers to China,” he said. 
Massicote, who works in biomedical research, said he had seen firsthand the effects of those policies in the loss of adequate talent. 
“I work on the sales end of things. All my customers — all their funding is stalled. They’re nervous for their jobs. There’s been a lot of layoffs.”
Against those stakes, Pappas, a relative centrist, has not impressed Massicote. “I feel like he’s had a run in Congress, and I don’t know what he’s done, to be honest,” he said. 
But to others, Manzur’s positions and biography were shadowed by a bigger factor: her ability to win. Liz Malone, a Durham Democrat, said she voted for Pappas “because I think he has the best chance to beat Sununu.” The recent inflation increases affected her daily, she said, from groceries to gas to medications. 
“I pray to God it will be a good year for Democrats,” Malone said. “And I think if it’s not, this country is in a heap of trouble.” 
In Wolfeboro, James O’Rourke, a retired college teacher, voted for Hollie Noveletsky in the Republican 1st Congressional District primary over candidates including Anthony DiLorenzo and Brian Cole, and Sununu for U.S. Senate. For O’Rourke, abortion is the most important issue.
“I’m hoping that Hollie Noveletsky will vote more pro-life than DiLorenzo,” O’Rourke, 86, said. “DiLorenzo seems competent, but the support for unborn life is important to me.”
DiLorenzo released a 21-point policy plan online with a promise to “Oppose federal abortion legislation and respect New Hampshire’s laws.”
O’Rourke thinks Sununu is sometimes “a little soft on the life issues, but I think he’s good, and he has a chance to win.” As a Republican, he really doesn’t want Pappas to win in November, and he thinks Sununu represents the best path to defeating him.
He voted for Dale Fincher for state representative because he believes he is “the more deliberate, the more intentional candidate.” Fincher is running for the state House of Representatives again after losing in a special election in March to Bobbi Boudman, who has now opted to run for state Senate. His primary opponent is Dallas Emery Jr.
Bob Mongan of Manchester said voting for Pappas was at the front of his mind going into the voting booth today. He said he believes he is the best person for the job. 
“The economy needs a lot of work, and I think Chris has got to at least attempt to fix it. Of course, they (the Democrats) could do it all alone, but he could work on a winning team.” 
Mongan also voted for Maura Sullivan, but said he would support Stefany Shaheen if she wins the primary. Down the ballot, he voted for Jim O’Connell for Executive Council. Despite the numerous election watch parties in Manchester, Mongan said he will be watching the results from his couch. 
“I’ll just wait til this evening,” he said. “See if I’m right or wrong.”

The two will face off to represent the western half of the state in the general election Nov. 3. It will be their second time […]
text:
Lily Tang Williams at her home on Tuesday, Sept. 8. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Incumbent Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat, and Lily Tang Williams, a Republican, secured nominations from their respective parties on Tuesday in the race to represent New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District.
The two will face off to represent the western half of the state in the general election Nov. 3. It will be their second time facing one another in the general election.
Democrats choose incumbent
On the Democratic ticket, Goodlander had 80.3% of the vote as of 8:55 p.m. on Tuesday, with approximately 32% of votes counted. The Associated Press called the race at 8 p.m. Progressive challenger Paige Beauchemin collected 19.5% of the vote. 
Goodlander is seeking a second term after she was first elected to Congress in 2024. Originally from Nashua, she has worked as an intelligence officer for the U.S. Naval Reserve, a law clerk, an attorney for the House Judiciary Committee, a foreign policy adviser for late U.S. Sens. John McCain and Joe Lieberman, and with the U.S. Department of Justice under President Joe Biden.
Beauchemin, her challenger, is a nurse and state representative from Nashua who during her campaign emphasized her support for Medicare for All, transparency in campaign financing, and immigration reform, calling the nation’s current policies “inhumane.”
Williams secures Republican nomination
Lily Tang Williams, of Weare, secured the Republican nomination on Tuesday, with the Associated Press also calling the race at 8 p.m.
Williams had 64% of the vote as of 8:55 p.m., when about 20% of votes had been counted. 
Williams has mounted a campaign for Congress twice before, participating in the primary in 2020 and in 2024, losing to Goodlander in the general election.
Speaking on Tuesday evening just outside her home, where she hosted a small gathering for close friends and supporters, Williams said her social media following and increased fundraising contributed to her primary success.
Victor Orlando, a business owner from Hollis, had 15.1% of the vote, while candidate Dan Nicholson had 12.6% and Michael Anthony Callis had 7.3%.
U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander will once again face off against Lily Tang Williams in November. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

title: Pappas and Sununu prevail in primaries, setting up expensive fight for U.S. Senate
description: Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will face off in November against Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu to be U.S. senator, after the two candidates prevailed in their respective primaries Tuesday. The results, projected by the Associated Press shortly after 8 p.m., solidified what will likely be a bare-knuckled, expensive general election fight for the […[...]
text:
Chris Pappas (left) and John Sununu (right) will face off in what promises to be a very expensive U.S. Senate race. (Left: Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will face off in November against Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu to be U.S. senator, after the two candidates prevailed in their respective primaries Tuesday.
The results, projected by the Associated Press shortly after 8 p.m., solidified what will likely be a bare-knuckled, expensive general election fight for the Senate seat, which is open after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement. 
Polls suggest the contest between Pappas, the current representative for the 1st Congressional District, and Sununu could be close, and both candidates had been positioning themselves for the general election months before the primary. As the polling has tightened, the race has taken on increasing significance to Democrats’ chances to flip control of the U.S. Senate, with Pappas’s shrinking advantage drawing national attention. 
In winning his primary, Sununu held off a challenge from Scott Brown, the former U.S. senator from Massachusetts who has since moved to New Hampshire, after Brown attempted to align himself with President Donald Trump and run to Sununu’s right. Trump ultimately endorsed Sununu in February, spurning Brown and propelling Sununu into a lead Brown could never overcome. 
Pappas, meanwhile, bested Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist from Exeter and first-time candidate who ran as a progressive. Manzur called for universal health care and attacked Pappas for his prior support of Israel; Pappas has since told the Bulletin he wanted “a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.”
In a statement after his victory, Sununu signaled awareness that the general election fight would be centered on the cost of living. 
“We will keep listening, keep working, and stay laser-focused on the economy, jobs, and making life more affordable,” Sununu said in the statement. 
“We will clean up Washington and hold politicians in both parties accountable,” Sununu continued. “I’ll push term limits, make Congress pay for the full cost of their healthcare, and cut Congress’ pay if they vote to shut down the government.”
Pappas had a similar message. “Growing up in Manchester and working alongside my family at our restaurant, I learned that you don’t get ahead just by making promises,” he wrote in a fundraising email shortly after his victory. “You have to be accountable. You listen to people, work hard, and deliver.”
“I’m running to make New Hampshire more affordable for working families; protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid; safeguard reproductive freedom; and stand up for the small businesses that are the backbone of our communities,” he added.
Both candidates had decisive victories: Just before 9 p.m., Pappas commanded 62.5% of the vote compared to Manzur’s 35.4%; around the same time, Sununu had taken 69.1% of the vote compared to Brown’s 25.6%, according to the Associated Press.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Former Franklin Circuit Judge Roger L. Crittenden dies at 81
description: Former Franklin Circuit Judge Roger L. Crittenden, who issued the landmark legal decision that requires the General Assembly to pass a budget, died Monday at his home in Frankfort. He was 81. Crittenden also was former chair of the state Executive Branch Ethics Commission and served as a special master to craft a distribution plan […]
text:
Judge Roger L. CrittendenFormer Franklin Circuit Judge Roger L. Crittenden, who issued the landmark legal decision that requires the General Assembly to pass a budget, died Monday at his home in Frankfort. He was 81.
Crittenden also was former chair of the state Executive Branch Ethics Commission and served as a special master to craft a distribution plan for a large class-action settlement involving former clients of disgraced attorney Eric Conn.
“He was a great judge and public servant, and even a greater human being,” said Franklin Circuit Judge Phillip Shepherd. “He was a wonderful role model and one of those rare judges who continued to become a better judge as long as he went.
“Many burn out. He kept going and going and got better and better.”
Shepherd noted that much of Crittenden’s legal career was in state government.
“He understood the balance among the branches of government.  That gave him extra insight in his role as a judge.”
Gov. Andy Beshear appointed  Crittenden to serve as a member of the Executive Branch Ethics Commission in May 2020. He served in the role through June 2024. Members elected him chair in July 2020 and he continued to serve as chair until the end of his service. 
The Executive Branch Ethics Commission presented Crittenden last December with the “Livingston Taylor Ethics Award” for 2023-25. The biennial award was established to recognize individuals, programs or agencies within the executive branch of state government for their outstanding achievement and contributions in promoting the ethical conduct of executive branch employees.
The late Livingston Taylor, an investigative reporter for the Louisville Courier-Journal, served as the Ethics Commission’s first chairman from 1992-1995. 
A long career
After three years of service in the U.S. Army including a tour in Vietnam, Crittenden graduated in 1975 from the University of Kentucky College of Law. He was inducted into the college’s Hall of Fame in 2007.
Crittenden served 26 years as an adjunct writing instructor at UK’s law college. The school honored him by naming one of its legal writing groups after him.  He joined such figures as Henry Clay, Benjamin Cardozo and Thurgood Marshall.
Crittenden began his legal career in public service at the Kentucky Cabinet for Human Resources and the Kentucky Council on Higher Education.
In 1980, Crittenden was elected as Franklin County District Court Judge where he served for 12 years before being elected as Franklin County Circuit Court Judge in 1992. He retired in 2006 and became senior judge of the Franklin Circuit Court. 
Prospect attorney Stephen Houston served three years as staff attorney for Crittenden and former Judge William L. Graham.
“Judge Crittenden was a perfect role model,” said Houston. “I am thankful to have worked for him.”
Crittenden also served as chair of the Circuit Judges Association Education Committee and was board chair of PUSH Infant Pre-School, an organization dedicated to early childhood education.
Budget decisions
One of Crittenden’s most prominent decisions as a judge forced the state legislature to pass a budget.
In 2004, the Kentucky General Assembly ended its regular session without passing a two-year budget. Then-Gov. Ernie Fletcher issued a continuation plan to keep state government running.
Crittenden ruled that Fletcher’s executive order could proceed but he said no state funds could be spent on building projects or expenses that were not approved by the legislature.
The ruling meant that a governor could not fully fund government operations or start major spending without the legislature’s enactment of a budget.
In 2020, Floyd Circuit Judge Johnny Ray Harris appointed Crittenden at the recommendation of Prestonsburg attorney Ned Pillersdorf to be special master in the case of Eric Conn’s multi-million-dollar Social Security disability fraud scheme.
Pillersdorf and a legal team had secured a settlement of about $750,000 with Conn’s malpractice insurer for about 1,500 former clients harmed in the scheme.
Crittenden delivered to the court a recommendation to distribute the settlement money to about 800 of the most vulnerable clients.
“He had a ‘Mission Impossible’ job,” said Pillersdorf Tuesday upon hearing about Crittenden’s death . “He got the assignment during the start of COVID and he did wonders with it.”
Pillersdorf also said he practiced several cases before Crittenden.
“He cared deeply for everyone,” Pillersdorf said. “He paid attention to details. He judged in a thoughtful, deliberative way.  He loved to get to the point and he reminded me of that quite often.”
Harrod Brothers Funeral Home in Frankfort is handling arrangements.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State debt collection strategy includes hundreds of potential driver’s license suspensions per month
description: A South Dakota state agency requests an average of 249 driver’s license suspensions per month as part of its efforts to collect debts owed to state government, a legislative oversight panel heard Tuesday. The figure hasn’t changed much in recent years, and many of the debtors enter a payment plan before their license is suspended. […]
text:
The South Dakota State Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota state agency requests an average of 249 driver’s license suspensions per month as part of its efforts to collect debts owed to state government, a legislative oversight panel heard Tuesday.
The figure hasn’t changed much in recent years, and many of the debtors enter a payment plan before their license is suspended. It’s an effective way to push debtors who’ve ducked multiple attempts to collect unpaid fees, said Jason Kettwig, deputy director of the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration.
Kettwig’s agency oversees the state’s Obligation Recovery Center. Lawmakers created the debt collection clearinghouse 10 years ago for things like fines and court costs, unpaid fees or tuition at state institutions, or other fees owed to agencies such as the departments of Transportation, Revenue, or Game, Fish and Parks.
The center’s operators, a private company called Reliant Capital Solutions, can ask the state to suspend the driver’s licenses of debtors who owe more than $1,000. Reliant, which has held the contract to operate the center since 2020, is paid through a 20% surcharge added to debt. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
License suspensions are “everybody’s least favorite thing to talk about,” Kettwig told the state’s Government Operations and Audit Committee on Tuesday at the Capitol in Pierre. 
“We don’t collect money because we get their license taken away,” Kettwig said. “We collect money because we are able to talk to them and explain to them what they can do to make it right. But sometimes the only way we can talk to them is to have something that they feel.”
A report on the center’s performance is presented annually to lawmakers. This year’s report noted that the center has tallied $34.7 million in payments since it began operations 10 years ago.
The state’s court system represents the largest share of that 10-year total, at $15.7 million. That’s more than four times higher than the figure for the Department of Revenue, at $3.6 million.
About 45% of the center’s collections are tied to the court system, whose debtors owe more than $102 million, the report said. Of the $4 million recovered through the center last year, $1.8 million was court debt.
The center’s strategy has also leaned more heavily on payment plans for the last three years, Kettwig said. About 60% of the 15,062 accounts resolved last year belonged to people who paid off their debt in installments.
There were about 176,000 outstanding accounts at the center on June 30, the end of the state’s 2026 fiscal year.
